I have to say that this game is not what I expected.  I expected a game where the player travels back in the old man's memories, and gives him a chance to relive his life - thus allowing the player to play through the man's life and make changes in it.  That is not the case at all.
To the Moon IS NOT A GAME!  It would be more accurately described as an interactive story. No, not a choose your own ending kind of story. The story is very linear, follows a laid out path and conclusion.  The player is not often offered a choice, and even when he is, it doesn't matter.  You can only follow one path, and that is that.  As such, not only is To the Moon a story rather than a game, it posesses no replay value.
So, is it worth buying? Yes, definitely.  Even though the graphics look like it came from the mid-1990s, the story is compelling, and the music beautiful.  It's a tear-jerker, and I often felt myself wanting to go through "just one more scene".
To the Moon has no keybinding controls, and even though that is a big bugbear of mine, its controls are bound to the number pad, not WASD. As a left-handed person, well done development team.
Also, there is no volume control for the music. Sole control over volume comes from your own speakers or headset.
In short, To the Moon is not a game, has no replay value, no control bindings, and no volume control.  But its compelling story and beautiful music more than compensate.  Definitely worth the price of admission.

Scribblenauts Unlimited is a VERY fun installation in the Scribblenauts series.  New to the game is the object editor, a very easy to use and creative way of making your own interactive objects.  You can change sizes, colors, and shapes, but the one thing that made me upset was that you can't DRAW your own objects.  This limits you to using only pre-made things in the game, forcing you to combine them if you want something unique.
Also new to Scribblenauts is its vast world.  From the city, to a desert, and even to space, you can take Maxwell (or one of his many brothers) on missions around the virtual globe.  Each level has challenges awaiting you that can be very simple or complex.  On the other hand, many missions have simple solutions.  For example, if a boy is unhappy, you can make a clown, video game, etc.  The possibilities are endless, but the entertainment level with some obstacles is limited.
All in all, I still like playing the game.  Even after you finish all the side-missions and campaign, you can still make your own objects and re-create your favorite characters and scenes from movies, video games, and books.  I highly recommend this game for anyone who wants to share their ideas with others and explore Maxwell's world.

PROS:

I really wanted to like this game because anyone making a coop multiplayer free game gets a thumbs up from me. I personally like the zombie genre but this game shows why this genre is tiring on PC and needs inspiration.

The problem here is there is a better free2play zombie game out there already called No More Room In Hell. These games are pretty much the same. The only difference I can see is this game has set classes you can pick from rather than just playing as a random... but both games have the same missions, levels and play theme. I only managed to play for 40 minutes but that was a enough... I'm not a massive fan of reviews after short play time but this was enough to see this is unfinished and a 5 out of 10 at best.
The Left for Dead games and the Killing Floor series are much better games so just buy those and pay you'll get a better experience. If you don't want to pay then No More Room In Hell beats this game in all areas. This game *COULD* end up being alright but not until it gets a lot of work and the devs put in some serious time. They need to add something to make it unique! Don't get me wrong this is free and it *HAS* potential but at the moment it's a bit naff. It feels like an alpha version or a game that should be in green light and is basically a very early release. If I had paid for it then I'd be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and want a refund.
My main two problems are as follows:
Firstly the game suffers from input lag and the hitboxes are really large but inconsistent, sometimes you have to shoot off to the right other times the shots land but your crosshair isn't even on a zombies head. Even on low ping servers with 10-20 latency this still happens. You press to shoot and there's sometimes a small delay or an annoying zoom glitch when you go to iron sights.
Secondly it has a horrible rag doll effect when you shoot zombies that causes them to fly off unrealistically. I think this ragdoll effect contributes to the horrible glide feeling I experience when jumping too. There doesn't seem to be a gravity effect in play, I do understand a shotgun blast knocks things back at close range but it's like someone turned physics off for a second when you fire. I did try hosting my own game and I played on 3 different servers just to rule out server or host problems causing the issues... it happened all the time and occasionally the zombies vanish.
This game pretty much does the same as No More Room in Hell just not as well. It has a basic wave survival mode which is simple and dull. We've all played wave survival about a million times on other games. The mission mode is where the game could be better it has 3 scenarios on a choice of several maps where your team must escape, find a location or get an item and evac.
To sum up the hitboxes, glide effect, ragdolls and input lag just ruin it. Classes are a nice idea but this is clearly a tired genre which this game does no favours for so stick to the tried and tested games if you must play zombies shooters. I played the technician and found the sentry gun only fires in one direction which is mildly annoying. I didn't try pointman, sniper, medic or assault. I suspect all the classes have little quirks and issues as someone on voice comms moaned about grenade throw lag.
I hope a developer, programmer or tester reads this and happily takes on board what I've said! Codename Cure has potential but not worth a penny at the moment and No More Room in Hell is better.

Downwell is amazing video game popcorn. It's brief: fast-paced action through a handful of environments, such that you can get in a full game in a short break without stressing yourself to speedrun it. It's accessible: as the man said, all you gotta do is jump and shoot, and since your gun is on your feet, those are both the same button. It's addictive and satisfying.
More impressive is how lean its design is, how it expends minimal effort to achieve maximum output. It's a single file less than 35 MB in size. Its palette uses only four simple, bold colors, but it uses them effectively to very quickly show you what you're dealing with as you hurtle down the well. Fall through black, land on white, and zero your attention in on red. Red squares are valuable gems and everything else that's red hurts you. Stompable enemies? White on top, red on bottom. Unstompable? All red: a clearly visible threat. (The fourth color is blue; it only shows up in the aquifer and it shows you where to find air supplies.)
It has gunboots, it has timevoids, it has pretty balloons. It's one of the gamiest games I've played, and it's only three bucks at full price. If you've got the stomach for fast reflex games, you don't really have an excuse not to buy it.

Divinity is the game to buy if you are looking for a modern spin on the oldschool RPG genre. It is one of the best games i've played in the last couple of years and i'm struggeling to find anything to complain about. Of course it has some weak points, like the generic main quest and the sometimes overly dialouge heavy story parts, but the good outweighs the bad. The value if great as well, providing a lot of playtime for a good price though there is not really any replayability (for most people one playthrough will be enough)
- Story/world -
The story of Divinity is nothing to write home about as it really is a generic fantasy storyline, but that does not mean that the world is not interesting. The world has a lot to offer with interesting characters, exploration and side quests that tie in to the story wonderfully. The main quest, even though it's generic, can be completed in many different ways (except for a few events, like the ending) and really reward out of the box thinking and patience.
Did I mention patience? This is a text heavy game, especially at the start and missing dialouge can get you stuck later on. it is voice acted so you don't have to read it if you don't want to.  You can play the game without a lot of the text if you as well (more on that leter) but you will still need to sit through a lot of it. The world overall is really colorfull and rewards exploration with hidden secrets, alternative ways to go about the quests at hand or maybe even new companions. Your companions also come with thier own storylines and quests.
- RPG elements -
Divinity has three big things that make it a RPG. The first is the skill and traits system were you can freely invest your points however you like. Do you want your character to be a tanky healer who summons blizzards and fights with a crossbow, but also stinks and can talk to animals? you can do that.
The second thing is the conversation system. Every time your making a descision in a conversation your characters personality changes and will affect future conversations. This makes it feel like your choices has immediate consequences and lets you roll play on another level.
The third thing is the world itself. I don't think that there are any invurnable npc's in this game except for a few characters which the story is built around. Remember that merchant that scammed you in another game? In Divinity you can murder that merchant and steal back your gold. Is a guard stopping you from crossing a bridge and wants you to retrive a necklace from someone? You could steal the necklace, gain it by doing a favour or just straight up kill the person carrying it. This combined with the many ways there is to solving the quests makes Divinity a great RPG.
- Combat -
The combat is the real "meat" of this game. While it is a storydriven game that a has a big focus on conversations and rollplaying, you will need to fight monsters and other enemies along your journey. Your party will consist of your two main characters and up to two other companions. The combat is turn based and uses a AP or action points system to determine what each character can do on each of thier turns. I recommend that you look up a video on how the combat works because it is hard to describe, but I will try anyway.
When combat is engaged, it happends on the spot and every character within a certain radius is now part of the fight. Turns are decided by your stats and so are the number of action points you start with an drecive every turn, you also have the health and mana to manage. The AP system works wonders and makes combat really interesting. Big spells costs a lot of AP and you might not even be able to use them for the first couple of turns, but if you wait around with one character for that AP to generate the party will be at a disadvantage overall.
The enviroment plays a big part as well. I remember a scenario where I was facing down some enemies of as much higher level than my characters, so I had my tank bait the enemies into a cave were i had planted a ton of traps and had my mages ready with lightning storms and freeze magic.
- Performance -
The game runs really well for me and apart from some bugs with the combat (nothing major, only smaller one time bugs) I have nothing to complain about. The first release of the game had performance problems for me and combined with there being no voice acting I dropped it early on. They have fixed all of that.

This game is fun for one or two playthroughs, but once you pass about 10 hours you begin to see the serious flaws in this game's mechanics. The basis behind game creation is chosing a combination of a genre, topic, and platform. Your game's success depends on how well the combinations match up. Some topics may work well as an action game, but not as a strategy game. Additionally, genres work better on different platforms. An RPG or Simulation game will work well on the PC, but casual games will not. Most of the best Topic/Genre/Platform combinations have real-world counterparts- a Millitary Action game on the Xbox 360 (Call of Duty) or a Fantasy RPG on the Playstation (Final Fantasy) have a good chance of being popular. But if you try to make a Wild Western Strategy game for the Wii, you're going to have a bad time. This is all very well done, and the best aspect of the game. There's a ton of topics and endless combinations to chose from.
When you've decided on a layout for your game, you go into development. This is where you decide what aspects you want to focus on. You can focus more on having good world design and story telling, or you can spend more time on a games AI and gameplay. Again, your success depends on the genre of game you're making. An RPG /Adventure game is better if you spend more time on Quests and World Design, while an Action game is better if you work on the AI and gameplay. You can also hire employees who specialize in different areas.
The biggest catch is: The game doesn't tell you any of the best combinations to start with. Game development from the beginning is completely trial and error. only after you release a game will you find out if you made the right choices. The problem is, the system is so unforgiving you'll be on the verge of bankruptcy by the time you figure out what works and what doesn't.
As you make games, your character levels up in different areas of game design, as those levels increase you unlock additional features you can put into your games. This all culminates into a custom game engine. You can build engines from the ground up that include various game features you unlock, that become more advanced as the game goes on. You add these features by spending research points (earned by playing) and money. As you progress, the features become more advanced and replace old ones, allowing you to add new things to your game. This sounds great in theory, but its incredibly poorly executed. Engines are incredibily expensive to build and it must be done fairly regulary if you want to progress. Also, there is NO WAY to upgrade the engine you already have. Unlock a cool new feature you want to put in you next game? You can, but you have to COMPLETELY rebuild your engine, which is incredibly costly in both game-time and $$. There is no worse feeling in this game than investing a million dollars into a new engine that only lasts you for 2 games before everything in it becomes obsolete.
By far the worst part of this game is the convoluted scoring system. The final review score changes depending on the scores of your previous best game. Say you hit it out of the park with your design and make a 9.5/10 game. Every game you make from that point forward will score poorly unless you make a big improvement over your best game. This means that the only way progress is to INTENTIONALLY make your games bad and incrementally impove them over time. There have been several times where I've purposely left out features I had available because I didn't want the game to be TOO good.
Example: You're far into the game and have a ton of money. You decide to make a new engine with all the best features money can buy, you make a Fantasy RPG for the PC called "The Olden Parchment: Oceanedge" and you put your heart into it. Every feature you have goes in, you use all the best employees and you make the best game you're capable of making. You release it and it gets a perfect 10/10. It breaks every sales record out there. Where you you go from here? Nowhere. You're actually completely screwed. You've put all of your best technology into your game and until you level up more and unlock newer better features, you have no way of possibly making a better game. The only way to continue playing is to pump out bad games with as little $ as possible until you can start over with a new engine.
That's the biggest flaw witht this game, and its really ruined it for me. The forced difficulty of the scoring system makes it impossible to be succesful and enjoy Game Dev Tycoon for what it is. Buy this game on a steam sale, donwload some cheat mods and mess around, and you'll have fun. Otherwise, you'll be disapointed once you figure out how this game works.
TL;DR- The awful game-scoring mechanic takes away from what the game does well. You're punished down the road for making good choices, turning the game into a counter-intuitive mess. Its not worth full price. You'll have the most fun with cheat mods, but even that gets old quickly.

This is my review for Fallout 3.
Please remember to give a like and enjoy the review.
The Story:
The story centers around you, the player. You're actions effect of how people think of you as a person and your actions also effect the world you are living in. The game opens up with your life in the vault and how you grow up and understand life, the safety and comfort of the closest thing you have to a home. Life is totally normal until you find yourself leaving the vault. Leaving the only life you've ever known while at the same time, entering a whole new life. A life of danger, adventure and much mystery within the world that you must figure out yourself. The basic story without trying to spoil anything major is your character trying to track down your father after he abandons you in the vault. As you go throughout your journey, you slowly get introduced to the many terrifying creatures that live within the world, the numerous raiders, Mutants that capture and kill anything in their way, and what's left of humanity and their struggle to survive and bring order in a new lawless world. Later in the game you find yourself trying to make a difference in the wasteland in an attempt to save mankind and the way you do so is up to you. In the end, you are either seen as the hero of the capital wasteland or another savage destroying it. It's up to you.
The game revolves around your choices to choose carefully.
The gameplay:
This game is an RPG at heart and it makes sure that you know it. The game provides you with a leveling system which includes different skills and perks to level up on. For example, how you level up determines your skills with guns, hand held weapons, how charismatic you are, lock picking, repairing weapons/ armor, health, etc. These help you play the game the way you want to play it which is where this game shines. In addition to this is to be able to choose dialogue/ interations with other characters and a lot of quests. Over 200 side quests along with the main story and dlcs which I highly recommend since they are so amazing as well. Player choice plays a huge part and so does the way you approach missions. Sure it would be nice to gun down all of those raiders to free the hostages but it would be just as rewarding to find a smart alternate path. Anyway you play the game is just as fun as the next which welcomes a lot of replays. In fact, you'd be missing out on a lot if you didn't replay this game in different ways. Do yourself and the game some justice. My only problem with the game is that ammunition can sometimes be hard to come by if you aren't looking in the right place.
The World:
The world is absolutely well done and beautiful in it's own way. With many points of interest and monuments to see, you could easily spend hours just exploring the Capital Wasteland with much more to be discovered. The more you put in, the more the game will give. Just keep your pistol loaded and by your side at all times because it's also, as I've said before, dangerous and lively. My only minor complaint with it is that there are many metro stations that you'll have to travel through but at the same time it provides a good dark and creepy atmosphere that vile creatures await you, lurking in the dark.
The Verdict:
For Fallout 3, this game deserves a solid 94/100

It's a fun game, but definitely not for everyone. It's all what you make of it. Honestly, I'm considering playing this game with my baby cousins (asking them to come up with the solutions), because I'm sure we'll have a ball coming up with silly scenarios in this fun little world.
Do I enjoy this game? Yes, I think it's great. Would I recommend it to any of my gamer friends... To be honest, no, not really, unless they want something they can play along with their kid on their lap, or enjoy playing silly games like I do.

To the Moon is a beautiful, emotional and sometimes comical tale with very little "gameplay", but a whole lot of heart. The tale of John and River continues to linger in my day-to-day thoughts even a year after playing it. Now one of my favorite games of all time, I can't stress enough how much you should play this 3-4 hour game.
Tips For Playing:
- Forget what you know about gaming. This game is about buckling in for a rollercoaster of feels through storytelling, not you more standard gameplay machanics. Keep an open mind going in and you should be fine.
- Play it in one sitting. It's a short game! Think of it like a movie; you'll want to finish it in one sitting or it just won't have the same impact on you.
- Turn off other distractions. The musical score is fantastic, and even necessary in setting the mood of the game. If you're the type to listen to your own music collection, a gaming stream, friends on Skype, or what else have you while playing games, turn it off just this once. You'll be glad you did.

Although Naval Action has some flaws, there are still many reasons to play. First, for an early access game, Naval Action is very well polished and recieves substantial updates and bug fixes each month. The devs are really good at listening to the community and making necessary changes. Along with that, the community is great dispite its small size. There are plety of new players joining the community every week and many will happy to travel and fight along side you in both PvP and PvE. The combat is the main attraction for Naval Action and is realistic and challenging.
There are a few problems that will likely be addressed in future updates. The open world travel is painfully slow and the world is massive. Most of the time you will spend is around your own coastal ports. In addition, there isn't a ton of variety in the combat, which is made worse by the long grind required to reach the higher ranks. For me, getting money is the easy part and you will certainly be able to by a first rate before you have the men to crew it. This is because the amount of crew you can have is dictated by your rank. One last thing is that I really recommend playing this with friends as it cuts down on some of the boring grind.
Overall, I recommend Naval Action despite its flaws. You have to remember that this is still early access and has been around for only a short time. The updates every month are refreshing and make noticable changes. For under $60, this game is tremendous fun for anyone interested in the age of sail.

A well thought out simulation of 'blue water' sailing of ships of the "Wooden Ships and Iron Men" era popularized in the Hornblower and Aubrey/Maturin novels and films, this provides the Player with the ability to captain his/her own trade ship or warship sailing and trading between ports or engaging in realistic ship-to-ship combat.  Both one-to-one, fleet-to-fleet, and Player-to-Player combat is enabled in the PvP version.
The game map is extensive, and includes all of the east coast of the Americas, the Gulf of Mexico and the Carribbean Sea.  One sails seamlessly over the entire map, encountering trading vessels and warships, some operated by other human Players, others by AI Non-Player-Characters.  In the "PvP" version, one is enabled to attack or be attacked by other Human Players from opposing national factions, or by the ever-threatening Pirate faction.  The trading simulation provides an economic model that enables the human player to earn money without fighting, or to win game money, Experience Points toward promotion (and larger, more powerful ships), and seize ships and cargo from adverse faction ships as prizes.
The game requires some patience, some understanding of the interaction between sails, wind and simple 'dead reckoning' navigaton.   A rewarding experience for those seeking some taste of what it was like circa 1800 in a warship or trading vessel going in harms way for the chance of adventure and gold.
Highly recommended.

This platformer is different. I recommend this game even if you are not into platfomers. The art and music are a pleasure. The controls are responsive. There are new challenges around every corner and they are never frustrating. Level design is an invitation to move and respond fast. I wished it were more difficult; don't get me wrong because it is not easy but the game is so free-flowing and rewarding that it leaves you looking for more. That is only downside; it ends.
There is a story, and don't let the fact that this is a 2D platformer fool you that it is your standard save-the-princess or save-the-forest-friends or find-the-item-that-will-save-the-universe. The story is simple and revolves around a powerful theme of a mother's love and sacrifice. It is told in short scenes that are accompanied by a heartfelt and moving soundtrack.
This is one of the best games that I have ever played and I enjoyed it more than many AAA titles on my GTX 780 Ti, 32 gb rig.
Finally I would express my thanks to the inspired team behind this project and tell them that I wish there were more of you in the industry.

is a Metroidvania 2D platformer that controls with an almost parallel beauty to the sublime visuals & incredible soundtrack as composed by Gareth Coker, with Aeralie Brighton, Rachel Mellis providing powerful vocals & Tom Boyd on Oboe. (Feel free to listen and/or download the trailer themes released on the composer's SoundCloud):
Capable of providing a great challenge, an engaging story, a great deal to explore that navigating is never too difficult,
is perhaps one of the most recommendable games I have seen in a fair while, and one that'll remain in memory fondly.
Highly recommended using a GamePad as your input. The game supports Keyboard & Keyboard & Mouse, but unfortunately limits itself to QWERTY & AZERTY presets, with no rebindable keys in or out of the game.
Despite running very well in my case & not been particularly demanding, Dean Dodrill's
remains to be outdone as the best PC port of a Microsoft Studio game.
From the very outset, Moon Studios emotionally grips with an outstanding prologue (Which their trailers were far too keen to try to spoil), then you are thrown into the gameplay and on a emotionally rich adventure.
The story is something I would consider to be very emotionally driven, as well as being probably the game's only notable weakness. To explain why would be a disservice to those whom have not yet had the fortune to play this game, so I'll leave that particular mystery to be solved by yourself (Or even find it's just me). As for the characters, their visual design alone makes them difficult to not fall in love with, with their unique animations & highly expressive faces enough to convey their powerful emotion & charm alone with great effectiveness, with only a particular set of characters with any words to provide.
But whatever the weaknesses, it remains strongest where it matters most; the gameplay. Although more tributary & iterative of the Metroidvania genre, it is one that provides a great deal of accessibility & ease of navigation without the fear of giving you a fair number of challenges to conquer.
Even though not being one for 2D platformers, even in my youth just before they made the leap to 3D, it was remarkably distinctive to the Metroidvania design it was so keen to pay tribute to, keenly reminding me of my experiences with the likes of
, and was also pretty astounding as to how beautifully it controlled for the most part (I say for the most part as early-game wall-climbing can be very tricky to pull off with precision due to requiring constant jump-button mashing to maintain a grip, especially when the game's pace skyrockets).
Despite the 12-14hrs I spent with the game completing it to 100%, it's a game that paces itself remarkably well, never demanding too much of your time & giving you a good moment to close down for another time, but always ensuring that no moment is ever a dull one.
I feel it's safe to say that whilst paying tribute to the timeless 2D platforming classics of the past, this one itself has gained itself the chance to become one along side them, with sublime visuals of a timeless quality, a soundtrack rich & raw with emotion, and gameplay & control that masters not only being accessible to many, but not afraid to make them earn their mastery of it.
If you're looking for a good ol' 2D Platforming Adventure, you cannot go wrong with this one!

Divinity is an absolute gem of a game that most RPG fans will find pleasure in. Best played co-op, it has provded countless hours of entertainment for me and my friend. it's one of those games where 12 hours can fly by without you realising.
What makes Divinity great is the emergent gameplay and tight balancing of the combat system. Elemental forces play a big role here; you'll find yourself planning your moves very carefully, chaining combos and making your party work together as a team.
This is why it works so well as a co-op adventure. Do yourself a big favour and play this with a friend - you'll find yourselves strategising and exploring the colourful and deep world to the wee hours of the morning.
I'm throwing praise at this game, but it certainly has some flaws. The story can be a bit convoluted (and long) at times, and it throws you into a big story-driven quest early on (you spend about an hour running around a town, trying to solve a murder mystery). This may not appear to most players, but once you're through that, it's pretty much non-stop combat.
A problem I often have with RPGs is a bloated story and complicated quests, but Divinity does a good job of keep the quests light. You'll spend maybe 15-20 minutes in town, getting quests and restocking your team, before a 2-4 hours combat session; this is a ratio I can live with.
It's also quite unforgiving early on; the harder difficulties really expect you to know what you're doing. But I find this tight balance really engaging as every move and ability really matter - you won't last long if you just try to directly attack everything in sight.
Which leads to another positive - the ability system gives you great freedom in customizing your characters. I have a melee character that wasn't doing much because the ground was so often on fire or covered in poison, so I gave her the ability to become an Avatar of Fire which not only makes her immune to fire but also lets her fling fireballs about. Having the freedom to do this in such a tightly balanced game is very refreshing.
I highly recommend picking this up, particularly if you have a friend to enjoy it with.

Fallout 3: Tunnel Snakes Rule
Although we all knew it was there hiding behind the curtain, it’s nice to finally know that Fallout 4 is, indeed, a real thing. And, surprisingly. coming this year at that! With the recent announcement, I thought I would write about one of my favorite Bethesda games, Fallout 3.
I think it’s safe to say that for many of us, Fallout 3 was our first introduction to the series as a whole. Not to say that Fallout 1 and 2 were not popular games, but being the fourteen-year-old I was in 2008, it’s easy to believe many gamers like myself were introduced to the series with Bethesda’s take on the famous franchise.
Going from an isometric turn-based RPG to a first person “shooter” is definitely a massive sea change. Although I wasn’t invested, I remember hearing some people were disappointed in the changes that a first-person perspective brought (and I can totally understand why), but Fallout 3 is still a game that I look back on, seven years later, with wonderfully fond memories.
One of the things, I think, that made Fallout 3 great was that while the world was rather vast and empty, that feeling of “emptiness” was very fitting for a world ravaged by nuclear war. There were pockets of life and activity, and you would randomly stumble across creatures or bandits out in the wilderness, but it wasn’t exactly “dense”. The game struck a nice balance between you finding encounters, and encounters finding you. It always seemed like, given enough time and walking, something interesting would happen. Whether it was being attacked by horrible Super Mutants in Downtown Washington, or stumbling upon a homestead that has seceded from what is left of the government.
The world had flavor. And that made it fun to explore.
Much like it’s predecessor, TES IV: Oblivion, Fallout 3 had a rather... ‘off’ feeling to it. Which was, in some ways, a great contrast to the bright 50’s aesthetic of the game world. While at the same time fitting for its post apocalypse setting. There was a nice conflict between what the world “was” and what it had become.
In Fallout 3, it felt like just about every abandoned home you entered had some kind of tragedy waiting to be discovered. Whether it was the remains of a family scattered through a home, or a suicide note left by a survivor. There were so many little details tucked away in the various places of the D.C. Wasteland. These touches made the world feel “lived in.”
Aside from the general “lived in” quality that Fallout 3 had, there were plenty of disturbing moments which were hidden in the world too. Walking into a school that had been taken over by cannibals, and seeing their “food supply” strewn across the floor… Exploring downtown and being ambushed by horrible mutants. Investigating a murder, committed by wannabe vampires… And of course, going down into some of the abandoned Vaults hidden in the wasteland… For a game made by a company notorious for stiff game design. There were some very good moments in the game, whether scripted or not.
For instance, Vault 108 was very memorable for me because it was full of Garys.
Gary had been cloned, many, many times, his clones were insane and hostile to all non-Garys. Eventually the Garys killed everyone else in the Vault, causing it to fall into disrepair. It was unsettling to walk into the silent rusted hallways of the Vault, only for the silence to be shattered by gunfire and unrelenting battlecry of: “Gaaarrrryyyyy? Gaaaarrryyy!!!!” And having three madmen, or truthfully three of the same madman, trying to rip your throat out.
Bethesda used the isolation in many of the Vaults to great effect. I specifically remember Vault 87. A crusty, dilapidated Vault, filled with Super Mutants and Centaurs. The isolation, the oppressively low ceiling and close walls. Combined with the darkness, large amounts of human remains, and the overall nastiness of the enemies made for a very memorable experience.
When the game was new, I remember playing through this area at two in the morning. While I was slowly making my way through the tense halls of the Vault, a dog started barking outside. I remember peering  through the blinds trying to figure out what was going on... Before I realized the game had stressed me out and I was reacting to the stress.
But nothing came close to the Dunwich building, although it wasn’t the scariest thing in the game, it was certainly the most upfront about it. In most cases the tension was due to thinking you’re alone in a quiet, dark, place and suddenly being shot or attacked by monsters. However, the Dunwich building had special scripting for its events. There was nothing like it in the rest of the game, and I think that’s why it was so memorable. It was a little, creepy, gem left to be discovered. Uncovering what happened to the people there was very interesting and, simultaneously, off putting with a wonderfully creepy easter egg waiting for you at the end. I highly recommend checking it out.
Well done, Bethesda.
While the world of Fallout was certainly fun to explore and become familiar with, the mechanics of the game itself were, unfortunately, pretty clunky. Shooting was stiff, and in some cases felt quite weak. There was nothing worse than shooting someone in the head, getting a bad damage roll, and watching them shrug off a bullet like it was a spit ball.
However, what made the shooting in Fallout memorable was V.A.T.S. or, the Vault-Tec Assisted Targeting System.
This is the mechanic that made Fallout 3 for me, V.A.T.S. allowed you to pause time and select individual parts of your opponents, then shoot said targets. Plus, V.A.T.S. would show your shots in amazing slo-mo cinematic glory! It made the combat feel pretty epic. There was nothing better that blasting an annoying NPC in the face with a shotgun, watching their head fly apart in slo-mo, and then reloading your previous save to continue on.
“This Moriarty guy is infuriating…” *quick save* *murder* *quick load*
Seeing your dude shoot at the enemy, watching the killing bullet travel from the gun barrel into their head, and seeing it explode into a chunky red mist all from a cinematic camera angle was… satisfying...
Throwing a grenade into a group of bandits running at you with murderous intentions, seeing it sail through the air, land at their feet, and then watching their feet fly in six different directions was… satisfying…
Running up to a guard, punching him to death, and watching his body explode into little chunks because of the perk “bloody mess” was… hilarious…
Unfortunately, V.A.T.S. didn’t completely circumvent the clunky nature of the game, but it did make it tolerable, and in many ways wonderfully endearing. V.A.T.S. was, by far, my favorite part of Fallout 3 It was, and still is, a unique and interesting mechanic, that spiced up combat. And the idea of using it in the upcoming Fallout 4 is getting me hyped.
And hype is bad, hype is the game killer.
Now, as you may or may not know, Bethesda games are famous for being incredibly moddable. They come with a complete suite of tools used solely for the purpose of creating new original content for the game itself. Fallout 3 is no exception.
There are some amazing Fallout 3 mods floating around out there… and some really weird ones. If you feel like the game is missing something, chances are someone made a mod for it. Just be warned… There are a lot of…
“adult” mods too. But, hey, if that’s your thing... They got your back!
The modding communities for Bethesda games are spectacular, there are some great gems out there on the internet. Sometimes you just gotta do some digging to find them.
Just go in with an open mind, remembering that the game is from 2008, and expect some amount of ‘jank’ and you’ll be fine.
It might look and feel dated, but damn there’s a fine game in there.

Skullgirls is a nice heavy dose of the familiar topped with a delicious, interesting theme and wonderful personality. The actual mechanics in play are nothing out of the ordinary, you'll be using standard 2D fighter controls to pull off mix-up combos, cancels, special moves and power-bar depleting "showstoppers." If you've played any other fast-paced 2D fighter such as Guilty Gear or BlazBlue then you'll be instantly comfortable with the controls and speed of the game. Skullgirls is extremely accessible with a detailed tutorial explaining everything a beginner fighter player would need to know. There's even in-depth character tutorials that explain what each character's special abilities are useful for and how to work them into combos. Within a few hours I was able to start stringing together 25+ hit combos and playing on Hard difficulty and I'm only an intermediate fighting game player.
While Skullgirls doesn't do much to innovate at its core, it makes up for this by hitting a home run in the area that matters the most in fighting games, the characters. Each Character is full of personality and is easily distinguishable from the rest in terms of visuals, motif and mechanics. No two characters feel the same. Even the stereotypical doppleganger character (who uses other fighter's skills) feels unique since the borrowed abilities aren't just copy-pasted from their source, they're more like attacks the source character would use but doesn't. I find myself interested in each character, wanting to hear what they have to say, to watch their personalities in action and the story mode, while short and linear, does a great job at showcasing these characters through beautiful still-frame cutscenes.
Speaking of the art, Skullgirls is gorgeous!  Its vectored sprites are crisp and the animation is silky smooth. The whole game operates under a jazzy, psuedo-noir/art deco/theater theme that infiltrates every aspect of the game. From the music to the menus to the cutscenes, Skullgirls stays consistent to it's theme and makes the whole experience a coherent one.
My only real complaint about Skullgirls is that there are far too few characters at the moment. Since you can play with up to three characters on a team at once, with a roster of about 9 playable characters, playing through arcade mode will have you seeing repeat upon repeat. Thankfully it looks like more characters will be added over time as there is already a DLC character up for purchase.
In conclusion, Skullgirls is a ton of fun. It may not do anything out of the ordinary, but what it does, it excels at. I would easily recommend this game as it is an accessible, addicting 2D fighting experience.

I'm going to be the contrarian here and write what I didn't liked about the game's story. If you want to read another review saying "To The Feelz" then feel free to move ahead.
That being said, before I explain which are my points of disappointment, I want to say that this is indeed an amazing game. It is short, standing at 5 hours of gameplay for most cases, so if you're looking for a lenghty visual novel, that's not the case here. However, it is a very good short story worth playing. It is mostly story though, beyond some minor puzzles and exploration. Also, it has a profound soundtrack. Overall, I would give this game 4 out of 5 stars.
Why not 5 stars? Keep reading, but I suggest you finish the game first.
*SPOILER ALERT*
Since you're exploring Johnny's memories, the story is told from his point of view. We see him dealing with River's illness and staying by her side until the end. We even see him granting her last wish, by allowing her to die to save their dream home. You know that this is going to be a sad story, since this is the story of a couple of scientists granting an old man's dying wish. However, I can't understand how the characters almost completely overlook the saddest point of all, which was River's ordeal.
Let me explain... while you play the game moving from the present to the past, you see that as part of River's illness she develops an obsession with creating rabbit origami. Every time she creates one of these she asks Johnny to describe what it is, but Johnny is unable to provide a satisfactory answer for her. At some point on the story, it is revealed that she started this obsession after Johnny told her something about their first meeting. You don't know for certain what he told her, but you know that his friend Nick knows about it. Since Johnny met Nick in middle school, you know that the event is something that happened at that time.
Now, when you learn the actual mystery of the game, you get to know that Johnny doesn't remember most of his childhood after the trauma of losing his brother and taking some medicine to forget about it. But here's the true tragedy: Johnny also forgot his actual first meeting with River when they were kids. It was the time when their connection started, the one that would last for all their lives. They were stargazing, they saw a bunny on the stars with the moon as its belly and Johnny ended up giving away the platypus stuffed toy as a present to River. It is the same platypus that she would keep for all her life. She also tells him about her love for lighthouses and how she would like to befriend one, one day.
So now, let's look at the story from River's point of view. She met Johnny when she was a little girl and they had a strong connection. He promises to meet her at the same spot next year, but that doesn't happens. She remembers about him, because she keeps her gifts. Later, by chance, she actually meets him again and they go out and eventually get married. And after they live almost a lifetime together, Johnny confesses something that makes her aware that he doesn't remember their first meeting and what may be the most crucial point of their relationship. But, River having a mental illness and being introverted, she doesn't just tells him: "What the hell, Johnny?! Don't you remember that time when we were kids?" No… instead she tries to show him. She makes paper bunnies and asks him to "see", to make him remember the moon. The last bunny even has different colors, because the moon is its belly. As final challenge, she asks him to throw away a bag Johnny has given her when they first met, and he does because for him it doesn't means anything. So in the end, she dies knowing that the man she married is not the same boy she met on the cliff that night when they were friends.
That's the true sad story here. River's story. And what I cannot understand is how the main characters of our story, the scientists, are completely ignorant about it. They saw it, they must understand what was happening, but they don't even make a reference about River's point of view. I know she's already dead, but not recognizing how hard it must have been for her it's the same as ignoring it. For me, it's like saying: "Yes, too bad for her, but this is Johnny's story, not hers".
In the end, I agree with Dr. Watts, Johnny didn't actually wanted to go To The Moon, what he wanted was to remember why he felt that the moon was special. He wanted to remember the moment that he actually met River. I think that would have been fairer to both sides of the story: Johnny's and River's.

I wrote a previous review in which I stated  my "Negative" was actually a "Neutral"
This is now a Negative review. Why? Well, I'll try for the first time ever to write a comprehensive review
Graphics: 6/10
This game is stunning to look at. The sea is dynamic and rolling (although I believe they removed storms from the overworld), and the ship models themselves are quite detailed and gorgeous to look at. They obviously did a ♥♥♥♥♥on of research and probably were able to get their hands on the blueprints and measurements for the actual ships. So why so low? Why not an 8 or a 9 or a 10? Well, if you've ever played Empire/Napoleon Total War, you know that ships show heavy damage as they fight; masts fall, holes are torn in the bulkheads, etc. In Naval Action, you can demast a ship, but 'damage' is reflected by pockmarks in the hull, like the bullet holes in Goldeneye 007 (N64). It really takes you out of the moment to realize that 32lb carronades (big honking guns) do no visible damage except for basically scuffing up the paint. It also denies you tactics such as firing grapeshot (think a shotgun blast from a cannon) into holes you blow into the ship to kill crew. Instead, blue bars in the UI show how much of a ship's armor you have destroyed. It feels cheap and isn't satisfying. You may be lucky enough to cause a fire and have an enemy ship explode, but I haven't been that fortunate to witness, so I cannot comment. Also, visible crew is limited to one animated sailor operating each cannon; this is understandable due to framerate issues, but it still looks a tad silly. The 'ports', if you can call them that, are indistiguishable from each other and are visually uninteresting. The user interface, once you enter a port, is a bland and uninspired blue-themed mess that looks like something from Windows 3.1 (Yes, they say they'll have a better UI on release. Yes, it's a lame excuse; take a couple days to whip up some nautical-themed graphics, if only as a placeholder, it *can't* be that hard). So, while the ship models and the sea may be absolutely stunning, everything else just seems cheap, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and uninspired.
Sound: 4/10
The cannons boom majestically, but there's no ambience aside from the sea itself; no seagulls, no whale or dolphins, nothing. There is no music, either. Some good sea shanties, epic battle music, or even some Celtic-style stuff that would fit the era would really add a ton of value and enjoyment. I rate this so low because, as the developers for the Total War mods called "Darthmod", they added some beautiful and epic music to their mods for Empire and Napoleon, and it's unacceptable that they wouldn't even lift *those* tracks, even as placeholders.
Gameplay: 2/10
Oh dear, oh dear, what could possibly be wrong? The answer: Everything. This game is the densest time sink you will ever play. It can take hours and hours of real-life time to sail the map, so grouping up with friends or clanmates means you will need to plan *far* in advance if you want to play together. Assigned missions can be up to 30 minutes away (thanks to the rotating wind direction); this, of course, assuming you can even find the missions. There are no tools for the in-game map, so if you want the exact bearing of where you want to go, hold a protractor to your screen; otherwise, you could overshoot your mission marker and waste a large chunk of your life looking for it. Some may say "But Sluggo, you tool, you have a compass in the overworld which shows your heading!" To which I reply "Yeah, but look at where your mission marker is on your map: tell me the exact bearing it's at." Because, especially if where you're headed is far away, a mere 10 degrees can mean the difference between reaching your objective or getting hopelessly lost. The battles themselves are fun, at first, but quickly grow repetative. There are also port battles, where nations fight to capture ports, but a wonderful mechanic to determine when ports are 'open' for battle means if you're in bed at 3am, you're not fighting.  Speaking of nations, there are 7 historical nations to choose from, plus a Pirate faction. All nations (plus Pirates) have access to the same ships, the only difference being the flag you fly. Pirates, amazingly, are an actual 'nation'; they operate exactly the same way as a real nation, without the high-risk/high-reward bucaneering you may be expecting. You can sail right past a British NPC fleet and they'll politely wave as you sail past; it's disgustingly immersion-breaking. If you're looking for a game where you'll be high-tailing it from Commodore Norrington with a hold full of Aztec gold, look elsewhere. You can choose to become a pirate when you create you character, or simply become a pirate by attacking a ship from your own nation. This is irreversable, as is changing your nation from any nation to anything except Pirate; there are no pardons, letters of marque, etc. So if you would like to be a privateer, er, independent contractor, you're out of luck. The in-game economy is completely broken; clans dominate the economy. The economy in the game is based on shipbulding and material trade, both of which are extremely time consuming as you must sail from port to port to port to collect resources and spend 'labor hours' from a limited pool to craft items and ships.  Because of the wealth amassed by clans, ships which should be worth no more than 100k gold cost millions and millions; anyone who would like to play on their own and not in a clan is at a severe, severe, disadvantage.
Aside from battles and economy, there is no other content in this game, and this is where it really falls apart. Visiting ports is pointless as they all look the same; there is no reward for, or need for, exploration or adventure, which, in the Age of Sail, is what this whole era is about. The developers have ruled out the possibility of there ever being a first-person component to this game; if you want to walk around your own ship, look at charts and maps in your cabin, walk around a port, meet your Admiral, participate in deck-to-deck fighting with the enemy captain, look elsewhere, because this game will never have it. The battles quickly become repetative, and all except the most die-hard will grow bored and move on to another game. The contect availbale in no way justifies the price tag. Development on this game has been very, very slow, with no major changes aside from tweaking of damage values; if you're expecting a bigger, better game a year from now, you're not going to get it, because all further contect will be within the limits of the current framework, which is itself extremely limited.  It honestly, truely feels like a proof-of-concept for a few mechanics of a bigger and better game that we're never going to get. I am longer ambivalent in my feelings for this game, and actively discourage anyone who hasn't bought it to not buy it and spend their money elsewhere. The playerbase is abandoning this game in droves with fewer than 700 average players, per
, and it continues to fall. In a few months I predict this game will be dead and just another failed Unity-engine project.
Not only to the developrs of Naval Action, but to the gaming 'industry' in general: This early-alpha-pre-access-beta-test-for-us-and-give-us-money extravaganza needs to stop. Now.

Would I recommend buying this game at this time? No
I will keep it short and to the point. This game has one of the best and most accurate to date naval combat simulations.
The problem is that since leaving combat test which was more MOAB style and the implementation of the 'open world' that combat is now gated behind a barely functional open world that is now depopulated, has huge exploitable mechanics loopholes, lacks content, and has a unrewarding and too fast paced realm vs. realm.
You will spend hours and hours searched for PvP only to have 99% of them run away and you in turn running away from the 5 to 1 gank squadrons. Depicting an open world of the age of sail this game does not do well. As an example my 1,000 plus hours of having the game running I have maybe at best 50 hours of PvP combat. The rest was sailing and watching something else or chasing players that didn't want to fight without their gank squadron friends even when they still overmatched me.
So while I have no regrets on the money I spent on the game and got my enjoyment out of it when the game had a more viable population, the current state of the game, the gating of what the game does well being behind a broken open world, and the lack of progress in development makes me unable to recommend to another to spend money on it. I can't even recommend buying it as an investment to the concept because it doesn't seem like the proceeds have been directed back into Naval Action in the slightest. While their studio is currently working on a new Ultimate General title.

TLDR: 7/10  (assuming 5 is baseline for a 'ok' title)
Quick View:
Its like playing Prototype 2 from the viewpoint of 'helpless army guy'.
Long View:
While I've played The Division primarily on the PS4, I have spent just enough time on the PC version to give what I believe is a fair point of view on how the game works for PC players.
The Division is at its core a good game. The story while only passable is not the focus of this title. Completing missions alone or with friends is the point and the game does that well.
The cover system and different enemy types give just enough variety that a player or team needs to introduce some strategy and cannot simply 'Rambo' it.
I have not spent much time in the dark zone (pvp area) and so cannot comment on that.
Overall this is yet another good game from Ubisoft, brought down by the 'AAA' B.S that they are known to inject.
Plenty of Micro-transactions (though overall cosmetic in nature)
Good:
Co-op with friends is robust, which is rarely seen these days.
The enviroment is amazing and well designed making you feel like your in New York after a virus outbreak or at least a decent sized riot.
The base upgrading is done in such a way that it feels organic and shows very real progress. The skills and character progression are linked to this in a innovative way.
Bad:
Micro-Transactions; in my opinion they are a plague on the industry and I will always look down upon a games that implement them. Feel free to disagree, but these alone bring this game down from a 8/10 for me.
The always online nature of the title will make it restrictive and will increase loading times for people with slower connections, even in single player.
Enemies tend to be a little 'bullet spongey' this is especially true while leveling and during missions set to harder difficulty.
It's definitely improved since release, but it can get boring if you only play by yourself.

This game is the biggest piece of indie rubbish I have ever played. The plot is mediocre at best and overly convoluted at worst. If you're the kind of person who thinks obscure pop-culture refrences can subsitute for good dialouge then you might like this game.
The game model's itself as "Inspired by Chrono Trigger" but lacks any of the aspects that made Chrono Trigger fun to play. There are no random battles, no leveling, no equipment. You play the entire game esentially trying to find the next person to talk to so that the plot will advance. The few times the game attempts to throw something that might qualify as  "gameplay" are poorly executed and frustrating.
The 16-bit pixel graphics are overly cliche and only serve to remind you that people made deeper, more entertaining, overall better games 15+ years ago. Every moment spent playing this game is a moment I could have spent playing a 12 year old game on an old supernintendo.
As I mentioned earlier, the plot is a boring mess of pop-culture dialog and awkward exchanges between characters that lack anything in the writing that would have you beleive the characters are alive. Plot twists are either boring, non-existent, or utterly predictable.
If you are a hipster who likes things that are terrible in order to make yourself seem quirky or interesting than you will love this game. Otherwise you will spent all 3-4 hours of gameplay hating yourself and regretting whatever decision lead you to purchasing this game.
In short: To The Moon is barely a game, and a terrible one at that. Don't play it unless you hate yourself.

So I set out my ambitious gamemaking career from my mom's garage. After making a bunch of more-or-less failed text adventures and 2D shooters with an 3-5 average score, I was about to fail miserably with my bank account hitting red after every pitiful attempt. But I wouldn't give up. I pushed all my energy and creativity into making just one more title in hopes that it would save me from bankrupcy.
And I did it. I was completely out of money and would probably have to move out of the garage and into the streets, but the game was finished. Upon release I noticed, however, that in all my creative flush and flow, I had forgot to name the game.
Nevertheless, Game #9 was an instant blockbuster! Reviews followed, praising the game (despite it's name) and calling it a masterpiece. Sales skyrocketed. With my newly accumulated capital of over 3 million, I decided to get a real office. Then I was prompted to hire new staff, so I started looking for a coding specialist to get some load off my shoulders.
The first name to pop up was Ashley Williams. Apparently one of my favourite characters from the Mass Effect universe had had a change of career and I would surely welcome her military expertise into my team. So that was a no-brainer, didn't even look at the others. I made another game with a publisher and with some ~7 million I thought I'd hire a few more people. I then got an achievement for hiring someone famous because I hired some dude. I still have no idea who that was supposed to be.

Unlike Assassin's Creed, Black Flag, that was entirely arcade-like in its sailing and battle dynamics, Naval Action endeavors to be more of a sailing simulator and has very sophisticated physics models for ballistics/ ship damage and other ship dynamics. This, combined with very good graphics, cements my interest in the game.
For the above mentioned aficionado, this should be enough to enjoy this Alpha release as  it stands.  For others it seems, perhaps wanting more polished nuance, a AAA game team of developers making leaps and strides of breathtaking advancements weekly, may find themselves  disappointed.
The UI is rudimentary, the crafting is basically looking at lists that resemble a spreadsheet.  In fact in the lower corner of the screen the developers have a little note the states ‘Please ignore the UI’.  I find this all forgivable at this relatively early stage in development.
There are many ships available in the game that you access as your leadership experience advances.  Every ship is modeled to have its unique strengths and weaknesses, this is fleashed out in more detail then you  will ever need at -

A recommended site to have bookmarked for quick reference if you play the game.
There is no way the game could be at its current state without dedicated passion from the development team.  This gives me great faith that, going forward, we will see the game evolve into an icon of the Age of Sail simulator/ MMO.
Again, highly recommended. I have my money’s worth several time over already.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Edit after 600+ hours in game
My interest in the game is increasing over time.  A rare quality in a game.
The developers continue to tweak the dynamics and add features.
A notable incident that speaks to the character of the development team happened recently when their ISP provider had a technical problem that took the Naval Action servers off line for something like 24 hours or so.  Although it was no fault of the game team, they gave every player in the game a newly developed ship of considerable game-value as compensation.
I have played many AAA MMOs that have been in full release for years and when they have similar server issues that ARE their responsibility, they do nothing, no compensation, not even to paid-up patrons.
So kudos to the Naval Action team.

Divinity is an absolute gem of a game that most RPG fans will find pleasure in. Best played co-op, it has provded countless hours of entertainment for me and my friend. it's one of those games where 12 hours can fly by without you realising.
What makes Divinity great is the emergent gameplay and tight balancing of the combat system. Elemental forces play a big role here; you'll find yourself planning your moves very carefully, chaining combos and making your party work together as a team.
This is why it works so well as a co-op adventure. Do yourself a big favour and play this with a friend - you'll find yourselves strategising and exploring the colourful and deep world to the wee hours of the morning.
I'm throwing praise at this game, but it certainly has some flaws. The story can be a bit convoluted (and long) at times, and it throws you into a big story-driven quest early on (you spend about an hour running around a town, trying to solve a murder mystery). This may not appear to most players, but once you're through that, it's pretty much non-stop combat.
A problem I often have with RPGs is a bloated story and complicated quests, but Divinity does a good job of keep the quests light. You'll spend maybe 15-20 minutes in town, getting quests and restocking your team, before a 2-4 hours combat session; this is a ratio I can live with.
It's also quite unforgiving early on; the harder difficulties really expect you to know what you're doing. But I find this tight balance really engaging as every move and ability really matter - you won't last long if you just try to directly attack everything in sight.
Which leads to another positive - the ability system gives you great freedom in customizing your characters. I have a melee character that wasn't doing much because the ground was so often on fire or covered in poison, so I gave her the ability to become an Avatar of Fire which not only makes her immune to fire but also lets her fling fireballs about. Having the freedom to do this in such a tightly balanced game is very refreshing.
I highly recommend picking this up, particularly if you have a friend to enjoy it with.

Well, what to say...
This game is in early access, so there is a lot about it that will be changed, will be improved, etc. etc. As it stands it is very enjoyable, if you are able to get it to work. Not that there isn't a way, as you can see, it is currently able to run on most computers, old and new, but I would highly recommend tweaking the graphics and whatever else before you play. As a game, it doesn't quite provide any real instructions, similar to that of, well, you know. Unlike the game I'm not going to mention, its controls can be trickier to master, and though I'm unsure whether or not it supports controllers currently, as mine haven't worked so far, it really needs them.
As for the game, let me explain the HUD, menu and controls to you.
The start menu appears to be what you'd expect from a LEGO game on boot, but you end up confronted with a new kind of actual menu past the title screen. Rather than the Save/Load/Options/Windows scroll menu we're used to seeing, it presents a new World Generation interface, along with a load of different functions in the top left corner. These include Options, Character Select, World Saves and a bunch of others I've forgotten. In the bottom right corner, there's world naming, coordinates (seeds, essentially) and a button to play.
The controls are strange; unlike most LEGO games, a mouse is required for the menu, but the keyboard controls are more or less the same as if you've played any other on PC. If not, it's not dissimilar to that... other building game, or you can always set the controls in the options.
Now the in-game HUD is strange. It allows you similar menu options to other LEGO games, but also gives you character customization, block selection, world editing and a shop in which to buy other things such as characters, decorations, etc.
Now, my computer has still had slight troubles running the game after changing the settings, as yours may also, and don't be too alarmed if it shuts down instantly after twenty seconds to an hour of play. It does that, but as it's still in development it will likely be fixed eventually.

Here's a genuinely sweet, fun little racing game. I don't particularly play racing games, but the graphics on this were adorable, and it gave me a pleasant surprise.
The AI is surprisingly good in races and I didn't notice too much rubberbanding going on with the game, and the multiplayer is some great fun, since all the rounds are elimination-based and can actually get pretty intense. Single player isn't terrible at all, and there are multiple different modes to make the game not monotonous. The game also does not overstay its welcome, with 100% completion taking me about ten hours, and that's with me being awful at racing games.
I'm not actually sure if it's because I'm just bad at racing games either, but the game does provide some actual challenge with its various modes. The time trials are absolutely brutal, and I finished all of them within a second of the required time to get a perfect rating, so even to people who play the genre all the time, this might be interesting as a grab for them.
There are so many little tiny details that were put into this game that I love. The cars have little screws on the bottom. There are a few cars that come with working sirens, and all of them have working horns which you can spam, if nothing else. The levels themselves are absolutely adorable, all clearly designed with the idea of your cars actually being toys in mind.
This is really just a cute, very fun game that I would recommend to everyone who wants a new little racing game to try out, especially if you have some friends who would want to give it a go with you.

sets to simulate the official 2013's WRC championship calendar, with full car liveries, classes, and their respective pilot's and co-pilot's.
A total of 65 drivers, 55 teams, 16 different car models and 78 stages, is what's waiting for you, through the different classes. 13 official rallies will put you to the test from ice, dirt, asphalt, and all the great landscapes of Finland, Australia and even the breathtaking Argentina, and much, much more.
The career mode lets the player feel like a real driver, or at least that's how was intended. Going trough the garage, reading emails, the calendar, results and adversaries, is something nice, but interaction is heavenly missed, even for a Junior WRC driver. The intentions were good, but ends up away repetitive over time.
Visually the game improves from
, which isn't available on Steam, and delivers a world calendar with an average to high in real-track detail. Hardly fair to compare to other games released more recently of course, but it's still a record of what the past WRC season had to offer in track challenges.
As gameplay goes,
delivers a very close experience to previous titles. The franchise is still directed to the soft audience, who look for a casual experience of the most prestige rally championships. Hard difficulty is still present, with the usual car adjustments to make your life easier, or harder, depending on how far you're willing to go for realism.
It's still worth mentioning that WRC franchise is far from the realistic rally experience, at least compared to other games on the market, from past and present. Car physics are average, and at this point in time outdated.
Flashbacks are still present, which is perfect for the less experienced players having issues with rough weather or night races, and can be equally turned off if none of those things can slow you down!
Being a console port,
didn't include many options, and the ones they did are so basic that aren't worth mentioning, otherwise this game wouldn't even be playable at all. In fact, would be more fair to state functions missing, like turning the vibration off from gamepad/controllers.
Online functions are terrible, not only because it requires online account validation everytime one want's to play, but because the service quality is just bad. Ping out of control, users unable to enter lobby due to "out of reach status", gaming crashing often... It's a mess of a service not optimized, and often used on console online services, where the players themselves host the match.
is still a good option but not at current price and only if you want to take the most out of an offline experience.
With really nice visuals, basic gameplay that will suit most players, enjoying a rally experience from low tier classes to top WRC drivers can be interesting.

This game is the biggest piece of indie rubbish I have ever played. The plot is mediocre at best and overly convoluted at worst. If you're the kind of person who thinks obscure pop-culture refrences can subsitute for good dialouge then you might like this game.
The game model's itself as "Inspired by Chrono Trigger" but lacks any of the aspects that made Chrono Trigger fun to play. There are no random battles, no leveling, no equipment. You play the entire game esentially trying to find the next person to talk to so that the plot will advance. The few times the game attempts to throw something that might qualify as  "gameplay" are poorly executed and frustrating.
The 16-bit pixel graphics are overly cliche and only serve to remind you that people made deeper, more entertaining, overall better games 15+ years ago. Every moment spent playing this game is a moment I could have spent playing a 12 year old game on an old supernintendo.
As I mentioned earlier, the plot is a boring mess of pop-culture dialog and awkward exchanges between characters that lack anything in the writing that would have you beleive the characters are alive. Plot twists are either boring, non-existent, or utterly predictable.
If you are a hipster who likes things that are terrible in order to make yourself seem quirky or interesting than you will love this game. Otherwise you will spent all 3-4 hours of gameplay hating yourself and regretting whatever decision lead you to purchasing this game.
In short: To The Moon is barely a game, and a terrible one at that. Don't play it unless you hate yourself.

+ Well designed in almost all areas and nice graphical effects on spells and abilities.
+ Polished and most aspects of the game mechanics are easy to use/get to grips with.
+ Voice acting is great and almost every character and NPC is voice acted.
+ Tone of the game and its characters is often brilliant. Very funny when your party banter with each other or when you dialogue with NPC's. As long as you're looking for a game that doesn't take itself too seriously.
+ Well fleshed out side quests.
+Character creation, customisation and class building is enjoyable while not being to in depth that it takes away from the rest of the game.
- Combat is far too easy and quite repetetive after tens of hours.
- A rather unoriginal and uninteresting main story arc that seems to drag on for far too long.
- Playing a story based game in co-op in this instance is pretty pointless. If you ever disagree on a dialogue option it it decided by playing rock, paper, scissors... what, even...
Summary - DOS:EE is an enjoyable game if you're willing to overlook how cliche the main storyline is. It can be very funny at times and there's no denying the developers put a lot of work into making the game feel like a good quality game. I recommend turning up the difficulty and maybe swapping your party around a few times to mix up the combat a bit otherwise it can get quite boring. Playing in co-op is really not worth it. The side quests can be just as, if not more enjoyable than the main story arc so make sure to try them all out. Overall I would give DOS:EE a neutral rating if I could but it certainly doesn't deserve a negative so that only leaves one option! :D

You can go anywhere, kill anyone or anything. Loot anything. There will be consequences for your actions of course, but the game doesn't try to protect you from making a game breaking mistake.
Cast a spell that spills oil everywhere and shoot it with a fire arrow to watch it burn. Or perhaps throw a poison grenade and then cast a fireball on the gas cloud and watch it explode! These are the kind of combinations you have to think about during combat. The game uses a classless based system, so while you build your character with an archetype in mind, you can really go anywhere with it.
The story is light hearted and fun. The voice acting is great. I'm very impressed with Larian Studios updating this game so incredibly well. Be warned though, if you buy this game, you're buying into the series.

A quick, downward-oriented, roguelike indie game. Wew, what a mouthful.
This game is one of those 'easy-to-learn, difficult-to-master' situations.
You make your way down a spooky well filled with all sorts of creatures that I assume are trying to eat you in order to... reach the bottom. Heh. You could probably finish the game easy enough just by winging it but I feel like most of the fun and challenge lies in making those sicknastyhuge combos (I think my highest combo was around 215-ish).
Collect gems from enemies and safe rooms, then purchase health refills/expansions, or more weapon charges. If you collect a lot of gems quickly this also gets you a 'gem high' which significantly buffs your weaponry. Choose from about a dozen different perks each time you complete a level. Mix and match them for crazy bullet explodey times. It's all good.
On that note you've got a respectable amount of weapons to choose from, but you'll probably just stick to a few you feel most comfortable with (shotgun and puncher for me).
Finally, where the game falls short in length it makes up for in replayability, easily worth the price they're asking I think ($2.99 AUD, full price at the time of this review). With that said, I got all the achievements in about 2 hours so I'm pretty much done with it. Your own play times may vary.

Coming from someone who doesn't usually pick up fighting games, this was a very enjoyable experience. The presentation is a sight to behold, with beautiful hand-drawn visuals and a lovely soundtrack that fits just about every location and event in the game (I really hope they release the soundtrack on Steam sometime in the future). The gameplay is certainly nothing small either. As it states in its description on the store page, it uses a 6-button interface that takes almost no time getting used to. Even if you're not big on the fighter scene, they have a lovely tutorial section in the Training Mode that shows you almost everything there is to know about not just the game, but I dare say the fighting genre in general. And the online mode; gorgeous! Skullgirls relies on GGPO, which in a nutshell is a middleware that creates almost no lag for various games. The only true problem I have with the game is the character selection, which doesn't even matter in the long run, as Lab Zero recently held an Indigogo campaign to fund DLC characters within the upcoming year. I love this game, and I would definetly recommend it to the fighting crowd. Even if you're just a casual gamer, this is still a game that you can pick up and play, provided that you look at the tutorial. You might end up loving it as much as I do.
