SKullgirls is a fun and challenging game with a lot of personality.
The premise is simple: There's a mystic artfiact that can grant wishes, but corrupts those who use it if they are not pure of heart, and various factions fight over it.
However, the game's art style and matching personalility really makes this typical plot line into a non issue. Every character has myriad influneces, from other fighting characters (Painwheel takes after voldo), to genres (peacock is a homage to early cartoons, such as Popeye and Steamboat Willie).
Addittionaly, the game has a huge amount of lore and backstory present in it, There is already over 40 characters with wiki pages and in universe concepts present on the wiki, despite the game (currently) only having 9 playable characters. Speaking of the story, I have found myself feeling emotionally invested in some of the characters, despite each character's story line only being a 30 minute ordeal.
As far as actual combat, I feel it's a very good fighter. I'm no expert, but I can tell it has the deep mechanics and skill required for fighting game pros, but without feeling overly intmidating or difficult for more casual players. Combos don't feel stiff with very small windows of time to add on hits, specials are simple to pull off, but despite all of this, there really is a lot of depth.
I highly reccomend skullgirls for just about anyone, unless they have a passionate hatred for the genre.

This is one of the best fighting games currently out there. Even if you're completely new to fighting games, this is probably the best choice to start with: Its tutorial is simply the best I've ever seen in a fighting game. Play with just one character or team up with 2 or 3 for MvC-style tag team madness. The game even balances each character's strength if your opponent picks a different number of characters for their team. With it's hand-drawn art style and Roaring 20's vibe, this game is simply beautiful to look at and listen to. With simple controls, this is a game anyone can pick up instantly, yet it has the infinite depth that you'd expect of the most competitive tournament fighters.

Amazing fighting game developed with competition in mind. The gameplay is great. So you can have an idea about what it feels: it plays more or less like a mix between Marvel vs Capcom 2 and Guilty Gear. Beautiful graphics in high resolution with fluid animations, amazing soundtrack with tracks by Michiru Yamane (Castlevania: SotN and other games in the series) and an INCREDIBLE netcode.
Right now it has a small roster of 9 characters (8 with the regular game, 1 dlc character as of now) but each character is unique (even Double who has sprites from everybody plays differently from the rest). The game has an extense tutorial where it teaches you meaningful things you need to know if you're new to the genre and also gets you started into learning how each character plays. More characters are in the making, you can even watch the devs streaming the developing process from time to time.
Meaningful gameplay features include:
-Variable-sized teams. You choose if you play with 1 powerful character, 2 average characters or 3 weaker characters.
-The ability to assign ANY attack to your assists (as long as it's not a super).
-A system that prevents infinite combos.
-A robust training mode with the ability to see the hitboxes, use savestates and slowdowns, etc.
-Steamworks integration for online lobbies.
And in general there's a lot of attention put to details that matter, things like an easy and fast system to configure controls or the inhability to pause the game by accident. And the game is constantly being tweaked (and by "constantly" I mean even daily), with the devs actually listening to the community.

As with nearly all Milestone's games, graphics options are minimal. The only things adjustable are:
and those can only be adjusted outside the game in the launcher prior to starting the game. Shadows are on by default and detail levels cannot be adjusted. Because of all the non-adjustable parameters, basic GPU utilization is quite high. The only significant ways to get better frame rates is to turn AA off and / or to use lower resolution.

Short version:
- Progress on the game is painfully slow, most updates add nothing new, but just adjust combat variables and even that is done seemingly carelessly.
- It's a timesink, heavily discouraging casual play. However, dedicated players aren't really rewarded since the game lacks features in a bad way.
- Combat system currently heavily favours attackers, leaving PvP servers as gank or be ganked.
- The game is bleeding active players. The last two months has seen the game's biggest server go from a daily peak population of almost 2500 players to less than 1000, even with a smaller server being merged into the big one. This means little to no community for many factions, as the players are spread out over 7 different nations plus 1 pirate faction.
Bit longer version:
The game definitely has potential, and in the hands of a bigger company/more productive developers, I think this would turn out very well. Having spent hundreds of hours on the game over several months, I don't think that will happen, unfortunately.
It's still very bare bones. There is little other to do than battle, and while the battle mechanics are quite fun, the game is open world  and generally set up in a way that makes it seem very dull and empty when battle is the only fleshed out part.
On the face of it, that's not a problem, though. This is after all Early Access, so you don't expect a full game. I do expect progress, however, and in the 2 months I've played the game, the only new 'feature' to be introduced was the ability to enter ports belonging to other nations as a smuggler, and from what I can read on forums, that is in fact all they've managed to add in about half a year.
The rest of their effort seems to be spent fiddling with damage, armour, penetration and other battle-related details, often messing things up immensely. A good example was a change to leaks that meant a light frigate could just ram a huge ship-of-the-line and that alone would sink the massive hulk in less than a minute.
It's also a time sink like nothing else I've ever played. You need hours to do anything interesting, as just travelling to and from a mission will often take more than half an hour on its own, especially if the wind is against you. You spend so much time doing absolutely nothing, but even then you can't actually let the game idle, as the wind changes and you'll have to adjust your course or you have to look out for enemy ships.
Speaking of enemy ships, combat very badly handled and I see no reason to expect the devs will change the current system. Combat occurs not in the Open World map, but in an instance, so to speak. The relevant players are removed from the Open World map and placed in a separate combat map. Other players not dragged in from the beginning can reinforce the battle, but only for a couple of minutes, then the combat is closed until it ends. This means jumping lone players with a group of ships will basically ensure an easy kill, since there simply isn't time for help to arrive. Ganking is the way to go in this game.
I could go on, but I've already wasted enough time on this game, hoping it would live up to its potential. It doesn't now and I have no reason whatsoever to think it ever will.

The too long; didn't read version is that this game is excellent and if you enjoy Total War and/or Warhammer you will enjoy this game a lot. Especially given what it will be like in 6 months time.
The latter point is really the only downside that this game has at present. It has some issues. Namely that the Mortal Empires update that was promised to include all the WH1 factions into a single giant map alongside the new world factions was released in an unfinished state and it has taken close to two months for CA to bring in the foundation update to WH2 and the Norsca faction that was arguably released as an incentive to preorder WH2 probably won't be incorporated until 2018. So if you're thinking of buying this game because you'd like to play the large combined map, I'd probably wait another few months. By then, Mortal Empires will hopefully be finished and there will probably also be Tomb Kings DLC to fluff the game up a bit. The factions also need some serious rebalance, especially the potential for factions like the Dwarfs from turning into behemoths out of nowhere. This will hopefully be fixed like they fixed the Wood Elves from dominating the entire Western side of the map in WH1, but it's still a bit annoying. CA does seem to actually care about fixing problems like this at least so it's unlikely to be ignored in future updates and will be dealt with eventually.
That aside, this is a great game that builds upon the strong foundation laid in WH1. The new factions are great, although the Skaven feel a bit too niche for my liking and I am struggling to enjoy them. Which is a shame because I really like their aesthetics. The vortex campaign is a lot of fun and does change the pace of the campagin quite a lot compared to previous Total War titles that all followed the same kind of playstyle every time unless you decided to roleplay or something. My only beef with it is that at present, there is no option to turn it off and just enjoy the campaign map without worrying about it. Technically you can just ignore it and gamble on being able to defeat the other main factions before they complete their rituals or you can gamble on fighting a final battle when one does finish, but the AI won't ignore it and it would be nice to be able to completely and uttlerly not worry about it at all. Overall it is a definite improvement to Total War and I look forward to seeing how CA expands on the idea of narrative-driven campaigns in future games.
Overall, this game is a solid 8/10 and I am willing to bump that score up as updates are released. This game has a lot of content and you can lose a day playing without really even noticing. All the new features like loot/mysteries/exploring ruins, improved magic, story, and little things like UI improvments have come together to produce one of the best Total Wars I've played. Its only real downsides are things that will be addressed in future updates.

Oh gee, lemme get right to the point - this game is SO much fun, and surely is one of the best RPGs I have played in a long time. So if you are into classic RPGs, if you like, eg. Baldurs Gate or the older Divinity games, GET THIS ONE.
Even though I am not even that far into the game, I already feel like I got my money's worth out of the game, as it's highly enjoyable. Even if you are new to RPGs or worry that this might be too "deep" or complicated, don't worry... the game does a good job at showing you how to play, and if help is needed, there are some nice resources online.
So, what do I like?
- The game looks quite nice, with a rather classic look and perspective.
- The combat is SO much fun... it's quite tactical, and there are quite a few ways to win fights. I try to have all kinds of skills and schools of magic, ranged, melee and the different types of casting available in order to be able to adapt to different fights. You HAVE to pay attention, even if you gear up and get better skills... oil on the floor? Set it on fire! Water? Use lightning! Or use rain to extinguish fire etc. Keep in mind that the environment can be used to hurt and kill enemies... but it might hurt or kill you too if you are not careful, as your enemies will use the environment against you too!
- The abilities and spells are pretty fun... summoning stuff, using the elements, etc.
- Big inventory
- Deep crafting with the ability to experiment and discover stuff
- Great writing and an interesting story
- Fun characters, and some interesting conversations
- Difficult, but not unfair. You might wanna start with one of the lower difficulties in order to learn how fights work and learn tactics, but then start a new game with higher difficulty for a more rewarding experience.
- Again, fighting, tactics, are so much fun. You can also learn all kinds of skills, and I think it's best if you do. So train your melee warrior some magic so he or she can heal or cast spells.
- Tons of freedom, even though some content is locked at first until you level up (you CAN go there, but the NPCs recommend not to, and they have their reasons for it)
- Music is nice
- Riddles that require a bit of thinking and experimenting
YMMV:
- A quirky sense of humor. The game has a few cartoonish elements in game, and some humor. If you want some incredibly tense and serious RPG, that might turn you off.
- Even though the game does a good job at teaching you how to play and there are SOME markers, quests actually require you to... QUEST. Think. Search. Experiment. Look around. Look for clues. I love it, but it might be a turn-off sometimes.
- Some fights really require you to be at the right level and prepare. One of the stronger quest bosses rather early on will obliberate your group quickly unless you are at a higher level. However, autosaves and frequent manual saving will help to figure that out.
So far, it's a TON of fun, and I am reminded of classic RPGs I played in the 80s and 90s (Pools Of Radiance, Ultima 4-7 etc), and so I really can't wait to play more and get more of the story, explore the world etc. And part 2 is already in the works (early access, release in 2017, you can buy the game already and play a bit of its content)
My current rating? 8.5/10, might even go up.

I've just completed the game on Normal and found it enjoyable. The story is meh but that's not what I came for. The gameplay was action packed, fairly similar to Gears of War third person shooting. The experience was linear as the developers intended, which I didn't mind. Sometimes it's nice to be spoon fed the content and just enjoy the gameplay.
The difficulity progression was fair, starting things off simple and introducing new enemies as the game goes on. Each enemy general has a basic weakness, i.e. armored enemies require piercing shots from heavier weapons.
There were also some unique sections of the game which I welcomed, kept things fresh.
The cut scenes were all pretty generic, the voice acting is mediocre but not bad. Maybe I would have appreciated them more if I followed the Warhammer 40k universe, but I don't. Some transitions seemed a bit off, audio occassionally seemed to cut abruptly.
Here's a list of pros and cons to simplify things and to maybe add some things I missed.
PROS
----------
Fun, fast paced gameplay.
Pacing of the game feels natural.
Different weapon types keep the challenge present.
Longevity of game worth what I paid (£5 during sale).
CONS
----------
A few too many lengthy walking sections with little action inbetween.
Dialogue is mediocre.
Story is meh.
Cut scenes are only worth watching to know whats going on in the story.
Summary: This game was clearly not "the next big thing" and I don't think it tried to be. It's just a fun playthrough, worth it if you fancy a linear action game.
I'd just like to mention the dedication to Brian Wood in the credits, one of the developers of Company of Heroes that tragically died in a car accident. It's very honourable his dedication is the only thing in the ending credits. The staff clearly wanted his name to be remembered and it will be for me whenever I think of this game.

SKullgirls is a fun and challenging game with a lot of personality.
The premise is simple: There's a mystic artfiact that can grant wishes, but corrupts those who use it if they are not pure of heart, and various factions fight over it.
However, the game's art style and matching personalility really makes this typical plot line into a non issue. Every character has myriad influneces, from other fighting characters (Painwheel takes after voldo), to genres (peacock is a homage to early cartoons, such as Popeye and Steamboat Willie).
Addittionaly, the game has a huge amount of lore and backstory present in it, There is already over 40 characters with wiki pages and in universe concepts present on the wiki, despite the game (currently) only having 9 playable characters. Speaking of the story, I have found myself feeling emotionally invested in some of the characters, despite each character's story line only being a 30 minute ordeal.
As far as actual combat, I feel it's a very good fighter. I'm no expert, but I can tell it has the deep mechanics and skill required for fighting game pros, but without feeling overly intmidating or difficult for more casual players. Combos don't feel stiff with very small windows of time to add on hits, specials are simple to pull off, but despite all of this, there really is a lot of depth.
I highly reccomend skullgirls for just about anyone, unless they have a passionate hatred for the genre.

This is one of the best fighting games currently out there. Even if you're completely new to fighting games, this is probably the best choice to start with: Its tutorial is simply the best I've ever seen in a fighting game. Play with just one character or team up with 2 or 3 for MvC-style tag team madness. The game even balances each character's strength if your opponent picks a different number of characters for their team. With it's hand-drawn art style and Roaring 20's vibe, this game is simply beautiful to look at and listen to. With simple controls, this is a game anyone can pick up instantly, yet it has the infinite depth that you'd expect of the most competitive tournament fighters.

Amazing fighting game developed with competition in mind. The gameplay is great. So you can have an idea about what it feels: it plays more or less like a mix between Marvel vs Capcom 2 and Guilty Gear. Beautiful graphics in high resolution with fluid animations, amazing soundtrack with tracks by Michiru Yamane (Castlevania: SotN and other games in the series) and an INCREDIBLE netcode.
Right now it has a small roster of 9 characters (8 with the regular game, 1 dlc character as of now) but each character is unique (even Double who has sprites from everybody plays differently from the rest). The game has an extense tutorial where it teaches you meaningful things you need to know if you're new to the genre and also gets you started into learning how each character plays. More characters are in the making, you can even watch the devs streaming the developing process from time to time.
Meaningful gameplay features include:
-Variable-sized teams. You choose if you play with 1 powerful character, 2 average characters or 3 weaker characters.
-The ability to assign ANY attack to your assists (as long as it's not a super).
-A system that prevents infinite combos.
-A robust training mode with the ability to see the hitboxes, use savestates and slowdowns, etc.
-Steamworks integration for online lobbies.
And in general there's a lot of attention put to details that matter, things like an easy and fast system to configure controls or the inhability to pause the game by accident. And the game is constantly being tweaked (and by "constantly" I mean even daily), with the devs actually listening to the community.

After two hours, three missions I dare to say it's worth the 5€.
Basically it's a real-time strategy where you're not playing a cigar-smoking general who commands armies of tanks, instead your units are medics, firefighters, policemen and other people who have anything to do with emergencies; maybe only Batman is missing.
The game has a sandbox-like campaign, where you are assigned as the man directing the city's first line of defense during calamities, and you will get - I presume - randomly generated emergencies including extinguishing fires of various sizes - from a few smoking bushes to blazing multistory buildings, catching pickpockets and restarting failing hearts. Time to time, however, a pregenerated larger scale operation will pop up which will certainly require a combined operation. For example in the first and second one you will need both medics and firefighters - with gasmasks in the second, while you need medics, criminal profilers and marksmen in the third. All in all, I have no problems with the variety of missions so far.
But the game has problems. The most important - for me - is that it lacks active pause; when you stop the time, you cannot issue orders. Many would say "it's called real-time for a reason", but I would answer: "If it was real-time strategy then an ambulance would reach its destination in 30 minutes or so, and not within seconds. So let's call these accelerated time strategy, and as such, they need active pause. Especially when you have to act for all your men and women, because they will apathetically suffocate in a smoke-filled building should you not order them outside." And with that last sentence we reached the topic of AI.
Well, it's simple, and not without problems. For example the firemen will target the nearest fire within a few a meters when they have a hose in their hands, but will gladly try to take the longer route to reach their assigned target, even if that way the hose will be too short. So don't try to send them on longer journeys unattended, which means a lot of micromanagement when your hands would be full even with a more proactive crew.
Another problem is that they just don't seem to comprehend the gravity of these emergencies. For example, in the third mission I had six marksmen ordered to riddle two mobsters with bullets. The culprits were of course running towards the edge of the map, and my unit of cold professionals, the tip of the spear, the edge of the knife, the crack of my ... eh... were walking after them. And I don't mean they did not take a vehicle or something, I mean that they simply did not feel like running. I had to order a donut-eating patrolman into the criminals path, and - luckily - they immediately opened fire on him, giving enough time to my SWAT team to finish sightseeing and catch up with them. My condolences to the widow, her husband died a heroic, although otherwise completely avoidable death. Bleh.

I was apprehensive about buying this game in early access because I've been burned by EA games before. But I'm glad I finally bought it.
-The combat in this game is solid naval combat. Except for the poor looking boarding menus. Boarding works but it isn't fun and they'll have to change it for it to be fun.
-It is open world and kind of reminds me of POTBS MMO if any of you played that.  There is a map but it doesn't ping your location so you have to rely on terrain and your compass right now. Also the missions are indicated by crossed white swords which can be hard to see during the day ( I suggested they change the color of those).
-The port screen is ugly but fully functional. It does have a little messege saying Test UI please ignore so it will change. Making it pretty is something probably low on their priority list and that is ok.
-The ships are beautiful but I'd like to see more customization of colors on the wood/designs, possibly sail color (but not a big deal), and a maybe a custom captain avatar sailing the ship. Right now every ship is the same color in its class, the deck's cannons do change style depending on what you have equipped,  and there is a very generic crew representation (which is ok enough for me, but some might want more here).
-Sound effects and smoking cannons are great but the game doesn't have a music track yet, so I use my own in the background.
-there is crafting, trading, and gathering resources to build ship which is nice. There is even a chance at making better ships such as exceptional.
-there is clans, PvP, PvE, and co-op play so it has it all there. Not only can you craft, sell/buy ships, but you can also capture them in combat which is always nice(again boarding isn't fun right now though).
Overall I enjoy  the game because I like naval combat and love playing it with friends over voice chat. However I also like customization and role playing which is lacks, but I can see them building on. I can see this game going a long way and recommend in its alpha state if you want a good naval combat game with the understanding the RPG element of it is growing and not complete yet.

I like this game a lot; but I can't recommend it.  Designed to, as accurately as possible, portray the Age of Sail in the Carribean and Gulf of Mexico, the game does that very well.  The devs are working very hard to tweak it, add balance, etc.
But authenticity comes at a price.  Unfortunately, the main cost is real time. This is a huge problem for the long term success of a game.  Just going on a simple PvP mission can take an hour or more.  By the time you sail to sea (crap - it's against the wind), get to your marker, conduct the fight, then sail back (crap - against the wind AGAIN), you have just spent 30-60 minuites (or more) in the game.  Seek out a larger PvE battle and the time goes even higher.  PvP battles can be even worse.
Any battle can last up to 90 minutes.  That means if you have 60 minutes to play before you go to work, before your next class starts, etc you can't play because you may still be stuck in a battle by the time you must leave.  And even if you get out of the PvP battles, you may well find friends of the enemy waiting for you as you leave - sucking you back into another up to 90 minute battle - sometimes 2-3+ times in a row.
For someone with no time constraints, that is fine.  For the majority of players with class, jobs, family, etc, the time cost is too high.
Yes, if you can only play a short time you can pursue your crafting skills.  But, it literally takes only 10-15 minutes tops to use up all the labor points you have for the day, so crafting can't fill the short time void very often.  You can also make trade runs, but smart players build their outposts so trade runs are rarely needed; why risk losing one's cargo when one can ship in complete safety using the automated delivery system that entails 0 risk to ship or cargo - and again can be setup in 10-15 minute tops?
And that really, is all you can do.  Fight.  Trade. Craft.
Even with the most well thought placement of your outposts, getting to an enemy port to raid or try to seige takes a long period of real time - followed by that up to 90 minute fight - or multiple fights back to back.
Not only can most players not afford the IRL time sink, many others can't handle the long periods of inaction.
You can select Small or Large fleet battles in port and skip the sail out anf back.  This helps a little but the battle can still go on for 90 minutes.
I'm not sure what the devs can do to lessen the time drain.  The overall concept of the game is outstanding.  Battles, especially between groups of frigates are great fun.   But the average gamer is going to acknowledge the game's potetntial then move on to other games that offer more fast paced action.

After investing approximately 5-6 hours (in 1 sittingish) I know regret not engaging with this title sooner.  I did hear alot of great things about it but it was another 'steam game' on my end less of steam games.  However this weekend I finally took the oppertunity to play through this title.
I was certainly not disappointed.  To begin as the descriptions suggest it is 'Story Rich' a sizeable percentage of the game is story driven.  There's also an element of 'puzzle' solving which I'm surprised isn't listed as one of the tags.  Overall the tempo of the game I think is varied based on the 'puzzle' element (which you'll either blow through them or spend some time in contemplation).
The story telling component was certainly compelling, the characters reasonably likeable, and the light humor deters the  seriousness of the situtation just enough to not have it weigh you down.  As mention in other reviews this game is filled to the brim with feels and for some the cup of feels will runneth over on to the table cloth of feels turning it into a giant moist towelette of feels.  In addition to the story the soundtrack is simply suberb and there are several scene which which can easily be recollected simply by hearing the compositions.    On a final positive note I'm sucker for pixel graphics which this pulled be right in.
Critiques / Suggestions:
Though with any great games I think its well worth providing some feedback in what could have potentially been better.  Controller support was a bit lacking.  I found myself after 5 minutes of game playing switching straight to mouse clicking and it felt a great deal more comfortable.  Though to note I am using a PS3 controller with some conversion software so that could partly be the issue.
This one's exceptional minor but I wish the puzzle explanations were a bit more forth right.  The 'ideal' concept comes to mind and wish it was explained from the get go.  Its obviously intuitive what it means once you jump into the 1st puzzle but the concept isn't elaborated on until the 3rd puzzle...found that a bit odd.
There were some minor UI things that could possible be improved upon.  It would have been a bit more interesting if there were certain mechanics in the game that allowed the user to highlight them to get the simple text.  There's some scenarios I found where I just wanted to quickly reference something but couldn't recall from where and found myself like running around in circles to complain the task.
Even with these tiny things I definitely enjoyed the game and look forward to any future content Freebird Games put out.

Anyways, if you guys are looking for a great Open World 3rd Person Shooter with semi RPG elements then The Division is the game for you. 10/10 you will enjoy the game in singleplayer, and 100/10 you will enjoy it in multiplayer with friends.

Well, I've played some rally games, They all felt slow and not action packed, But WRC 4 Solves this, WRC 4 is filled with action packed tracks and first person which i love! I would play this game, So many cars, a bunch of different times in one day. I reccomend.

WRC4 is the official 2013 WRC game and was developed by Milestone games.
+ All official WRC, WRC2, WRC3, and WRC Junior 2013 drivers and cars.
+ All 13 official WRC 2013 countries, with 6 stages each.
+ Nice modern Rally car list.
+ Stages are varied and challenging enough. (they also feel narrow and dangerous, as rally should be)
+ Long and fun Career mode, you start at junior WRC and make your way to the WRC 3, WRC 2, and finally the main WRC.
+ OK graphics. (See the screenshots and videos)
+ OK Sounds.
+ Decent Arcady Handling physics. (Played with X360 controller)
- Less cars than previous games, the 70's 80's 90's and Group B cars present on previous games are missing, leaving us with only the modern WRC 2013 cars.
- Many stages share the same sections on each country, and some are just reversed stages that are treated as new.
- No weather variations (each country is fixed to its weather, like snowy, raining or dry).
- No night races.
- The Co-driver has some pacing and consistency issues sometimes.
- I wish the AI times were more varied, 99% of the times Loeb is the fastest AI driver, followed by Ogier or Latvala. that makes championships too predictable.
- The rewind feature is welcome, but not very well made, if you make a mistake you have to wait some kind of cooldown time, so if you crash, rewind, and crash in the same place, you will not be able to rewind again for a while, and this can be very frustrating for more casual players.
- Having to use a Launcher is annoying.
There are better rally games on the market, but overall this is a decent Rally game, more focused on the 'official' side of rallying, and I can recommend it if you are a fan of real-life WRC and can get a nice discount (75% off).

At first glance, this game might look like those abysmal simulator games that you find decorating the local GameStop's bargain bin and the Steam Greenlight page in equal measure. However, 911: First Responders couldn't be more different. What appears to be a mild-mannered and simple simulation is a surprisingly realistic and hair-pullingly tough game of skill and judgement that plays out more like an RTS than a traditional sim. Well-researched subject material, a lengthy and challenging campaign, and exquisite sound and music design go hand-in-hand to create this gem of a game that deserves far more recognition than first appearances might suggest.
In 911: First Responders, the player assumes the role of an emergency dispatcher in an unidentified, accident-prone urban sprawl somewhere in Europe - presumably the Netherlands, considering where developers Sixteen Tons Entertainment hail from. It's your sole duty to command and micro-manage emergency responders of all professions and roles, ranging from police marksmen to fire department marine divers to tow truck technicians. The mammoth campaign is comprised of twenty assignments that are broken up by short sessions of responding to low-level emergency calls inside the city, with each success granting the player some of the funds needed to buy vehicles and upgrades that are imperative for the next big assignment. Though they start out easy enough, these large-scale missions quickly become damningly hard and will push even experienced RTS players to their multi-tasking, micro-managing limits. A very wide range of emergency situations and responses are represented in loving detail, giving the game just enough complexity to be engaging without being overwhelming to people who aren't educated in emergency service operations - despite the plethora of vehicles and personnel on hand, most of the tools the player is given have an obvious and easily comprehensible application. The open-ended nature of each assignment is also something to be noted and applauded - though some missions may have clear solutions, others require creative use of the tools at your disposal in order to save  as many lives as possible.
Of course, fun as it is, the game isn't flawless. The eight-year-old graphics can't help but show their age upon close examination (though they aren't 'bad' by any means), and the pathfinding of the game's larger vehicles can become problematic in enclosed areas - which feature heavily in some assignments, occasionally resulting in Tetris-like scenes in which the player must manually guide their confused emergency vehicles out of a tight spot in order to release an urgently-needed automotive at the bottom of the metaphorical heap. The game also has a nasty habit of giving the player new tools or personnel without giving much notification, which wouldn't be so bad if those new tools and personnel didn't tend to play very critical roles in the mission in which you're given them. One notable example is the fifth assignment, in which the player must clean up after a road bridge collapse - a task in which the fire brigade's marine divers are essential for locating sunken cars in the river below. The game, of course, doesn't tell you that it's given you these divers, so they're easy to miss when you're loading up a fire engine to send onto the map.
These flaws, however, pale greatly against the immense fun that I've been having with this game so far. The surprisingly steep challenges that it offers seriously surprised me as I progressed further into the campaign, and part of what motivates me to overcome every nail-bitingly tense challenge and assignment is my curiosity over what the next assignment will hold.  At the asking price of £3.99, this game is an absolute steal for its quality and a must for strategy fans and anyone who's enthusiastic about the work of the emergency services. Definitely get this game.

Combining a rather unique Japanese inspired aesthetic with a familiar genre of metroidvania and fast paced mobility based gameplay, Ori and the blind forest creates a very rare game, the one you simply have to experience.
Ori and the blind forest tells a touching story of an orphaned tree spirit given a bigger purpose in restoring the dying forest back to life. Using the hero's journey template and a couple of nice additions of their own, Moon studios manage to deliver a deeply touching story while also resolving all the presented conflicts and ending the game with a very satisfying conclusion.
The game looks stunning, every level presents a unique theme and pallet which keeps the game fresh. Animation quality for Ori is incredible, i absolutely love the twirl when you jump of a wall and front flip after a running jump. Graphics quality is very high and the game uses the engine to it's fullest. However on the technical side there are reports of slowdown and frame rate issues, despite that i was able to run Ori on my lover end laptop with 60 fps on a lover resolution so the problems should be fixable by just tinkering with the settings.
Music and sound design create the needed atmosphere in every level. Music tracks fit their respective areas really well and at certain points help deliver the story. One of my personal favorites is ginso tree track with a looped raising bass line reflecting the climb to the treetop as well as first major challenge Ori faces.
The sound and feeling of dread Kuro creates is a testament to how you can make an antagonist really scary purely with sound, and a couple really good camera angles, seriously Kuro, get out of my face, you're really scary.
Gameplay is fast paced and centered around Ori's very swift and agile movements. As you unlock new moves the skill ceiling just keeps going higher and higher allowing crazier and crazier movements and certain parts of the game can be beaten without ever touching the ground.
Boss fights are swapped for "escape sequences" - tightly timed puzzles that require you to use your mobility to the limit. Ori is not an easy game, but i never got frustrated because the game controls really well and lets you save at almost any point so it's really hard to justify blaming the game or even just getting frustrated.
There is of course a metroidvania part, with a big map and lots and lots of secrets hidden all over the place, searching for hidden places and fake walls is as fun as traversing the levels since most secrets will have some sort of a movement puzzle leading to them. You also won't need to backtrack as much since game gives you quite a lot of shortcuts you can open to just breeze through the levels.
You can have all the mobility in the world but if level design is lacking it will be meaningless. First levels of the game have to be more simplistic since Ori has less movement options but it will make backtracking through those levels kinda boring. Luckily Moon studios found an elegant solution. As the game progresses and Ori unlocks new moves the forest changes opening new movement options in the older levels.
I've been praising this game for quite some time, but it doesn't mean there is no room for improvement.
The game is really short, while it's completely justified by the game's budget and price tag ultimately i really wish there was more of it.
Music can be a little bland at times. Level design is great overall but certain levels are worse than the others and can be improved upon.
Escape sequences are amazing and i feel there should've been at least one more in the very end.
But all of this are minor complaints that take almost nothing from the overall quality of the game.
I really want a sequel for this game. You may wonder why? The gameplay is just THAT good, i feel we need more of the cool escape parts, more flying through the levels using all the sick moves, more hide from Kuro, And i believe, that with bigger budget and more time on their hands, Moon studios can deliver even better Ori game. We NEED more of this.
Oh, and if you need a score - 98/100.

Overall a satisfactory title, but apart from the absolutely amazing art design and beautiful soundtrack it leaves much to be desired. The gameplay, while extremely fluid, is relatively simple and becomes increasingly predictable after obtaining the dash ability. The metroidvania elements are weak, with exploration rewarding health (which is made increasingly redudant as more and more ways to die instantly are introduces), energy (equally redundant, you'll have more than enough for a save point before and after every minor segment) or ability points (for the RPG elements; I imagine most players will aim firstly for the triple jump and ignore the other trees). The world lacks any sort of interconnection, and it's a chore to make way from one side of the expansive (for better or worse) map to the other. The story shoots itself in the foot fairly hard around the end, which dissolved what remained of my interest in it after the basic premise of "collect the three plot devices".
Still, credit where credit is due. It's an absolutely gorgeous game, graphically. It's just the right length for its content. The difficulty curves perfectly, peaking at a comfortable if punishing level of challenge that makes the later areas rather satisfying to complete. I'm also extremely impressed with how the "cinematic" sections were handled, they were ultimately some of the hardest parts of the game and served as both intense and tasking. It doesn't do anything outright poorly, there's just a lot of things that it doesn't do too well.
Worth playing, and worth the time it will take to finish. At the current price I'd advise waiting on a sale, though.

It's a good game for those who enjoy participating in grand battles but aren't necessarily into the base-building aspects in real time as well, since the grander campaign is turn-based. How to create a new Fallout 3 dungeon
1) Write a note that defines the storyline of the new dungeon in story terms
2) Select a standard building that will contain the dungeon (generic vault, office …)
3) Decorate the dungeon with appropriate props and junk
4) Cut and paste the same monster over and over
5) Add just enough loot to keep the player from quitting the game
6) Post the design note at the bottom of the dungeon as a computer file or tape recording
Repeat the following steps fifty times to create the foundation of your own Fallout game
There is merit to this game, it's just buried under a ton of post apocalyptic dungeon crawling. If your idea of a fun game is digging through your septic tank and drainage field to find your lost diamond wedding ring, then this game is for you

The squeeze and I were looking for something to play together when we watched Jesse Cox, Dodger, Crendor, and Sam tackle Divinity II on a Twitch stream. We were instantly hooked. It took us no time to burn through the first chapter of the early release, so we returned to the games origin here with Original Sin. The turn based combat, the beautiful AOE and CC effects, the salty/sassy in party banter, engaging game story, down to the rediculous ambient enemy chatter made it an absolutely amazing experience. We logged just over 60 hours completing the game (though not without missing a few quests by enraging and murdering people... ♥♥♥♥ you, Lawerence).
Dozens of saves, standing just before boss fights and strategizing over how to best position ourselves, bickering over plot points (I ended up guessing the mysteries of how the end of the world got started, but I'm a writer myself, and the developers made all the same decisions I would have story wise <3), and fretting over talent choices reminded us both of times when we were younger, ploughing through DnD campaigns, MUDDS, Baldurs Gate and so on.
I cannot recommend this game highly enough. It was lovingly crafted by people who love this genre as much as its fans, and worth every penny. It's fun solo, but even better with a friend. The both of us can't WAIT for the release of Divinity II, and you can bet we'll bring more friends next time. <3 :D

The concept of Scribblenauts is fantastic, and the graphics are awesome, but this game is really let down by how unbelievably easy the "puzzles" are. And yes, being creative is half the fun, but if puzzles are as easy as "oh no a pipe is leaking we need something to catch the water", or "my dog is hungry" then the novelty of something as strange as a pipe leaking into a swimming pool, or dogs eating enormous waffles wears off really quickly. What's more, an alarming number of the problems can literally be solved just by typing the word "gone", which takes another level of fun out of it.
Everything else about this game is great, and I think it'd be fantastic for teaching kids about spelling and problem solving, but how unbelievably easy it is just ruins it completely for me. A few harder puzzles here and there, even if they were optional, would make this game infinitely more fun.

After being forced to kill what amounted to a severely mentally challenged man-child, complete with extremely uncomfortable whaling for his mother, I stopped playing this game and played a few other games to completion. The entire situation left me feeling odd and a little sad and not at all heroic. And I'm a combat veteran. It was one of the most uncomfortable moments I'ver ever had in a game and I've been gaming since the 70's. Since I already had well over 100 hours into the game by that point and I knew the end was coming up I forced myself to complete the main story. The only thing I could really recommend about this game is that it's "turn based" and I enjoy turn based RPG's. And the story is sort of interesting even if the execution and terrible attempts at humor are lacking. Otherwise everything else seems to miss the mark.
A lot of times, especially near the end, I found myself watching the game play itself as enemies and NPC's with twice as many action points as me made their moves. And the crafting is tedious, unituitive and sort of pointless aside from a handful of armor and weapon upgrades. Seriously, who will actually wear a the "barrel with rope suspender" armor? Just because you can make a couple hundred useless items, food and potions doesn't necessarily make a crafting system "deep". But my biggest complaint is the obtuseness of almost everything. "This game doesn't hold your hand" is code for "better get used to using alt+tab and Google to figure out this puzzle that has absolutely no ingame reference point aside from spending countless hours on 'trial and error' in order to figure it out". This is pretty much the whole game: find a two page book (among literally hundreds of books that all look the same) that vaguely (and I do mean VAGUELY) mentions a trap you'll encounter several hours later, stumble upon said trap barely remembering that you read something about the trap somewhwere, search through your unwieldly inventory for the correct book only to not find it (or maybe you do but it won't really matter because...), then realize that the book is way to vauge on explanation, spend an hour trying to figure out how to get past the puzzle and then say "screw it, I got work tomorrow" and look on Google. Of course that's for about 75% of the puzzles because the other 25% is nothing more than "use the teleporting pyramids".
Some of the other things that bothered me, in no particular order is as follows: character developemen is boring and confusing. Everything sounds cool and useful until you realize that most of the non-combat skills aren't really needed and can be worked around pretty easily and the game pretty much will be played by the typical "tank, heals, ranged-dps/mage" party RPG enthusiasts have come to know so well. And one of the biggest problems I had was that there was no way to trigger combat manually. I've played tons of games like this andthis is the first one I can remember playine where I there wasn't some way for me to enter combat mode so I can set up an ambush.
I'd recommend this game to die-hard RPG fans like myself but anyone else should pass or at the very least wait for a sale and do plenty of research on which sites and Google phrases will be the most useful to get past a puzzle. Usually you can just type "Divinity (level/dungeon/mission name) and instantly come up with a solution because you aren't the only person to have trouble understanding why your character is suffereing frrom "insta-death" when he steps on that blue floor. Heck, you won't even be the thousandth person to wonder that.

Downwell is essentially a hybrid of a reverse-shmup and platformer. Shooting is also just as much about stalling your descent as it is about taking out the baddies.
This is a game that takes some time before the gameplay feels fluid. During that time though, you will be rapidly unlocking both palettes and styles, the latter actually affecting gameplay. When your "floaty" style is unlocked (slows your descent), is likely the same time you'll feel comfortable with pulling off combos. Combos are risk/reward-based, as keeping one alive can often be dangerous, but will yield substantial benefits depending on what you manage to pull off.
This combo system is what really makes the game for me.
Also, my eyes are much more keen on reading what is going on with older (80s/early 90s) shmups and platformers, where explosions, debris, and other effects didn't hinder my vision too much. Once you're eyes adjust to Downwell's palette, it's very easy to tell what's what and play effectively.
Play control is perfect.

I usually put on a NES music playlist or a retro game soundtrack, depending on my mood. Believe it or not, doing this really helps me in this game; it sort of gets me in the zone in a way that the stock music doesn’t.
20 hours in, I can’t recommend this game highly enough, even to those not sure they’d like a game like this. Most retro-revival games are thoroughly lacking. As simple as this game is, at least on the surface, it is, dare I say, one of the deepest retro-ish games I’ve played on PC to date.

In 911 First Responders you take control of emergency forces in their mission to help people in need. A challenging Singleplayer Campaign will see you rescue hostages, extinguish forest fires, deliver humanitarian aid in a 3rd world country and even fight chemical disasters. The games engine is outdated by now and pathfinding of units is sluggish at best but it's still pleasing to look at your units rushing down the roads flashing their sirens. You will be able to take control of the Police, Fire Brigade, Medical Services and even technical help centres that can tow vehicles, use cranes to get crashed vehicles out of rivers, SAR Helicopters, Technicians to fix broken traffic lights and railroad crossings and much more. The game still has a very active modding community. Truly the best aspect of the game however is it's multiplayer with its challenge and endless mode. You can team up with 3 other people to take control of a city's emergency forces and help prevent disaster... and you'll know disaster when a riot starts or a chemical plant catches on fire, you'll need good co-ordination of all forces to make it through.
A great multiplayer, an alive modding community and very fun gameplay make up for the small bugs you can encounter here and there. It's cheap and it's fun. If you always wanted to see how well you can manage emergency forces (by yourself or with 3 friends!), give it a go! 4.5/5

This idea has a LOT of potential, and for an early access game it's polished enough to have fun with. However, most of the fun comes from terra-forming (some of the best tools to do so since Magic Carpet), as trying to build your own structures is going to be a lesson in tedious camera correcting and axis monitoring. Once these things are practiced though it starts to become second nature, and most of the problems with the game (damn camera) can be easily fixed in time.
Something I am nervous of is if there will be microtransactions. Right now all unlocks are bought with in game coins (found buy interacting and destroying things just like in the other Lego games) but the menus hint at a purchase setup for complete build sets especially. Though a really nice one is included already, I can easily see Lego charging arm and leg for more (after all this game has real potential to cut into sales of their physical sets).
It's pretty amazing that the entire world, sans sky and water, is completely made up of Lego bricks. It is mighty impressive that destruction or addition of pieces is easily handled by the game's engine, but the framerate can often stutter as distant terrain and objects load in. It's not enough to ruin the experience but it's always noticeable.
Here are some cool tips for a newbie:
- Use the bulldozer vehicle to clear large swaths of land for flat building. Keep in mind that vehicle controls are view-relative, so always keep the camera behind the player when steering. You can also use the delete function but that doesn't work too well for removing generated terrain. Bulldozer is also good for setting up terrain for roads for the car.
- Use a certain flying creature's attack to create natural looking caverns and valleys.
- Infinite cash flow can be had by interacting with the light post object in the house set, over and over again.
- Don't touch the orange glowy stuff. However feel free to place the glowy stuff by painting with the bright orange texture (only found in main paint menu, not block painting).
- When trying to build up in a vertical line, restrict to Z and X axis / When building lines horizontally, just use the view-relative axis control. Hold Shift before placing down a block and then drag to create a line.
- When matching heights of several blocks using the line feature, listen for the "click" sound that accompanies a correctly placed piece.
- Utilize switching between Overlap and Non-overlap modes. It can really save you a headache when editing small mistakes or gaps in the structure as you probably won't have to find the exact piece that will fit.
- Avoid using copy/paste because it's kinda screwey how it currently selects things and its camera is even scewier. The camera is not coded the same way as the other building modes.
- Bears are easier to control than horses, and faster at climbing hills too.
- If you get stuck, scroll to Options in the main menu and activate sky-dive

Overall a satisfactory title, but apart from the absolutely amazing art design and beautiful soundtrack it leaves much to be desired. The gameplay, while extremely fluid, is relatively simple and becomes increasingly predictable after obtaining the dash ability. The metroidvania elements are weak, with exploration rewarding health (which is made increasingly redudant as more and more ways to die instantly are introduces), energy (equally redundant, you'll have more than enough for a save point before and after every minor segment) or ability points (for the RPG elements; I imagine most players will aim firstly for the triple jump and ignore the other trees). The world lacks any sort of interconnection, and it's a chore to make way from one side of the expansive (for better or worse) map to the other. The story shoots itself in the foot fairly hard around the end, which dissolved what remained of my interest in it after the basic premise of "collect the three plot devices".
Still, credit where credit is due. It's an absolutely gorgeous game, graphically. It's just the right length for its content. The difficulty curves perfectly, peaking at a comfortable if punishing level of challenge that makes the later areas rather satisfying to complete. I'm also extremely impressed with how the "cinematic" sections were handled, they were ultimately some of the hardest parts of the game and served as both intense and tasking. It doesn't do anything outright poorly, there's just a lot of things that it doesn't do too well.
Worth playing, and worth the time it will take to finish. At the current price I'd advise waiting on a sale, though.

This deceptively simple arcade-style game is simply one of the best action/platform games I've played in years. The action is furious and constant, and there's almost always something happening: an enemy to avoid (or stomp on), a secret cave to head towards, an obstacle to work around or blast through. Whenever there *is* any breathing room, like when you duck into a cave for a power-up, visit the shop, or choose your upgrade between levels, you get a welcome sense of momentary calm before you jump back out into the pit of blobs, bats, ghosts, and weird monsters. The pacing is just spot-on; every level is the perfect length, so Downwell never wears out its welcome for a second. In addition, each level is procedurally created in a rogue-like kind of style, so there's a lot of variety and every run is a bit different. This makes the whole experience into something that is really addictive and rewarding. You can even unlock different playstyles, which allows you to personalize your play and try out different tricks and strategies.
I honestly can't think of a single real criticism of this game. The graphics are simple but very expressive and memorable (love the Shopkeeper). The game is hard but fair...whenever you die, you know that you made a mistake in the heat of play and you either stomped on an enemy that you shouldn't have or took a breather on a platform when you really should have kept going. I do have to admit that I really hate the bats, those things have a way of finding you and flying right over head just as you bounce off of something. Remember: *around bats, watch your backs.* The game is tough enough that it's going to take me a good while to beat it, but I don't think that this is the sort of game that you play through, beat, and then put away. It's something that I want to come back to over the years, getting a bit better each time by learning the best strategies and how to properly react to certain situations.
If you like action games, arcade games, SHUMPs, platformers, or rogue-likes, you should absolutely get this game. It's without a doubt the best 3 bucks you'll spend on Steam. It shouldn't even be legal for a 3 dollar game to be this good.

HOWEVER, even with all this polish and how good I think the game is, I now have a personal problem with how the health works. In a recent patch, the health system is similar to that of Killer Instinct's(2013 version on XBone). When someone dies in a 1v1 fight, their health DOES NOT reset to full, giving the other person a clear advantage, as they will be reset to full for the next round. This system, in my honest opinion, is ♥♥♥♥ING. TERRIBLE. This applies to everything; story, arcade, and Online play. If you were thinking of buying this game to play online, then I would recommend you stay away from it and get a different fighting game, like Street Fighter x Tekken or something. The online community is filled with people that infinitecombo and isn't very friendly to beginners, even with Lobby play.

I'll cut to the chase: go buy Skullgirls right now. It's incredibly fun and you'd be hard pressed to find a better value for your gaming dollar. The sheer amount stylishness, polished gameplay, and raw originality on display here is truly remarkable.
I've always enjoyed fighting games, but I'm not an expert by any means. I like to learn as many special moves and combos as I can, but my actual "strategy" usually ends up being semi-coherent button mashing. I own Street Fighter IV and Mortal Kombat and have had a lot of fun with both. Skullgirls is similar in many ways to its big-budget cousins, but it's also very much its own game. The neo-Art Deco art style is very well done and the characters are designed and animated to perfection. It's an absolute joy to watch classic Warner Bros.-style cartoon chaos unfold as cars race across the screen, heads roll, and giant balls of twine wreak havoc on your character. The voice acting is limited, but suits the mood of the game to a T, as does the 1920s-era jazz soundtrack.
I do have a few tiny nitpicks. I would like to see a few more characters, a little bit more voice work, more graphics options, and maybe some polishing done on a few of the stage backgrounds. Honestly though, I get why there are a couple of minor weaknesses like this. Clearly the developers spent a huge amount of time and money perfecting the core gameplay, and as a result they've come up with something really special. If a few secondary things fell through cracks or got pushed back then that's totally reasonable. It just makes me look forward all the more to future patches/DLC and (hopefully) Skullgirls 2!

A friend of mine and me started looking for a good co-op game to play together when we stumbled upon this game. I had my doubts of the game as I'm not much of a guy for these classical type of rpg games, but boy did I get amazed how entertaining this game is especially if you play it with a friend.
You start the game by creating two heroes (
) and you can customize their looks, stats and what kind of spells they have. There is enough of variety on the spells so you mix things up to make some different paths for your hero. For example my buddy made a knight that is more of mage than a knight.
In the begining of the game, you get guidance how to play the game which is necessary if you are new to these kind of games. There is little of fighting in the beginning and more of exploring the world and getting to know the world so you can live up to it. The humour in the game is good and the dialogues you get between the two heroes is a lot more fun when playing with a friend. You just might find yourself beating the life out of a innocent dog if you start arguing with your friend about digging up graves.
The turn-based battles are somewhat challenging in the classic mode but you get more difficulty to it if you take the tactician mode. Once you get out of the first town (which took awhile because we had to explore every corner... Born explorers that we are) you get a lot of more battles which is great because the battle system is superb and there is a lot of different things to consider when you are fighting. The environment, enemies, resistances, type of damage etc. You can actually make things a lot of worse if you dont pay attention if there is water on the ground for example.
Exploring is a big part of the game as you get most of the quests by speaking to someone or something. And there is a lot to explore as the world is large and there is a lot of books laying around and stuff. Thankfully there is a teleport system in the game so you don't have walk from area to area, but be aware that there is still a lot of running to places.
My advice is that when you start the game make sure you have the ability to speak to animals. Yes you read it right, you can speak to all kinds of animals in this game such as hens, pigs and a lot more.
I don't know how long the game is as I haven't played it through yet but with 30hrs of total playtime I would dare to say that it is worth of your money. You may play the game a bit faster if you play it solo but the game is much better with the kind of friend that likes rpgs too.
So as the summary for this review I would like to say that you definitely want to play this game if you are atleast somewhat interested of rpg games. Talk to a friend of yours and try to talk him/her to get the game also and enjoy your time in the world of Divinity: Original Sin! And I hope you don't have to kill as much of innocent people in the game as I have had. That savage knight..

This is my introduction to the Emergency series, and I am blown away! It's such a simple concept- respond to various situations and instruct your crew to save lives. And yet, it's nearly impossible to master. I will send an ambulance to a seemingly ordinary cardiac arrest call, but in minutes, the whole block could be up in flames because a bomb went off!
There is a wide array of emergency vehicles to dispatch, and each have their own advantages. It's up to you to learn them. It can definately be challenging and frustrating at times (I once had a riot that had over 50 causalties to attend to), but it's a fun game with many hours of replayability. The campaign mode is fun and immersive (while challenging).
Yes, the game does have a few flaws. Occasionally, you may experience a crash. Other times, the graphic interface may flicker. There is definitely room to improve on, which is why I can't wait to buy the newest of the series.
It is worth the $5- I have personally invested 12 hours as of this review, and won't be quitting soon.

1. Best Age of Sail combat simulation there is.

3. Play as Pirates, USA, Great Britain, French, Spanish etc.
4. The map is huge centering around the Gulf of Mexico, Bahamas and the Caribbean Sea and travelling across the map would take hours. Each of the 100+ port is conquerable.
5. Graphics are great. Sea and weather looks realistic and ships look detailed and authentic.
6. Wind condition plays important part in sailing, so are ship sailing profiles.
7. A large selection of ships, ranging from tiny cutters, to small brigs, to midsize frigates, and to large ships of the line, including the HMS Surprise, HMS Victory, and USS Constitution.
8. Trading & ship-crafting is also important in this game.
9. Some ships are only craftable by players, such as the trader ship Indiaman and other high grade ships.
10. A large selection of armaments, ranging from tiny 4 pd cannons to 308 pd mortars.
11. Combat, albeit slow paced, is very realistic and deliberate, down to the very details of boarding.
12. The game is early access but very playable, though the UI is a bit rough.
13. The game community is very helpful and active, and does regular port battles in large 10+ ship fleets.
14. The game is constantly improving and even if a bit expensive is worth the price for something so special.

Naval Action is the best you're going to get if you're going for a historic naval game.
Many people complain about the grind that is Naval Action, but this is for the best, It's a simulator and sailing will take long, battles will take long, because that's just the way it was back then.
This game does not take the casual approach many game developers take these days, It's not made for you just to shoot some ships and quit after a week. Sailing around the caribbean is not danger free, you will get attacked if you do not pay attention, and you will lose your ship. Other way around, you can take ships.
(On the other side of the grind, If you own a decent ship, getting money is as easy as taking candy from a baby.)
Many people complain about the developers because they don't "listen" to the community, this might be true on some occasions, but to say they don't listen is complete b*llsh*t. Just take a quick look on the game-labs forums, everything the developers do is based on player opinions, they players even vote for which ship gets added to the game next.
This game is everything the 18th century caribbean had to offer, beauty, danger and hours of sailing. If you are looking for a historic naval game that's not a casual, easy peasy point and click shooter, Naval Action is for you.

When it comes to post apocalyptic, this is the game series you want. I personally prefer this game over the others in the series for its Patriotic themes & therefore epic storyline. The crafting, combat, and dialogue systems may not be the most finessed, but they are still well executed especially with the Fallout unique, V.A.T.S. combat system (slowing down & spefically aiming at body parts of your enemies in limited intervals.
Set in a post apocalyptic version of the Washington D.C. - wrought with nuclear destruction. This is a rich world stuck in the 1950's golden age of America - a futuristic past if you will. You most make your way along the wastes salvaging supplies & fighting tooth and nail for survival and toward your chosen goal. You will encounter various factions you can join at your leisure, and build your character in various ways to suit your playstyle. This also applies to the moral allignment of your Vault Dweller, you may be the paragon or the ultimate villain of your own world. There is no skimping on content here - not only a rich main storyline, but of course extensive side questing available to those interested and even some lovely DLC packs. You may also have a traveling companion of your choosing - A dog, a Ghoulish Zombie-like mercenary, Human Merc, a member of the Power Armor wearing Brotherhood of Steel, or even a bright yellow Super Mutant, etc.
The enemies vary from irradiated Ghouls, Super Mutants and giant Behemoths, to Raiders, Mercenaries & Power-Armored Boy Scouts - Not to mention the giant firebreathing ants, mole rats, and the dreaded Death Claws. A refreshing bestiary especially in reguards to the zombies not being of a viral origin like so many other games dragging the over used concept through the modern mud.
The story is that of a Vault Dweller ascending into the real world from a secluded / nuclear protected population who, (depending on your playstyle) destined to save the wasteland from itself and to fight for America the Beautiful itself, or to become the Bloody King of all Raiders - spreading misery and tyranny through the wasteland with the terror of his extended weapon collection. Or...somewhere in between! As you leave the safety of Vault 101 you are searching for your Father, (voiced by Liam Neeson) who has "Taken" it upon himself to embark on his own quest to help save the wasteland.
Your President, John Henry Eden (voiced by Malcolm McDowell) elegantly explains to you throughout your journey over the Enclave Radio Station, through your Pip Boy 3000 the current state of the country, its capitol and the questions that have arisen over his presidental office - enforced by Enclave Soldiers - Power Armor clad guards hell bent on strict adhearance to any and all laws of the current administration.
You even have the option to build yourself a home wherever you see fit in this vast world - and there are even a few actual choices of property to purchase or earn depending on how your individual story unfolds.
This is likely one of the best RPGs ever to be made - despite it's aged graphics, slightly clunky gameplay at times - this title is not to be missed by gamers of many types!!

Reviewing this is kind of tricky, because the real focus here is on the story of the game, and the gameplay is sort of a second thought. Thankfully, the story they made in To The Moon is good. Damn good. Great. Yeah, so maybe I cried a bit, what's that to you? So yeah, it is a very feel-filled story, and may make you cry too. Thankfully, it's not all tears, as the dialogue between the two lead characters is very funny and believable, which is something I applaud the writers for.
Unfortunately, the gameplay is... Well, a little lackluster. It's based on simply clicking around to explore the world, with the occasional puzzle to solve (which I thought were pretty easy, but that's up to interpretation). But hey, if you like clicky-eplorey-puzzly games, then you may still get a kick out of it. I assume the gameplay was put on the easier side of things so players would be able to breeze through the game in order to get to the next part of the story, rather than being stuck in the middle of the narrative during a particularly difficult puzzle.
Now, since they wanted to convey a good story, and they definitely succeeded, I'd say that this is undeniably worth your money. The main draw comes from whether or not you're willing to sacrifice a bit of gameplay for that good story, which, frankly, I think you should be, because the story really is that good (And hey, the game lasts only about 4 hours tops, so if you hate the lack of gameplay, but like the story, then you don't have a marathon of a game to plow through, haha). Give this game a shot!
(Oh yeah, and get the soundtrack! It's technically simple, but very well-made and compliments the game perfectly. Give it some love too)

I'll cut to the chase: go buy Skullgirls right now. It's incredibly fun and you'd be hard pressed to find a better value for your gaming dollar. The sheer amount stylishness, polished gameplay, and raw originality on display here is truly remarkable.
I've always enjoyed fighting games, but I'm not an expert by any means. I like to learn as many special moves and combos as I can, but my actual "strategy" usually ends up being semi-coherent button mashing. I own Street Fighter IV and Mortal Kombat and have had a lot of fun with both. Skullgirls is similar in many ways to its big-budget cousins, but it's also very much its own game. The neo-Art Deco art style is very well done and the characters are designed and animated to perfection. It's an absolute joy to watch classic Warner Bros.-style cartoon chaos unfold as cars race across the screen, heads roll, and giant balls of twine wreak havoc on your character. The voice acting is limited, but suits the mood of the game to a T, as does the 1920s-era jazz soundtrack.
I do have a few tiny nitpicks. I would like to see a few more characters, a little bit more voice work, more graphics options, and maybe some polishing done on a few of the stage backgrounds. Honestly though, I get why there are a couple of minor weaknesses like this. Clearly the developers spent a huge amount of time and money perfecting the core gameplay, and as a result they've come up with something really special. If a few secondary things fell through cracks or got pushed back then that's totally reasonable. It just makes me look forward all the more to future patches/DLC and (hopefully) Skullgirls 2!

Currently in an
, Kitten Rampage is a kitten simulator reminiscent of a similar game of the goat variety that offers destruction at an epileptic level with an aside to scatological (toilet) humor.
It is important to understand that this game may induce epileptic seizures. The warning is hidden in the extended “About This Game” section in the Store page and the game fails to emphasize this upon launching. Kitten Rampage utilizes strobing lights upon shooting (which is almost always consistently activated), and the explosions present variations of intense particle effects.
Kitten Rampage offers 4 main game modes: Time Trial, Free Roam, Expert, and Survival. Each mode contains a set of objectives that must be completed in order to clear the level. Some of these objectives may be achieving a certain score, killing a number of enemies or reaching a location. Throughout the game, there is also a hunger, thirst and health meter that “needs” to be maintained. The objectives are attained with the help of two shooting weapons that can fire simultaneously and indefinitely. Grenades can also be “puked” out for higher firepower. There are only 12 achievements in this game and most of them can be attained in half an hour.
The maps and levels in Kitten Rampage are pretty generic, utilizing ordinary objects and locales. Often times, there is a lot of empty space making traversal a bit of a chore. Also, the sprint button cannot be toggled, a much needed quality of life improvement, making most of the gameplay uncomfortable from constant pinky usage.
Some of the objectives, such as killing X enemies, get extremely tedious due to the level design. Some rooms seem hidden, and many buildings blend into the background making these enemies annoying to track down. Having to redo levels due to the inability to discover the last couple enemies is extremely frustrating. A time bonus mechanic upon killing an enemy would help remedy this.
The graphics and aesthetics for Kitten Rampage are really poor. Stock assets were used, and the objects seem too two-dimensional. Upon closer observation, most of the repeated patterns that the assets utilize are either color gradients or basic low quality textures (no shading/light variation). There aren’t any thematic colors or styles used to decorate the levels either. The kitten can, however, be personalized to an extent (fur/eye color).
The physics engine is also very weak in this game. Clipping occurs everywhere, collision detection makes no sense and object disintegration are too similar which each other. Everything seems to be made up of flat panels or boxes, as observed upon destruction. Portions of the level can cause the kitten to clip so badly that it will get permanently stuck.
Although the game has not been released for long, the patches seemed to have waned from launch. For a developing game in Early Access (especially one that is in its alpha stages), it is crucial to be transparent with future content. The developer(s) do seem to take part in the Steam Discussions board; however, there hasn't been any updates for quite some time. Currently, there seems to be no one playing Kitten Rampage, according to Steam's community statistics. With such a strong similarity to another certain animal simulator, and having the same price, it will be very difficult to grow the player base without a lot more content/refinements added.
It is imperative for any simulator to have a strong physics engine and intriguing maps along with an ample amount of varied goals/objectives/achievements to add longevity to the game and improve re-playability. This game has neither, making it very difficult to find an audience that can manage to overlook the frustrating bugs and tedious nature of the gameplay in order to enjoy Kitten Rampage.
