This is a great game, albeit with a few significant problems.
The Gameplay is the best part of it, where you have to simultaneously deploy and manage multiple response units including firemen/firetrucks, Ambulances/Paramedics, Police, Negotiators, Salvage vehicles etc.
You start in a suburban area where you respond to numerous events. The game quickly manages to scale up and has you managing multiple units at the same time, in different areas of the city, all earning you money to purchase new equipment. When you have the required equipment it unlocks a "mission" that takes you into a separate "mission map" and you get a more complex mission. When you complete the mission it takes you back to the suburban area again, to manage more random events until you have purchased the required hardware for the next mission.
This gameplay is quite fun, and even though it is the same incidents, the map is quite large and always has you thinking on "where is the nearest hydrant?", "what resources do i need for that?" or "where is that criminal running?" so each incident is still quite unique.
Now, the "significant problems" I mentioned earlier (from least significant to most significant)
Firstly: Audio is ok. It repeats a lot of things a lot of times and has some interesting things (like every vehicle you click on sounds the "ambulance sirens", even if you click on a car on the side of the road)
Secondly: Graphics are ok. It doesn't have any options above 1024x1280 and on a full HD display it is somewhat grainy, but I don't think this significantly detracts from the game
Thirdly: When doing the more complex "Mission scenario" I still haven't found a way to restart it without quitting to windows. So when you make a big stuff-up and all your firemen are dying with a wall of fire between them and the paramedics, you actually have to deal with the situation... or you quit to desktop and start the game again
Next: Each individual will not really do anything unless you have told them to. ie: A fireman will watch a fire burn, unless you have told him to equip an extinguishing device (hose or extinguisher) and is within range. If a fire moves out of range, he won't follow it. Same goes for Paramedics and Police. I'd love to see a little bit of automation, such as: tell the fire-truck to "CONTAIN" the fire and they setup automatically to stop the fire spreading, or tell the paramedics to "TREAT" the casualty, and when he is ready for transport they should automatically load him into the ambulance and take him away.
Oh, and firement shouldn't stand in one fire when trying to fight another fire... yeah this can happen.
Lastly: Traffic routing. If you order ten ambulances (yes, i made a few mistakes fighting a fire once) and tell them where to go, after the first two arrive, then the others keep driving around in circles because they can't get to the spot where the first two ambulances parked. Sometimes they'll drive around a building on fire and blow up because they are trying to get to that exact spot.
And sometimes they get "jammed" because they drove too close to a pedestrian and then you have to manually "unjam" them so they can drive again. (not too common)
But, all in all, a good, enjoyable game, just be warned that some things are frustrating

Reviewing this is kind of tricky, because the real focus here is on the story of the game, and the gameplay is sort of a second thought. Thankfully, the story they made in To The Moon is good. Damn good. Great. Yeah, so maybe I cried a bit, what's that to you? So yeah, it is a very feel-filled story, and may make you cry too. Thankfully, it's not all tears, as the dialogue between the two lead characters is very funny and believable, which is something I applaud the writers for.
Unfortunately, the gameplay is... Well, a little lackluster. It's based on simply clicking around to explore the world, with the occasional puzzle to solve (which I thought were pretty easy, but that's up to interpretation). But hey, if you like clicky-eplorey-puzzly games, then you may still get a kick out of it. I assume the gameplay was put on the easier side of things so players would be able to breeze through the game in order to get to the next part of the story, rather than being stuck in the middle of the narrative during a particularly difficult puzzle.
Now, since they wanted to convey a good story, and they definitely succeeded, I'd say that this is undeniably worth your money. The main draw comes from whether or not you're willing to sacrifice a bit of gameplay for that good story, which, frankly, I think you should be, because the story really is that good (And hey, the game lasts only about 4 hours tops, so if you hate the lack of gameplay, but like the story, then you don't have a marathon of a game to plow through, haha). Give this game a shot!
(Oh yeah, and get the soundtrack! It's technically simple, but very well-made and compliments the game perfectly. Give it some love too)

When it comes to post apocalyptic, this is the game series you want. I personally prefer this game over the others in the series for its Patriotic themes & therefore epic storyline. The crafting, combat, and dialogue systems may not be the most finessed, but they are still well executed especially with the Fallout unique, V.A.T.S. combat system (slowing down & spefically aiming at body parts of your enemies in limited intervals.
Set in a post apocalyptic version of the Washington D.C. - wrought with nuclear destruction. This is a rich world stuck in the 1950's golden age of America - a futuristic past if you will. You most make your way along the wastes salvaging supplies & fighting tooth and nail for survival and toward your chosen goal. You will encounter various factions you can join at your leisure, and build your character in various ways to suit your playstyle. This also applies to the moral allignment of your Vault Dweller, you may be the paragon or the ultimate villain of your own world. There is no skimping on content here - not only a rich main storyline, but of course extensive side questing available to those interested and even some lovely DLC packs. You may also have a traveling companion of your choosing - A dog, a Ghoulish Zombie-like mercenary, Human Merc, a member of the Power Armor wearing Brotherhood of Steel, or even a bright yellow Super Mutant, etc.
The enemies vary from irradiated Ghouls, Super Mutants and giant Behemoths, to Raiders, Mercenaries & Power-Armored Boy Scouts - Not to mention the giant firebreathing ants, mole rats, and the dreaded Death Claws. A refreshing bestiary especially in reguards to the zombies not being of a viral origin like so many other games dragging the over used concept through the modern mud.
The story is that of a Vault Dweller ascending into the real world from a secluded / nuclear protected population who, (depending on your playstyle) destined to save the wasteland from itself and to fight for America the Beautiful itself, or to become the Bloody King of all Raiders - spreading misery and tyranny through the wasteland with the terror of his extended weapon collection. Or...somewhere in between! As you leave the safety of Vault 101 you are searching for your Father, (voiced by Liam Neeson) who has "Taken" it upon himself to embark on his own quest to help save the wasteland.
Your President, John Henry Eden (voiced by Malcolm McDowell) elegantly explains to you throughout your journey over the Enclave Radio Station, through your Pip Boy 3000 the current state of the country, its capitol and the questions that have arisen over his presidental office - enforced by Enclave Soldiers - Power Armor clad guards hell bent on strict adhearance to any and all laws of the current administration.
You even have the option to build yourself a home wherever you see fit in this vast world - and there are even a few actual choices of property to purchase or earn depending on how your individual story unfolds.
This is likely one of the best RPGs ever to be made - despite it's aged graphics, slightly clunky gameplay at times - this title is not to be missed by gamers of many types!!

You are born (literally) in a post-apocalyptic world where the Cold War has destroyed everything with their nuclear weapon use. Luckily there are plenty of Vaults build, and you find yourself in one of those vaults. No one can enter, and no one can leave. At least, that is what they want you to believe. Your father gets out, and you will have to follow him to find out why he left, and why he lied to you about your past...
From that moment on, it is your world. Your choise on what to do. Do you follow your father, or roam the wasteland, loot old abandones houses and come across NPC who need your help? Do you settle in the first town you come across or stay on the move to see as much of the wasteland as you can? Are you a good person or a bad person? Choise is a big factor in this RPG, and that is one of the main reasons this is one of the best RPG's out there. One of the best maritime war games i have played. Sound quality and visuals are on point and gameplay is close to accurate as actual 19th century naval combat. A little expensive but well worth it in the long run.

While the game is still in development, and the dev team are interested in feedback from the players, their obstinate refusal to offer anything close to realism in the way of maritime navigation is the deal-breaker for me. No matter how pretty you make the sunsets, no matter how detailed the ships, no matter the accuracy of the eye-candy for the period, having to rely on landmarks for navigation is possibly the stupidest game mechanic decision they have made. They give you a compass and what amounts to a speedometer, and tell you to navigate by sight. No concession to anything realistic about sailing is made. The world map is lovely, yet worthless in regard to getting from A to B. Yes, you can see the port you just departed from, and yes, you can see the port you may be attempting to reach. You can even see the crossed sabers indicating the position of the ship(s) you are instructed to sink, etc. What you are not given, and what you will be never given (unless the dev team comes down off their high horse) is any indication of where the hell you are on that same map.
I played Pirates of the Burning Sea at launch, and then again 2 yrs ago. While Naval Action is in the "simulation" category, and PotBS was not, for all of its faults, PotBS was a better game. It had character and style. NA has plenty of screenshot-worthy moments, but the ludicrous and intentional lack of navigation realism cannot but render this game to me anything beyond a mobile Geoff Hunt painting. If you want to sail a pretty ship around scanning the horizon for a landmark to fix your position, then buy the game.  I think I'll uninstall for now and come back when the game is finished. Maybe, by then, the devs will realize that their desire for players to experience being "lost at sea" because navigation tools like an octant or a sextant would make it too easy is a cop-out.
I have not, and will not say anything about the lack of tutorial, etc. because it IS an Early Access game.
If you have a couple of spare $20 bills lying around, buy the game. If you would rather see your money put to better use, send it to me and help me pay off my student loans.

Downwell is a unique take on the sidescroller genre, actually it's a verticalscroller. That's because you progress through each level by dropping down a well, hence the title, Downwell. You have these gunboots allowing you to shoot enemies. Landing on platforms or stomping on enemies reloads and there are various types of weapon modules that change the way the gunboots function. The game has real tight controls allowing for precise movement and the levels are procedurally generated, so each time you play it keeps you on your toes. The game can be played at any pace and it all works. You can be patient and meticulous or you can be fast and rythmic (my preferred method). You can also play it in long strides or short bursts to pass the time.
All of these elements come together to create gaming bliss. I love this game and it's only 3 dollars. Just get it.
Bats are now my mortal enemies...

Watching a few seconds of Downwell can show you the general gist of the game; it is deviously simple in design in this way. You fall down a (seemingly) bottomless well, dodging and killing enemies as you fall. The same button used for jumping is used for firing your weapon, therefore, you can only fire while airborne. You rack up "Gem High, which boosts your firing power, collect power ups, and so on so forth, dealing with a brutal difficulty. It's your standard rogue-like affair, all done very well, with tight controls and a series of engaging mechanics that encourage fast and franctic gameplay as you plummet endlessly.
Ironically, my only qualm would be a lack of real depth to its mechanics and gameplay, and other players may also feel like this. But in a way, this is a completely null argument. The game is elegant and minimal, and that is why it is such a good game.

Well this came out of the blue didn’t it?
Lego Worlds is more or less if Minecraft Sandbox mode was made with 100% Lego.
Now I personally have always been a big fan of Lego, I still to this day have a huge box of Lego stored away for the rainy days when I need a little pick me up and need to create something cool, the fact that you can just create almost anything you want, has always been a big thing for me personally and I know that many other people share the same with me, but now for the game itself.
When you start the game and create your wold, you are literally dropped in to the world and off you pop to explore and build.
There is no story as of what I know, the whole entire goal of the game is for you to just roam about, explore, build and create. When you encounter a new object, it is automatically put in to your library of objects.
There are small chests littered around the place and when you destroy an object or a character, they will drop silver, golden and blue Lego bits that work as your currency that allows you to unlock the things you’ve found in the world and to unlock more skins for yourself you need to buy the characters with these bits to unlock the costume for you to freely use.
Usable items can be found in big chests and the first time I found an Item I found a bazooka, the game clearly knows me well enough not to argue and gives me a bazooka straight off, first game to understand that that to keep me mildly entertained for a while is to allow me to randomly blow stuff up. However the items you get are purely random so you have no idea what you will get when you open a big chest.
In addition you will find vehicles and animals to ride on to help your exploration and make it slightly faster and here is the cool part, any animal can be rode upon and that includes dragons, fireball spitting red dragons, I shall call you Charlie. Hey Ho Charlie Awaaay.
Unlocking minifigures and skins for your character requires you to actually find the characters in the world and if they are friendly, go and talk to them and if they are hostile, blow them up, but I guess it works for both.
The world itself is divided in to biomes and different biomes for the most part have different objects and characters in them, these biomes also house a variety of buildings placed around sometimes and some of them will have a big chest in them so it’s always a good idea to explore them.
In addition to exploring and just roaming about, you can colour up the place and free build things or if you are lazy, build things from a list of pre-made structures. There are no limits to what you can do, so build whatever you want, where ever you want, when ever you want.
Now for the gripes, which there are only two.
The first gripe is fairly simple, as much as I know, no first person mode. The one thing that I really would of wanted out of this is to be able to play in first person and I know the third person mode is a staple of the Lego Games, but exploring houses is a pain in the posterior because the camera is a very very very stubborn creature to control and most of the time ends up clipping through terrain and buildings.
The second gripe is to do with the games optimization. It’s quite bad and for the first time I have had to actually turn around and say the following “A Lego Game is tanking my fps” On a high end machine it has no problems, but to a medium range machine it seems to have a bit of an fps issue and the game even tells you when it’s struggling. I can’t imagine what the game would be like to a low end machine.
Other than the two gripes I personally have about the game, it is great fun and I will most likely return to it every once in a while to explore and to build more things. The lack of multiplayer is a slight over sight, but even so it’s still great fun for the whole family.
I would give this game 10/10 because it is fantastic, but because of the poor optimization I am going to drop my review down to 8/10 because some people won’t be able to play this properly and enjoy it to it’s fullest because of simply running the game on a low end machine.
But that is all for this time folks, Go out there and build something amazing.

Skullgirls is a great fighting game. The game itself is a well stylised 2D fighting game with smooth animations and good soundtracks. Character pool is limited, though it will continue to be expanded in the future, and each character does have their distinct playstyle. It comes with a good AI difficulty range so it can be challenging to pros while forgiving to newbies, and its tutorials are even more newbie friendly as it teaches the core mechanics of a fighting game.
Skills and combos in this game are relatively easy to pull off, though a controller or a gaming pad is recommended. The Xbox 360 controller works fine with this game.
The character rolster is currently all-female, though there seem to be plans for male characters in the future. The character design may not appeal to everyone (sexualised is the word that comes to mind, though which fighting game isn't?), but the story modes for the characters are enjoyable for the most part.
It's definitely worth a try if you have a casual interest in fighting games and don't want to go fully hardcore and spend 2 years in rage just to have enough practice, while the combo variety might still appeal to the more dedicated fighting game player, though I wonder if they might find the game too easy in terms of controls.

Fighting games -- aside from the more-casual ones, such as Smash Bros. and Soulcalibur -- have always been a genre I've avoided somewhat due to not wanting to dedicate the time to learn the theory behind how to play them competitively (ie, not button-mashing). They just drop you in raw, and you are never really properly taught anything.
I decided to pick-up Skullgirls mostly because it had a very in-depth tutorial that teaches you the mechanics and the theory behind how to play the game, and it forces you to reliably apply and repeat what you've learned so that your progression is never a fluke. Granted, for other competitive fighting games, I could have searched the Internet and read Wikis or something, but Skullgirls' excellent, beginner-friendly Tutorial mode (which is still difficult, as it should be) being built straight into the game was enough to finally get me into the genre.
I'm still getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked. A lot. But I at least know why now, and I'm constantly improving.

Time Disclaimer -- I have played 911: First Responders / Emergency 4 for hundreds of hours prior to the Steam release.
Emergency 4 is a Real Time Strategy in which the user is tasked with controlling a number of German Emergency Services; Police, Ambulance, Fire, and Mechanics. Using these, it's up to the user to deal with a number of disasters in the main campaign ranging from simple fires to earthquakes, hostage situations, airline disasters and more! Alternatively, the user can play an endless mode in which they must deal with random emergencies which will grant them the finances to purchase more vehicles and deal with bigger disasters. One great aspect is you're not penalized for doing a bad job so if you get bored, you can use your police units to cause havoc.
The game is easy to get into but difficult to master as controlling a number of different emergency units can quickly become overwhelming. The assets have also aged well since release.
Emergency 4 is definitely a unique game and is an often looked over gem, it's a game that is both engaging and enjoyable, even if you're not a fan of Real Time Strategies.
Additionally, the game is VERY moddable. The '
' is definitely recommended as it adds dozens of additional units and missions.
To put it simply, this game is a must play and for the price it's being offered at, it's definitely worth grabbing. There are rumors of emegency 5 being released next month (October 2014) and hopefully it's a better game than the poorly done Emergency 2012/2013/2014 games and hopefully, the release of Emergency 4 on Steam is a good sign of Emergency 5 being released on Steam sometime soon.

Your childhood, now in 3D!
The fact that codemasters still care about this classic series brought a tear to my eye.
Seriously though, this game is pretty great. If you're a big fan of the old 2D MM games as I am, you'd probably enjoy the ride.
First of all, the graphics. You've probably seen the screenshots, and to be honest, it doesn't seem to look all that impressive. It's certainly far behind in quality to codemaster's other racing games, say, GRID or DiRT. That's certainly what I thought. But make no mistake -- once you play the game, you will see that the graphics aren't bad at all. The game was designed to be lightweight and welcoming, and that's exactly what the graphics on this game does: it makes you feel good. It's the kind of game you'd want to play waking up on a saturday morning. The upbeat music also helps. One of the reason I wasn't too fond of MM V4 was because of the danky graphics and techno-electronic music tracks. This game has none of that.
Then there's the gameplay. While racing through an environment of tabletop items is pretty fun in itself, the game adds a few elements to make it more interesting, such as items and different race modes. I don't have much else to say on this aspect, other than that it's very faithful to the MM games of old (it even has a retro camera!) which is never a bad thing.
Of course, the game isn't without its caveats. The single player campaign is very short, it has too few tracks (18), and the difficulty curve can be pretty overwhelming. The one thing I was most dissapointed about though, was the lack of variety. The old MM games had many different types of tracks, including gardens, sandboxes, and even bathtubs (personal favorite), each with its own set of challenges. Even the traditional tabletop levels were much more creative (music boxes and whatnot). This game does away with that, and rather just offers you a few different tracks of 3 themes -- breakfast, school science lab, billiards, and construction playground. While there's nothing wrong with the tracks themselves, they can get pretty old pretty quick. This game would have benefited greatly if codemasters had included workshop support, but I guess that's asking a bit much from a niche game such as this.
Another thing I find annoying about the game -- though this is purely subjective -- is the use of a mobile-game like scoring system. You got 1st place? 3 stars. 2nd place? 2 stars etc. Then you use said stars to unlock more levels. While there's nothing technically wrong with this system, I'd prefer that my PC games stay away from mobile game mechanics.
In conclusion, if you're a die hard MM fan, then consider buying this game. If you're just a casual racer looking for some quick fun, you'd better wait until it goes on sale. For the latter, it's not really worth the asking price.

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a Third Person Shooter with great story and great gameplay.
The game follows a Command Squad of three of the Ultramarines, 2nd Company Commander and playable character Captain Titus, his immediate subordinate Veteran Sergeant Sidonus, and a relatively inexperienced and by-the-book Tactical Marine named Leandros.
Initially upon arrival the squad provide assistance to the outnumbered and overrun Imperial Guard regiments fighting on the planet's surface, which after the loss in battle of all higher-ranking officers are now being led by the sole surviving junior officer, Second Lieutenant Mira
The Space Marines then move on to continue with their own mission and, amidst securing the Titan Invictus, a weapon that can destory the orcs. The titan need a power source that can found in a reactor. Titus retrieves it and activates the Psychic Scourge, but the Orcs doesn't die, but a Warp Gate to the world of Chaos and unleaches a horde of demons.
Later the Chaos Lord Nemeroth emerges from the portal. Using his Warp powers, he subdues the Space Marine squad as Inquisitor Drogan arrives via lift and approaches Nemeroth, revealing his allegiance to the Chaos Lord.
The Scourge opened a growing Warp portal around the Orbital Spire, allowing Chaos forces to pour in; seeing this, Titus forms a plan to destroy the portal and the Spire by using one of the Titans they had secured earlier. The Titan Invictus is brought to full activation by the Power Source, and destroys the Spire. However, Sergeant Sidonus is killed by Lord Nemeroth, and the Power Source is stolen and taken to the floating remains of the Spire.
The reinforcement fleet now having finally arrived, including a company of Blood Ravens Space Marines as well as the rest of Titus's company and large numbers of Imperial Guard, Titus leads them in an attack through the remaining Chaos forces to stop Lord Nemeroth from performing a ritual to ascend to the status of a Daemon Prince using the power of the device
Nemeroth has partially ascended to Daemonhood when Titus finally faces him again; both are knocked off the spire in the struggle, and the Captain defeats him in single combat while falling towards the ground. He then breaks the experimental device in half with his hands. Titus survives the exposure to the raw Warp energy again, and is rescued by a Thunderhawk dropship before he can impact the ground.
The end scene of the game involves a new Imperial Inquisitor by the name of Thrax, accompanied by Leandros and escorted by several Black Templar Space Marines, who places Titus under arrest. Leandros believes that his Captain has been corrupted by Chaos, based on his resistance to warp forces.

First off, this is an early access game. I realize the price is steep for an early access game, but this is quite simply one of the most fun games I've probably ever played, both in the open world MMO genre and in general. I've easily gotten more enjoyment out of it than the last $30-$40 full release titles I've purchased, and the hours speak for themselves.
The Awesome:
1. Combat is absolutely amazing. It plays somewhat like a chess match, in both large fleet actions and single ship actions. Each side makes a move, to which the other side attempts to counter. In a large battle, this mainly comes down to your side's shot caller attempting to give as many of his ships as possible a shot on the opposing fleet. In single ship fights, much of  the skill comes down to maneuvering to rake your opponent's stern to kill crew and dismount cannon until he can no longer fight, while preventing him from doing the same.  The combat is definitely the most polished part of the game, and it shows.
2. Development: I say this mainly because the game already is in development, but I've seen very few games capable of treading the thin line between giving the players what they want, and doing what's best for the players and the game as a whole. These devs have done an amazing job on this, and many player suggestions throughout closed alpha and even early Steam release have found their way into the game. In addition, the development cycle is very regular, with a major content patch around the middle of each month, along with usually 2 ships added to the game. In addition, the devs have added multiple player-made ships to the game.
3. The Open World map: This is probably the most important part of the game. The open world map is a scale representation of the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico, based off of maps from the time period of the game (early 1800s-late 1700s). This is how you get from port to port and find other players to sail or fight with. When engaging other players, your position relative to them and both of your positions in relation to the wind translates directly into the battle instance, making positioning in the OW almost as important as actual combat skill. A recent update now translates any land you may be nearby into the battle as well, meaning cunning captains can pin smaller and nimbler ships against land when they would otherwise be able to sail away unscathed. In addition to that, major fleet AI battles can be found quite easily in the open world as well (but make sure you bring friends).
The Not So Awesome (outdated, see EDIT):
1. Finding a fight: One of the biggest complaints is the difficulty of finding a fight in the open world. This can be a challenge, but it does depend primarily on where you are trying to find fights. Generally, the closer to Cuba/Jamaica you are, the better the change of finding a fight (this primarily concerns the PVP1 server). Free Ports (uncapturable by any faction) allow you to base ships closer to these areas to get into the action quicker. In addition, duels can be set up in the port screen (just ask around in national or local chat for a dueling partner, and remember your ships must be the same battle rating to duel), which gives a loss-free way to practice handling your ship before jumping into real danger in the open world.
2. Game Economy/Crafting: This is probably the least polished portion of the game, meaning everything I say here is subject to change. The economy is inbetween a full player driven economy and an AI driven economy. Money can be made quite easily by your production buildings, and those resources in turn supply the shipbuilders. Ships require resources to build if you want an above average one, otherwise basic versions with a minor flaw or minor improvement (to speed, crew space, rigging, etc.) can be bought for very affordable prices from the AI. AI only sells up to 4th rate 60 gun ships however, anything larger must be built by a crafter or captured from another player. If your objective in buying the game is to become a major crafter/trader and nothing else, you may want to wait for this feature to mature before purchasing.
3. The "Grind": You'll find many reviews that complain about the game's grind. At the end of the day, the game is only a grind if you make it one. Unlike War Thunder, World of XXX, or other arena games where you are forced to play a vehicle  to unlock the next, the only limiting factor in Naval Action is the crew you can command. You start with 40, and this increases as you go through the ranks. You can still purchase any ship on the market if you have the money to do it, and some ships can be used without much downside with less than maximum crew due to crew management mechanics added to the battles shortly after steam release. In addition, the thresholds for how much experience (earned by damaging and sinking/capturing enemy ships in battle) is required for each rank was recently reduced by a large margin. All that being said, don't fall into the trap of thinking "bigger ship = better ship." The captain's skill ultimately decides the battle. Even a cutter (starter ship) can make the difference in an open world battle, and I know this from personal experience.
EDIT FOR 9.8 PATCH:
With the 9.8 patch, finding a fight in OW is no longer an issue. Teleport timers have been completely removed when going from outpost to outport, allowing players to jump around the map to various hotspots as they please (so long as they have an outpost in the area). This makes it quicker and easier than ever to fight PVP.
In addition, ship durability/HP has been compressed, meaning there is no longer as much of a difference in the punishment each frigate can take compared to each other, or for how much each ship of the line can take compared to each other.
Also, many new upgrades were added to further allow players to customize their ships, as well as all the other awesome changes in the 9.8 patch notes.

This is an epic WW2 strategy game.  The economics in this are tight.  The battles are simple (panzer general style).  You won't be wowed by graphics or anything but this is a gem of a game.  You have to be looking for the right thing and I'll try my best to explain it.
- Events.  This game is loaded with historical events and there are choices you can make (like a choose your own adventure book) and those choices allow you to impact the game one way or another.   For example, Germany could be building a carrier and an event will ask you if you would rather convert it to a battleship and that then saves you some economic impact)
- You can control all the sides of an alliance (Germany + Italy for axis; UK, US, USSR, Poland, and France for Allies)
- You can tell the AI to control specific pieces.  Russia, for example can be AI controlled while you manage the western faction
- This game has a decent technology tree that impact the game
- The diplomacy in this game is a roll of the dice but you can invest money to influence countries to join your faction
- The economics is tight.  You will have to make tough choices.
- The AI is good.  It will kick your butt if you aren't on your toes.  It will not do something stupid.  I don't feel I can manipulate it
Naval Combat is fun, BUT, the designer even admits he beefed up Germany for game balancing purposes.
- I love how the convoy system works and how you can raid it
- I think the naval combat could be a little better, but I find it to be fun.  With Italy and Germany, you tend to either dominate or lose it all...it is really tough to keep a naval presence in this game!!  (As it should be for them)
- It has a supply system I've never seen before.  Be sure to really read the rules on supply or you will get destroyed and feel the game is unfair.  It is fair, and it is winnable, but you MUST understand supply.
Now, for my final thing.  I complained about how long it took the AI to take their turn.  A developer contacted me, wrote me privately and worked with me and he changed the code!!  He cut the AI time in half!!  You just don't find dedicated support or service like this very often any more!!
Of course, I recommend this game.  But it is challenging.  And it handles WW2 at an epic grand strategy level.  THe tech trees and diplomacy are functional but not flashy.   It all goes into what you are looking for.   This is a cross between Panzer General and Order of Battle, but covers the whole European theater versus a mini combat map.

Differnet doors and routes are used each time, so its never the grind that destiny or other shoot em ups become, and it alternates between relatively calm advances to what I affectionately call 'Chaos Mode', where shedloads of zombies spawn all around you, forcing you to defend your position while doors open, or just while trying to advance, and your teamwork is really put to the test, especially on higher difficulties. For an early access game the ballistics are excellent, although there isnt any recoil on the sniper or the shotgun, but it doesnt detract from it at all. The hitboxes are excellent as well, modeled almost perfectly to the sprites. And to top it all off, the soundtrack is absolutely badass, with the chaos mode track being awesome, and the track that plays in the last minute of the bombs timer is so good i have to concentrate on not raving and concentrate on not dying. Kitten Rampage:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

If reincarnation is an option, then I want to come back as a kitten with laser beams and a mini gun! It is fun to create havoc in the human world.
Kitten Rampage is an action / cat simulator game where you play a fluffy, little white cat and your goal is to destroy as many things as possible with your laser beams and bullets from your mini gun. This game is currently under development, but you will be able to play a couple of missions. In the first one, you will have a time limit to destroy as much as possible and achieve given objectives. The second one is pretty much the same without the time limit.
The game play is really fun, as you go on a rampage and literally ravage the household and it occupants (they are actually agents). You will be able to Meow, sit, jump and of course poop in your litter. If you can’t find your litter . . .  don’t worry, you can poop everywhere! As you know by now, you will be using laser beams and a mini gun but . . . you can puke grenades for good measure - let me tell you, you are going to laugh playing this game!  You will see your kitten in a third cat (person) perspective and you will need to make sure it eats and drinks well during your rampage. And, as you are a very clever kitten, you will be able to enter cars and drive them around the house. Also, with each Great Kill, 1 second will be added to your time limit.
Graphically, it is nice (still in development). Nice soundtrack too. The controls could be better but overall they are ok.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Fun gameplay and interesting concept
-	Nice graphics
-	Plenty of explosions
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Repetitive
Kitten Rampage shows great potential, it is fun and will give you the giggles more than once. I can’t wait to see new levels.
7.5/10

Space Marine is a third-person, over-the-shoulder shooter. You play as the Adeptus Astartes Ultramarines Captain, Titus. His mission is to save the planet by doing what no human could ever do: brutally murder Orks and Chaos forces by repeatedly shoving  a chainsword in various orifices. Is this game good? Definitely. Is it fun? Fantastically so!
The gameplay is your simple shooter affair: center the middle of your screen on something you want dead and pull the trigger to watch it be made so. Accompanying that is a wonderfully gory melee system using chainswords, power axes, and thunder hammers to wonderful effect. The bolter rounds feel like they punch the enemy and the melee weapons can send them careening across the map. The combat is most excellent and definitely worth the money for that, if you enjoy rampage.
The story is equally compelling. While it is set in a "parellel timeline" where Titus is captain of the second company as opposed to Cato Sicarius, it still feels just as real of a Warhammer story. Titus is strong, dutiful, and is more than ready to destory xenos and heretics in equal measure. He comes off as abrasive, but that only adds to his character as a soldier eager for battle. The other characters, however, are not so noteworthy. The game tries to make us like them, but none of them really hit home or even provide much more than expositional dialogue. The over-arching narrative was also quite excellent, but it did feel like it went on too long and one story was abandoned for another halfway through. I understand the reason, but it really felt hollow.
Now, my biggest complaint is with the difficulty, namely that there isn't any. My first playthrough was on Hard, and I performed quite admirably. The few times I did die was do to my stupid mistakes rather than the game being difficult. For me, this felt too easy. Fun, but without enough challenge. For experienced shooter players, Hard difficulty should be an easy ride.
I happily recommend this game to veterans and newcomers alike. The gameplay is easy to get used to and fun to play and the story is interesting and keeps moving forward, if slowly at times. The multiplayer will also provide hours of enjoyment either before or after the campaign. Now go purge some xenos filth in the name of the Emperor!

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a 3rd person shooter.
I've played all Warhammer 40,000 video games. Some were good, and others were so great that I still play them, even several years after their release.
This is one of the best 40k games, period. It nails everything- from what makes a good 3rd person shooter, to what makes a true-to-lore 40k game.
To start off, This isn't your standard 3rd person-totally-not-gears-of-war game. Whilst most 3PSs focus on a cover system, Space Marine removes that entirely. You ARE the cover. You can wade into a mob of enemies, without dying every 3 seconds. It perfectly encapsulates what makes a space marine a space marine, and lets you experience that firsthand.
The combat is divided into two parts- ranged and melee. You are given a wide variety of weapons to slaughter your enemies in different and uniquely brutal ways. Each weapon feels (and sounds!) exactly how it should. The shot of a bolter, the hiss of a meltagun, and the roar of a plasma cannon. And although the ranged weapons are cool, the melee weapons are even better. Chainswords (chainsaw-swords) evicerate and rend flesh whenever they strike, turning a large horde of orks into a bloody mess very quickly. Thunder hammers, although slow, deal tremendous damage and completly pulverise your enemies. The combat (especially in single player or the horde-mode) is immensly satisfying and one of the best parts of the game.
The game has both a single-player and a multiplayer. The single player has a decently lengthy campaign (10-12 hours) with a pretty good story. It does have its faults (unfinished story arcs that will probably never get finished b/c r.i.p THQ). The multiplayer, although good and reasonably well balanced, gets repedative with the 4 maps (excluding expansions). You also can't choose which side you are on pre-match, meaning you might not even get to see your shiny new color scheme for a couple matches. The multiplayer also follows the standard 'level up to improve' philosophy, with special perks unlocked by completing challenges (some of which are brutally difficult without help).
Overall, this is a fantastic 40k game that really makes you feel like you are playing a space marine.
It's practically a badass simulator, 10/10 from me.

I've purchased this game quite recently at the time of posting this review, and the negative reviews posted right before did make me waiver. I'd like to go over why I am so happy that I decided to try the game for those that waiver as I do.
I've played Sid Meier's Pirates for well over 1k hours before it was added to steam, this game sort of comes across as a much more in depth MMO version of that. Choose a nation, participate in PvE missions (small and large scale), capture ports of Pirates or other nations for your nation, fight people or capture traders/player ships in the open world, participate in a player driven economy. All of these aspects of the game accompanied by fantastic feeling combat and a true sense of accomplishment along the way, something I've found missing in a lot of games.
It's true that you don't show up as an X on the map, and must use your compass as well as landmarks to get around. I have yet to get lost (perhaps other than a couple minutes of questioning my exact location), and honestly navigation feels great and after a day of playing I could find missions far off of land easily.
There are several nations as well as pirates, and each one feels like a unique community. As you play throughout the day you see server wide messages of port battles, cities being conquered, you see in global chat people mentioning huge expensive ships being captured by pirates. The world feels alive, actions seem to matter and when you see a first rate ship sail by or you see people taking part in these huge battles with huge perma-loss risks and rewards, it excites a new player to want to continue.
I already feel part of a national effort, I already feel a sense of accomplishment after getting a new ship and crafting enough to make a lot of gold. The combat feels fantastic, and though 10+ minutes may feel slow to a lot of people for missions, it never feels artificially slow. Each mission is still fun to me, fleet missions feel rewarding and sailing back to port with the risk of pirates jumping me and taking all of my rewards is honestly fun to me. (though very rare, but the possibility is there)
I'm very happy that I'm playing this game, though it seemed hard at first it very quickly became a fluid and fun experience. Though people said missions were super slow, nothing has felt anything but natural and entertaining. This is a game that feels rewarding, the faction system makes me feel like I'm a contributing member and honestly this is the pirate game I've been wanting for years. I hope the development keeps going strong and adding more, but either way I've already gotten more out of this than a lot of games and plan on continuing for quite a while.

I've been playing Naval action for a bit now. I'd like to say that I could endorse this pretty looking game but I can't.
There are quite a few unsavory elements to the game. And here's a few.
1. Unrealistic and overpowered AI.
The NPC ships in the game routinely break nearly EVERY sailing rule of physics in the book, maneuvering like hydrofoils even in a headwind. And if THAT isn't bad enough, their gunnery puts even present day warships with their guided missiles to shame with a near 90% hit rate even at extreme range with maybe 2 out of every 3 hits landing criticals. Also they seem to have a higher rate of fire than most players.
The devs DID recently reduce the AI accuracy on small ships such as cutters and brigs hoping that less experienced players won't notice that all frigates and SoTLs still have the "sniper elite" level AI and dance around like fairies.
2. Toxic and hostile player community.
The game is supposed in alpha stage, which means that people playing the game are supposed to be providing feedback and making suggestions. However the player community will usually try to shout down player suggestions, throw insults and name-calling around, and attempt to derail the suggestion thread by leading it off topic into wild and immature tangents. They also seem to celebrate on the forums when frustrated players announce their intention to leave <like good riddance or don't let the door hit you in the *** on the way out, etc>.
3. Devs alienate PvE and Independent players.
With only a single PvE server and no access to alt characters if you want to experience something new, for example playing another nation or just plain want to play a new character they give you only 2 options either completely delete your old character and make an entirely new one sacrificing all your gold, ships, crafting resources and all that even though you still retain both your rank and crafting xp or be forced onto a PvP server where only 3 of their 7 or 8 playable nations are even viable and where ganking and griefing runs rampant.
They claim that this is designed to prevent economic exploitation but that kind of exploitation already exists in the game in the form of the current guild activity.
4. They are setting the stage for total disaster for the game economy and solo playability with their future economic goals.
In their most recent patch they did away with player ability to sail captured warships. Instead players now have to auto turn in warships they have captured in boarding combat over to their respective nation's admiralties for a tiny sum of gold and only allowing players to commandeer merchant ships. They also have future plans to completely do away with NPC resource vendors and allowing players to have the complete run of the economy. This action coupled with the canned ability to sail captured warships will inevitably open the door to massive overpricing of ships, and other items and make it impossible for any independent player to survive and be competitive.
It's like Pirates of the Burning Sea all over again.....Perhaps even worse.
At least portalus games has since begun to offer means of solo player survivability (if only to line their own pockets with real-world cash).
With this all said I can not in good conscience recommend this game to anyone.

Finally finished my first playthrough of the game and I loved it. It's an adventure roleplay that's quirky and, at many moments, just plain silly.
At a classic level, it wasn't difficult. I beat the game at level 20 and haven't even dipped into a lot of the other elements in the game like crafting, blacksmithing, or restarting your stats. The world is open enough for you to explore wherever you want to go, which can result in completing certain story events before the cannon order. The game allows for it all pretty well but take it from me, if you stumble into an area where everything is two levels higher than you, it's absolutely possible to beat them but you're most likely meant to be in a different region.
A lot of the puzzles can take some time if you miss the hint they give you such as in a random book lying around, note you collected eariler (among the series of notes/books you'll find yourself collecting out of habit), or dialogue from a previous encounter. This can lead to a lot of running back and forth, attempting to find what you're meant to do. There is a safety net, however: there's almost always more than one way to complete something. Person you need to get past? Kill them or talk them down. Need to get past a magic barrier? Find the spell or teleport past the barrier. Problem with this? Sometimes your solution may screw you over to being able to complete an optional puzzle (in my case, broke a statue I needed to stay on a pressure plate and saved right after). Or other glitches can occur like not getting a certain spell you need for whatever reason. But for the vast majority of the time, there's no problems.
While I didn't complete all the quests and really enjoyed the game for what it was, I'm not currently enthused about spending another 60 hours going through the same story line and making some aribrary quest differences. The ending is probably the weakest element of the game for me, just because I had roleplayed my two main characters as sisters but the cannon ending I got, they were made to be lovers so, you know, kind of breaks that whole idea of roleplay freedom.
Apart from the ending, they did have a neat roleplay aspect, as you could choose a few options often that would give your character different characteristics like 'blunt' or 'considerate', which provides different stat changes. Ie. blunt made a character immune to charm. They also let you choose 'AI's for your characters, which helps mould them into something different and make their own choices. My main didn't have an AI, but her witch sister had a 'free spirit' AI which fought with me about everything - which, in all honesty, was enjoyable to rock, paper, scissors it out to see where our story will lead. Lesson I found? Her sister was generally an idiot. Sometimes I'd just 'ungroup' her from my troop and make her stand outside the building till I was done talking. I could have avoided this whole thing if I didn't give her the AI but I liked the unpredictablility when the mains reflected on their situations.
And after this review is five times longer than I had planned at four in the morning, I'm gonna conclude with this: if you're looking for a fun-spirited, turn-based roleplay game, this is an fantastic option.
I had a lot of fun playing it. It's not for everyone, but for those who like ths genre of games it's great. Can't wait to start playing the sequel.

Before going in-depth with my review for the game, I want to sum it up with that one word alone:
.
Upon purchasing the game, I didn't know what I was getting myself into. Sure, I've heard praises about it some time ago and it was on sale recently for a very reasonable price. So, I bought the game along with its soundtrack bundled in without any idea what to truly expect. And after just finishing the game recently, I can safely say that what I got was an experience worth every penny.
Keyword: "experience".
I'll start off by discussing what I think is the main problem that people seem to have for the game (based on the negative Steam reviews).
This game is labeled as an "Indie Adventure Role Playing Game". It was also designed through the RPG Maker XP engine. So it is of no surprise that people expect at least a bit of RPG Maker gameplay elements that are typically found elsewhere. But this game doesn't have that. In fact, aside from very simple puzzles, this game doesn't have much else in terms of 'gameplay'.
And therein lies the problem. It's hard to call it a 'game' when it barely has any gameplay elements to it. Heck, as long as you keep playing there's no way to lose the game. It's more like a movie with a few interactions added here and there. I personally expected a bit of a challenge too but the game was too easy and too linear. But is that necessarily a bad thing?
No. In my opinion, it's not.
In fact, because of how straightforward the gameplay is, I was able to progress through the story very quickly in anticipation for what's going to happen next. All I had to do was overcome a bit of a hurdle in order to progress through the story and it didn't bother me at all.
That is why I prefer calling it an 'experience' as opposed to calling it a 'game'. It is a
. The lack of any complicated gameplay made all the other aspects of the game shine.
The graphics may be your typical RPG Maker stuff, but it's better-looking than most of the games made through the RPG Maker engine.
The story...well, without spoiling much let's just say that there are a lot of feels found in this game. One minute I'm laughing at the interactions between the two main characters, and the next minute I'm trying my best to hold back my tears from too much feels (and most of the time failing to hold back said tears; no shame in that).
And the music? Oh man, the music...the music in this game is arguably its greatest asset. The music found in the game is very beautiful. Each soundtrack served its purpose in making every scene of the game much more enjoyable and memorable. If you buy the game, I implore you to buy the soundtrack as well. It's worth it.
It's a short game; only took me around 4 hours to finish. But every second of that 4 hours was worth it. It was a short but sweet ride.
I highly recommend this game.

Ubisoft and Massive have put a ton of effort to make the core RPG experience a lot more accessible and fun for everyone. You don't need the DLCs at all to enjoy the base experience.

Oh boy, where to start...
If you want a short version of this review I'll just say this; 11/10 Would 100% complete again.
Now here's the long version.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a platformer which has a slight tendency to incorporate puzzles, requiring you to put your skills to the test and combine all of your unlocked abilities to get every single collectable. These puzzles aren't neccessarily hard, but you're certainly going to have to remember every single one of your abilities to 100% this game.
The music is just brilliant, I've never desperately wanted to buy a game JUST for it's soundtrack. The music in the trailer is just fantastic, and as soon as you hear it, you'll be cracking into a smile in no time. The transitions between music is also really smooth, as all the music seems to run at a similar tempo (except for a select few tracks) so the transitions seem to be just substituting some instruments with other instruments, instead of loading screens with the track changing as the game loads.
The graphics are just as beautiful, with almost everything interacting with Ori when you run by them. I once jumped by some vines, only to see them sway with Ori as I flew through the air. Everything is very detailed, as you can see little bats hanging on the ceiling in caves, water flowing in the background, individual rocks, and even a strange creature appearing in the foreground. Any hazard is very well detailed, and you'll really only run into them if you're simply not paying attention.
The gameplay is also really good. While this game seems to be one of those games that you should only play with a controller, the keyboard and mouse work just as good, if not better! This is a game I certainly recommend picking up some time. I don't care when you buy it, what system you buy it on, just buy it at some point in your life span.
Oh, one thing I should mention. If you plan on getting this game, but just so happen to have a not-so-powerful PC, or don't have an XBOX One on hand, this game will definitely slow down for you. My PC is a pretty low-end one, so the game's video runs slower to keep a consistent framerate. (I actually really like that idea) This becomes ESPECIALLY apparent in the cutscenes, as the music will play faster than the video itself. There are some sweet spots that will run smoothly for you, and some areas that'll make your FPS drop from 30-40 to 10-20 just by walking into the area. Basically, if you have a low-end computer, and no XBOX, but still want to play this game, the game'll run for you, but it won't run at a fast speed, so make sure that other graphic-heavy games such as Skyrim run at about 60 FPS without breaking a sweat. As a general guideline for whether the game runs well for you, if the game is running over 45 FPS, you're pretty much set. (Steam has an in-game FPS counter if you want to use that) Apart from that tiny setback, the game is definitely worth the purchase. I hope Moon Studios produces more content that are equal to, or are better, than Ori and the Blind Forest.
Edit: After actually playing the game on the 360 myself, low-end PCs and the 360 both have slow down.

I played more than 30 hours and then removed the game from my hard drive. About half the way in I only played on to have something to show for my frustration and to beat the game in spite of its large shortcomings. This game looks like a more in-depth version of the more casual classic "Clash of Steel" (CoS), except CoS was much better in the end...
I'm not a grognard but I played my way through games like "High Command" or "Hearts of Iron" (1 and 2) or Gary Grigsby's original Pacific War/War in the East, etc. I appreciate a good grand strategy game and I know at some point you have to abstract somewhat or even a lot but this game makes all the wrong compromises.
Pros:
* Simple yet fun research system
* Diplomacy system works (pretty much like CoS except no instant results)
* Units are upgradeable as technology advances
* Clean and uncluttered interface
* Resource management makes nice mix between research, buying new units, shifting units between fronts and overseas
* You can switch off a lot of scripted events
* Air cover, interception, and escorts work
Cons:
* Bad performance - AI turns take very long, even saving a game gives you two waits
* It's scripted - free units for the British when Axis reaches Egypt, no need to attack Norway or Denmark, just click a button
* Varying turn lengths - instead of properly implemented weather effects turns in winter take longer... yes, it takes longer to build units during the winter...
* Hot-diggity infantry - entrenchment happens fast and is the biggest obstacle in the game. Dominating factor.
* No stacking - the biggest limit for support units for the attacker is that each unit takes up one huge hex
* No coordinated attacks - instead of issuing a common order for all attacking units you have to attack one by one, have the first units absorb lots of losses. also: I hate the unit swapping rule
* Fog of war off + spotting rule = broken submarines - moving next to a sub results in spotting it
* Crazy Zone of Control - units with ZoC impede movement around them. Infantry can prevent armor from breaking through gap a because it projects ZoC even "behind itself." (It can even make moving next to it so expensive you can't finish your move next to it.) Makes armored warfare pointless, mostly minor encirclements also because in most places on the map there's no space to maneuver either. In this game armor is mostly useful for striking twice and its high attack value, not so much for bold moves behind enemy lines.
* Navy has no impact on amphibic assaults - you can evade entire Royal Navy by only moving port-to-port every turn. Only way for RN to prevent: line up in the channel blocking every hex.
* UK surrender conditions -  You control Egypt. You push through Palestine. You have to push from London all the way up to Scotland to make UK even retreat to Canada. What gives?
* Don't invade the UK! Any success in Egypt or the UK just gets both the US and the USSR into the war.
* Game-y AI: Some say the AI is good. I think it's just built to exploit the game's broken entrenchment and ZoC rules.
* Super-huge support units - Artillery, anti-tank, and air-defense units so big they can fill huge hexes - and nowhere to fit them in any front line. Cannot attach artillery or anti-tank directly to infantry to give it more punch, but can add better "infantry weapons" and air defense.
* Silly scale - Just like the casual CoS infantry armies and corps share the same scale - and only occupy one hex. Also: Infantry corps super expensive
* Silly air units - you can have four dedicated fully upgraded naval bomber fleets (Germany's max) and they can barely, without enemy fighter cover, sink one battleship without taking moderate losses. Bombers take losses from attacking entrenched infantry with no anti-air of any sort. Bombers can eradicate land units completely from the air - not organization loss, but complete obliteration.
My list goes on and on, and I might add to it, but the point is: If you don't take it for historic, it might be a game of limited fun. As a "what if?" game it lacks appeal because it's so heavily scripted and even turning events off can only do so much. Even more casual games than this have the ability to stack units or do coordinated attacks, or to have some kind of flanking attack. A game that does not support stacking units or has a good flanking rule is pretty much a lost cause to me.

I admit that i was hessitant to buy it at first as its kinda pricey, but man, after 73 hours (and counting) i can say its worth every penny.
You see, this game doesnt concentrate its efford in shinny graphics and cool animations, instead it focuses on whats important for a grand strategy game: its gameplay mechanics, enemy AI, and overall desing, and it is brilliant in these aspects.
I love that it manages to be complex, challenging and "complete", but with
of the micromanaging required in other grand strategy games.
Somehow all the concepts of the game "make sense" and are very easy to understand. You dont need to spend 50 hours watching videos and reading some incomplete, outdated "wiki" to learn how to play it.
Dont get me wrong, the game is simple to understand, but there isnt a simplistic bone in its body. If you expect to win, you
to consider your military production, diplomacy,  your technological research level, the supply level of your troops, the terrain you are attacking on, their morale, weather, combat readiness, your fighting tactics like encirclement, cutting enemy supply, reinforcing your units, etc. Its all there! But yet somehow the game manages to present all these aspects in a way that is intuitive and easy to understand.
Another aspect of the game i quite like, is that you can control all the countries on either side, not just their main powers. For example, if playing as Germany, you can control Italy, Bulgaria, Romania, etc. I havent seen other games that allow you to do this.
If you were to ask me what i dont like about the game? well there aint much. I would like to see more flexibility in the diplomacy department, not to do idiotic stuff like conquering all the world via "influence" in a ridiculous matter like "some" games allow you to do (e.g. "influence the ussr to become fasist in one year" lol yeah right), but to for example keep other countries neutral. Yes i know the game has options to disable/enable each and every scripted event, but i would have prefered it if it had a simple option at start to keep other countries random or neutral. Like previous strategic command titles had.
Overall, i can say that of all the Grand Strategy games i own, this is my favorite so far. If you like WWII Strategy games, i strongly advice you to give it a shot. Also, the support provided by the developers, is simply the best ibe seen in years. Just check out the forums if you dont belive me!

I used to play grand strategy board games back in the day, one of my favorites was Third Reich by Avalon Hill. Ever since I have been searching for a computer game version that captures the same interesting decision making. Most of what is out there right now is pretty bad, and I have tried many. Hearts of Iron was probably the best, but suffered from poor AI, as nearly all of them do. After purchasing one of these games I would immediately test the AI by playing the Allies, because playing Axis at the start of the war requires a very aggressive strategy, which is always the weak point for the AI in these games.
I have to say that the AI in this game performed extremely well. Poland was conquered by October 1939, and France by June 1940, despite my best efforts. After the invasion of the Soviet Union, it went on to capture Leningrad and I finally stopped it just outside the gates of Moscow and Stalingrad. After that I was able to turn the tide and conquer Germany by December 1944. Contrast this with the same experiment I did with Hearts of Iron IV, which took four months to conquer Poland and failed completely to conquer France.
I would definitely say this is the best WWII grand strategy game on Steam right now. I heartily recommend it.

*Single Player* Review only,
The game has two modes.
Non interactive cutscenes, or "semi interactive" cutscenes.
1) The "story" of this game is fully in service of the "Warhammer 40k" license. Mechncally the story isn't trying to do anything you haven't seen a million times in *all* other types of media.
However, the story is very good at providing you with the "feel" of the Warhammer 40k setting. If you are not interested in this license, don't get this game for it's narrative experience.
The graphics engine, some of the art assets, and physics engine all feel like they were in a lot of other games in the ps3/xbox1 generation.
The sound and music are not trying to make an artistic statement of note.
2)
This game is a third-person restricted shooters (only carry 3 guns at once, and one of these guns is never going to be used).
This game is also a third-person melee combat.
The amount of verbs you can use seems extremely empowering for the first 1/3-1/2 of the game.
But
The third person shooting becomes tedious because you have so few guns available.
The melee combat becomes tedious because you only really get 2 combos to use. The melee combat also has "execution" cutscenes, but only has about 6 -8 of them total. You may execute well over 100 enemies in a playthrough.
Ideally the game wants you to interchangbly use ranged and melee so as to not over rely on any one system.
However
The fatal flaw of the "gameplay" of this game is that toward the halfway point of the game, the game starts to give you many enemies with very powerful ranged weapons.
This creates a "trial and error" type of gameplay loop. Because if you're about to get into a situation where there are several of these types of enemies, you will probably die because you don't realize where they are all located before you can shoot them.
However, once you know where these enemies will stay, then it becomes quite easy to just target them at the start of an encounter.
Ranged enemies with heavy firepower  is the main way that the game creates challenge from 1/3-3/3 of the game.
If the game had made the melee combat system more robust, then they could create challenge through melee combat, while allowing the shooting to just be a secondary system.
But you will mostly win or lose in the late game based on your ability to quickly shoot things which do 90 percent of the damage toward you otherwise.
3)
I still recommend this game, it tries to be an experience. And it feels a lot less cynical than many other big-budget games of that console generation.

To begin, I must state Warhammer 40,000 is possible my greatest obsessions, I've loved playing Blood Angels, Kult of Speed Orkies and the Tau. I even wear the Imperial Aquila, for the God-Emperor will rise.
OK, OCD warning over with.
Warhammer 40,0000: Space Marine: having played through the single player enough times to get the single player achievements (minus the 40k kills one), I can honestly say that I have found only five issues with this game. And this actually bugs me the feth out of me, I could find more problems with the Legendary Half-Life. Even on the third playthrough (forthe weapon achievemnts) I found I was still enjoying the story, Relic might have choisen the wrong chapter, but the story was still good. Maybe not as indepth as Dawn of War (but after two games and four expansions of a RTS, that's not a surprise).
Gameplay:
I found this to a fun third-person shooter, with the melee smoothly included. The weapons is quite good, would prefer more, but I do love my dakka-dakka-dakka (*quickly beats down his inner Orkie*) so would have liked more, but the ones in game are nicely balanced, ammo drops are balanced IMO. Using the Thunder Hammer to smash throught the waves of Orks was so much fun.
Issues:
1) "'ere boyz, we bleed red??" Space Orks - they be plant based organisims (seriously, they grow like fungus), and so, GW made their blood green (like Vuncan blood).
2) "For da WAAAAAAGGGGHHHHHH!!!!!!!!!" Orkies, they don't speak Imperial Gothic (or the local language for your area), the few that have learnt it speak in really poor broken speak  (see Dawn of War for examples)
3) "For Macragge, for Roboute Guilliman, for the Emperor" Really, Ultramarines??? The most boring chapter of them all? The only semi-decent characters in the chapter are those that break from the teachings of Roboute Guilliman, just like the player charater in this game. I would have loved to have seen this with Bllod Angels or maybe Space Wolves, but then I could never choose between those two.
4) "May the Emperor be with us, Captain." Any human found saying "Emperor" instead of "God-Emperor" would be shot on sight by the Ecclesiarchy or their agents (Background: the Ecclesiarchy view the Emperor as a living god, and have spend thousands of years teaching the Imperial that He is the one true God, and anyone deviating from this view are seen as heretics, this also includes the Imperal Space Marine chapters, who view Him as the man that created the Primarchs and the Space Marines, to united Humanity across the stars.
5) "With me, Battle-Brothers" By the time I started playing this, the multiplayer had more or less dried up.  I was able to get a few games of the Dreadnoght DLC maps, and I can honestly say it was the most fun PvP modes I've come across in a long time.
Would I recommend this to non-40K obessed fans, well, I think I'll quote my non-geek, non-gamer brother "Space Marine? oh, the third-person shooter with the guy in big blue armour? That was so much fun, can't wait for the sequel."  My brother doesn't do games normally, but this e took time out to complete it (a first for him to my knowledge).
Would I recommend this to 40k obsessed fans: if they can look passed the first four points above, then yes, yes, and fething hell yes.
Thanks for reading, I hope you find this useful, and not put off by my "slight" obsession.

Namely, the ability to use any kind of LEGO element, and create your own vehicles/creatures/whatever the heck you want to ride. This is a huge draw for me when it comes to playing with LEGO in real life, and I'm a little dissatisfied that I haven't found that feature in this game in some capacity at the moment, considering it's supposed to be a big virtual LEGO playground.
I realize this may take some effort to program in, but imagine being able to build your own super mech from scratch with drill arms for tunneling, and jet boosters for flight! If the team at TT can manage to implement this feature, or at least a relatively close approximation, then I will be quite ecstatic.
Until then, I will say this is quite an impressively-realized sandbox game with a ton of customization options, even at this stage. And when you're building static objects with brick elements, it almost feels like playing with real LEGO! First the caveat; the game is clearly not finished and there are a number of rough edges including the fact that any sort of instruction or guidance whatsoever is absent. Secondly, the controls, especially the menu system for building, is a pain in the rear to use which makes it difficult to create your own structures with any degree of accuracy. Oh, and the vehicles are limited to those you find in the game; you can't build your own sleek jet or eighteen wheeler.
Ok, all that being said this game is awesome. It took me a while to really get into things and then the next thing I know three hours have passed. There are going to be the inevitable comparisons to Minecraft, but this is a completely different game. The focus is not on the crafting or even building, which is a bit weird for an open world Lego game, but rather on exploration and adventure. You travel the world unlocking animals, equipment and new looks for your minifig while traversing a variety of landscapes and fighting a few types of enemies.
What really makes this game great though is not the bazooka (and that thing is freaking sweet) but how well the controls work. Oddly enough Lego World manages to be the best 3D platformer I have ever played as well as better and more intuitive vehicle controls than many racing games. Frankly, this game is in a whole different world from Minecraft, not better or worse just different, or really anything else and I am looking forward to the updates as development progresses. If Tt and WB play this right they could be looking at a game that becomes a whole new paradigm that helps redefine what gaming is, and if the price for that is wonky building controls I'm fine with that.
Oh, and if you think you might ever want to play this game I'd suggest getting in now while it's cheap, because with the incredible level of depth and immersive to the gameplay I could easily see Lego World retailing for well over $60. Plus, the fact that you would have to wait at least six months for the final version, and that's half a year of missed awesomeness.

Personal Rating: Solid Rally Game
Classic Rating: ★★★★☆
Latest Rally Game I played on PC was Richard Burns Rally and that was a terrific Sim; other rally games I played on Playstation are the Colin McRae's Rally Series: those were mostly Arcade games and even though you cannot compare them to RBR, I enjoyed them quite a lot at the time.
Now, WRC 4 FIA WORLD RALLY CHAMPIONSHIP is a very well balanced game, it cannot be defined as a Simulator but it's not even an Arcade. I'm playing with an XBOX 360 Gamepad - no wheel here - and I'm using "Durazno" to change acceleration/brake from left/right trigger to right stick: I can't really get used to the triggers; I also have the handbrake an "A" and it feels really comfortable now.
This game can be played in different ways:
● Fast stage: single run on a random SS with a random car
● Single Stage/Rally: you can chose a single SS or a complete rally with a car you like, in the category you like
● Career Mode: You get contracts from your manager, start low in the Junior Category and go up till WRC Championship
● Multiplayer
One "big" problem I (and many other users) have is that online features (not talking about MP, because I usually play solo) is often down: the game cannot estabilish a connection to the server and you can't save progress online - yes, you need to register an account in the setup screen, before entering the game.
I bought this game on a Summer Sale, even though it was quite expensive for my wallet, but I'm very satisfied and feel like I can recommend it to anybody who likes Rally races - newbies and pros.

You can solve puzzles in very creative ways, but there is no incentive to try because the game rewards you exactly the same way no matter what you do. You could create a giant burning zombie made of bacon to melt an iceberg in your way, but using a flamethrower will net you exactly the same result, so eventually the appeal of using your imagination wears off and you'll settle for the easy solution just to push through faster. Even playing with friends or being inebriated (which usually make anything awesome) only extends the fun for so long.
If you're still curious and want to try it, at least wait for a sale, because $19.99 is just way too much of an asking price.

This is a great WWII strategic game. It is quite easy to learn, but harder to master, as these kind of games should be.
So, if you are looking for a game with an I-win-button, this is not it. If you look for a game where you need to think about what you do, and make a plan, this is a very good game.
First choice, do you play as the Axis or the Allies.
Second choice, what will your initial targets be? Aka, do you go for Poland, then France, then UK as  Germany?
Third choice, what do you focus your research on? Tanks? Infantry? Production?
Fourth choice, what do you build? Tanks? Infantry? Airplanes? Ships?
and so on.
But, all your choices should be made to play into a master plan, if not you might quickly be in a bad situation. So, you have all the aerial units on the board, but no tanks. Taking USSR might be  a tad hard then don't you think?
Is it the most complex strategy game I have ever played? No.
Is it a fun game? Yes.
Are the devs helpful with any isssues? Yes.
Is the game well made? Yes.
Are there many bugs? No.
Do I take a brief pause to think about what course to take from here? Yes.
