I've been playing Naval action for a bit now. I'd like to say that I could endorse this pretty looking game but I can't.
There are quite a few unsavory elements to the game. And here's a few.
1. Unrealistic and overpowered AI.
The NPC ships in the game routinely break nearly EVERY sailing rule of physics in the book, maneuvering like hydrofoils even in a headwind. And if THAT isn't bad enough, their gunnery puts even present day warships with their guided missiles to shame with a near 90% hit rate even at extreme range with maybe 2 out of every 3 hits landing criticals. Also they seem to have a higher rate of fire than most players.
The devs DID recently reduce the AI accuracy on small ships such as cutters and brigs hoping that less experienced players won't notice that all frigates and SoTLs still have the "sniper elite" level AI and dance around like fairies.
2. Toxic and hostile player community.
The game is supposed in alpha stage, which means that people playing the game are supposed to be providing feedback and making suggestions. However the player community will usually try to shout down player suggestions, throw insults and name-calling around, and attempt to derail the suggestion thread by leading it off topic into wild and immature tangents. They also seem to celebrate on the forums when frustrated players announce their intention to leave <like good riddance or don't let the door hit you in the *** on the way out, etc>.
3. Devs alienate PvE and Independent players.
With only a single PvE server and no access to alt characters if you want to experience something new, for example playing another nation or just plain want to play a new character they give you only 2 options either completely delete your old character and make an entirely new one sacrificing all your gold, ships, crafting resources and all that even though you still retain both your rank and crafting xp or be forced onto a PvP server where only 3 of their 7 or 8 playable nations are even viable and where ganking and griefing runs rampant.
They claim that this is designed to prevent economic exploitation but that kind of exploitation already exists in the game in the form of the current guild activity.
4. They are setting the stage for total disaster for the game economy and solo playability with their future economic goals.
In their most recent patch they did away with player ability to sail captured warships. Instead players now have to auto turn in warships they have captured in boarding combat over to their respective nation's admiralties for a tiny sum of gold and only allowing players to commandeer merchant ships. They also have future plans to completely do away with NPC resource vendors and allowing players to have the complete run of the economy. This action coupled with the canned ability to sail captured warships will inevitably open the door to massive overpricing of ships, and other items and make it impossible for any independent player to survive and be competitive.
It's like Pirates of the Burning Sea all over again.....Perhaps even worse.
At least portalus games has since begun to offer means of solo player survivability (if only to line their own pockets with real-world cash).
With this all said I can not in good conscience recommend this game to anyone.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Kitten Rampage is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was 0.145.
"Invade and Persuade with cuteness and cuddles."
Kitten Rampage is first-person shooter with you playing a kitten bent on mindless destruction using your twin lasers and chaingun. No, I'm not sure where a kitten got twin lasers and a chaingun either.
Graphics - Graphics are relatively simple, but do the job they're supposed to. Everything looks reasonable, although I didn't see any fancy effects or anything like that. And there's some very weird scaling: ducks as big as people and a wolf as big as a car.
As far as settings go, it's another Unity game, so the standard Unity settings are available: detail level settings from 'Fastest' to 'Fantastic', resolution settings, and the like. FPS was mostly good, although I experienced a little bit of stutter in some situations. I would expect a more powerful system than my laptop to have no problems whatsoever.
Sound - The first thing I noticed was the menu music: a rock riff played over and over again. It was mindless, but okay, and set the scene for the rest of the game. Within the game you can currently select from five soundtracks, but they're all a bit samey, with obvious rock and metal influences. Still, the choice is definitely appreciated. Sound effects are functional, with lasers 'zapping' and chaingun 'budda-budda-ing'. Your kitten's meow is pretty cute, too.
Gameplay - Typical WASD first-person shooter gameplay, but with a kitten as the protagonist. You choose a level (this version only has one time-trial level available, plus a free-roam version of the same, but from the menu options it looks like there will be seven in total, with both time-trial and free-range options for each) and then you run around destroying all of the objects in the environment. And that's pretty much it at the moment.
The level so far implemented has a number of goals to reach in the set time limit, with available time being increased by a couple of seconds with each object you destroy. There are some 'agents' that walk around the level, but other than that everything is static. The level includes vehicles that can be controlled (how!?), but so far there is little point in commandeering one except for a brief change of pace.
Your kitten has food, drink, and health indicators, but other than food and drink decreasing steadily and being renewed with collectibles from within the level, they don't seem to do very much yet. I'd like to see a bit more variation than just running around mindlessly destroying stuff, and some enemies to avoid as well, but hopefully they're on the way.
Pros:
+ original themed FPS with some weird ideas
+ developers have a clear path laid out for improvement and addition of gameplay
+ developers are actively fixing bugs and working on content
Cons:
- not much to do yet; only one level
- no plot to speak of; gets repetitive once you've achieved the stated goals
- a couple of crashes, some minor grammar errors in the menus
- grenades are pointless and cause very little damage
- Steam achievements don't seem to work
For a game that makes no sense at all, Kitten Rampage is kinda fun. There's not a lot to do yet, but the developers are active. Recommended if you're into weirdo FPS games and don't mind taking a punt on another Early Access title. Otherwise, you might want to wait and see where the developers take this one.

Just finished this game, and jumped straight to writing this review. I will try to be relatively spoiler free, so no worries on that.
To start, im a huge Warhammer 40k fan. Ive played all the RTS games, the MMO, and even tried my hand at the boardgame. I picked this game up preeetty late after its release, grabbing it on a 75% off sale. Let me say, it was worth it from a fan standpoint. Yet if this is your first Warhammer game, or dont know much about the factions or any general backstory, you might not exactly understand most of the game. Hell, even if you're a fan, you'll notice some things are a little out of place or dont make sense. Ill touch on that, but first the pros and cons.
Pros:
- TONS of action and blood.
- Plenty of enemies to kill on screen
- Factions present like Imperial Guard, Orks, SpaceMarines and Chaos.
- Good story length (roughly 7 hours)
- Challenging sequences and fights.
- People still play the multiplayer, and its fun.
- Different weapons to choose from, so you can pick and choose what you like.
- Very WH40k esque scenery and locations.
- 3rd Person with aiming and melee was done nicely and smoothly.
Cons:
- The hordes of enemies coming at you are just clones of one another. Same models for each "class" of enemy (Slugga Boyz, Shoota Boyz, ect.)
- So. Many. Elevators. Seriously.
- The story can be predicted easily, and leaves out or throws away tons of relevant details.
- Some enemies (im looking at you, Chaos) you've never seen in a WH40k game before. Trust me, its weird.
- Very linear. Lots of hallways in certain chapters. You can never choose another "path" to get to the objective, theres literally only 1 way there.
- You wont see any other Space Marines until a certain point in the game. Even then you fight with them for a measly 5 minutes. I would have loved to fight alongside them for longer in more badass locations.
I wont go into story details. If you are a WH40k fan, get this game on sale. Its sooo worth it so play as a singular Space Marine. You'll die occasionally, even in Normal difficulty. The story was kind of meh after the first half but oh well. It has potential for a sequel.

---- If you dislike reading lengthy reviews, you can skip to the conclusion for #/10 and tl;dr at the end --------
Of the 13,318 reviews given to this game, 97% of them are positive. As a game overall it has recieved an 'Overwhelmingly Positive' response. With a game like this -it seems to me- it is almost sacrilege to give it a bad review, and it's quite hard to find a balanced one among the pile. All you generally seem to read is why it is awesome,why it will change your life,etc,etc... which generally aren't that helpful in terms of an actual critique.
To that end, I will endeavour here to give my honest -and hopefully balanced/critical- opinion.
Overall, I found this game really good, and I liked it a lot. You play as two scientists who make there dying charges last wishes' 'come true' by delving into their memories and finding a way to make it happen by implanting the impetus in their childhood. To this end, the altered life created by the two is the only thing patients remember before they draw their final breath( which, quite subtly, forces one to think about one's own life and choices). Their current case concerns Johnny, a dying man who wants to go to the moon, but the catch is he doesn't know why. This premise sets up your objective: go backwards through his memories to find the reason, and make it happen. Throughout the course of your journey, this man's life and character are fleshed out by bearing witness to key moments in his life. To 'leap' back through his memories you must collect 'links' to activate a certain memento which brings you to another past event.
This mode of storytelling is highly captivating, as the plot unravels by going back in time(so to speak), and kept me engaged throughout: you're not playing to see the effects of actions, you're playing for the causes, which adds a certain depth to the game. However, I did find that this came across as slightly voyeuristic at times, which cheapened the experience a little( i.e. it's feels a lttle stalker-y). For the most part though, I felt suitably immersed. Within each level('memory'), collecting the links is not that difficult, and provides a small yet gratifying sense of reward so you get to continue on. After collecting them one must solve a puzzle by piecing together the memento to form a complete picture, which did seem slightly superfluous, but to interest of those(like me) who like puzzles. Some reviews have raised the issue that the gameplay is overly-simplistic, but I would argue it is just simple enough. Ultimately it is the story that drives this game, not the game mechanics. Take out the latter and you have a visual novel, but leave them in and you have just enough participation to feel like a part of the story. It is a delicate balance, but one that I think it struck quite well.
In terms of Aesthetics, I was not a huge fan of the graphics. A listed key feature is the 'classic RPG aesthetics', but this is not an RPG, nor does the game lend itself to this type of look. Having said that, I'm not sure what would have looked better, so I cannot offer much by way of constructive criticism here. The graphics did grow on me after a time, but something just felt not quite right.
The game's soundtrack is pretty beautiful, but the main theme ('River's Song/'To The Moon') is featured prominently throughout, to the point that it really is the only memorable tune from it.  A little musical variation would have been nicer, though they use the song at just the right moments so it doesn't feel over-used like the are shoving it in your face. It is subtly poignant and simple, which adds to the overall tone of the game.
One of the best features of the game is the dialogue. Though the two scientists have the standard 'one-is-serious-one-is-a-bit-of-a-clown' dynamic going - which has been seen in countless mediums before- it still seems to work well such that one isn't completely put off by the characters. There are some utterly hilarious moments( such as an extremely random RPG meta-game-instance near the beginning) and wise-cracks( which pretty much all come from Dr. Watts) that punctuate the sombre, sentimental storyline. Yet at the same time there are also some beautiful scenes between Johnny and his wife that balance this out.
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game. It is an achievement in story-driven gaming, and one that deserves to be played. Fine, it can be a tad cheesy/cloying at times(which might put some off),but at the end of the day this is a love story, and love can be cheesy sometimes. It is set up and plays out as a sentimental ballad( I don't mean that in a derogatory fashion), which it accomplishes beautifully. Judging it by the ending alone, I would give it a 9/10; it is a spectacular conclusion which does not fail to tug at the heartstrings( some will say it made them cry, but to me that is a tad strong). However it be wrong to judge a work based on a single instance. Overall I woud give this game a 7/10: it is a gem to play through and one that should be treasured, yet- despite the rave reviews- nothing absolutely life-changing.
tl;dr Go play this game. It's truly great. Just try not to buy into most of the hype.

I picked this up on sale thinking I would make a quick playthrough of 10-20 hours in between other games and not hoping for much considering all the negative reviews, but I’ve been hooked since the first moments I started playing. The graphics, level design, detail, lore and general atmosphere are amazing. Just running around in half destroyed NY-city without shooting a single bullet is an experience in itself.
There are some great original missions, and yes, there’s a lot of repetition, but that’s the nature of this type of games where grinding is necessary IF you wish to max out your gear. Personally, I enjoy it and the game offers lots of different ways to obtain this gear. The amount of weapons, gear, mods, talents, currencies, crafting materials ...etc can be overwhelming but it also offers depth and complexity.
Despite what some people say, everything is doable SOLO, even the Dark Zone which is the PVP zone. Yes, you will die often, that’s what happens in a high risk and high reward PVP zone. That’s what makes it fun. And in my experience most players will rather work with you than against you. Matchmaking doesn’t really work but you can easily group up with other players once you’ve entered the zone.
Yes, there are some bugs, server disconnects, AI sometimes acts stupid, and other small quirks. But if you get tilted on these you might as well stop gaming all together and start a new hobby, like gardening. Tomatoes never bug out ... I think. Never seen one in real life.
The “Underground’ DLC is also worth it, offering a new way to grind for high level gear: random missions will be generated based on some settings you can define: difficulty, length of the mission etc... Haven’t tried the other 2 main DLC’s.

In the pantheon of WWII Turn Based Games, SC:WiE hits the sweet spot between too simple and too complex. You have a wealth of research & build options to customize any kind of historical army you can conceive; but you lose the tedious and demanding micro required by overly complex engines like Hearts of Iron.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who appreciates turn-based WWII games. It is very easy to learn. More importantly, it is very difficult to stop playing.
Out of the box, the game is compelling. Immediately, you are grabbed by the 'one more turn' bug that all good turn-based games possess. Replayability is extremely high. Both factions, Axis and Allies, are enjoyable in and of themselves. The Research/Upgrade path is so flexible there are far more than one way to victory.
After that, Fury includes a full blown game editor. It will take you an hour or so to figure out the outlay of the editor, but once you grasp the basics, using the editor could not be more simple, Want to give Germany a Heavy Tank brigade to start the war? Easy. Britain to have a full blown airforce? No problem. Don't like your starting technology, change it. Maybe build an entire industrial complex in North Africa, or anywhere else you darned well please. Very doable. You didn't know there was oil next to Warsaw? You didn't look hard enough!
Again, my highest recommendation. Well done!

Excellent strategy game in WW2 arena. Its is deeper than appears on the surface and good planning pays dividends, but not too much to detract from instant playability. The multi player aspect is excellent, look on the matrix/slitherine forums and you can find players to go head to head with.

This is an old school wargame: turn-based and hex-based. Easy to learn and easy to play. Yet elegant enough to be just as credible as a strategic simulation of WW2 as many other games that have a steep learning curve or that require a huge amount of micromanagement.
Military technological advancement, diplomacy, naval and submarine warfare, aerial warfare, supply, weather effects, historical events and decisions, historical commanders ... : it's all there.
You can play both sides in five different campaigns (set in different years of the war). There are many different paths to victory and you can experiment with different strategies.
Just as much fun playing against the AI a against a human opponent.
There were a few bugs in the game, but those were ironed out before the release on Steam. (I've been playing the game since its release last year by Slitherine).

I ve been playing turn based strategic games since the early 90s and I must say thisone is a true masterpiece. Since game is part 3 of the series, and after spending 100+ hours playing it, I must say its easy to learn basics and quite hard to master. Multiplayer is very challenging because game contains loads of possible strategies for axis/allied player (instead of first part of the series - SC1) .
From a grand strategy scale point of view - this game implemets MPP - military production points which Your side earns each turn from cities, mines&ports, used for purchasing various types of units (armies, panzer groups, corps, garnisons, AA, fighters, various bomber units...), research and diplomacy. Adaptability of usage of MPPs may differ from each game, since You must carefully watch research/diplomacy of the opponent to be able to counter it. Also, there are force limits, entrenchment, weather (very important) and various other factors which may be different from game to game and all this factors insuring that each new game will feel fresh and challenging.
Land, air & naval combat are also well balanced , although some players feel that axis bombers are a bit too strong, forgetting that they could have had that annuled with investment in AA research and upgrading units. This is what makes this game so unique, there are tonnes of possibillities how and  where to go, but it doesnt make a big confusion. Decisions are relatively quick and easy to be done.
Great + comes from the historical events that occur from turn to turn. For example, Axis player may choose to occupy Norway by event, with no need to position and transport units. But if You choose yes for that event - U loose some MPPs. Allied player may choose for example weather to attack Vichy fleet with some percentage for success, loose some Mpps but also alligning Vichy government towards the axis.
Experienced players may find single player games a bit dull, but AI is very capable in dealing damage to unexperienced players.
Cheers for Hubert Cater and Bill Runacre, amazing game, game feels so good that I can hardly see possiblity of making SC4 ever (only graphics may improve)

I love parts of this game but just cannot reccomend it as it stands. The devs have a fantastic setup for the future of this game and will surely make a game that will go down in history. But as of right now, there is just too many flaws that make me rage quit this game every time I try and get into it. I'll list some of my complaints below. Keep in mind that I have been playing this game quite a bit to try and see if maybe I am doing something wrong, but I am convinced that this game has too many issues for me personally.
1. There is no tutorial at all.
This game has a very very steep learning curve, almost like hopping into IL-2 1946 on max realism for your first time. You are dropped into the game and are on your own immediately. They don't even tell you how to open your sails to move. You are forced to get in touch with a clan who can train you and provide you with some basic knowledge about how to even use the port menus. Joining a clan isn't too bad of an idea since almost all of the larger clans are happy to help but if you like to be a lone wolf it can be very frustrating.
2. The AI is extremely overpowered if you try to battle by yourself.
This is perhaps my biggest pet peeve about this game. If you are by yourself trying to do a mission on your level it is nearly impossible to sink the AI. I did a battle in which I was in a Navy Brig, the AI was in a regular Brig. I had 37 leaks on his ship and he was at near zero armor. He was still floating like nothing happened. He could even sail into the wind at 8 - 10 knots while the second I turned into the wind, I came to a dead stop. I was at around quarter armor all around and had 0 leaks and I was taking on water at crazy rates after one broadside. I have never been able to take on an AI in battle unless I had a fleet with me or took on a low level mission while using a large ship. The AI seems to be way too accurate, way too maneuverable, and have armor that seems like it's made out of cast iron.
3. The optimization is absolutely terrible.
Not much really to be said on this subject. The game has pretty bad optimization.
4. The game is extremely grindy for XP
If you want to level up within a day you have to get used to doing back to back missions. It's not bad at first but once you reach level 4 or 5, it takes forever to level up. If you want to get this to play for only a couple hours a day, you might want to get used to the cutter because it will take you weeks to level up. While this can be a con, it is also understandable since you don't want everyone rolling around in the best ship.
I have many more complaints, but I am really not trying to go on a b*tch fest here. I'm just trying to say what I don't like about this game. I will probably continue to try and like this game but as I said before, unless you are constantly with a couple of people to help you in battle, it is near impossible to win fights unless you go against a small ship. For $40 I would personally say wait until this goes on sale for at the most $25 and pick it up then if you really want it.

The visual fidelity isn't the best, but it doesn't seem to matter much as the camera is relatively zoomed out and usually moves quite fast. The feel of the driving is spot on, and the multiplayer is an absolute blast.
Toybox Turbos is a fantastic little modern take on overhead racers of the past and well worth your time.

Ugh. Where to begin? This isn't a fanboy review so is you're looking for a quick read maybe look elsewhere.
The Division was released to much hype, controversy and mixed expectations. Par for the course for a Ubisoft game.
The good, the meh,bad and the ugly at a mere 70 hours in.
: The graphics in this game on ultra look pretty damn good. Great sun rays and reflections running on a 1070 gtx. Others have reported glitches; I cannot. Then again I purchased this when patch 1.7 came out. The snowdrop engine looks fantastic on a high-end rig.
it is clear that the devs at ubisoft put incredible detail and effort in the layout of the map. The city is incredibly detailed in its openness. Everything from flashing lights, mist from sewers, animals roaming the streets and killing other animals, to dynamic weather system. The blinding snowstorms are amazing and reduce your visibility. The lighting in this game is incredible. The reflecftions are incredible. When an enemy AI is crouched behind cover in back of a light source, you see his reflection movement for movement. For an open-ended game streets are littered with abandoned cars, the destitute, the ill, the dead and enemy AI.
not bad. Each level offers decent cover and concealment options. You can go in guns blazing or covertly. Some notable missions include Napalm site and the Russian consulate.
Individual campaign missions are fun I have to say. With the amount of grinding and levelling up previously difficult missions will become easier. The AI on normal or under your level are too easy. But I've found challenging missions with enemy AI levels 4 levels higher than mine to be a challenge worth repeating. One thing I enjoy with this game is trying missions with higher enemy AI and being forced to repeat it with different tactics. Some missions are simply too tough, but when you return later with a higher level and better gear, it becomes doable. The fact that you can
missions on different difficulty levels along with friends is a great aspect. This I found highly satisfying.

you get a limited array of weapons that deal increasing amounts of damage. At first it's exciting to get better weapons. Then as you progress you get classes of weapons, be it specialized, etc. AI and NPCs will drop clothing articles that you can equip which are frankly useless. A one-minute firefight as you reach a high enough level means you get some XP, guns you can sell and useless clothing articles.
pretty fun when you can find someone to matchmake on missions. Obviously this game is more fun the larger group of friends you have. Once you hit the higher levels, finding similarly levelled people and going on missions is fun. I have to say, the people I have met and gamed with online have been nothing but polite, respectful with a sense of teamplay and collaboration. This for me is the most fun aspect of the game: making friends, connecting, hitting up Daily Missions, High value targets and redoing missions with different tactics.
this is the meat of the game. You can go rogue or in large groups and essentially become a fast moving shooting machine. If MP is all you want this may be your thing. You get the chance to acquire high-value weapons but also lose them. Can be highly frustrating because it is a no holds barred shooting arena.
Side quests are boring and fast repetitive. How many times do you have to protect and defend a) supplies, b) inept JTF soldiers who can't fight c) rescue civilians? Boring!
: Clothing is frankly useless. The Division is insanely detailed in really
options, like how you can get cypher keys to open vanity items.

After running around on main and side quests, the game becomes so convoluted you forget just what the hell is going on. The campaign itself frankly sucks. Side quests are repetitive with the exact same mission (turn on water, fetch and defend supplies, etc).
The Dark zone after awhile. Shoot, respawn, acquire loot and rinse and repeat.
. At retail price of 79.99, it is blatantly overpriced. Given the amount of grinding, lack of cohesive campaign, for that price you are paying for a great looking repetitive grinding MP experience.
: The trailers showed a team of 4 people hitting up the police station, chatting as if they were talking in real-time. We learn later that this was all staged. AngryJoe does a great job categorizing the lies and half-truths in comparison pre- and post- launch game options.
On higher levels, the enemy AI are total bullet sponges. While this forces you to use tactics on the fly, emptying my Black Market AK light machine gun with extended magazine twice in the face of one guy and then having to reload is downright ridiculous. On some missions I have emptied my LMG into AI only to be killed with one shot while under cover.
For the first I would say 10 or so levels the game is fun as you are acquiring more gear in leveling up. But after level 20 unless you really get into the dark Zone the game becomes its worst enemy which is a grind Fest.
And finally as many people will probably agree, the worst thing about this game is that
Ubisoft as per standard operating procedure hyped the s h i t out of this game. The trailers which have now been debunked made this game seem like it was something it wasn't. The voice acting we all saw during the trailer was staged and we were all led to believe the game was different. Rather than develop a really well fleshed out campaign the devs dumped all of their money into visual assets and multiplayer. This to me is the direction of billion-dollar gaming companies which is to develop high-end looking games that are hollow inside except for of course the multiplayer experience which sells. Instead of making a continuing immersive story which I think they could have done Ubisoft has yet again fulfilled its mandate of overhyping, misleading and disappointing serious gamers who want something aside from multiplayer. It's a shame because I still believe that gaming can also include a single player campaign or Co-Op campaign instead of the cliched multiplayer route. Today in my opinion the only series of games that' Ubisoft has made where they combined visual Aesthetics with the single-player campaign is the Far Cry series. That and maybe the ANNO series.
: If Ubisoft can go on to
off of one game, the least they could is write a halfway decent campaign.
Long story short: at $80 retail price this game is not worth it. What started out as a promising game turns out to be a grind Fest which only can last so long. If you manage to buy this game on sale like I did at 60 percent off at 23 USD, then this for me makes it a bit more worthwhile time and energy-wise even with the grinding.
This game has its fanboys and its haters. Based on the price and the strength of the visual layout and the level design along with some of the more challenging missions like the Napalm site and Russian consulate,  I would give this game a 6 or 7/10 and therefore a weak thumbs up.

---- If you dislike reading lengthy reviews, you can skip to the conclusion for #/10 and tl;dr at the end --------
Of the 13,318 reviews given to this game, 97% of them are positive. As a game overall it has recieved an 'Overwhelmingly Positive' response. With a game like this -it seems to me- it is almost sacrilege to give it a bad review, and it's quite hard to find a balanced one among the pile. All you generally seem to read is why it is awesome,why it will change your life,etc,etc... which generally aren't that helpful in terms of an actual critique.
To that end, I will endeavour here to give my honest -and hopefully balanced/critical- opinion.
Overall, I found this game really good, and I liked it a lot. You play as two scientists who make there dying charges last wishes' 'come true' by delving into their memories and finding a way to make it happen by implanting the impetus in their childhood. To this end, the altered life created by the two is the only thing patients remember before they draw their final breath( which, quite subtly, forces one to think about one's own life and choices). Their current case concerns Johnny, a dying man who wants to go to the moon, but the catch is he doesn't know why. This premise sets up your objective: go backwards through his memories to find the reason, and make it happen. Throughout the course of your journey, this man's life and character are fleshed out by bearing witness to key moments in his life. To 'leap' back through his memories you must collect 'links' to activate a certain memento which brings you to another past event.
This mode of storytelling is highly captivating, as the plot unravels by going back in time(so to speak), and kept me engaged throughout: you're not playing to see the effects of actions, you're playing for the causes, which adds a certain depth to the game. However, I did find that this came across as slightly voyeuristic at times, which cheapened the experience a little( i.e. it's feels a lttle stalker-y). For the most part though, I felt suitably immersed. Within each level('memory'), collecting the links is not that difficult, and provides a small yet gratifying sense of reward so you get to continue on. After collecting them one must solve a puzzle by piecing together the memento to form a complete picture, which did seem slightly superfluous, but to interest of those(like me) who like puzzles. Some reviews have raised the issue that the gameplay is overly-simplistic, but I would argue it is just simple enough. Ultimately it is the story that drives this game, not the game mechanics. Take out the latter and you have a visual novel, but leave them in and you have just enough participation to feel like a part of the story. It is a delicate balance, but one that I think it struck quite well.
In terms of Aesthetics, I was not a huge fan of the graphics. A listed key feature is the 'classic RPG aesthetics', but this is not an RPG, nor does the game lend itself to this type of look. Having said that, I'm not sure what would have looked better, so I cannot offer much by way of constructive criticism here. The graphics did grow on me after a time, but something just felt not quite right.
The game's soundtrack is pretty beautiful, but the main theme ('River's Song/'To The Moon') is featured prominently throughout, to the point that it really is the only memorable tune from it.  A little musical variation would have been nicer, though they use the song at just the right moments so it doesn't feel over-used like the are shoving it in your face. It is subtly poignant and simple, which adds to the overall tone of the game.
One of the best features of the game is the dialogue. Though the two scientists have the standard 'one-is-serious-one-is-a-bit-of-a-clown' dynamic going - which has been seen in countless mediums before- it still seems to work well such that one isn't completely put off by the characters. There are some utterly hilarious moments( such as an extremely random RPG meta-game-instance near the beginning) and wise-cracks( which pretty much all come from Dr. Watts) that punctuate the sombre, sentimental storyline. Yet at the same time there are also some beautiful scenes between Johnny and his wife that balance this out.
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game. It is an achievement in story-driven gaming, and one that deserves to be played. Fine, it can be a tad cheesy/cloying at times(which might put some off),but at the end of the day this is a love story, and love can be cheesy sometimes. It is set up and plays out as a sentimental ballad( I don't mean that in a derogatory fashion), which it accomplishes beautifully. Judging it by the ending alone, I would give it a 9/10; it is a spectacular conclusion which does not fail to tug at the heartstrings( some will say it made them cry, but to me that is a tad strong). However it be wrong to judge a work based on a single instance. Overall I woud give this game a 7/10: it is a gem to play through and one that should be treasured, yet- despite the rave reviews- nothing absolutely life-changing.
tl;dr Go play this game. It's truly great. Just try not to buy into most of the hype.

I missed all the old CRPGs, but loved the Dragon Age Inquisition tactical combat.  This game has an incredible story, and the turn-based tactical combat fits a very unique and fun niche.  The game isn't hand-holding, and some quests can be very difficult to figure out (I'm still amazed how hard the nick quest was to figure out).  Combat is never dull, and death can strike fast if things aren't planned well.  There have been multiple occasions where I'd try and die multiple times before coming up with an actual sound strategy; it's almost a puzzle to figure out the best path to defeat the enemies--the interplay with spells is fantastic.  A simple example of this interplay, calling the rain, then grouping enemies in puddles with my tank before zapping them with lightning stunning them all, I can't think of any other game I've played where tactics were so strong.  The lack of hand-holding, and attention to detail is great, there are no quest markers and relying on wits to deduce locations is great the layout is always sufficiently described to derive the location, and something I've missed in other games.  This game has shot to the top of my all time favorites, and is well worth playing.

Original Sin is a rather classic RPG with no "hand-holding", an amazing turn-based combat system, a load of well written, fully voiced dialogs with vocus on character development, an detailed crafting system and a Coop-Mode. If these are the things you enjoy in gaming, you should buy this game, trust me.
A few more words about the combat system: It is defenitily the highlight of Original Sin, especially the magic system. There are dozens of different spells with different synergies, which you can combine to manipulate the enviroment and your enemies. Here are a few examples: Oilfiled + Fire = Fire AoE, Waterfield + Thunder = Stun AoE, Waterfiled + Ice, Ice AoE (Enemies slip and fall over, my favourite). All these combinations led often to funny ( and sometimes not intended) effects, I acutally enjoyed every single fight.
The difficulty ( I played on normal) was challenging and fair in my opinion, but if you're new to the genre, I'd recommend the easy mode, since most enemies can get quite tough, espically in the late game.
The dialog system offers a ton of written text, which might put off some people, but you can always listen to the excellent voice-over instead.
However, there are some negative aspects, I'd like to mention. The story is rather generic and although is started quite interesting, it flatend down towards the midgame. In my opinion, most of the sidequest were actually much more entertaining than the main plot.
There are also some bugs, which I encountered during my playthrough, such as not working crafting-recepies or
dialog-options. Still, a simple reload always solved the case for me, so no game breaking bugs.
In conclusion: an amzing game with a great combat system and a few minor flaws, so if you're a fan of classic RPGs, I would totally recommend you this game.

This game is mostly great and if you enjoy a good RPG with interesting turn based combat, then you should give this game a try.  For me, the combat was the highlight of the game as the classes and related abilities make each battle unique.  Furthermore, the synergies between spells, abilities, and environmental elements make combat highly unpredictable, constantly keeping you on your toes.  That being said, this game has some flaws that I need to mention so that potential buyers aren't caught unaware.  If you can look past these flaws, then you'll enjoy this game.
First and foremost are the bugs.  I find myself constantly annoyed by something that doesn't work right.  Whether it's a crafting recipe, a combination of spells interacting erratically or not at all, or some random effect that happens inexplicably (i.e. dealing poison damage by shooting a silver arrow).  The turn order indicator at the top of the screen will sometimes get stuck and you'll have no idea whose turn it is.
Knowing the type of surface you're standing on is extremely important, however, many times I found that the surface texture wasn't showing correctly so I end up standing in an electrified puddle, or poison, or fire, when there's nothing showing under my character.  What makes this even more problematic is that your characters will happily run right into these hazards instead of pathing around them.  There are further annoyances, however these are a few examples of what to expect.  I've also had some crashes on rare occasions but it's mostly the in game bugs that are the most problematic.  The key is to save often.  Thankfully the game lets you save at almost any time, even during combat.
The reason that the above issues are more than minor nuisances is that the game can be very hard.  There's nothing wrong with a difficult game, but when you have to constantly contend with the problems mentioned above, it takes away from the fun and makes the experience more aggravating.
Finally, the difficulty curve is all over the place.  One moment you'll be ripping through a group of enemies with ease, and the next you get destroyed before you've had your first turn.  It just feels completely random.  This appears to be done purposefully as there are some events\encounters that just outright kill you, and you have to reload, so prepare to quicksave\quickload often.

Downwell presents itself as a little hidden gem, which you can pick up and play with enjoyment. Professional reviews showered the game with praise and I decided to yell CHECK on it.
Unfortunately Downwell, while not bad, doesn't blow my mind either. It fails on three levels. The easiest to describe is a technical one. You are playing the arcade, presumably skill based game and the last thing you want to experience as a player are the framerate drops when you get hit. Stupidly enough, those framedrops seem to be intentional on the behalf of the developer and I seriously question, if someone thought this was a good idea.
My second gripe is an unsatisfying gameplay loop. Imagine... You jump into the well. There are enemies that like to ambush, chase and attack in most annoying ways possible. Bats are an epitome of unfairness, when they can attack you off-screen or be placed in the most inconvenient places. You will get hit and your health pool is small and hard to recover. Controls are hyper-sensitive and as you try to get use to a weapon upgrade you don't like, you die... and the process starts all over again.
It's not really satisfying enough. In other good perma-death games you feel that you are getting better and that next try will be more successful... or you figured out the new strategy. However, in Downwell, you will find yourself blaming the game more than your lack of skill. Game gets slightly better on later levels when game decides to be fairer and enemies are far more predictable. Still, you will spend far more time in Caverns and Catacombs and get frustrated with those bats and skulls and other annoyances (and coincidently, the music after level 2 becomes much less painful for ears)
At last, what happens when you make a good progress or finishing the game? You get nothing. There are unlockables, but they are so obvious afterthought that it's counterproductive to mention it. I walked away from the game being angry and relieved that I'm finally done with it. I had similar experience with Spelunky, which are a platformer that likes to emphasize luck over a genuine skill.
And you tell me that some game journalist gave this game a 10/10? I struggle to find anything remarkable in Downwell's design or execution. I would suggest avoiding this game. It's not worth your time and effort in my opinion, but it's not a trainwreck, so maybe you will find something in it. I fold.

Great fun but priced too high because singleplayer is short.
I never played any 3D MicroMachines games so I can't compare that gameplay for you. But I was a massive fan of the first 2D MicroMachines growing up and that game's DNA can be found here despite being quite different on the surface. This game just "feels" right and is plain FUN! There's a wide variety of cars that do feel quite different, but there's a nearly screen length massive drafting system. So you can catch most cars with most cars and keep races close. Then while they went big on the amount of cars they dropped the ball on track amount. Most of the track themes are there though and provide a wide variety of fun scenery. I do really wish they would've included outdoor and garage tracks. And then there's enough modes to keep you interested throughout the campaign (Race, Overtake, Time Trial, Survive, and some other time related one). It was simple fun that brought back some good feelings.
I did manage to 100% the singleplayer aspects within 2.5hrs which doesn't thrill me. The original MicroMachines was pretty much unbeatable as the difficulty increased. This rarely posed much of a challenge. Which is where we come into the price discussion. $14.99USD is too much. I would feel pretty bummed out at the singleplayer lack of a challenge if I forked over that much. But that's what sales and bundles are for! This was a superb bundle toss in game for me and became a hidden gem because of the bargain.
Simply put; I had fun. Lots of fun. But not full price fun. Shop wisely!
Edit 1: Played some local multiplayer. Good fun. Only one game mode which is "elimination". And car choices are limited to one of the classes at a time. These consist of 4 or 5 car choices. So it ends up another shallow experience. Fun! But shallow.
Edit 2: Finding some good times on online multiplayer while its populated from the recent Humble Bundle crowd. Still just one game mode, and there can be host lag. But eh, its another couple hours of fun. Receommended for sure. :)

If you know me, you know I love Fallout. And Fallout 3 is my absolute Favorite for the series. The game was great on its own, but with mods, it has become an order of magnitude better.
If playing with mods, this is how I recommend your story should go, ignoring actual distances involved.
Escape the Vault, have no idea where dad went and get scared down to a boat with a friendlyish face.
Run away to Point Lookout (You are new out the vault, the wasteland scares you and you like the sound of greenery. Plus rednecks should be easier than raiders, screw artificial hitpoints).
Wander back to the wasteland feeling cocky. Hear a radio call for help, decide "hell yeah, I'll free some slaves". Head to the Pitt. Kick♥♥♥♥♥and come back to wasteland a hardened warrior.
Feel ready to wander the wasteland bit. Meet the outcasts, use your Pip-Boy to help them and get some awesome loot and training. Step forth on to the Capitol wastes, now a total armored badass.
Head back to Megaton to pick up dad's trail (Having been gone a while it makes more sense it should be as cold as it is in game). Play though the main game picking up companions.
Complete broken steel. Wander the wastes admiring your good work as the Lyons Brotherhood expands. Catch a strange signal, the zeta crash. Being abducted it makes sense you leave behind your companions. Complete Zeta.
Make sure you have Mothership Zeta Crew Installed. Play through whole new game section as you secure the Capitol Wasteland in the name of your new army.
Such is a glorious playthrough.

I really struggle to understand the negative reviews of this game......I understand the frustrations at release but the game now is fantastic.
It is so rare to get a complete open world, rpg open world shooter. The Campaign is brilliant and confronting, the attention to details is beyond words and will make your skin crawl. I had fun all the way to the end and was actually gutted to see the story finish.
The loot system is great, it is easy to get end game gear, what is hard is grinding out the perfect stat roles. End game gear has sets like any other MMO RPG, 3, 4 set bonuses eg. You have your legend weapons but they are basically useless which is a bummer. Lots of loots drops to the point it is like Borderlands. You craft weapons, armour and mods.
You can fully customise your guns and armour to boost certain stats and adapt your guns to situations or your style of play. Whether you want to boost range, accuracy, damage eg.
The map is huge, heaps of enemies pop up who are easily defeated so it is still fun but doesnt feel like a chore to kill them, they also drop gear that is useful so it isnt just kill and move on. End game you will find mini bosses wandering around or events will pop up like a supply drop of rare items and you have to kill the enemies guarding it.
The darkzone (PVP area) is brilliant, it makes me feel like i am playing a survival game, knowing you can be jumped for your loot is exilerating. Chasing down people who have gone 'rogue' is also fun.

Having only played the original Scribblenauts on the DS prior to this game, it's really nice to see where the series has progressed. Controls are simple and intuitive, though sometimes a bit slower than need be. Level design and exploration is creative and engaging, with fun visuals that are unique for most levels.
The downside of this game is that there really isn't much challenge. Most of the time, solutions are painfully obvious as soon as soon as the puzzle is presented. Even though there are hundreds of possible solutions to a puzzle like "The student is hungry!" there's limited fun in finding out the most obscure food that the game recognizes.
Levels are expansive, but predictable. Within each larger area, you'll find a handful of sub-levels that contain a handful of starite fragments, as well as a full starite earned by completing a sub-sub level. Although the locations and characters you encounter are varied and interesting, this continued structure leaves the game feeling flat...almost bringing up memories of games like "Mario is Missing."
Although as an adult I've always been drawn to the charm of Scribblenauts' promise to allow the player to create anything, this game's vocabulary seemed more limited to me than the initial title. Yes, you can apply adjectives now, but that's rarely important to gameplay.
Scribblenauts Unlimited is a good game, though it's formulaic gameplay could end up turning a lot of people off. There is some appeal to gamers of all ages, but this feels distinctly like a game for children.

This game is pure imagination!  A huge improvement over previous Scribblenauts games, especially for how it encourages you to think outside the box by adding adjectives into the mix.  It's also a ton of fun, which is a plus.
Plain busywork with no real payoff. You wouldn't think solving puzzles with dead babies would be unrewarding but there you have it.

I feel somewhat torn about this game. On the one hand it is a competent rally game we had not since Colin McRae Rally 2005 and Richard Burns Rally. On the other hand it has some serious flaws. The game has quite arcady driving physics, and if it is good or not for you, it depends on your personal preferences. This is a proper rally game, so it does not have any Ghymkhana, rallycross or baja nonsense. It contains 4 classes (WRC, WRC 2, WRC 3 and Junior WRC) and 13 rallies with 6 special stages each.
On the other hand the amount of roads is quite limited. Each rally has 6 stages, but there are driven mostly through the same pieces of road, so there are only about 2 unique special stages per rally. The fact that kept us playing old rally games was great amount of special stages and vehicles, there just is not enough of that. The game is capped to 30 frames per second, what is unacceptable for a PC driving game nowadays, but there are some methods to remove this cap. The game still has some bugs, which are not game braking, but still can be annoying for some people.
The bottom line is that if you are into rally games, get it on sale. It has too much flaws to be recommended at full price, but if you can get it cheaper, it is worth playing.

Reviewing an early release is notoriously hard, the game is still in development and who knows where it is going to go. But Naval Action, while still an Alpha, is shockingly playable for a game so early in its development.
Game play is rather unique, and by unique I mean SLOW. Combat is slow, travel in the overworld is slow, crafting is slow, and that slowness is probably one of the greatest points of this game. If you are a fan of most modern games MMO or otherwise this slowness can be a schock. This is not Call Of Duty, or War Thunder. Naval Action is more a game of chess than a game of whack a mole. You plan your attack, you turn a few points off the wind and you wait for the enemy to roll into your broadside. A single ship to ship combat can take up to half an hour, a multi ship battle can take over an hour. Travel in the overworld takes planning and time, a trade route may take you hours of real time to travel. Nothing happens fast and in this quick twitch game heavy world the stately if slow action in Naval Action is a welcome change.
Factions are a fact of life in Naval Action, there are no independent ships. You will have to join a faction in character creation but that does not mean Kill On Sight for every other faction; French Privateers will peacefully cruise past Spanish ships of the line in neutral waters, but you do need to watch your back. Just because you don’t attack does not mean you will not be attacked.
Overall this is a pleasing game, but you do have to set some time aside to play a good session. I for one look forward to the further development of Naval Action, it has a lot of great potential.

When you were younger did you ever play “the floor is lava” or some sort of similar game?  Hopefully someone else out there did, because for me it was second perhaps only to the “jump over cars with your fingers while looking out the backseat window” game.  Any way, of course the floor wasn't actually lava. When you inevitably touched it you ideally didn't do so in a manner that caused injury.  That game is sort of what Japanese indie developer Moppin's Downwell is like.  Well, Downwell is actually a lot more entertaining although certainly not as physically exerting as climbing on furniture.
You play as a young man that has hopped down a very deep well.  There is a little more to it than that but it's best left unspoiled.  The well is procedurally generated and each area features different terrain and enemy types.  He is equipped with nothing other than a pair of gunboots, which are useful for destroying blocks, killing enemies, and slowing his fall.  As he makes his descent there are several different types of upgrades, alternate gunboot shots, and stat items to be found.
The key to Downwell is falling with style.  While you could cautiously make your way down the well, it isn't in the spirit of the game.  The player is encouraged to avoid touching the floor by instead bouncing off of enemies.  If you manage to chain sufficiently long combos, you will be rewarded with gems (the in game currency), health, and additional charges for your gunboots.  With practice it is possible to combo entire levels (and possibly the entire game) without ever touching the ground.  Shops and side caves have time bubbles at the entrance that allow you to preserve your combo even though you've technically hit the ground.  It all amounts to extremely fast-paced game play that will require all of your attention and reflexes.
Visually, the game is simple but pleasing.  The default palette style's heavy emphasis on red and black reminded me of playing the Virtual Boy.  I liked it, but fortunately there are plenty of palette swap options in case it doesn't agree with you. On the default palette (which is the only one I used) it is very easy to tell which enemies you can land on and which ones you can't (bright red enemies).  It's good because it's important to be able to easily differentiate between them as you'll likely be moving at high speeds.
Downwell is a great ride that left me wishing for more.  It's a short game that will only take a few hours to complete for most players, though there is a hard more that provides extra challenge.  The fact that it is procedurally generated adds a fair amount of replayability.  Although I would have liked to see more, all the content that's there is great.  Downwell is an outstanding game and at such a low price point you really can't go wrong with this one.  It's one of my favorite finds in recent history, and I'd recommend it to anyone that likes fast paced platforming action.

First of all - game is very short (takes ~20mx2 to finish normal and hard difficulties) but at the same time is very hard, so it can take 20h+ to actually finish, maybe more, depends on your skill and luck. So if you're a person who's into challenge - game is certainly for you.
Pros:
1) it's randomly generated, so you can't finish the game by just remembering exact path, and you have to actually learn how to beat enemies in different situations with different weapons - and you'll need to pick up different weapons to keep your life and charge up.
2) enemies are diverse, as well as environments, they even change with difficulty too. all guns (10) are pretty effective if used right, so in that sense it's nicely balanced.
3) overall difficulty is pretty great, so you can actually feel good about beating it, not like in 90% other games, where skill means next to nothing and it's all about repeating easy actions.
4) 8-bit graphics are pretty nice and cute.
Neutrals:
1) music - i suppose to each his own, some may like it, some may not. it's a but depressing and repetitive, but atmospheric too, so can't really say it's bad thing.
2) game "skin" changes - again, can't say that it's bad, i suppose it's good thing to be able to change colors of things around you, the only problem is, most of those colors are too bright and hurt eyes, so no one will use those anyway.. some of those are ok, some are really wierd.
Cons:
1) as usual, cons are logical consequences of pros - so it's about being random. sure, stages themselves are ok, guns are balanced, enemes (with very rare exceptions) spawn so you actually can kill them without taking damage. but then there are upgrades after each stage - 20 of them in total, and you can pick only 1 out of random 3, and some of those upgrades are _way_ better than other. which turns game in luck based to some extent.
2) if you don't like "hit the wall" in any game - maybe it's not for you, because in this game you certainly can. there are no saves, you have to run game through start to finish. it's not quite "con", but beware.
So in the end - even with some flaws, game is pretty solid and well-made, therefore deserves recommendation.

I usually never buy games on release, but "Ori and the Blind Forest" was an instant buy for me and I absolutely don't regret it. Due to college circumstances I didn't get to play this game until recently and just finished it a moment ago. Now I want to tell you people what I think about this game:
Ever fell in love on first sight? I did! The moment I saw the trailer of "Ori and the Blind Forest" I was hooked!
The reason for this is the very beautiful and detailed artwork in combination with its music. These two elements manage to convey a lot of emotion through the screen. One realises that a lot of work has been put into these. And it definitely paid off! This is a game where getting the OST is recommended IMO.
The storyline is very interesting. Also they way it is being told/experienced was much to my liking. It consists of a combination of movie-sequences, sentences from a narrating voice and also explanations from your "little helper".
One should have no problems following and enjoying the storyline to its fullest. (The movie-sequences can be watched again in the menu.)
The only thing that bothered me a bit later on was the gameplay/controls. With bigger game progess one gets a lot of skills/abilites. I had some trouble to not accidently use the wrong ability/skill, but this may just be me and my inability do to so. This is only a minor negative for me.
Another thing that I think should be pointed out is that this game has "moments & places" where the difficulty may be a tad too much, but this may also be due to me just not being all this good in this kind of game. The game usually autosaves before harder/more difficult parts, so that shouldn't be a problem. One can also make a lot of safepoints during the game if needed. I still managed to finish it all without help, so it's allright I guess. And without any challenges the game would become too boring anyway.
I finished this game in under 10 hours (in which I died more than 500 times). I will definitely play it again after some time and try to clear some more achievements.
All in all I would highly recommend this game to anyone who has an interest in these kind of games. It is definitely worth the buy and also for people who are not fans of this genre I would recommend this as a game as worth trying out. Maybe you as well will get hooked by it.
My expectations were fullfilled and even more than that, exceeded!

How many racing games have you played with
1. No cheating AI?
2. No imba powerups/cars?
3. No frustrating gamemodes?
This is it.
Instead of cheating AI, there's slipstreaming, just like GTA Online (driving in the trail of your opponent makes you go faster). Unlike GTA Online, once everyone is bunched up together, the race gets more fun, not less, so it's not an issue here but rather a very big plus. The powerups are all balanced and the receiver even has a chance to negate some of them (i.e. being set on fire actually speeds you up, so you can use it to gain a massive lead, however you also get very slippery controls and if you touch an obstacle, you die, so only do if you're not on fire). This is a game of skill, not luck, so no matter what powerup you get, you're not any worse off than the other guy.
The cars are divided into groups depending on their speed, so you can't under any circumstance race against a superior car. At the same time, various cars in a group are all different in their handling and you're guaranteed to find your favorites. They went complete nuts with their designs so racing bulldozers, tanks or moon buggies is a normal occurence (they're all reasonably fast despite not looking the part).
I've only played through the campaign alone, and I had a blast, in fact I find myself playing Elimination just for fun even now. I can only imagine how fun multiplayer would be, but alas, I've yet to catch an online game that doesn't lag so much it's unplayable, and my dear roommate thinks inviting him to play is an assault on his loyalty to Need for Speed. But I assure you this is the game you want to play with friends, there is absolutely nothing standing between you and the fun. There is no fat, no frustrating stuff, just pure fun, fun like we may not have again in a long time.

Bought the game for around 18 dollars through♥♥♥♥♥with the UPlay version. I suggest you do the same, because although The Division has hours of content to go through most of it is the same kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Now, you might like it and you might not like it. For me, this game was a great game to play while listening to podcasts. Actually, even without podcasts, listening to the story and intel was sort of captivating for an MMO.
That being said, the story itself is decent, interesting enough for a game of its genre. The intel, such as the holographic memories, the evidence you get from completing the main story missions, and♥♥♥♥♥♥like that is worth listening to if you're mildly interested in the world.
And, to be honest, you should be interested in the world. The game is ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful. Given you can run on it on decent settings, there are times where the snow is falling and the christmas lights placed before the virus catastrophy gives a stellar vibe and impeccable atmosphere. It truly captured the state of New York. Well, as best as it could in a post-apocalyptic setting. Even after hours of grinding, the occassional weather change with the blizzards and the snowfall still somewhat catch my attention. I found myself standing in the game observing the engine's capabilites at some points during grinding the same missions.
The music is quite the eargasm as well. It has a more space kind of theme though, like that No Man's Sky type vibe. The tunes and rings don't remind me of the urban setting the game places itself in, but it does carry the hope everybody in the city posseses and is a good nod to the story with how it's orchestrated. It's very upbeat and has that marvelous "look at the extremities of New York" deal. I can't really quite explain it, although I tried my best to. It's a little thing worth checking out. The fast travel music is real nice to listen to as well, but unfortunately abruptly ends cause my computer loads in the game too quickly.
Now, the gameplay itself is repetitive. There's no suprise there. Once again, it's an MMO. But, in my opinion, it is well executed for what it's worth. The gunplay is smooth and the cover mechanics are simplistic. There are many ways to go about playing the game, where there are gear sets that cater to certain skills, weapons, and conditions. If you enjoy organizing and thinking logically about where to put stuff, you'll most likely enjoy collecting, stashing, mixing, and matching the variety of gear builds that The Divsion has to offer.
But, that's where the complication and actual effort ends. Well, if you consider doing the same missions constantly "effort". You see, RNG is a big thing in The Divsion as you may know. It will take a while to get the gear you need to maximize your power in your character, or you might never even get the sets required to even try new builds in the first place.
You know that saying where the journey matters more than the destination or whatever gypsy♥♥♥♥♥♥ It applies exactly for this game. I had good times figuring out how things work, upgrading my equipment, wondering what's going to happen for The Divison in the storyline, and overall exploring the New York play area. But, things can get stale once you've reached the end. Actually, part of the bore leaks in the journey, because there are things called side missions and encounters which are pretty much the same thing. In The Division, the side missions have no depth to it whatsoever. It's kill this, kill that, help this, help that, go here, and go there. There's slight differences between the side missions and encounters, but not that big to really separate the two. All side missions and all encounters throughout every area of the play area is the same. It's a bummer. Even if you don't want to do it, you have to to access some stuff that are part of the endgame grind. And just going through the side♥♥♥♥♥♥will get boring, but then again it depends on the person.
It's the same with the endgame. Same missions, but harder. Harder than the hard presented to a new player. You can do it solo or with a team, but most of the time I find randoms useless and the matchmaking can be very... scarce. I guess it depends on peak times whether or not you can find a group. But even then a group can make things harder when your team doesn't know what they're doing, has a powerless build, and doesn't use cover at all. Seriously, how could you not use the cover system?
Moving on, most of the content is soloable. Challenging missions will be difficult to solo if it's your first time going through one, but eventually you'll develop a sort of "cheese" or technique, given you have a useful build. As far as I know, unless you're using the cheesiest of builds Legendary and Heroic missions might as well be impossible. That goes for incursions as well. All these legendary, heroic, and incursions also take quite a bit of time, so you have to dedicate yourself and try really hard not to rage quit when you've sunk so much time in a mission. And, with Massive apparently nerfing everything to oblivion it might get tougher here on out, but as a relatively newish player I haven't experienced my builds getting destroyed or even experienced them at there upmost potential in the first place.
Just know going into this game that the endgame will consist of you farming. I really hope they add new content to the game because going into it for a week, it's getting stale. For what it's worth though I've had some great times and even made friends with the PvE content.
The PvP content is a different story, however. Absolute cancer. Middle-aged men and children using the easiest builds just going around killing everything in their path for the purpose of PvP. You can't complain though, it's a PvP zone for a reason. Fight fire with fire! Just know that not everybody you see in the Dark Zone is not going to be farming. Be ready to defend yourself. It's part of the game, just get over it and get used to it.
That's all I have to really say. Sorry for the unorganized format, this was more of a thing I can do to waste time while I wait for Destiny 2 to download. Let's see how this goes.

This is the sort of game I'm been waiting years for. I remember using the old digital LEGO builder back when I was a kid, and LEGO Worlds offers a much more in-depth, intuitive experience to building with LEGO's without the risk of killing yourself by stepping on a LEGO brick.
I was impressed, for the most part. You can easily tell going into the game that it needs a lot of work. The camera controls are fairly clunky and irritating. The graphics aren't entirely there, but they're decent enough. The variety of bricks in the building menu could use some... expansion. As far as I was able to gather, we were limited to stationary, generic bricks. There were no doors, no specialized window bricks, etc. that exist in the real world. Basically, I was disappointed by how limited the brick library was. I prefer making complex, moving builds with LEGOs, you know, ships and contraptions and mechs and all those sorts of things. This game would be perfect if it allowed you to make your own vehicles from scratch (I still dream of the day where I can design my own Star Wars-esque capital ship and pilot it over my empire) and had the vast customizability and options that real LEGOs give you.
I also wish that your LEGO character could interact more with the world without having to go into the other menus to do so. Aside from riding animals and punching skeletons, there's very little you can do without using something from the build menu. That's just my opinion on the matter, at least.
Overall, I'm interested to see where this game is going. I understand it's still in development, and I know that it isn't entirely done yet. I hope some of these issues are rectified by the time the final product is released.

"Space Marine" proved to be far better game than anticipated. To the point I regret that both sequels were canceled. It's not only a game for Warhammer 40k fans but for everyone who likes 3rd person action games. And what's more surprising - multiplayer still lives! It's nothing mindblowing but it's nice and fun - it should keep you with game after the campaign is over (which takes around 8h on Hard).
"Space Marines" offers fast, meaty and satysfing combat that of melee, shooting and explosions that remains challanging till the end (at least on hard difficulty). The game does awesome job at reflecting both, how it is to be a Space Marine - the god among man, the very best manking has to feer for warfare - and how it is to fight Orks, savage beast born only to  wage war called "Waaagh!!!". While you are superior at firepower and armor, your enemies are numerous, unyielding and skilled in combat. Follow the teachings of Codex Astartes, - prioritze targets, use cover and tools of ware wisely, thinking one step ahead and you will be victiorius. Or throw yourself blindly into combat, putting faith in your superhuman abailities and fail miserablly.
When it comes to graphics - models are really nice, well made and holding Warhammer 40k aesthetics. But the levels and your sorroundings are only fine. They clearly lack polish, some sort of final touch or greater vision. They keep Wh40k athmosphere but do it at the lowest price possible leaving you with the feeling that level designers just ticked few guidelines they had and did never put any effort in their work.
Audio is fine, nothing to complain about. Dunno how good is musi as I tend to turn it off ASAP.
Plot? Yes, there is one. But it's not worth mentioning as it is as "warhammerish" as possible. Seriously. If you have ever read a single book about Space Marines, you most likely already know the plot ;) So there is war, there are Ultramarines as the spearhead of counterattack and there are few, easy to predict plot twists. Characters are generic and unremarkable.
So to sum it up - while it's fine game, there is still room for improvement, mainly in non-direct gameplay department - things like cutscenes, plot, level design, overall epicness - stuff that improves immersion and athnmosphere. And paying 20eur for it is a bit high. But during sales, its definitely one of those "go for it!" titles, I can recommend without a doubt.

I have heard the crafting system labeled "deep", however "varied" does not equal "deep". There are a lot of items than can be combined... but there is no flow or progression to the crafting process... it's simply "make something magic, then wear it as a necklace". I'm probably being too harsh, but given the amount of frustration at just trying to enjoy myself in a lengthy rpg, I have completely failed to see the positives this game does possess as a reason to recommend it.
The story does not carry it... the battles, while fun and rewarding at times, ususally fall to one extreme or another. Sometimes you are hopelessly outmatched, other times enemies fall at a sneeze. The voice acting is a-typically hokey and uneven. Character builds are forced into tight, streamlined classes... which wouldn't be so bad, except they insist in their promotion of the game, that you will not be locked into standard classes like other rpgs. This is an outright lie.
All in all I have sent a good deal of time with Original Sin, and have played the prior Divinity games to relative satisfaction... this is by far my biggest dissapointment... a damaged part of my brain that sends OCD impulses will probably make sure I finish it... but it has become a chore, instead of an escape...

Skullgirls, an indie fighter project. The game itself actually plays quite well, with characters having unique skillsets which are well animated and the game is relatively balanced (with the exception of a few characters which are obviously weaker). The developer  is continually rebalancing and reworking the game however and this is a good thing, although it may invalidate my previous statements. This game also has a moderately high learning curve, sure the base story can be breezed through, however learning and mastering the combat mechanics is quite difficult. Beyond the pretty artstyle in combat, the story is told through still cinematics and text, that being said the stories are very fragmented and it feels that even despite completing everyones stories there is still subtantial parts of the story missing. This combined with a very low roster of characters (8 playable + dlc characters), makes for a brief story experience running approximately 3-4h for everyone. The game offers standard story mode, arcade, training and online modes. The online mode is where the majority of your time will be spent as you will complete the other aspects of the game and view all the unlockables relatively quick. There is local multiplayer, as well as online lobby system and ranked matching. The matchmaking and search systems need to be refined as there often seems to be mismatches of players albeit the game does relatively well in offering lag compensated games. Overall the game is an enjoyable fighter game, but unless you plan to practice with one character then go online (and don't mind losing badly when you get mismatched), it will be a brief experience. As such it is recommended conditionally if online brawling is your thing.

A great remake of the classic Micro Machines in all but name, Toybox Turbos delivers wacky non-stop action. Basically a crazy racing game with a variety of customizable miniature (toybox) cars and suped-up weapons (e.g. giant hammers on the roof of your vehicle!), TT features a range of tracks such as the pool table, science lab, kitchen etc. All of the features that made the original Micro Machines games so good are here, plus some new game modes such as 'overtake' and 'escape' in single player, and (of course) online play. The multiplayer facilities in TT are quick and simple, meaning you can jump into races easily and race as few or as many tracks as you like. Plus, you can still play on the same computer with a friend, using controller(s)/WASD/arrow keys. Overall, a very fun game that is really great value on steam sale.

It's a casual game, short and simple, not the kind you play for more than a few days.
The game leads us on a nice nostalgic romp through the evolution of gaming starting back in the day when the Commodore was expected to put the PC out of business.
It contains a model of game development, which is interesting even though it's obviously simplistic.
You research technologies such as multiplayer and saving game and cut-scenes and 3D graphics and stereo sound. At any point you can write a game engine which is capable of supporting any number of known technologies. You can write many games using a single engine. A game engine that can do a lot of things is very expensive, so there's a temptation to write specialized engines for different game types.
The work is divided into 9 categories:
Story/Quests
Engine
Gameplay
Dialogues
Level Design
A.I.
World Design
Graphics
Sound
You have to choose how much time to spend on each of these for every game you make. The games have a topic like Aliens or City or Sports or Dungeon, and a genre or two, a platform or three, a target audience, etc.
Game Dev Tycoon itself would be categorized by itself as category Casual-Simulation with topic of "Game Dev".
Fallout 3 would be Action-RPG on the topic "Post Apocalypse".
After your games are published, you get to see them rated and reviewed, and you can research this and learn things such as Casual games are not a good match for the PC platform, Strategy is not a good match for the Wii.
Occasionally there's a demand for a certain kind of game. At one point there was a demand for offbeat and bizarre game types, so I made one. When the reviews came back, this is what I learned:
"Dance Adventure-Strategy is a terrible combination."
