Beautiful visuals for a retro-styled pixel game, addictingly fun gameplay, a simple soundtrack that sounds awesome, and very unique zones that noticably stand out from the previous (My favorite being 4 and 5). While the game seems very basic at first you'll quickly find the level of depth through combos, risk/reward siderooms, and the upgrade system which can cater to your personal playstyle. Every run is different because of the randomly generated levels that never seem too unfair or difficult. The game is difficult since you need to beat zone 1-5 without dying to truly beat the game and you only start with 4 health initially from the usual style.
Speaking of styles there's 5 total that are unlocked by your gem total after you win/die and are also excellent ways to play the game how you want it (more difficult? Easier to get combos? More health? Gun fanatic?). There are also unlockable palettes that change the visuals of the game, it's a welcomed cosmetic change and considering the game only works with four colors it's not too difficult to distinguish the red hurt barriers in each one, in addition to the DOWNWELL style my favorites are GLOW, AQUA, and VBOY. It took me 14 hours to 100% the game and I can honestly say that I had a lot of fun doing so and thought the additional mode was fairly challenging and fun.
Definitely pick this one up if you're either up for a challenge or if you want to try something brand new!

I own and enjoy the first WRC game by the same developers which came out in 2010, so I thought I would get this when I saw it cheap in a sale for 80% off.
The game seems to have changed little since then  - the graphics are slightly improved but not much.  In some respects I think I prefer the original's graphics which aren't quite as colourful perhaps, but look more realistic as a result.
There is still no weather to speak of, most stages are dry with clear skies - no heavy downpours or snowstorms here, something which the Colin McRae Rally games had since the late 1990s!  I would say that Colin McRae Rally 2005, in fact even Colin McRae Rally 3, had better graphics than this game as well despite being much older.  Unfortunately Codemasters stopped making semi-realistic rally games like that, and went full arcade.  Dirt 1 was still somewhat realistic but by Dirt 3 it dropped any pretense of realism and lost me entirely.  If you hanker after old school rally games like the Colin McRae series then WRC is all that's on offer today.  I would say it's better than Dirt 3 (except graphically) but inferior to the others.
The car handling seems to have taken a step back since the first WRC game and the cars are now much harder to drift without using the handbrake - even full throttle while steering on ice it is very hard to get the car to drift, perhaps this was dumbed down to make the game 'easier' and more casual but it makes the cars less satisfying to drive for me.  (I did make sure stability assist was turned off.)
There are 6 stages per country but in my view this is very misleading because essentially, and I'm not exaggerating unfortunately, all stages look and play the same.  You don't have the feeling of progressing across a country but of driving the same tiny part of it, 6 times!  It's really very lazy I'm afraid.  Also the stages have FAR too many corners and not enough straights - the first WRC game and indeed real life WRC isn't like this.  So you are constantly bombarded with corner after corner after corner which becomes monotonous and tiring, and there are none of the exhilarating exciting super fast sections of the first game.
WRC 4 lacks the group B cars of WRC 1, like the RS200 which is disappointing.
Overall the game feels like a budget release, despite its full price tag and I would only recommend getting it when heavily discounted, and even then you probably won't be fully satisfied with it.
I gather that WRC 5 is coming out this year but by new developers.  Hopefully they will put a lot more effort, polish and love into their game than this has had.

Before you start looking my review being stinky and unfair because I only played 2 hours, it's because I already have 50+ hours on PS Vita cause there's where this game was intended for, so let's begin.
Pros
+ Very nice graphics for a game that's a port from consoles. Kudos to Autodesk Beast.
+ Very easy career to folow: Win the 6 Special Stages and ascend in the rangings. Easy, simple and effective to achieve fun.
+ Not powerhouse PC requiremends in order to play. Good for people with mid-range PCs who want 1080p resolution.
+ Good variety of cars to choose while you unlock better rep.
+ Online leaderboards that sync with an account IF you want to create one (GFWL sucks, no way around it).
+ Nice voice acting. You can hear really good the instructions from your partner.
+ Loads fast (again port, so on a HDD the load is way quicker)
Cons
The cons are mostly revolve around the fact that this is a port and a quorky one at that.
- Very VERY sensitive controls, don't try keyboard even if your life was depended on it. With controller things get better but still if you are low tempered you will surely throw the controller out the window. That's because PS Vita analog sticks have very small area of reaction, 1o in PS Vita corresponds to 10o in controllers so you have to somehow amend to that and the solution is to make the controlls very sensitive. Don't try to change the sensivity, you will make things worse.
- Repetitive gameplay. Same tracks 80% of the time and no other modes like 1vs1 race or something else.
- No team pros and cons. It would give the game a bit depth to the team you choose but only car power (also uninteresting) matters.
- Weird way classes of WRC are shown. Junior I get, but what's the difference between WRC 1,2 or 3 ?
- If the game crashes for no reason, you might be welcomed later with a message saying "Your save game is corrupted", also for no reason.
- If you get stuck while trying to upload your times inbetween races you either lose the race or your save game, again, for no reason.
- Way to pricy for a bare bone experience. 30 dollars ? You mad son ? DIRT 3 costs 25 and since yesterday the GFWLess version with all the DLC included just got released for 22.5 dollars. Pick it up only for 50% sale and above only.
- Did I mention the save games get corrupt easy ?
The only reason I give it thumps up is because I bought it on sale both in PS VIta and for my traveling PC, otherwise I prefer DIRT 3.

I've always been a huge fan of the Lego Games from the 90's, and even though I've enjoyed many  of the previous Traveller's Tales lego games, I've oftentime been frustrated by their repetition and with the lack of actual building they have compared to the original series of games like Lego Racers and Lego Creator. Lego Worlds is not only a fresh of breath air, playing very differently from Traveller's Tale's other lego games, but feels like a modernized version of the Lego Creator concept, which was always one of my favorites. This is an open world exploration game that lets you build things, which is awesome. I've seen Lego Worlds compared to Minecraft, but I actually wouldn't say that's a very apt comparison. Lego worlds has a very different feel, being focused on unlocking and building things, whereas minecraft, while still very exploration-focused, is about, well..... mining and crafting. In it's current state, you can drive a handful of vehicles, explore several different biomes, unlock several characters, place several pre-built creations, plus build your own things, albeit with a very limited selection of bricks. Overall the experience is fairly polished for an early access game, but content the game currently provides, although varied in some aspects, kind of wears thin after a while. I don't doubt that there will be a ton of stuff added soon though, so I think it will be interesting to see how this game develops and it seems like the developers are keeping good contact with the fans and listening to feedback. Right now the biggest issue is the painful lack of brick types to build with. Despite this, it's super fun to explore the world and see which characters you run into and what props you unlock, plus the vehicles are extremely fun to drive. The game also features a fairly robust platforming system, allowing you to climb and hang from cielings with amazing agility. Normally, I don't go for early access games, and maybe you shouldn't quite rush out to get this one yet, but this Lego Worlds is polished and promising, and I'd say 15 dollars is a good price for what you're getting.

If i could leave a "mixed" reccomendation, i would put it. Unfortunately Steam is forcing me to put either yes or no.
It's uh... Not exactly the game i was buying back then, now that it's released.
We were having a completely different game, where we had exploration and procedural worlds, where building and exploration was the main point, whole destructible and procedural worlds with various biomes, think of it like Minecraft but instead of focus being on survival, it was just building and exploration.
The current game is well... Forcing you to play in prebuild worlds and "discovering" new thing, which well, sounds the same right? But well, it's really not, you are being put in a small prebuilt area, where you have to complete quests to get access other prebuild areas. Which somewhat kills the exploration aspect, instead it feels like they just give you a few levels, make you do a few quests and move you onto another one.
Also your movement is always being limited by the tool you chose, back in Early Access you just had to come to something and it'll be discovered, then you can do whatever you want with it.
however i am not sure if that would be the old version of game with infinite generation and biomes. It also costs 100... 100 golden bricks, meaning that you'll have to go through a lot to get to the good part, the Sandbox part, if it's still the same as it was before, then i guess it would be worth to get through all the other pain, however, if it were not for the optimization issues.
Framerate is, surprisingly worse than it was in Early Access with procedural worlds, which is kinda strange, considering that the prebuild areas are noticeably smaller and less detailed.
(18 frames in the second prebuilt world with prehistoric stuff, what the hell? It also doesn't change no matter what you do with your settings.)
But on the good note,
The game actually feels like a "game" now, it has content to play with, it has an objective, it's no longer just a pointless exploration and sometiems build a thing game.
The menu got a major overhaul, too, and it does look fairly nice, as well as intro cinematic, and all that fluff.
They also seem to give a light hint on that there will possibly be other expansions for the game, because all "explored" items are now being in "sets", so maybe someday if you are a fan of Lego Batman or Harry Potter or Star Wars, you might be able to get an expansion for Lego Worlds and play the game with different content. Kind of reminds me of the whole idea of Dimensions in a way.
So... While it's not the same game we were promised, it's still... kinda good?
The only problems i see with the game, is the fact that optimization is still fairly awful, and that to create your own world you have to get a LOT of golden bricks, but other than that... Changes seem to be okay.
So if i were to tell you to get it or not... i wouldn't even know if to say yes, or not. I'd say wait a few patches for them to fix the performance first, and add some improvements to some systems, then we'll see.
Personally, i think they should just give you a go into sandbox mode straight from the main menu, and that would probably remove a lot of conflicting reviews.

Normally I do not review a pre-release game after so little playing time, but on this one I feel that I have to warn people before spending a massive 30-odd pounds or equivalent on this game.
After reading the reviews and looking at the screenshots I was exaulted! This would be my new favourite game.
Maybe my expectations where a bit too high? But in the pre- and reviews things like accurate sailing physics where mentioned more than a few times.
This is the greatest disappointment of all, sure you need to tack your ship by hauling the masts in the correct seaquence. however even if you have no clue what that means, just leave auto-skipper on and your ship will happily sail like in any other arcade shooter game.
Being a sailor myself (no longer proffesional but still for hobby) I tried some tactics on the cutter only to find out that they don't work. One of those tactics would be to sail opposite to the enemy, turn into wind, push out the spanker, opposite rudder and drift backwards. Although all these mechanics exist in the game, the ship doesn't respond correctly to those stearing inputs. instead the direction relative to the wind only has infuence on the total speed of the ship, the stearing relies 100% on the rudder (apparently no effect of heal etc.) and as a result the ship becomes uncontrolable going backwards at 0.2 knots.
Sure this is a pre-alpha release but as this is the very core of the game I can only hold faint hope that this is merely an unpolished aspect.
If you like arcade pirate shooters, go for it. if you like Age of Pirates 2 multiplayer? go for it. If you like scentec sail simulator 5? stay away from this... at least for now.
I will keep this review updated if the sailing physics improves, but for now, alas, thumbs down :(

I have decided to add to my original review since many changes have come to pass as the devs continue to add, modify and change the game.  See the bottom for added comments.
I have had the pleasure and sometimes the pain, yes pain, of playing Naval Action through the original battle sim on to the launch of the open world.
Visually the devs have done amazing work. As you sail around the detail astounds you.  You need a nice graphics card and machine to truly enjoy it.  Last night I noticed that the shallows near islands had become sand beaches and rocky shoals.   Another upgrade to the whole visual aspect of the game.   Watch some of the videos.
There are a few negative reviews regarding the grind and the time it takes to sail from place to place.  Also about nothing being fast and taking too long to complete.
Have you ever sailed in a yacht on a sunny day? You really do not get anywhere fast.
Real life age of sail battle could take all day to resolve if they even were resolved.  In Naval Action you could be in a battle well over an hour  and then sink if you can't escape a losing battle.  It is the age of sail after all.
If you want instant gratification and super powerful ships the moment you buy and join the game then you might as well go elsewhere.   You need to earn your place on the seas and there is a lot of help for you to get where you need to be to have fun in larger ships and sail with skill.
The initial grind can be very frustrating but everyone in the game has to do it. There are legal in game ways to make it a bit faster but as you get better it goes faster and you gain a larger crew which allows you to sail larger ships and gives you more options as to how you want to interact.
Some trade mostly and build ships. Others constantly organize port battles and manage the wars against enemies. Several like to backstab fellow pirates and pay the price.
The world is in flux. Ports change hands, Power bases grow and shrink and ships get lost.
We all have lost our best ships in a battle but live to fight again.
If you want to join a game still being improved (and sometimes in ways we might not all like being tested), still growing  with a good base of skilled people in all of the nations from all over the world, then give it a try.
I have played in "free" games and pay games where bots have taken over the game and completely ruined them.  This game depends on your skill and your clan and country's ability to hold important ports for supplies and staging and not on some computer bot working against you.
Join the grind, join the community and enjoy the game.   There is nothing more enjoyable than after an hour or more of tough battle with cannons firing, smoke wafting across the water and hearing your crew cheer when the dreaded enemy loses a mast and then you sink or board the ship and seize it!
New to this review.
You will read some fairly negative reviews on this game and some of them do make a point about some of the changes taking place in Naval Action.
In my opinon as a game in flux through continuing development it is still a great game with some new wrinkles.
Graphically they added shoals, seagulls , rocks and other fine details making the whole environment richer.  New ships are being added all the time.  Tweaks for battles keep us on our toes as well.
Many are unhappy that fleets are back as they prevent good single player battles in open water.
Others complain about buying crew you lose in battles or if your ship gets sunk or taken.
There are many options in the game from pure battle to trading or crafting that are still viable but you must take care and do some planning or yes incur huge costs for repair or replacement of your ships and crews.
All in all still a great game that I enjoy very much and when you add the social aspect of clan membes from all over the world working and fighting together in game it makes all the rough spots and complaints go away.
Still say give it a try and join the fray!

If I had to write a review in 3 words; BUY. THIS. GAME.
An amazing game. Doesn't hold your hand, and can feel frustratingly difficult at times, and this makes it that much more rewarding. Classes dont really matter, as you can (and SHOULD) make each character multi-use. Going full warrior-melee and having no spells will get you nowhere. Anyone can be killed (including Quest-giving NPCs) which can result in having quests you are unable to complete. Kill wisely! The game gives you lots of freedom to roam wherever you want and collect tons of loot from containers and mobs. Don't listen to the complainers who cant level up high enough to defeat certain enemies. Its not all about level; its strategy too. You can get slaughtered in a fight with a few wrong moves, or you can walk away with your party unscathed. There are over 75 side quests to explore and every NPC has something to say or sell. The game requires careful management of skills and abilities as a few points in the wrong abilities can hinder your team substantially. I restarted the game multiple times to get it right and I've enjoyed every moment of the game. Combat is great (though, as mentioned, it would be nice to zoom out a little more) and the top-down perspective highlights your allies and enemies for easy identification. The story is interesting, the characters are unique and how much/little you explore is up to you. There are tons of funny little easter eggs (Such as a man in an imp prison who talks about his television and his car and not knowing how he got there. Your party decides this man is just crazy and doesnt know what he's talking about). The choices your character makes impact not only the outcome of quests and reputation among the townspeople, but grant you bonus stats. Ex- making Cautious choices will improve your sneaking ability. It's an unforgettable game and even at 100+ hours I'm not ready for it to end.
The game truly is a unique experience and highly recommended.

Beautiful visuals for a retro-styled pixel game, addictingly fun gameplay, a simple soundtrack that sounds awesome, and very unique zones that noticably stand out from the previous (My favorite being 4 and 5). While the game seems very basic at first you'll quickly find the level of depth through combos, risk/reward siderooms, and the upgrade system which can cater to your personal playstyle. Every run is different because of the randomly generated levels that never seem too unfair or difficult. The game is difficult since you need to beat zone 1-5 without dying to truly beat the game and you only start with 4 health initially from the usual style.
Speaking of styles there's 5 total that are unlocked by your gem total after you win/die and are also excellent ways to play the game how you want it (more difficult? Easier to get combos? More health? Gun fanatic?). There are also unlockable palettes that change the visuals of the game, it's a welcomed cosmetic change and considering the game only works with four colors it's not too difficult to distinguish the red hurt barriers in each one, in addition to the DOWNWELL style my favorites are GLOW, AQUA, and VBOY. It took me 14 hours to 100% the game and I can honestly say that I had a lot of fun doing so and thought the additional mode was fairly challenging and fun.
Definitely pick this one up if you're either up for a challenge or if you want to try something brand new!

I promised myself I wouldn't get the feels, I swore up and down I'd be the strong woman that my mommy raised me to be. I knew when I hit play that I would be able to take anything that this game threw at me and shrug it off with a "oh well, that's life. Big deal."
And then this cute little thing popped up on my screen. A fat, bear like thing with a undulating stomach as it walked managed to smush its way into my feel factory. As it found Ori (a glowy little creature thing that is slightly reminisent of Mew) and began to take care of this little abandoned creature; I began to let down my walls. I sat in my room and happily watched as the two unlikely creatures made a small little family. They built bridges together, gathered foods and played together, it was the cutest thing I had watched in a long time.
And then, they just HAD to punch me in the gut. They just had to lie to me. I had unsuspectingly been sucked into a false sense of security, only to have my world crushed in the worst 5 minutes of my life. I watched horrified as the giant fat bear gave up its last bit of food to the unsuspecting Ori, only to die before Ori could return with an armful of berries to feed his adopted mother. He curled up on her stomach, depressed and alone. It was like a train wreck; I couldn't look away as he ran back to his dying mother with the images of them playing flashing up in the background. It was possibly the most gutwrenching and life altering moment of my life. AND I COULDN'T STOP WATCHING! Ori, alone and depressed ran off into the now destroyed woods to DIE. He had given up. And I WASN'T ABLE TO SKIP THIS PART!!! I was forced to take part in every depressing, emotional, moment of this story. It brought up flashbacks of when I was a child and had to watch The Fox and the Hound, I suffered intense emotional trauma from the first 5 minutes of this game. I suspect that I'm going to have PTSD from this prolouge alone.
But now into the actual game. It's really good. I've always liked platformers, I've been really good at them for as long as I can remember. Most often, once I get the hang of a platforming type game I can beat it within a few hours. This one has actually kept my attention and on more than one occasion gotten me quite frustrated during gameplay. I'm normally not one to get angry at a game, this one had me pretty close.
The game is extremely beautiful. Everything is a pool of color and light and sometimes I would actually just sit in one place or on the title screen and just enjoy the graphics. Don't even get me started on the soundtrack; where the graphics end, the soundtrack picks it up and keeps running with it. The music is one of, if not the best soundtracks I've heard in a game in a very long time. It's right up there with Castlevaina, Okami and The Witch and the Hundred Knight soundtracks.  It makes the whole game somehow surreal.
The fact that while playing, you are able to unlock certain moves, and perks to Ori while playing just makes this game even more detailed and worth the time and effort you put into it. While some levels of gameplay become almost insanely difficult as you progress through the storyline; after beating a boss you get that satisfaction sense and continue to press forward to see what's going to happen next. It's almost one of those games that you want to stop playing but can't because you have to see what Ori is going to accomplish next.
In all, this game is a solid 8 of of 10. Everything I want in a platformer.

There is a major spoiler alert for this review since I will be going into a lot of detail, so if you're just looking for the abridged version, then it is this:
Get this game. Immediately. The chances of another game trumping this for 2015 are low. $20 is not a bad deal for this game, so you're doing yourself a favor by picking it up.
Now that that's out of the way, it's time to go into why this game is my current pick for game of the year for 2015.
First of all, the gameplay is solid. I used an Xbox360 controller to play, and the only issues I could find were very minor things such as sticking to walls when I didn't want to and rarely having a slight analog push register as a full push. Beyond this, the controls are crisp and intuitive, which is absolutely critical to a platformer where most of the abilities you unlock are based on increasing your ability to move around the maps.
It helps that the game is very well tutorialized. Every time you gain a new ability, you're given an opportunity to use that ability in every way that the game could possibly expect you to do within minutes of picking it up. Even if you forget how to use the ability fast enough or are returning from a hiatus from the game, the status menu will allow you to see the abridged version of how to use the ability at any time.
Even outside of abilities, there's no place in the game where you simply are expected to know something that's not intuitive. A lot of things in this game that damaage you have either a spike type of texture or a glow, and you're given a lot of time and room early on to make that connection. The game doesn't hold your hand by telling you the rules, but there is enough wiggle room that it's easy to figure out the rules of the game.
Ability points are the way you upgrade in this game, which is further split up into three trees. The Combat tree increases your ability to deal damage with Sein, who is essentially an outside damage dealer that hones in on enemies nearby. Some of your other abilities also deal damage or interact with enemies in some other way, both of which fall under this tree. The Efficiency tree is all about convenience in finding all the hidden upgrades strewn throughout the world; maxing this tree will show every single secret in the game on the map (provided you have explored near the area) and allow you to see through hidden walls. The Utility tree is all about convenience in general; you use less energy, gain health when you save, and take less damage among other things when you max out this tree. Note that maxing every single tree is absolutely overkill, but it's a fun challenge and will make things much easier in the long run. It's very difficult to miss when you gain a skill point since Sein will send out a shockwave across your entire screen that will do a lot of damage to all nearly enemies.
Now it's time to talk about the defining feature of this title and a largely significant reason that this game is generating buzz: the atmosphere.
The game is gorgeous. The graphics, while not fantastic, fit the gameplay itself like a glove. Parts of the scenery are dark and foreboding, yet will become lighter and greener after reviving the Ginso Tree and cleansing the water. Everything you can interact with is distinctive, at least the mandatory things. Some of the secrets are trickier to figure out, but that's not a negative as there are other clues to lead you in the right direction. Plus, secrets are placed the way they are for a reason; it wouldn't be much of a secret if you could find it without any trouble.
The animations are what truly set the graphics apart. Ori's animations especially are top notch. Despite to having a healthy size of abilities that all require their own animations, it's impressive how smoothly they blend into each other. It's a blast to just run around comboing your abilities together to get around just to watch Ori move, which is only a good example at how good the animation quality is. The background will also move when the situation demands it; the best example is if you level up in a grassy area. When the shockwave hits, virtually everything on the screen moves along with it the way it would in real life. It's mindblowing how much effort went into this type of minor detailing, but it truly adds an extra layer of depth and immersion to the game.
The soundtrack. There's no doubting it; this soundtrack is fantastic. A lot of the tracks don't sound as impressive by themselves as they do in game, but they complement the mood they're in so well that it's difficult not to be swept away in what is currently going on in the game. One clever thing I really like about the soundtrack is how much of the ambeance is in the sound effects of the situation; listen to the Forlorn Ruins escape sequence and then listen to the song by itself. The song doesn't sound anywhere near as epic by itself. One other small touch I like about this game is that the songs will loop sections of it during a cutscene where you have to move to a destination to continue, but will immediately transition to a new section of the song once you do in order to sync with the actual 'cutscene' section.
Don't even get me started on the syncing. I don't even want to know how much effort and care it took to make the music and video match up as perfectly as it does, especially since a lot of cutscenes in the game have a single song for the entirety of it.
So the graphics, animation, and sound all combine together to create a fantastic atmosphere of the game, but all that does is showcase the single best part of this game and the true reason I would consider this game a fantastic example of how video games can be art:
The story.
Note: This is where the majority of the spoilers will be from, so be very careful if you don't want the story to be spoiled.
This game takes several concepts that are incredibly difficult to pull off and succeeds with flying colors with all of them. The prologue introduces two characters and kills one of them off within minutes, and yet they manage to craft it in such a way that it makes the player emotionally invested enough to be sad at their loss. I know enough about story-telling to be very aware that this type of plot point so early in a story is extraordinarily difficult to do well, and when it doesn't go well... it completely fails.
The reason it works is because of how much care went into crafting the prologue. You control Naru as she finds Ori in a storm. You control Ori's walk to see Naru to create a bridge towards a feast of fruit. You control Ori's walk to investigate the ominous light. Finally, you control Ori's trek back to deliver the final batch of fruit in the nearby area to try to save Naru's life.
The ingenius thing about all of this is when the game gives you control over the characters. The first two instances are directly and blatantly happy things. The second one is ominous, but it feels like the resullt is nothing you could have any control over. The fourth is a bit different, but it drives home the overall theme of this story:
Hope vs. Despair.
Ori sees a total of four flashbacks of memories with Naru that you have just seen before the forest began to die. Ori is worried about Naru's life... but there is still hope within the fruit in Ori's arms. It's only after Ori returns and happily presents them that it becomes clear, first through confusion, then panic, then realization, that Naru had died and Ori gives in to despair. The rest of the prologue is Ori stumbling through the forest, dejected and weak, until the last breath is drawn and ends in Ori's own death. It's clearly showing that giving in to despair will erode the will to live.

Cons:

Definitely worth the price-tag for a 10 hour metroidvania though.

These spirit shards can then be spent on new abilities and power ups in Ori's skill tree. Also, deathin this game is not really punishing at all as Ori has the ability to create his own save points and respawn after a death are nearly instant. In conclusion I find that the gameplay as a whole is helps to create a fun and enjoyable experience.

When I learned that I missed out on Lego Universe, I realized that I really wanted to have a video game where I could build and explore a Lego world. This game is the answer!! Thank you Lego Company, for creating such an awesome game!
Okay, now that my fan-boy is out, lets cut to the chase.
Pros:
+The game is well done. It's not fully done, but it has an amazing start!
+Randomly generated worlds. I realized quickly that this game could get old very quickly, but with random worlds, you can start a new adventure easily.
+Cheap unlockables. In this game, you collect 'studs' from destroying plants and discovering chests. These 'studs' allow you to buy unlockables such as vehicles, playable minifigures, props, and animals. The prices seem reasonable, so I don't think that it'll be an issue to unlock them.
Cons:
-Camera and controls are sluggish. It's very hard to move smoothly and the camera gets in the way a lot.
-Not a whole lot of interactivity with npcs. There are npc minifigures scattered across the worlds. All they seem to do, however, is move around and attack skeletons.
-Not much of a tutorial. Now, there is a helpful info box in the lower right hand corner, but the game could benefit from a basic tutorial.
-The worlds could be a bit larger, if not have more than one island. I don't know if I simply haven't found the right world yet, but I don't like that all the ones I've found are a single island.
One big thing about this game, is that it's only single-player. I know the game is in Early Access, so I hope they add this feature soon. The game gets very quiet with it only being one player. One thing they'll have to get around is how easy it is to destroy terrain. So I hope they make a way to prevent a player from destroying another player's builds on accident... Or purpose... >:)
Anyway, I would definitely recommend this game to any Lego enthusiast. This is the game we've all been dying for!
I give it a 7/10. It's a birlliant idea and I hope it all works out! But they need to fix the clumsy controls and it HAS to have multiplayer! It wouldn't be Legos without interactivity with other people.

There is a curious exhilaration here. Most cheaply described as part rhythm game, part platformer, RUNNER has you leaping and sliding as Commander Video with the soft pulse of electronic music bouncing along with you. Power ups don’t just increase your score, but also add new, dramatic musical flourishes and ideas to your every move. The game is at its best when you are in sync with it, bounding and dancing along to a living musical world.
The game is also difficult. Dying not only halts your progression, but brings your musical journey to a stifling halt. For all of its musical prowess, the game doesn’t have control of its pacing. Every death feels less like a opportunity to learn and more like a broken record, that will only play the whole song half of the time. The boss battles are similarly uninspiring. They rob the primary game of its colorful, musical joys, replacing them with the tedium of its bare mechanics.
Despite its shortcomings, RUNNER is thrilling and fun, as long as you have the chops to not break its rhythm.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a super fun game that I hate and that makes me hate myself. The basic premise is that you're a running man (Colonel VHS) who just can't stop running. You need to help him through this addiction the same way all addicts do: ducking, jumping, and kicking. You sync up button presses to get through obstacles like a visual Simon Says, hoping to God you didn't try and jump over another goddamn kick target. The soundtrack is designed to sync up with the sound effects produced by your button presses, turning what might otherwise be a pretty simple excercise in game design into some sort of sheet music nightmare. I'm not kidding, this is basically one of those lazy mobile runner games elevated by the fact that they hid Guitar Hero in it.
Visually BTR tries to tap into that sweet sweet pixel biz we've been stimulating our nipples with since at least Shovel Knight (but definitely since before Shovel Knight), but does it in a cool, somewhat more 90-s centric way. While player character Sergeant Betamax is himself just pixels, the world around him is made of simplistic 3d models of rectangles and triangles and such. The effect is an aesthetic that is almot nostalgia-themed without actually imitating a graphical style that ever actually existed. The environments don't look like Nintendo 64 or Playstation polygons, but crisp, clear models that just happen to be intentionally simple.
The soundtrack keeps in with this aesthetic, being comprised of electronic beats with a slight 90s hip-hop edge to them reminiscent of the more public-domain tunes schools would play during pep assemblies. It works really well, especially with the gameplay integration. Someone less rhythm-, tone-, and basically music-deaf than me might even be able to even use the soundtrack to help them time button presses.
So yeah, pretty good game probably. I mean, I can't be sure everything I just said is correct, or even something I remembered from this game in particular.

In Scribblenauts you have to find solutions for problems by creating or altering objects/persons with your magic notebook. The amount of objects and adjectives available is enormous, but unfortunately the puzzles are lacking. In fact they are not even worth being called puzzles. Someone wants to chop down a tree? Give him an axe. Someone wants to fly? Give him wings. Someone wants a gift for his girlfriend? Give him flowers. And that's it. Of course you can use weird solutions, like giving the guy with the tree problem a 'huge pink funny demonic chainsaw', but the fun in doing things like these wears of pretty quickly. Especially since it doesn't change the outcome, the guy still chops down the tree just like he would with an axe. Often your weird creations aren't even used and standard objects are created instead. If you give a girl who wants to dress up nicely a pink miniskirt for example she'll just put on some default clothes instead of the object you created.
The game can be fun for a few hours if you just mess around, but it gets boring pretty quickly. It is certainly a nice game for little children (age 5-10) though. So no recommendation for adults from me, but recommended for children.

After a patch that - last summer - chased out almost all players due to a too harsh hardcore approach, the game was becoming more and more enjoyable. Personally I always liked it (as you can see I have a lot of hours ingame), but in last months it was becoming way better than before. Plus the community is - as always - very friendly with new players. Yet the game is rather time demanding: it takes a lot of time to do everything. Population is still somhow low at the moment so the (huge) open world feels sometimes empty and open sea PVP action is not very common (outiside some "hot" ports where people usually gather to brawl). The good of PVP is that, even a lowbie in a medium ship, can be very effective in PVP action (both solo and group). PVE is difficult only when you begin, but becomes somehow a routine when you learn how to play (always the same mission, rinse and repeat) but - that's the good point - it is now very rewarding in terms of gold/items/exp. Levelling through the ranks requires a slow paced grind, but acceptable. Endgame PVE content is simply inexistent. When you reach max rank, you have to throw yourself into some PvP/RvR action ... or you trade/craft or you farm NPCs to get good drops or ... you freeze the account. Crafting has been recently revamped, and it's good (even though the grind through the ranks here is very very slow). The naval combat - both PVP and PVE - is really accurate and challenging and - toghether with the marvellous  graphic design of the ships - it's definitely the best thing of the game.
Faction conquest (the so called RvR) is a different beast: it is very lively on EU server, but the decision to merge the servers due to the lack of players in the Global server is likely to bring back some flaws (the so called "nightflips" that some months ago spoilt the RvR and caused a mass quit of players). Odds is that to please a vocal minority (some players of global servers), devs chose to adopt a model of RvR that in the past really screwed the game for the silent majority of players involved in RvR. Same story with the models of sailing: in order to please the (smaller number of) fans of simulative aspect of the game, ships have become more difficult to handle for the average player.
TBH, the trend of satisfying minorities at the expense of the interest of the larger base of casual players seems to be the actual reason why this game is not having the sucess that it could have.
In example: for some weeks a half dozen of PVP players (actually, they are just well known gankers) have been flooding the forums with the request to abolish safe zones around the regions around capital cities. What is likely to happen is that the Developers, with no discussion or anticipation whatsoever, one day will suddenly announce that they will wipe the safe zones. Then - due to this choice - population will drop and Devs will then get back the safe zones. This "one step ahead and two steps back" attitude has plagued the development of this game since the very beginning.
And this is also the reason because - even though I like the game and still play it - I suggest to think twice before engaging in this game. Better waiting at least the launch of the final product or you wll bear the risk of playing a game that will change 100 times without any possibility to tell how it will be at the end. This thing is the most disappointing one, since does not let a player even decide if they like the game or not, since it changes too often in too many features to let them evaluate it objectively.Moreover you risk to buy something that will become more and more difficult to enjoy for a casual player.

GDT is primarily a game of slider adjustment. If, for example, you wish to produce a game of the Action genre, then during Stage 1 of development you'll wish to set the Engine slider to 100%, the Gameplay slider to 80%, and the Story slider to 0%. Meanwhile, your only competition is yourself, and every time you outperform yourself, you raise the bar. If you don't exceed the standard you've set for yourself, improving every game over the last, then your ratings will suffer, and so will your sales. Critics and customers aren't concerned about whether or not you've produced a good game, or an entertaining game. They're interested in whether or not you've produced a game that was statistically better than your last. You'll find yourself frustrated in no time, getting real cozy to all the GDT strategy guides and spreadsheets that litter the internet.
My first game started out enjoyable. I was fascinated by the nostalgia of the Comadore 64 and Nintendo. I liked giving my games titles and momentarily daydreaming about what each would be like. It didn't take long before I adjusted a games sliders luckily and scored my first big hit. Little did I realize the critics and customers would never be accepting of anything less after that. From that point on it was all frustration, confusion and work, eventually leading to bankrupcy during the PS2 era. The next game, I spent most of my time reading those guides and refering to those spreadsheets I mentioned earlier, strategically planning everything with precision. I even downloaded a series of mods that did such things as display percentages in the sliders, for precision purposes. I left nothing to chance, and yet I again found myself bankrupt during the PS2 era.
Before the third playthrough, I must've spent an hour scouring the internet like an NSA agent reading and rereading Vladamir Putin's autobiography and hacked personal correspondance. Finally, I tried one last time, nearly found myself bankrupt during the PS2 era again, but I won with $4.5 billion in my account. Was it worth it? No. There's a lot of examples of "the wrong execution of the right idea" here. That bar raising I spoke of earlier being one. GDT is unmercifully, artificially and ridiculously difficult. From what I've read, that seemed to be more true with each update released for GDT. They found any patch of fresh air within the game, capped it off, and left the player suffocating. For example, MMO's have been nerfed to the point that insane, rapid and unending rises in server maintenance will leave you broke in no time flat, expansion packs or not. This is, in essense, a game of gaming the game, never playing the game. It's work, not fun. From what I've read, the game used to be fun, but in it's current and apparently final state, it's not. You'll find no joy here.
Unless you're a masochist: steer clear. Find something to play that'll actually be fun.

This is a fun RPG which feels a lot like a modern version of Ultima 7 (even the story starts with investigating a murder).
You have your 2 main characters whom you create, and can add other party members. There's a lot of text dialogue with NPCs to get story and proceed in quests. A lot. I like that because I like to read & learn about the world & lore of my games; however it's also almost fully voice-acted.
I really enjoy the turn-based, action points-based combat system. It feels like the original 90s X-COM but more streamlined (but not so streamlined distilled down to "2 actions per turn" like the new XCOM is). There's a lot of strategy available, especially if you want to play with the synergies of your party. Fun!
The elemental effects and how they interact are the "killer app" feature of Divinity: Original Sin's combat IMHO. Make it rain with one spell to get everyone wet (wet is a status, a buff/debuff), then cast an icy spell on an enemy and they'll freeze. Say the enemy has fires around, giving everyone the "warm" status (and therefore easier to get lit on fire). Now the enemy shoots a fireball and lit your character on fire -- cast that rain spell to put yourself out, and all the fires in that area.
The music is great! Fitting and melodic. Just writing this review conjures up one of the tunes in my head.
The Enhanced Edition fixed the sluggish movement issue I had with the original version of the game.!  \o/
My only real complaint is that you're nearly locked into combat once combat is triggered. You do have the option for each character to try & run away, but turning your back on an enemy confers a large bonus to the enemies' attack, so in my experience you're more likely to die than escape. Time to reload the last save!
I only point it out as a con because you have little to no direction for where to go outside of town and can very easily trigger combat with multiple enemies of significantly higher level than you if you just blunder around without caution. To some that's a challenge, to others it's a learning experience (followed by a reload!), and to the "hold my hand every step of the way" babies it's a point to whine about.
Just get used to hitting F5 every couple of minutes, and set your Quick Saves number to 10.

- Very bad controls (both on mouse+keyboard and gamepad), slow reaction on player's actions, non-intuitive hotkeys like Esc or "B" button on gamepad. Controls are so bad, that I ran into fire pits at least 2 times instead of throwing fireball there. Very bad mouse cursor interaction: all the time path to cursor is shaking (if it is on the edge of max radius), some paths can't be reached from current camera view.
- Zoom is too bad. It's like a strategy, but I can see only 2-3 meters near me on top and bottom. Yeah, it's very useful to see details of my character right now, when I'm fighting those guys, who is not on screen (sarcasm). Let me see all the battlefield please.
- Bugs. First helmet that I found showed me the world around me without any textures (only curves) when I weared it. One time I was waiting for end of turn of enemy for about 2 minutes, he was just staying (until I pressed a mouse button and suddenly his turn ended and my charatcer ran away right into all enemies).
- Very unfriendly to new players. 2 difficulty from 4 is like – if you missclick one time, you are in deep shieeet and will have to relo. Took something from box near guard? – it's ok, never mind. Took hammer from random bench in the city while nobody sees? – "Take him!" 10 citizens stop extinguishing the fire on the ship and now they want to kill you!
- Localization is pretty bad: bad translations, layout is made only for English, other languages will suffer (do I need to read my ability description fully? YES of course I need it). Well, I can switch to English, but guys: if you do localization, please, do it qualitatively.

I have mixed feelings.
The art is great, the music feels good too though can be a little repetitive at times.  Movements feels great, it's a platformer where for most parts (minus a few a little frustrating sections with no checkpoints) I enjoy the platforming quite a lot, especially certain moves/abilities you obtain later (dashing in midair) are fun to use.
However there is also a feeling of shallowness. The intro sequence is emotional but relative eyecandy as you will hardly see similar events over the course of the game. There isn't much of a story to speak of, and according to my progress indicator I'm already near the end of it. You get tossed into a decaying forest, presumably you are somehow at fault for it going down, and you must restore certain elements (wind, water, etc.) of it. It's rather predictable how it works out.
I don't feel much responsibility or guilt though, and while I see some efforts from the devs to make you feel something for the world (for example by turning enemies into "friends" and by showing that their aggressive behavior towards you is ultimatively only an effect of your presence having ruined the forest and their places of living) there isn't much of narration or anything else substantial to hold onto. On the contrary the gibberishy whining of my spirit companion and the godlike (again gibberishy) overworld voice that narrates certain events with one-liners feel close to being pretentious to me sometimes. It doesn't feel as bad and artifically bloating as for example in "Nihilumbra", but it's not exactly something that captures me either.
Also, the game doesn't feel optimized too well. It's hardly an Assassin's Creed: Unity, yet I can seemingly only run it in windowed mode (fullscreen keeps crashing) and/or with VSynch enabled. But even then cutscenes keep stuttering/lagging.
So, if you expect a constant tear-driver like the intro sequence would suggest, or a deep and actually engrossing story, or a world that you can properly relate to, maybe look elsewhere. If you like Metroidvania-style platforming and find a relatively superficial "magical" world appealing enough go ahead. Sadly I will probably forget this game quickly as soon as I'm done with it. It's not bad, but not as special as I would have expected it to be either.

When I saw that
had announced a game that could be considered a Minecraft "clone", I was skeptical. I love
, but was worried it would be a cheap ripoff. Sure, this game is early access, and you can't be sure of the full product, but when I landed in my procedurally generated world, I instantly fell in love with the recognizable blocks.
That was, until I saw my first skeleton. I immediately found myself surrounded, and not just by mindless bones. They were bobbing and weaving, with their bony fists raised like they were trained by Mike Tyson. I couldn't land a hit, and was forced to run. Luckily, I was saved by early access bugs, as the skeletons ran into trees and were glitched so badly they fused into them, becoming prisoners of the bark. I used Mother Nature herself to survive.
I also rode a horse. That was neat.

A truly impressive early-access title that is worth your hard-earned dollar. The developers are already active with the community, and statements have been made about possibly implementing steam-workshop for game modification in the future. If you want to feel like a kid again, buy this game. You won't regret it.

It's June 1st and this game just hit the Steam Store with a BANG!
I had been waiting ever since the Lego Skateboarding games on PS1 for a Lego game with no theme, no story, just an open world to discover and create things in (kinda like minecraft).  This game does just that, which makes it amazing.  With minecraft-esc randomly generated worlds and over 4 different biomes this game is a real treat.  Now lets get down to pros and cons
Pros:
-Randomly generated worlds
-Tons of vehicles to drive around and explore with
-Tons of outfits to collect and customize
-AI that reacts differently to the outfits you wear (ex. Skeletons wont attack you when wearing a skeleton head)
-Tons of handheld weapons and tools to collect
-And you can freaking ride dragons!
Cons:
-Buggy early access game (microstuttering, texture popping, navmesh errors, etc)
-No workshop support
-No multiplayer
Since there's only 3 cons those 3 should be fairly easy to fix and I bet in about a years time this game will be as polished as ever.

Altough graphics are somehow oudated, game itself bring some nice arcade rallying fun. For first time from ages (and I mean ages, Mobil 1 Rally Championship I think was last rally game with some part of license) we got official FIA licence which helps build rally mood, we got original WRC drivers in original cars battling on four WRC orignal levels. There is something like career mode which will guide you trough all four levels of World Rally Championship from Junior WRC to the top. Locations are official WRC sites but Milestone didn't recreate stages but simply make some variation about it keeping national character. Stages are disappointingly short, max 6km on one stage and 6 stages on one rally which gives us merely 25-30km of rallying on each locations. But stages are packed with action, so we still got fun twitching fingers on endless hairpins. To be not mistaken - this is not a simulator, stages are too short and setups too basic, but game itself could pretend to title of semi-simulator in which nicely done arcade parts like steering, setups or maps got added a pinch of simulation in physics and handling. There are some bugs, mostly in collssion detection and in handling but cautious driver could ride trough whole rally didn't noticing any part of it. Graphics are moderate, cars looks good, some stages also looks nice but some stages looks like unfinished (maybe they will finish it in console game Sebastian Loeb Rally Evo).
Concluding - really nice rally rcade game with pinch of simulation reminding last rally oriented CMR game - Colin McRae 2005 (in first Dirt on 56 events only 18 were rally oriented with next 6 hill climbs).

Very simple but fun game. I cant imagine how successful this game would have been in the arcade. Its format and gameplay would have fit perfectly considering theres only 3 buttons; left, right, and jump/shoot. Also considering how addicting it is.
The game is very fast paced and takes some time to get good, so I'll give some tips.
1. there are several upgrades that are quite useless. here are the ones you shouldn't get:
- hot casing: Makes bullet casings do damage - pretty much useless, don't waste an upgrade on this.
- Gem Sick: Gemhigh lasts for longer duration - since its pretty hard to lose your gemhigh anyway you won't be needing this.
- Reverse Engineering: Lets you shoot a gun module to resuffle it once - after some time you will find a good weapon and you just wont end up using this one, because you'll like sticking to one particular gun.
- Drone - This ones iffy. If you have a high RPM weapon like the Machingun or Noppy it can be usefull, but the most powerfull weapons, the shotgun and laser, dont shoot very fast so the drone will only shoot one bullet.
- Rocket Jump: lift off - this one is iffy too. the main thing you want to be doing in the game is building a combo so you wont be touching the ground very often.
2. These are the most important upgrades
- Safety Jetpack- lets you float for a little while after running out of ammo. - this one is especially good for the laser and shotgun because they have low ammo capacities.
- Blast module: creates an explosion after stomping on enemies - this one is what will mainly be damaging enemies.
- Popping Gems: Shoots bullets upwards when you collect gems - If you also get Gem Attractor it can be very effective in getting the enemies that you miss.
3. Get as much health as possible.
- It took me a while to learn this but when you have full health and you get more hp it adds it to a little bar under you HP meter. Once you get 4 more hp at full health it permanently adds another HP to your Health.

"BIT.TRIP RUNNER" is a 2D platformer, in which you control "CommanderVideo" through 36 different levels divided in 3 worlds.
The worlds are designed in an 8-Bit style, also the soundtrack of each level is well done.
After every level the path gets harder, besides jumping there is also sliding, kicking and protection with shield. The combinations of different key combos make the levels really hard and frustating. There are no checkpoints or any other save points during a level. Even a mistake in front of the "Finish"-line lets you replay the whole level.
In conclusion is "BIT.TRIP RUNNER" a fun little platformer, with awesome graphics, soundtracks and a challenging difficulty. Its not a game what i would play every day, but sometimes it can be really enjoyable. I would recommend this game to everyone who likes classy old school 8-Bit style and challenging gameplay. But for players who get frustrated easily and rage a lot... not really.

GDT is primarily a game of slider adjustment. If, for example, you wish to produce a game of the Action genre, then during Stage 1 of development you'll wish to set the Engine slider to 100%, the Gameplay slider to 80%, and the Story slider to 0%. Meanwhile, your only competition is yourself, and every time you outperform yourself, you raise the bar. If you don't exceed the standard you've set for yourself, improving every game over the last, then your ratings will suffer, and so will your sales. Critics and customers aren't concerned about whether or not you've produced a good game, or an entertaining game. They're interested in whether or not you've produced a game that was statistically better than your last. You'll find yourself frustrated in no time, getting real cozy to all the GDT strategy guides and spreadsheets that litter the internet.
My first game started out enjoyable. I was fascinated by the nostalgia of the Comadore 64 and Nintendo. I liked giving my games titles and momentarily daydreaming about what each would be like. It didn't take long before I adjusted a games sliders luckily and scored my first big hit. Little did I realize the critics and customers would never be accepting of anything less after that. From that point on it was all frustration, confusion and work, eventually leading to bankrupcy during the PS2 era. The next game, I spent most of my time reading those guides and refering to those spreadsheets I mentioned earlier, strategically planning everything with precision. I even downloaded a series of mods that did such things as display percentages in the sliders, for precision purposes. I left nothing to chance, and yet I again found myself bankrupt during the PS2 era.
Before the third playthrough, I must've spent an hour scouring the internet like an NSA agent reading and rereading Vladamir Putin's autobiography and hacked personal correspondance. Finally, I tried one last time, nearly found myself bankrupt during the PS2 era again, but I won with $4.5 billion in my account. Was it worth it? No. There's a lot of examples of "the wrong execution of the right idea" here. That bar raising I spoke of earlier being one. GDT is unmercifully, artificially and ridiculously difficult. From what I've read, that seemed to be more true with each update released for GDT. They found any patch of fresh air within the game, capped it off, and left the player suffocating. For example, MMO's have been nerfed to the point that insane, rapid and unending rises in server maintenance will leave you broke in no time flat, expansion packs or not. This is, in essense, a game of gaming the game, never playing the game. It's work, not fun. From what I've read, the game used to be fun, but in it's current and apparently final state, it's not. You'll find no joy here.
Unless you're a masochist: steer clear. Find something to play that'll actually be fun.

This is a very lovely game. It is very detailed and always nice to look at. It isn't easy, neither gameplay itself nor the (still alpha) interface. The developers contiously do their best to improve gameplay but also always keep track on realism. If you look for real bugs (more than some suboptimal clipping or balancing issues), try another game. This one simply works:)
A bit more than a year later, I can add a little to my review:
The game has two servers: a "fully functional" PVP Server and a PvE Server, that offers slightly reduced funtionality (It doesn't offer port-battles. So the national harbors don't change and players can't be attacked).
The balancing between beeing a game and a simulation seems to be very difficult and Naval Action is more on the simulation side than on the game side. But it still is much fun and nice to look at.
Lots of people complain about the changes the balancing brings. But that's the reason, why the game is still in early access. The engine works fine, the models are detailed, it works. On the PvP Server players have to deal with others, on the PvE Server, some content is missing. But thats ok.
The only real point I see, that compromises my impression of the game is the "TEST-UI" Interface. It's functional but ugly. There are no descriptions for Tooltip-Stats so lots of people have no idea what upgrades are about.
So please read between the lines of negative reviews. Lots of people love the game, even if they write "red reviews" ;)
Have fun!

A complex game revolving around mathematics, gear score, and multifaceted gear combinations as well as stats, perks, and talents. The division can be played infinitely, and always has a new mode of gameplay. For example , story missions, high value target missions, incursions , the underground , survival and the most recent addition  global events.
Experience manhattan in a post apocalyptic landscape , as you battle the many factions in free roaming areas.  Discover incursions as you and your assembled team work together to take down names bosses. Gather and grind high end gear in the dark zone as you or your team battle to extract your loot out of the contaminated zone. Will you follow the division ,or  give in to the temptation to go rogue.

Intro
The Division is a pretty good game that just didn't come to all its promises at start and is a little short. I've finished the game twice on PC and almost 3 times on Xbox so I have a pretty good story to tell y'all.
-----
What stuck out about it and should it be played solo or with friends?
The game really stuck out with its tactical combat/movement and where it was set. The game itself when played alone is an exciting challange when in the right area and is twice as exciting when played with friends that are near or at the same level. Plus, its pretty cool that its based off the real-world Manhattan.
-----
Graphics, how do they look?
Honestly, I think they look beautiful. They really set the mood and fit the game very well and look very very nice even at Medium. There isn't much to say about them besides that they look good and performs well.
-----
How is the combat and weapons in it?
For me, the combat is very smooth and really neato since I haven't really seen this in many games. Its also very tactical which is, again, really cool. You can do♥♥♥♥♥♥like make a run for new cover, dive and roll across short areas or to suprise an enemy, or dry fire if needed.
When speaking of guns, you have a lot of choices spanning from assault rifles such as the ACR, M4A1, AK47, SCAR-L, etc to SMG's such as the Kriss Vector, PP Bizon, MP5, TEC-9, and more. Its a quite wide selection at the beginning but slowly narrows down to mainly AK's and SCAR-L's as your primary with a Vector as your secondary and maybe a shotgun and sniper in your backpack for backups. Oh, and there are also LMG's but they are kinda hard to use unless its an L86 LSW.
-----
Whats the story about?
The main story isn't all that perfect but is pretty neat for somebody like me who gets engaged into any story.
There was a plague called "The Green Poison" which mysteriously broke out around Black Friday. About a month into it many people were sick and started to riot. CERA and JTF tried containing it with a large wall but the street gangs and riots had been slowly picking at them. Then, the first wave of Division agents was activated. About another month later, CERA and most of their checkpoints had been destroyed and JTF was in shambles by all the street gangs and casualties they had along with the first wave of Division agents being magically wiped out. So now its up to you, an agent apart of the second wave, to help get the city back on its knees and take back what was once yours. Skipping the first scene aka tutorial, you are set at Camp Hudson and need to make a Base of Operations in this case being the post office. You need to rescue 3 different people all being in charge for every part of the place: Defense, Tech, and Medical. Once you rescue them, you slowly do all sorts of encounters and missions which during them you take out 3 different gangs: Rioters, Rikers, and LMB. The 3 major gangs running the street. Your mission is to take them out and restore humanity to the city.
-----
Is there PVP? And if yes, how is it?
The PVP area aka the Dark Zone is okay but is FILLED with scummy and jacka** players upon entering at level 14 and under. You may meet people who are level 14 in the normal area outside of the Dark Zone but are level 99's just so they can kick your tiny a** and be total c***s. In this area as well, you cannot just take loot and go. You need to put it in a different little bag that has a certian number of slots which needs to be extracted via calling in a helicopter and getting it decontaminated and picking it up at your stash. Oh, and I forgot to mention, when extracting, EVERYBODY IN THAT AREA CAN SEE IT. So you either be ready for a fight or you'll get lucky and meet nice people which is EXTREMELY RARE. Most of the time, its okay at higher levels since not many people go in there then but when you are a low level, its just hell and not really worth it.
-----
In all, how good is this game?
Honestly, its a little bit of a mixed bunch here. It promised a couple things at launch that never happened but nowhere close to as bad as No Man's Sky. People say this game is bad but honestly, I don't think its all that horrible. Sure there are some things that aren't very good about it but from what I can tell, its a fun game that is very good with friends, has a smooth and a exciting tactical combat system, a wide selection of weapons to choose that narrows down at the end, and a fun but kinda dead stop story line.
Total rating: 7/10

Skullgirls is a fast-paced, drop dead gorgeous fighting game with an interesting and growing roster, one of the best tutorials for a fighting game and a helpful community. It's a must buy if you're interested in getting more serious about fighting games and a blast for playing casually with friends.
Despite never having played a 2d fighter beyond a really casual level, (although I do have a small competitive Smash Bros. background) it was very easy getting into the deeper parts of fighting games. The in-game tutorial gives a very good starting point. It explains basic and more advanced fighting game concepts and beyond that, there are brilliant guides and helpful individuals at
, the dedicated forums.
The cast, albeit small, is intriguing and diverse, ranging from an amnesiac schoolgirl and her hairy parasite to a little girl-turned-cyborg wielding weaponry inspired by old cartoons. and soon, a saxophone man, dropping the beat on his opponents. The currently 9 characters have more than enough charm to make up for their lack in numbers, but there are 4 more characters (the sax-man Big Band, the egyptian songstress Eliza, the wrestler Beowulf and his trusty chair, and the enigmatic robotic version of Ms. Fortune) to be released over the following year that each have a free-to-download period thanks to the Indiegogo campain. And even after that, there is a sheer limitless character pool of astounding variety in the mind of the universe's creator.
The gameplay is fast and offers a vast amount of tools to be creative with your combos. No character plays like the other while the roster in it's entirety is incredibly well balanced. You can choose between fighting as one strong, two medium or three weak characters, allowing you to employ a variety of tactics and easing you into a team-based fighting style, should you be interested in such. The community and the developers have a great deal of interaction. This, along with the often updated beta version allow for fine-tuning and steady improvement of the already great underlying systems.
No matter how much you are interested in fighting game, Skullgirls is a great place to start, and a great place to stay! Still true!

"Awesome" is one of the many adjectives incapable of describing this game if used alone. With gorgeous visuals, beautiful music, challenging yet fun gameplay and an incredibly emotional beginning (seriously, anyone who DOESN'T cry after it needs to see a psychologist), Ori and the Blind Forest is quite the experience for fans of action platformers.

Enjoy playing Dust: An Elysian Tail? How about LIMBO? You know, those side-scrolling multi-layered background games with plenty of puzzles and rich, if sometimes dark, storylines? Those games with characters that draw you into their world with or without words.
Ori and the Blind Forest is the newest in this genre of games, with its sprawling map to explore across the vast Forest of Nibel, to the tip of Mount Koro and the deepest depths of the Moon Caverns. Endless secrets to be found, a streamlined and straighforward leveling system, visually appealing gameplay and combat mechanics, and best of all, the adorable main character Ori, whose goal it is to restore the Forest of Nibel to life by reviving the Spirit Tree.
Never before has a game drawn me in so deep or captivated me with enchanting music, encouraging me to sit still and play it all the way to completion.
If you enjoy the powerful, deep, range of music and moods in Dust: An Elysian Tail, everything from mournful strings to cheerful oboes, then the music alone should compel you to play this game. Go check out the soundtrack if you need some convincing.

I've had so much fun with this game that I (almost) regret buying it for only half its Original price. Undoubtedly the best RPG in my gaming history ever.
I got hooked as the main menu loaded for the very first time and I was greeted with nostalgic music. Then I proceeded to create my characters. It took me a good hour to decide what they should look like, be called and what role they will play ("Today a wizard, tomorrow a battlemage!" is not really my style). Next thing I knew, I was ensnared in Rivellon.
The world is simply beautiful. Colorful. Coupled with exquisite soundtrack, just wandering about is a pleasant experience. I dared not set the difficulty to Honor Mode, as I prize my sanity, but early- and mid-game battles on Tactician were quite challenging. Sometimes I had to repeat them using new strategies until I won. One flaw is that after reaching level 15 and obtaining certain spells, the battles became too easy - I could actually beat some of them before they even started. But the battles weren't the hardest obstacle in my way - the puzzles were. Switches, levers, hidden buttons, fake walls... I would spend half an hour in some areas looking for a way in or out, examining closely every wall and floor to find THAT button. I absolutely loved it, the puzzles are very absorbing and solving them gave me lots of satisfaction, as the clues aren't direct and nobody holds your hand. Another thing I was disappointed with is the crafting system - not the way it works, but its existence at all. During these 100+ hours in game, I have never felt the need to craft something. Loot was abundant, and you can equip yourself with good stuff at most NPCs. I am a hoarder, I always rummage through every possible container there is and pick up everything, so my inventory was cluttered with unneeded ingredients.
The game is full of good humour and has tons of easter eggs, it never failed to amuse me. Dialogues are solid and well voice-acted. The main story and side quests are engaging, so there is "Never a dull moment in
Rivellon"!

Pros:
Combat is fun in Divinity. The elemental magic system was cool and I like that if you mix elements (like electricity and water or poison and fire) there's a reaction.
The abilities and character creation are simple, but they work well within the game.
The graphics, specifically the effects and the glossy nature of the images, are on point.
The soundtrack fits the game well.
Cons:
The story didn't pull me in at all. I did like the idea of time and how it the characters worked within that, but otherwise it just didn't interest me.
Group members will actively run into lava or traps, even when there is a simple route around, that set them on fire or blow them up with pie-eyed glee (killing an entire party).
UI is super clunky and involves a lot of tedious dragging and clicking (with the exception of the recipe crafting).
Several character attributes (like blacksmithing) are mostly pointless. Technically they have a purpose, but they are really just a waste. By the time you get good enough to craft a decent blade, bow, etc. you can find something much, much better. Actually, due to the linear nature of the game you WILL find weapons much better than anything you can make. The only reason crafting is useful is to make arrows or potions. Potions alone will save a ton of money. Dinners are helpful in a pinch too. Beyond that, I found the skill to be pointless. Same went for lockpicking (just set the safes and doors on fire).
Trying to talk to animals was fun, but chasing rats was a pain.
All in all it's a fun game, with some novel mechanics, but I have no real desire to finish it. So, if you are itching for a group-style RPG ala Baldur's Gate (sans epic story), then this is a decent game.

I suppose this is a rhythm platformer, although you don't need to know the rhythm to accomplish the goals. Don't let that dissuade you from trying this out. A timing platformer that creates a beat/rhythm to correctly timed actions is more or less what this is. There is some artificial difficulty mixed into the levels that irked me the wrong way at times, especially some that are late into the final levels. These points are rare, if frustrating, but shouldn't have any real bearing on the overall experience at the end.
This game is fun, and it is solid on its mechanics and its gameplay. The additional extras at the end of levels add a certain competitive spirit to get all the gold you can. If greed hasn't done that already. The graphics are good enough and have a retro feel to it. The image blur can have some negative effects, but the representation of speed gives it a faster pace that is worth the tradeoff.
The way the music stems from your actions, hit or miss, is where this game really shines. The music is awesome to listen to, and coincides with correctly timed maneuvers. The gameplay offers tight and responsive controls that make this a delight to play and except for the few artificial points in the game offers a well thought out level design that offers plenty of challenge. The end levels offer a very specific set of challenges that will require all the previous skills learnt through the course of the game, as it should be.
All-in-all, besides for a few spots this is a solid platformer that is sure to offer plenty of fun with plenty of the wackiness that is a welcome distraction from the main game. With a difficulty that impresses at nearly every level to go with strong gameplay, music, and controls, this is one you should check out.

Toybox Turbos is a fun little arcade racer and spiritual successor to the classic Micro Machines. There's a nice selection of vehicles ranging from cement mixers to moon buggies and around 7 exquisitely designed environments for you to traverse in about 5 or 6 different game modes. That really is the biggest draw for this game, racing around these wonderfully crafted cartoon environments feels fantastic and it's hard not to be distracted at times trying to take in all the details crammed into each course. The vehicles all handle differently and there's definitely a degree of strategy in selecting the right vehicle for each race but experienced players shouldn't have too much difficulty achieving gold medals in every event. Overall I played for about 5 hours and managed to 100% the game so if single player length is an important factor to you be aware of the relatively short playtime. Big WARNING though, multiplayer is a shell of the single player with just a single game mode available, Elimination, with up to 4 players. This didn't bother me as I mainly bought the game for the single player experience but for those hoping this will provide a compelling online experience, look elsewhere.
I loved my time with Toybox Turbos and for the sale price I paid for it I would absolutely consider it money well spent. I'll probably dive back in every now and then to improve my times but for most part I've had my fill.
