This Jakarta developer found here
likes to put two words together such as 'Almightree' and 'Plantsportation'. Which ironically is fitting for a game which also entwines a number of concepts together too. Its a 3D grid platformer decorated in an artstyle that respects the classic games such as Zelda, Bastion and Catherine. Granted the story doesn't really make a lot of sense. You 'the last dreamer' have to save the world in which you live and which is falling apart literally beneath your feet. Why is everything falling apart? I have no idea. In any case, you need to keep ahead of this quake that threatens your very existence and which has already killed all that you have known and loved.
As the last man standing your given a vision that the almightree (some big badass tree) can save your world as long as you get to all of it's withering saplings (20 of them) and touch them in all the right places and bring them back to life, so that they can pull your world back together again. The sap that you are, you agree and branch off onto an adventure where you must traverse 20 levels which demand that you solve block moving problems while on the run.
The gradual difficulty is well presented here, the first 5 levels literally lets you find your roots in the game, while the other later levels from 13 onwards will send you barking mad and will probably have you stumped at times. There are three difficulty levels  easy, medium and hard and I would strongly suggest playing the game hard from onset. As only the toughest difficulty will unlock a further 40+ challenges which also demand your gaming expertise. These stem from levels needing to be done by a certain time requirement, levels needing to be completed with no damage taken, levels being completed with a certain amount of sunspheres collected, and finally levels being completed within the minimum block transportation moves possible.
The puzzle mechanics gradually get harder and harder too, from simple bridging the gap to moving specific blocks so that your shielded from the effects of certain obstacles, such as shooting flowers or electric plants. One false move and you can find yourself in a very serious predicament as you start to feel the ground tremble beneath your feet and the musical score starts chanting that 'danger, danger, run, run, your going to die!' melody.
Before you know it 'TIMBER!' and down you go.
There's also multiplayer, but these are just the same 20 levels randomly being selected. It would have been a nice surprise if the multiplayer had a more random perk to it, by chopping up the levels that we have already played in the single player mode, and delivering them in a more splintering offshoot, with sections randomly jumbled up and maybe even mirrored. This way it would have been more exciting constantly thinking on your feet more, while being pitted against a worthy adversary online.

Skullgirls is a fast-paced, drop dead gorgeous fighting game with an interesting and growing roster, one of the best tutorials for a fighting game and a helpful community. It's a must buy if you're interested in getting more serious about fighting games and a blast for playing casually with friends.
Despite never having played a 2d fighter beyond a really casual level, (although I do have a small competitive Smash Bros. background) it was very easy getting into the deeper parts of fighting games. The in-game tutorial gives a very good starting point. It explains basic and more advanced fighting game concepts and beyond that, there are brilliant guides and helpful individuals at
, the dedicated forums.
The cast, albeit small, is intriguing and diverse, ranging from an amnesiac schoolgirl and her hairy parasite to a little girl-turned-cyborg wielding weaponry inspired by old cartoons. and soon, a saxophone man, dropping the beat on his opponents. The currently 9 characters have more than enough charm to make up for their lack in numbers, but there are 4 more characters (the sax-man Big Band, the egyptian songstress Eliza, the wrestler Beowulf and his trusty chair, and the enigmatic robotic version of Ms. Fortune) to be released over the following year that each have a free-to-download period thanks to the Indiegogo campain. And even after that, there is a sheer limitless character pool of astounding variety in the mind of the universe's creator.
The gameplay is fast and offers a vast amount of tools to be creative with your combos. No character plays like the other while the roster in it's entirety is incredibly well balanced. You can choose between fighting as one strong, two medium or three weak characters, allowing you to employ a variety of tactics and easing you into a team-based fighting style, should you be interested in such. The community and the developers have a great deal of interaction. This, along with the often updated beta version allow for fine-tuning and steady improvement of the already great underlying systems.
No matter how much you are interested in fighting game, Skullgirls is a great place to start, and a great place to stay! Still true!

Well, I'm not sure where to begin. Ori and the Blind Forest exemplifies all that makes the Metroidvania genre so popular. It is a game that follows a fairly linear story, yet allows a considerable amount of exploration beyond and beside the intended path. It is a platformer that presents intimidating challenges, yet is consistently fair and forgiving because of the life bar and portable save points. Most of all, it's an absolutely gorgeous thing to behold, and the wondrous atmosphere puts any other platformer to shame. You needn't take more than a cursory glance at the trailer to realize this.
Progression comes in the form of powers and abilities. The powers are what you'd expect from a classic Metroidvania - wall jumps, double jumps, and a downward smash technique that obliterates foes and obstacles alike. They all have multiple uses in travel and combat, and the mid-air bash in particular is highly enjoyable and unique. Abilities, on the other hand, are more like passive bonuses that offer assistance in various ways, such as revealing more secrets on the overworld map, increasing your attack damage or causing collectibles to float towards your character. Notably, none of the passive abilities are required to finish the game, so if you're a sucker for punishment you could get through it without spending a single point on them.
To figure out anything to complain about in this game would be a challenge in itself. Truthfully, it's about as close to perfection as the genre will get. If you don't enjoy Ori and the Blind Forest, it's because you don't like Metroidvanias at all, and that's fine. But those of us who do could have asked for nothing better.

Toybox Turbos is essentially a rebooted version of the old Micro Machines games in all bar the name. These were fantastic top-down view racing games that used everyday locations to create the race tracks. Toybox Turbos continues that trend and adds vibrant levels with plenty of new obstacles to make things more interesting (or irritating, depending on your preference).
The game modes are split into Classic (a simple race to the finish line), Escape (outrun a wall of death for as long as you can), Time Trial (complete a number of laps with no competitors as fast as you can), Overtake (as the name suggests, overtake as many AI cars as you can in the time limit) and Elimination which is typically a boss battle. On these the goal is to either destroy your opponent or get far enough ahead that they fall off the screen. Both players start at 5/10 points and you gain a point for getting ahead/lose a point for falling behind. First to 10 wins. These can be a bit irritating if you use the classic top-down view as you often can't see far enough ahead to dodge obstacles in time. Still, it's a minor flaw.
I've not tried the multiplayer yet but the single player is great even on its own. If you're looking for a casual, fun to play racer in the vein of Mario Kart and/or were a fan of the original Micro Machines games then do yourself a favour and pick this up. Great little game. Taking the best element from Baulder's Gate, Diablo II, Dungeon Siege II, and D&D.  There are numerous games that stress dexterity, and real-time combat systems and very few of these treasures that stress strategy and cunning (Final Fantasy Tactics anyone?).
Taking your time to enjoy every corner of a game is what the adventurers of our time dream of.  Cast aside your speed-runs, your competative natures, and your rush to get to max level.  ENJOY your stroll through this game and truely become attached to your characters.
The only Cons for this game are really the learning curves (if you've never played any of the games mentioned above, you will die early on and frequently).  They start you with 1 resurrection scroll each and the tutorials will come up AS they are happening.  In a nutshell, that means you won't learn that standing in oil and lighting it on fire is a bad idea until someone is burning.
Another Con would be that despite being beautifully programmed and coded, the optimization has limits and playing the game for anything longer than an hour risks memory leaks and crashes.  Save frequently and restarting the app alleviates this.
Ultimately an incredible purchase and the Enhanced Edition adds all the bug fixes and perks that the consoles received (included in the price).  Grab it when it's on sale ($20 I've seen it at times) and you'll kick away weeks of your life... well spent and enjoyed.

I know a lot of reviews say this game has no "handholding" and is not for casual players, but don't let that neccessarily turn you away. I've never played one of those old-school CRPGs this game hearkens back to, so I entered the game pretty blind. It was very challenging at first, but once you get the hang of things and your characters have access to more tools and lower cooldowns, the combat aspect at least becomes much, much easier. And more fun. Every turn is like a puzzle. You don't just spam attacks (although I have two pure fighters who largely do... my two control mages support that.)
If you enjoy exploring every nook and cranny of a mysterious world, leaving no stone unturned, you will adore this game. While there is no quest tracker or markers or such modern amentities, the game actually does a good job of planting hints in the world (as well as updating your journal) so you're never left completely lost and confused. You get a great sense of satisfaction from figuring something out, putting the pieces together, following hints and clues, but nothing is completely obtuse. I've had to Google a couple times, but it's always been a "DUH" moment. Never a "how the hell would anyone ever figure that out" moment. Google isn't neccessary though... the answer is always in your inventory, in an NPC's dialogue, or hidden somewhere nearby!
I also like how I don't feel punished on normal difficulty for not building characters optimally. You have total freedom to build your characters as you choose, and it seems as long as you have a basic idea of what you want that character to do, you'll be fine. It seems like all the skill schools are pretty OP in their own ways. And you have a lot to play with when it comes to environmental effects, scrolls, grenades, etc. There's no battle you can't win, you just may have to try different approaches. There's a respec option available eventually, but I never thought, "oh, I really ♥♥♥♥ed up and I NEED to respec." I've been tempted to do it just because there are so many possibilities and things I want to try...
It's really difficult for me to feel compelled to finish a game these days, and I just can't get enough of this one. If you're a fan of RPGs of any sort and familiar with the basics, don't pass on this game. It's immersive, fun, rewarding, and best of all, you can play it with one hand. ;)

Beautiful, emotional storytelling. It's a story first, and a point and click game second. The game is simply the medium. It's funny, serious, dark and hopeful all at once. A simple concept experienced masterfully, games don't normally affect me but this one struck a chord. The soundtrack is only a couple of very basic tracks, but it is hauntingly beautiful, and deserving of the pickup. In many ways, this game is like a movie experience with the added benefit of your own input and interaction. Visually, it's retro look gives it charm, and it's impressive how much emotion can be conveyed with pixelated animation.
You take the role of a pair of specialists who enter peoples memories, specifically dying people, to generate an experience from them that they express as a dying wish. In a style reminiscent of Inception they dive into the life of John, to fulfill his wish to go To The Moon. They have great chemistry, with fantastic pop culture references and lots of one liners. The story they discover is touched with meaning and emotion. I can't say what makes this game so great without revealing anything that happens, but it brought me to bittersweet tears.
I bought this on a whim, a whim I now very greatful for. It's a truly enriching game, and it will make you cry.

Overveiw: In Space Marine you are a Ultramarine from the Warhammer 40,000 universe, and you go to Forge world Griaia to stop an Orc invasion

Simply amazing. If you're 40k fan, the opportunity to play as a single character rather than at a tactical level (as we have so many times before) is brilliant. Combat is an unusual mix of third person shooter and frantic melee combat, which sounds odd in theory but really makes for a great experience.
Yes, the campaign is a little short (a good couple of evenings play if you don't rush it), but the voice acting is first class and the story is memorable and true to its roots. Graphically rich and violent in its depiction of the waves of enemies you will righteously purge, it indulges 40k fans with one of the best depictions of the game universe I've yet played.
After completing it I dabbled a bit with the multiplayer on Exterminatus mode, 4 players versus wave after wave of enemies or upto 8 man teams versus 8 other human players and that gives the game a bit of extra longetivity.
Ultimately, its a game you will want to replay for the campaign or pvp blast. Enjoy it, finish it and then load it up it up again whenever you feel like purging xenos (or human opponents).
***EDIT*** I want add the multiplayer is really good. You can play with others against waves of computer controlled enemies as I mentioned before or on two opposing teams of human player against each other. This adds another level of enjoyment.
I would STRONGLY SUGGEST you play the co-op game mode "Exterminatus" first to get all the weapons unlocked. "Versus" mode is pretty unforgiving if you don't have access to the Weapons and Perks. Killing the cpu mobs is fun and reasonably easy. With practice I can now complete 2 and a half waves solo, although no doubt there are others who can do better.
***/EDIT***
Finally, my recommendation.
I picked up the game when it was on sale and frankly I wish I had done so sooner. Grab it whenever it's on sale and don't worry about the DLC, it's not necessary unless you want to look cool in multiplayer.

When I started this game, I enjoyed it... at least for a little while. The game itself isn't necessarily bad. The core mechanics are decent and fun but I found a couple of issues that ruined the entire game for me and made it something that I just can't recommend.
The game is a 2D autoscrolling runner. If you aren't familiar with that, basically, you just avoid obstacles coming towards you from the right hand side of the screen and your character runs automatically for you. My main issue with the game is how unforgiving it is. I know it is supposed to be difficult but most of the difficulty comes from pressing a button a frame too early or a frame too late. It made the game extremely frustrating at times.
On top of that, it gets repetitive really quickly. Each stage is made up of a couple of different patterns which are just ordered differently across each level. Most of these patterns are bearable but get annoying when you have to do them repeatedly but the difficult patterns are ridiculous when you add the fact that you have to have frame perfect precision (you don't control movement so I wouldn't call it pixel perfect). Usually the more difficult patterns come at the end of the level which means that if you fail, you'll have to redo the entire level and when you get to the later levels that become exceedingly long, it just becomes frustrating. Also, the music becomes repetitive as you play the same level over and over again.
I enjoy this type of game but this one is just too frustrating to recommend. If you want a game like this, I would suggest you get Bit.Trip Runner 2. Its a lot more enjoyable and all the issues I have with this game are fixed in that one.

"Write a review for Bad Rats: the Rats' Revenge." The command was clear, succinct. The words of a force that knew exactly what it required of the universe, and knew exactly what it needed to do to get what it required.
As soon as I read those words, I knew I had been chosen. That I had a responsibility to tell people what I had discovered, what I had been taught.
Bad Rats: The Rats' Revenge is a game without peers. It defies all typical notions of what a game, or even what a work of art, can be. Released in 2009 to little fanfare by unproved developer Invent4 Entertainment, a Brazilian Developer based in Porto Alegre, it was not an overnight success. Of course, people who were lucky enough to play it at the time realized quickly that they had a masterpiece on their hands.
The game was developed starting in late 2008, with development being led by creative visionary and media influencer Augusto Bülow, a name that will surely in the years to come ring with as much clout and prominence as the likes of Hideo Kojima, Todd Howard, or Shigeru Miyamoto. Mr. Bülow holds a bachelor's degree in computer science, and this technical know-how shines through in every aspect of Bad Rats. From the painstakingly recreated and highly realistic physics, to the biting and sometimes scathing social commentary present throughout the experience.
For those who haven't been made privy to the core concept of Bad Rats, it is as brilliant in its' simplicity as it is elegant in its' execution. This is a tale not of Rats that were born bad, but good rats, honest, patriotic rats that have been driven to go bad to defend themselves and those that they love. The storyline expertly plays with the dynamics of how far down a dark path good intentions can take you, and may leave you questioning the very nature of the morality and ethics that we often take for granted. These rats have no inherent, born hatred of cats. In the eyes of each young rat burns a desire for a more just and verdant society, where someday cats and rats could live together, free of hatred and conflict. But as they witness the atrocities perpetrated by the previous generation, the seeds of hatred and the acid of vengeance slowly fills their hearts. It's an emotional experience that far exceeds the likes of other efforts by games to show the darkness of the human condition in times of war, such as Spec Ops: The Line or This War of Mine. The emotional honesty and character development presented here is matched perhaps only by the greatest works of wartime fiction ever written, such as the works of Tolstoy or Boris Pasternak.
Cleverly, and somewhat tragically, our gameplay experience explores the darkest part of the generational conflict between the titular rats and their longtime antagonist, the cats. I refer of course to the treatment of prisoners of war during total war. The primary goal of the gameplay is to carry out executions on the cat POW's, often in increasingly gruesome ways. The content is extremely disturbing, and it's rich framework truly places you in the position and mindset of a young man bound to his duty, despite the clash with his own ideas of moralism and the value of life. It surely served as a partial inspiration for the later title Papers Please, as the parallels are clear with that game's depiction of life as a servant of a fascist government in increasingly tumultuous times.
This game is an experience that will test your skill, your intuition, your intelligence, and perhaps most of all, your humanity. It is not a piece of work that should be missed by anyone interested in psychological horror, philosophical questions, or masterpieces of artistic expression in digital media.

Cutting right to the Minecraft comparisons:
First of all, my kid loves it already.  Any problems I have are nitpicks from an adult perspective who can see the potential for a true Minecraft 2.0 killer.  That said, I like it, and will be back.
My first impression is that it plays a lot like the Lego story games set in a minecraft world.  Fighting destroying and collecting coins have been ramped up.  Creation, destruction, exploration and unlocking new items is fun, but will run out.  Longevity will rest on the creation toolset, and I have a thought.  Minecraft is addictive because of how easy it is to build.  Redstone ensures that you are only limited by your own creativity.  So how does LEGO Worlds stack up?  "Building" is more or less a three click affair.  Once something is unlocked and paid for, you can build it anywhere and the terraforming and creation is done for you.  This is a double edge sword.  On one hand building a town will be a piece of cake, and once multiplayer is implemented, you will be able to populate large areas very quickly.  On the other, it takes away from the guarenteed uniqueness each minecraft world.
The individual brickbuilding tools are there, but they are as clunky as trying to build with a pile of bricks on your living room floor where your are only allowed to use one of those arm extending grabbers instead of your hands.  I'm sure this will get refined.
This game mirrors Minecraft in it's lack of physics, this makes me sad, because as a kid, I would spend hours with my brother building catapults.  We would launch rocks at eachothers catapults until one was too broken to work.  I don't see how that is possible here.  There may be motorized parts, but the interaction between objects is nonexistant.  I also hope there is a way to build your own vehicles at some point.  Multiplayer is going to put this game to the test.
Pros:
The LEGO look has been nailed.
The biomes are varied, dense and detailed.
The world is made of the tiniest bricks, which adds to the detail.
There are no rules.
Creative and Survival modes exist at the same time.
Explore to unlock.
Potential to unlock realworld kits for use in game.
Destruction is satisfying.
The sheer volume of figs, props and creations.
Riding a dragon.
Mowing lawns replaces bumpy bricks with smooth flat ones.
Steamrollers lay roads.
The driller, wow, it is fun to drive.
Eagles, planes, motorcycles.
Cons:
No physics engine.
Mouse and Keyboard control doesn't play well with controller controls
Selection tools are pretty rough.
The obvious setup for microtransaction after microtransaction.
No MP yet
World creation options not present yet
No aiming retecule.  Not a big deal till you blow a hole in the side of your castle when you were aiming at a skeleton
No first person mode
Brick building tools are really tedious

This game has so much potential, and it is soooooo fun! I highly recommend it! Even though it is in early access, I would get it now before the price goes up lol. If you love Minecraft, you will LOVE THIS!!

Now tha tthe game is out of early access, here's my final thoughts:
TLDR - Do NOT get if you enjoy building things.  This game is more about exploring and adventuring.
The GOOD
-Exploring is extremely addicting.
-The game aces the lego feel and is really charming.
-I play with most graphics maxed and the game looks pretty good for the most part, it's especially refreshing seeing all the different block shapes instead of standard squares in most of these games.
-I like the new brick progression system for the most part.  Makes it feel more like a game than a really rough beta.
The BAD
-Camera needs a lot of attention, althouth it's not the hell that it used to be.  Make sure to switch to a different mode in the ingame menu.
-Controls feel off a lot of the time.  Flying vehicles keeps resulting in me moving up instead of forward since the control schemes are inconsistent.  And your character easily grabs and tries to climb onto anything it bumps into which is extremely annoying when navigating close areas, why hasn't this been given it's own dedicated button yet?!  Even Assassins Creed has that.
-There's a "Quest" system where characters want to be given an item and than you can unlock their discovery.  But there is no reliable way to get most of the items, especially since a lot of the items don't spawn on each world.  Worse yet you literally give them the item from your inventory, so you have to collect it all over again each time.  Note, talking to a character while walking around with the item in your hand gives it to them, even if it is the wrong item it is gone now.
-Doesn't say which biomes are in the world you generate.  So you have to load into it each time to see since the picture is ulta generic and vague.
-LOTS of quests spawn underground it seems.  Since digging isn't a very intuitve or precise process it can be annoying finding them.
-Underwater chests are extremely hard to open.  Terrain generation and a limited air supply means multiple deaths while you try to maneouver or remove terrain stopping it from opening.
The UGLY
-The building mechanics.  Still are unchanged since day 1.  They took a game that should have simple block placement like Minecraft or Startmade and gave it an overly convoluted building system.  To keep this short, you can build lots of impressive things.  But even something really simple will take ages to make and require you to fight both the camera and having to carefully make sure you place EVERY block in the right place.  Even for a simple wall it is insanely easy to snap them everywhere but where you want
-Combat just isn't fun.  Ranged aiming is insane, even when zoomed into their nausiating first person mode it still trys to auto aim, spear chucking I'm completely unable to figure out for example.  And melee is just as bad somehow.  Lots of enemies hit way harder than you and you are just trading blows in typcial lego style, basically your goal is to buy more hp so that you can wishstand their hits long enough to kill them.
-No vehicle creation yet.  Seems like a massive oversight.
Final Thoughts
I wanted to like this game, I still enjoy playing it a bit and don't regret getting it cheaply during EA.  But I can't see most kids enjoying it for very long, the controls are overly complicated and unintuitive in places yet the game is too simplistic for adults to keep interest for long.  Frankly the building system is what killed it for me, they haven't improved it at all sicne the beta.  Here's a few final tips if you do pick it up:
-I heavily suggest playing with a controller.  Game feels lot better with one, sometimes the keyboard controls don't seem to work when you press them in the build modes.
-After doing a quest for a creature you can usually "Discover" it.  This is ANY quest not just the give me X item ones.
-Zooming all the way in goes into a first person mode.  It can help a lot even if I find it nausiating.   With mouse and keyboard you reeeeeaally have to keep scrolling in, it seems to have a hump you have to get over to reach first person.
The mechanics and the gameplay are just as tight as their clothes.

Seeing that this was available as a free download for a weekend, I almost ignored it even then, marking it down as just another wannabe team-based fighter. However, I caved in and gave it a go after all, and I must say that I was very pleasantly surprised.
Boasting some of the most fantastic HD artwork and animation in a 2D fighter I've ever seen, this game is also full to the brim with stunning, high-octane quickfire combat the akin to BlazBlue, Guilty Gear or, given the team mechanic, Marvel's VS. series.  It's a finely balanced piece of fighting gold that, while lacking in characters, punches the personality of each of its combatants through the roof.  You'll find yourself grinning at quips and one-liners, as well as face-palming over terrible puns and reminiscing with one character's particular fascination with 80's and 90's cartoon quotes.
Overall, this is far worth the asking price of $15 (given that you're not buying it on sale), as it offers up more than its fair share of fighting goodness for the cost. If you're a fan of fighting games at all, especially fast paced ones, then this is a given.

A potentially good game utterly ruined by a single bad addition.  TRAPS.
For some reason, the developers of this game decided to stuff sections of it completely full of traps and environmental hazards that the game engine was clearly never designed to handle.
The problem is that you can only control a single character at a time, and you can't queue up or issue simultaneous orders.  So if getting past an environmental hazard or trap means doing 3-4 actions, you have to sit there while your characters do them one at a time, including going through full animations every time.  If you make a mistake or step on one of the many (MANY) hidden mines, then it's game over, since even if you theoretically have the healing skills to save your party, the engine doesn't allow you to act quickly enough to do so.
Geting past a simple fire-totem-in-a-pool-of-oil trap, for example, means destorying the totem, which might take 30-60 seconds depending on how you do it.  And there'll be several of these in a row in places.  BORING.
It's a huge shame, because the game's got a great combat system, a decent story, and a fun tongue-in-cheek approach to dialogue, but unless you're willing to spend hour after hour tediously crawling through dungeons at an utter snail's pace, you'll drop the game long before you get to fully enjoy any of it.

Having aspirations to become a naval officer and chagrined I will likely never have the chance to captain a warship under independent command (given my country's pitifully small navy), I took great interest in Naval Action. While rather pricey for a game still in an open alpha, the game itself is quite fun – with new content being added regularly.
While still a game in active development with quite a few flaws and the sometimes painfully repetitious grinding for higher ranks/manpower/resources to make components to construct ships, the freedom afforded in the game is outstanding. Learning optimal angles to sail in the wind, manoeuvring to ripple off broadside after broadside at foes with great plumes of gunsmoke obscuring your vessel, your battleline - and ominously, that of the enemy. The ability to board an enemy vessel to take a grand prize for yourself and the crew. This game exudes the spirit of the Napoleonic era.
More than that, nothing quite beats the exhilaration of participating in a PVP fleet action in a wee 7th rate cutter against 4th and 5th rate enemy ships.  The stark terror of the sea about your small ship awash from a 25-gun broadside of 18 pound shot, with a mere six-gun broadside of 6-pounder shot to reply with.

Beautiful, emotional storytelling. It's a story first, and a point and click game second. The game is simply the medium. It's funny, serious, dark and hopeful all at once. A simple concept experienced masterfully, games don't normally affect me but this one struck a chord. The soundtrack is only a couple of very basic tracks, but it is hauntingly beautiful, and deserving of the pickup. In many ways, this game is like a movie experience with the added benefit of your own input and interaction. Visually, it's retro look gives it charm, and it's impressive how much emotion can be conveyed with pixelated animation.
You take the role of a pair of specialists who enter peoples memories, specifically dying people, to generate an experience from them that they express as a dying wish. In a style reminiscent of Inception they dive into the life of John, to fulfill his wish to go To The Moon. They have great chemistry, with fantastic pop culture references and lots of one liners. The story they discover is touched with meaning and emotion. I can't say what makes this game so great without revealing anything that happens, but it brought me to bittersweet tears.
I bought this on a whim, a whim I now very greatful for. It's a truly enriching game, and it will make you cry.

Hands down - best, most fulfilling RPG of the past few years. This game has everything that every classic RPG should have - a huge, interesting world to explore that lives and breathes, fascinating and often funny characters and dialouge, an intruiguing and ever unfolding story/plot, a satisfying and rich combat system, a deep skill and crafting system and loads of unforgettable "moments" that you will put right up there with your best memories from all the classic RPG's you've ever played. I give this gem my highest recommendation. It brought back and even rivaled all those great memories of playing the gaming classics like the Ultima series in the 80's and Baldur's Gate in the 90's. A must play for any true connoisseur of the RPG genre. Some newcomers may be thrown off by the difficulty of some of some of the bosses (that Braccus Rex battle was ridiculously hard) and puzzles, however. I did have to resort to combing through a few forums for answers to really obscure puzzles... i.e. the "weight/balance" puzzle comes to mind as well as a bunch of really lame   "push buttons in specific (but nevertheless arbitrary) order" puzzles - with no clues or hints so it's all trial and error in which you may waste an hour or two just trying various combinations. Hopefully they got rid that nonsense in the sequel. Nevertheless... 9/10

-CONTAIN SPOILERS-
This game had one of the greatest storylines added to an 8-bit game. (Short summary, two employers of a company named "Sigmund Corporation" help an elderly named John Wyles fufill his desire to go to the moon.) Now these two are to travel through Johnny's memories collecting energy from specific objects to get to his earliest memories. That would allow them to plant artifical memories, making it seem like he had the desire all along and had already acheived it. Understanding this, I had a feeling it would be another typical game, just a bit different than the other ones.
Oh how was I wrong.
This story had much more feeling to it, much more meaning. It's so weird knowing how it all is going to end, yet looking forward to the process of getting to that point. Looking into a person's dark past is really heart racing, really shocking. I'd have to say a few of the most shocking things in that game were; (not in order)
1) Finding out River had Asperger's Syndrome.
2) This should have been obvious but I didnt quite catch it, Johnny having a deceased brother.
Another great aspect to this video game was the comical moments to sort of relieve the tenseness. Nicely timed, not too silly to ruin the whole development but not too "ha, not funny". Eva was so cute in her little battle against a squirrel. hehe.
I'd also say the artwork was beautiful, and the backround music was a giant bonus. (Especially because they use the piano as the main instrument, no words needed to set the mood. ) For River (Johnny's Version) & For River (Sarah and Tommy's Version) is definitely a recommended song! The only unsatisfying part to the game is the ending. I felt pretty empty and left confused at it. Episode 1? What is there going to be a series of games? Is this Final Fantasy? (It's never final, lol.) And how the screen flashes like they are still in a memory, whaat? Well, it was intended to confuse the audience but it left me irritated.
Well enough of me rambling, I conclude that this was a wonderful game and I definitely recommend.

Great game. Well, it´s in EA obviously but the devs are pretty active and also very communicative, have frequent polls for new features/ development steps and so on going, so i´m not worried the game will grow to maturity...
That being said, for me as a PvE player there is not (yet) very much to do, going on missions or hunting ships on the open sea are the activities that i can do so far, but tbh, that´s exactly what i bought the game for. More PvE stuff is to come,like more mission types and other activities. Right now the production focus lied (and probably still lies) on the combat (pve and pvp) mechanics as well as economy/ trading and crafting, the latter being really complex already. So if you are a designated crafter, you´ll feel at home here as well...
the combat and sailing mechanics are what the game shines at. It takes a rather realistic approach. It features a manual aim system, where each gun type and also each ship has a certain way to aim...combined with the need to take your ships stability and the conditions of the sea into account, aiming takes a bit of practice. Each single cannon ball seems to be tracked, means not only it "hits the hitbox,applies damage and that´s it",but it might hit, penetrate the hull, run halfway thru the ship, kill some crew on its way to the magazine... you get it... or it might just bounce off and drop into the water...of course there are also chain shots for destroying the sails,as well as grapes, especially to decimate the crew of an enemy vessel, available... what ever suits your needs :)
the gameplay/ combat is very slow paced and has a most realistic age of sail feel to it, so if you are looking for a quick combat game,where you jump into a match and 5 minutes later leave again with 20 kills on your count, this is NOT your game...
if you´re the type of guy who throws a party when you land a beautyful broadside barrage after outmaneuvering that large vessel over there, then yes, this is for you :) while we´re at cannon barrages: the sound of a 20 cannon volley alone is worth 100$ :D
So yea... the game is far from feature complete, especially PvE players feel the lack of content pretty quick, pvp players who have no issues with finding a guild might have an advantage for now :)
But that´ll change, since they have PvE servers as well as pure pvp servers, the devs are showing the same interest in both parts of the game... But as i said at the beginning, i´m here for the ship fights anyway, and those are unmatched by any multiplayer game i have played so far...
btw, the recently added open world is H U G E ... a trip from southern cuba up to Cape Canaveral (Florida) took me almost 2 hours :)
There are several playable nations (including Pirates, which might change,meaning them being handled differently in the future...for now they´re "just" a nation as the others), which -on pvp servers- fight for the control over the MANY dozens of towns all around the caribean sea... but as mentioned, i´m a PvE player, so i´ll leave the PvP review to others...

I'm a huge rally fan and for me, this game ticks some boxes but is lacking in key areas.
Gameplay experience is generally good, I play in the hood view and its easy to get enjoyment from the sense of speed it creates. The car set up option is also good and fairly thorough.
The handling of the cars (I use a controller) is, although, a bit sloppy and I would've liked the kind of percision evident in games like the DiRT series.
My biggest problem and the most frustrating thing about this game is the pace notes. If you arent very familiar with rally outside the gaming world, perhaps this wouldn't seem like a big thing. The pace notes in game are HORRIFICALLY inaccurate and vague. The developers clearly gave little thought to individual stages and instead recorded all the notes and threw them in haphazardly into the rallys with little thought. Many of the corners in game tighten and are rarely mentioned, to get out of recording specific stage notes, there is a chicane (left/right or right/left) note and a very vague Turn Left/ Turn Right junction note with no specific severity of bend. Without a course map it becomes extremely difficult to successfully navigate a stage as crests and tightening corners are never mentioned and its largely left to guess work.
I could go on about the various problems with this game but the fact of the matter is if youre looking for a decent rally simulator with good gameplay, great graphics, and decent gaming experience, buy DiRT.
This game has a long way to come before it can compete.

At its core, Superbrothers is a 2D point and click adventure game. You click on places to move, try to find objects to help you progress and experience a story mainly told through the music and pixelart. Said pixelart is a very dense affair and can take some getting used to. Combat is handled in a 1v1 mini-game where you need to time your attacks or defense with what the enemy is doing. It’s ok, a bit annoying but otherwise harmless and you, thankfully, won’t encounter it too often. The game is on the short side, clocking in at about four hours but I felt I got my monies worth.
The game follows the adventures of a Scythian and her adventures in locating a mysterious object called the “Megatome”. She is nameless and her past is unknown. Well, that goes for most everyone you’ll encounter. There’s not a learning about pasts, just experiencing the here and now. You interact with a few people in the game, but the game mostly focuses on exploring the world and trying to find objects as you go through it. There are a few occasions where you’ll fight a wolf and an object known as the Golden Trigon but they’re few and far between. The game also likes to insert amusing jokes and references as well as break the fourth wall. Overall, the story is fairly ok.
The puzzles weren’t too bad on difficulty, so long as you could figure out how the game wanted you to interact with it. There is a bit of a learning curve to the controls, especially if you’re new to the genre. While there was the occasional puzzle that could be difficult to solve, I managed to get by most of them just fine. They usually require you to move your mouse in a certain way or click on the right places of the screen in the right order. Sometimes the game can be frustrating because it won’t clue you in on whether you’re trying to solve the puzzle correctly so that can lead to a lot of brute force guessing.
It made the port to PC rather reasonably but it’s still missing quite a bit. What it does have, is a plentiful amount of resolution options, fullscreen on/off, Twitter integration (though I have my doubts this works anymore) and a single volume slider. It would have been nice to see multiple audio sliders and the ability to configure graphics. The game handles itself well on both the desktop and mobile devices though I think the touch experience is preferred. Though, I doubt you’ll really feel like you're missing anything when using the mouse. There weren’t any serious porting issues reported and the game didn’t have any major bugs or crashes when I gave it a go.
The visuals presented in Superbrothers are a rich and dense pixelart design and are quite interesting to look at. Combined with the atmospheric chiptune/electronic soundtrack, it really creates a unique experience as you travel through the levels.
Point and clicks like Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery are a mixed bag for me. I always seem to get really intrigued by the concept but the execution doesn’t always gel with me. Sure, the game was oddly engaging for me when I first played it back in 2012 and I think it still holds up now. I also won’t deny that a lot of the homages/references to the Legend of Zelda series probably helped me enjoy this game more than I normally would. That said, the combat is pretty lacking and it can feel like the game is being unnecessarily obtuse at times. Puzzles can be confusing or downright frustrating, requiring you to force brute them or look up hints online. Which I’ve found is pretty typical of minimalist point-and-clicks like these. It’s why I don’t like playing them too often. As for Superbrothers, I still think it’s worth giving a go if you’re into this genre or want an introduction to it.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a challenging yet addictive jump and run game in pixelart-style, with a nice soundtrack, you can play to kill some time.

Be warned: this is not a rhythm game.
It's a timing game.
What's the difference? A rhythm game would have you press buttons to a musical beat, and you would be rewarded for pressing those buttons in tempo. Bit.Trip Runner will actually get you killed if you ever try to follow the rhythm.
The beat of the music corresponds to the obstacles as you pass them by, NOT when you need to press a button to execute a move. I am a drummer, and I have good rhythm, and I promise you that your button presses will be desynchronized with the music itself, and you always have to press a fraction of a second earlier than the beat to clear the obstacle.
And in the final third of the game, the timing required for button presses is so pinpoint precise that I actually found it easier to MUTE THE GAME so I could get through it, concentrating on the position of the character rather than the music. The first two thirds of the game are easy enough to get through, but the difficulty spikes to an astonishingly punishing degree at the end, sapping all fun out of the experience. In this section, the timing needed for your moves varies wildly depending on the obstacle, and I am talking literal tenths of a second will mean the difference between success and messing a single move up, forcing you back to the beginning.
The Pitfall-inspired bonus levels take the challenge to an even more drastic degree, and to prove my point, they feature no music at all. I think the developers know that their game has NOTHING to do with rhythm or music - it's all about executing a series of moves with ABSOLUTELY EXACT timing, and music gets in the way of that.
(It's worth noting that you would have to be an absolute masochist to attempt perfecting this game. These bonus levels are only accessible by completing a main level and obtaining all of its collectibles in one run - and then if you make even a single mistake on the bonus level, you have to redo the main level again to reattempt it. This type of design is so disrespectful of a player's time that I pity anybody who will find themselves going for it.)
Aesthetically, each environment is rendered with very basic geometric shapes, and while some are more interesting than others, they lack the psychedelic colors and movement of Beat and Core that works so well as background material. The music is also significantly less varied in tone from previous Bit.Trip titles - the game's three songs all have the same feel to them, a sort of bubblegum chiptune major key sound that will likely get on your nerves before the end.
The more I think about it, the more I dislike this game. There's really nothing good to say about it, beyond its ability to give you that feeling of exquisite relief tied to finally getting through a tough sequence, when you know you never ever have to play it again.

Skullgirls is on sale, but should you buy it?
Now, if you play fighting games, you probably already know if you like skullgirls or not. If you don't play fighting games, should you get into this wonderful genre and should Skullgirls be your entry? Let's take a look.
First off, a lot of people I know always say the same thing when I talk to them about fighting games, "I'm not very good at them." Putting it lightly, they're wrong, and you probably are wrong too. It's not that you're bad at fighting games, it's that you don't know how to play them.
Are you bad at playing an instrument you've never learned? No, you just haven't learned how to play it.
So at this point you probably know that you don't want to buy fighting games and play fighting games. After all you don't want to spend time learning how to play, learning what to do. Often people buy special controllers to play fighting games (arcade sticks) which can cost around $100 and right now you are feeling overwhellmed.
So why would you want to get into a niche part of a hobby where people tell you to spend $100 on a controller and you need to spend a lot of time learning how to play and what to do.
The gameplay of fighting games is without a doubt the most rewarding competitive video game multiplayer experience. If you like the aspect of directly proving that you are better than someone else by beating the crap out of their virtual avatar then fighting games are for you.
In many games such as MOBAs or FPS games people will often whine about their bad team caused them to lose, in fighting games there is no team, if they lose it's because they're crap.
Now, winning in fighting games appears very simple. Just don't get hit. However it isn't that simple in reality.
Skullgirls is centered around broken and unfair mechanics layed out by Capcom's VS series, where long combos are king and if you can't execute these combos you will not win. It doesn't matter if you can hit him 10 times while they hit you once if their one time takes all your life and your 10 hits barely scratch them.
On top of that Skullgirls has a long and rocky history involving dramatic changes to how each player combos and how many subsystems interract.
At the current installment I find skullgirls has rediculous requirements for combo execution, learning how to preform you combos and the gameplay isn't better than direct competitors to demand these things.
Previously my review featured an in depth breakdown of the game, the systems, and did reccomend it  however in my opinion the constant development and changes has really hurt the game and forced people to relearn their combos, relearn their teams, relearn what their assist calls do.
For even FGC fans I would call that unforgivable and for new players even more so. Learning fighting games doesn't have to be as hard as skull girls makes it, so do yourself a favor and pass this game up.

Game Dev Tycoon is a simple game with an interesting plot. The player begins in his/her garage in the early days of computing and computer games (probably late 1970's or early 1980's). As time progresses, the technological boom of computer gaming evolves.  The various platforms, graphics, sound and a variety of other aspects of the industry become available to the player to utilize once his company has researched the topic. A series of random events are sprinkled trhoughout the course of the gameplay as you attempt to become the industry leader. I found that even though this little gem of a game is seemingly simple on the surface, the intricacies and sometimes humorous combinations of genres and types of games as you move from your garage to an office and beyond is extremely engrossing and captivating. Overspending can have disastrous effects causing your company to go bankrupt and I did lose my first few games. It is well worth the small amount of money to purchase this game. I pay as much for a movie ticket and derived many more hours of pleasure out of this game. Highly recommended!

The amount of work that was thrown into this...It HAS to have been at least a year of work for all of the developers....The amount of detail that goes into each animation, every enemy, cutscene, and attack is utterly astounding and beautifully made. I never had any bugs that occurred to me, or any game-breaking glitches, and the game was fun all the way through. I sat up from 8 PM until 6 in the morning playing it because I wanted to find every nook and cranny there was, to find more and more of the map.
Overall, this game is a lesson in itself while going through the plotline. Whether it be the values of family, the constant threats of nature, and the darkness inside of us that can drive us to do things we aren't normally supposed to do. I just...Couldn't get enough of the game. I wish that there will be DLC added to this game, perhaps another storyline after the fact, or even a prequel beforehand. Whatever happens, this game hit my mark, and I actually plan on doing a gameplay video of it shortly after posting this...
The workmanship of each individual map scheme flowed fluently between one another, SEAMLESSLY. I give props to the producers for this...It is not often you find a game where there is a seamless map without ANY cutscenes in between where the level has to load up to a new portion. I was able to fully enjoy this game with every second I played, and plan on putting more hours into it as well.
Props to the producers, you did an AMAZING job on this game. And those who have not played it, I encourage you to! The game is well worth $20, and perhaps even more, as it isn't your standard "You have a plotline and you have to follow it" kind of deal like Metro, Call of Duty campaigns, or other storyline based games. It's more of an ADVENTURE than anything, and the ending nearly made me cry (No spoilers!), that's when you know you've made a good game. When somebody gets emotionally attached to their character, and when an ending finally comes, you match all of your original experiences with them and take them to heart.
Props to everyone who made this, and once again, for those who have NOT played this game, PLAY IT! Take your mom's credit card, pull from savings, anything. This game is WORTH every cent that you put into it.

A supremely grueling exercise in patience, memory, and repetition.
After playing off-and-on for three years, I've finally beaten it.  While sweet, the punishing difficulty borders on insane.  With no checkpoints or second chances, perfection is demanded for complex stages that can last for ages.  Worse, the visuals sometimes hinder the player's accuracy from lack of clarity.  You'll find yourself hitting brick walls hard, only to punch through them from playing a level over and over for dozens of times.  However, the eminently charming graphics and dynamic soundtrack will keep you motivated to come back.
If you can endure the challenge, you'll find an extremely artistic and challenging experience that you can't put down - and that's just the base game.  For even greater masochists, there are higher difficulty modes - including Perfect mode - with collectable gold and additional after-levels.  With all this value, a recommendation is easy, if not highly pained.

This is like the Simon electronic memory game from the 80's except with better visuals, music, and an occasional chance to mitigate bad memory with hasty reflexes. That is to say: it's better than Simon, but that's a pretty low bar. The problem is that it passes itself off as a rhythm-platformer –– an acceptable label until the level length and difficulty becomes such that memorizing the hazards is the key to victory. "Okay, duck twice in row.. then 3 jumps and a kick and then...." forgetting makes you freeze and you plow into an obstacle.
You might find this kind of misery to be something at which you could excel, and I'll grant that the gameplay has a certain appeal. But there are other misfires which prevent me from really recommending the title. One in particular:
places heavy emphasis on "perfect" completions of the levels (rewarding it with achievements and the like). Nabbing all the collectibles in a given level gives you subsequent access to a "retro level" –– an additional challenge postfixed to each normal level. If you mess up anything in one of these retro levels (which you most certainly will do), the game offers no chance to have another crack at it. It immediately queues up the next normal level and starts. If you want to attempt that particular retro level again, you must exit to the level select menu, choose the previous normal level you played, and complete that one with a perfect score to give you one additional shot at the retro stage. Having to repeatedly complete (perfectly, remember) one level to have individual chances at another will make you grind your teeth to powder. Is this negligence by the designers or leveraging time for difficulty (a member of the gaming Rogues Gallery)? Neither of those explanations is satisfactory.
That's all to say, this game will make you mad. But I think it's often for the wrong reasons.

Great game. Well, it´s in EA obviously but the devs are pretty active and also very communicative, have frequent polls for new features/ development steps and so on going, so i´m not worried the game will grow to maturity...
That being said, for me as a PvE player there is not (yet) very much to do, going on missions or hunting ships on the open sea are the activities that i can do so far, but tbh, that´s exactly what i bought the game for. More PvE stuff is to come,like more mission types and other activities. Right now the production focus lied (and probably still lies) on the combat (pve and pvp) mechanics as well as economy/ trading and crafting, the latter being really complex already. So if you are a designated crafter, you´ll feel at home here as well...
the combat and sailing mechanics are what the game shines at. It takes a rather realistic approach. It features a manual aim system, where each gun type and also each ship has a certain way to aim...combined with the need to take your ships stability and the conditions of the sea into account, aiming takes a bit of practice. Each single cannon ball seems to be tracked, means not only it "hits the hitbox,applies damage and that´s it",but it might hit, penetrate the hull, run halfway thru the ship, kill some crew on its way to the magazine... you get it... or it might just bounce off and drop into the water...of course there are also chain shots for destroying the sails,as well as grapes, especially to decimate the crew of an enemy vessel, available... what ever suits your needs :)
the gameplay/ combat is very slow paced and has a most realistic age of sail feel to it, so if you are looking for a quick combat game,where you jump into a match and 5 minutes later leave again with 20 kills on your count, this is NOT your game...
if you´re the type of guy who throws a party when you land a beautyful broadside barrage after outmaneuvering that large vessel over there, then yes, this is for you :) while we´re at cannon barrages: the sound of a 20 cannon volley alone is worth 100$ :D
So yea... the game is far from feature complete, especially PvE players feel the lack of content pretty quick, pvp players who have no issues with finding a guild might have an advantage for now :)
But that´ll change, since they have PvE servers as well as pure pvp servers, the devs are showing the same interest in both parts of the game... But as i said at the beginning, i´m here for the ship fights anyway, and those are unmatched by any multiplayer game i have played so far...
btw, the recently added open world is H U G E ... a trip from southern cuba up to Cape Canaveral (Florida) took me almost 2 hours :)
There are several playable nations (including Pirates, which might change,meaning them being handled differently in the future...for now they´re "just" a nation as the others), which -on pvp servers- fight for the control over the MANY dozens of towns all around the caribean sea... but as mentioned, i´m a PvE player, so i´ll leave the PvP review to others...

You won't see "Micro Machines" mentioned anywhere in this game, but if you played the MM games in the 90's and miss them, you will love Toybox Turbos. Codemasters have done a really good job in replicating the feel of the original. Replacing the old tile-based maps with 3D ones really adds to the feel of just racing cars around whatever was lying about on the table. It's full of nice details too. Some of the spoof books and fake brand names on the track are quite witty, and when you score a point, the car bounces and spins just like in MM. The single player is longer than it looks. There's the usual kind of unlock-driven progression that you expect from modern racing games, but that is very much downplayed: you unlock by driving through coins in-race, so you can't ever run out; unlocks are cheap, so there's no "grinding".
But if you're buying this game it won't be for the single-player alone. Multiplayer is where it's at. Because there's no real in-game communication, playing against randoms is not that fun, but great Steam integration makes it easy to play with up to three friends, whether they're near (at the same computer) or far (playing on their own computers). Multiplayer can be a bit unfair occasionally: sometimes the physics is a little implausible, and the wrong player gets taken out or one player survives a crash they really shouldn't be able to, but TBH Micro Machines had just the same problem, and this element of randomness actually helps stop the gameplay feeling overly competitive.
An update added Oculus Rift support. I wouldn't say the Rift is ideally suited to what is at heart a social game, but it's a neat addition. You feel like you can reach out and pick up the little cars. The scale feels a bit off, and the loading screens are really disorienting, but apart from that it's a good integration and an unexpected bonus.
The only shortcoming really is that the only controller supported is the XBox 360. I hoped I could use it with some no-name controllers, but I was disappointed. It only really needs a stick or D-pad and a couple of buttons for accelerate and brake (and you won't be pressing brake often), so it's hard to see why they couldn't have added support for arbitrary controllers. You can still use the keyboard, so even if you've only got one 360 controller, you can just fight over who gets it. Other additions I'd like to see are helicopters (remember the helicopters in Micro Machines? they were really hard), and even a map designer, but the game is complete as it is.
I've already had lots of fun with this game: having a quick race on my own, with friends when they come to visit, or at a LAN party (bearing in mind the four-player limit). I don't know anyone who hasn't enjoyed playing it, and if you remember saving up your pocket money for one of the old Micro Machines games, you certainly won't regret spending a few quid on this spritual successor.

This game is generally solid. But to me it seems the developer shows not too much love for this game. First of all, the advertising for this game was nonexistence. This is basically Micro Machines (MM), mostly a solid remake of the PSO MM V3 version. The original MM video game series was Codemasters most successful installment during the glorious generation of 16-bit consoles in the 90s. Nowadays they produce professional racing games like Grid, DiRt and Formula One. It seems like someone at Codemasters feared a loss of reputation by releasing a fun racer like this but still smelled the extra cash that is to be found here. The game itself is technically absolutely first class. I discovered no bugs so far, the game flow is steady and controls are fine. But after inspecting the surface you can almost feel that this child has been abandonded half the way. It has that "get this one done ASAP!" feeling all around. There are some missing features from the original series: no Time Trials, very short tracks, only one multiplayer mode. Online multiplayer feels almost absent. You may play online: but there no one ever around. But after all these negatives one can say this game revives the old spirit very well. The game is charming you right from the start with its colorful and vivid graphic and the easy listening music. The racing tracks feature some funny themes and once the race starts everything gets instantly hysterical. After all this is a easy-to-pickup-game to race several rounds and put it aside after. Do not expect hours of excitement in single player. It is quite uncompetetive. If you can gather some friends locally this rather will provide its real potential. If you are unsure if you want to buy this, play the provided demo. The business department of Codemasters will see this product as cashcow, for the case they require quick cash. So I bet you will see this game in 2-3 months in sale for a nice discount. Just stay patient ;)

It's like someone turned a bucket of legos upside down and said, "do whatever you want". It's a pretty random game and really fun for all ages.
(Below is a few opinions and review details for the sake of Lego Worlds' developers, if they are looking at reviews.)
It's pretty optimized for controller use, although it lacks some minor functions. Additionally, the game's effects that start with the sandard video settings can be seriously taxing, and I would recommend turning some off to play, unless you have like a R9 295X or GTX 980 or above, or a meaty i7. I'm serious, I use a 4gb R9 290x and my friend uses a 4gb GTX 970 and they have an issue playing this game on max with all effects activated. It could be that the game is just a little buggy with effects, but still, turn off at least 2 effects and the game runs at 60fps smoothly.
One thing I really appreciate is the 3D platforming aspect of it, which includes small things like Backflips and double jumps, butt-bombing and body slams. Oh and the ability to climb anything, no falling damage and being able to interact with a lot of things. I grew up on 3D Platforming, so this game is great for me.
Things it needs though are:
- Multiplayer
- a "view map" function (to see where you are in relation to the rendered space)
- the ability to use the items like the telescope.
- quick controls for rotating prop pieces (there's currently none for the controller, or at least none that are listed or functioning)
- Manually firing the guns in the direction you are aiming at, even if its not at a targetable object
- More "sets" to place
(If I think of anything else, I will add it to this list later on with a date added.)
Also, the amount of Legos needed to make this game's enviornments and structures in real life would cost you like the entire economic value of the world. This will save you money on Legos.
Overall:
A lot fun, 3D platforming adventure and builing game - It will consume a lot of my time to come.

For the short version; This game is pretty bad, not worth it's WRC license.
Decided to finally give it a go. I had quite a lot of fun with WRC2 a few years ago, hoping that this would continue on it. Well, and that is exactly what it does, and not in a positive way. It is common that wen developers get the hang of a license, they improve on it, but not with Milestone!
Graphics are pretty bad, they would be doable in 2007-2008, but we are quite a few years past that. The game literally has no graphic settings apart from V-Sync, FXAA and resolution and there are very few settings outside of that as well. To make matters worse this game is performing like absolute crap and is capped at 30FPS.
I also had borders on my 1680x1050 resolution, I mean, seriously? I can understand it in videos because of the way they are rendered but i was having those borders in the actual game itself.
The menus look rather cheap and with me the background videos werent playing properly. Could be my graphics card, but still, the first time I actually had issues with videos not playing properly.
And then we get to setting up a driver. I don't know what they are thinking over at Milestone but it is very common to have a last name of more than 9 letters. It's sad that in 2013, game devs(only Milestone, apparently) are still not adapting to longer text boxes. Seriously, even old games had text boxes to 16 characters, but not with Milestone! This small thing just shows the abysmal quality of the game engine.
Driving physics are doable and there is enough in terms of setup.
Sounds is bad, but better than the average game. I don't know what they did with the Co-Driver, though, but I wouldn't call it good.
The stages seem okay, although I seem to be getting a lot of the same parts. It seems like they have just reused the same parts over and over again.
The pacenotes are pretty bad and are hardly ever correct, I've come across so many errors and inconsistencies in the pacenotes that there is very little point in actually listening to them.
And if you are thinking of making an error and rolling down a cliff, something that is always a danger in real world WRC, don't worry, the game will reset you before you're actually falling down!
This game is pretty abbysmal and way, way behind in tech. This game is just not worth it's WRC license.

You can play as a trader and make your money, you can also combine that and be a crafter making ships for others to buy from you. The crafting aspect is actually very good, one being that you don't just get automatic rights to craft anything you like, it creates more thinking and a tech tree to follow, one part makes this part and you only get a certain amount of labour you can use per hour which means people can't gain silly amounts of advantage. Also you have to craft certain types of ships with just a small % of a chance you'll get the blue prints to other ships meaning it takes time and tactic to be able to craft different ships.
Now if you go for the battle side this is a very broad game play. We have port battles, PvP or just plain old hunt the AI. I must admit alot of thought has gone into this; you need to be able to think, control and watch. The devs keep patching this area and adding or smoothing out the tweaks and doing an amazing job for it. When sailing in battle you have to think which direction you are going, where your sails are pointing how much sail you have, how many people on guns, how many people on plugging leaks. It really is in depth as a game gets for this area you quite literally can control everything.
Overall I would extremely recommend this game and urge anyone thinking to get this. The price tag is worth it!!! Constant patches and planned improvements that are set this game to be one you won't get bored on. I've clocked so many hours and the worst part is I never saw those hours go by, its truly addictive when you join the right clan community; my main tip is to join a clan to maximise every aspect of this game.

Game Dev Tycoon is a simple game with an interesting plot. The player begins in his/her garage in the early days of computing and computer games (probably late 1970's or early 1980's). As time progresses, the technological boom of computer gaming evolves.  The various platforms, graphics, sound and a variety of other aspects of the industry become available to the player to utilize once his company has researched the topic. A series of random events are sprinkled trhoughout the course of the gameplay as you attempt to become the industry leader. I found that even though this little gem of a game is seemingly simple on the surface, the intricacies and sometimes humorous combinations of genres and types of games as you move from your garage to an office and beyond is extremely engrossing and captivating. Overspending can have disastrous effects causing your company to go bankrupt and I did lose my first few games. It is well worth the small amount of money to purchase this game. I pay as much for a movie ticket and derived many more hours of pleasure out of this game. Highly recommended!

Scribblenauts is an ingenious little game.
This is exactly the type of creative game I expect to see in almost 2014. If you aren't familiar with Scribblenauts the game is basically a puzzle game that you have to use your imagination to solve the puzzles.
The story revolves around a boy who gains ownership of a magical notebook. Anything that the boy writes in the notebook becomes real. Similarly, the words you type into the game appear before your eyes. If I were to type floating spotted firebreathing bathtub, then thats exactly what I would see appear in the game.
The puzzles are mostly very simple, though I would still say its fun for all ages as I am an adult and even I had fun playing it.
The only flaws the game has are that many of the puzzles are very similar and you tend to solve them the same way. The game usually doesn't put any kind of restriction on how many times you can use a word, which means i can solve 10 puzzles the same way if I wanted to which I feel takes away from the puzzle aspect of the game.
For instance, once i found out i could add attributes to my own character, i made him "invisible superspeed tiny flying invincible" which lets you beat the missions in probably half the usual time or less but again takes away from the fun of the game. My only other complaint is that theres not much in the game that can kill you, even the things that do attack you take so many hits to kill you that you can easily stop them. They should have included a difficulty setting in the games menu.
Conclusion:  Over all I would give Scribblenauts a 8/10 in the category of childrens puzzle games. I would value it at up to 15$. Great game!

Toybox Turbos is a very fun, but short racing game.  As others have said, it is the spiritual successor to the old Micro Machines games.   I loved the original NES Mirco Machines so I was excited to try this one.  The game has good graphics, fairly interesting vehicles, and bright and clever course design.  The campaign starts out quite easy but gets challenging, especially for the last two cups.  Unlike the original Micro Machines, there are some power ups scattered around the track.   Luckily, they are not so overpowered as to take over the racing / skill element, ala Mario Kart.   The campaign has a variety of different challenges, so it's not just racing.  There are time trials, picking up clocks, and an interesting mode where you try to pass as many slow cars as possible in 3 laps.  Each level also features a boss level where you must win a series of short, head to head sprints vs. the boss.  The game features bright, cheery graphics and the music and sound effects are appropriate for this style of game.  The game also runs very well on my rather older pc, which is a plus.
There is also multiplayer.  Depending on the time of day, it can be hit or miss finding a match.  The game also features local multiplayer which might be very fun on big picture etc, but to have more than one player requires Xbox 360 controllers.  Multiplayer races are short sprints run on a single screen, with the slowest cars falling off the screen.  It plays a bit like a party game, not a serious racer in MP.  This game's campaign is pretty short.  I finished it in 4.2 hours, getting 100% achivements, except for local multiplayer.  Achievement hunters beware, you need an Xbox 360 controller to get the local multiplayer achievement, which kind of sucks.
Overall, I liked the game a lot, but I do have some criticisms.  My biggest complaint would be the lack of customization.  Races are always 3 laps, which is quite short.  Courses themselves are really short as well.  You must always choose a "class" of racecars, which is preset.  There is no option to use all of the cars or custom classes which would add variety.   The game is missing a lot of the classic car types from the original.  Powerboats, Road Warriors, helicopters, etc. are all absent.   Overall, most of these issues could be easily fixed with some DLC or the inclusion of Steam Workshop.  It's a solid game with a lot of potential and offers a lot of racing fun.  It's the type of game that you can play for 10 minutes after a long day at work and just relax.  It might even cheer you up!  For 4ish hours of gaming without counting multiplayer, you may want to wait for a sale, however.

This platformer is pretty...pretty difficult. It makes other classic platformers like Sonic the Hedgehog or Super Mario Bros play like Tetris. It's unforgiving in its mechanics and level design. If you don't own a controller, don't even think about playing this game. There's people posting reviews whining about having a difficult time navigating the game with mouse and keyboard...godspeed. I use an X-box controller (arguably the best one designed for systems) and I still struggle with controls in this game. I can recall one segment in particular - the tree of Water where you have to constantly jump through about 20 screens to escape a fast-climbing rush of water. One misstep or mis jump and you die...for an added element of stupidity you can't save at any point during this segment either. It's what I consider poor level design at its best.
The one thing this game has going for it is the art direction. It's gorgeous, but ironically this backfires during gameplay. Your character Ori is essentially a white speck of bright light on the screen, and guess what...the enemies all glow and shoot various other bright specks of light at and around you. It's pretty darn easy to actually lose track of Ori on screen during some of the fights or mad dashes. This will serve to further frustrate you, and cause Ori to die and respawn only to force you to grind through the same segment again and again. There seems to be a fair share of bugs that come with this title as well, in my case I get booted from full screen to desktop frequently or the game will simply turn into a black screen and freeze. These are frustrating but can be overlooked depending on your level of patience.
All in all a stylish, beautiful and devilishly challenging/frustrating platformer with its share of drawbacks on the gameplay and level design front. Caveat Emptor folks.

If you are the kind of person that enjoys playing the Street Fighter Series, Marvel vs Capcom, Darksouls and more, then I highly recommend you give this game a go. The roster is full of well designed and created characters each with their own unique personalities and abilities. Action is fast paced for old school hardcore veterans with its online versus mode, while also providing the rich story telling setting and game play for a more casual audience, without ever giving up one of the two groups. With content being released at a steady pace and at Triple-A fighting game companies pace, the gameplay always remains fun and enjoyable without sacrificing the feel of the game. Plus, coming from an indie company, the quality put out is comparable to even the standard of Konami and Capcom, perhaps even better since the game is always being attended to and any bugs prominent are fixed on a matter if days. Lastly, the staff of the game is always ears open, attending to your needs and request, tweaking minor segments of the game to provide a more comfortable experience for any gamer looking to try or commit to the game.
Also, the art style is something different compared to what your would see in most fighting games. With a first ever "dark-deco" style, you can expect beautiful art work on both the characters and the backgrounds of the many "arenas" you would fight in, guaranteeing your eyes will never be too confused nor bored with the scenery at hand. Even when it comes to the motion animation of the characters the character movements are fluid and well connected, so you will never experience static imagery which would ruin your game experience.
Overall the gameplay is fluid and it fulfills the core element of what every fighting game should be, while also venturing away from common practices and going in a different direction, a better, brighter and more creative direction. And that is why I give Skullgirls, a solid and well deserved 10/10
