While I don't usually think of myself as a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥, in this particular instance I'm almost forced to be given the fact that the graphics in this game are terrible compared to your DiRT 3s et al.
I've also come across those who claim DiRT 3 is more of an arcade-style racer whereas this is more of a simulation, however this couldn't be further from the truth. If you wanted to play a proper rally simulation, then you'd look no further than Richard Burns Rally which will test your ability to even drive along a straight line for more than a couple of seconds.
So where does that leave WRC 4 exactly?
Well Codemasters have had years of experience creating games that hit the right balance between gameplay/playability and realism (including the likes of TOCA and even Micro Machines), however WRC 4 seems to want to accelerate in a direction that facilitates neither of these core features; obviously content in the hopes that the WRC license alone would be enough to carry it through. Well it doesn't work I'm afraid.
Also throw into the mix the weird sound effects which sound 'tinny' due to its poor quality and implementation, and what you're left with is a game that couldn't possibly be recommended to anyone.

WRC 4 by Milestone may not have the polish or production values of a Codemasters Title, but it's an excellent Rally game in it's own right.
It looks great, runs well, has a ton of content and a solid Career Mode. I've really been enjoying my time with the game.
I don't understand the seemingly negative reactions to the game, I would easily recommend WRC 4 to any fan of Rally Racing.
My advice to those seasoned in the Genre would be to disable all driving-assists, set the difficulty to 10 and damage to Heavy. Those are the settings I play on (using a 360 pad) and I find it to be a good challenge.

There are major audio problems that start at the end of almost every stage which require a restart in order to make it go away I don't think they are going to fix this since it has been known about for a long time.

I only recommend this game if you are a hardcore rally fan and tired of all the extra crap in dirt 2 & 3.  If you can power through the frustrating control issues (see below) its still pretty fun if you get it cheap (humble bundle for $10 - I wouldn't pay more for it)

Toybox Turbos is the latest micro racer from the house of Dizzy or Codemasters as they are more commonly known. It is Micro Machines in all but name, but still manages to capture the look and feel of those classics.
Racing takes place on courses in various rooms of the house just as an imaginative young mind might create. Most of the courses are fun and feature lots of big jumps and tight corners and are set in some imaginative locations such as a dinosaur park, a kids party and dad's snooker table. Most of them have hazards such as train tracks to jump over, oil slicks to slip on and even a volcano spitting out lava onto the track. There are also a great selection of vehicles which include the usual sports cars and hatchbacks as well as diggers, earth movers, police cars and tanks.
As you race around you can collect power ups which you can then use to blast the living daylights out of any other racers who happen to stand between you and an ill deserved first place. Remember that they can give as good as they get and will shoot back. Races are quite short at only 3 laps and over within a flash.
In the single player game each championship is based around a certain type of vehicle such as emergency or construction vehicles. These include the normal finish first races, time trials and overtake challenges. Each one ends with a one on one boss race where you have to outrun or blast your opponent to win. Do this a set number of times and you win their car and unlock the next championship. The game also features a good multi player mode with all of these types of races and more.
Unfortunately the game is quite short – you will finish the single player game in a couple of hours and even the multi player doesn't really give you that much more to do. It has a sort of "seen it done it" feel to it which becomes a little monotonous after a while. Having said that the game is fun while it lasts.
It does have a fairly low price tag and Micro Machines fans will probably get more out of it, but the short play time hurts it a lot – if you really want it get it on sale...

Where do I begin with this one?
Think of the game like it's Dust: AET; a fantastic looking game with a few flaws holding it back, but with more focus on puzzle-solving and platforming and less on combat.
To start, Ori and the Blind Forest is obviously a beautiful looking game; there's no denying that. The animations are stunning, and are a huge reason I stuck around with it. The soundtrack accompanies the gameplay quite well, and really drives some set-pieces home.
The story is...mediocre. I won't be giving any spoilers, so I guess I can say that the prologue is rather well done. It is quite heart-wrenching, but then the game kind of forgets it soon after, like the developers just wanted to get your attention for the rest of the game by adding something sad. Not to say that the story is bad overall, however. It just feels like they didn't work on it as well as they could have. And the ending is also touching, but is so cliche that I ended up being disappointed with it.
Where the game truly shines is in the puzzle-solving and gameplay. There were many times that the game offered a puzzle that made me say, "Wow. That's actually pretty clever. I wonder what they'll do next."
The gameplay often revolves around platforming, and has a constant Metroidvania feel, and a difficulty that, in my opinion, respects you as a gamer. You may think the death you suffered was cheap and unfair, but in reality it's because you jumped at the wrong moment, or didn't use an ability correctly. The game doesn't hold your hand, outside of telling you where to go in the story, and it's a welcome change.
Overall, Ori and the Blind Forest is a steal at the price it is now. It isn't perfect, but it is very good overall, and a welcome change of pace for indie games in general.

Ori and the Blind forest is a metroidvania-esq game with a greater focus on platforming than on the other aspects of games in that genre, and a gorgeous aesthetic that really sets it apart.
The game has excellent performance but there are a few technical issues with the game.  The game doesn't bind the mouse to the game window when in fullscreen, so if you have multiple monitors you can mouse outside the screen.  There are only a few graphics options but that sort of comes with the whole package as a 2D title like this.  You can't take away much because all the assets are more or less a core part of the game.  Controller and keyboard + mouse mappings are not rebindable so if you do not like the control scheme you may find yourself at a bit of a loss, I personally did not find it to be to bothersome despite some accidental inputs on my part.  The default controls for Windows may cause you to trigger the Sticky Keys by pressing Shift too many times so save yourself a little trouble and turn that off before you play.  Lastly, the game does not alt-tab as you'd expect and will force itself into windowed mode instead, but pressing the old alt+enter shortcut to put the game puts it back in place without much trouble.
The presentation and aesthetic of this game are amazing.  An artist's touch definately went into the making of this game, which says a lot I think because many modern games have difficulty achieving this with 3D graphics due to the way those games render.  This game presents some amazingly lovely scenes with great color and detail, much like a wonderful work of fantasy art.  A lot of little touches go into the game's other parts too, with good sound design (Ori's gasp for air when surfacing water especially stands out in my mind) and a lovely soundtrack I can't wait to buy.  Its not quite on the level of Transistor or Bastion where the soundtracks play a more integral part of the game, but this game's score does not dissapoint and adds so much to the game.  The story of the game is far from original, but it is well-presented and meshes with the gameplay that I don't feel like that harms it at all.  My only critique here would have been that a little longer of an intro-prologue might've let me feel more attached to the characters before the game unfolds, but I think they made the right choice here in not delaying the player from the core of the game too long.  I have always had the opinion that you don't need an original story or unique gameplay to make a good video game, it just has to be robust and people will enjoy it.
Gamplay is where I think I want to get into the nitty-gritty.  This game has been described as a metroidvania, which is in some way right and in some ways wrong.  This game doesn't have a lot of the mainstays of that genre.  There are no boss battles, enemies aren't particularly varied and are kind of forgettable with a few exceptions.  There is no uniqueness of collectables to backtrack for like in the castlevania titles, only health and energy upgrades and skill points.  The game gives you major mobility changes at quite a few points like in game.  Instead of gear, the game has a skill point system which functions more like ease-of-life progression (adding map markers for undiscovered powerups), and isn't required to finish the game but still presents enough to be meaningful (like adding a triple-jump).  As an additional note, you can save almost anywhere, and save points are also a health restore mechanic in this game and relevant in my next point.
What the game opts for instead of enemies is platforming.  Metroidvania title's aren't particularly known for their platforming, but instead for their gating.  You only need double jumps and wall smashing to get past certain barriers, but they aren't particularly core parts of the game in Castlevania.  In Ori that IS a huge chunk of the gameplay.  Gliding and jumping around rooms filled with spikes, bouncing off enemy bullets to climb chasms, and other activities are the challenge the game will present.  Sometimes this will be calm and sometimes it will be hectic.  The real boss battles of this game are dramatic sequences where you will either need to jump and bounce and dodge away from perils whilst certain death chases behind, or carefully platform in pseudo-stealth sections between safe spots.  In both cases, these need to be performed flawlessly as you cannot save midway through.  This is where some people may find the game a bit too frustrating from repeated failures as there is no way to tone down the difficulty of these sections.  I personally did not find them difficult enough to be problematic, and when fully completed I really appreciated the thrill and excitement that the scene was trying to convey.
All in all, Ori and the Blind Forest is a game that I have confidently placed among my favorite games.  The metroidvania genre is one I quite enjoy and this is an excellent title in that genre with its own beautiful aesthetic and platforming twist.   The game clocked in about 9 hours of gameplay for me with almost total completion, however the game does not permit you to revisit a few areas of the game nor leave the final dungeon, nor can a clear save file be reloaded and there is no NG+, so completionists may find themselves necessitating a second playthough.  There is not a particularly high replay value unless you simply want to enjoy the game again, but as a game that is likely to become a classic I think it will be a title you will happily come back to a year or two down the line.  Even at the full price of $20 I would absolutely recommend this game.
Lastly, thank you to the friend who gifted me this game.  I absolutely loved it.
EDIT : A recent patch fixed the fullscreen resolution bugs among others, and added some save backup options.

If you have ever wanted to stride through the battlefields of Warhammer 40K then this game is for you.
There aren't enough games like this for the 40K universe and this is one of the best entries in the genre. The action is intense and fast paced, mixing the feeling of being a nigh invincible Space Marine with the sense of being overwhelmed by Orks in their untold horde as you fight to protect vital Imperial assets from the ravages of their WAAAGH!
The atmosphere of the game is spot on and you get a real sense of the desperation of the characters involved as you and they struggle to survive amidst the carnage and ruin of the battlefield.
Ultimately the only thing that I found wanting was the lack of other Space Marines. Save for a few instances you are alone with two others against the enemy. It would have been nice to have fought alongside others and some of the more powerful warmachines of the Adeptus Astartes as well.
The gameplay is rudimentary but that doesn't detract from the experience as you are often too busy trying to stem the tide of enemies to really pay attention to the controls as they become second nature as you execute devastating melee attacks and furious barrages of bolter fire to push the Orks back and there are many minor mechanics such as suicide squiggs and Orks holding up sewer grates that add little tactical choices to mix up the combat.
All in all I would say play this game if you like 40K and definitely play this game if you love Space Marines.

Firstly, let's just make two things clear: this game was released in October 2013 - it costs, currently, £24.99.
Now, bearing in mind the release date, you might expect the game to look fairly nice. It doesn't. At all. It's passable for 2005, but in 2013 I expected a little more, and considering how dull and uninteresting the game appears visually, my PC kicks out volumes of heat when playing it - perhaps that's due to not using the game's v-sync option which locks the frame-rate at an absurd and choppy 30FPS. It's that, screen-tearing or using a third-party tool to force v-sync. Again, 2013 - £24.99.
At least the game works, until it hangs on menu screens, or until upon loading a stage it goes deadly silent unless you're willing to exit out and start it up again. A couple of bugs, we can look past those.
The gameplay, though, is where it counts, and for WRC 4, where it fails further. There is no satisfaction to be found here. In a rally we have six stages, most of which are the same stage, just with different start/finish lines, and all of which are drab and unappealing. The driving gives no palpable sensation of the road you're on, the jumps are floaty, the layouts are packed with hairpins (I hope you like the sound of the rev-limiter), your co-driver bleats monotonous directions at you, and irritatingly, loves to comment when you can't pick the road texture out from the not-road texture and drive into things: "whoa, careful". 2013. £24.99.
But, perhaps you really love the WRC and your options are limited to pretty much this or, at a leap, Dirt 3. This is better than nothing, right? It isn't. It isn't at all. Go sit in a puddle and I guarantee you'll have a better time. I know Dirt 3 has "Gymkhana" which is as detestable as forcing "drifting" into racing games, but the Trail Blazing events make up for it. Whilst Dirt 3 isn't a good game, it has a few really enjoyable moments, whereas WRC 4 is a frustration throughout.

Before you read this keep in mind that this is a review in 2015! This game was probably amazing for its time, but I can't say that it's worth playing today. Let me explain why...
With Fallout 4 coming out just around the corner & a steam sale deal I couldn't miss out on, I decided to pick up this game. Everyone said it was a great game and it may be, just not in 2015. I just feel like this game is so outdated now. For example, the HUD was terrible. It was basically a comapss. I had to keep opening up my Pipboy (the game's user interface) and looking at the map on there, and that really killed the continuity. And to continue on about the pipboy, it felt like I kept having to go to it for everything. For example, healing myself, switching weapons (no, you can't even switch weapons with the number keys), basic things that you need to do. And the worst part about the gameplay was probably how slow it was. Your character moves so slow and can't sprint. You'll need to get to a new objective and spend 5 solid minutes walking there from your nearest fast travel spot.
Then, there's all the stuff you need to do before you even play a minute. There's a whole guide on steam on how to get it working on your computer. For me, I followed everything and still had crashes every 20 min-30 min. You have to keep saving (manual saves only of course because quick saving will cause even more crashes), and that's just even more pausing.
The story was meh. Wasn't a fan of the ending.
I don't know, maybe this game was great for its time. Only people who played it then know the answer to that. As for someone who played it for the first time in 2015? I'd say no, to be honest.

This is one of my favorite games of all time.  I often play it whenever I need cheering up.
It has lackluster reviews, and I've noticed almost everyone that rates it mediocre or bad plays it differently than I do.  You could consider this both a review and a guide to having fun with the game.  Don't worry, there won't be spoilers.
If you're out of elementary school, and play the game in the most straightforward way, it will be too easy.  It amounts to a graphical adventure where you can access almost every item in the game by typing the name, letting you bypass anything resembling a puzzle.  While this might be viewed as a problem by teenagers and adults playing the game, it's actually a good thing for children, who can use it as a fun way to exercise their vocabulary skills.
Teenagers and adults playing the game should use their creativity.  The game is usually surprisingly flexible in how you can achieve a goal.  The only restrictions it normally has are: you can't use real people's names, or anything involving drugs, prejudice, or sex, and you often can't kill anybody.
Suggestions to get you started:
Played this way it should have you laughing your head off.  You may lose the level (usually due to an accidental death), but have so much fun you won't care.
The game does have some flaws.
It doesn't recognize every correctly spelled word.  That would have been impossible to program and create art for.
Some goals are too restrictive to allow creativity.  Sometimes there is only one solution.  There should be at least three significantly different solutions.  Better playtesting could have caught this.
There are “fetch quests”.  They involve going to some part of the map, which is usually unobstructed, picking up a item, and carrying it back to the person that asked for it.  You can't use your magical notebook to do this, and it's unhumorous, uncreative, and unchallenging.  Hopefully the authors will stop including these in the future.
While I love what the object editor can do, I hate how it does it.  The primary pain-point is how difficult it is to “draw” a new object.  You have to do it by lumping together existing art assets.  The second worst pain-point is how difficult it is to get the behavior you want.  You can only create new behaviors by tuning settings on existing ones.  While you can argue this is “creative problem solving”, it fits poorly with the design of the rest of the game.  Making a item in game is as easy as typing the name.  Making items in the object editor should be similarly painless.  We'd be better off with a design that imports SVG and allows scripting in some common, efficient, sandboxable, programming language, like JavaScript or Lua.
There is no way to create new levels at all.  This could have greatly extended interest in the game.
Overall, I think this is one of the finest games ever made, and look forward to more in the series.

Toybox Turbos is a mobile game masquerading as a nostalgic iteration of the MicroMachines franchise of yestayear. There is nothing inherently bad about the game, but nothing particularly spectacular either. The shallowness of content compared to its predecessors will perhaps turn a lot of nostalgic fans wanting a new and improved MicroMachines game away.
As a mobile game, the content ticks all the familiar boxes; races are short, are rated with three stars, collecting coins unlocks vehicles, etc. Its biggest problem, as I have previously mentioned, is that it is nothing spectacular and oftentimes feels as if the developers were playing it just a little too safe - In other words, everything Toybox Turbos does as a racing game of its kind has already been seen before with the previous MicroMachines iterations (and in some cases, was done somewhat better).
I would reccomend this game, however, in the hopes that codemasters develops a proper sequel more in the spirit of MicroMachines V3. What is old is new again. The negative review simply reflects a personal (subjective) disappointment.

So I'm updating my previous review which was written at 112 hours of playtime. At present I have just about 548 hours on this game and have to say it's absolutely fantastic if you enjoy Warhammer 40,000 and can get over the occasional lag issues, you will also want to look into joining a clan or a group in order to play the game more frequently.
The game's story is good, lengthy and an enjoyable slaughterfest of carnage in the Emperor's name, there has not and most likely may not be any game to come out in the near future that will allow you to wield as much power as you do in this game without being overpowered, you never feel that there's no chance of death and tactics are required even though you can cleave through your foe as though they were made of paper, the singleplayer also allows you to perform epic feats through the use of a slow-mo system called "Focus" that allows you to slow down time when in aim-down-sights mode and increase your melee damage by an incredible amount that allows you to cleave through boyz, nobz and meganobz with ease, the game does lose some of its touch when you finally get to the last few levels where you fight Chaos Space Marines, they are much harder to kill and do not feature any sort of gore which leaves a lot to be desired, but the game is pretty good overall even for just the singleplayer, It'll take you about 8 hours to beat if you play on normal, may vary depending on skill of course.
Now. Onto the multiplayer, while it is a laggy pile of crap that often causes desyncs and frustration when people use ridiculously overpowered weapons, it is also bloody fantastic and one of the best and most easily accessible 40k games featuring the Adeptus Astartes to date, no game I've ever played allows you to feel this powerful whilst still being on equal standing with your enemies, you feel like an absolute beast of a man who can tear through an entire team given the right loadout and skill, I've personally gone on 20:0 (K:D) rampages with a stalker bolter with precision shooting in both long range and close combat, it's absolutely visceral and I love it. There are of course the issues of lag which cannot be ignored, every other game will lag worse than playing with Dial-up, remember downloading a 1 minute youtube video for about 8 minutes? that's basically what this multiplayer can be like, people warping around, instakilling you but taking no damage and even receiving no damage even though they stand still. It's very buggy and can get very frustrating but with a group to play with, it's absolutely amazing.
Now, I wouldn't recommend buying this game at full price unless you're satisfied with the singleplayer content as the game's multiplayer is becoming less and less active with the upcoming release of Eternal Crusade, I'd say pick this game up on a sale if you can, play it and enjoy some multiplayer games if anyone is still playing but I'd recommend anyone who loves Warhammer 40,000 keeps an eye on Warhammer 40,000: Eternal Crusade, it's an upcoming MMOTPS in the style of Planetside 2 set in the 40k universe, it's shaping up to be absolutely amazing and definitely a game people will want to pay attention to if they love the 40k universe as much as I do.

The first thing I want to say, this isn't a minecraft clone, I wouldn't compare this to minecraft at all, this is its own game. I'm not saying everything in the game is innovative, or original, but I did not feel like I was playing minecraft at all while in this game. Minecraft is very much a survival game. This is not at all a survival game, however Minecraft is.
to start my review, this game isn't perfect. Its not fantastic, however It's not bad. Its okay. Don't let the over whelming positive reviews immediately sway your decision.
There is no tutorial system. There are little tips that kind of tell you how to operate things (how to walk, turn your camera, control your vehicle)  but there is really nothing explaining switching between your tools, different menus, and honestly what you're supposed to be doing.
The game is honestly kind of complex.  Thats not necessarily bad, its just more reason to add a little tutorial. To add on to this point, but there is a lot of Lego products that are directed towards kids, which, to me, means that there are going to be a lot of kids buying the game. Not necessarily going to be the easiest thing for them to jump into.
Honestly the biggest thing for me is that there is no clear goal at the start, and like I said, this isn't minecraft, sure there is no actual objectives, but there is a goal. and it is to go around and find everything, find new people, buildings, treasures, etc.
On to controls,   the controls aren't bad. Camera movement isn't that fantastic, its actually quite slow.  Honestly the game right now can definitely be played with keyboard and mouse, but in the future i would very much like it if the developers made it so you can play with only the keyboard. Its about 3/4 of the way there at the moment to full keyboard functionality. You can't freely control the camera with your keyboard (but you should be able to with analog keys) and you can't control the tool bars (which you should be able to with the tab key and the 1-4 keys)
Building isn't exactly fluent, its hard to work with, building should feel very intuitive. Its not. Feels quite clunky, and a lot of it has to deal with the camera not being super good.
For performance, as most early access games aren't, its not entirely optimized graphically however its playable even with some low profile builds.
The game has tons of potential. They should definitely add multiplayer functionality to it in the future, as well as mod support so we could add our own content to the game.  The biggest thing about this game,
Things I'd like to see
-First person mode,
-Multiplayer (in multiplayer I'd like to see custom game modes, a lot of them, different ones)
-Maps (something a lot of these open world games lack are maps, not full huge maps, just a minimap. this way you can explore the world and be able to find your way back after)
-mods with workshop support (this game honestly can be so much with mods, and having them available in the workshop would just be so convenient)
the game has a lot of work, as I said above, tons of potential, I would recommend getting this, Can't wait to see how much the game evolves in the upcoming months. Keep in mind this isn't made by an indie developer, WB, Lego, all large main stream companies that are with this game. If you are afraid of this game dying, I wouldn't be.

I saw this game on Twitch once and immediately fell in love with it, an RPG Masterpiece and a great example on how a good remaster SHOULD BE DONE. Not only did they add voice dialogue and squashed bugs, they added new CONTENT as well, which is a rarity in gaming these days.
Divinity is an amazing strategic RPG whereas you can play by yourself with two characters, or have you and a friend each take over one, later adding on to your party and assigning which of you gets to take control of THOSE characters. The writing is comical, as if the game knows its an RPG and likes to exagerate it a bit (as you'll see with status effect quips and general banter) but it never gets old and personally, I think it's hilarious when my friend is sneaking through somewhere and all of a sudden yells "LOCKED DOOR!" and the homeowner none the wiser. The combat is fluid and strategic, using the environment and impressive ways to manipulate battle. For example, if I summon a spider and it happens to get set on fire, I like to hurl it straight at enemies and then throw a flask of oil after it, catalysing my spider and engulfing the horde in flame.
It may seem odd that I'm writing this review with currently 14 hours logged (09/17/2016) but it all that time I've only done the tutorial and entered the first town! The city is so full of life and events and oppourtunity, you're going to want to solve every mystery, talk to every person (and animal), unturn every rock, and dig up every grave before you even THINK of leaving. I can see myself loving this game, and doing multiple playthroughs as different characters, solo and co-op.
Overall, you should DEFINITELY buy this game as you will not regret it, especially if you're into fantasy D&D Combat mixed with a rich story :)

Codename CURE is your average free-to-play zombie  survival game, with a few additions that really make it a great game to play. First and foremost is the fact that so far I haven't found any DLC purchase options in the game, or any of those addons that companies really want you to buy (such as gems in Clash of Clans, or Gold Bars in the Adventure Capitalist.) The game is 100% free and there isn't really that typical need-to-pay-to-get-good-items like you see in a lot of free games nowadays.
There are a few different types of gamemodes, one of which is PvP which every game with guns should have, although less popular than the other gamemodes it's still nice to be able to shoot a few other people instead of focusing on hordes of zombies that are sprinting at you. The second is the storymode type gameplay in which you have to plant a bomb and get to the helicopter before the bomb explodes, reminds me quite a bit of Left 4 Dead in how they made it. The third type that I've played so far is the casual horde gameplay, in which a team of however many are in the server work together to get to as many waves in the horde as possible. The amount of different playstyles is a plus for any F2P zombie killing type of game.
The community on this game is rather quiet, I've only met one other player who uses a mic ingame, I guess that could be because it doesn't have as many players as DayZ or Unturned or other games like this. The community, however, is quite helpful and friendly, there is a type-chat that I got all the questions I had answered every time I joined a random server which shows that it's not a bunch of prideful, immature 9 year olds who control the community.
It's fairly easy to get the controls down, the one thing that I couldn't figure out how to do without reading the controls is to throw a granade, which was glitchy even after I learned. Half the time it'll throw, the other half it'll do nothing despite pressing the right button. That should probably be looked into, @game developers. The loot crates on horde survival, and the classes on the storymode type gameplay are fairly easy to understand, and come with enough information to ensure players don't get confused and quit the game.
I've played 5 hours so far on this game, but I plan on playing a lot more of Codename CURE. For a free to play game, this one exceeds my expectations and should be a model for similar games to future game developers.

In my original review (when this game first hit early access) I stated that it was hard to not recommend this game. I made this statement based on potential and what gameplay was available at the time.
This was 2 years ago and now not a whole lot has changed. This game needed 3 things to really shine (in my opinion) and I will explain why.
These things were buildable vehicles, a survival mode complete with crafting to make you keep coming back, and water physics.
Water:
The water has improved since launch, as you can now go under it and explore, but the surface water isn't fun, it is still lego blocks (which might please some people) but I was hoping for some beautiful liquid looking water complete with waves and foam to make building ships and other watercraft (if this was ever going to be implemented) much more fun to use, and gorgeous to look at with droplets spraying up onto your bricks and reflecting sunlight into the camera lens (Don't have the hardware? turn this feature off in video settings). Using games like Banjo-Kazooie: Nuts & Bolts and GTA V inspiration for water with a bit more spray and effects going on would have been a nice example.
Survival:
Lack of any survival gameplay just means that your progression is based purely on exploration of randomly generated maps with randomly placed characters, tools, plants and props to descover. As you discover these, they unlock in your interface and let you place more of them in the world. After you have done this, there is nothing really else to do besides build land or structures out of bricks, all of which aren't interactive due to lack of survival mode and objects that would be useful for that, such as workbenches, cooking appliances, beds, manufacturing etc.
The bricks you build structures and land out of are infinite, which again may appeal to some, but as a result of this, they do not feel earned, therefor making these buildings and structures feel unrewarding and pointless (in my opinion). The game does offer a nice variety of blocks to use though, which is nice for people who like creative mode style building with no limitations, but what comes after you build this stuff? Not a whole lot for gameplay, besides blowing it all up I guess.
Vehicle building:
Why this was not implemented is confusing. Someone finally makes a lego game about building stuff, and most of the stuff you would actually build out of lego, you cannot actually build. But why?
This is where most of my time would have been spent. In survival mode I would have worked hard to earn the necessary parts to build a vehicle to help me explore, then as I would progress, I would have added things like storage and better parts allowing me to use this vehicle to progress further to the point where I have enough resources to experiment with other vehicle types and start building ships and large transportation vehicles. That is just me however, but the community would make far better use of these features than I would have and if done right, could have extended the life of the game for years, and it didn't even have to be a hard to use feature. Games like Banjo-Kazooie and Scrap Mechanic among many have proved that this feature can be very accessible as well as deep and rewarding to use, so that was obviously not a limitation.
TLDR?:
Bringing these features into the game and making it a physics playground with actual progression, would have made it the lego game of my dreams (as well as many other people) but after 2 years of being in early access, the game has taken it's foundation, optimized it, added a few minor features and is basically now ready to be moved out of early access (according to the developers) and sold as a full game, although a very, very shallow one.
It is with great sadness, I must now say this game, if you could call it that is only recommended for creative mode players, and not for people who want an actual game that's going to keep them coming back for years.
I will still casually play it from time to time as a distraction, but I think most of us can agree that this didn't end up being the Lego game most were hoping for, which really sucks, because it's the closest one to it since Lego Creator came out many years ago and has now only fuelled my desire for a good Lego game about building Lego even further.
Someone, please just make that game already?

Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautifully composed game, with stunning scenery and a lovely soundtrack.
The story begins as the little spirit Ori gets separated from its father, the Spirit Tree, during a great storm. Ori is then raised by Naru, a bear-like creature, who finds Ori deep in the forest and takes it in as her own child. Years later, the Spirit Tree calls out to find Ori, and shortly after the forest starts to decay and die.
Another series of events happens and Ori, with the help of Sein, a guiding light, is set to uncover the mysteries of the dying forest and what caused it's decay. All while combating the dark owl Kuro, which holds a grudge against the Spirit Tree and therefore Ori.
I enjoyed this game very much and completed it after 12 hours of playing. The story is gorgeous and has a nice development and a little twist to it, which makes it all the more compelling.
The puzzles are simple, yet solving them often requires good timing and skill. Although I sometimes got frustrated because I lack both, I still could only stop playing for a short time :D
The only thing that bothered me a little, was that the last level - at least to me - appeared too hard for the pace and difficulty set throughout the rest of the game, but that's just a little detail which didn't limit the fun I had playing it in any way.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a very beautiful game that fans of the genre will love and I hope a lot more people too.
If you're not sure about it, at least give it a try and if the beautiful story doesn't get you, the scenery and atmosphere will.

I have played this game a decent amount and while it's not terrible it's not great either.
The game looks somewhat decent, I personally have found no bugs that way. The physics are very, very far away from being a true simulation. Front wheel drive cars do not actually behave like they are front wheel drive. You have to try to actually make them understeer. The different road surfaces do not always feel all that different either, the cars never seem to lack grip no matter what surface you are on. There are occasional issues with physics that make you spin in weird directions too ( like turning right and grabbing the handbrake and the car suddenly spins left).
Car tuning is very basic and does not save between stages. Big changes to the setup of a car don't effect it that much. No choice of tires, no varible weather. I feel that even with steering lock at maximum the car always seems to react slowly to my input (xbox 360 controller). The car just turns to slowly even when you move to full travel of the stick you wait for the car to catch up.
Tracks are generic, all of the stages are the previous stage reversed or pieces of the other stages combined ( apparently they all take place in the same 3-5 mile stretch of road) which is an issue I had noticed in the previous WRC games. The stages are a great deal longer than those in Dirt 3. In Dirt 3 the stages are over far to fast and never really felt like a rally, this does improve on that at least. Co-driver is not always synced with the track and can be telling you about the corner you are currently in not the next one even with maximum delay. Some of the co-driver notes are wrong also ( saying left for a right turn, hairpins when its really a 2 or 3 etc.)
The Career is far to easy IMO. I have played on the hardest settings from day 1 and never really had an issue winning any stage. I was able to skip WRC3 completely and even when driving a "lower performing" car in the same class I had no problem beating the other cars by 10secs or more per stage.
The game is not all bad, but is definitely not a great game either. There have been far better in the past, in fact I think WRC 2 was a bit better. It does trump Dirt 3 in the track length department, though I feel Dirt 3 stages are apallingly short. I wouldn't pay full price for it by any means. I think you would get a better more real experience picking up an old Colin Macrae game for Xbox than this.

Quite often, we hype ourselves up for a new game; we craft an absurdly idealized image of it in our heads. Naturally, it is very rare for a game to actually live up to these expectations. This is one of those that does. Warhammer II is the realization of the potential we saw in Warhammer I.
This is not to say Warhammer II is without its faults: there are only four playable factions, which makes me suspect scads of faction DLC, a la every other TW game. The game is also something of a cpu hog (although it still feels better optimized than Rome 2). Moreover, some people are angry that the mortal empires campaign requires buying both Warhammer I and II. (I am not one of those people but understand the criticism).
That being said, this game truly lives up to the hype. The campaign objective is a novel and fast-paced departure from the usual "conquer everything" format of previous TW titles. The different factions actually FEEL different, and damage dealing magic is actually impactful in battles now. The overly restrictive (IMO) territory capture system from WH I has been replaced with a climate system that allows one to capture anywhere but ensures that some territory is better suited to some factions than others.
On the whole, this is an excellent addition to the Total War IP. It continues and improves upon Warhammer I's aim of taking the Total War model in new and interesting directions. The game is polished, well optimized and, most importantly, fun.

I saw this game on Twitch once and immediately fell in love with it, an RPG Masterpiece and a great example on how a good remaster SHOULD BE DONE. Not only did they add voice dialogue and squashed bugs, they added new CONTENT as well, which is a rarity in gaming these days.
Divinity is an amazing strategic RPG whereas you can play by yourself with two characters, or have you and a friend each take over one, later adding on to your party and assigning which of you gets to take control of THOSE characters. The writing is comical, as if the game knows its an RPG and likes to exagerate it a bit (as you'll see with status effect quips and general banter) but it never gets old and personally, I think it's hilarious when my friend is sneaking through somewhere and all of a sudden yells "LOCKED DOOR!" and the homeowner none the wiser. The combat is fluid and strategic, using the environment and impressive ways to manipulate battle. For example, if I summon a spider and it happens to get set on fire, I like to hurl it straight at enemies and then throw a flask of oil after it, catalysing my spider and engulfing the horde in flame.
It may seem odd that I'm writing this review with currently 14 hours logged (09/17/2016) but it all that time I've only done the tutorial and entered the first town! The city is so full of life and events and oppourtunity, you're going to want to solve every mystery, talk to every person (and animal), unturn every rock, and dig up every grave before you even THINK of leaving. I can see myself loving this game, and doing multiple playthroughs as different characters, solo and co-op.
Overall, you should DEFINITELY buy this game as you will not regret it, especially if you're into fantasy D&D Combat mixed with a rich story :)

Kids today are oppressed.
They didn't get to experience the joy of Micro Machines. This sucks because Micro Machines were the best thing. Now they got stupid crap like anime and bad video games and hippies telling people that LEGO is sexist despite the fact that nobody really cares what you buy your stupid kid. Give Johnny a Barbie Doll and give Lacie a Tonka Truck.
Ok, but Micro Machines were the best. Even their licensed crap was the best. So it was '90s, back when video games needed effort to make. Someone thought "You know, Micro Machines are cool as hell. Let's go and put them in a video game. And have them race in bedrooms, on tables, at school, in the bath, and out in the garden. And, you know what? It was awesome. Then they did it again and again. Then they made V4 and that was about as disappointing as your average Kickstarter.
But, now MicroMachines are gone and kids have to grow up playing with Non-Threatening Civil Peace Corps Joe and Empowered Gender Studies Professor Barbie. Someone at Codemasters must've been like "We want another Micro Machines because that game was cool, but there aren't any more Micro Machines. But, because someone there isn't an idiot, they said "Ok who cares about the branding. Just call it Toybox Turbos and make the tracks and such be desks and tables and such, and make the cars toys.
And it worked. Toybox Turbos is essentially Micro Machines V5. It's not as good as the original or V3, but it's still great and easily worth $15.
The controls are tight and responsive, the visuals are colorful and inviting, and it's a lot of fun to play. It's a bit more challenging than the previous games, too.
But, why do I say it's inferior? Basically, the track variety is all limited to being indoors. And, all wheeled vehicles. Racing helicopters in the garden or powerboats in the pond doesn't happen. Not only that, it's nice to be able to select vehicles instead of being forced into the track flavor like in the original, but it's all limited with in classes. In fact, there's an entire class dedicated to Taxi Cabs. That's kinda lame. Not only that, but the elimination boss characters do love to cheat and stay utterly uneffected by both the stats of their vehicles and track obstacles. This is a pretty lame way of padding out the game time. It serves to only give the player an agonizingly long and unenjoyable boss bout that leaves you longing for just standard racing. In all, the game could've used more classic racing instead of the tacked-on game types.
Sure, it's not as cool as the first, but that was a long time ago. This game is still great. If you're as cool as Spider was, then you'll probably check this out.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER pushes the boundaries on sound design, gameplay, and atmosphere. Where should I start?
The BIT.TRIP series is well known to be part of the "rhythm game" genre, so not surprisingly, the sound design is absolutely superb. You can tell how much dedication Gaijin Games put into this specific installment. Every obstacle you face has an associated tone that adds to the melody of the song, where collectable + signs give you a score boost and make the rhythm of the music more basey. Every + sign you collect, a robotic voice declares that you are "Mega", "Super", "Ultra", and finally "Extra", which really helps with my self esteem issues.
Hence the name, BIT.TRIP RUNNER is about running. What the title fails to convey, however, is the sheer amount of dodging, blocking, ducking, and kicking you will be doing throughout your adventure. Some levels are easier than others, and there are many instances where there are massive difficulty spikes (*COUGH* ODYSSEY). The main objective is to dodge all enemies, but for all the completionists out there, every level has a certain number of gold bars, and you will score PERFECT on a level if you collect them all. If you accomplish that, you can even get a double PERFECT by getting all gold in the insanely difficult bonus levels that follow. What can be concluded from all this: Gaijin Games has a capitalist agenda that they're trying to push on the media.
Upon first analyzing the game, the graphic design is very jarring. Commander Video is a sprite, and yet the entire world is in 3D! Yet, it is that juxtaposition between his appearance and the world that allows us to appreciate the environment for what it is. Make the main character too realistic, and you would focus on him. Considering there is no dialogue in this game, much of its story and impressions rely on noticing subtle details in the background. Meat Boy even makes a cameo in one level! For this reason, I think it's simply genius that they made that gameplay choice.
All in all, I think this game should be nominated for Game of the Year 2016. It's a must buy.
Easily the greatest runner ever, unless you have no sense of rhythm whatsoever.

The Dark Souls of automatic runners...
It starts out as a challenging, but doable, automatic runner with great style. Jump over stuff, collect stuff; perfect arcade fun. THEN you get to the last few levels. The difficulty spike is so great that I put the game down for a couple of years. I came back because I realized that I had a Steam code for it as well as my DRM-free version. Finally, I beat the game, but it took a heck of a lot of muscle memory training.
It's not the difficulty that bothered me, it's the spike at the end of the game. Dying constantly at the middle of the level after a split-second mistake and doing the first half again gets boring. I recommend that you try to get "Perfect" on several levels to tide yourself over and come back to the harder levels. Or do what I did: put the whole game down and come back to it. There are three difficulty settings, but they just govern the bonus collectibles, and not the obstacles that kill you. Also, unlocking a level on harder difficulties does not unlock it on easier ones: you need to play the game over again if you want to switch difficulties.
My game time doesn't include the time I spend on the DRM-free version: I'd guess it took me at least six hours of playing total before I beat it.
Thanks for listening to me rant. I enjoyed this game greatly; just be ready for some frustration!

One word to describe this game would be "Potential". I can see this game could go very far. In its current state It is a building game with experimental combat. There is no inventory, no resources, no progression of any sort. What I mean by this is that in most sandbox games you start with nothing and progress towards the bigger and better things. That is currently not part of the system (Hopefully it will be at some point). Right now you wander around discovering different props and use the building system to create terrain (Just like the creative version of Minecraft). You do not have to gather materials, everything is available at the start (With the exception of props).  There are vehicles that allow various functions (Dig terrain, pave roads, etc.), which I love.
Don't get me wrong as I said this has great potential, I can see this going very far. I just don't want people to hate it because it is missing so much content.
Now I am not one to point out flaws and not provide something constructive in return, so here are thing I think could be added in the early stages to make the game more desireable (Please note my reference to brick is a base 1x1x1 lego piece, and Block is referring to larger parts such as a 4x2x1):
1. Inventory and resource management. By this I mean the player should have to collect 10 dirt bricks before they can place 10 dirt bricks. These mechanics are the base of what makes a sandbox builder successful. The sense of accomplishment is important to keep players interested.
2. Crafting of bricks into blocks. Each block harvested is worth a proportionate number of bricks. For example a 4x2x1 block would yield 8 bricks.
3. Place limitations on early building, and incorporate tools that help advance building and gathering. For example if you want to harvest and build metal structures, you need certain tools (Forge, Anvil, Strong Pick etc).
4. Resource renewability. If you chop down a tree, there should be a way to replace that tree or the world should replace that resource randomly (I'd advised against the latter as it could cause problems with players designs. Who wants a tree sprouting up in front of their door?). Easier to let players re plant a new tree where they want.
I know that these mechanics take a lot of programming and work, but I feel they are essential to keep players interested while developers work on other content.
So in closing I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys unrestricted creative mode building. However if you are looking for an adventure mode game, I would hold off for now.

Before I get into the cons I'll get into whats good,  On the fly character customization, Lego based terrain and buildability, variety of mount/vehicles. Discovery; small cash chests and "LARGE" unique item based chests, think Zelda. The ability to be able to 'spawn in items that you have come across in the landscape, and use the parts from npc's you have met to look like then or have their ability, like the mages fireball attack. There is more good/great ideas here but now to the meat of the thumbs down.
CAMERA and CONTROLS, being the main offenders here. This is a console game not a pc game, the controls are terrible for mouse and kb, the camera is a complete mess, you are unable to really zoom in or out, and the camera auto centers immediately. I found myself constantly having to keep my mouse sliding while mounted or in a vehicle, not to mention trying to steer while tunneling since the direction of the camera controls you direction, you will get the spinny jumpy inside your own skull spaz camera and driving of doom underground. Also spawning in vehicles is a bit hap hazard, if your in a tight space and need a vehicle facing a certain direction... too bad, it spawns where and how it wants.
You will find quite a few "thumbs up" reviews praising this game, which it is a fine game, but stating you really need a controller to play this properly, or to use the UI properly, "personal note I found the UI easy to manipulate with a mouse",  Releasing a game thats currently only on PC, and then building it around a controller is just disrespectful and wrong, This isn't a fighting game where your expected to use a controller or arcade stick, or a flight sim that requires a yolk or HOTAS to be enjoys correctly, its a proclaimed "Minecraft killer", that yes the world is beautiful and fun, but cant get the simple controls and camera of the established genre down, there are popular standards for a reason.
Once the controls and camera issues are worked out, this will be a fantastic game that i would endorse whole heartedly, but if a game looks like a gem but plays like♥♥♥♥♥♥ whats the saying, you can polish a turd but its still a turd, lets hope its only fresh manure that something great will grow from.

Unreal 2: The Awakening (a subtitle that, thinking about it, doesn't actually have anything to do with the game) is the sequel to the original Unreal, which is odd because that game didn't do incredibly well and Unreal Tournament did, so you'd think they'd stick with that. Maybe they thought Unreal Tournament's success could jump-start another try at this single-player thing. Anyway, it probably wasn't worth the effort, because Unreal 2 is mostly forgettable and dumb.
The story is insipid, and cobbled together from pieces of Aliens and Aliens ripoffs, with some other 80s action IP for good measure. You play as some military♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥who makes trite, sarcastic quips and doesn't play by the rules but gets results. You're surrounded by other military stereotypes, including a drunken ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a tragic past, a naive new guy who proves himself, and a sexy matronly female commander with anger issues and a problem with authority, which I think is actually two stereotypes rolled into one. The premise is some ancient-master-race-with-a-secret-weapon stuff, and goes about as you'd expect it to. To its credit, the story has one moment I liked and another that suprised me some, but other than that it's completely disposable.
The gameplay is only slightly better. It's a fairly standard old-school FPS whose main distinguishing feature is a movement speed that's about 2/3 as fast as it should be. A bunch of weapons and enemies are carried over from Unreal with new appearances but identical gameplay functions; unfortunately, Unreal's solid atmosphere of alienation, displacement, and vulnerability isn't also carried over. It's also hard to avoid taking damage, but to make up for that you have tons of health and health items are everywhere. Enemies share this quality, so you have to carry lots of ammo, too. The difficulty curve's all over the place—the second to last area is ♥♥♥♥ing punishing (mostly because the enemies there can put out damage like nobody's business and revive if you don't kill them hard enough), while the final couple of levels are almost a walk in the park. Occasionally there's a level where you have to defend something or protect someone, but they're mostly just a chore.
Like Unreal, it feels more like a tech demo than anything.
On the whole, Unreal 2 is like the Alien versus Predator 2 to Unreal's Alien versus Predator: mostly the same, but with a dumbass plot replacing the effective atmosphere and tension of the first game. Unfortunately, it's not nearly as good as Alien versus Predator 2; not bad, exactly, but just so bland and prefunctory that it's nigh-impossible to feel anything about it besides vague contempt. I recommend it, but only so that you can get some perspective on how good good games are, and better appreciate what makes them good in the first place. Buy it, but absolutely know that you're not doing so for a good time.

It's a very expensive game, especially for one in Alpha that has a long way to go. However the main gameplay mechanics like combat, PVP, trading and crafting are already well implemented, especially the first two, which are the highlight of Naval Action and why I think the money isn't wasted if you can afford to buy it and are interested in such a game. There is PVP and PVE servers, but I can't see the point of playing a game like this on a PVE server, so those patient and interested in the high risk reward, heart pounding PVP battles, are who I recommend this to the most.
EVE online is the game that comes to my mind when comparing Naval Action with another game, but in my opinion, while it is an alpha, has gameplay mechanics that are a lot more intelligent than EVE online, which has problems with getting people into the game, stagnant PVP and imperialism etc. Those who liked the idea of EVE and found it either too complex, or wanted more direct control over their ships and combat, will also enjoy Naval Action, so I recommend it for those also.
The main problem with the game right now aside from the lack of content is the terrible UI. It's not only the fact it is laid out so poorly they must have tried to make it that bad, but also how slow it is. Buying something quite literally takes 10 seconds for the server to register that you have made a purchase, which is just absurd, this is also the case for when crafting things. Crafting a ship in this game for example, takes ages, because you might have all the stuff, but you have to craft multiple things, each time taking 10 seconds for the server to register your commands. They also have sliders to choose how many of a certain thing you want to craft at a single time, except they cap out at a really small number, like making 16 ingots at a time, added with the stupid 10 second delay, it takes a very long time to process a lot of ore.
Dev team are a bit weird, but I guess that is Ukranians/Russians for you, they are pretty quiet in their development, nobody really knows what is going on, what is coming and whether or not their suggestions are being considered. I'm not one of those people that think Early Access is a place for developers to create a game based solely off what the selfish loud rabble are demanding, but more insight into what they are planning would be nice. Also development is most certainly not fast enough at this point, especially considering the core game is clearly well implemented at its base.
I'm certainly enjoying my time, and I'm confident I will get my money worth, at this point I'm already aproaching 40 hours played and have no intention of stopping yet, I just have to hope they don't stuff it up like Early Access game developers often do.

Very pretty game that is currently missing key features that define a 17th-18th Century naval game in the Carribean such as:
- Exploration of any kind
- A meaningful and detailed trading system and economy ( The thing that defines this era )
- Trading Vessels ( Currently, 3 converted, reskinned warships are the only options available )
- A useful open world navigation UI ( You sail blind most of the time, you get a crude map of the world though with no markers )
- Dedicated areas for new players to avoid being ganked and griefed
- A meaningful progression system geared towards those that like either combat, trading, or exploring. ( Currently, you just shoot ships. It gets pretty mundane really fast )
What you will get if you pick this up:
- Highly detailed warships
- A gorgeous open world with very well done weather effects and ocean effects that actually effect you
- PVP or Missions or a super simple trading system geared towards warship construction
- Long sail times between ports
I am not recommending this at this time due to the fact that the devs seem to be unsure of what to turn this game into or maybe they just don't want to share their roadmap and the current lack of content for the era it takes place in just makes it feel very empty. If you like shooting things alot and sailing for long periods of time and seeing very detailed warships, then you might like it at this moment.
At $40, I recommend you give this game some time to sink or swim.

This game should be about naval strategy and tactics. Living life on the ocean. Finding quarry and pursuing it, and instead finding yourself at the mercy of a better ship and needing to flee. Dealing with situations like that is what I wanted. Instead, this game is mostly about doing missions and grinding XP so you can get a better ship.
You are stuck in the worst ship (quite literally) for ages, grinding up small amounts of XP until you can adequately crew a less terrible ship. At which point you'll begin a longer grind for another less terrible ship. At which point you'll do it again, etc. The problem with progression like this is that for one, it limits options. It creates a linear path for Captains to follow that is inescapable, and this game purports to be about options. The second problem with this is that if every player can eventually captain any ship, there's no reason to have smaller ships. Players will only ever consider themselves viable when they're able to captain the largest ships, because that's the cap, and indeed, those ships are better suited to a fight. If every player can reach cap and get the best ships, all you'll have are the best ships; why would anyone come to a fight without the best? And the third issue I take with this is that the first couple of Ranks simply aren't fun. Nor are they thoughtful. They do not present you with a feeling of advancement (from your Midshippman to Ensign Ranks which require hourse of work you can have a max of 40, then 60 crew, which is so slight an advantage as to be laughable). They just aren't enjoyable, and I don't have any desire to put any number of hours into a game so that it becomes enjoyable. A game must be learned of course, especially if it has any depth. But you will learn Naval Action and still find that there are hours left before you can do anything worthwhile.
I will refuse to propose a solution here because this is a review. And in review I'd say that there are a few advantages to having a multiplayer-only game. The first is the living economy. The second is that it creates multiple layers of interaction. But the downside of all this is that to prevent uniformity in players, a scale of progression must be established. Unfortunately the implementation in Naval Action is bland, uninspired, and hopelessly repetitive. It is worse that because of it, you are so limited in your available activities, and worse still in that it forces obsolescence onto every ship you captain until you reach the apex of progression.
If you are looking for a game about sailing and fighting and privateering in an open world, my advice is to Follow this game if you are interested, and see how or if it changes. I would not advise a purchase.

"Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine". The game where you're supposed to be the best of the best. One of the strongest thing in the Imperium of Man, however. That is not the case. I bought this game on release a few years ago when it was released and stopped at just at the beginning of Chapter 3. But as the years passed. I couldn't exactly remember why I put down the game, I saw it in my library and figured I'd reinstall it. I couldn't phantom why I put the game down without finishing it. So I booted up Singleplayer again to finish my campaign.
I recall watching an interview for the game before its release. I remember them saying, "You're a Space Marine. Cover is for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Space Marine is designed to keep you in the fight." They completely failed on this. The combat is awful. You aren't a Space Marine, you're a ♥♥♥♥♥. Your shields go down in an instant until you get the Iron Halo (which is at the end of the game). You can be torn to shred by Orks no problem. Even the standard Chaos Space Marines you encounter later on the game are tougher than you are.
Combat is flawed from the very beginning. Since you aren't supposed to be in cover, you're getting shot all the time. No matter where you are. There is no rest in a fight. You're always being hit unless you retreat back and hide behind some crates. Even then, most of the enemies. including the orks have unnatural accuracy. You'll learn to despise the Orks with Rokkit Launchas and Chaos Marines with Plasma Cannons, as they'll volley over any cover you're hiding behind and hit you directly. But then, it doesn't matter. Since the game doesn't focus around cover, you'll still take damage from any rockets or grenades that explode on the other side of what you're hiding behind. One hit is enough to completely remove your shield, and two or three more will outright kill you. So if you get hit by all three rokkits at once? You're dead.
The game largely revolves around staying in melee combat and preforming executions to keep yourself going. However, if you try to preform one while in the middle of combat, you'll either get the same amount of health you started with, or you'll just die. As I mentioned, enemies have an unnatural accuracy with all their weapon. During the cut scenes for the executions, you can (and will) still get hit by any ranged or unit within melee range. The unnatural accuracy also extends to the point where they can fire through their teammates and still hit you without killing their buddies. (Excluding Grenades and Rokkit Launchas). Later on in the game you'll start encountering chaos pyskers, they'll fire a beam at you and if you're hit in the open by one. You're as good as dead.
Fights are all designed around this type of encounter. An extremely powerful ranged unit in the back (or several). While you get swarmed by melee infantry which can quickly over run you. So most of the game is just back peddling into corners to deal with all the melee infantry before you can peek out and take a few pot shots at the ranged units, as staying out for more than a few shots will generally get you killed. This if course, gets worse along in the game as you go from dealing with Orks to Chaos. At some points you'll be getting bombarded by plasma weapons, pyskers and swarmed by traitor guards and regular chaos space marines. Most of those fights require simply dumb luck and very slow movements to progress through. Dealing with Chaos is simply a cluster♥♥♥♥, as when you're distracted with those who pose a threat, you'll be getting shot by traitor guard, who serve no purpose other than to take up half of your screen with the hit indicator.
So the game is about 6-8 hours of the same combat over and over, ontop of artificial difficulty. It quickly gets frustrating as the game has no actual save system, just check points. Which is extremely annoying as dying some times will put you back right before a lengthy cut scene. (Looking at you, boss fights). Which are unskippable. The game is the same story as literally every other Warhammer game. You're under attack by orks, then SURPRISE ITS CHAOS, even though it was completely obvious from the beginning.
Even the very end wave fight is awful, and insanely harder than the last boss.It consist of going through several waves of enemies with little to no cover. Each wave having more♥♥♥♥♥♥tacked onto it. Toybox Turbos gets a lot of the fundamentals of the original Micro Machines games down quite well.
The tracks are fun and populated with an all manner of daily items and some not so daily ones.
You race with a variety of fun little cars, ranging from Double Decker Buses to Monster Trucks and Tanks.
The race modes are entertaining and the Boss Battles at the end of a chapter are a nice change of pace.
Unfortunately, the game has very little content. About halfway through the game you stop seeing new tracks and are just playing through the same variety of modes across the same tracks, just you go a little faster. It took me about an hour and twenty minutes to get 3-stars on all of the tracks, beat all of the bosses and grind up the rest of the coins to buy the remaining 2 cars at the end of the game.
For someone who hasn't played a racing game before, it might be quite challenging. I'm sure the game is targeted towards children who don't even know what a Micro Machine is.
But for me, who does know what a Micro Machine is, I felt it was missing quite a lot. There were no wacky cast of characters to choose from as your racer, the AI all did the same thing every race, including driving up against walls and flying off the track in Head to Head mode and there's only one track in the entire game where you get to drive in the pockets of the pool table and you only get to race on it once.
For a remake of the classic Micro Machines games it presents to you the absolute minimum. Small cars driving on familiarly themed but equally tiny tracks.
For $10, it's a fun little nostalgia trip with a few funny references tossed into the event names, a charming aesthetic and some great miniature cars you can paint up how you like. But the overall game itself is very lacking and I wouldn't recommend it to anyone except children and fans of the older games.

The tabletop chanpion by Codemasters is back! Toybox Turbos is the name of the game, but under the name simmering is the true successor to Micro Machines V4! Rack em' up and lets race on the pool table!

Charge your flux capacitors because we're going back in time.
It's 1994, Blur's Park Life is echoing in through an open window, a portable TV chatters away to itself in the corner advertising a new show called FREINDS.
A movie stub for Pulp Fiction sits on a desk and a fresh faced future games reviewer is hunched over a keyboard playing a game called Micro Machines on his shiny new Pentium PC.
Micro Machines was cool.
There's no denying the attraction of racing a toy car around a kitchen table, the track made from kitchen utensils, spilt sugar and the like, so much fun!
You could tear around a corner, skid on some milk and fly off the edge of the table!
There was nothing else like it.
It was a ground-breaking game which helped establish the top down racing genre. A genre which hasn't seen too much love in more recent times.
That is until now!
Back in the present, it's easy to look at Micro Machines with rose tinted glasses.
It was a different time back then, games were simpler, mechanics less sophisticated and consumers less demanding.
How would a game like Micro Machines stand up in todays market?
Similar titles have been few and far between over the last decade, maybe that's for a reason, or maybe we've all forgotten how much fun this type of game is and it's time to rediscover the genre...
It seems like you can't read a review these days without coming across the phrase "Spiritual Successor".
Civ Beyond Earth was the "Spiritual Successor" to Alpha Centauri, Next Car Game is the "Spiritual Successor" to the Flat Out series, Evil Within is the "Spiritual Successor" to Resident Evil 4, the list goes on and on.
Not being one to buck the trend, I'm going to jump on the reviewers phrase of the moment and call Toybox Turbos the "Spiritual Successor" to Micro Machines.
It's with this in mind that I approach Toybox Turbos with some trepidation.
I loved Micro Machines, so could this be the reinvention I'm hoping for or a hollow copy that will diminish my fond memories of the franchise.
Let's fire it up and find out!
The first track you'll come across will have your toy car of choice racing around a breakfast table, tearing around dirty plates, avoiding the odd stray baked bean and negotiating the various utensils as you try make it across the water-filled kitchen sink.
You'll find various little gift boxes floating around the course which, if you manage to pick up, will temporarily modify your vehicle by giving you a speed boost or bolting some sort of weapon to your roof enabling you to try and take out the cars in front (or drop mines to take out the cars behind!)
You'll also find gold coins littering the track which you'll want to try to collect.
After each race, the coins you've managed to collect will be added to your total kitty which you can then use purchase new vehicles.
There are 35 for you to choose from, each fitting into one of seven different categories from construction vehicles to race cars.
As you browse through the selection you will be treated to a view of each toy packaged in its own toy box which will open once you purchase it.
It's nice touches like this that really help Toybox Turbos shine.
There are slight differences in the handling of each vehicle too, a tractor isn't going corner the same as a race car, even if it is a toy.
Toybox Turbos fields 18 tracks, all of them bright, colourful and well designed.
You'll be racing around school desks, kitchen tables, science labs etc. each with their own short cuts to learn and each with their own special touches to make you smile.
You'll jump over ramps made from cake, be fired into the air by toasters and dodge run-away trains. You can tell that a lot of time and effort has gone into creating these tracks and it really shows.
Sure I've got my favourites but all of them are fun to race around, just don't spend too much time admiring the scenery or you'll miss your turn or find yourself trapped behind a stubborn baked bean.
It's not just about classic races either, there are end of level bosses, time trials, overtake challenges and escape runs to name but a few.
If this isn't enough to keep the game fresh for you, then you can take your driving skills online and invite 3 friends to join the fun.
There's nothing more satisfying than ramming a competitors taxi cab off the edge of a school ruler bridge before accelerating away over a text book and there's not many games you can say that about!
Another plus is the fact that Codemasters have announced that Oculus rift support is planned for this title.
I'm not sure how this is going to work with this genre but it doesn't stop me being excited about it!

With regards to criticisms, I'm really going to have to nitpick here.
You'll unlock all of the content pretty quickly, but after you finish the single player challenges you'll want to take this online anyway so I don't really see that as an issue.
There's a first to the edge of the screen race mode which can be awkward when your winning because you can't see what's coming next.
That's really about it, neither of these things are real issues and I only mention them for the sake of balance.
Back at the begging of this review I was nervous that Toybox Turbos might take something away from my fond memories of Micro Machines and I'm happy to say that this wasn't the case at all.
This is a title that knows what it wants to be and doesn't fail to deliver.
It's an honest, charming and nostalgic experience which captures the feel of the original micro machines titles perfectly.
Whether you were around for the original micro machines or not, I still think you'll find a lot to enjoy here.
