---------------------------------Full Review
Annual games are becoming more of a norm now a days as developers push less risky ideas and even though I am not the biggest fan, I do approve if it is done right. To be able to introduce enough new ideas on an annual basis to warrant such a yearly purchase is hard, but not impossible.
Sadly the WRC series is not such a series. It was made extremely clear to me by WRC 2 (2011) that recycling content was a normal thing. Now, 4 years since the first of the WRC games I still feel the effects. But fear not, as this year’s game feels fresher than ever. Whether or not this is acceptable however, is up for debate.
WRC 4 starts right out of the gate with a few very welcome changes. Gone is the boring dreary campaign that forces you to slowly crawl up the ranks. In WRC 4 you can get to the top level of the WRC in only a few hours, but also allows you to go down to the lower levels if you wish. This gives you a bit of freedom in your style of play. Like the real series, the higher the division of the WRC you compete in the more events are played out before seasons end. So by the time you compete in the top level you will be running the whole official calendar before one of these seasons is over.
This year the developers went with authenticity; something that is always welcome in an official racing game. Everything from the main menu (which shuffles real slow motion shots of rallies past) to the 3 day breakdown of each rally makes the game feel more realistic then it ever has.  The stages themselves too feel far more varied. Most rallies have a unique flavour to them. Finland is flying with many blind crests, and the UK has deep mud and rain. Gone is the mirrored feeling of many of the stages in previous games. Instead you are fought with tight hairpins, and Cliffside falls. This gives the game a sharper feel of power and control; allowing the player to truly push as hard as he dares.
Even though the new stages are impressive, many issues around come into focus. Some of which has never been addressed since the very first game. The main issue is replicating certain turns. Although not as bad as previous games or the horridly copied game that was WRC 2, there are still many segments that have either been seen before in previous game or are blatantly taken from other rallies! I found a perfect example with an uphill double hairpin that was in Sweden and then again in Australia. I have never had a problem with reusing the same stages in different configurations to create multiple runs of one rally, but to copy the same turns and then paste them elsewhere in a supposed other country is just irritating. It creates a heavy sense of déjà vu, creating fast player fatigue.
The audio in game also creates a step forward for the series. Gone are the horrible electronic songs that felt wildly out of place and instead you hear more of a smooth sounding beat. The problem here however is that there is only one song. You think they could have added a few more. Worse than the single song soundtrack is the horrible co-driver which makes a shocking 4th straight appearance in this series. They have not changed the horrible sounding co-driver… EVER. This being a rally game your co-driver is essentially to the game. You have to listen to him to know what is coming up. The problem here is he sounds so mechanical that it is hard to get into a groove. He says turns in such a choppy fashion I am dumb founded that the developers have not made a better sounding co-driver after 4 flipping games! He also has a tendency to call notes too late causing you to miss a turn.  I guess they never expected people to drive faster than the co-driver.
On a positive side for the audio is not all bad. The engine sounds are a big plus. All WRC cars sound very unique from one other making them a joy to listen to. From the smooth gear shift of the DS3 to the harsh pop shift of the Polo, it’s a real treat to listen to the vehicles in action.
This year’s game has also taken a huge step up graphically. Even though it is still not even close to the level that which was set by Codemasters DiRT games, it is still a hefty step up from last year’s visuals. The damage model however is still lacking and the water effects are still pathetic but other than that the game looks great.
The problem with the game is: it clearly is not ready to be sold. The game is littered with broken content; the main one of which is multiplayer. To enter multiplayer you first must register for their online service. This pointless step forces people to register their username and emails before entering. This also complicates things as they do not tell you this in any shape or form upon attempting to get online. Instead upon entering multiplayer they will notify you that your “nickname” is incorrect. It wasn’t until I used help forums that I realized I had to register prior to entering online. You would think that once registered that would be that, but it gets better: once I registered I was able to play online for only 3 days at which point again they told me my nickname was incorrect. I am not interested in re-authenticating my email 2 times a week for their stupid system. What little time I was in online events I would frequently encounter game crashes and disconnections. What little I played online told me that the online structure is a very basic model. With up to 16 playera and offering only ghost vs game play it is not worth the pain of entry. Online simply doesn’t work; sufficed to say, I have given up on it. These issues continue in other modes however. My final straw was when the game erased my career for seemingly no reason.
Now I did start this by stating the series is NOT a good contender for the yearly model which might seem odd as most I have said so far was positive apart from some broken content. The game is a step up for the most part and the game (when it runs) is really fun and tight, but you don’t buy an apple for a few bites and that’s what this game is: a few bites and nothing more. A game that struggles this much to bring working content and not requiring constant recycled content should not need to release a game on a yearly basis.
I would recommend this game ONLY if it is not listed for full price. What the game offers is amazing, but losing my career and not being able to play online is enough for me to not recommend it to people who want the complete experience. A series like this needs to take a year off and rethink its strategy.
I give this game a 6/10. It is really fun and the game play is really enjoyable but with only half the content working it’s hard to recommend it to everyone.

"Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine". The game where you're supposed to be the best of the best. One of the strongest thing in the Imperium of Man, however. That is not the case. I bought this game on release a few years ago when it was released and stopped at just at the beginning of Chapter 3. But as the years passed. I couldn't exactly remember why I put down the game, I saw it in my library and figured I'd reinstall it. I couldn't phantom why I put the game down without finishing it. So I booted up Singleplayer again to finish my campaign.
I recall watching an interview for the game before its release. I remember them saying, "You're a Space Marine. Cover is for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Space Marine is designed to keep you in the fight." They completely failed on this. The combat is awful. You aren't a Space Marine, you're a ♥♥♥♥♥. Your shields go down in an instant until you get the Iron Halo (which is at the end of the game). You can be torn to shred by Orks no problem. Even the standard Chaos Space Marines you encounter later on the game are tougher than you are.
Combat is flawed from the very beginning. Since you aren't supposed to be in cover, you're getting shot all the time. No matter where you are. There is no rest in a fight. You're always being hit unless you retreat back and hide behind some crates. Even then, most of the enemies. including the orks have unnatural accuracy. You'll learn to despise the Orks with Rokkit Launchas and Chaos Marines with Plasma Cannons, as they'll volley over any cover you're hiding behind and hit you directly. But then, it doesn't matter. Since the game doesn't focus around cover, you'll still take damage from any rockets or grenades that explode on the other side of what you're hiding behind. One hit is enough to completely remove your shield, and two or three more will outright kill you. So if you get hit by all three rokkits at once? You're dead.
The game largely revolves around staying in melee combat and preforming executions to keep yourself going. However, if you try to preform one while in the middle of combat, you'll either get the same amount of health you started with, or you'll just die. As I mentioned, enemies have an unnatural accuracy with all their weapon. During the cut scenes for the executions, you can (and will) still get hit by any ranged or unit within melee range. The unnatural accuracy also extends to the point where they can fire through their teammates and still hit you without killing their buddies. (Excluding Grenades and Rokkit Launchas). Later on in the game you'll start encountering chaos pyskers, they'll fire a beam at you and if you're hit in the open by one. You're as good as dead.
Fights are all designed around this type of encounter. An extremely powerful ranged unit in the back (or several). While you get swarmed by melee infantry which can quickly over run you. So most of the game is just back peddling into corners to deal with all the melee infantry before you can peek out and take a few pot shots at the ranged units, as staying out for more than a few shots will generally get you killed. This if course, gets worse along in the game as you go from dealing with Orks to Chaos. At some points you'll be getting bombarded by plasma weapons, pyskers and swarmed by traitor guards and regular chaos space marines. Most of those fights require simply dumb luck and very slow movements to progress through. Dealing with Chaos is simply a cluster♥♥♥♥, as when you're distracted with those who pose a threat, you'll be getting shot by traitor guard, who serve no purpose other than to take up half of your screen with the hit indicator.
So the game is about 6-8 hours of the same combat over and over, ontop of artificial difficulty. It quickly gets frustrating as the game has no actual save system, just check points. Which is extremely annoying as dying some times will put you back right before a lengthy cut scene. (Looking at you, boss fights). Which are unskippable. The game is the same story as literally every other Warhammer game. You're under attack by orks, then SURPRISE ITS CHAOS, even though it was completely obvious from the beginning.
Even the very end wave fight is awful, and insanely harder than the last boss.It consist of going through several waves of enemies with little to no cover. Each wave having more♥♥♥♥♥♥tacked onto it. If you fail it, you have to start back down the hallway so you have to run back and watch the same few minute long cutscene again. The Boss fight after it is a compete joke, its an on-rails quick time event where you fall down a spire. A few moments have free movement where you can dodge stuff thrown at you. For some reason you can fire, but Titus just holds his gun to the side and all the bullets fly off the screen.
The secret to killing the boss is this:
1-1-1, hit space, 1-1-1, hit space. Hit F, cutscene. Repeat x2-3 times.
Congrats, you win.
TL:DR?
- You play as a weak♥♥♥♥♥Space Marine Captain.
- Muh Ultrasmurfs.
- Awful, repetitive combat.
- Extremely accurate orcs.
- Demons are somehow weaker than Chaos Marines.
- Same exact story as any of the other games.

If you're a 40k fan, you'll find several annoying flaws in the game. So I'd recommend passing this game up and go play Dawn of War or Chaos Gate. Something else worth your time.

I've played Naval Action on and off since Sea Trials, and I have thouroghly enjoyed every moment spent in game.
That being said, most of the players who have been playing consistently throughout that time have become seriously concerned about the games direction.
Right now a lot of things are in bad shape.
* GUI is still very rough. (only slightly improved since my previous review. Still placeholders.)
* End game content is limited to port battles which are locked during U.S. prime time.
* Developers have gained a negative reputation for favoratism, ignoring player feedback and otherwise bad PR.
The Sailing is still excellent, and combat is fun, if a bit grindy due to lack of varied content.
The ships and game world are really beautiful, and the performance has improved a bit (at least for me)
I am maintining my positive recommendation because I have personally gotten more than $40 worth of enjoyment out of it, and because I don't want negative reviews to kill this game before the Devs have a chance to sort out the problems they have created.
If you are considering a purchase, I still recommend you read and carefully consider the *many* negative reviews that have been submited recently.
My Original Review From Last Year Below:
In some ways acting as a successor to Pirates of the Burning sea, Naval action is a far more realistic voyage into naval combat. The game has a large focus on trade, and the major nations must struggle for control over all of the major trading ports in their attempt to acheive naval superiority. Large scale naval battles are acheived in a grand fashion, with beautifully rendered oceans, and ships. Smoke billows off of freshly fired cannons, and drifts away slowly with the breeze.
Battles in Naval action require a bit of practice, and an understanding of basic seamanship will help asspiring captains greatly. The action here is slower than many games, and requires a bit of tactical positioning; it is critical that players learn to use the wind to their advantage if wishing to avoid destruction.
Naval action is still in early access and has a number of issues at the moment.
While the game is lovely, this graphical fidelity comes at a performance cost; further optimizations will hopefully reduce the strain on mid-range systems such as my own, but with my rig the game is perfectly playable. The UI leaves much to be desired as well, as the developers have opted to use a placeholder GUI while they work on core mechanics. This issue should easily be resolved in the coming months.
CPU:i5-3750k 2.6ghz - OC 4.0ghz
Nvidia Geforce 660ti
16gb ddr3 ram
While It might not be for everyone, I personally rate Naval Action at ~ 9/10.
Technical issues keep me from giving it a perfect score, but I fully expect those to be resolved at a steady pace.

I hate this game. Not because it is a bad game, but because my expectations were through the roof after having literally everyone saying how much of a masterpiece it is.
Truth is, this game does a lot of thing well. Combat can be very tactical, the graphics are beautiful and you have a lot of freedom ... of sorts. There is a lot of random thing you can do in the world, steal, kill etc. and the game will allow you to deal with the consequences. Unfortunatly, there is very little in terms of story that actually matters - as far as I can tell. Quests sometimes offer a choice or two in dealing with issues, but from my experience there is usually just one good way of completing them. Once I was tasked with finding evidence of a crime in a certain widow's home, where it turned out the only way to find it is to go to the basement and literally click on every piece of furniture and random items, until a secret door opens. No talking my way through, no alternative way of proving guilt or innocence, nothing. The usual illusion of multiple choices are 2 or 3 doors to a certain place, which you can find with some luck and investigation skills. Underwhelming, to say to least.
Now to my biggest issue with the game - the writing and the story itself. Although I was intrigued at first having been tasked with conducting a murder investigation, it quickly turned out to be a random string of events with poorly written characters. Cartoonish is the best way of describing basically every person and every event, it is like the developers could not take their game seriously even if their lives depended on it. Imagine going to a party with a group of people that constantly throw semi-funny corny jokes and just are not be able to have a serious conversation for even 5 minutes. If you have a similar sense of humour then you will have a blast, otherwise you will get tired, fast. It is hard for me to immerse in a world that does everything with the tongue in a cheek. If you are like me, try out the game first before even considering buying.
I will once again remark on the poor writing of the game. The dialogues are just bad and do not even bother taking the perk for talking with animals - their's is a partically poorly written one and does not give you any substantial reward for indulging in it.
Another example of the game's wackiness is the crafting system. You can combine many items to create new ones and in theory, it is robust and fun. In practice, you either try everything on everything in hopes of making sense of the system's logic or you simply look it up online. I am not saying it is impossible to find out thing on your own, but damn if I ever thought that carving a tooth with a knife and putting it on a stick can create a stun arrow.
To sum it up - if you want a game where you can play with a friend and just screw around, it is a good choice. Otherwise try to get a few hours test play and then decide. As for me, I will certailny not return to this game, ever.

Toybox Turbos is a very easy game. Now, easy doesn't necessarily mean bad but I just can't see myself recommending this game to anyone except die hard fans of the Micro Machines V games. And even then... I was a huge fan of V3 when I was a kid. And this game does make you relive the nostalgia you had during those times but the game fails to really expand on anything or make itself stand out.
The biggest disappointment by far is the tracks. Not only is there not many of them, but they're insanely short. A single track could take just 20 seconds to complete each lap for a grand total of minute long races. I can't recall if Micro Machines had longer tracks but, in this game, the tracks are just way too short. The visuals are nice but you'll get tired of seeing the same scenery over and over again especially when the design of them aren't exciting or challenging. Every track feels roughly the same and doesn't keep the races fresh. Shortcuts are rather weak and don't have any sort of creativity put behind them except for maybe one or two. Most of them just involve creating a small micro shortcut that let's you skip a hairpin turn.
There's not much to really complain about the driving other than the really dumbed down physics. Colliding with other drivers doesn't cause much penalty to you or them so trying to play dirty doesn't work. That's left up to the weapons and they're honestly really boring when you stip them down to their basic principle. There's a hammer which destroys anything in front of you in one hit, a machine gun with autoaim that can kill you and mess up your handling, an emp ball that is supposed to short out the controls but is so minimal it's useless, a magnet that let's you instantly snap to any other driver, and rocket boosters. That's really it.
The game's music is okay I guess. It's nothing too exciting there's really only about 3-5 music tracks to go around so get used to that. The music varies depending on the mode you're playing and... well there's only 5. You have your standard races (which only go to a max of 4 for some reason), time trials, race against the clock, overtaking and escape. Escape is by far the best mode but eventually you get to a point where the blue aura of death goes much faster than you and kills you automatically making fighting for the leaderboard rather impossible.
Apart from that the game is just too easy. It has a spike in difficulty once you reach the 4th or 5th cup but for the first few cups you'll be whizzing right through every challenge with ease. Despite the spike in difficulty I still managed to beat the game and unlock every car within 3 hours.
The multiplayer is decent enough. I've yet to play classic mode but they made the smart choice of taking the Elimination mode from the boss-battles and made it between 4 players which is nice. Players fight for points as one person either A. Has to leave the pack behind in the dust or B. Be the last one still alive. But it's hard to recommend because no one seems to own this game and the only one online battle I was able to find was on launch day.
Overall Toybox Turbos does a fair job of being reminiscent of the old Micro Machines games but fails to capture the same charm and fun those games had. It just doesn't do anything new or exciting to make itself stand apart. Again, if you're a true Micro Machines V fan then I suggest checking out the demo, but even then I'd be wary of making a purchase.
Toybox Turbos gets a 6/10.

Toybox Turbos has all the heart of Micro Machines but very little of the soul.
The single player mode offers very little challenge and the tracks are far too short, there are irritating filler modes such as Escape where you have to stay ahead of a wall of blue deathy stuff for a certain distance. Countdown in which you start off with little time and have to collect clocks to get more time BUT you must cross the finish line on your last lap with a certain amount of time to get Gold. And then there's Overtake which is the most stupid mode; you have to overtake a certain number of AI vehicles within the lap limit.
Boss battles are the only time in the single player game that the classic 'Elimination' mode is utilised in which you either destroy your opponent or gain enough lead on them that they are off the screen.
Physics are a little too floaty at times and you'll be frustrated by the amount of time it takes to right your vehicle if you're knocked over and there's no button to quickly reset your car.
Track design is a little too simplistic, they're all too short and all of them taking place indoors. Beating the single player mode enables mirror mode in multiplayer but it would have been nice to vary things in single player with mirrored tracks.
Vehicle types are really limited (there are no water based vehicles) and the weapons are fairly boring and useless.
You do get a feeling that Codemasters made this game with tons of DLC in mind which, if is the case, I think they have perhaps shot themselves in the foot for not offering a more stripped down version of the base game as a free starter pack. But the asking price isn't actually that bad and there is fun to be had.
I think multiplayer is where this game will really shine but I don't except the flame to burn that long and wouldn't be surprised to see this game heavily discounted in the coming months.
Final verdict? A fun but very short lived spiritual successor to Micro Machines with too little of the actual spirit.

Toybox Turbos may not carry the MicroMachines name, but in every other way it is a true successor... for better or worse. While other games will try to make you feel in charge, Toybox Turbos makes it very clear that the developers are running the show.
Other games try to give you an explanation why that camera is at that ungodly angle, or why THAT enemy has to have three times as much health. Not TT. The reason why the camera won't let you look ahead, is because the developers wanted to make it slightly frustrating. Ditto on the strange car physics... and let's not even speak about how the camera is always NOT right behind the car, leaving you slightly disoriented.
Accept that this as the real challenge you've been given and TT will be a lot of fun. Or at least as much fun as you can have with 18 tracks. Yes, the game is very short. Four hours and you should have received every car, track and achievement that's available.
What makes Toybox Turbos different from the hundreds of mobile games that try to imitate Micro Machines is that it does not ever apologize for its shortcomings. With a camera that limits how far you can see, you'd expect long straight streets with virtually no obstacles. You'd expect environments that never block your view. You'd maybe expect a mini-map. And you'd definitely expect the camera to tightly follow your car at predictable angles.
TT will have none of that. Instead you're given confusing environments with sharp turns, narrow straights, hundreds of deathtraps, a lot of stuff that is only designed to get in your way or block your view and a camera that will make every tight turn an exercise in multitasking.
And it works. It's a kind of challenge I haven't seen in years and it is oh so refreshing to encounter it once again. True, in the day of Micro Machines, the technology of the day required this kind of limitation, while it's just an artistic choice now, but it still feels good. And in a way, you feel like every match is a personal match against the designers.

This game is simply amazing, it takes everything well done in the first chapter and improves it. It's not a perfect game for sure:
- The Vortex mechanic imo is pretty annoying, there are factions that are in a far more favorable position in the map for the quest of collecting scrolls. The whole campaign ends up being "Win the battle after every major faction finishes the fourth ritual until it's your turn". At least this was the impression I got, but it's still nice to innovate and probably many people liked this mechanic; and if you don't there's the "Mortal Empires" campaign anyway which is plain awesome.
- For some reason unknown to me, cpu's armies are able of moving a freacking lot around the map and still be able to attack me in the same turn, while every time I move I end up being 1 inch away from the enemy. (I know you can upgrade the movement in the map through the commander, but still..)
- Compared to the first one, some of the lords are astonishingly strong (Malekith+Seraphon <3), so their influence on a battle is much stronger. This is not necessarily a bad thing, it's just a difference, more evident if you like the historical chapters.
Apart from these small cons, the game is amazing: nice graphics, nice gameplay, awesome map (mortal empires), increased importance of naval movements (even though you still cannot fight in water, i really don't mind the absence of this feature, but someone might nonetheless).

After 150 hours I changed my opinion.
While the game has many to offer (good graphics, combat, etc.) I need to change my recommendation from yes to no. After 150 hours of grinding to finally unlock some content, you'll see where the problem of this game is: it has no goal. None at all.
Yes, you can level up, and work closely together with a clan to get some big ships. And with these big ships, you can try to participate in the port battles. However, this expects you to do two things: grind xp, and start belonging to your nations elite. Your either in, or your out, and if your not in your not going to have any fun. Anyone who's not fulltime addicted to this game, makes no chance of ever joining.
Then there is the trade disaster. There is no rewarding trade system what so ever in the game. Yea, some missions and crafting, but these things are pointed at one goal: make money and ships to join port battles. In which I can't participate. And selling things for gold makes not a lot sense, as you can't do stuff with the money.
So what else is there left? PVE combat missions. In which you, over and over again, grind your combat level to higher. While the first battles were trilling and fun, you will quickly learn one thing: only pick battles in which you are completly dominating from the start. If you try to take a battle that's somewhere near challanging, you have the risk losing your ship with upgrades. As this is bloody expensive (mostly the upgrades, since they need lot's of crafting hours), you'll quickly learn not to join exciting battles, as you'll need atleast a week trading and crafting to regain your ship back again.
So probably the community is nice? Well, one year back, it was: people were helpful, etc.. Now it's plain evil. If you read on the forums, flaming is the norm. Not my ideal leasure time activity. And to make it worse, the developers are flaming as well, in stead of working hard. In the last year, so little changed to this game. Yea, new ships and a lot of effort of rebalancing ships combat. But before this game will get its final shape, it might be 2030.
In conclusion: do not get this game. Dev's are not interested in your opinion, and development is so slow.... Furthermore, you've no goals, and most likely, you will not find the epic combat your looking for, as the risk in losing your ship has such an economical impact that you'll not dare to ever use it. Except for the nation's elite, of course.

The sound and graphics are nothing to write home about. They would feel at home on any mobile device. But the art is cute and smooth, and works for the game style. (since there's very little movement)
The mod community is what takes this A+ game into some other realm of awesome-ness. My advice? Play through it once, and then think about what would make it better. Then... GOOD NEWS! There's a mod for that.
My ONLY complaint (and it's microscopic) would be that I'd like to see a bit more options in the initial game creation screen. Picking topics and genres is great. But what about the presentation? Is it a 4X game? Rail shooter? Sandbox? Grid or Hex-based tactics? This game is simple by design, so I'm not expecting it to be THAT deep. But maybe in the sequel???
In summation, this game is... it's just great. and that's saying a lot when coming from someone who generally shies away from casual games.

Fun game to play if you have an itch for sci-fi shooters. Not a long game, probably 6-8 hours, so definitely get it on sale. Solid all around with a few really cool and unique missions and weapons. I have a few complaints, but overall the game makes up for them.
The movement speed in this game is insufferably slow (slower than Halo), and there is no sprint ability. To rememdy this, you can bring up the console with the ~ key and type in "setspeed 2". This will double your movement speed and make this game feel much more like the original Unreal and UT2004. You may consider this cheating, but the maps in the game are simply too big for how slowly you move. It really comes down to if you want to spend the game walking really slowly toward your next objective, or actually playing the game and enjoying the combat.
My main complaint is how weapons switching works. Weapons are bound to your number keys, 1-5. But there are more than 5 weapons in the game so they decided to bind two or even three weapons to the same key, forcing you to press a key multiple times to access certain weapons. It really breaks the flow of the game and I wish they did it some other way. There is not even the option to use all 10 numbers keys.
Story is so-so, but nobody plays these games for the story. The main gist is that you have to go to different planets to collect 7 ancient mysterious artifacts of power. The bad guys want them too and are trying to stop you at every turn. The crew on your ship have interesting personalities and backstories of their own which  give the game a little more personality, but it's nothing special.
Not a bad game, but it had much more potential. I recommend you buy this game at a discount.

Some things to keep in mind.
Unreal II was NOT developed by Epic. It was developed by Legend, who is now kaput.
This is not really a sequel to Unreal in any way, shape or form. You can't really compare the two - in fact, if this was called ANYTHING else it would be a blessing. Sort of like Far Cry 2, in that it also has nothing to do with the first game of the series, and if anything marks a sort of spin-off point.
So, Unreal II.
What can I say? It's awesome, really it is, I'm still struggling with the fact that people have actually said anything except 'it's great'. I mean, back in the day, I thought it was great, and so did the critics, and now all of a sudden people are badmouthing it. Hmm.
I don't think half the reviews for this game have been fair, to be honest. There's nothing technically wrong with this game, and there's plenty of fun to be had with it - the weapons are just so cool, I mean you have an unlimited inventory system, which is nice to start with, but you get a gun, that shoots spiders. SPIDERS. That's awesome no matter which way you look at it.
The enemies in this game are really cool too, most humanoids will flop over into a ragdoll (which was pretty neat for the time) and you can walk over that corpse to sap some of the power left in their power-armor and add it to yours. Instead of like, dropping a medkit or something, you straight up sap whatever life was left in them. That's also awesome.
The AI design is absolutely perfect, agile heavily-armored melee warrior-caste aliens will sprint up to you, dodging left and right, reflecting your bullets while shooting back at you, closing in on you and strafing at close range to dodge your attacks. Mindless trash mobs will gang up on you and straight charge into you aggressively.
There is some really great level design here too. You really get a sense that the devs kind of mapped out everything in their heads... the ship itself that your character, John Dalton lives on with his crew does certainly seem like the interior matches the exterior in terms of size, shape.
And the graphics? The graphics are awesome too. Not everything has as much detail as games released today, but sometimes they come pretty damn close. The lip-syncing for instance is also really good. Legend did a certain kind of thing with this game... all of the big things tend to have less detail, so that small things and character models can have much more detail.
Know what else does this? Metal Gear Solid does this. If you look at a space floppy disk or whatever in Unreal II, you can actually make out all the lettering on it. Maybe not because it;s important, but the higher resolution on the smaller objects of the game help immersion greatly, because your brain can fill in all the blanks on big, less detailed textures, but it's harder when you're dealing with text. This game gets around that wonderfully.
So, the character you play as in this game... in a sort of compensation for being a walking tank - a dude in power armor - you're not that fast. Not as fast as running in Unreal Tournament, but that's okay, this isn't a UT game after all. Whether you like that sort of gameplay or not, it's quite fair I think. Especially since, you really shouldn't be comparing this to Unreal or UT99. This is an Unreal Engine game, but I don't know if you should really consider it an Unreal series game.
I mean, I don't really feel like I'm biased here. I don't. There's just so much passion that went into this game, so much love and dedication, and I feel like the developers really tried their hardest to make the best game they could... we might not quite have the multiplayer that we were promised, but honestly, I'm fine with that. I think Unreal II is a great game, and apparently in 2017 it's a highly underrated game.
Back in the day, it wasn't just about making a quick buck. It was about making games. So I give you Unreal II. Enjoy.

This is an excellent RPG in the vein of classic PC RPGs of the late 1990s, such as Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, and Fallout.
It earns this classification due to its focus on plot, dialogue, interesting characters and settings, and deeply impactful player choices.  It executes these core aspects very well.  The plot is fascinating and at times unpredictable.  The dialogue is not only dynamic and consequential but also unrelentingly cheeky (and fully voiced in the Enhanced Edition!).  The characters are many and varied, with distinct personalities and motives that bring the game to life.  The settings exhibit a remarkable attention to detail, with good design for their main purposes and numerous hidden curiosities and treasures.  All of this is tied together by a game engine that enables and encourages you to play it your way, exploiting every available path and tool to achieve your objectives.  This last point is taken to a greater extent than in most games in this subgenre: there are very few restrictions on where you can go; enemies are not leveled to your character or party; (nearly?) all NPCs can be killed; and most combat encounters are challenging enough to require some trickery to win.
On top of these familiar traits, this game adds a remarkably well executed combat/puzzle system based on interacting with the environment: moving objects around, creating surfaces and clouds of various elements, and exploiting the effects of numerous statuses that can affect combatants.  The number of elements and statuses is vast, and all of them have meaningful interactions with each other that can be exploited to turn the tide of a battle—or used by the game against you.
In a nutshell, this game encourages the player to explore, to tinker, and to choose his or her own adventure.  Somehow, despite the complexity inherent in that goal and in the game's execution of it, it doesn't feel engineered.  For an RPG, it's easy to just pick up and play, and it's a pleasure every time.
The Enhanced Edition added—for free—numerous enhancements that truly improve the game.  Fully voiced dialogue, reworked and expanded areas, improved and rebalanced skills, new equipment options, a completely overhauled crafting system, controller support…  None of these changes were strictly necessary, but all of them are extremely welcome.  Actions speak louder than words, and this upgrade truly demonstrates how deeply committed Larian Studios is to this game and to its fans.
My only major point of criticism is that it's sometimes unclear how to answer the question, "What do I do next?"  This game is very much not on rails, and it makes little or no effort to hold your hand or tell you where to go, even if you know which quest(s) you would like to pursue.  To a large extent, this is clearly intentional, as the game's plot- and subplot-driving sequences are meant to be discovered and progressed on the player's own terms and with the player's own comprehension.  However, I believe it would be possible to retain loyalty to this spirit while providing a little more guidance: better map indicators, or more detailed log entries, or more pertinent dialogue sequences.  On occasion, I find myself choosing my next destination solely based on the levels of the enemies that are there, which somewhat breaks my immersion.  I'm curious to see how Larian responds to this common criticism in the upcoming sequel.
Bottom line: if you want to play an excellent RPG that has offers heaps of discovery, challenge, and free-form play, do not pass up Divinity: Original Sin.

This game is not player-friendly at all.
10 hours on Normal difficulty and all I've done is get my butt handed to me.  The difficulty curve skyrockets after the tutorial and you'll quickly find yourself sauntering in to combat where you're so heavily outnumbered and outgunned in every imaginable way and there's nowhere to get to farm XP off easier enemies.  So far, I'm utterly stuck.  Gameplay has ground to a halt while I quick-load over and over again trying to take on a force I shouldn't be touching for two or three more levels yet.
All the weapons you find are hands and feet better than what you had five minutes ago; sadly they're too powerful for you at your level and are therefor much more difficult to use and drain your Action Points much faster or leave you with no feasible attacks.
Enemies equal to your level will come at you in swarms and if they win the initiative they can easily wipe out your team in one go and there is nothing you can do about it.
While the game's features are nice and well-done, the voice acting is horrendously annoying after a while and the inventory management will give you NIGHTMARES.
If you liked the old Ultima Games before they were horrifically butchered by EA, then this game is for you; but if slow, RTS-style combat, horribly unbalanced progression and ear-gouging, cockney-accented NPCs are your bag, then go for it.  You'll be saving and loading so often, though, it's practically a part of the gameplay.
Still, I recommend it.  It's not ENTIRELY the game's fault that I keep dying and I'm sure there's people out there that are walking all over this game and reading this review thinking "dis n00b ned 2 g3t gud lol"
Update:  You know, I was right.  It "is" me.  It's been 'decades' since I've touched a proper RTS/RPG and this 'is' a proper RTS/RPG.  All too recently these types of games allow you to skip the majority of content by providing you with steadily increasing gear and the powers of your party are typically enough to get you through all the way to end game.  I rarely used potions or bought anything off merchants in games like Dragon Age when all the best stuff was found lying around and the classes were powerful enough to take you through the whole game without needing artificial support.
This game breaks that concept and I STRONGLY recommend you buy every damned grenade, specialized arrow and scroll you can find.  You also don't get skills for your class handed to you.  Whatever you don't get at character creation, you have to find.  So if you ignore the merchants you're only hurting yourself.
While this game is kicking my♥♥♥♥♥and as much as I hate the voice acting, this game IS what it IS and it doesn't shy away from it.  I was only making it hard on myself because the last 10 of years of this genre, the developers were making it easier from the genre's 90's predecessors.

Toybox Turbos is a game where you play with toy cars on various location such as kitchen sinks, school tables, toy train sets and more. The game provides 35 cars and 18 tracks and there are various game modes but they are for single player only. For some reason multiplayer has Elimination mode for both local and online multiplayer.
The game has 7 tiers of cars, the first tiers are a bunch of taxi, london cab and buses while the second tier are a set of off road vehicle which provide SUV, moon buggy and even a monster truck. The cars gets faster every tier, the final tier of cars are race cars which provides a classic F1 car, dragster, sportscar (which looks exactly like a low poly GRID 1 and GRID Autosport drift Mazda RX7) and a hot hatchback.
The cars feels very floaty and all of them drive similarly, they are a bunch of Micro Machine scale toy.
In the single player mode, there a total of 7 cup and each cup has 5 race. Each cup are restricted to specific tiers of vehicle and specific set of races. There are 6 type of game modes here, Classic Racing, Overtake (like the ones in GRID 2), Escape, Elimination, Time Trial and Countdown.
Classic Racing also includes weapons, weapons can be used to overcome your opponent. There are a few weapons in the game such as hammers, EMP, rifle, turbo boost, mine and magnets. Magnets could pull you closer to your opponent cars, hammers lets you wreck your opponent cars and EMP could slow down the cars around you.
Overtake mode requires the player to overtake a bunch of cars around the track which acts like traffic. The player wins by overtaking an amount of cars set by the game.
Escape mode has a wave of water or force field like thing chasing behind you, the player requires to drive the furthest distance possible before your car being covered the water or force field.
Elimination mode is also the boss race in the single player mode, weapons are provided in this game mode as well. This mode plays a bit like NFS Underground 2 outrun mode, the player requires to drive as fast as possible until your opponent car is not seen on the screen and the player loses when the car is not seen in the screen, got destroyed by weapons or flew off the track. A score is given when the player wins and 1 score taken away when you lose, the player win this race by filling up the score bar. If the race takes too long to end with constant plus and minus 1 score from you and the opponent, the game will starts putting mines around the track and losing will no longer deduct a score but every win still adds 1 score.
Time Trial mode ask the player to clock the fastest time on the track but the tracks has mines to disrupt your racing line.
Countdown mode is similar to Time Trial mode, the tracks has mines placed around it as well. The difference is the player requires to pick up "clocks" to add time to their timer, the player lose when the timer ran out of time and wins by reaching the finish line with most time left.
The single player AI starts off to be very easy and they dont seem to use the weapons they pick up at all but it gets better and faster as you progress through the cups.
One of the problem for the single player is the lack of proper quick race mode, you cant pick a set of cars and track combination you wanted to do a race or any other mode. The special game modes are restricted to the "Single Player" section which act as the career but the local multiplayer can be used as a "quick race" mode. You could start a local lobby yourself and the game will fill the opponent with AI, you could chose the tier of cars you and tracks you wanted to race but the multiplayer is resticted to Elimination mode only. The hard AI in the game is pretty challenging and could provide a couple more hours of fun.
The game provides both online and local multiplayer up to 4 players, the only game mode for multiplayer is Elimination mode. It plays the same way like in the single player mode but instead of having 1v1 you are having a 4 player elimination race.
I'll highly recommend this game if it goes on sale for around $10, the game length is really short. It took me 4 hours to finish the game with all stars and all achievement (the achievement are super easy though). For the full price Codemasters is asking for now, it is still pretty good if you are a fan of top down racer, likes the toy cars feel with bright colours and casual racing.

The DNA of Mashed, Circuit-Breakers and Micro-Machines are all present with their best features employed to great effect. Connectivity is solid and we've experienced no de-sync as of yet. Game settings give you lots of scope for play experience, including the amazing "Retro Top Down" mode which re-creates the effect seen in only the earliest versions of Micro-Machines (i.e. the camera doesn't chase-follow the cars so when you are racing down the screen left and right are reversed). Circuit design is also first-rate. Excellent title, a throwback to front-room console gaming from a by-gone age. I really can't recommend this enough.

Lego Worlds is an interesting take on sandbox games from the ultimate physical sandbox from my youth.  Before Minecraft, before virtual worlds, there was the physical joy of building something with Legos.  However, there are a few cons for this BETA release.
PROs: 1. HUGE world.  Got lost a few times just trying to explore it.
2. Everything is destructible. (if you have the right "items".)
3. I found, flew and destroyed things with a DRAGON....nuff said.
4. The vehicles are awesomely fun.
5.  It's fun to just tool around in.
CONs:
1. Controls are a little wonky.  Breaks the momentum when you have to go back into a menu to rotate a brick instead of mapping it to a key or button on a controller. (I played with the Xbox 360 controller and it was pretty intuitive other than that)
2. I got lost.  Flying over water in a dragon, seemed like I was flying forever over water.  About 10 minutes infact and never saw land.  A map of some sorts would be nice.
3.  Digging down would be cool.  was able to blast tunnels with the Warlock's fireball, that was fun.  However, even when I found the drill vehicle, there wasn't much ability to dig down.
4.  Not enough options for minifig creation.  You have to discover minifigs throughout the world before you can get their options in a custom character.  My kids LOVE making minifigs, this would definitely turn them off.
5. Multiplayer and maybe some sort of purpose to being/discovering.  Other than wandering the map, killing skellys for no apparent reason and seeking out items/minifigs; I didn't feel much of a drive to DO anything.
Overall, great game that I can only see getting better with new content, workshop support and of course...multiplayer.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER definitely exceeded my early basis of the game prior to buying it. Originally not thinking much of it, believing it to be a small indie endless-runner type game, with a low-cost budget iterated by its supposed low-pixel character, I was for certain surprised with what I ultimately played.
The game is definitely more complex than it looks at first glance. In a sort of ironic sense, this low-pixel character is thrown into this retrospective, high-detailed world, and ultimately creates this strange contrast that excels admirably.  Gameplay-wise, it actually has its own stage system to it, to which you run at a fixed pace non-stop in an attempt to reach the end goal, while maneuvering over certain obstacles. Failing to overcome an obstacle sends you back to the start, which is both aggrevating and relieving. In a sense, I could probably bring comparisons best with this game to Geometry Dash. Now, that being said, early levels are far from being as difficult as Geometry Dash, but you'll soon find yourself having to duck, kick, and soar over large gaps, and soon after having to combine all of these in swift movements.
Personally, I'm relieved to find a game that allows itself to be difficult for gamers, but not in an "artificial difficulty" sort of manner. It never really seems to rely on luck, if at all. It's completely memory and skill based, which adds to the gameplay value of practicing the game until you can surpass a point you're stuck on.
So all in all, I would definitely recommend this game.

If feels like somehow a few developers who learned to code from YouTube coding lessons managed to cut and paste their way into something that resembles a game. I’ve tried to like this game for 3 months but its been a horrible experience overall. This is a mediocre game at best. Further, they insist on degrading the user experience further by forcing secondary logins & game registrations.  You have to create an account with them, verify you are who you say you are, and all that junk. This stuff never works right and is especially true with this game. Oh, and get this, you must use a gmail account for registration.  What?? I have gmail but still what kind of flaky spaghetti code are they writing that can only handle registrations from gmail? None of this has anything to do with the game either its just some kind of old school foolishness. They don’t even maintain multiplayer game servers (see below) which would at least be a valid excuse for this account registration nonsense. Aside from registering the game and perhaps being forced to do so multiple times because they have an inadequate registration system that forgets who you are and loses all of your game info you’ll have an even more difficult time trying to do anything that requires hitting their servers like saving race results and getting anything to do with multiplayer to work.  Even the achievements seem straight up bugged presumably because their own system doesn't remember who you are and refuses to pass on the achievement information to Steam.   Even the most mundane of achievements are hit or miss to ever get to pop.  Some basic achievement as simple as opening the car repair menu may never pop and likely a more significant one like a well earned victory achievement will never be realized.  Achievements are not that big of a deal but if you’re going to advertise them as a feature then you know what? They better work.
All this developer imposed nonsense aside, the game itself is average for a 10 year old racing game. The graphics are lackluster but passable.  On the highest settings performance is almost decent BUT it looks so dated. The controls are fine using an XBOX wireless wheel or just a regular XBOX wireless game pad.  What is an issue, however, is once you do any remapping of controls the game menus do not properly represent your remappings. It uses the default prompts in the game even after you change the mappings. It’s also really easy to get stuck in the simplest of menus and the prompts just don’t make sense sometimes. Come on, at least get the MENU system right.  Then it’ll read something along the lines of press A for OK, B for Accept, etc.  So you have multiple options that would appear to do the same thing, but of course they don’t and good luck trying to figure out what the devs were thinking with that.  You can’t tell half of the time if you’re continuing to the next level or about to forfeit a race. Once in a while a button just stops working in the menus. You might have to abandon a race if, for example, you’re on the race stage info menu but the right dpad stops working so you cant navigate back to start the race or tune and repair your car. No other key or button will help either and you’re only choice is to quit which hurts your overall standings which in turn hurts your ability to advance in the campaign. Magically the button starts working again once you've done exactly the opposite of what you wanted to do. Sometimes the sound cuts out entirely. Not just the car sounds, but everything in the game including music, the crowd, etc. Silence. Then it’ll suddenly start working again 30 seconds later. These things have been complained about on the forums for months to no avail.
I’ve never been able to start a multiplayer game.  The system insists I need to create an account and verify it which has been done.  I did it when I first started playing in November 2013 and have done it again since. Doesn't matter I don’t exist apparently.  None of my race results get uploaded and after every single stage of a single player race I face “an error occurred during upload” message.
Support doesn't seem to exist.  They haven’t replied to any emails, facebook, or in the Steam forums. In fact I think some of my posts were wiped away instead of being replied to. The attitude feels like, “thanks for the cash, now leave us alone.”  Also I’d take whatever they put on the store page with a grain of salt. “78 courses in 13 different countries,” they say?  Well maybe if you count that ½ are just reversed courses or slight variations on the other courses. There are nowhere near 78 ORIGINAL courses. Also from the store page, “Online multiplayer mode for up to 16 people” but this is from their own readme: “ARC 4 FIA World Rally Championship has no dedicated servers for multiplayer.” Huh?  So it’s peer to peer? How do you even establish a peer to peer connection if you can’t even start multiplayer mode at all?
There are plenty of great racing games out there with a lower price tag. This game is a bit specialized but not terribly so that its a must have. I guess I could go on about how much I don’t like this game but if you made it this far there is no sense in beating a dead horse. Warhammer 40k Space Marine...Well, this is going to be predictable as hell. For those of you that know what I mean by "predictable" I mean over done, and here's why:
The Space marines have been on almost all the marketing for Warhammer 40k. Because of simple box art this usually results in people outside of the fanbase thinking "oh hey, those are the good guy Spartan people from Halo of duty fighting demons in Hasbro reskin armor....Let's go make a chess game out of it...With grenades and AOE attacks...Ya'know, just like chess."
So you better like the Space marines 99% of the time because that's what you are going to get until someone revisits Fire Warrior, or release a game about Eldar, Imperial Guard, hell the Orks sound fun! ♥♥♥♥ it, let's begin the review.
You play as captain Titus, an ULTRAH SPHESS MEHRIEN! sent to this Forge world with a mission to retake the city from the massive Ork horde. But wait! Turns out the Orks are being led by someone with a brain! Just so you know I'm being sarcastic, it's no surprise who it really is and the videos on the store page give it away before you even purchase the game.
There isn't much to talk about the campaign for Space Marine, it's simply 'meh' it's not bad but it isn't good either. It's just...Decent, at least enough to keep you going, unless you get tired of getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked by Nobs in tight hallways.
To be honest I'm a little disappointed. The execution animations get tiresome after a few hours so that means you'll be playing this game in sips.
The ranged weapons also feel dull, and campaired to the awesome power of the melee weapons within the game I felt like there was no point to the guns. It's like giving the player Excalibur at the very start of a game then tell him/her that he/she should use a squirt gun instead...Chances are you're going to go with the over powered weapon they just gave you.
But if that was the only flaw within the gameplay I would call this just nit picking. Unfortunately this is a console port...Best way to say that is "♥♥♥♥ keyboard players!"
I rarely use controllers since I play 70% of the time on my desktop/laptop. But there are games out there that are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to play without a controller. So, how bad is it? Well the mouse feels slow and unresponsive. The keys are placed in odd areas on the keyboard, for example: by default the 'ctrl' key is the aim button. Character movement on the keyboard is sluggish and hard to control, espeically while sprinting- (I feel like I'm driving a heavily armored gothic bumper car with chainsaws attached! and there are no breaks!)
And then there is the audio...The XBOX360 version of Space Marine's sound is perfectly fine, but on the PC? Sound tearing everywhere! This happens generally when there are a large amount of enemies in the area, this is a game about fighting Orks by the way...Enjoy the sound of- "WAAAAAAA-RIIIIIIIP*STUTTERSTUTTER*-AAAAAAAH!!!!" I assume Space Marine suffers the same problem Source games have, but I can't confirm this so I won't go into too much depth about it (god knows I get enough flame wars on these reviews just for saying Hack'n'Slash instead of Hash'n'Slash...Yeah don't ask)
Normally I'd say the more content the better, but I think multiplayer is the reason why less attention was placed into the singleplayer. But besides that, you start off with a class selection and a long♥♥♥♥♥road of unlocks (oh joy)
Tactical, your basic soldier with a bolter rifle and a selection of grenades. After progressing for a while in multiplayer you'll find yourself with a wide selection of guns to use such as- the Plasma gun, sniper rifle, storm bolter, and finally a grenade launcher. Sadly other bolter varients from the lore are not in the game. Also the flame thrower isn't in there either which I have a hard time understanding.
Heavy bolter marine, he starts out with a heavy bolter but eventually you get a las canon and a plasma cannon. Although I don't know why because the only "vehicle" in multiplayer is the Dreadnought, and that's a 9.99 DLC!
Finally the Assault trooper, this is the most fun you'll get in multiplayer, jumping around from place to place with your jetpack. You start out with a chain sword but eventually you unlock stuff like the power axe and the thunder hammer. Sadly he dominates the other two classes once you get the hammer and it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥just killing one of them.

Fallout 3 is the
Movment is painfully slow now, but added some of the coolest weapons to the series.

It's a fun single-player campaign.
There are a TON of weapons to choose from, probably more than any other shooter I've played. And all those weapons have alt-fire modes as well, so there's a huge variety. You've got everything from rail guns to deployable force fields to black hole generators, it's really impressive.
The solid gameplay that we know and expect from other Unreal games is here too -- expect some great firefights!
Some of the music tracks were pretty catchy; I particularly liked the Suferon music track (I'm listening to it now as I write this review).
I played on Windows 7 64 bit. There were a few minor bugs but all could be rectified by going to an earlier save. Graphics are mildly dated by 2016 standards but it's very playable.
The two main complaints about the previous game were nonlinear levels and lack of a strong story. These issues were definitely addressed in Unreal 2! The levels are very linear so it's hard to get lost. The story now involves interactive choices (for flavor only, as the levels will always play out the same way). There are also downtime missions where you interact with your crew and get briefings on your spaceship.
I found it hard to relate to the protagonist, but overall I found the story enjoyable. Buy it if it's $5 or less!

TL;DR Surprisingly solid, enjoyable game. Graphics are spot on, handling is just right, difficulty has challenge without being too hard. Features 4-player local/online multiplayer with plenty of options and tracks. Also top-down retro view for fans of the old Micro Machines games. Would recommend to people who like fun!
I've spent the past year looking for modern-day Micro Machines-alikes but nothing comes close to the originals, I found myself replaying those instead. When I saw that CodeMasters were making a new game (albeit with the license), I was incredibly excited but also very weary. Turns out though, that it's a fantastic little game.
The difficulty is not overboard like the old ones tended to be but still challenging enough, I often found myself tantilisingly close to a higher place on the online leaderboards too, which added some extra life and replayability to the game.
I realised all too late that you were able to change the camera view to a retro-topdown one but I was surprised actually by how much the new camera view suited the game, I'm usually strictly retro-isometric but I'd happily play this game as-is!
Altogether, this is a well put together title which has clearly had some love lavished upon it, especially considering the low pricepoint. You aren't paying the triple-A money of the original games but you certainly get the quality. The graphics are just right, the handling is great and there are several noticably nice touches in the track design.
I've yet to try out the multiplayer but that is usually where Micro Machines games shone so I have no real worries there.

Ask yourself a very simple question: Do you love the old Micro Machines games?
If the answer is yes, then chances are you'll love this too.
It's pretty much everything you loved about the old games: fast, close and fun races; innovative tracks based on breakfast tables, playrooms, school rooms and pool tables.
You can even set the view to the classic 'top down', which makes it a lot easier to spot short cuts but isn't really how the game is meant to be played.
The single player campaign is rather short. I finished it in less than four hours, which is something to be aware of.
I also found online to be a little bit buggy and laggy, though this could have been my connection rather than a server side issue. I'd have to play more to find out.
I haven't played local multi-player yet but it should be a hoot!
If you're not sure, try the demo.  For me it turned this game from a 'wait until it's on sale' to a 'I need this right now!'
It may be a short and quite simple game, but it's very, very sweet.
I can't wait to get this game on with three other peeps, it'll be an absolute blast!

Overall a surprisingly well put together game that captures the feel and the nostalgia of the old Micromachine games.

This game is not player-friendly at all.
10 hours on Normal difficulty and all I've done is get my butt handed to me.  The difficulty curve skyrockets after the tutorial and you'll quickly find yourself sauntering in to combat where you're so heavily outnumbered and outgunned in every imaginable way and there's nowhere to get to farm XP off easier enemies.  So far, I'm utterly stuck.  Gameplay has ground to a halt while I quick-load over and over again trying to take on a force I shouldn't be touching for two or three more levels yet.
All the weapons you find are hands and feet better than what you had five minutes ago; sadly they're too powerful for you at your level and are therefor much more difficult to use and drain your Action Points much faster or leave you with no feasible attacks.
Enemies equal to your level will come at you in swarms and if they win the initiative they can easily wipe out your team in one go and there is nothing you can do about it.
While the game's features are nice and well-done, the voice acting is horrendously annoying after a while and the inventory management will give you NIGHTMARES.
If you liked the old Ultima Games before they were horrifically butchered by EA, then this game is for you; but if slow, RTS-style combat, horribly unbalanced progression and ear-gouging, cockney-accented NPCs are your bag, then go for it.  You'll be saving and loading so often, though, it's practically a part of the gameplay.
Still, I recommend it.  It's not ENTIRELY the game's fault that I keep dying and I'm sure there's people out there that are walking all over this game and reading this review thinking "dis n00b ned 2 g3t gud lol"
Update:  You know, I was right.  It "is" me.  It's been 'decades' since I've touched a proper RTS/RPG and this 'is' a proper RTS/RPG.  All too recently these types of games allow you to skip the majority of content by providing you with steadily increasing gear and the powers of your party are typically enough to get you through all the way to end game.  I rarely used potions or bought anything off merchants in games like Dragon Age when all the best stuff was found lying around and the classes were powerful enough to take you through the whole game without needing artificial support.
This game breaks that concept and I STRONGLY recommend you buy every damned grenade, specialized arrow and scroll you can find.  You also don't get skills for your class handed to you.  Whatever you don't get at character creation, you have to find.  So if you ignore the merchants you're only hurting yourself.
While this game is kicking my♥♥♥♥♥and as much as I hate the voice acting, this game IS what it IS and it doesn't shy away from it.  I was only making it hard on myself because the last 10 of years of this genre, the developers were making it easier from the genre's 90's predecessors.

Lego Worlds is an interesting take on sandbox games from the ultimate physical sandbox from my youth.  Before Minecraft, before virtual worlds, there was the physical joy of building something with Legos.  However, there are a few cons for this BETA release.
PROs: 1. HUGE world.  Got lost a few times just trying to explore it.
2. Everything is destructible. (if you have the right "items".)
3. I found, flew and destroyed things with a DRAGON....nuff said.
4. The vehicles are awesomely fun.
5.  It's fun to just tool around in.
CONs:
1. Controls are a little wonky.  Breaks the momentum when you have to go back into a menu to rotate a brick instead of mapping it to a key or button on a controller. (I played with the Xbox 360 controller and it was pretty intuitive other than that)
2. I got lost.  Flying over water in a dragon, seemed like I was flying forever over water.  About 10 minutes infact and never saw land.  A map of some sorts would be nice.
3.  Digging down would be cool.  was able to blast tunnels with the Warlock's fireball, that was fun.  However, even when I found the drill vehicle, there wasn't much ability to dig down.
4.  Not enough options for minifig creation.  You have to discover minifigs throughout the world before you can get their options in a custom character.  My kids LOVE making minifigs, this would definitely turn them off.
5. Multiplayer and maybe some sort of purpose to being/discovering.  Other than wandering the map, killing skellys for no apparent reason and seeking out items/minifigs; I didn't feel much of a drive to DO anything.
Overall, great game that I can only see getting better with new content, workshop support and of course...multiplayer.

TL:DR:  This game is like dating a gorgeous blonde bombshell who has the IQ of a flea.  It's really awesome when you first start but in the long term you can't handle the stupidity. Originally I was split 49/51 not in favor.  However with a friend the fun intensifies and the DLC seems pretty decent.  I am in favor of the game now after giving it some more time.
The good:
- The emersion is great.  The feel of desperation in the city is awesome
- The visuals are stunning
- They did an awesome job on recreating a pretty real NYC.
- The story and missions are done well
The bad:
- This game is in my top five for clunky controls.  I never would've thought that a AAA game would push a game with such clunky controls.  This is my number 1 gripe.  It's a tethered style so it looks smooth but feels clunky.  You find yourself trying to stop and turn and you're still running forward into a wall.  Or you grab an item from a chest, get up to turn around and you find yourself doing the running man on the chest.  Also, it's so annoying getting in cover behind something and suddenly finding yourself needing to jump out of the way of a grenade and your body doesn't respond the correct way all the time.  It's hard to explain without going into great detail of how to break off, dive, etc.  Needless to say it's annoying sometimes. Theres also the healing issue.  ISay I finally get up from cover and take off running, try to begin healing but it won't let me because I'm getting shot.  I'm button smashing trying to get my heal to go off.  Then one of the heals you can shoot towards something or heal yourself.  But in a hurry you find yourself trying to shoot it instead, trying to cancel it, or trying to use a medkit instead.  Just frustrating.
- The community is not the greatest.  It seems like a good mix of mentally challenged kids and self titled elitists.  So PUGs can get frustrating because you can easily find yourself grouping with the mentally challenged.
- The chat system is difficult to use in party because it's not pronounced and people usually don't see it.
- PVP can get very frustrating if you are alone. Unless you know a friend who wants to play, teaming up seems difficult in the dark zone.  Sometimes you get lucky and find a couple people to roll with once you're inside but usually you'll find a group of players running around going rogue and taking peoples stuff over and over.  They just camp spots and wait for you to try and extract.  If you want to go solo, I recommend going in the DZ at slow hours (early or late) and building your gear so you can take on the rogue players when they show up during normal hours.

A polished and full-featured offering to the Scribblenauts series. Being on PC and having access to things like the keyboard and the Steam Workshop greatly improve the game. It is somewhat annoying to have to figure out what the game wants you to say, as its understanding of words can be limited at time. For instance, one puzzle needs you to evaluate a piece of art and typing "art expert" doesn't work, but "expert" by itself does. A mechanic can't repair a robot because a mechanic repairs cars, but a scientist can because science. Little things like that. Luckily those issues aren't usually a huge barrier to progress.

The game is cute and the dictionary is a novelty you won't find in any other series, unfortunately the game's selling point is also kind of its downfall since it makes all the puzzles incredibly easy. There's no penalty for using the same words over and over and the game doesn't really reward cleverness, you can solve pretty much everything with adjectives or the same obvious solutions. A game with limitless potential for creativity isn't worth much when it offers no incentive to actually be creative beyond self-amusement. The controls are also pretty bad, you'll find yourself repeatedly accidentally opening menus and pausing the game when you try to attack things, although this game is very light on reflexive action as it is.. It's an alright sandbox if you get it in a sale, though if you've played any of the other Scribblemans games then you've already seen everything it has to offer.

Game gets boring after little time playing it.
It's basically a Half-Life with multiplayer, sights, no sprinting and no story at all.
Weapon animations are poorly made, with bad stats and headshots seem to do no increased damage. Don't try using the sights as it will only slow you down and obstruct your view.
In-Game sounds are low quality and have different volumes, some are too low, some are too high (to the point where playing the game more than 15 minutes on the lowest volume setting will severely hurt your ears) and the background music really doesn't fit the playstyle.
The default keybindings are somewhat confusing (melee is on F key, for example, whereas Grenade/Especial Item is on MOUSE3).
Maps are also confusing and difficult to get around, the zombie spawn mechanic is really bad, you'll quickly get surrounded if you don't have your back against a wall/corner as the zombies spawn anywhere you are not looking at and at very fast rate.
There are no "Official" servers, which means you are subject to modded ones, no VAC Protection servers and the like.
In my opinion this game is nothing but a short demo and should only be played if you, for some reason, can't play any other free game of the genre.
In conclusion, the time spent is not worth it and won't add anything for your gaming experience or something else, except for increased frustration and occupied disk space.

The game plays out more like a 2D-pixel art movie than anything else. No action (except maybe the zomb-evas) or strategy, except the occasional easy puzzle. This game wasn't designed to be like other games you can find on Steam, but rather was meant to take you on the journey through the protagonist's life. Bit-by-bit the story pieces together the memories of Johnny's life all the while reccuring objects tie them together. The ultimate question is, "Why does Johnny want to go to the moon?" The answer to that question was definitely a tear jerker. Rarely does a game make me cry. The last one I can remember was Final Fantasy VII when Aeris died. "To the Moon" is in a league of its own and I would buy this game again to support FreeBird developers to produce a more in-depth update version of this game and possibly another episode.
Who should buy this game?
1 - People who can appreciate a well written story.
2 - People who appreciate well composed semi-classical music.
3 - Anyone who cried from a good story line in a game... ever.
4 - Someone who wants to help an indie developer produce storylines like these.
5 - Also someone looking to spend 3-4 hours in casual gameplay.

I have just finished the game and can honestly say Ori and the Blind Forest is an amazing game. I am not a fan of platforming games. Rpg & rts are my thing, but after seeing some gameplay footage of this game I had to try it out for myself.
The two things which made me want to trying this game is the absolutely beautiful artstyle & music. The animation quality of this £14.99 game puts many triple A developers to shame. For example, simple things like when you walk to the edge of a wall you can climb or jump up, Ori will put her hands on it and look up as if to prepair. Also as I jumped through some vines she put her arm out to touch them as she went by. Simple things like this make such a difference and makes the world you are in feel alive.
Exploration is encouraged and rewarded, if you dont find some of those hidden places I doubt you will max out the skill tree has some nice upgrades which are make a difference to how you play. For example you can unlock underwater breathing or upgraded vision, which allows you to see hidden rooms.
The save system in this game is pretty good. There are static save area (shrines), but you can use your mana to create a save point, which also gives you acess to the upgrade tree. You will need to learn when best to create one, or you may find yourself loading up ages away from where you died.
You will unlock many new powers as the game progresses and the puzzles leading to the end of an area will give you ample practice to perfect your use of that power, before you face the *boss* moments where you need to use all you have learned to escape. Each new area offers new challanges & encourages you to think. Every time I died, I never felt like the game was screwing me over as it reacts well to the input you give. On a whole Ori and the Blind Forest is a ray of light in the massive pile of bug filled, micro-transation loaded or dlc milking releases which have plagued us this year. You can see the developers have put their heart and soul in to making this game & I would say this is a game everyone should experience atleast once in their life.

The short version : Gamer grade (as in, it's no cakewalk) Metroidvania with Nintendo-like polish and precision and Studio Ghibli inspired art style.  10 to 12h for a first run, absolutely fantastic game, go buy it now.
The longer version : I have just completed Ori & The Blind Forest (OTBF).. and within the confines of a drab gaming landscape, filled to the brim with uninspired sequels, overhyped and disappointing (allegedly) triple A titles, continuously pushed back for months if not years and completely broken with bugs when they finally come out, it is incredibly refreshing to finally play a true video game !
Inspired in every sense of the word, OTBF is blessed with a stellar presentation (the introduction was so emotionally crushing I actually cried within the first 10 mins); technically proficient and artistically stunning graphics who put even the latest Rayman games and Child of Light's UbiArt Framework to shame; an enchanting, memorable and absolutely fantastic soundtrack; and gameplay, although nothing revolutionary and a little old school, is nothing short platforming heaven.
Similarly to Guacamelee back in 2013, OTBF is the latest heir to the proud Metroidvania legacy.  A legacy it seems, that simply refuses to die (thank the gods).  People not playing OTBF would clearly be missing out on a landmark.  The kind of landmark that will be durably etched in gaming's Pantheon for years to come.
In closing, a word of caution though : OTBF is not designed to cater to the casuals, as it is a rather difficult game (albeit never frustrating from my point of view) that requires some level of skills.  Other than that, buy and play this game.  It gets my highest praise and recommendation.
