It has clipping issues - muzzle clearance is often not how it looks when you're close to scenery. It follows a tried and tested but very dated format of running through the hoardes of baddies to get to an `end of level Boss', who is then defeated by following a set pattern. Even the final Big Boss (spoiler alert) turns into something far less, with flying in a circle avoiding his blasts until you automatically close, then just following the on-screen button-press prompts. It's like you've been guided to win. It's definitely enjoyable, but there's no innovation, it relies on an old format and suffers from it - you just want so much more. Especially when it takes such a short time to complete.
So what about the multi-player? The online play? This seems to be where the game can really come into it's own. Colour schemes aside (it has ALL of them!)The options for customising your build are fantastic, really make a difference to both the way you play and feel of the game. With comms you can make very effective teams, even a pair can cause havoc when side by side with complimentary builds (I recently had a game where our team were winning easily until an Assault marine paired with a Melta bearing Tactical Marine annihilated us repeatedly). BUT (you knew it was coming) all of this is wasted. Because the Peer to Peer (P2P) matchmaking system, lifted directly from console games, means you have ridiculous lag and rubber-banding for far more games than you don't. "Waiting For Host" becomes the bane of the game. Even when you don't "migrate hosts" you're still strafing in a circle expending clips into stationary targets and suddenly just dropping dead for no apparent reason. The good games are very very good, but they're few and far between and this is not just my opinion. People are typing words to this effect in the chat channels all the time and my own gaming community, who embraced this hugely on release have pretty much stopped playing it because of the P2P lagfest.
Space Marine is a classic case of expectation not being met because some basic concepts were not addressed in either the Alpha or Beta stages of the game. This is "working as intended", and it's not good. The freely downloaded extra content of "Exterminatus" (4 player co-op games facing waves and waves of enemy) is immensely fun but quite a small addition. You'll get huge kicks from this game, but it's such a shame the system is flawed right where it should let the game shine...

I cannot recommend this game more. The cute, but very serious story is astounding, the art style is... breathtaking, to say the very least, but most of all - the gameplay is fluid and fantastic.

4 Words.
You're missing out by not playing this game. I have not had this much fun in a single-player platformer game in a long time. While the story is very simple and generic, the execution through all the other factors of this game molds one of the most cohesive experiences in a single-player game.
on the story.
I have not tried the keyboard controls, but I can say in great certainty that the controller button mapping is excellent; though, it would be nice if there was a feature to customize controls. The handling of Ori in the game is very fluid and smooth; Ori is a very flexible and acrobatic character and is able to maneuver gracefully through the entirety of the map. I personally had no serious trouble with the handling and controlling of Ori, and despite having felt cheated on certain portions of the game due to the controls, I look back at that and realize that it's not because of the controls; the game places an emphasis on replayability and challenge.
on the controls.
The difficulty of this game depends on the player's skill. You will die a lot die a lot when you first play this game. If you're great with platformers, this game will not feel as difficult; if you're new or not that as skilled in this genre, you're going to feel like this is the hardest game ever made. All the enemies and environmental hazards still feel like a threat even when you have upgraded Ori's HP and skill tree; environmental hazards will deal the most damage to Ori. After overcoming the obstacles in this game, you feel like you've accomplished a challenging task; it's quite a satisfying experience.
on the difficulty and gameplay.
Lastly, the graphics and the sound/music are amazing in this game. Before writing this review, I was questioning myself if I should review the graphics and the sound/music in different categories. However, I find that this game has created a very cohesive experience with the graphics and the audio. Hearing the soundtrack is like listening to the story of Ori play out. Looking at the graphics of the game gives you the imagination of what the music is like. The content of them both are so well intertwined; the experience created from it is one of perfected beauty. I cannot say anything that is con of the graphics nor can I say anything negative of the sound and music. Gareth Coker did an amazing job on the soundtrack. Play this game and you can see and hear for yourself how a story plays out.
perfection on the graphics and sound/music.
Overall, this game gets a 9/10 from me, but an extremely close 10/10. This game is near perfection and one of the highlights of this year. Buy this game and play it. You will not regret it.

100% credit to AuldWolf for saying it perfectly.:
I'm going to miss this game.
For me, this was one of the greats.
It was like I'd entered a vortex to a parallel reality where gaming hadn't given into the mainstream; it hadn't become creatively bankrupt, desaturated, dead-eyed, xenophobic rot that one could complete in their sleep. Yet it had retained the best values of contemporary gaming form our reality. Fair, even-handed, challenging without ever punishing (it reminds me of VVVVVV in that regard).
There are certain games of each particular age of gaming that stand out as being something unique. Of this ilk, I can think of Okami, Knytt, and Ecco off the top of my head. Though oddly it shares most in common with Ecco. Once you've got at least the triple-jump and the dash, the movement becomes so precise and fluid that it might as well be underwater. It's a beautiful thing to watch.
I'd rather seek egress from this place and find that reality where this sort of thing is commonplace. I'm a soulsick old fart, I admit. I have an imagination and worlds within my mind, I'm almost nauseated by how distressingly boring the average person is. Their mirrored minds each mimicking the last in grotesque displays of abominable extroversion, as though that were some kind of achievement. None of them with a word worth speaking.
For a while, playing this, my heart sang. I'll admit, I'm rarely happy. It comes with being introspective, creative, and intelligent. Sorry. Many people like myself have stated something along the lines of 'show me someone with those qualities whose often happy and I'll show you a liar.' Which isn't as eloquent as I could put it, but it'll suffice. What I'm trying to say is that this is a thing of rare beauty. I feel most entertainment creators these days simply don't care.
And it was nice to play as something other than a human for once, too. I'm not fond of my species. I mean, if you'd experienced what I had, you'd understand. I'm mentally disabled, and physically too if you consider motor problems/the shakes to be a physical disability. I'm of a class of person so utterly despised and reviled that I'm wondering how long it'll be before we're all stuffed into gas chambers and flowery excuses are made of it. So I don't often relate to humans in entertainment.
It's worse, too, that they're often toned, Aryan in appearance, flat, extroverted, and as one-dimensional, soulless, hollow, fallow, empty, and paper-thin as they are 'beautiful.' These are homunculi. Not so different than zombies. Just zombies that the mainstream masses find appealing. It's a sort of conformist zombie, a Barbie & Ken zombie with bleak eyes. That's what gaming focuses on, today, so much.
I think that as our brains are shrinking[
] we're just becoming more narcissistic, extroverted, oxytocin-pumped, and generally xenophobic. And when I say xenophobic I mean ermahgerrd it's something I can't relate to, KILL IT WITH FIRE. So it's quite an achievement to create something like this that all those people can relate to, where they've been unable to relate to similar things in the past.
I don't know how you pulled that off. But it's quite amazing. Gives an old fart just a sliver of hope.
But yes, I won't forget this game. I can't. It's today's Ecco the Dolphin. It's singularly unique, and it's unique in how singular it is. It's a thing untainted by what the mainstream might want, by what shareholders might desire. It's an alien, foreign, impossible creation. So it may not sell well, if that's the case, I'm generally sorry. We're kind of a crapsack species at the moment, what with all the greyscale serial killer simulators selling so well. So I'm sorry if you won't be able to make more like this.
But I appreciated it. And I know I can't be alone. And I know I'll miss it. I'll come back it at some point in the future. Likely a year or two from now. I might make it a case just to drop in and wander around, like my yearly sabbatical into Uru: Ages Beyond Myst to see Shroomie.

This game is beyond fun. Skullgirls has the fighting genres staple character types like the grappler, ranged, and all around while still having unique characters with their own mechanics that change the way they play. Whether throwing your head as Ms. Fortune to change your combos and gain a extra hand in battle or using your own skeleton to change from Elizas' slow heavy attacks into fast pace quickstrikes this game has diversity. Diversity in alternate costumes which are easily obtainable by playing arcade or just as the character alongwith the great reference skins from anime, videogames, comics, and even other fighting games! There is no shortage of costumes and no shortage of ones to call your personal skin. I love this game due to these aspects and appreciate it more for the amazing tutorial and practice mode with frame data, hit box and hurt box options alongwith character specific training teaching every button and special aspect of the specific character. Skullgirls is a great entry fighting game while still being veteran friendly, I've played fighting games every since I could hold a controller and my friend has only played smash, yet he can access information on his character, not get frustrated with multi page combos and have a enjoyable experience with the story and arcades multiple difficulties. All in all, I would HIGHLY recommend skullgirls for a first or even eleventh fighting game. The visuals are also something that astonishes me but you should get this game, it's worth every dollar and its cheaper than other fighting games ive seen on the market.

CALL OF DUTY INFINITE WARFARE REVIEW.
(Pros and Cons, Personal opinions and Useful Information about buying)
TL:DR: Call Of Duty Infinite Warfare does not deserve all the hate it is getting, If you played it yourself you'd find it the one of the best damn games in the series.
Pros:
-Great Story
-Game Mechanics are top notch
-Weapons are awesome
-Really well designed
-Vehicle mechanics are better than most games
-Gives kind of the star wars feeling
-Fast paced action
-Amazingly optimised
-Awesome characters
Cons:
-It does take 76GB of space
-First time startup takes a while to load, after that launch it doesn't need to load much anymore
-Does freeze for a few seconds every now and again to refresh steam overlay. Easily fixable
-Some weapons sound the same
-Kind of short main story
SINGLEPLAYER:
Single player campaign has got to be one of the best I've played. Aside from Black Ops 2.
The characters in the story are just plain badass and really awesome to play as, you play as Captain NIck Reyes, he was promoted to captain of the UNSA fleet after the recent Captain had been killed alongside the general due to an SDF invasion. The SDF forces are the main enemy in the game, they attacked your homeland and terrorised the planet. You have to evacuate from the planet using your mothership and continue your raid in outer space. You can ride various customizable JACKALS. Jackals are spaceships similar to star wars, they shoot missiles, rockets, flares and MACHINE GUNS that you can use in ship warfare in space which is EXTREMELY fast paced and all action fun. I shouldn't be spoiling too much else of the game, basically take down the enemy forces from the ground up, literally.
MULTIPLAYER:
Very, very fun! It is sort of hard to find a game since the multiplayer servers aren't as active as before. But when you join you have a massive variety of weapons to choose from and really awesome action gamemodes. Consisting of some of the classic modes like Deathmatch, gun game and  capture the flag. Even introducing EXTREMELY fun NEW gamemodes like gesture warfare which is funny and fun to play. Overall, the multiplayer in this game is a BIG upgrade from multiplayer in games from the other series. If people played more then maybe they'd see the brighter side of it. The AI isn't bad either, better than a lot of other games AI. I would highly recommend to try this out whilst playing, I can guarantee you'd have a lot of fun. WE JUST NEED MORE PLAYERS.
ZOMBIES:
Zombies... oh my lord it was amazing. This game gave the zombies mode a new shine of light. Never seen before in other games and one of the best improvements to the mode in the series. It introduced different MOVIE BASED situations, which were EXTREMELY FUN. Reminded me of the early days with Left 4 Dead 2. In the new zombies move you play as a gang of 4 people, almost sounds like scooby doo. And there are many zombie situations and maps to choose from including bonus DLC to buy and they ARE WORTH GETTING. Overall the zombies mode is an epic upgrade from the other games including STORY BASED appocalypses and characters which have different personalities and equipment. You'd enjoy this mode very much trust me. After playing the other versions in other games. You'd be freaking overwhelmed by how good they've made the mode in this game. The zombie weapons are very effective and useful, there is a big variety to choose from and all do sustainable damage. It is just undescribable of how good this game is and this gamemode in particular. You should really try this.
OVERALL:
Call of duty: Infinite warfare is almost one of the best games in the series, you should really try it despite the bad reviews. It is sooo amazing. There are a few buggy startups which are easy to work around once you start playing. This is game is just so amazing I don't even know the words for it. I encourage everyone to try this game out and you'd be suprised at how goddamn good all the developers worked on it. Did I mention? There are so many people that put their hard work into this, a lot of companies, devs, publishers, customers and the community. I'd like to say a personal thank you to all the people that worked on this game. This is one of your best games yet. PLEASE PLAY THIS GAME YOU WON'T REGRET IT!

This is only surpassed by my ability to put chain shot through existing chain shot holes in an enemies sail and cause no damage whatsoever. I've also had the moral quandry of whether to run away or just surrender my vessel. Surrendering is todays favourite as it's quicker to just start again rather than wait to flee, wait to sail allllll the way back to port and then get repaired. Only to pick up another mission. Trade--- difficult to turn a profit. You can buy an entity produced in one place and needed in another only to find it's cheaper to buy in the needed place. That's like buying water from a man in the middle of the sahara desert cheaper than from a man living next to a river. Yesterday I actually bought something and sold it instantly in the same port for a profit. The Sell was higher than the Buy price. So when demand exceeds supply in a port the Sell prices go down?

AI--- An AI ship can tack through the wind twice to put two broadsides into you before you've done it once and brought your cannon to bear.

Plus the larger heavier Privateer can turn on a sixpence and the small Cutter takes 1/2 a mile to do a half circle. Personally I've never seen an oil tanker at sea out turn a speed boat.
I know now why Cortez burnt his ships when he reached the New World. He'd played Naval Action on the way over. If you've ever seen any youtube videos about people reacting to this game, you will see various reviewers either crying their eyes out or desperately trying not to. This is a very emotional game, with a script and story that would move even the most unemotional of gamers and has been one of my favorite stories in a game since playing Shadow of the Colossus on PS2 back in 2003.
To the Moon isn't a video game in the traditional sense, mainly because it focuses almost exclusively on it's soundtrack and story, which is where this game shines. Some people claim the game is worth buying for the soundtrack alone, and in my opinion, is one of the most moving and evocative scores i've heard in the past decade of gaming. The gameplay revolves around exploring small environments, finding small clues and items to advance to the next area. The controls are a little awkward, and would benefit from controller support and might take a while to get used to, but it doesn't take away from the experience. The visual style reminds me of Chrono Trigger for the SNES, while sporting far more detailed environments with character sprites that convey the characters emotions and body language amazingly well. The visuals are excellent, the audio is even better, and the only thing that is slightly in need of improvement are the controls.
The actual story revolves around Johnny, a man dying of old age, and his final wish to to go To the Moon. This is possible thanks to technology that allows two scientists to change the Johnny's memories, granting his wish inside of his mind. What follows is a trip backwards through a dying man's memories. I don't want to reveal too much about the story, but it is a little slow paced and takes some time to pick up. Once it does though, the story writing has as many "Aha!" moments and twists and turns as a Doctor Who or Sherlock BBC Episode. There are many points in the game where Johnny does or sees something that seems irrelevant, but the further back into his memories you go, it takes on a totally new meaning. I could go on for hours about how excellent and brilliant this game and its story/soundtrack, but it would be easier for you to just buy this game, because its definitely worh every cent.

Assassin's Creed is a franchise centered on an action-adventure video game series developed by Ubisoft. It depicts a centuries-old struggle between the Assassins, who fight for peace with free will, and the Templars, who desire peace through control. Featuring historical fiction and characters, mixed with real-world historical events, and figures. The series took inspiration from the novel Alamut by the Slovenian writer Vladimir Bartol,[1] while building upon concepts from the Prince of Persia series.[2]
The franchise began in 2007 with the release of Assassin's Creed. The main video game series consists of nine entries, developed by Ubisoft Montreal (single-player) and Ubisoft Annecy (multiplayer), released on PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox 360, Xbox One, Wii U, Microsoft Windows, and OS X platforms. Many spin-off games have been made for Nintendo DS, PlayStation Portable, PlayStation Vita, iOS, HP webOS,[3] Android, Nokia Symbian Windows Phone platforms, the handheld games are developed by Gameloft and Gryptonite Studios, with additional development by Ubisoft Montreal. The series has been well received by critics, and has sold over 100 million copies as of September 2016, becoming Ubisoft's best selling franchise and one of the highest selling video game franchises of all time.
Additionally from the video games the series has been expanded into a film, comics and novels; all of which take place within the same continuity as the main video games series.
he Assassin's Creed games primarily revolve around the rivalry between two ancient secret societies—the Assassins and the Knights Templar—and their indirect relation to an ancient species pre-dating humanity, referred to within the games as "those who came before", whose society, along with much of Earth's biosphere, was destroyed by a massive solar storm thousands of years before the games. The games' real-world chronological setting begins in the year 2012.
Within the franchise, Abstergo Industries is a mega-corporation conglomerate with multiple branches, secretly run by modern Knights Templar. The company is the present-day main antagonist of the franchise. Abstergo secretly created a device called "Animus", that allows its users to "re-live" and experience the memories of their genetic ancestors within their bloodline through a virtual simulation. Overexposure to the animus causes the "bleeding effect", which results in giving the user skills and abilities of his ancestors, but is also dangerous for the user as it can damage their mind, causing symptoms such as dementia, insanity, dissociative identity disorder or brain damage. Abstergo is seeking to discover the location of several historical artifacts, known as the "Pieces of Eden". Such artifacts hold great power, and are capable of controlling free will. Abstergo seeks to use them to remove free will and bring humanity into one single unified group, while the Assassins oppose them. In order to find the Pieces of Eden, Abstergo is abducting people whose ancestors are suspected to have had historically confirmed or suspected interactions with such devices, forcing the kidnapped person into the Animus and searching for clues on their ancestors' memories within the Animus.
While the games are often presented through protagonist Desmond Miles, the bulk of the game is played as Desmond experiences the memories of his ancestors through an advanced device called the Animus. This provides a means of a diegetic interface, showing Desmond's ancestor's health, equipment, goals, and other features as part of the Animus interface. The Animus is based on the player controlling the assassin to maintain the synchronization between Desmond and his ancestor's memories. Performing actions that go against the Assassin's way or dying breaks the synchronization, effectively requiring the player to restart at a previous checkpoint. Furthermore, the player cannot explore outside areas that the assassin has not experienced yet. There are also abnormalities within the Animus from previous users of the device.
While playing as the Assassin characters, the games are generally presented as third-person in an open world, focusing on stealth and free-running. The games use a mission structure to follow the main story, generally assigning the player to complete an assassination of public figureheads or a covert mission. Alternatively, several side missions are available, such as mapping out the expansive cities from a high perch followed by performing a "leap of faith" into a haystack below, collecting treasures hidden across the cities, exploring ruins for relics, building a brotherhood of assassins to perform other tasks, or funding the rebuilding of a city through purchasing and upgrading of shops and other features. At times, the player is in direct control of Desmond, who by nature of the Animus use has learned Assassin techniques through the bleeding effect, as well as their genetic ability of Eagle Vision, which separates friend, foe and assassination targets by illuminating people in different colors. Through the Animus interface, the player can go back to retry any past mission already completed; for example, in Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood, the player achieves better synchronization results by performing the mission in a specific manner such as by only killing the mission's target.
The games use the concept of "active" versus "passive" moves, with "active" moves, such as running, climbing the sides of buildings, or jumping between rooftops, more likely to alert the attention of nearby guards. When the guards become alerted, the player must either fight them or break their line of sight and locate a hiding place, such as a haystack or a well, and wait until the guards' alert is reduced. The combat system allows for a number of unique weapons, armor, and moves, including the use of a hidden blade set in a bracer on the Assassin's arm, and which also can be used to quietly assassinate targets.

TLDR – Space Marine is a third person hack & slash shooter taking place in the world of Warhammer 40k. If you’re working your way through the games in the Humble Relic Bundle, Space Marine is a great way to round out your Warhammer experience after beating the Dawn of War Real Time Strategy games. Remember Starcraft Ghost, the first person shooter taking place in the Starcraft universe? Me neither because that game was cancelled. But Space Marine is a decent approximation of what I think that game would have been like. You encounter the distinctive enemies of Warhammer and lead your squad through a war torn world beset on all sides by alien hordes.
In this chapter of the Warhammer 40k saga, you play Captain Titus of the Ultramarines (like regular Space marines, but more ultra I guess). Your mission is to infiltrate a planet under massive Ork attack and secure a vital strategic asset before the Orks can get their grubby mitts on it. The Orks (with their British accents) are generally scavengers and will pick apart any technology they can get, including the super secret weapon that happens to be on this particular planet, so it’s up to you to stop them.
The game is played in the third person perspective, like Mass Effect but with no real cover system and much more emphasis on melee fighting. You have a small selection of guns and a few melee power weapons that will be familiar to people who’ve played the Warhammer games, for example the chain sword and power axe. The guns are reasonably powerful and you can mow down waves of enemies with your limited ammo before getting to the hack and slash melee fighting. At key points in the game you also get access to the badass jetpack that you often see space marines run around with in the RTS games. The Orks almost always come in large numbers so get used to the melee portion, it will make or break your game experience. Orks aren’t your only enemies though, and you’ll find yourself under attack by forces of Chaos closer to the end who are significantly more difficult to deal with.
Pros:
+Greater immersion in the Warhammer world since you won’t be getting an overhead view like the real time strategy games. You’ll actually be dropped into it playing as a single person fighting xenos in the name of the emperor. Enemies from the Dawn of War games like Nobs and Chaos demons are real threats, unlike their counterparts in the other games.
+Decent story, and some flavor added through “servo skulls” which act as personal logs (similar to the recordings in the Bioshock games). These give you some background on the world you fighting for, and the enemies you’re up against.
+The game has multiplayer with some people playing, so I was able to join a few cooperative matches when I wanted to try it out.
Cons:
-This might be a personal problem, but I seemed to get headaches when playing this game for more than an hour. It probably has to do with the movement of the camera as your Space marine stomps around in his power armor.
-There’s a bug with one of the servo skulls if you’re going for the achievement to collect them all. Just get this one last and you should be good. Fortunately you can load specific chapters from the start menu.
Note that the difficulty of the game skyrockets in the last half hour or so of the story. The rest of the game is pretty straightforward and you can take your time, but suddenly you’re all alone up against a horde of powerful foes. Overall though, the game is fun and I would recommend it to any fan of the Dawn of War games or action games in general.

Anyone that knows me even a smidge knows that i'm a huge warhammer fan, and i enjoyed space marine quite a bit. both melee combat and ranged combat are just as viable as the other and flows seamlessly between the two, allowing for entertaining and gory combat while purging the enemies of the Emperor. The story within the campaign is decent as is the voice acting and soundtrack, and there a lots of nice little touches within the game such as even the random battlefield objects such as ammunition boxes being actual games workshop models in the present - something i thought was a cool little feature.
Character development is interesting; which is why we all hate Leandros and love Sidonus/Titus.. and there are some highly unexpected plot twists, ones that you wouldn't normally suspect from warhammer! Even the warboss Grimskull is fricking awesome, likewise with the chaos lord Nemeroth.
The bolter was done so extremely well that it just has to be mentioned - a doof-cannon of explosive destruction with a realistic rate of fire for such a large shell being loaded automatically and the chainsword is just as satisfying as you "vroom" your way through orks and chaos. In fact the entirety of the sound design is top notch, such as the heavy stomping of casual marine steps and the general atmospheric sounds.
However, despite these gems within the game it does possess some things i found to be issues...
- Now, while the combat in this game is rather highly acclaimed, it does not have a parry button; the only way to stop your opponent's spamfest of attacks is to stun them. This is rather...weird... as in multiplayer it's basically just two marines constantly shanking eachother and then throwing in the odd backhand to knock them back for a moment. This results in no skill needed to effectively melee..at all. It's just spam the attack button.
- The game isn't too accurate to lore either. In saying that it's not exactly butchering it though. For example Lascannons only instand kill marines on headshots. If it was more accurate to the lore it would kill a marine outright. As would the plasma cannon...and melta...
- THQ no longer exists and SEGA isn't doing much, so no updates apparently to fix any bugs/issues (despite myself not actually discovering any bugs but anyway)
- DLC has segmented the already splintered online playerbase somewhat
Now, don't let these negative words sway you from the game itself though, i found it to be quite fun, the campaign is of a suitably long length and remains fun if you play it in bursts of an hour or so, the combat is oh so much fun and last but not least...it's warhammer! What isn't to love in the grim darkness of the far future!?

Unreal 2 starts very real, introducing your character, an ex-marine that patrols space for the Terran Colonial Authority with his cozy little spaceship, a funny pilot and a hot female companion (oh and the techie that gives you a bunch of new guns and mods after each mission). The dialogue is fun and the graphics holp up very well but the gameplay is slow and the loading times ridiculous (maybe it has something to do with my system but playing on 'hard' means you will see more of the loading screen than the actual game even when returning to a quickload). LOADING-STANDBY-INITIALISING...The psychodelic intro is nothing like the game. It was probably hard to top the creepiness and sense of alienation you had in the original, as well as it's speed and agility.  Still, the game has enough variety in the settings (very different planets and climates) and the weapons (very cool stuff including a flamethrower, turrets, and even a spiderthrower) to make it worthwhile.

Unreal 2 is an underrated little gem that was overshadowed by Halo (which in turn was influenced by the first Unreal). The major difference between the two is that while Halo sucks, Unreal 2 doesn't. The graphics are better, the combat is better and there are no tedious driving segments or pitiful attempts at an epic story with Disney enemies. The story is simple, involving chasing artefacts throughout the galaxy, which serves as an excuse to showcase some epic and varied environments that still impress. Despite the low-key story, there are some good character interactions and a very gutsy ending. The only downsides I can think of are the rather slow walking speed (a sprint function would have helped a lot) and a soundtrack that doesn't live up to its predecessor's reputation. Also note that the game's human enemies are annoyingly difficult on the hardest skill setting so take that as a word of caution if you're planning on yanking up the difficulty level.

Skullgirls is...an interesting fighter to be sure of, and I don't know how to really declare my stance on it.
On one hand this is a very 'fluid' fighter, every attack has a large amount of frames of animation, there's a lot of small details in movements and actions, every input 'feels' like it has weight behind it. It also has things set up to 'prevent' a lot of things that seem to plauge fighters of both yesterday and today (Justace, Jojo ABS, and MvC3 being the current examples of writing.) and to try to encorage more 'dynamic' fighting.
...On the other hand this game kinda 'forces' you to learn long strongs of attacks and very selectivly timed inputs to get 'garenteed' damage, with most even low-mid level fights being desided by two connecting hits leading towards said combos. It also has a very limited roster, meaning you'll chances are see all the tricks in the book in a very short time.
it want's to try to welcome new people into fighters, but it seems to cater more towards those who have been doing fighters for a long time...thought in turn, seems to not be 'enough' for them to sink their teeth into and feel gimped by the experance. This is in no way a 'bad' game, but it sits in a very akward placement where one has to ask: If you try to please everyone, will you in the end please no one?

Why ? ...   Let me tell you some things you might need to know before purchasing it:
Pros:

+ the first thing you'll notice are the waves. the water is so realistic to watch.. and even more realistic during battles, where u'll have more details
+ steering a ship is fun too, there are a great variety of ships you can purchase during the game with many upgrades and different looks

+ you can be dutch, danish, sverige, american, british, french, spanish or join the pirates, which is the only faction who can attack eachother.
+ day/night cyclus
Cons:
- the waves could be much bigger at the sea
- as nice as the UI is while outside on the sea, once you are in a Harbour/Port/Outpost the UI is big and confusing.
- You gain 50 ish xp for a successfull mission in Level 1, and not more. You need 1000xp to Level 2 = Pure Mission Grinding!
- There ain't alternatives to grinding missions, but to attack players of other countries, which you shouldn't do in early levels anyway, cause you have no effin chance
So if you don't have mates to help you out in those missions wich are 1vs1 battles against AI Ships and 50% of them will destroy you in the beginning, you have a problem
- one of those missions ( 1vs1 battles ) will last for 30minutes or longer until finally a ship is destroyed and will sink, whether its yours or the AI ship.
- there are only 3 things to do in this game: missions ( which are always the same procedure ), pvp battles ( will be interesting in higher levels / you can attack Harbours too ) or you can just farm Gold by buying and selling goods in different Ports, but you cant gain xp from that and there ain't trading quests yet.
If you decide to farm Gold first, you might be able to puchase bigger ships, but bigger ships need a bigger crew, and the amount of crewmember will increase with your rank/level only! so don't even think about joining a battle with a ship that needs 150+ crew and you only got your 40 member in level 1. Cannon reloadtimers will increase drastically, your turning and steering will be horrible, and you can't even manage to repair it either.
So.. if you're already a fan of ships , especially old ones and don't care about the difficulties during the game, get it and travel the carribean sea!
Otherwise, give it a couple more months and check if they added more content.

This game is AMAZING. This game has everything you want if you want to have a more realistic touch to being a captain of your own ship. I am going to get right down to the point of why this game is amazing.
Pros-
Captain your ship, your way. You can choose to be a faction or be a pirate. Some of the factions are the French, the Spanish, the Dutch and the Americans. There are several others as well. If you want to be a factionless person you can be  a pirate and kill anyone, but that goes double for you as you can be killed by a fellow pirate and any other faction in the game.
PVP and PVE. New to the game? Not to worry. There is a PVE mode where you can join up with people and learn from them as you fight AI ships which can give you a run for your money. There is also a PVP mode (Of which I cannot cover as I haven't done that yet.)
Realistic damage. The damage to your ship does affect what happens. More damage equals more holes and easier to shoot grape shot (To kill crew) into that side. Chain shot can destroy sails with ease and slow you down, making you a sitting duck for cannon shot.
MIssions and free roam. In this game, you start with a basic cutter class, the lowest of the low. In the start you can't exactly go up against a high level ship such as a frigate and expect to win. To rank up you need to do missions against the AI and get money and XP. Doing this will help you get to your next ship and buy your guns for it.
There is a lot of goods, to many to name off in fact but the game does have some minor gripes.
Cons-
Teleport. There is a teleport system in the game that does send you back to your capital city. Now this is optional keep in mind and you don't HAVE to use it, but this is a gripe because...WHY IS IT IN THIS GAME?! I understand people might get lost or confused in the game but thats part of the fun of being in a time when GPS or things like map markers don't help. The fun is the adventure and the thought of finding yourself fighting a high skilled enemy because you don't know where you are.
Confusing at first. Once you join the game it thrusts you into it without any real indication of what you are supposed to do. It kind of just gives you a menu and says "Have at it" Which isn't bad but in a game like this, you need a tutorial or some help leaning about it. While it isn't impossible to learn by yourself, I suggest youtube or guides on how to start first before you do anything.
These are only a few gripes and of course as it is Early Access, things are going to change. The UI could use some spit and polish, perhaps even a reboot, but it isn't exactly impossible to use. All in all, the game is great to play and fun to just shoot each other.

As stupid as this sounds, LEGO Worlds is THE Lego game.  It is like having every single piece of Lego ever created right in the palm of your hand.  You are always mere clicks away from building castles, cottages and Wild West Saloons, as well as having the ability to build something one single Lego brick at a time - Which will take a lot of time and dedication.
In the beginning you will be able to randomly generate a world that you would like to play in.  My world had a small forest that was home to cavemen and cavewomen, a desert biome that housed warlocks and vampires and one corner of the world was dark, it looked evil and was spewing lava. Once you have generated your own personal world, you will be able to skydive in, Just Cause style and just play with Lego.
I was running around and constantly finding new and exciting things.  I came across horses, sheep, dogs, vampires, cavemen and women, skeletons, cars, bulldozers, boats, a swimming pool, snowmen, etc.  From the short time I have spent in the game, there is a lot here already for a Early Access title.
The world renders every single individual lego brick.  That means, if you use the tools that the game gives you to edit the terrain as you see fit, you will find more lego bricks.  Take away a huge chunk of the world?  You will still find every single individual lego brick has been rendered underneath.  Unfortunately, this may be wear I began to have my only performance issue - I have experienced some pretty bad framerate issues, even when trying to mess around with the settings and lower quality (My PC should be able to handle this game at the highest anyway).  However, I give LEGO Worlds the benefit of the doubt as it has just released and is still in Early Access.
One other weird issue: Pressing 'S' when In a vehicle does not put the vehicle in to reverse, the vehicle instead just goes in a circle until it is facing the opposite direction that it was before.  I suggest this is changed to the 'S' key reversing a vehicle. EDIT: THIS SEEMS TO ONLY BE WITH THE BULLDOZER VEHICLE.
Nice audio with soothing music and fluid game animations are present.  You can really tell that LEGO Worlds has high production values and that TT and Warner Brothers are really backing this title.
I believe that if this game gets the love and attention that it deserves, it could truly be a fantastic game.  With updates, patches and more content this could be great.  The game is fun right now with a lot to do, but more content in this type of game never goes to waste.
I would also love to see some sort of survival mode - For example, like Minecraft.  Something where the player has to collect materials and resources to build shelter, mining tools, etc.  As well as harvesting food or something like that.  I believe that a survival mode along with this current creative, free roam mode that is in the game just now, would be incredible.
If you enjoy sandbox games like Minecraft and of course Lego and also like to be creative and build your own world with it's own buildings and communities - You may have a great time with LEGO Worlds.

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a 3rd person shooter based in the (suprise!) 40k universe.
I've played several Warhammer 40,000 video games. Some were good, others mediocre, and others were so great that I still play them, even several years after their release.
This is one of them.
This is one of the best 40k games, period. It nails everything- from what makes a good 3rd person shooter, to what makes a true-to-lore 40k game.
To start off, This isn't your standard 3rd person-totally-not-gears-of-war game. Whilst most 3PSs focus on a cover system, Space Marine removes that entirely. You ARE the cover. You can wade into a mob of enemies, without dying every 3 seconds. It perfectly encapsulates what makes a space marine a space marine, and lets you experience that firsthand.
The combat is divided into two parts- ranged and melee. You are given a wide variety of weapons to slaughter your enemies in different and uniquely brutal ways. Each weapon feels (and sounds!) exactly how it should. The shot of a bolter, the hiss of a meltagun, and the roar of a plasma cannon. And although the ranged weapons are cool, the melee weapons are even better. Chainswords (chainsaw-swords) evicerate and rend flesh whenever they strike, turning a large horde of orks into a bloody mess very quickly. Thunder hammers, although slow, deal tremendous damage and completly pulverise your enemies. The combat (especially in single player or the horde-mode) is immensly satisfying and one of the best parts of the game.
The game has both a single-player and a multiplayer. The single player has a decently lengthy campaign (10-12 hours) with a pretty good story. It does have its faults (unfinished story arcs that will probably never get finished b/c r.i.p THQ), and the last boss fight is pretty lame. The multiplayer, although good and reasonably well balanced, gets repedative with the 4 maps (excluding expansions). You also can't choose which side you are on pre-match, meaning you might not even get to see your shiny new color scheme for a couple matches. The multiplayer also follows the standard 'level up to improve' philosophy, with special perks unlocked by completing challenges (some of which are brutally difficult without help).
Overall, this is a fantastic 40k game that really makes you feel like you are playing a space marine. It has a few issues (mostly with multiplayer), but you can easily get many hours of enjoyment out of this game.

Warhammer 40k: Spacemarine is a game so caught up in doing a half-arsed job of emulating other successful games, it has no identity of its own. The gunplay is a poor knock-off of Gears of War and the melee combat is a poor knock-off of Arkham Asylum, and the difficulty alternates between snooze fest to rage fest between each encounter.
Melee combat has only half a dozen moves per weapon (with just three weapons) and performing the same goddamn finishing move over and over again to regenerate health is a wearying necessity to stay alive, so wading out into the fray is more of a chore than the visceral joy it should be.
This is especially true when the ork rocket troopers are introduced en masse as, with no a cover system and a character who moves with all the speed and grace of a sack of potatoes, you'll be obliterated in seconds flat if you aren't constantly leaching enemies for health.
The story is uninspired, too. No spoilers here but if you're familiar with the 40k universe, it's pretty predictable stuff.
If I had to say something positive about this game, it would be about how appealing the art style and lore is. Then again, considering that these was borrowed from Games Workshop and aren't added to in any meaningful way, it's not credit which the developers are due. The guns feel ok, I suppose, nothing to get too excited about though. Seriously, if I weren't such a fan of Warhammer, there's no way I would have soldiered on to the five hour mark before quitting for good.
There is no reason to play Space Marine. Play one of the Gears of War games or Arkham games or, if you want to play something set in the 40k universe, one of the Dawn of War games. Relic should stick to strategy games, they're out of their element here.

The very core of gameplay, fighting ton of bad guys, is put together very well and doesn't use the ♥♥♥♥ing arkham asylum "press RMB in the right time to win" style. Instead you have the choice of three melee weapons, with power hammer as my favorite, and a lot more in the guns department, with classic boltor and some more exotic weapons; like melta gun, mixing it together in glorious gun kata. Enemies come in variety; from orcz who rush you naked with an axe and just die, through berserkers and armored orcs, ending with ♥♥♥♥ers with missile lunchers. There is another faction aside from orcs that you will fight later, but I won't spoil it for you. Story is what you would expect from that kinda game, being bitter-sweet and straightforward save the world, no time to philosophy when there's war to be fought!
Now let's get to issues that this game is flawed by. And believe me when I say, that there are many of those. First of all, mentioned by me before, repetitive nature of this game. Now you may say that is the genre's fault, but subjects as Devil May Cry or MGR : Revengence show that it is not the case. The difficulty spikes and unbalanced melee to gun prowess of the emenies ratio is worth mentioning too. You may find yourself taking out dozens of orcz with axes when later be taken down by 2 baddies with rifles and a supportive rocket spewer in the back. Also the problem for me was that while carrying a power hammer you can only use 2 out of 4 ranged weapons, and that being the more powerful ones, which in most situations kills the joy maker that is power hammer, and forces you to slowly take down ranged units one by one, insted of headshoting them with sniper rifle otherwise. The music is just kinda there, mediocre at best. Also the whole game is on rails and contains not even a sliver of open worlds.
Would I recommend this game? Well, if you're at least a little interested in the warhammer 40k universe and is looking for mindless massacre of greenskinz, then yeah, absolutely! Is it deep? No. Will you remember any campaign moment when you finish it? Not likely. Will it blow your mind? I don't think so. Is it any fun? Yes! Just don't hope for too much and you will be satisfied. :)

I remember on January 2003, I got an early copy of Unreal 2 at Hastings, I'm guessing they had a review copy or something like that. Anyways, I remember playing it, liking it, but then again, I was 9 when I played it.
Now years later went by and I'm an adult now, is Unreal 2 as good as I remember it?
HELL NO.
Let's get the positives out of the way first, the graphics of Unreal 2 are good and weapons are unique just like the environments, from a gun that shoots spiders to a grenade launcher with multiple ammo types, the guns are good.
But that's about it.
Unreal 2's story has nothing in correlation with it's predecessor, Unreal 1 and RTNP.  In fact, the only thing that Unreal 1 and 2 have in common is the fact there's Skarrj, and that's about it. U2 does try to add Liandri, Izanagi and Unreal Tournament references in there, but it goes over the head like the comedy.
Characters are nice, but bland.
And then there's the gameplay.
U2 is single-player only (unless you get the XMP pack of the net), and while the environments are nice looking and unique, it doesn't help that each mission is about the same; go in, kill a bunch of dudes and aliens, solve a puzzle and get the artifact.
In between missions, you can talk to your crew aboard the USS Enter... I mean Atlantis, to get briefed about your next mission, learn about your weapons and learn about the backstory of the crew, that's it. It serves it's purpose.
But sometimes when normal missions aren't enough, U2 likes to throw a curve ball in the form of defense missions.. and these can BURN. IN. HELL.
Defense missions asks you to defend an area or a person for a certain amount of time, using force fields and turrets and Marines with Derpy AI to guard the objective from waves of enemies. The problem is that not only do they break the boring flow, but some of them are a pain, be it the derpy AI marines, the derpy targeting system of the Turrets, the fact that it takes little time for the enemy to plow through your defense with ease or all three.
And let's not forget that one DICKWAD on Janus named Meyer... The biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in U2 who constantly ♥♥♥♥♥es about everything. EVERYTHING.
With all these things combined, I cannot recommend Unreal 2: The Awakening to anyone, from veterans on Unreal to new players.

I highly recommend this fun for all ages kinda game. It is like mad libs come to life. You wander around what is basically a 2D open world mad libbing people's issues. Spawning a zombie to solve one puzzle might chase away other NPCs. Unless you add the adjective, friendly zombie. Its really the interactivity with the world that makes the game such silly fun. Did your zombie make a fire? Well have a firefighter put out that fire. Its a silly fun game that I can imagine would be great for kids. Simple controls that really thrive with a keyboard when you're typing things like 'pretty pink princess.'  There are good area settings too, everywhere from standard city areas like hospitals and a fire station, to more creative areas like Jurassic Park, a haunted house and a castle. Overall, the game is pretty easy. Easy enough that anyone can see it through to the end.

Scribblenauts is a fun puzzle game with inventive solutions to problems others are having. You (Maxwell) must save your sister by collecting starite which you collect by helping people. You can help others by using your magical notebook that alows you to create anything* that you can think of. Many of the solutions to these puzzles require some knowledge of many different topics and is a really fun way to test your memory bank and problem solving skills. I recommend this game if you want to be given a problem and must figure out the solution only using nouns and adjectives to modify those nouns. The pencil is mightier than the sword, especially if that pencil, paired with Maxwell's magical notebook, can create Excalibur.

The real lure of Scribblenauts is in its stories.  The flexibility and variety of available words mean you can conjure up just about anything you can imagine.  And if the word isn't included, you can build the object yourself, or likely find it in the fantastic Steam Workshop library.  It all adds up to some pretty fantastic experiences.  Here's a few of my favorites:
I had to finish a painting to please a gnome.  I wrote "stinky dotted underpants."  He loved it.
A girl wanted something romantic.  I gave her "sparkly jealous vampire."  It did not end well.

Returning to the start of the level every time you screw up makes the game very repetitive. Part of the reason is the lack of music variety between levels. If you replay a level 20 times hearing the same bit of music and then move on the next level only to hear the same song, it gets more than a little monotonous.
Also, the game is much more difficult than I'd anticipated. When I purchased the game, I expected a sort of casual platformer, but it demands Guitar Hero like precision to progress beyond the first world.

I really wanted to like this game, but after playing three sessions across 2 hours, the game really started to drive my patience; and it's not because it's difficult, on the contrary I like difficulty in my games, but because it's tedious and repetitive.
You start off with one world with 12 levels. After going through 8 of them, you'll start growing tired of the lackluster visuals you'd see after countless deaths, and the uninspired pattern of (jump over tiny rock, jump over tiny rock, jump over tiny rock, jump over ledge) x 10. If there is challenge to be had in this, then it's not an interesting or visually appealing one. You'll also grow sick of the music, which has a 3 second electro synth loop with single piano notes that play whenever you jump, duck, etc. Just imagine playing the same level over and over again with that kind of music! Needless to say, it's irritating at best and loses it's charm after 10 minutes.
You'll then face certain levels like 1-11.
1-11 has the worst level design I have ever seen in gaming.
Hear me out here.
There are 8 similar rocks to jump over, then stairs, then 8 rocks, then a ledge, (then 3 rocks, then a ledge) x4, (then 8 similar roofs you need to duck from) x2, then more rocks. Each rock has average 2 seconds interval between them. This is about 15% percent of that level.
I guarentee that you will die countless times in that level, again not because of it's difficulty, but because it drags. For. So. Long.
This is an example of level design that favors replayability rather than variety. Basically, this is f*cking Flappy Bird.
Just get yourselves Runner 2 instead. It has great visuals that will keep you interested, and level design more complex and diverse then just straight rows of rocks and ledges.As for this, if you got it in a bundle, knock yourselves out to the torture. Otherwise, avoid this if you don't want your time and patience wasted.

As stupid as this sounds, LEGO Worlds is THE Lego game.  It is like having every single piece of Lego ever created right in the palm of your hand.  You are always mere clicks away from building castles, cottages and Wild West Saloons, as well as having the ability to build something one single Lego brick at a time - Which will take a lot of time and dedication.
In the beginning you will be able to randomly generate a world that you would like to play in.  My world had a small forest that was home to cavemen and cavewomen, a desert biome that housed warlocks and vampires and one corner of the world was dark, it looked evil and was spewing lava. Once you have generated your own personal world, you will be able to skydive in, Just Cause style and just play with Lego.
I was running around and constantly finding new and exciting things.  I came across horses, sheep, dogs, vampires, cavemen and women, skeletons, cars, bulldozers, boats, a swimming pool, snowmen, etc.  From the short time I have spent in the game, there is a lot here already for a Early Access title.
The world renders every single individual lego brick.  That means, if you use the tools that the game gives you to edit the terrain as you see fit, you will find more lego bricks.  Take away a huge chunk of the world?  You will still find every single individual lego brick has been rendered underneath.  Unfortunately, this may be wear I began to have my only performance issue - I have experienced some pretty bad framerate issues, even when trying to mess around with the settings and lower quality (My PC should be able to handle this game at the highest anyway).  However, I give LEGO Worlds the benefit of the doubt as it has just released and is still in Early Access.
One other weird issue: Pressing 'S' when In a vehicle does not put the vehicle in to reverse, the vehicle instead just goes in a circle until it is facing the opposite direction that it was before.  I suggest this is changed to the 'S' key reversing a vehicle. EDIT: THIS SEEMS TO ONLY BE WITH THE BULLDOZER VEHICLE.
Nice audio with soothing music and fluid game animations are present.  You can really tell that LEGO Worlds has high production values and that TT and Warner Brothers are really backing this title.
I believe that if this game gets the love and attention that it deserves, it could truly be a fantastic game.  With updates, patches and more content this could be great.  The game is fun right now with a lot to do, but more content in this type of game never goes to waste.
I would also love to see some sort of survival mode - For example, like Minecraft.  Something where the player has to collect materials and resources to build shelter, mining tools, etc.  As well as harvesting food or something like that.  I believe that a survival mode along with this current creative, free roam mode that is in the game just now, would be incredible.
If you enjoy sandbox games like Minecraft and of course Lego and also like to be creative and build your own world with it's own buildings and communities - You may have a great time with LEGO Worlds.

A solid FPS game, great campaign, funny-themed zombies mode, and your average annual multiplayer mode brought by yours truly Infinity Ward.
I don't know why many people hate this game. The campaign is superb. I wish E3N (Ethan) can be more "robot" like BT from Titanfall 2. E3N is just like a human but with a robot shell, so I can't sympathize more with him.
A game with good cinematics, its like watching an action packed movie by Michael Bay.
Watch how Kit "Snow" Harrington pulling strings behind the scenes, making you look at how all of  your achievements from the start is taken from you, slowly and painfuly. It almost made me cry when the roll credits came in, and listening to all of the fallen teammates last words.
Cool side missions, not that long and it's not really repetitive. The air combat system is one of the most coolest things of this game. It will keep you on the edge of your seat for a good amount of time.
"When you wanted to save something, you need to sacrifice something more in return" --That's what I learned from playing the campaign.  Compared to the COD:WWII which campaign feels a little bland and rushed, this one is much better in general.
I can't really tell much for the multiplayer mode. It is okay, the weapons is not really that powerful. I just use the stock weapon fighting all the guys with those microtranscations thingy and still win somehow, but not all the time.
It is somewhat like Titanfall 2, I recommend playing that over this if you like multiplayer, it has more "destruction" than this game.
Zombies? Well its a good adition to the game, but I'm planning to get COD:Blops3 if COD:WWII doesn't bring better additional zombie content.
Worth the money? I think so, I bought the legacy edition on 60% off the original price at my local store on Black Friday.  I don't really recommend getting the DLC and other microtransaction stuffs, as you will better of buying other games at that price.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of the most beautiful games I've played in a long time. And I don't just mean visually so; it is challenging and exhilarating in ways that provide intensely gratifying rewards merely from the experience of the gameplay itself, and in a time when far too many games make us trudge through various frustrations to be rewarded with some pretty cinematic or a tool that lets us trudge through slightly-more-difficult frustrations, this virtue gains even more significance.
That alone would be enough to make it beautiful in my eyes, but it takes another step. Ori and the Blind Forest follows in the spiritual footsteps of Super Mario Brothers and Metroid, channeling the energy granted by a gorgeous world where the experience of each region is entirely unique and feels like its own game. That energy is conveyed along with glorious pacing, granting new, amazing abilities that center around mobility and traversing terrain. This means that the Metroid-esque backtracking is made all the more entertaining as you approach old ground with an invigorating and fresh prowess.
Though it is perhaps unfair to Ori to say that it merely follows these iconic franchises -- rather, it blazes a fantastic new trail in the same direction with its beauty and execution, not merely pandering to my nostalgia, but exceeding it in ways I never thought possible. I am both thoroughly impressed and deeply moved.
TL;DR -- Ori and the Blind Forest is amazing and you should play it.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a real treat. Perhaps the most striking thing about this game at first glance is the presentation. It is gorgeous, like a painting in motion. Ori and the other characters move very fluidly, and the visual effects, from the various explosions of sparks to the projectiles, are striking. The music is dramatic and moving, giving the game the feel of a high-quality animated film. The plot, as simple and sparse as it is, helps to keep you moving to restore the forest.
If you're worried that Ori is all style and no substance, fear not - there's plenty of challenging platforming to be had here. This is a Metroidvania, so you'll gain your traversal abilities as you progress through the game. By the end of the game, you'll be tasked with bouncing off walls, enemies, and projectiles through cramped areas where spikes and lava surround you on every side. Mercifully, you have the ability to create a checkpoint on any solid ground, so if there's a section you're having trouble with, you don't have to replay long stretches of the game just to get another shot at it. Just remember to actually use the ability - I know I've lost significant progress a few times because I forgot.
In short, Ori and the Blind Forest is an incredible product in every aspect. It hits it home with the presentation, and it'll put your platforming skills to the test. If you like beautiful games with challenging gameplay, this comes highly recommended.

An improvement over the original in every way. If you have any interest in strategy or fantasy, let alone Warhammer you owe it to yourself to give Mortal Empires a try (assuming of course you have several extra dollarydoos burning a hole in your pocket).
The Eye of the Vortex campaign can't be overlooked either, it has a very different dynamic to the typical conquest-focused sandbox gameplay you'd expect from a Total War game. I only wish that for Mortal Empires the Old World races were given the same amount of support the new ones received, especially unique start positions for legendary lords (I love the Empire's army roster and HATE their start position, was sincerely hoping for something different).
A final piece of advice, I'd strongly encourage installing this game on an SSD if at all possible. Loading the campaign map in the first game could take upwards of 7 minutes (I timed it) until I purchased an SSD specifically for the upcoming release of this game, which reduced load times to around 35 seconds. With the Mortal Empires map being nearly twice the size of the Old World from the first game, I shudder to imagine trying to load it on a regular HDD.

Oh, dear lord, what a game. I was really excited for this one, and rightly so. The visuals are beautiful without being too rough on the hardware, the music is incredible, the story is gut-wrenching and touching, and it deserves every penny it makes. It did feel a bit short (I finished it 100% in about eight hours; my play time is a bit off because of idling), but for twenty bucks it's worth the cost.
I do have a few gripes. This is a difficult game. I like it that way, but some may not. It's fair, but it can get a bit frustrating. Sometimes the foreground gets in the way of the action and enemies and projectiles can be obstructed by the scenery. The world is fairly large, so some kind of fast-travel system would be nice. Am I nitpicking? I'm nitpicking.
All in all a wonderful little project. If this game were full-price, I would tell you to wait for a sale, but for $20, it's a steal. If you like fast-paced, skillful platformers, this will make an excellent addition to your library.

Lets see if I can't discribe this game in four words...dull, dull, dull, dull, dull, dull, dull, dull, heart pounding fun, dull, dull, dull, dull.
Huge open world that might as well be the surface of the moon for all the content it lacks. Wonderful graphics when it comes to the sailing ships and ocean content. On the flip side, its like playing a DOS game whenever you are in port. A complete lack of a texural old world feel. Almost as if the developers said screw it. The developers are thin skined and vindictive. As long as you kiss their rears everything will be fine, but question their glaring inability to hit deadlines or choices and watch out.
This game was highjacked by a player base that wanted realism at the price of playability. At every turn they chose making it duller over making it playable. Open world speeded would have helped...nope. Quick transports to your other ports as apposed to a 45 minute sail...nope. This group likes staring at the stern of a ship for hours on end. If you yearn for the feeling of sailing for long unbroken expanses of time through a barron world, then brother this is your game.

This game is easily one of the best things I've ever downloaded.
That may sound like a bit of an exaggeration, and it very well could be in some regards, but this is a game that I honestly feel left a lasting impact on me in a way that very few other games ever have. Let me cover what possible few faults anyone could have with this game, just to get them out of the way before I move on. Yes, this game is short. A full playthrough will clock in at roughly 5 hours. However, this isn't a complaint, as that's all the time the game needs. It doesn't feel too long and drawn out, but it doesn't feel rushed either. Yes, this is an RPG maker game, and while it's graphics and gameplay aren't exactly ground-breaking, it still does more than enough to accomplish what the game sets out to do. So, keeping that in mind, what is it that To The Moon sets out to do? The short answer would be, "to tell a story", but honestly, that small explanation wouldn't do justice to the world... no, worlds, this game creates.
To The Moon Primarily focuses on Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts, a pair of scientists who work for a company known as Sigmund Corp, out on their daily routine, which usually consists of them being called to the homes of people who are on their deathbed. The people who call them do so because they have a final wish that time won't grant them. Using specialized machines developed by Sigmund Corp, Eva and Neil manipulate their clients' memories so that they can relieve there lives from the beginning inside their own minds, only with a few changes. After giving them a chance to achieve the dreams they couldn't in their real lives, the patients pass on, presumably happier than they would have been otherwise.
On this particular day, Eva and Neil visit the home of a dying elderly man by the name of Johnny. Already comatose and only slated to live for another day or two in his cliff-side manor, the doctors arrive and are greeted by his caretaker, Lily. Upon meeting with the comatose Johnny and his at-home physician, they find out that Johnny's last wish was "to go to the moon", but for some odd reason, he couldn't remember why. After this, Neil and Eva enter Johnny's memories through the machine and go through his life in reverse, looking through his memories one at a time and trying to find where his desire to go to the moon originated from so that they could alter a memory from his far past and change his perceived future. What follows is, bar none, one of the deepest, most emotionally charged stories I've ever encountered, and I don't just mean that in the sense of stories in games. This is easily one of the best short stories I've ever come across in any medium. Despite the game's short run time, its narrative gave me more surprises, twists, and turns than I'd ever expect from such a simple looking game. Despite its overall minimal presentation, the story and characters carry this game from start to end, and they do it in the best way possible.
While we're on the subject, let's talk about the characters; specifically Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts. Eva is the clear straight man of the dynamic duo, usually trying to focus on the job at hand and taking a few things too seriously, while Neil acts as the primary comic relief character, constantly spouting nonsense, doing potentially life-threatening things due to a lack of perspective or tact, or breaking the fourth wall with references to other video games and pop-culture (seriously, the amount of references he makes is honestly a little jarring... though I kinda liked it... Don't judge me.) Throughout the game, you get a sense that these two have worked together for a long period of time, constantly giving each other a hard time and poking fun at one another's flaws and insecurities. While some of it might come off as mean spirited, you can really tell they have a deeper bond as the game progresses, not just as co-workers, but as partners and friends. Through small bits of swapped dialog here and there, you get an idea of how these two met, came to work together, and even a few bits about their pasts and presents that the other may not even be aware of. But in the end, all of those hints really are just hints, as very little is said out-right about them. While that could easily be a complaint for some, I honestly didn't mind it, as the game's main focus isn't really on them anyway. Its on Johnny... and this is where I knew I'd have trouble writing this review. Johnny, as a character, is so well written that I want to give any and every detail that I can about him, but as it stands... I really can't say anything about him at all. You see, because he's already in a coma by the time Eva and Neil arrive, Johnny's character, personality, and history are all essentially revealed by playing the game, and while I may want to go into more detail about him and other characters from his past, I simply can't for fear of spoiling major plot points in the game. So, I'm afraid the best I can put here is this: I really like Johnny. He's an interesting guy with an interesting past, and he truly is what makes this game as amazing as it is.
Then there's the gameplay, which is honestly the game's biggest weakness. It works a lot like most classic point and click games. in order to progress to the next stage, you'll have to find and touch 5 items, and then use them to unlock a main item. Once that item is unlocked, you will have to solve a puzzle in order to use it to progress to the next memory (And, sadly, no. The puzzles don't get very challenging). Rinse and repeat. While maybe a bit too simplistic, I honestly think the narrative pay-off does make the monotony worth it. you can also pick up and keep certain items, which usually come with small bits of info, references to earlier sections, or funny joke descriptions. Simple, yes, but it is still fun.
As far as the presentation is concerned, well... it is what it is. Like I said, it's an RPG Maker game, meaning the simple 16-bit visuals don't really reflect the deeper tones of the story. However, where that might be the downfall of other story-heavy games, I think it works to this game's advantage. Because the graphics and characters are simple, it leaves you to rely a bit more on the story to keep your interest and get a better idea of who they are. Now, don't take that the wrong way. The character designs are very well done and unique, ensuring you can relate anyone's style of dialog to a specific face. Additionally, the set designs were both functional and beautiful, serving the purposes of the game while still being easy on the eyes. The amount of detail put into the settings really show the time and effort the developer put into making this game's visuals. They are simple in style, but very complex in design. And where would the presentation be without a soundtrack... in this game, non-existent, because the entire soundtrack was composed by the game's creator, Kan Gao (Save the theme track of "Everything's Alright" by Laura Shigihara), and it honestly shows, as the compositions are amazingly well done and really help prod out the emotions this game already pulls from you. Regardless of my opinions on the game itself, I highly recommend downloading the Soundtrack.
So, yeah... I freaking love this game (As if it wasn't obvious by now). The Story is beautifully crafted and easy to get drawn into, and the characters are all amazingly written and believable with real personalities and character traits that will make you want to learn everything about them that you possibly can. The visuals, while simple, are clean, crisp, and incredibly detailed and colorful, and they more than hold up the underlying themes of the game. For 10$ (and usually on sale), I honestly don't think you could do much better than To The Moon. Highly Recommended and TK Approved!
Also, I recommend playing the game in one sitting to get the full effect. Have fun.

I'm not gonna lie - this game is a lot better than everyone makes it out to be. While yes, it may be another future-set FPS, and yet another Call of Duty installment, this game does a lot right. First, Infinite Warfare refines the implementation of the movement mechanics introduced in Advanced Warfare and expanded in Black Ops III (wall-running, thruster jumps, etc). Compared to the previous year's installment, it definitely makes great strides in fixing the major problems involved - for example, Infinite Warfare provides a "Tactical Mode" in multiplayer, meaning that the updated movement mechanics are disabled - the map plays like it would in Black Ops II or any games before that. However, Tactical Mode doesn't need to restrict the playable map area or need to be played on only select maps - it works perfectly on all maps, as if to prove that it doesn't need the updated movement mechanics to be playable, unlike Black Ops III. Second, Infinite Warfare also introduces some very interesting concepts - among those being outer space-based gameplay. When I say that, I don't mean something like Mass Effect, where you fight aboard a spaceship. I mean combat that utilizes the low-gravity environment that outer space provides, with accurate simulations of what movement, gunfire, and physics would be like in outer space. This is something that is rarely seen in other FPSs, and definitely not in the "3D" manner that Infinite Warfare constitutes of. This is not to say that Infinite Warfare doesn't have its flaws - there are some features I don't agree with, the biggest of these being the implementation of pay-to-win mechanics - but it certainly does correct quite a few of the mistakes that the previous Call of Duty installments - especially Call of Duty: Black Ops III - have made.
