Bad Rats is a revolutionary first person shooter that sets a new standard for this era of gaming. This is game published by Electronic Arts and is developed by Dice on the new Frostbite 4 engine to provide a superior graphic fidelity compared to other marvellous titles including Crisis 3. The story of the game takes place in the year 2035 when North Korea officially ends the cease fire for the Korean War and launches a series of surprise attacks on the United States of America and South Korea. North Korea launches an overwhelming amount of long range ballistic missiles towards major metropolitan areas in the United States which devastates the population and cripples the infrastructure of the government to be able to function properly to contain control of the United States. North Korea launches a full scale aerial campaign on Seoul with a relentless wave of troops pouring across the DMZ of North Korea and South Korea. China and the rebuilt Soviet Union organized by Vladimir Putin has been supplying North Korea with highly advanced military technology and expertise has secretly been supporting North Korea for a war since 2006! You play as a squad in the Navy Seals for the United States called “Bad Rats” Your objective is to assassinate all cats in the region of Asia to cut off all food supplies from the North Koreans and collapse the regime of Kim Jong Un. Using the destructible environments from the Frostbite 4 engine you must use the environment for a tactical advantage to exterminate all cats from Asia. Fan favourite maps return including Seige of Shainghai where you must collapse a skyscraper to kill all cats in the building. Facial scanning technology from LA Noire returns to add an extra layer of realism with realistic facial animation movements to add more emotion to the already immersive world. This is a highly addicting shooter that takes place in locations across the world from nuclear wasteland America to the glorious lands of North Korea. You have a massive arsenal of over 500 weapons to use with thousands of gadgets and gun camouflages. Bad Rats is integrated with the Steam Workshop which has created thousands of community maps and gun skins to be submitted into the game for future free DLCs called “Operations”. Each operation adds an extra layer of immersion into the game with a huge variety of community maps and skins to be added to expand the already masterpiece of a game. Bad rats is a very skill based shooter and requires extensive training to truly shine in multiplier. Bad Rats is the only first person shooter on the market to add a innovative competitive mode with ranks to determine your skill level. In multiplayer there are 2 teams. Counter Cats and Cats. The counter cats must plant a bomb on one of the two locations on the map to kill the population of cats in the area. The cats must prevent the counter cats or the “bad rats” from planting the bomb by either killing all the Counter Cats or defusing the bomb to save the population of cats in the premise.Bad Rats is a highly addicting shooter that any seasonal gamer should try out but I assume you already have! Bad Rats global sales have exceeded 1 billion on the first day outselling the Call of Duty franchise. It is very rare to see game a game this flawless since the release of Half Life 2. If you like first person shooter games you already own bad rats, if you don't you are missing out on one of the most brilliant game of this century.

The party emerged from the German nationalist, racist, and populist Freikorps paramilitary culture, which fought against the communist uprisings in post-World War I Germany.[6] The party was created as a means to draw workers away from communism and into völkisch nationalism.[7] Initially, Nazi political strategy focused on anti-big business, anti-bourgeois, and anti-capitalist rhetoric, although such aspects were later downplayed in order to gain the support of industrial entities, and in the 1930s the party's focus shifted to anti-Semitic and anti-Marxist themes.[8]
Pseudo-scientific racism theories were central to Nazism. The Nazis propagated the idea of a "people's community" (Volksgemeinschaft). Their aim was to unite "racially desirable" Germans as national comrades, while excluding those deemed either to be political dissidents, physically or intellectually inferior, or of a foreign race (Fremdvölkische).[9] The Nazis sought to improve the stock of the Germanic people through racial purity and eugenics, broad social welfare programs, and a collective subordination of individual rights, which could be sacrificed for the good of the state and the "Aryan master race". To maintain the supposed purity and strength of the Aryan race, the Nazis sought to exterminate Jews, Romani, and Poles along with the vast majority of other Slavs, and the physically and mentally handicapped. They imposed exclusionary segregation on homosexuals, Africans, Jehovah's Witnesses, and political opponents.[10] The persecution reached its climax when the party-controlled German state organized the systematic murder of approximately six million Jews and five million people from the other targeted groups, in what has become known as the Holocaust.
The party's leader since 1921, Adolf Hitler, was appointed Chancellor of Germany by President Paul von Hindenburg on 30 January 1933. Hitler rapidly established a totalitarian regime[11][12][13][14] known as the Third Reich. Following the defeat of the Third Reich at the conclusion of World War II in Europe, the party was "declared to be illegal" by the Allied powers,[15] who carried out denazification in the years after the war.

-Disable Visual Themes
AND
-Disable Desktop Composition.
then click APPLY

Awful. A true insult to the Unreal series.
Unreal and Unreal Tournament are my two favourite FPS's of all time, Unreal offers a beautiful fast paced single player adventure with Awesome Multiplayer and Unreal Tournament IS Awesome Multiplayer. Unreal 2 is Neither.
This game has no reason bearing the name 'Unreal'. The ONLY connections to the previous games are a few similar weapons and the incredibly forced appearance of the Skaarj. That's it. The only other reason it has the name is because it uses the Unreal Engine, which is absolutely stupid, it would make as much sense calling XIII Unreal 3 or Dishonored Unreal 4!
Storywise the game offers nothing, you play as a generic Space Marine whose role is to fly around the universe with his Stripper/Captain, an engineer who was probably homeless before this job and the Unreal universes version of Jar Jar Binks. None of whom have much in the way of personality, general likability or interest.
Weapons in a Nutshell: The Dispersion Pistol from the first game, Except it can't be upgraded and is never used. A pistol which delivers a lot of damage but has low ammo, rarely used. A generic Assault Rifle (how creative). A shotgun that fires both regular rounds and fire rounds (kinda cool). A Flamethrower that can also fire flammable liquid and then be ignited (or you could just set the target of fire initially showoff). A Rocket launcher. A Sniper Rifle. A Gun that has interchangable rounds, yet you rarely find a use for each individual round, ultimately creating a mess of a weapon, 2 alien laser guns. A gun that shoots spiders (less coll than you would think). And a Black Hole Launcher that is only used in the last level.
There is an Escort mission in this game, and the guy you have to escort makes Natalya from Goldeneye seem like Elizabeth from Bioshock Infinite. He is such an annoying whiny ♥♥♥♥♥ and you just want to kill him, but killing the guy results in a game over. To rub it in your face, when you beat that level there is a cutscene where Blandy McSpace-Awesome is told to kill him, and he refuses, you don't even get a choice, you just watch as the game gives you the finger.
Levels are slow and empty, they usually contain few enemies, the game appears to be playing like Half-Life yet the enemies are all laid out like Splinter Cell, this is a Bad Thing. There is no exploration either, one of the things that made the first game so good was that you had to explore to survive, you found something new each time you played, this game does not, and as such has no replay value.
The Biggest sin of the game is that IT IS SOOOOOO SSLLLOOOOOW
Your character moves like he is wearing Lead Armour and there are sections of the game that make you roam your ship just to talk initiate random chatter with people you don't care about, This coming from a series famous for it's fast action gameplay. Oh and the game is 6 HOURS LONG! The fact you move to slow feels like a cheap way to artificially lengthen the game.
To Spoil the ending (Because this is one of the worst games I have ever played); Your Crew gets killed (I think you are supposed to care) and you are then sent to see some alien mutate into an uncontrollable beast, This is the Final boss btw. When you kill it you get the aforementioned BFG Black Hole gun and you kill a bunch of identical and now inferior mutants, against an artificial timer as the ship heads to a sun. Oh and turns out some random guy you forgot about betrayed you and you kill him in a cutscene. Offscreen. You don't even get to see the impact. And you escape.
Honestly one of the Worst FPS games ever, and it's a shame because the developers clearly put more effort into the art design than the actual game. Yes, despite everything I've said the sole positive feature is that the game looks REALLY good. But other than that there is NOTHING. Oh and there is no Multiplayer either, yes, the series that managed to redefine multiplayer experience has a game with none at all. Perhaps if it an alternate name then perhaps it could jsut be forgotten about as a Generic FPS, but the fact it shares the name with two of my favourite games is insulting.
Don't buy this. Play Unreal or Unreal Tournament instead.
FINAL VERDICT: Garbage.

This is one of the best multiplayer co-op RPGs I have ever played.  That co-op element is going to be the focus of my review.
The game follows the fairly standard fantasy RPG plotlines.  The co-op aspect works very well with the story in this game, in that it actually gives both the players some semblance of input into the story.  Other games either lock up one player to watch the host make all the choices, clone one player or make them a tagalong with no input, or sometimes dont even give the second player any view of the story action at all.  D:OS gives both players input in the story in the form of personality perk effects that are decided on each player's dialogue responses to the events that occur in game.  Both players may (but are not forced to) view conversations that occur.  This lets each player role-play, run around town and find their own quests or do shopping while another works on dialogue or participate if they like, and the input both players give is also meaningful to the gameplay instead of merely flavor.  If ever a major gameplay decision must be made and the players disagree, there is a rock paper scissors 'diplomacy' battle.  This works pretty well for friends playing coop, and really gives a much better co-op experience.
Combat is turn based, and while it doesn't explicitly benefit or change from it being a co-op game it does let both players strategize together.  The combat has a fair amount of interesting terrain effects and positioning-relevant abilities, so working together with a friend to overcome fights can be pretty fun.  Mis-used abilities lead to laughs, and there's a good amount of variety in abilities that both players can feel like they can pick a role they like and fill it.  If there is any complaint here it is that individual abilites dont improve, they only scale with player stats, and thus can sometimes feel a bit underwhelming as they don't always feel exceptionally good until later in the game.  Some skills also feel underwhelming, as diplomacy never really has a big impact on the story.  Crafting can create some neat items, but the UI could be cleaned up and managed better and require less head-against-wall discovery of recipe, especially since some crafting recipes are also underwhelming.
The game ran well, with crashes occuring only rarely.  I don't recall what framerates I had, but I can't recall the game ever looking poor or running poor because of my higher settings.  Occasionally abilities that list over 100% success rates would fail for no understandable reason (rogue ability that turns the character invisible for a few turns, for instance), and sometimes minute positioning in combat could lead to accidental moves wasting action points, but these gameplay gripes are minor and I never was so frustrated as to lessen my experience with the game.  The story, while perhaps a bit trite, is still very passable.  Full voice acting for both characters and NPCs really helps as well and was robust.
A mostly-full clear co-op playthough (of every side area and quest we could find) ran about 75 hours, with some extra hours on my part spent solo fiddling with crafting and the like.  It was overall a very fun experience.  You don't see many good co-op games these days, and this is one of the better ones.

As for the game's factions, i've finished my campaign as High Elves and the character models, colors, small intricate details are well taken care of. This faction has a particular feel of being the guardians of the Vortex. Ulthuan is well designed. Tyrion and Teclis are great characters. The game has significant improvements and streamlining than the first game, you just hover over the events and a scroll will open to inform about the event. Armies now get regular traits for exuding a particular behavior, like marching, recruiting a lot, or defeating a particular faction a lot gives you additional buffs.
To think that CA developed this game in just over a year after the first game, i'd say it's a well done game. Great work CA.

Igra sa kojom Skullgirls deli najviše sličnosti je Marvel vs Capcom 3, praktično ukoliko ste imali prilike da igrate Capcomovu VS igru, znate da igrate i Skullgirls. S obzirom da je igra krcata potezima i specifičnim terminima, prisutan je i vrlo iscrpni tutorial mod, na žalost u vidu ‘’zidova’’ teksta.
Ipak, ono što očigledno dominira igrom je njena specifična prezentacija, u stilu animacija iz 40-ih godina prošlog veka propraćena džez soundtrackom, sa likovima koji kao da su izašli iz Max Fleischer crtaća. Trenutno u igri postoji samo devet likova ali svaki ima specifični stil borbe i poteze tako da nema ‘’deset Ryuovih klonova”. Autori su najavili još četiri borca, ali kada ih možemo očekivati kao ni da li će i koliko biti naplaćeni se još ne zna (prvi DLC lik, Squigly, je besplatna do kraja novembra).
Igru bije glas da pokušava da stvori kontroverzu gotovo perverznim prikazom određenih likova, naročito Valentine (tipični kliše seksi medicinske sestre). Neosporno je da ovakav dizajn likova škodi ugledu igre koja mainstream publici već izgleda uvrnuto ali ovo nije ni prvi ni poslednji put da su cure u video igri prikazane kako jesu. Mnogo bitniji problem igre je što često dolazi do slabe preglednosti, da li zbog opšteg haosa koji nastaje korišćenjem nekih specijalnih poteza ili čudnim dizajnom nekih likova.
Fanovima borilačkih igara neće biti potrebna posebna preporuka da nabave Skullgirls, pre svega zbog drastično niže cene u odnosu na konkurentne igre. U pitanju je naslov unikatnog izgleda i,mada ne potpuno originalne mehanike, zanimljivo osveženje u žanru.

Still, the game pack some tight mechanics and very impressive fights. Seeing as it's one of the cheapest fighting games on market, purchasing Skullgirls is a no-brainer for most serious fighting game enthusiast and competetive players.

END UPDATE
I am not going to review the game itself, as it's far too early for this, but I'm going to review how the "Early Access" of this game is being handled.
It clearly states on Early Acces that you can get involved with this game as it develops. This couldn't be further from the truth. Every major decision is already set in stone, pretermined by polls from early backers. There is pretty much no Developer interaction - the only known Developer admin is hardly posting at all on either the Steam or the official forum.
There is no dialogue about future game mechanic changes. Giant threads of people remarkably unhappy about design decisions made in the past being broken (such as pirates not being a nation like the other 7 but very different from them) are just growing without any official word being taken into account. If a poll like the pirate mechanics vote has the overwhelming majority of 71% against pirates capturing ports, and hundreds of replies in it, it really can't be without a dev response at all.
There was a response, but you had to watch a certain twitch stream doing a Q&A session (not advertised on the forum) with an audience of 50 viewers. Not the way to do it.
There has been a single blog like post since the EA Launch six weeks ago, talking about upcoming features. One.
If you want information, you need to befriend moderators who are also close to the dev team, who will then feed you information that is generally kept secret so far - such as the very near economy wipe and the new economy system - e.g. Steel Sandwich on the official forum. I've received far more information that turned out to be true at this point from this hush hush source than I've received by following the developer announcement posts.
Another issue is that it is marketed as a sandbox, when that also isn't correct. There is one way to advance: sink enemy ships. Other gameplay mechanics might be in place, but they do not advance your character whatsoever. Also, they're designed in a way that you can't do them as long as you want, as you will run out of a finite, non-replenishable resource and have to wait for it to grow back - as if this was Farmville, not a full price game. Admin is also completely mute on this subject, making many economy players wonder if this game is even for them, despite it clearly being marketed as a sandbox.
This is not an Early Access game, this is basically a gofundme campaign where the developer asked for pre-purchases so he can keep developing the game that he wants. You're not paying to have your opinion heard about the game, you're not paying to help design it, you're paying to be an Alpha Tester for a game that is already finished on the whiteboard. I don't know whether that game will actually be good, because he's also pretty quiet on that subject.
I do not believe this to be in the spirit of Early Access, therefore I am not recommending it.
As to how that could change: Communication can't be a one way street. The developers need to actively engage the community. Information is key. Share your roadmap. We're left in the dark what's happening within the next four weeks at this point.

First off I want to say I know this is early access, and hopefully some of these things will be addressed in time. That said, let's get the bad stuff out of the way first;
No control/camera options!
I *think* this might be because this will be ported to consoles eventually. I say that because the messages "Press any button/key" and the option of turning on or off "Vibration". Now sure some people play PC games with gamepads, and that's great, but I hope this PC version of LEGO Worlds will get some options for how we play. An irritation so far for me is that the right mouse button is for looking as well as pointing (ie movement). So if you want to go straight but swing the camera to the right to look at something, you have to correct your movement by strafing or something similar. Another annoyance is how low the camera is to the ground, so you're looking at the horizon all the time rather than your immediate surroundings.
Intricate building with individual bricks is a bit clunky!
Again this may be because of the possible console like control scheme, but trying to build something is a bit more tedious than it should be. The interface for the brick selection and color selection aren't designed very well (scroll the mouse wheel to go through them, but that also zooms in your view, grr!). I prefer the dedicated building programs that exist more than this, even the Google Chrome LEGO builder. The low framerate doesn't help matters either, and I don't have all of the bells and whistles on maximum.
No way to affect the world without going in to build mode!
I really wish a had a shovel or something that just dug where I was standing. Or maybe even dig with my hands, or *something* rather than nothing at all. To alter the landscape you have to go in to one of the build modes, and either remove bricks one at a time via clicking, or delete huge chunks at a time in a somewhat clunky interface (that interface again!).
This is *not* like Minecraft!
I mentioned MC again because, if you're like me, you might have been hoping that this was a LEGO version of Minecraft. It isn't, so get that out of your head right now. What's more like is an open world, no story mode TT game. You explore and if you run in to a NPC you haven't collected yet, you unlock them for purchase. Ditto for vehicles, little models (ie plants, various decorative objects, etc.). You get studs for destroying stuff, and use those studs to permanently buy one of the things you've unlocked. You also get studs for interacting with one of the supplied builds (a lovely little home with a pool and BBQ). These studs come pretty freely, so I never felt low on 'money', however all this paints a somewhat different picture than what Minecraft does; there's a lot more video game here than just building.
Now on to the good stuff shall we?
Genuine fun!
I actually enjoyed exploring the different landscapes, even if they were somewhat barren for now. I had a rush of glee when I found a NPC I hadn't encountered yet and quickly harvested their sweet parts for myself. I enjoyed riding the dragon and blowing up craters in the mountains. I enjoyed mowing the lawn (aforementioned pre built house object), and giggled when I saw what it did. I liked finding the big chests that yielded me a hand held item (though the gun mechanic of shooting is a little odd for now). Basically there is fun to be had here, and it should only get better.
Beautiful views!
Both the theme areas as well as the character models themselves look wonderful. Luckily we have ambient occlusion already for us (no need to fake it for nice screenshots like MC!) as well as gorgeous lighting effects. Everything looks amazing and really sucks you in to the world.
Ok now on to the stuff that isn't even in the game and my personal opinion/hopes on what happens, you can skip this bit if you want.
Multiplayer?
Unfortunately it doesn't *seem* like this will be like MC again. There won't be any 64 players joined here, I'd be very surprised. There isn't even (unless I'm blind and/or not smart enough) chatting of any kind yet, but as I said I could be wrong. The game certainly didn't prompt me to say hello or anything like that, and I couldn't check the control scheme. There was an option to 'search for worlds', though I didn't look in to it. I fear it might just be something similar to Little Big Planet, where players upload their world to the server and let other people play *in* it, rather than *with* other people. And since multiplayer was technically at the bottom of the list of 'features to add', I'm worried it'll just be basically co-op. Certainly not the social juggernaut that MC had become even in beta, LEGO Worlds multiplayer seems like a footnote rather than core feature of the game.
I guess that's actually the only bit I'm not certain about. I hope we can get some good multiplayer, but we'll see!

Set in the vast and deep Warhammer Universe, you take role of Ultramarines Captain Titus - extremely well voiced by Mark Strong - and are immediately sprung into a war on global scale when Orcs attack a planet. Which planet? No need to know since it matters not. As an Ultramarine you are not supposed to "ask question", let alone "question orders". Not that it would change much to be honest as I couldn't tell you the name of the planet if I wanted. Anyway, soon you learn that scientists have managed to encapsulate the mythical warp energy and all kinds of monsters are now throwing their bodies like blood-filled waterbaloons to secure this for their respective faction.
A deep, long-standing lore as Warhammer's would surely put many devs in a peril to cram at least the important parts into a game one would think. Unless you don't even try. Which is the case here. You won't hear where you come from, why you fight, who the factions are or the characters. Nothing. But then again, as an Ultramarine you ought to fight for the Machine Gods (whoever them might be). Don't ask questions, there is only
.
It is a third-person-shooter with a very hefty dose of melee combat thrown in for good measure. It is in no way an afterthought though. In fact many times you will realize that brawling your way out of combat is the better choice. Very good that the variety in melee weapons is formidably well as to classic weaponry. Speaking of, you start with only a pistol and add a rifle shortly to your arsenal. During the ~7 hours you'll play the campaign there will be frequent and steady additions to it. At the half-way point even glorious energy-type guns. These especially feel fittingly powerful against the huge hordes of orcs rushing at you during the constant barrage of firefights. Make no mistake, this game is about shooting things and it does not stop until the credits keep rolling. It is refreshing to feel extremely overpowered at times. Movement shows this too as you feel like a walking tank with humongous armor. A tad slow but it conveys the feel of heaviness nicely to the player.
One very clever mechanic about combat is melee as mentioned before. Apart from just being a very powerful type of attack, it also serves as the only way to heal yourself - which might sound weird at first. It works like this. After putting your an enemy into a staggered state you can kill it with a gratuitous finishing move and regain a good portion of your health-points back. It is a refreshing mechanic which leads to an extremely offensive playstyle. Don't come into this when you like planning and cover. It's full frontal combat. Set-pieces and sweet jet-pack sections give you nice amount of variety as well.
Space Marines is a good game with very satisfying combat mechanics. To my disappointment did the devs not put any priority whatsoever into showcasing the deep Warhammer lore. A big shame as this lack of knowledge makes you care significantly less about characters and events unfolding. Why would I care about the machine gods, the imperium, the codex when I never get to learn more about them? There is huge potential with the lore but it was wasted here sadly. The story as well looses importance with this. A very rudimentary construct keeping me go from level 1 to level 2 at best. In the end I only wanted to get to the next area to bash some orcs head. So far, from what I've played, this is a really fun game. The combat is smooth and responsive, melee combat is fun as hell, and it isn't very taxing on your system at all. There's only a few problems I have with the game. First, it has pretty much no graphical settings. The game looks pretty good already, but I would have liked a more robust graphical settings option. Second is the lack of weapons. You get a pistol, an assault rifle, a sniper rifle, and a grenade launcher. There might be more later in the game, but there is only four weapon slots that I can see, so I doubt it. The last gripe I have with it, is that they give you cool things, just to take them away like 5 minutes later. I got this really cool jetpack, got to use it for like two areas, then lost it. So the bad parts of the game in my opinion are very small, and don't detract from the overall fun you'll have with this game. Oh, the game is pretty damn easy too. There's a health regen system in the game that allows you to regenerate health by executing enemies, and it's really easy to do. Also, there's ammo caches all over the place, so you never have to worry about running out of ammo or grenades. So I recommend setting the difficulty pretty high if you want a challenge. Overall, pretty good game. Not really worth the $30 it's at right now, but I'd say it's deffinately worth around $20. So if you're interested, wait for it to on sale.

I personally was thoroughly surprised by how much I enjoyed
. There is actually a decent sci-fi narrative in there; albeit one that is a bit cliché. And the characters actually have personalities that manage to be mildly interesting. Mix that in with classic
FPS gameplay and you get a pretty enjoyable experience.
The narrative will escort you from mission to mission (level to level), as you explore various worlds in the vastness of space to accomplish your goals.  In between each mission you return to your spaceship where you can interact (mildly) with your crew and arrange your armament for the next mission.  Having conversations with your crew allows you to gather background information and expands on some of the lore aspects.  In this way, there are some parallels with the early
games.
The different missions will take you to diverse environments with various objectives, but the core gameplay doesn’t evolve much throughout the game. However you will be able to unlock new weapons and armaments as you progress, which allows you to keep things fresh as you finish up the campaign.
One main complaint with
is that the movement speed is much slower than in other
games. To be honest, it didn’t bother me that much. Luckily, if it does bother you, there is a way to increase the speed of the game using the console.
So it is true that
isn’t perfect, but I still really liked the overall experience quite a bit.  I think if you enjoy sci-fi FPS games with decent narratives, and need something new to play: this is a good game for you to consider.

This is one of the best multiplayer co-op RPGs I have ever played.  That co-op element is going to be the focus of my review.
The game follows the fairly standard fantasy RPG plotlines.  The co-op aspect works very well with the story in this game, in that it actually gives both the players some semblance of input into the story.  Other games either lock up one player to watch the host make all the choices, clone one player or make them a tagalong with no input, or sometimes dont even give the second player any view of the story action at all.  D:OS gives both players input in the story in the form of personality perk effects that are decided on each player's dialogue responses to the events that occur in game.  Both players may (but are not forced to) view conversations that occur.  This lets each player role-play, run around town and find their own quests or do shopping while another works on dialogue or participate if they like, and the input both players give is also meaningful to the gameplay instead of merely flavor.  If ever a major gameplay decision must be made and the players disagree, there is a rock paper scissors 'diplomacy' battle.  This works pretty well for friends playing coop, and really gives a much better co-op experience.
Combat is turn based, and while it doesn't explicitly benefit or change from it being a co-op game it does let both players strategize together.  The combat has a fair amount of interesting terrain effects and positioning-relevant abilities, so working together with a friend to overcome fights can be pretty fun.  Mis-used abilities lead to laughs, and there's a good amount of variety in abilities that both players can feel like they can pick a role they like and fill it.  If there is any complaint here it is that individual abilites dont improve, they only scale with player stats, and thus can sometimes feel a bit underwhelming as they don't always feel exceptionally good until later in the game.  Some skills also feel underwhelming, as diplomacy never really has a big impact on the story.  Crafting can create some neat items, but the UI could be cleaned up and managed better and require less head-against-wall discovery of recipe, especially since some crafting recipes are also underwhelming.
The game ran well, with crashes occuring only rarely.  I don't recall what framerates I had, but I can't recall the game ever looking poor or running poor because of my higher settings.  Occasionally abilities that list over 100% success rates would fail for no understandable reason (rogue ability that turns the character invisible for a few turns, for instance), and sometimes minute positioning in combat could lead to accidental moves wasting action points, but these gameplay gripes are minor and I never was so frustrated as to lessen my experience with the game.  The story, while perhaps a bit trite, is still very passable.  Full voice acting for both characters and NPCs really helps as well and was robust.
A mostly-full clear co-op playthough (of every side area and quest we could find) ran about 75 hours, with some extra hours on my part spent solo fiddling with crafting and the like.  It was overall a very fun experience.  You don't see many good co-op games these days, and this is one of the better ones.

This is one of the best RPG experiences I've had thus far. Very few games have made me want to play a second playthrough, and even fewer have made me want to begin a second playthrough immediately after finishing the first!
Firsty, Divinity is a co-op campaign-focused RPG. Many of its elements are enhanced by a co-op experience while still remaining perfectly enjoyable for the solo player. It rewards different approaches, and its conflict resolution system is not just limited to NPCs: players are encouraged to discuss and debate major decisions, even if it results in a charisma-based game of rock-paper-scissors to decide. The enemy and environment designs are beautiful, and enemies (including bosses) are loathe to force players into brute force combat of one type or antoher. The voice acting is excellent and the world is fleshed out well.
It has its flaws, sure. The music is limited and can get repetitive, there are still a number of bugs (especially for non-host players) that will force reloads or reconnects, and the UI makes it insanely easy to accidentally tresspass or steal things when you're simply trying to explore. The crafting system can occasionally prove too vague, forcing either cluttered inventories and constant experimentation or looking up guides online. And some quests have unclear objectives, forcing - yet again - either a guide-lookup or lots of experimentation. You can even bug out a quest or two if you're not careful.
But overall, I am happy to recommend this game and look forward to playing its sequel. If it's more of the same but with fewer bugs, I'll be more than happy.
Some spoiler-free tips, for those reading this far. First, read everything you can. There's a lot of lore and fluff, sure, but there's even more hints for complicated puzzles and quest objectives hidden about in parchments and books. Secondly, don't be worried about having more charisma than 5, and try having most of those points come from gear; it's effectively worthless after 5. Finally, learn how to use environmental effects and statuses! Even bosses aren't immune to all effects or hazards.
Have fun!

Now before you listen to people on certain forums crying that SKULLGIRLS IS♥♥♥♥♥♥or LOL GREEDY DEVS just listen.
Yes, Skullgirls borrows a lot from games like Marvel vs Capcom and guilty Gear- Airdashing long combos, stylish attacks, air dashing... list goes on. But think about this. It's an indie game that admittedly was funded in help by IndieGoGo (but with the big boom of crowd funding, almost everything is) and has amazing mechanics for a game like such. IPS prevents stupid infinite loops that can be abused (Looking at you UMvC3) and also has a great movelist for just about every character. Combine that with a cast of characters that are significantly differnt and each unique in their movelist, and you have the basis of a winning Fighting game. The animations are hand colored, animated, and drawn, so enjoy all the glorious beauty of the smooth as silk flow of the fights in HD.
The game has some flaws- For instance, some parts of the game still need work. Lobbies constantly break, there are a few matchmaking glitches here and there, and most of all, a new player can get matched against a professional in a heartbeat. The positives out weigh this for me though.
All in all If you like fighting games with Style, gorgeous animations, great combo system, high skill ceiling, and is easy to get into, this is for you. Sprinkle a little story and developers who care about the game like it's their child ontop, and it becomes even better.

This game is one of the smoothest Alphas I've played. What it occasionally lacks in content it makes up for in game mechanics. Naval combat is realistic, fair and most importanly skill based. The map is giant; it takes hours to sail from one end to the other (upwards of 10 hours I hear). Naval combat itself is the core of the game; there is not much to do other than fight NPCs or other players. There is a level progression system that allows you to unlock bigger and better ships (if you have the gold). This progression eventually leads to the possibility of having giant battleships that are rarely seen. A second part of the game is crafting which is relatively straightforward, but very rewarding as it leads to the ability to craft ships that have unique stats which you can sell or sail for yourself. And don't worry, if your hard earned ship is sunk due to pirates or another country's fleet attacking you, you get 4 more chances with that same ship before it is permanently gone. Lastly, one of my favorite mechanics is the ability to board and commandeer a ship, which at times can be an effective way to make gold.
Pros:
*Excellent/realistic naval combat
*Quite a large amount of ship customization
*A large variety of ships (with more to come)
*Very skill oriented game
*Has some nice ambience
Cons:
*Requires patience and time
*The UI has Alpha written all over it
*Skill gap may be overwhelming to some
*Sometimes you run out of things to do if you are tired of naval combat
Tons of potential and a lot of fun in its early state

Many ask now-a-days, "where have all the good [RPG] games gone, and where are all the [developer] gods? Where's that [Playable] Streetwise Hercules to fight the rising odds?", and ain't it all too true? Gone are the golden days of the old school RPG's that made the genre the gods of Olympus in the world of video games: Fallout, Neverwinter, Wasteland, all genre defining titles. Where have they gone? Well, they have been replaced with fast paced 3D, in your face, Action RPGs, that look pretty with their special effects and complex skill trees, but lack the depth of the, "choose your own adventure in an open world", style of PRG gameplay that everyone grew up on, and grew to love. Well, the wait is over!
Divinity seeks to place the genre back on Mt. Olympus with its phenomenal engineered throw back to the old school era of RPGs, but with its own, unique, "new school flavor"; all wrapped in a pretty bow - as in the interactable world and environment built around it. Dvinity plays just like the "oldies, but goodies", yet with a refreshing approach implementing new elements to modernize the dead genre while breathing new life into the RPG's of old.
Despite bridging the gaps by filling in the missing components of the early century Golden Age of "bird's eye view RPG's", Divinity reaches beyond the limitations of the earler "industry defining" releases in the open world RPG genre. Divinity offers an unpredented depth to character development by offering a plethora of archtypes, styles of play, and even so far as each character's personality through an AI setting to be available at release. The "AI" setting is your characters disposition, which I look forward to experiencing the impact it will have with NPC interactions, and the game play as a whole. Divinity makes the world around the player character come alive and cooexist with the player character's choices offering a synergy unlike what you have seen before in an open world, "choose your own adventure", RPG's.
Combat is of course turn based, and strategic to say the least; in many situations, survival is contingent on casting spells on the environment for special bonuses and effects against your combatants. Spells, certain weaponry - particularly arrows bought or crafted by Rangers - as well as skillsets also help the player navigate and negotiate dangerous environmental restrictions such as, poisonous areas, grounds scorched by fire, or frozen over by ice, and environmentally hastened, strengthened, and even weakened, enemies. Only by negating or taking advantage of these effects can your characters safely gain passage whether they are navigating through dangerous environments, or fighting certain combatants requiring the player to use thought and purpose to progress through the game.
You start with two fully customizable characters based on existing archetypes, or you can build their skill sets and spell pools to your own style of gameplay. During your travels you will be introduced to other companions who will join your crusade with their own personal disposition towards your actions and inactions with ongoing interactions with your player characters as the game progresses. Your chacters themselves will also interact through dialogue to support one another's choices or to contradict eachother using skills gained during gameplay through these interactions and their AI plays a role in their decisions.  Will they support your actions, take opposition, or will it lead them to despise everything about you and what you stand for as a person?
Divinity offers a deeply rich environment. The backstory is that the player characters are "Source Hunters", or investigators that quell threats of people using an evil form of necromancy magic called, the "Source". It all begins with the investigation into a murder at Cyseal, requiring the player character to interact with several NPC's to unravel the mystery until their investigation leads to fruition with answers to satisfy the residents of Cyseal.
Quests, in general, are multilayered requring the player to embrace and comtemplate their interactions with NPCs as they progress through the story of unravelling the mysteries to find the answers their quest-givers seek. These quests are not at arms length or fetch quests. Rather the quests contribute to the finality of the game and your cause as the protagonist. Most of them, even the side quests, represent a link in the chain of steps to achieve your ultimate goal of completing the game. This provides a sense of unity and singular purpose in discovering the solutions whereby what you decide to do in one quest may ultimately affect the results of another or multiple quest chains. This offers a very unique experience to RPG players both old and new. Players generally have to interact with most of the NPCs in order to decipher what needs to be done to complete each quest, while certain quests still maintain a simple and direct passage offering diversity. Once you have completed the quests in one area, they transition to the next area, and so on and so forth until you reach the finality of the game as the protagonist. Notwithstanding the many stages, quests feels organic and intuitive and whether they are substantive or minute, you feel a sense of accomplishment as you tally forth into the unknown.
To advance the experience further, Divinity includes crafting similar in scope and application from genre defining games like the Ultima series. You can craft an innumerable number of items, from clothing to weapons, potions to scrolls, magic items to non-magical items, all based on your crafting skills, the necessary components, the recipe books you have uncovered, and through the simple function of trial and error by mixing various ingredients to discover new compounds. The crafting component offers an entirely additional layer and value to the game that can keep you entertained for hours, if only to learn more combinations to create items, potions, weapons, and then twice over by mixing crafted items with crafted maigcal items to create magical properties within crafted items.
Divinity: Original Sin is truly the RPG borne from and infused with old school RPG DNA. If you are a purist when it comes to isometric RPG's, you will not be disappointed with the depth, novelty, and versatility of this game. Not only does the game offer a core storyline for you to playthrough, but additional tools to afford players to create their own environments, NPCs, characters and quests to upload to developer servers for others to play. These tools offer the level of depth that most online games with similar tools could only dream of providing to their player base.
You would probably expect that I would be wrapping up this review, but there's more. The game can be played single player. One of the more defining characteristics of this game is the opportunity to have one player character controlled by a second person. You can play with a friend and divide and conquer, performing whatever actions you choose free from the other player and all across the environment.
Your decisions do not weigh lightly in this game, but rather define the your experience through to the finality as well as how the world may interpret your actions for the better and for the worse. This is worth every cent if you are an RPG lover, and Divinity truly sets a new precedent and the bar high for all RPG titles released after its full publication.  The next iteration of this game will be released in the last quarter of 2016, so if isometric turn based RPGs shares a special place in your heart, buy the game now and lead your way into the sequel that is expected to be released later this year.

Game is extremely fun and interesting. Challenging puzzles, spell combos, the humorous writing all blends well. 10/10!

- Find out an NPC took a bribe that led to a Bad Thing happening
- Tell him he should turn the money in
- He beats me at paper scissors rock and refuses
- Try to pick the money from his pocket and turn it in myself
- He catches me and attacks me
- Knock him on his♥♥♥♥♥br>- Beat him to within an inch of his life
- Flee the battle
- Go tell the Legion Captain about the bribe
- He gets arrested
- Ransack his shop while he's in prison
- Almost every little decision you make has some kind of impact. Even minor dialogue choices affect your characters through putting tallies on certain personality traits that affect in-game bonuses. You're presented with a number of challenges that you can solve creatively, and the method you choose actually has some bearing on what kind of people your main characters become.
- Combat requires you to think and manage resources, unlike many modern games that hand out health potions like candy and make it easy to get by without them to boot. The element system is a cool way of encouraging players to alternate their spells, using combos such as drenching the enemy with rain to set them up for a lightning attack. This aspect also gives wizards something to do in battle besides blast enemies, as their area spells are sometimes needed to clear up hazardous conditions so the party can advance or create hazardous conditions to deny routes to the enemy.
- When I came into town, I met a cat wizard who likes turning into a cat and making cat puns. I figured he was the comic relief character. I now realize that they are all the comic relief character. Goofy characters and goofy writing constantly undercut the game's efforts to get you invested in the story. The setting actually looks pretty interesting (other than the hilariously-named "Sourcerers" and "Source Hunters"), but I can't bring myself to care. This is a particularly major flaw in a game that's supposed to be an old-school-style RPG.
- There are some quirks in the combat interface that take some getting used to, and the one-click command system combined with the delay time after some combat animations makes it a little too easy to accidentally commit a character to burning all of his or her action points walking across the screen to a useless position or firing an attack spell off at a corpse or barrel. You've seen the trailers, right?
Few games really live up to its trailers and all its marketing nowadays. This one surpasses it. The realism is there, to a much higher degree than any even remotely similar game I have ever seen. You have your physics, the sea and the wind and the structure of your ship, to take into account in every move you make. You have your graphics, as beautiful as you could wish. And the immersion is there - every battle you fight counts, for good or for bad.
The ships range from the smallest cutters and schooners to the heavy first rate ships-of-the-line, and the variety in gameplay is enormous as you raise in the ranks. Furtheremore, the game offers other aspects of the naval Caribbean life than combat between nations - trading, crafting, plundering and politics.
This game already has ten times more to offer than the average AAA game, and so far the game has been growing furiously in both size and quality, from the match-based combat game it once was, during the Sea Trails, to the masterpiece it already is, despite a few bugs and a very rudimentary GUI. And this despite its still being considered an alpha version. It offers no tutorial as such, but instead it gives you a cutter to do with as you please, and which you can replace for free once you manage to sink it or blow it up. In my personal opinion, this is the best tutorial you could wish for.
And lastly, I know the price is by some people considered rather high for an early-access game, but I assure you: if you would be willing to buy any of those AAA games for 150% of this price, then you should not doubt going for this one too. And contrary to so many of those games, there has been no talk about any DLCs, suscription fees or any other of that crap yet. And that detail alone is very encouraging.
See you on the high seas, captain.

So Game Dev Tycoon was released on December 10th, 2012 on Greenheart's website as a standalone game. I played this game after 2 months of it's released, it was amazing. I remember Christmas being over and I had cash to spend, I decided to buy Game Dev Tycoon for it's unique idea. I realized that I was taking a risk since this wasn't on Steam, wasn't really on anything besides their website. I'm so glad I did buy this game because I simply love 'creating' games. I mean you can make a company from scratch, start in a garage and climb all the way to the top with your money over 1B+. I played this game at least 100 hours, yeah I know that it isn't showing on my steam record, remember I got this game when it came out. I am a game developer, so when I came across this game I was like "Yeah this is an instant buy". I kinda use this as a guide for not creating a stupid game, I think of a game idea, I give it a name and I create it in Game Dev Tycoon, if it has a good score then I'll attempt to create the game in real life, but if the game gets a bad score, I'll just scrap the idea. I know that seems strange to others but I use it for that haha! Now for the reasons in a nice list like all the other reviews do...
-Friendly cartoonish graphics
-Fun & perfect gameplay music
-Simply easy to learn
-Great fun mods
-Runs smoothly for Mac & Windows (I don't know about Lynx since I don't have one)
-Game price is good (If the game would cost $30, I would still buy it)
-Hours upon hours of non-repetitive gameplay
-Create your own goals and strive to complete them (Something I found that fits perfect with this game, for example, like trying to obtain a "11/10" review from a game reviewer which is also a achievement)
-This game is something that anyone can play, when I say anyone I mean anyone (My dad is 81 years old, he played this game and loads of fun...)
-No huge bugs
-Mods can be an easy way to ruin the game for you (Like the Cheat mod...)
-Once you complete everything, it gets boring unless you haven't unlocked all the achievements
Honestly this game is pretty good, it even got a 4.5/5 from Microsoft!
I really got the best out of this game and the price is so worth it to have so many hours of fun. Now i know that people may have their opinions about this game either in a bad/good way. I'm a game developer so I really REALLY like this game.
Well their you go, you can purchase this game and have fun or you can miss out on hours of fun.
The choice is yours...

- Almost every little decision you make has some kind of impact. Even minor dialogue choices affect your characters through putting tallies on certain personality traits that affect in-game bonuses. You're presented with a number of challenges that you can solve creatively, and the method you choose actually has some bearing on what kind of people your main characters become.
- Combat requires you to think and manage resources, unlike many modern games that hand out health potions like candy and make it easy to get by without them to boot. The element system is a cool way of encouraging players to alternate their spells, using combos such as drenching the enemy with rain to set them up for a lightning attack. This aspect also gives wizards something to do in battle besides blast enemies, as their area spells are sometimes needed to clear up hazardous conditions so the party can advance or create hazardous conditions to deny routes to the enemy.

Goofy characters and goofy writing constantly undercut the game's efforts to get you invested in the story. The setting actually looks pretty interesting (other than the hilariously-named "Sourcerers" and "Source Hunters"), but I can't bring myself to care. Scribblenauts Unlimited is a title in its own genre: to the general public there is no game quite like it (and to this day I have not found any alternatives myself either). While the gameplay should be known to most of my readers, for the sake of completion I will elaborate on the game's objectives and means to succeed in them.
The protagonist is Maxwell, a kid that gets his hands on a notebook with a magical power, being that everything written down in the notebook will magically appear. As ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and malicious little children are, he seized the opportunity to make the lives of others miserable, that is until a magician curses his sister and she is slowly consumed and converted into rock. The only way to stop this from happening is for him to make people, as well as animals and sometimes even inanimate objects, happy again. The player is presented with a sidescrolling 2D level including Maxwell, the aforementioned entities, and loads of hints that should indicate the player what to spawn for those in need. Some of these entities initiate a small storyline, while others are as simple as spawning a glass of water for someone that claims to be thirsty.
There has obviously been a lot of work put into the levels as to not make them linear, and while this succeeded, the overall premise of the game makes it that it will still appear linear to the player. After all, your mission is to spawn the things you're asked for. The sandbox aspect of the game has some potential as far as humor is concerned (have you ever worn a pants that's armed with a sword and is fighting your t-shirt?), but to some this will be entertaining for a shorter period of time than it is to others. The music and sound complements the visuals and while these aspects aren't exactly extraordinary, they are good enough.
In general I'd spend €10,- to €15,- if I was less cynical of a person. The reason I wouldn't scoop out that small amount from my budget is that I easily got bored with the sandbox aspect, but you'll have to keep in mind that I'm one of few uncommon gamers that is unable to enjoy the sandbox aspect of many other games like GTA1/4, Saints Row III and Just Cause 2, so I'm sure this will still appeal to a lot of folks out there.

OYE great game of course, but if you buy it you need to fix it, here's how my friends (i have done this and now it works perfectly):
Open up the fallout.ini file in: My Documents\My Games\Fallout3
Find the line:
bUseThreadedAI=0
change it to:
bUseThreadedAI=1
Add another line after it and insert:
iNumHWThreads=2
This will limit the game to 2 cores and prevent the engine bug from causing the game to freeze.
*If the game still crashes write this iNumHWThreads=1

I recommend the game for all fans of the Warhammer franchise. Players who are not familiar with the lore at least a bit, it is still playable and they can have real fun with it, but they might not understand the whole story or the importance of some characters. Gameplaywise it is still massive fun.
The story is rather simple actually, but that doesn't mean it is bad. The whole franchise deals about war between the parties and this game is no different. You play as Cpt. Titus of the ultramarines. For more info you need to check the pretty deep lore. It is quite extensive and you should read it if you are into scifi stuff. Anyway, you are sent out to cleanse a planet of an orc invasion. I don't want to spoil too much, but there will be more to it later on. *cough* Chaos *cough*.
The gameplay is pretty simple. You run through easy-to-follow levels and shoot or slash your way through hordes of enemies. Once you are into the first battle of the game you notice two things. First the amount of enemies are a bit bigger than in other 3rd person shooters, Second, melee combat is way more effective and more often used than in other games. Both fits wonderfully into the game. The hordes that storm you are quite overwhelming, but never unfair and when you go into a horde of that orcs with a big♥♥♥♥♥energy hammer and just smash their skullz you feel like a badass. The slow motion effects when you cut an orc in half or behead one even helps feeling like a killing machine.
The shooting is solid. It feels good and when you shoot any weapon you can feel the high calibre.
The fury system is a basically a boost which increases your strentgh and heals you for a short period of time. You need to fill a fury meter first before you can activate it. Well, and how do you fill it? Correct. You murder enemies. In Melee you fill it way faster than in ranged combat tho. This can be tricky. Especially in harder difficulties.
The controls feel a bit clunky more so with controller, but you are a space marine with a big♥♥♥♥♥armor. So i guess it was intended. You can dash, you can sprit and with a jet pack you can jump high in the air and then dash down. For the melee weapons you can use different combos. There is also a stun attack which lets you finish your foes off with a brutal finisher.
The health system is something uncommon. You are protected by a shield. So far so standard, but if the shield runs out and you lose health, there are only two way to regain your health. You have to use finishers on enemies. This way you have to be offensive, because despite all the sniper and ranged weapons it is hard to be not involved into a melee battle. The offensive way is also betterto gain fury.
the weapon arsenal is ok. You have 4 melee weapons (each with its own combos and strengths and weaknesses) a bolter (a machine gun) a grenade launcher, grenades, sniper rifles, plasma weapons you can fire fast or charge for more power and a melta gun which is basically a shotgun. So i missed nothing while playing,
The graphics are solid. The game isn't the newest, but they still look nice. The space marines feel a bit stiff in its animations, which is forgivable since they are in heavy armor, but the normal soldiers could feel a bit more fluent. The effects of explosions and the gore level is quite ... detailed. Shame about the brownish setting. Every level looks too alike. It has this brownish tone. Has to do with the planet and the city you are on, but a bit more variety wouldn't be that bad.
There is also a Multiplayer. Which is asically a deathmatch. You can built your own Space Marine and customize him in color and armor a bit. Since it is only deathmatch it gets a bit boring after a while, but i bet die hard fans don't care :)
Also shame about the length. I played it on hardest difficulty and was through in 7 to 8 hours. I guess for a few bucks it is still really entertaining.
I really recommend the game, but it is double the fun if you have at least a small clue about the whole lore.
It's a bit repetitive at points, and some of the deaths will feel cheap, but this game's combat system feels absolutly amazing. Any 40k fan willing to drop the $30 should check it out.

First off I"m giving a thumbs down only because it's Early Access and many issues have not been fixed that I feel should have been many moons ago.
Well, you can see how many hours I've played, it's not  hundreds but it's enough to see what's going on. This game is very pretty, VERY pretty. So pretty in fact, I have to run it on all low graphic settings to squeak out 16 FPS. My gear is AMD 4300 quad core 3.8ghz 8GB RAM Radeon R7 250 w/2GB video RAM, it's not the fastest but I shouldn't have to ride the little bus just to run the game though. World of Tanks I run on high settings and get 25FPS and it's every bit as graphically intense. A minor quibble, let's get to other things.
The levelling system is a tad grindy, maybe not Korean MMO grind, but tedious enough that unless you're a fan it will take weeks of steady game play to get from the starting 7th rate ships to 5th (grinding all the way to 1st rate is for the no life crowd). The combat, while immersive, is using the same tired old tricks every dev uses to make the AI "difficult", in other words it cheats. Nobody uses anything other then Round Shot, and there's a reason why. I took a Privateer down to 47% Sails using Chain Shot (the preferred method of anti sail attack) and it continued to achive 10 knots, in close haul to the wind, This flys in the face of the Bernoulli effect on sails...with a dozen melon sized holes in them. The entire point of using Chain Shot is to reduce their use of anything but running with the wind and reduce their speed to a crawl, making them easy prey (a lot of ships during the period would strike their colors once their ability to maneuver was removed). I guess the devs decided that was either too hard to code (or maybe not 'sexy' enough) or ran out of funding when that part came up. By way of another players account of using Grape Shot (think big shot gun) to reduce a ship that started with 155 crew to 25 crew, and they were still able to maneuver the ship and reload and fire all canons as if nothing had changed. Yet again, another option removed for expediency of coding I suspect. I think they incude these ammunition types for historical accuracy street cred, but in reallity the AI doesn't pack it in until the hull is gone, and the only thing that does that is Round Shot. Remember, the whole reason to use Grape Shot is to remove the crew without damaging the ship to much, because then you now own a slightly used ship which is often times worth tens of times more then the cargo it's carrying.
Now, lets get to the strategic map, shall we? For some reason, after months of Alpha and Beta testers complaining that open Faction enrollment was leading to grotesque Zerg factions skewing strategic game balance not one jot has been done to fix that. I get it, it's hard to tell people they can't play their favorite nationality in favor of sucking more EA sales and turn a blind eye to the steam roll that is happening with the ports, but the end game is not fun for anyone, even the umbrella factions as they will quickly run out of opponents. Soon, everyone is bored and quits to play something else. As the French I watched the Pirate faction in the USA PvP server take half of Martinique in 2 hours. After logging on before writting this they own most of the eastern French, Swedish and Dutch ports, the USA faction owns the coastline to Mississippi and a dozen ports encroaching on Cuba, Great Britain owns half of the Mexican ports, it's just kinda ugly. There's competitive and there's one sided, the abscence of any balancing makes for these weird one sided steam rolls. The thing is this has been covered by every MMO that's come before and failed to deal with the gorilla in the living room issue of faction balance, we know how it ends, writing your resume for the next game company.
I cannot comment much on the Crafting or Trade aspect of the game, but port control is a huge facet of Trade, and the juggernaut steam roll of the ports has left many to give up on Trade if they aren't in the few zerg factions. Crafting requires for the most part a reliable resource influx, which is often tied to...wait for it...Trade. As you can imagine, quite a few have switched sides to the zerg faactions simply because that aspect of the game they like dictates they do so.
What can I say, this game is still in Early Access so there's a possibilty these issues will be resolved before release, but don't bet on it until you see a video of some old Alpha dog telling you it's safe to go in the water again. I keep thinking, all they needed to do was pay some German board game designer 10-20 thousand Euro for consulting fees and implement his/her ideas regarding game balance, because those German board game designers know how to make a good playable fair game.

Outstanding game so far. Naval Action captures the difficulty, chaos, and terror of naval combat unlike any other game since Silent Hunter III. Its open world is influenced heavily by EVE Online and Mount & Blade, and while systems are rudimentary, they are all in tact and functioning. The size of the world is truly impressive -- the entire Caribbean, modelled precisely. It takes about 3 real-life hours to cross the map, if you have the wind... The political system is very intriguing and already shaky alliances have formed between certain nations.
Gameplay is remarkably tight for an early access title -- I have encountered literally no bugs, glitches, freezes, etc. The combat is difficult but accessible for new players, and the graphic fidelity in the battles is basically AAA quality -- think a cross between Wargame: Airland Battle and World of Warships at max settings but with MUCH better ocean, sound and smoke effects. Ships are modelled in much more clarity and detail than WoWS and waves and storms can dramatically influence battles.
This game needs more press and exposure. I've played every major war game, sim, etc., and Naval Action is the most promising I've played in a long time.
Is it worth $40? Absolutely. The test UI is clunky and certain features need iteration, but the game is pretty much there and without the glitchy nonsense that afflicts most Early Access titles. This is 100% more polished than Day Z SA.

Start with a lowly cutter and fight your way up the ranks until you have earned the crew that allows you to outfit a 1st Rate Ship of the line Nelsons Victory, Or the spanish giant Santissima if you can build or afford one. But dont rush it as every ship type has its advantages and drawback and testing them all are a large part of the fun.
You can also advance your crafting talents and become a ship builder that help your nation by supplying your fellow captains with ships for trading or cannon thunder, for a fee to be negotiated.
Or a shrewd trader that buys low and sells high, Transport needed goods from a port with a surplus to a port that lacks your commodity and is willing to pay a premium price.
Join a Clan to seek adventure or combat Pirates, take part in RVR vs other Nations on which your nation and clan is fighting. Join a Fleet to stage a Portbattle and conquer a enemy region filled with ports and resources for your nation and deny the enemy of its use.
Now you can pass the time with fishing while on the open the seas for exotic and valuable fish and the very rare Bottle with a map that can lead you to a shipwreck filled with treasure.
The choices are yours, But remember The open sea can be a dangerous place.
There be captains of other nations with whom you are at war, The smuggler who is trying to bring contraband to your nation or is smuggling for your enemies, or even the Pirates who wish to plunder your ship and its cargo to pay for a night in Tortuga with his ladies and rum bottles.
The adventure is there but remember, Once you leave the safety of your nations port who knows what lies beyond the horizon.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a fantastically designed infinite runner game (A genre that seems to be very popular nowadays).
Graphics: 10/10
The graphics are an amazingly designed, psychadelic (BIT.TRIPPY, if you will) mix of 8-bit, modern-ish, and 3D-pixelated (Yeah that's totally a thing), depending on what you are looking at. It blends together so well that it's just very pleasant to the eyes.
Sound: 10/10
Just listening to the title screen theme, you can already tell this soundtrack is going to be great. Also I love how the music changes depending on what you do in the level. That's a very neat addition.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
The game, although it is just another infinite runner, is amazing. It is very fast-paced and fun. The only problem is that it takes forever to complete a level.
Now that I have sung praise for this game, here are some cons:
-No checkpoints
-Gameplay can seem a bit too fast-paced at times
-Controller thumbstick isn't compatible; you can only use the D-pad.
-Game won't run at my computer's resolution. You can change your resolution (Unlike Pac-Man CE, which is a review I will do another day), but when I changed it to 1440x900, it still ran in 16:9 ratio. This is only a very minor nitpick though.
So in conclusion, this is probably the only BIT.TRIP game worth the series' asking price of $10. The other games are good, but not worth $10. Plus the whole collection as BIT.TRIP SAGA is available on 3DS for $15 and on Wii as BIT.TRIP COMPLETE for however much it is.

I have over 500+ hours clocked on the first Total Warhammer game, and ever since the Mortal Empires FREE expansion launched, I have no doubts Warhammer 2 will povide me with the same (if not more!) endless hours of enjoyment. I simply love the combination of Total War gameplay in a Warhammer setting. My only hope is that CA eventually picks up the license to make a Warhammer 40,000 installment.
So far I have mainly played Skaven and a bit of High elves with alot of interaction with Lizardmen AI and some Dark elves. The new factions in Warhammer 2 bring a new style to the currently existent factions from the orignal game.
High Elf units are honestly the most balanced and well round troops in all respects, everything you could want from archer units, frontline units, siege, and calvary is there. Honestly in my opinion High Elves are OP not because their units are overly buffed, but because all the entire unit roster is simply "perfectly balanced", I simply found no noticable weaknesses in any of their troops. Take a moment to look at each unit card and compare it to how other faction cards look, I found a very compariable balance to every other faction in the game yet without any shared weakness that factions suffers. For example, High elves have fairly similar top notch range units as Wood Elves but do not suffer the Wood elf draw back of having poorly armored frontline units. This perhaps makes sense and fits in with the High Elf lore, but gameplay wise I found them super easy to play and boring because of this; there is simple no challenge to them.
Skaven on the other hand, wow. In my opinion they are as hardcore mode as you can get initially. Very weak early game units overall that result in very risky plays against far stonger enemy units (high elves and lizardman) and are an interesting hybrid between Chaos Horde and managing a growing amount of provinces. What I mean by this is the Food mechnic, which I disagree with in a few respects but the one thing it does well is force players to be very selective on which settlements / provinces you want to settle and which one you will raze; traditionally most faction and their players will want to just outright settle every habitable settlement to expand their empire. This system forces you to spend more time razing nearby settlements and only risking growth for the sake of highly desirable settlements.
Skaven are however very enjoyable to play for the simple aspect that its extremely satisfying to use Plague Hero's to inflict major amount of disease on a very well defended settlement and infect it's garrison and any armies nearby, after a few turns the enemy losses are so great that by the time the disease runs it's course nothing is left but a skeleton crew; at which point Skaven army can attack-attack and feast on their enemies to their rotten hearts content.
It is a fun and addicting game.  It is worth more than $1 for every hour of fun.

I'm writing a negative review not for the actual game itself, but for the poor version I inadvertedly purchased as a German buyer. You see, in Germany, we still have very narrow views on what is acceptable or harmful in a video game. Not everyone – not me at least, but the official canon is that violent games can't be advertised, so a lot of publishers censor their games for the German market, so they can overcome this hurdle, at the cost of quality. This is unfortunately what happened with Fallout 3, that can only be bought in a "low violence version" and, worst of all, can only be played in German language. This is completely inacceptable for a game that old, as it will certainly never ever be the object of an advertisement campaign and, anyway, publishers nowadays, even Bethesda, have realized that a good game should be sold as it is and it will advertise itself better than any billboard or advertisement. Why they have not chnged this poor version of Fallout 3 to be on the height of its quality for the German market, I don't know but here you go, Bethesda. Update this version at last and I promise, I will update my review. Until then, I'm not touching the game and it will gather virtual pixel dust until it sees better days.

That leaves way for the upper level management "CEO" branch to step in which is being promised in the next update which I'm excited to wait for, honestly. The auto-runner genre is one that’s filled with all sorted of titles so to really stand out you’ve got to create something special
BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a rhythm / music platformer with a fully character-based adventure that’s the latest chapter in the award-winning critically acclaimed BIT.TRIP series.
Run, jump, slide, and kick!
Another fun well paced game that’s only challenge is you get into the rhythm of the level! As with many auto-runners, the pace picks up as you progress and the challenges become more complex.
What’s rather nice about this game is the cameos from other Indie Game characters such as Super Meat Boy, these pop up in all sorts of places so you’ll have to keep your eyes glued if you wish to spot them all!
Sometimes we don’t often talk about when highlighting features of a game is the soundtrack and really it’s one of the most important parts of a game. It keeps you immersed, add to the emotion of the game and even makes you jump from time to time. BIT.TRIP RUNNER has one of the best soundtracks from the Indie Game Genre it’s simply perfect for the gameplay.
A rainbow of colour delivered in well crafted blocks, whilst side-loaded it still creates enough depth that the story can interact with the landscapes in ways that help to make this game feel very modern even when it reflects a retro feel.
Speaking of retro, one of our favourite features about this game is if you perfectly finish a level you get to go on a bonus retro adventure, it’s like having two games in one!
With more than 50 levels, new easy and hard modes plus leaderboards and achievements you will find yourself not only challenge your friends but yourself in your quest to be on top with the perfect score!

Do note that this review is written in regards to the campaign only.
Call of Duty Infinite Warfare is an example of Infinity Ward learning to apply the positive changes Treyarch added to the franchise with Black Ops, putting their best foot forward, and producing a genuinely good campaign as a result of it.
The characters are likeable and well-written for a CoD story. The villains, though quite one-dimensional, fulfill the exact role Infinity Ward CoD villains should. People come to these games to feel like a hero, not to sympathize with Space!Nazis. The story is simple, not bad.
The gameplay is very much restrained compared to the likes of Advanced Warfare and Black Ops 3, with only a very limited version of wall running and the double jump returning, and in non-intrusive ways at that. The Space Fighter missions are actually quite entertaining, if generally on the short side.
There are actual stealth sections which do not overstay their welcome, and the ability to modify one's load-out with unlockable weapons and attachments at the start of missions greatly expands upon the campaign's replayability.
Nick Rehes, the protagonist, has an actual narrative arc he goes through over the course of the campaign; and unlike the sociopaths of Ghosts, is a geniunely likeable character despite the well-intentioned mistakes he can and does make.
Infinite Warfare is up there with Black Ops 2 in campaign quality, and despite what the masses say, is absolutely worth your time if you play this franchise for the campaign.
