Review re-written for the current state of the game, and pre-wipe/pre-PVE server shutdown.
First things first. Game Labs is a Russian company. Russian company is Russian. Which means they operate by a few specific rules:
- This is our game, we just let you play it.
- We did you a massive favor by letting you play the game, don't you forget it.
- Any and all feedback can and will be taken personally, because we did you a massive favor (see above), you ingrate.
- Bugs may be forgotten about, they may someday be fixed, or they may be declared features.
- We are SMARTER than you, don't you forget it.
- Long-term planning, consistent vision, UI design and tutorials are all for losers. What are you, some kinda LOSER?!
- Gamers are overgrown man-children, therefore professional conduct is unnecessary when interacting with them.
- If you don't like it, the uninstall button is over there. We don't care, because we are SMARTER than you and also did you a huge favor.
This behavior is consistent across nearly every game design company hailing from the land of vodka, bears and balalaika. This ought to help you set your expecations for Naval Action and its developer Game Labs.
Important note: the game consists of two modes, battle (where ships actually fight in an instance) and open world (where you can sail on a very large map).
Now then to the game. The good parts first.
- NA is probably the best looking and the most true-to-form Age of Sail battle simulator you'll find. When in a fight, you won't be sailing a motorboat with sails attached mostly for looks (looking at you, AC4, Tempest and others). The wind matters, the integrity of your sails matters, your ship's rigging matters (a fore-and-aft rig sails markedly differently from a square rig). You really get a chance to see what it is like to get your ship moving in the right direction (or just MOVING) while at the same time also shooting and being shot at.
- Ship models used in combat are not just pretty, they are GORGEOUS. If not for all the cannonballs flying around, you could spend time just admiring the tallships. The only problem is with the crew - you can only see the cannonneers, and they perform the same looping animation over and over again. Nobody climbs the masts or turns the wheel or pushes the tiller, but given the overall beauty of the ships it's not much of a distraction.
- Ditto for the water, weather effects and land (both in battles and in the open world) - there's something about coming up on a lush green island on a sunny day after sailing in the open sea for a while.
- Combat is sufficiently visceral: cannons boom, cannonballs fly, wood splinters, sails rip and tear. It is very satisfactory to see your enemy set on fire or dismasted (which happens fairly rarely), or just pound them into a scrap heap that slowly sinks beneath the waves. Beyond major rigging damage such as dismasting and loss of bowsprit, the damage is modeled primarily through decals (meaning that your ship can end up covered in a multitude of splintery holes from cannonball strikes, and that conveys the image well enough (though could be better).
- Sailing and fighting are just complex enough that it feels satisfying to figure things out, but not so much so that it becomes overly difficult. Ships of different sizes feel differently and it takes a bit of time to come to grips with your new boat's behavior when you trade in your old ride, however the overall techniques become second nature after a while.
- Open-world navigation has been much improved; the world map now has a coordinate grid, and while you don't get a "you are here" GPS blip, you can see your own coordinates. This makes finding locations a lot easier than before, and you can actually go sailing in the open sea with a reasonable degree of certainty that you will arrive exactly (or nearly exactly) where you intend to arrive. No more timidly creeping along the shore or using third-party tools to find your way; coincidentally, finding mission objectives is also noticeably easier.
The bad and the ugly now, and the reasons for the thumbs down.
- "Russian company is Russian" - see above. Features are missing, bugs go unfixed for years, developers openly play favorites with segments of player base and silence any dissent. Their conduct in general is unprofessional, petty and childish to the extreme.
- The game does its best to turn off the new players. As soon as you log on, you are presented with the ugliest and least intuitive UI you'll ever see (proudly labeled "test UI please ignore). There is no tutorial of any sort - so off to Youtube with you, matey; better hope that the guide videos you find are not out of date. Your first ship is a tiny, wobbly and woefully undergunned Cutter. The only way to learn how to sail and fight is to take this silly little boat into combat and learn by trial and error, which can be challenging to say the least. In low-level missions, your opponents also sail small, fast and maneuverable boats, and seem to sail circles around you while you still try to figure out how to make the damn thing go. All the while you are getting shot to death of course. It can be SUPREMELY frustrating - yes, you can replace the cutter for free, and the game now grants you "assistant" ships in lower-level missions, but still, getting repeatedly sunk before you figure out what you did wrong can be trying. Oddly enough, as you gain ranks and get larger ships, things get notably easier as you gain more survivability and heavier armaments.
- Boarding, the quintessential part of Age of Sail experience, is reduced to a kludgey rock/paper/scissors game presented via - you guessed it - another terrible interface. And the developers can't seem to make up their mind whether you should be able to keep a captured ship, or send it to the "admiralty" for a reward, and whether a captured ship should be useful or a cruddy "basic quality" barge.
- Open-world ship models are severely simplified versions of the models used in battle. Some ships look fairly nice; others are downright awful. All open-world models have no collision (meaning you can sail straight through other ships), there is no crew visible on decks, gun ports are open and sails don't behave realistically. It is worse for some than the others; the Niagara, for example, always looks like it is about to sink, with the waves rolling right over its top deck.
- While the large open-world map is nice, traveling takes a VERY long time. Hopping from town to town on the coast can take between five and ten minutes; if you are planning a longer jaunt, better settle in for 30+ minutes before you see land again.
- Inexplicably, NPCs ability to attack players has been removed. You can still attack NPCs outside of combat missions, but for some reason the majority of them roam around in fleets that include multiple first-rate ships of the line.
- The community overall is tiny (daily average number of online players is well under a thousand), and a large portion of that is the incredibly toxic PvP segment.
Which brings us to the latest brilliant idea by Game Labs.
It has just been announced that the dedicated PvE server is going away. Instead, a portion of the map (about 1/4 of it) will be reserved as a "PvE ghetto", limited to a choice of 3 nations. Want to sail the whole map? Better prepare to deal with gankers.
Game Labs seems to think that this will turn NA into "EVE with sailboats" and bring them the same level of success as EVE.
Game Labs may very well be delusional.

The ships in the game are absolutely magnificent. They really put effort into making them and anyone who loves building models of these old but majestic ships will certainly love the amount of detail and work put into the ships, not to mention being able to see the ships "come alive" as they sail across the sea in the game.
Another beautiful (though some might say terrifying) part of the game is the combat. Watching a ship as it turns with the wind, all it's gun ports open, the barrels of every cannon aimed directly at your ship and then seeing the rolling broadside as each gun is fired in succession is simply fantastic (and, yes, terrifying). The muzzleflashes light up the side of the ship and the sails, but is quickly hidden within a thick cloud of gunpowder smoke. Often the smoke from the gunpowder is so thick and heavy that entire ships can be hidden behind it. And the sound of the cannons is brilliant. They have loud, deep booms which scale as you get larger cannons, or even carronades.
The part of the game that still requires the most development though is the Open World part. This part of the game is still very barebones (the basic framework is up but it requires more work for certain, but then again, it IS alpha stage). The UI is largely, perhaps even entirely, a placeholder UI. The functionality is there, but it is not very appealing (again, it is alpha so beautification comes later).
Is this game worth it ?
In my opinion, absolutely! If you like sailships, definitely. If you liked the old Sid Meiers Pirates or Pirates of the Burning Sea, then absolutely.
However, as always, I encourage people to watch Youtube videos, reviews, twitch streams and so on to get a better idea of what the game is about, how it works, what it looks like and so on to make a decision.
Anyways, long wall of text, but then again, it's meant for someone curious about the game :)

Super Arcade Football is, yep you guessed it, an arcade football game that has recently launched through Steam’s Early Access program. SAF’s style of football is fast-paced, foul-filled and frantic, making it incredibly exciting for those playing single-player or with friends with the game’s local-multiplayer. With Quick Matches, Preset Tournaments (The World Cup and The Euros) as well as Custom Tournaments, there’s already a fair bit of bang for your buck with more to come as the game continues through development.
Please note: While I will mention what the devs plan to add several times in this review, my overall opinion, and therefore this review, is based entirely on what is currently in the game.
The game’s graphics are simple but suit it well, it’s a bright and colourful game which goes well with the overall feel of the game as a casual arcade game. The UI simply consists of the score and time played of the match in the top left, it doesn’t take up too much screen space so no complaints from me. The menu is also easy to navigate and a basic settings menu is now in place. The settings menu has two audio options and also lets you choose between a landscape or portrait camera. While there’s still a lot of settings which need to be added this is a good start considering it launched with no settings menu at all.
SAF currently features four different modes for playing a match, they are as follows:
The three different game modes all have a default time for a half (which is three minutes) but there are a few other options: 1 minute, 5 minutes, 10 minutes and No Time Limit (this last one would be for if you wanted to set a score limit). There are other match options now as well, you can choose what pitch surface you want, you can set a score limit, choose between 11-a-side and five-a-side and add modifiers to the game. The game currently has somewhere in the region of forty national teams with plans to bring more national teams as well as European 1st-3rd Division Clubs sometime in the near future. You’ll also be able to edit teams as well as create and share your own, presumably that’ll come with the team management update.
As for the game’s content, there is as I said earlier a fair bit to do, the reason I’ve only played two hours is because of a [seemingly] rare bug. The Tournaments are a lot of fun and the Quick Matches are perfect for killing a few minutes here and there. The general rule for sports games is that there’s a correlation between how much replay value there is and how much you enjoy the game’s sport, the same can be said for this game. SAF’s main appeal in its current state is for picking up to kill some time and while that will probably provide you a fair bit of game time over a long period of time. While the Tournaments are also enjoyable I can’t imagine wanting to play them more than a few times, though you could make them more interesting for yourself by trying to beat them with some of the lesser skilled teams in the game.
Speaking of lesser skilled teams, as you’d expect there are different skill levels of teams (a rating out of five in the game). As far as I can tell, the only thing affected by your team’s skill level is their speed though there may be other things, I’m not sure. Having a lower speed than the team your facing definitely doesn’t make the match impossible but there is a noticeable difference in difficulty.
On to the game’s controls, I haven’t tried M&KB but SAF is great with an Xbox One Controller. The controls are tight and responsive, as you’d want from a fast-paced game, and thankfully the default controls are good seeing as you can’t change them. You move your player with the left thumbstick, switch players with the left bumper, pass/kick with A (the longer you hold A down the harder the kick) and you also have a slow-mo kick with the B button. Holding down the B button lets you control the ball after you’ve kicked it, you’re not going to have it flying around in circles but you can curve it in to the goal which is awesome! It may sound like it makes the game too easy but you can only stay in slow-mo for a certain amount of time (though it’s usually more than enough to go from foot to goal) and goalkeepers move at roughly the same speed as the ball so you still need to be careful with your shots else it’ll just end up in the keeper’s hands.
Circling back to fouls, there’s a hell of a lot of them. This is undoubtedly where the game is weakest and I’m hoping that an option to disable fouls comes about as has been suggested by others in the forum. There are two main problems with fouls. First off, the only kind of tackle is a slide tackle. No big deal at face value but if the slide tackler makes contact with the slide tackleee (is that even a real word?) then a bone snap sound is heard and the player is incapacitated for a few seconds. You can have most of your team wiped out, leaving you defenceless, especially in the Indoor Madness mode, which is rather frustrating. The second problem is a weird one, there are too few foul calls as well as too many. If you’re going to include foul calls from the ref then every foul should be called, though like I said no fouls would be preferable. The thing is with SAF, not all of the fouls are called. This can be incredibly frustrating, especially in situations where your opponents get away with several fouls and you end up getting red carded. Plus, stopping play for a free kick or penalty completely kills the generally fast-paced nature of the game which is one of the best things about it. UPDATE: While fouls do still remain a problem in normal, unchanged game modes, one of the modifiers that has been added is a No Fouls modifier which works well for the 5-a-side games but I’d still like to see something done to fouls so they can be kept on in 11-a-side where they fit in a little more.
Lastly, as I said earlier I’ve only played two and a half hours (at the time of writing this review) due to a bug. The bug makes the game freeze during loading which means you have to force quit and restart to play a new match and it happens every two or three matches. It’s particularly frustrating for Tournaments since you then lose your progress. However, this seems to be a very rare issue as there seems to just be one other person who has complained about it in the forums. UPDATE: It looks like this bug has now been fixed which is awesome! Figured I’d leave this section in since it demonstrates that the devs care about the game due to the issue being fixed reasonably quickly.
Super Arcade Football is already a cracking fast-paced, arcade football game, though there’s still a lot that needs to be added. Even in its current state, its well worth the price of admission!

After seeing some early screenshots and videos I was eagerly awaiting the release of this game, but on first play I wasn't impressed.  However, coming back to the game a couple of days later I was hooked.  Sure, there are a few things that need attention, and the cons outweigh the pros at the moment, but the heart of the game is in the right place and with improvement this is surely going to be a great game...
Pros
- Stunning design - everything looks beautiful, cool kits and hairstyles, brilliant pitch textures (particularly the 5-a-side courts).  Would be nice to have an option to choose your kit in a tournament though as clashes are going to happen (you can choose in an single game)
- 5-a-side option - probably the best I have seen in a game
- Brilliant sounds & chants
- Fast and furious
- Fun to play
- Slo-mo shooting camera - works quite well and is a nice touch... but would be good to be able to turn it off
Cons
- Little too fast at times
- Difficult to pick a pass, might as well dribble through the whole team
- Goalies fly across the goal to make unbelievable saves
- No deflections - if your shot hits an opponent they walk off with the ball stuck to them
- Replays - Waaaaaay too long and can't be stopped, if a game has a lot of goals it can double the game time
- Gimmicks - Ice pitch?  Never gonna use that.  Hope that decent features aren't delayed for gimmicky elements
- Referees - very inconsistent, and don't even look at the player they are booking half the time.  But then again, most games have this problem, and have you seen John Moss, Lee Mason or Anthony Taylor trying to officiate a match?
- Tackling - it's all or nothing.  Sliding tackles are too violent and slide too far.  Should have the ability to make conservative tackles
- Team database - no way to get to the files so I can't have a look at them to edit.  Would also love to be to have more than two kits to help avoid kit clashes
- Team management - can't reposition players leaving gaping holes when someone is sent off.  And in 5-a-side it seems as though the only tactic is full on assault of the goal, leaving you stranded if you lose the ball
- Crashes - I've had quite a few on both my old PC and new Mac.  You can live with it in an early release, but there is no save option so losing your league is frustrating
- Ghost goals - Both myself and the AI have scored goals which definitely hit the back of the net but haven't counted, and I've also managed to score through a goalie and through the side netting on occasions
- Orientation - would like to be able to choose vertical or horizontal layout for all modes
As it stands, this is a great game for the price, and I'll use it to have a laugh with my mates in five-a-side mode so we can marvel at the bone crunching tackles, bad refereeing, goals that don't count.  I'm very much looking forward to new domestic teams being added, and finding out how custom teams can be created and loaded.  But I think this needs a lot of work if the management side is to be added... it doesn't sit right that my best option in a full match is to pass the ball out to my right back who will them weave round the whole of my opponents team before trying to beat the keeper.  If you are going to build a team, you want to be able to use all the players and for me the passing and tackling elements needs a drastic overhaul... either that or allow us to slow the game down so you can try to pick a pass or make a tackle.

To play football you basically have to able to do four things: shoot, tackle, pass, dribble.
The shooting and tackling in this game are fine. But i have serious issues with the passing and dribbling.
Passing: it is impossible to play crosses. In the old days you would pull back the joystick and shoot. But in those days you would be playing games with a digital joystick and i can understand that it is hard to emulate those controls on a gamepad.
Simple low passes is also really hard to do, because the game is paced waaay too fast. There is simply no time to play a decent pass.
The way i try to solved this was by playing "Postman Pat Football". When one of your players gets the ball, run with it acros the field and deliver a shot on goal. Which brings me to the next problem, dribbling.
Dribbling: the style of dribbling reminds me of Dino Dini's Kick Off games. What i mean by that is that the ball does not "stick" to the player, which makes dribbling a bit of a balancing act. Attackers are superior at it, defenders are pretty poor.
The solution to that would be to let your defender pass the ball to the attacker. If you could pass the ball that is.
Maybe when the game allows me to put my strikers on the wingback position, i will be able to be competitive with this game.
For now, i am not sure where the arcade stops and the football begins in this game. But i don't think that the  playability resembles the classic football games of the 16 bit era. And for that reason i can't recommend it.

This game really elevates the heist formula to a new level. The guard AI is amazing, no "what was that?" here. The mansion is absolutely beautiful, and has hidden secrets in every crevice. You really get a lot of choice of how to go about it stealing the emerald. Do you shoot the guards? Be stealthy? Break the water pipe and drown everyone (to be fair, that was an accident). Go in through the ceiling? And then the plot twist with the tiger and the emerald, which I won't spoil, is really fantastic. Ends with a really great car chase. There were a couple bugs though, the lazers seemed to activate in the mansion before the lights even came on (which really just added challenge), and the elevator took AGES to start moving. I could hear weird shuffling sounds behind the wall too. Anyway, 6/10, 7/10 with rice, definitely buy it on sale.

It only is a two- three hour game, but it has such an incredible story that it feels less like a game, and more like an interactive movie. Some may see that as a plus, others as a negative. For the subject matter, an old man wishing to go to the moon and a company that grants these wishes in their own way, really works for a story rather than a game. The makers really knew how to go about making the game something incredible.
In the end, the game is very creative, brilliantly executed, and so full of emotions from the main characters, to the side characters, and even the story in of itself. I'd recommend this to anyone who just enjoys games.
The only negative I see in this game is that it doesn't have much replay value. Maybe for playing through with others, but the actual game is so direct and short, the only parts that can be replayed are the puzzles for lowest turns. Otherwise, I don't have an issue with the game.

New Review: Originally the game did not work at all for a couple weeks after release. It's recently been fixed.
Proviant appears to be an ant colony survival game. It has a tutorial, but the tutorial is literally a single screen with some vague, Engishy info. The single screen also tells you to then start a new game for more info. The game guides you on WHAT you should be doing, but doesn't do that great of a job telling you HOW to do it. I'm STILL not sure what all the buttons do, I've figured out the dig button, and how to make it dig ramps. And I figured out the build button. As far as I can tell, it just lays dirt blocks down that your ants walk right past as if they weren't there.
You are told to make a large room for your queen. I have not gotten to this part because digging is VERY SLOW. You can only mark ONE tile for digging at a time (Unless there's a way to do more that  I haven't figured out) and the ant has to actually reach the tile to dig it. The ant will make almost no effort to get to the tile. The ant will walk to directly above it, and dig at the ground. It will not move to a lower area, or a better angle, and you do not get to choose which ant will dig. If the ant cannot touch the EXACT tile you are trying to dig, it will just paw at the ground forever.
You are told to double click your ants to assign them either a worker or soldier job. You cannot double click an ant that is walking around. Your ants are almost always wandering around. This makes assigning jobs REALLY annoying, in particular because you can't see what ants already have jobs until you double click them.
This game is absolutely terrible. It's poorly made, has bad music, has a lousy tutorial, and is just plain not fun. I somehow thought better of this game when it didn't work at all.
For the record, I have given up on figuring out how to play this game. If someone else figures it out, and it turns out I'm just a moron, I'll fix my review.

More buildings can be built in major cities and every Legendary Lord is now a seperate playable faction.
There are still some downsides to this game, namely that siege battles are still a huge step down from the historical Total War games. The lack of naval battles is also more noteworthy in this title due to the huge expanses of ocean there are on the Vortex Campaign map.
The Mortal Empires campaign, the combined map of both the first and second game, makes up for a lot of shortcomings though, not by fixing them, but by the shere amount of playable content without additional charge and will keep being improved and updated. But it has recently been announced that the pre-order bonus for this game, the Norsca race pack that got added to Total War: Warhammer, has now been said to not make it to this game at all until 2018, months after release of this game. And that feels like an odd decision.
Overall this is a great game, and the fact that these minor issues come up at all is saying something about the quality of the game. It's a huge step up from Total War: Rome II at launch, it's been flawless for as flawless a major title release can be in these times.
I'm happy to own both games and to look to the future and see more factions make it to Total War and to hopefully one day get a full playable map of the World-That-Was and remember an awesome time with huge Warhammer lore and depth out factions, characters, religions, cultures and locations without all the Age of Sigmar nonsense Games Workshop is now forcing down on everyone.

Super Arcade Football is a fantastic game even at it's current stage, the gameplay is smooth, fun and easy to get the hang of, of course the game isn't all there yet but there is still a lot to do.
--Gameplay--
The game itself runs well without any Frame rate issues, the gameplay is fast paced but easy to get the hang of. There isn't much to say except it's football but very fast paced, the game has a slow motion shot which allows you to curve the ball around the keeper and works very well. The keepers are for the most part very good and react fast enough to stop most shots but not fast enough to stop well placed shots which is good though as of this review they are a bit buggy and can get confused from a shot at an angle but the Developer has said they are working on it though it's not a massive issue. The only major complaint is the Auto switching but the Dev has also said they are working on something better and will be releasing it soon so that won't be a problem soon!
You can choose from 'Quick Match' 'World Cup' 'Euros' and Custom 'League' and 'Knockout' meaning you can choose how many teams are in it and what teams are human controlled, you can for Custom autofill the teams and just see who wins without playing which is a nice feature. There is NO saving currently, meaning if you're 15 games into a league but need to stop you will lose all progress, an annoyance at the moment but of course that will change so be wary of that!
Tackling is a bit odd but fun, it's pretty much random whether it will be a foul or not same with a booking or red card. There are also Penalties.
--Visuals--
I didn't see any graphics options though you shouldn't have a problem running the game, the game has a nice touch with the sliding tackles by adding in dirt lines where you slide which looks really nice especially when you get near the end of the game.
--Bugs--
Pretty much just the Goalkeeper bug I mentioned above, that's it, the game is very well put together and the developer obviously cares a lot about their game which is great to see!
--Conclusion--
So far this game has made a great impression with its initial start on Steam EA and I can't wait to see how this game develops especially with Career Mode! I give the game a 9/10 for being fun, fluid and nicely polished which is great to see for an EA game, if you like Football games or Sensible Soccer styled games then pick this up!

In their simplicity, sprites can carry a hell of an emotional wallop. Back in the glory days of 16-bit RPGs, every game had its tearjerker. -- SPOILERS FOR 20 OR SO YEAR OLD GAMES TO FOLLOW -- Think of Celes' attempted suicide in Final Fantasy VI or Lucca's mom's legs being crushed in Chrono Trigger. --SPOILERS END--
To the Moon repurposes that style into combat-free, gameplay-light interactive story about the compromises we make to our dreams to be with the ones we love. Taking a cue from Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (and a bit of We Can Remember It For You Wholesale, P.K.♥♥♥♥♥♥s short story that became Total Recall), the player takes control of a pair of specialists trained to alter memories of the dying so they can feel like they had no regrets in their final moments.
The story has a lot to say about memory, life, death, love, autism, social expectations, and the responsibilities of science. A lot to unpack in a short amount of time. Worth it if you don't mind crying like a baby.

This crowdfunded RPG shouldn't be missed.  Larian deserves a lot of praise for this.  What stands out the most is how well designed, coded, and implemented the gameplay mechanics are.  Lots of attention to detail here, and so much interactivity, such as the use of the elements (heat, water, air), being able to pick up and throw any reasonably sized object with ease, all of the different statuses.  The UI is also good, although the hotbar should be expandable as it's annoying to have to cycle through them.  This game has many different classes and a fairly complex leveling system, so that every character build will at least feel somewhat unique (although not quite as much as say the Neverwinter Nights games).
With all that being said, I can't help but feel this game is somewhat overrated by the press.  It doesn't have the most role-playing in the world, and not even close.  Yes, it has considerably more role-playing than the very limited Witcher franchise (they are based on novels after all), but compared to the all time greats it can be found lacking.  Compared to Pillars of Eternity, it is also lacking in role-playing.  There isn't much freedom in defining your characters' personalities, less than more recent BioWare games even.  You are always a pair of Source Hunters out to save the world from evil, and there is only one dialogue "skill" which is Charisma; however Charisma itself leads to three different dialogue options (each drawing from your Charisma score) which are Intimidate, Charm, and Reason.  What you choose, and what you do throughout the game will alter the effective of these, putting points into traits such as Individualistic, Pragmatism, and more, but all these do is give you boosts to either Intimidate, Charm, or Reason, as well as a boost to certain other stats like Willpower (which is used only for resisting mind-affecting abilities).
At the end of the day, the dialogue is quite restrictive compared to games like Fallout, Fallout 2, Fallout: New Vegas, Neverwinter Nights 2, and Pillars of Eternity.  Also, the game has two protagonists which you make at character creation, yet it lacks a party dialogue system found in games such as Neverwinter Nights 2: Storm of Zehir and Wasteland 2.  This means, only one of your characters can be in a conversation and the other cannot freely intervene.
The quests are quite restricting compared to great RPGs.  In order to beat this game I had to do things I didn't want to do, things that my character in my mind would not do.  This game, despite the open level design, forces you down a specific path.  Disappointing for an RPG.
Level design is very open.  You are rarely limited in where you can go.  However, enemies do not scale down to your level so many places will be utterly inaccessible just for this reason.  Balance is a bit of an issue in this game, as generic human enemies of the same level have far more AP than you can ever have at that level, and wield weapons that are much higher level yet used with no penalty (and usually have more initiative too).  In combat, enemies can open doors with no AP cost despite being nowhere near them.  Then there are things such as one human enemy who is able to cast a master level spell with no cooldown.  The imbalance is so obvious when (SPOILER ALERT) Bairdotr turns on you; one second she is part of your party, the next she levels up, has top tier equipment, and has far more AP than she should (unless her build changed to have most attribute points spent in Speed).
A shame, a mistake, and serious design flaws that don't affect smarter turn-based games.  And then some enemies just have essentially no real weakness (not even talking about Source demons obviously since they do have a weakness and that's plot related).  So there is some synthetic difficulty in this game, but not game breaking.  A general balance issue is that archers are overpowered on both sides, enemy and player.
But many of these imbalances are somewhat offset by how stupid the AI is.  The AI is nowhere near as smart as XCOM 2 and Enemy Unknown.  Not that this is consolation mind you, this is just another flaw.
Furthermore, leveling up in this game is an extremely slow process.  Far slower than any other RPG I've played.  Too slow even, as it can slow down the pace a bit and it restricts the amount of combat abilities you get.
Speaking of combat abilities, I'd say there is less than Dragon Age: Origins and Pillars of Eternity.  I'm used to Neverwinter Nights 2 so I'm spoiled and wish for more, but at least all of the abilities in this game are well designed and none seem useless.  Some classes will have far more than others, naturally.
Writing and character development are not a focus of this game.  Its tone is lighthearted, the real focus is on gameplay and exploration.  Art design is pretty good, locations stand out a bit but nothing blows my mind and environments can seem more repetitive than some other games.  The scale is large; locations are big and have a decent amount of detail and hidden places, but again nothing mind blowing.
Enhanced Edition contains many incremental improvements over the original, and they really add up.  This game was crafted with a lot of care and programming skill.  Now if only it had industry leading writers and directors.  The second game has Chris Avellone on board, so I can't wait for that!

BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a rhythm based endless runner by Gaijin games which has spawned a sequel and a whole bunch of spinoffs. I personally didn't really enjoy the game. It's simply not very fun to play. It's definitely challenging and according to the statistics less than 1/3 of players ever beat the first world. In the games detriment, I get the feeling that's because people have realized by that point that the game isn't fun enough to try to beat rather than the game being too hard. The rhythm aspect of the game might make it more enjoyable if the music were better, but frankly the music does little to improve the game. It's not a terrible game, seeing as its highly polished and feature complete but I wouldn't really reccomend it to anyone unless you really love endless runners.

Bit.Trip Runner is a game I recommend to whoever has patience. A single error brings you back to the beginning of the level, and some of the levels have tricky obstacles. Some of the harder levels added hours to my playtime just to beat them. That aside, the game runs well and has a remarkably small download size. It's a good game, and I have enjoyed my time playing it.

A great addition to the musical-runner genre, and leads by example as to how these games should be made. Visuals are unique and highly-rewarding. Music when running at full speed in more active levels is fun. Teaches through gameplay rather than dialogue boxes, keeping the flow going.
Very repetitive if being sent back is your worst nightmare in a game; one mistake and you're unceremoniously placed back at the beginning of the level. No checkpoints, no second-tries. Lots of artificial difficulty.
I see this game stagnating in people's inventories often. It's easy to open up, but hard to pick back up after the long breaks it ends up sending you on out of rage. If you don't have patience, you shouldn't pay full price.
You may rage-quit, but you'll be back. They always come back.

This package includes Gravity Bone and 30 Flights of Lovin. Both are extremely short, linear, first person narrative experiences that I didn't find particularly interesting.
The full package had some wonky sound balance, doesn't display correctly at full screen on my duel-monitor setup, and doesn't seem to track my mouse very well. On pause menus and ingame the games would react as if my mouse was moving even when it was still. This resulted in the first person camera drifting.
Gameplay for both games amounted to walking, poor first-person platforming, an uninteresting activities like "take this picture" or "use x on y." Interspaced throughout were sudden jumps, obviously intended to act like jump-cuts in film, that were often fairly disorienting.
The plots, a large focus of both games, is explained chiefly through action instead of text. However, even under such limitation, there is a strange lack of detail. The player is bounced through moments that vary from ridiculous to serious in seconds. The result feels extremely half-baked.
After playing and enjoying Jazzpunk I thought these games would be right up my alley. However, the technical issues, poor gameplay, and plot have left me wondering why these titles are so highly regarded.

A thoroughly magical game experience, both from a storytelling and game mechanics viewpoint.
Sure, one might say the story is a generic tale of cameradie and altruism but the combination of visually stunning, fairy tale like artwork supported by dreamy, orchestral musical score just clicked with me.
I think a big part of that came from being instantly reminded of the Mononoke Hime / Princess Mononoke anime. ;-)
The Jump & Run side of the game is expertly crafted, sporting crisp and very precise controls (I played with a Xbox 360 pad) so that even in parts of the game where for instance you face a deathly time trial you never feel like your demise was the game's fault. It is also worth noting that the game has a very innovative (for a jump & run) save feature which practically allows you to instantly save your location/progress at all times - short of time trials within the storyline.
The "Metroidvania" aspects of the game give you typical progression where the further you go within the main story line the more abilities you unlock which in turn allow you to backtrack and obtain previously unobtainable upgrades. This does not feel tedious at all but is actually fun - a fact which I believe also comes from the way how you can seamlessly explore the world without loading times.
This adds even more to the impressive (level) art style when you dash at breakneck speeds using, all your skills, while the scenery changes from an underground spider cave to lush overland greens, rocky passes, etc.
Via the in-game save file my very casual play time (did not try to collect everything) was recorded as circa 10 hours, which you might say is not too much.
However, considering the price tag AND how I was practically immersed, motivated and glued to the screen over the course of this play time I can high recommend "Ori and the Blind Forest."
An instant classic. Fantastic artwork and mechanics. Not to miss, even if you are 30 like me.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER is the fourth entry in the BIT.TRIP franchise, and the first that I played. You play Commander Video, an alien humanoid who crashes onto an odd planet. The goal of the game is to run to the end of the level while dodging hazards and acquiring gold. Getting the gold is optional, but getting all of it lets you play a bonus stage at the end of the level. The game is divided into three zones, each of which contains twelve levels, the last of which functions as a boss fight of sorts. The story isn't of note unless you've played the whole series.
The big clencher in my decision to recommend this is the difficulty. If you hit an obstacle, you are forced to start at the beginning of the level. This isn't a problem for most levels, as the obstacles don't get too tough early on and most levels last around a minute. However, certain parts of the game feel downright frustrating (1-11, for instance, has only been beaten by around 13.9% of game owners as of writing) as the level of reflex demanded climbs higher and higher. At times, it feels less like I'm getting better at the game and more like I'm memorizing the level's patterns.
If you're the patient sort who likes games requiring reflex or just wants to experience the series, I'd get this game on sale. Otherwise, I'd stay away.

At first glance the four factions of Warhammer 2 seem less distinct. There are two flavours of Elves, High and Dark, and two kinds of animal-people—the dinosaur-riding Lizardmen and the mad science rats called Skaven. All are good at magic, all have a mix of melee and ranged specialists. In play, they're more different than expected. Like the armies added to the first game as DLC, extra care has been made to make them mechanically distinct in both battles and campaign.
The Skaven, for instance, spread corruption like the Vampire Counts did, but this corruption affects their own troops as well as enemies. Instead of squatting in a castle brooding while the surrounding lands turn dark and then finally slouching across the border, the Skaven are constantly moving, ruining each province—literally, their settlements appear as ruins to casual inspection—and moving on. They struggle with hunger as well; their food supplies run low if they stop raiding. Playing as the Skaven you're discouraged from settling down.

I love this game, I have put about 40 hours into it now and I got hooked to it the day I bought it. Naval Action is a open world ship sailing MMO simulator. It is very similar to Eve if anyone knows about it, but it isn't as overwhelming as Eve. There is several different nations you can choose from, from the major players back in the 1700s like Great Britian and Spain, to the smaller nations like Sweden, Dutch, and even the Pirates. There is trading, crafting, and conquering territory with other people in the nation that you choose. There are PVE and PVP servers, both in US and EU.
The map is the entire Carribean, with the entire coast line from half way up the Eastern US, all the way down to the Northern coastline of Brazil. There are a huge amount of ports you can travel to and see what they produce and in what quantities as you plan out trade routes to make money or to craft ships, items, upgrades, etc. As you level up, you can sail bigger ships more proficiently as you are able to command more crew to sail these larger ships.
Surprisingly, I have yet to see bugs besides a small graphical glitch when sailing around. One thing thing that can be a pro or a con is that traveling to different places takes time while in the open world part of the game. You can simply alt-tab or watch a video on another monitor, if you have one, to pass the time. When you are in the open world sailing around, the wind matters a lot in how you travel around, so you must plan accordingly or it will take forever to get to the place you want to go, and wind defintely matters in battles you get into. When you get into a battle, you and the other party will be put into an instance and other people from the two nations can join the battle while it is going on, but they have five minutes to do so before the battle is locked to the players or AI within the battle. In battle, you can sink other ships, board them and capture their ship, or run away if you feel the battle isn't going into your favor, but the enemy can stop you from running away if they can hit you at least once every one minute and 30 seconds.
It is still far from finished and the devs seem pretty decent as they listen to the feedback the community gives. Also, they have plenty of ships being added into the game as the game moves through early access, along with UI changes and other features added to the game.
I just have to say I am addicted and can't wait to play more of this game.

Naval action is a early access public alpha that takes place in there sailing era of between 1600-1800 in the Caribbean.
The main premise of the game is to bring the age of sail to people who love naval combat.
Pros: a massive MASSIVE map to explore, raid, trade or sink you way around in ships ranging from the civilian to heavily armed warships.
Great amount of factions instead of just Britain, Spain, Netherlands and France. There are 8 at this time.
Combat is heavily based on three things. Which is good. Speed, skill and teamwork. ( a group of small ships working in unison can literally sink a 3rd rate warship.)
The Dev team have clearly done their research by reflecting the fact that the amount of guns didn't always win.
A trade system which works on supply and demand much like Port Royale franchise. It is hard however as prices don't stay the same as players and wars affect both.
Cons: there is no marker on the map to show your position in relation to mission markers. (I had a mission near Jamaica but I found that I was next to Bermuda)
There is no way points to help with navigation which both these points can cause huge stress when trying to get to your mission. Especially when you get storms around you.
There is no way to test drive ships to see if they are for you and you how they are played.
Base resources are too expensive and experience gain from battles is low. It takes 20 missions to get 1000 experience points.
You should be able to ring the ships bell any time with each button press to ring it. ( make use of morse code)
There should be a progression table to show what you gain from promotions.
It is highly function and extremely thrilling with combat and sailing physics and cannon and projectile physics too. It is worth as an early alpha £25-£35 due to its currently working and huge amount if features alongside a already vast community and friendly and dedicated Dev team.

There is a term thrown around in gaming that refers to moments, or segments, as "cinematic."Those people usually are referring to large and epic set pieces that involve a lot of explosions and lots of action, something that'd you'd see in a typical Hollywood summer blockbuster.
Thirty Flights of Loving, much like Chung's first game, "Gravity Bone," utilizies cinema's most precious and powerful gift, editing. Chung cuts scenes together that not only builds tension, but suspense and excitement in a truly invovative and creative way.
It is a short experience, but well worth your time if you enjoy caper stories and a truly "cinematic" experience.
It's a game that lends credence to the argument that video games can be considered art.
Your choices don't matter, the graphics aren't good, and the story is barely there, but somehow this dreamlike caper manages to be mesmerizing.

*Update 28/07/2016
Skullgirls was released in 2012 for Xbox Live and Playstation Network for both Xbox360 and PS3. When the game launched, I supported this game with all my breath. Its a fast, fluid, and easy to pick up fighting game with gorgeous art and a kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtrack by Michiru Yamane. However, as the years went on, the community for this game made me put it down, time after time again. The game was Re-released on PS3 and Xbox Live as Skullgirls: Encore, and then RE-Re-released on PS4 as Skullgirls: 2nd Encore, which basically just added a voiced story mode, an art gallery, and a challenge mode, which have all found their way into the PC release by now.
What made this game's community more toxic than some of the other fighting game communites (I'm looking at you SF IV, DoA V, and MK9), was the endless amount of drama on the SkullHeart forums, on the Steam Discussions, and on Steam Groups. Fighting games as a WHOLE have always had some of the worst gaming communites I've ever seen because everyone becomes so hyper-competitive that no one had fun. Do not let the art style discourage you from playing this fighting game masterpiece.
Under the hood, this game combines my favorite gameplay traits from Marvel vs Capcom 1 and 2 and mixes that with its own unique features such as the Infinite Prevention System and the variable battle system.
If you are a newcomer to fighting games, this game has easily the most comphrehensive fighting game tutorial I have seen. It will teach you not only how to perform specific actions but why and when you should do it. There are even character specific tutorials, so you can have a better understanding of the characters which best interest you. When you are ready to play with others, the online play is handled by the fantastic GGPO netcode.
Based off the success of the Indiegogo campaign, expect semi-frequent updates and free additional characters in the coming year up to a total of thirteen. The PC edition of the game also not only operates the smoothest, but will get all the content updates first, so you can be among the first people to discover new characters and their technology.
The fact that this is going for $14.99 is honestly a crazy good value. Heck, the two-pack and the four-pack are even more mind boggling. I honestly feel this game is a lot better than many fighting games that have been released on many platforms over the years at full retail price.
Mechanics are a little repetative, but still a decent story line.  As far as multiplayer, I don't enjoy the randomness of the race you play.

You are a space marine, a power armored super warrior. Fight space orcs with chainsaw swords & gyrojet rocket machineguns. Kick the alien scum off the Emperor's planet & save the day, hopefully things don't get any worse.
Despite how it may look, this isn't a 3rd person cover shooter. It's more of a run & gun/hack 'n' slash game with an emphasis of getting up close & personal w/ the enemy. Sadly, multiplayer is mostly dead.
Brilliant character design along with the most well written script all put into a well executed fighting game.

The only fighting game that will be able to beat this game will be Guilty Gear Xrd, but it'll take quite some time before it's released. Seriously, this game is awesome. It offers plenty of combat style variety, interesting modes, perfect execution, great technical realisation, great competitive scene, and, what's really important, great tutorial system so even the complete newbies to fighting games can quickly pick up on some of the advanced gameplay aspects. The only drawback I can find right now is somewhat limited roster, but that will be expanded with soon to come DLC characters (there's one already available for free).

This is an semi-rhythm, auto-scrolling platformer where you time your actions to avoid death.  Your basic actions are jump, kick, block, and duck -- and combinations of those.  Pretty simple stuff, but the challenging part is to do this quickly without too much error.  This is really a test of hand-eye coordination and memory (due to the levels being the same each time).  Rhythm and music are a key part of this game, but the game also relies on non-rhythmic actions as well.  As for any negatives, I have read some complaints about levels not having check points.  The lack of level check points is actually part of the appeal!  But do consider that the levels take no more than three minutes to complete so it's not as if you are losing a lot of invested time here when you die.  And speaking of dying, you will die a lot but in a fun and challenging way.  In the end, this is one of those games that doesn't look all that fun until you actually play it.  I've fallen in love with this game, and indeed, it is highly addictive!

In their simplicity, sprites can carry a hell of an emotional wallop. Back in the glory days of 16-bit RPGs, every game had its tearjerker. -- SPOILERS FOR 20 OR SO YEAR OLD GAMES TO FOLLOW -- Think of Celes' attempted suicide in Final Fantasy VI or Lucca's mom's legs being crushed in Chrono Trigger. --SPOILERS END--
To the Moon repurposes that style into combat-free, gameplay-light interactive story about the compromises we make to our dreams to be with the ones we love. Taking a cue from Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (and a bit of We Can Remember It For You Wholesale, P.K.♥♥♥♥♥♥s short story that became Total Recall), the player takes control of a pair of specialists trained to alter memories of the dying so they can feel like they had no regrets in their final moments.
The story has a lot to say about memory, life, death, love, autism, social expectations, and the responsibilities of science. A lot to unpack in a short amount of time. Worth it if you don't mind crying like a baby.

Causing magazine explosions really seems to be just random chance luck. Ammo like grape shot is very problematic and you'll often times kill more enemy crew with regular balls than grape. In the end you are buying potential. If the devs do not execute, it'll be forgotten and another dev, maybe even Sid, will come out with something that will make this look something a kid barfed up. This game is Grand Strategy incarnate. When I think of the phrase "Grand Strategy" I get this image in my head of massive armies moving accross the world bringing everything under the control of a single force while a mastermind sits behind the scenes directing everything, planning out every encounter, scheming for the future.
Total War: Warhammer 2 is the best possible visualization of that mental image.
When I play strategy games, I like having stuff to do, and Warhammer 2 provides PLENTY. The turn-based system allows me the chance to think about everything I'm doing and plan ahead instead of just going through the motions up until something happens, I feel like every choice I make is working towards the greater goal and seeing my territory expand outward is satisfying and fun. Building up my lords and heroes and completing missions for them gives a sense of attatchment to my strongest heroes, and watching them grow from nothing to hulking gods of war is an experience all on it's own.
And then the direct real-time battles provide an amazing mix between turn-based and real-time that lets you get in the middle of the action and direct everything personaly, watching those armies you've been growing and those heroes and lords you've been strengthing up decimate opposing forces, leaving massive piles of corpses in their wake, I find myself saving replays frequently just so I can go back and re-watch the carnage again.
Warhammer 2 is an amazing game on it's own and is the best example of what Grand Strategy can be if enough love and care is put in to it.
If you like Warhammer and Strategy, then this is your new favorite game.

This game...I don't even know where to begin.
1. The game was very heart warming and extremely wonderful. Each scene had you begging for more of an experience, more pieces to the puzzle, more events that would open up the world just a little bit as well as tugging on your shirt to check everything and anything in every moment.
2. The game is so...Emotional. I was in tears at some parts, and outright laughing at others. This game tugged on my heartstrings more than any other game ever has, and I really enjoyed it throughout the entire story. THE FEELS MAN, THE FEELS.
3. The concept of this game is so surreal in what it truly is. If I could have a single wish before I died, that would be so cool! Provided, people going into my head isn't so appealing...But it was so lightheartedly emotional up until the very end.
4. The atmosphere of the game, regardless of the pixelated graphics, was gorgeous. It goes to show that it doesn't take fancy graphics to lure people in. I couldn't believe the amount of detail that went into each scene, whether it be the lighthouse all the way down to the small squirrels running about...I couldn't ask more from a game.
All in all...The game is amazing. For some, it'll be a one time playthrough. But for me, I would do it again and again and again, because the story is just that wonderfully great. I wish for them to make a second episode in the series, and not just leave it at that. I loved this game, and I won't regret purchasing it, even after the multiple times I said I wouldn't. Naval Action is a very addictive, slow-paced, deep game with plenty to do that all comes together to make for a very enjoyable experience that is best enjoyed in a group.
As it stands now, only about a week out of Early Acess, Naval Action is a healthy, promising game with a friendly and invested playerbase. The game focuses a lot on basing its mechanics on players' actions in the game world, and as such you can expect to see a vibrant world form as a result. The game's features are still being fleshed out so there is certainly still room to give players more control over the world they play in, but you see from developer's responses on the forums that they plan to give players the tools we need to make this world ours.
So what can you do exactly in Naval Action's giant sandbox? First off, you can fight basic battles with AI. These battles usually come in the form of 'missions', or Naval Action's equivalent to a quest. Missions simply order you to defeat the enemy at a given random location in the sea in exchange for bonus XP and gold. These rather mundane missions are the mainstay of the grinding experience for most players as it is a straightforward way to progress and gain the experience and gold needed to get the next best ship. Battles with the AI can also come in the form of hunting down AI trader ships or patrol fleets by yourself or with a group. Engaging with traders is a good way to try and make some money by “commandeering” valuable goods or ships, and engaging with patrols is a good way to get yourself killed; unless you bring friends.
You can also of course fight with other players. You can do organized PvP in the form of Small or Large battle queues that you sign up for every few minutes in any port, or you can hunt down players in the open world. You can also participate in large port battles with other players against other players to wrest control over cities and the resources they provide.
And of course, you can trade and craft in order to make lots of money. These latter options require a lot of knowledge and time to do right, but can pay in dividends. It is also important to note here that any decent ships you might wish to command must be player-made, and crafting ships is no small task. The economy of this game is one of great potential for the budding capitalist.
Combat as a whole is very well done in Naval Action. It is deep and too complex to go into detail here, but know that this is no arcade style ship game. It is slow paced, but can be incredibly intense, especially in PvP and in large battles. Ships are detailed and well designed, the open world is a delight to sail in, and there are plenty of friends and enemies to be made playing this game. I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone interested in games like EvE that maybe are looking for something more than context menus in their combat scenarios.

I'd like to start off by saying this game is WORTH A TRY. Much like reality, the first few games were hit and/or miss, but none-the-less a learning experience. If you pay attention and invest in the right research you will slowely start progressing until you have enough money to do as you please.
Upgrading to a new office sounded nice at first, but the game suddenly introduces new elements with little-to-no explaination as to what the benefits of each are. I didn't know what the point of training myself and my employees was because I was too busy trying to develop profitable games, and saw little to no effect of training in their production quality. I wish this was more explained and clearly reflected in productivity of the employee.
Research in innovative game ideas comes slow, but that is because you forget what historically was available at the time. I found myself looking for things I wanted my game to have, forgetting that the technology had yet to develop. At the same time, I felt that I wasn't going anywhere with little to research and not knowing what I needed to do to unlock something as simple as 3D graphics.
The music is quarky and fun, but the 2 tracks noticeably repeat, and I wish there was even just 1 more track. (It would be cool if the background track reflected your current financial situation)
The graphics are what they are, but that's not to say they aren't appropriate. I have no complaints with the style, and appreciate the small gestures your character makes when thinking during development.
Overall, I am very pleased and have enjoyed this game thus far. The random topics offer some replayability, and I always want to see if I can get just a little further before going bankrupt.

God this game is just the biggest meme of the year isn't it? Especially for the PC community, however even though this is DO NOT BUY THIS GAME review, the game had a few things right about it.
So to start off with the positives:
1.) Supply Drops: Supply drops should be a negative thing for a COD game right? Even though I would rather have no supply drops, this game did them better than the others. The fact that DLC weapons could be rightfully unlocked to a season pass owner was the main reason I made supply drops a positive thing for the game. You could also get MOST weapons with scrap which isn't too hard to earn in the game.
2.) Zombies in Spaceland: Zombies in Spaceland is actually a good zombies map not only for infinite warfare, but IMO zombies in general. For me in zombies I look for a well balanced map of challenges, and easy tasks to complete. Zombies in Spaceland wasn't a serrious map by any means and was just fun and layed back. The map to me had a really good vibe and getting higher rounds was a bit of a challenge for certain people. The easter egg was also really easy but the boss fight was a little difficult. I did not really like the other zombies maps however as you may read later on.
3.) The Zombies Leveling Up/ Keys System: The tittle itself is pretty explanitory, I like how there are no prestiges and you don't have to end your high round game to prestige for more XP. Also the key system is really fair in zombies.
Now onto the negative things about IW
1.) The Optimization: The PC port for this game was actually really good for a COD game, however the game just did not run well on many systems including mine. The game always had stuttering and lag issues for me in zombies and multiplayer.
2.) The REST of Zombies: Now this is going to be a long one since I am more of a zombies fan than a multiplayer fan. The zombies for this game was complete dog♥♥♥♥♥♥ The only good map was spaceland, and everything after that was downhill in terms of inovation, and the good vibes for the maps. Rave in the Redwoods to many people was there favorite due to it being easy, but it was TOO easy to get to a high round on the map. Shaloin Shuffle is OKAY I guess, but not at all up to standard of a zombies map and I would say down as one of the worst zombies map if this game did not make any more maps. Shaloin just has a bit too much in it for the casual fanbase IW zombies was thriving off of. I do like a challenge, but I feel this game had a casual fanbase and this map turned them away from the game. Attack of the Radioactive Thing is just as aids as the name of it implies. Everything from the easter egg, to the size, to the lag issues on the map are there. The map is extremely hard and only for hardcore zombies players which if you stayed after shaloin, this map 100% turned you away if you are a casual player. The map is hard and boring to put it simply. Now Beast from Beyond I just could not play for 5 minutes without getting SUPER BORED. The map is just bad, everything about it including the extinction aliens. I couldn't even get power on without quitting it.
3.) The DEV'S Lack of PC Support: They simply did not care about the PC community as COD usually doesn't. They did not listen to us, and we got updates weeks later than even xbox did. Lack of communication and a community to talk to, killed this game on PC after the first 2 months.

Perhaps the most well-known Bit.Trip game, Runner is a.. music-influenced runner where you go left to right to reach a certain goal.
From the start, it seems like a cool game but with almost no replayability, no checkpoints, and difficulty based on memorization it definitely isn't a title I can suggest.
So its a runner, but not an endless runner. There isn't randomized stages or anything that varies from each playthrough. That's fine, but the levels are extremely linear. No alternate paths or anything to mix it up.
So in the levels themselves, you jump, dodge, and.. Actually, I think that's it.
Its fairly entertaining, but its nothing special.
The biggest flaw in this game is the difficulty. Once you start getting through the game, the levels will become much more difficult with ridiculous obstacles. One mistake and its all the way back to the beginning.
Yeah, no checkpoints.
The difficulty isn't so much about testing your reflexes, but about memorizing the stages. That's all it comes down to. Remember exactly which order you have to jump or dodge in.
This leaves the gameplay experience to be horribly repetitive and just tedious.
For that reason, I don't consider this a good game.
I would have much rather seen the game branch out with open paths and be more about perfecting your performance and scores with extra music aspects - similar to Guitar Hero, but as a runner. Unfortunately, its nothing like that and has almost no replayability.
No story, as with most games like this.
The visuals are decent, but I really dislike seeing a combination of such a low res sprite with full 3d backgrounds. I just don't think the combination works very well. Apart from that, it looks alright.
The music is probably the game's best part. Some of the tracks really sound great. The game itself has music tones play through the levels so there's definitely an influence of it in the design, but it never feels like an actual rhythm game.
fine
I felt like this game was just wasted potential. It should have been built around fun levels with multiple paths rather than memorizing patterns.
I don't recommend this game.
However, I do recommend its sequel!
Bit.Trip Presents: Runner 2 adds almost everything I wanted to see. Better visuals, multiple pathways in levels, checkpoints, a bunch of characters, and a much smoother experience. Its a pretty good game.
If you're interested in a runner, skip this one and check out Runner 2.

Ok, as you can see this game called bit trip RUNNER is pretty much that, a platformer on rails where you dodge obstacles  and -only if you want to unlock everything like I did- collect floating gold bars, and not much else. This game works great, super fluid, and is compatible with a 360 controller, sadly that's the only thing that I can appreciate from it. Its funny because some people claim that this game is "hard" and "fast paced", and let me tell ya, is none of those
1) Its not really hard, with some practice you will end up memorizing the secuence of the obstacles, you are just avoiding them without having control of your character, other than kicking, jumping, ducking, reflecting (you have some kind of orange bar that reflects only one kind of proyectile), or jumping higher from a spring, and thats one of the cheapest flaws in the game that makes it "hard". There are some kind of pink tiles that work like springs, all you have to do is press up or the Y button and you can jump higher than the regular jump, obviously there are sections that you need to do this in order to beat a level, how can you screw that up? usually you'll need to press the button right before you miss the pink tile because if you press it too early you'll land 3 pixels behind of the very spot you need to land on because, most of the time, in the spot where you should have landed there was a golden bar that you have to collect and if you landed right behind it you won't touch it and its game over for you if you're playing it on perfect difficulty and you lose whenever you miss anything you have to collect. Another cheap flaw is the perfect difficulty, because as I said before whenever you miss anything like the golden bar you lose, thankfully when that happens you can try again because it takes you BACK TO THE BEGINING of the level.Every.Time. This game wants you to be sooo perfect that when you press one button one instant before or after the instant the game wants or if you don't land on one magical pixel the game wants, hell even if you are almost half of a second late you lose and you have to restart the level at once. That's what make the game hard, because if you play it on normal or easy its pretty much, no, its the same crap, with the only difference of not having to collect EVERY GOLDEN BAR.
2) fast paced? no, simple as that, this ain't sonic, is just commander video. You can see whats ahead you, unless you're playing the bonus stages where your field of view is reduced
People claim that the gameplay is brilliant, I didn't find it like that, at all, not even close. This game gets repetitive in a few hours, there were times where I could tell that the developers recycle some sections in many levels, to the point that I could even guess the algorithm that dodges the obstacles
I gave this game and its sequel a chance, bought them during the sale so I did't spend too much money, but I was so dissapointed that I feel it would've been the same even if they were free
Then again, you can pretty much tell what kind of game it is ny just looking at it, but I saw some many positive reviews saiying that the gameplay is brilliant, fast paced, and unique. I bought that and ended up dissapointed because I found this game average at its best. Even at the end of the day I didn't expect too much from it, no matter how many people recommended it, but still deep inside I expected something at least better than what it looked like, and this wasn't the case
Bit Trip Runner is a bad game? nah, its not, just because you see that red downvoting hand doesn't mean that this game sucks, not really. You may find it entertainingand all but thats about it, not a really memorable indie game tbh
This game took me around 30 hours to unlock everything, including the freaking achievements because whenever I buy a videogame I want to beat it and unlock everything that I can, and these achievements weren't that hard, just annoying, and made my experience way longer that it had to be, because I couldn't find any replay value, once you unlock everything that's it for this game, same thing happened me with the sequel. And speaking of which, people also claim that the sequel was uperior because they made runner "better" and with more variety, and the only variety there were some minimal thing that didn't make it harder, hell I thought it was way more easier since they made the hit detection more merciful on the sequel, because on the first runner whenever you thought you collected the golden bar you ended up losing because you missed by one pixel. The only variety on Runner 2 is that you can play as other characters and actually find alternative exits that you need to follow in order to unlock stuff
Boss fights are pointless, they are basically an extra level for each zone
One last thing, this game is supposed to be a rythm game but Guitar Hero was more of a rythm game than this, here you have a generic bgm for each zone (there are 3 zones with 12 levels each, including the "boss" level) and whenever you collect these red crosses the bgm changes a bit, and every obstacle that you dodge makes a silly sound. When you keep dodging the secuence it kind of plays a melody but it doesn't have that kind of an impact unlike GH, some people may find it charming but not me
TL;DR meh, wouldn't reccomend this nor its sequel

Wow.  This game is beautiful.
If you hated the Assassin's Creed naval games for being too fast paced and comically unrealistic (massive ships turning in place and ignoring the wind, for example), this game is for you.
Starting out there is a bit of a grind.  However, with how beautiful the game is and the engaging combat (for those that love combat from the age of sail and feeling like Captain Jack Sparrow raking an English trading brig), I haven't found that to be an issue.  With a full time job and real life engagements, I've been blowing through the ranks for the past week.
It also helps to play PvP and explore the
map.  From the East Coast up to North Carolina, the entire Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico, all the way down to the northeastern coast of South America.  All owned by several nations and pirates.  All at war.

The game that opened the gate to the Warhammer universe for me.
Warhammer 40K: Space Marine plunges you into the dark, dreary Warhammer universe as Captain Titus of the Ultra Marine Chapter with the mission of cleansing a planet of an Ork invasion, but as the mission progresses, mysteries unfold and reveal that there was so much more going on behind the scenes...
With Space Marine being the first Warhammer game I ever played, there was a lot I didn't really understand, but years later, after having come back to it on Steam, I can appreciate it a lot more. This game is a fantastic hybrid between a hack n' slash and TPS that appeals to fans and strangers of the series, alike. If you're into the series, this is a no-brainer, if you don't know what to think about Warhammer, this is a great place to either get into the series, or to just play for about 8-10 hours through the campaign.
On top of the campaign, there's also quite a hidden gem of a multiplayer mode to be had. The only downside to this entire game I can think of, is that there is such a thin crowd online. Space Marine offers a very clean and balanced community and the ability to customize your character to a pretty good extent. Absolutely worth the full price, and if you're into the multiplayer, the DLC is something to pick up, too.

Even counting the entire Dawn of War series, this is probably my favorite Warhammer 40K game.
The single player campaign is rock-solid. It's not going to knock your socks off in terms of narrative depth, but it absolutely nails the look and feel of WH40K.
This game covers all of the Warhammer 40K bases. You fight Orks. You fight the forces of Chaos. You blow things up and you kill tons of bad guys.
When you get to multiplayer, you have a wealth of options in terms of weaponry and armor. You can choose paint schemes from the old tabletop and miniatures games, or you can create your own. Armor comes in sets, but you can mix and match the pieces to create a space marine who looks just the way you want.
Loadouts are made up of a class, a weapon, a backup, and some perks. Each class has its own built-in abilities, but it is your weapon and your perks that really dial in your playstyle.
The Assault gets a jetpack, and it's just as fun to use as it looks and sounds. The Devastator gets the heavy and long range weaponry. They have high damage potential and can be a little tougher than the other two classes at the cost of being a little slower. The tactical marine is surprisingly maneuverable, and falls somewhere in between the other two. Not quite as mobile as the Assault, not quite as tough or as good at long range as the Devastator.
There's a nice balance to the multiplayer, though the population is pretty low this far out from release. Also, there's often "that guy" you'll run into with a cheap, super effective, or heavily-practised loadout. The early matches in multiplayer can be a bit rough due to some of those cheap and/or veteran players combined with most of the gear and perks not being unlocked yet. If you stick with it a little bit, you'll unlock more of the equipment and you'll find your niche. There are definitely certain playstyles that hard-counter others, but for the most part teamwork and positioning matter more than the gear you bring.
The only issue specific to PC multiplayer is the effectiveness of sniper-type weapons. They weren't used much console-side and still have their drawbacks, but with mice being so accurate some of the sniper-style weapons have become way more effective in PvP than they really should be. It's not often a problem, but on certain maps you may find yourself being killed from across the map or at any range as soon as they spot you; due to the ease with which they can hit you. Space Marines are big, bulky, and a bit slow. Most of the combat is designed around this, but players using these sniper-type weapons will often find the nearest vantage point and begin mercilessly destroying you and your team at all ranges. Sometimes, sneaking up on them isn't even enough. If they spot you coming up on them or if you don't kill them before they realize you're there, they can fire just as accurately at close range as long range (even if most of the other weapons outperform in speed or raw damage). It's annoying, and so are some of the Assault players when they catch you alone, but those are hardly deal-breakers.
If you decide to purchase this game, do it for the excellent single-player campaign and the co-op horde mode (which you can play solo and can use to farm some of the weapon challenges). "Annihilation" mode sometimes has players, and it can be very fun, but it's more of a nice bonus than a guarantee.
