Few points to clarify first:
First: I bought this game solely for single-player campaign (I'm not interested in COD-styled MP, zombies, or any other BS)
Second: The last time I played COD was the very first one (yep, the oldest, the WW2 one)
So I finished the campaign, and I got mixed feelings about it. Some things were great, some were quite awful, overall, it was so-so. I'm big sci-fi fan and was looking for good sci-fi story and it was a sci-fi indeed, but the story itself was far too cliche. Acting was incredibly good (10/10) but not all characters are well developed (especially disappointing is the main villain aka John Snow, which is completely shallow, he is just a bad even guy, because... reasons). The rest of the main characters are quite good. The main story ark (4/10) is just dump- bad guys attack, good guys retaliate. Bads are bad and evil, goods are good and heroic. Nothing to see, the story is worthy of cheap paperback sci-fi flick, and saved from being completely awful only by main characters. Ground combat is highly disappointing - I heard this is the way COD are made now: they encourage slow cover-crawling, punishing anything else. This is not fun at all. Every time you get a little ballsy - you immediately got shot. The number of times I died from an enemy I haven't even seen is was way too much. I guess there people who like this type of combat, but I find it extremely tedious and boring - I much prefer run-n-gun approach of a games like new Wallenstein or Doom (or old-school shooters). Guess it is the matter of taste, and I don't like it. Zero-gravity fights are nice idea, but they are even more frustrating, as you don't have a proper cover to hide behind (3/10). Space-flight sim parts were kind-ok (5/10) but a very shallow and simplistic - two weapons (one for small ships, one for big), no inertia/momentum simulation (there is, for example, not problem "reversing" in space) and "ace pilots" which are objective in several missions can not be hit by missiles, they have to be hunted by gun, which could be quite frustrating, especially as there is no 3D map to give situation awareness, so very often as soon as I settled tracking the target, some other ship was locked on me, and I needed to evade, and start hunting over. To an old X-Wind/Tie-Fighter fan like me - it was boring and repetitive. Graphics in the game (especially characters and the settings) were amazing (9/10).
So for simple player campaign - I find it hard to recommend. Besides amazing actors and graphics there is not too much good to say about it. Don't bother unless you get it at a very good discount and are really into sci-fi (I do, but still can't say I enjoyed it very much).
Total: 6/10

Naval Action is not a perfect game.  It's still unpolished, with a rough UI, grindy and clunky level progression, repetative missions.  They just throw new players in, with no explanations or direction.  Obtaining even a moderate size ship is the result of many long hours of combat.  Battles are slow, with small ones taking 30 minutes and larger battles nearer to 90.  Sailing a ship to a distant port can take literal hours of tacking against the wind, with no navigational hints or visible land at where you are in the vast carribean, left guessing your position.
Yet still, this is the best game I have played in a very long time.  Just a few months ago, before I knew of this game, and in the middle of the Aubrey Maturin series, I found myself wondering "Why isn't there a good, multiplayer age of sail game?"  I asked my friends, and they all agreed this was strangely missing from the world.
Naval Action is everything I had hoped for.  The games slow pace means that combat, particularly PvP, is high stakes and suspenseful.  Rushing in towards an enemy, closing the distance while their broadsides crash into your ship unanswered, only to swing around at the last second and run yardarm-to-yardarm beside them, firing your carronades loaded with grape shot onto their decks as they bear, and boarding them in the smoke, is potentially one of the most gratifying experiences that modern gaming has to offer, with the possible exception of large battles.
Imagine 40 ships, some of them with over 100 massive cannons, running with wind, all firing at the enemy fleet at the same size a quarter mile away. closing in to a chaotic 80 ship melee at close quarters, blinded by thick clouds of smoke, fighting both sides of your ship while trying desperately not to smash head-on into friends and foes alike.  This routine occurrance is one of the most epic sights I have ever encounted in any videogame.
I have found myself wary of Early Access games as of late, due to abandonment or extremely bad development decisions.  But not here, the devs seem to pay attention to player's input, and the game, though unfinished, is already in a very playable state.  Though there is not much 'content' as far as missions go, the sheer fun and complexity inherent in sailing battles keep it fresh, and skill very much matters, as a more experienced player in a smaller ship could win through maneuvering and tactics alone.
I can't recommend this game enough.  If you like the age of sail, and are looking for a game to sink quite a bit of time into, this is it.

Although being in Early Access, Naval Action has a very good foundation upon which the game is being built upon. They started with the very basics by first developing, fleshing out and testing the combat module years ago. It is clear that this is where Naval Action shines.
It's not a true simulator by any means, however, it takes whatever realism it can and molds it into a fantastic gameplay experience. Sailing mechanics such as manually controlling the yards is extremely fun and rewarding as your maneuvering the battlefield trying to line up a perfect broadside. Constantly keeping an eye on the direction of the wind, the angle of your yards, the angle and direction of your targets yards and ship. Outmaneuvering your opponent can be a truly rewarding experience and most definitely will help you in coming out on top and surviving a battle.
The 'overworld', or 'open world' part of Naval Action is very much so a work-in-progress. However, it shows us the potential of Naval Action as a large-scale war between multiple nations trying to outsmart eachother through stategical prowess and manipulating the political landscape. Naval Action has a long way to go but it has shown us that the concept works, beautifully so, and they plan to make it so much better.
Albeit a tad bit pricey for being an Early Access game, I personally believe it to be one of the best we've seen thus far. So if you like the Age of Sail in general, perhaps the masterpiece film 'Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World', the great series 'Black Flag', you might want to check out this game.

Game Dev Tycoon is exactly what you expect: a videogame developer tycoon. You are supposedly warped back in time to 1985 to a reference-filled (hint: flux capacitor) garage, where you begin your endeavour into the gaming history books. Like any developer who travels in time to 1985, you are absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥at programming because the technology is so different.  You have a computer that's literally worse than a modern graphing calculator, yet you decide to make games. If you are successful, you can grow your garage into an actual company, with actual people, and actual results. You have to strategically market your games for specific audiences (you know, like "T for Teen" or "E for Everyone") and try to match genres to different gaming platforms to different audiences.
For example, kids. In the real world, devices like the Nintendo DS (which reminds me, tell you later) or the great old Gameboy are very popular. Add a role-playing/ adventure game like the Legend of Zelda, and you're all set. Target marketing at young people, and kaboom: ez skins, ez life. Although "skins" probably means nothing to the world of the 1980s and 90s.
So, now, about the NDS. The developers, in an effort to give you a good laugh, and avoid copyright infringement, have sort of parodied every console on the market. If I'm correct, the Nintendo GameCube's counterpart is the GameSphere. It's actually kinda freaking amazing.
I'll give GDT a solid 8, maybe an 8.5 because of the extensive workshop mod support.
TL;DR: Time travel to 1985, make games, ♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥es, get money. 8.5/10

You know, I'm fine with the whole "short story as a game" thing. There isn't much actual gameplay here and that's really OK. I'm ok with there being no dialogue, just a wah-wah sound like when the adults talk in Charlie Brown. It's like a silent movie. I'm fine with the comically bad art style, where everything is boxes and rectangles and polygons. Graphics don't make a story. I'm even fine with an incredibly ambiguous story that leaves you to piece together flashbacks and fragments.
What I'm not OK with is the complete lack of
here. You can see that I played this game for 30 minutes. That's all there is to it. 30 minutes covers two "stories," one in which you relive the last days of a heist team, and one in which you are a secret agent of some kind, doing missions for a "contract agency." I played this game for 30 minutes and saw everything there was to see. I didn't speed-run the thing; I wanted to drink in the little slices of life the developers were giving me, but there was barely a thimbleful to drink. The second story especially could have done with more missions. The first one was short, but involves you stealing a waiter's uniform at a party and literally "bugging" a VIP. The second mission has you breaking into rooms with freon and a hammer and taking pictures of birds before they explode. But, instead of allowing you to spend a little more time in their world, the developers simply have you get shot at the end of the second mission and tell you it's over.
I found the whole thing intensely unsatisfying. If you're going to tell tiny stories with games, then great, DO THAT. Tell stories. Make a whole anthology. Build a world and let me play in snippets of it. Don't charge me 5 bucks for two incredibly short experiences that blow up their premises within ten minutes of starting them.

If you're used to playing normal difficulty at other games, I recommend playing easy on this one, and don't try the most difficult setting unless you are a god.

When I first saw the trailer (long before it was on Steam) I fell in love with this game.
I could barely wait for the English version to be announced, I was/am playing it from the time of the close beta. I even got several friends to try it and at most of them played it beyond level 40 or 60.
At first there were only 3 continents, the quests and stages there are in perfect balance as you level up ... meaning just as you complete the quests for your level you almost instantly gain a level up. Very rarely a replay of a stage is needed, and where it is, it is because of greater dificulty or some big quest so you do get proper reward for the replay.
Up to around level 45-50 the gameplay is like a symhpony both in pve and (specially) pvp for people of similar (+-10) levels.
Then updates came ... continents 4, 5 and now even 6. Each of them required more and more unneeded grinding, each introduced more luck (money) needed to gain the strongest of items. The management (be it Webzen or the developers) ruined the present and/or the future of the game.
If you have friends to play it ... I would highly reccomend it for the pve and pvp experience to level 50, but if you only rely on the community you will either find too weak (rarely) or too strong (some of them "pay to win") players. Almost nothing in between to properly compare and measure your skills.
Notable cons:
It's not easy (unless spending real money) to get inventory extensions or skill resets or class changers. For the last two you can get them sometimes by not logging for 30 days as part of "returned player" rewards.
Inventory space can be tight even with few extensions.
Changing characters is a bit slow.
Notable pros:
Great combo system, useful professions, fun and/or challenging achievements/legends.
As there is only town space and "stage" space, if you are action hungry you wont have an empty stomach. Even if you want to wander around, you can wander in the town and the stages, there are beautiful landscapes, buildings and so on.
The "ultimate" skill, the rage skill, the visuals and the storyline to obtain them were damn well worth it for me.
INTRUSION as the ultimate combination of pve and pvp experience.
Problem of this game is its repetition. After you finish some area, you are going there 2 more, 3 more, 4 more times on increasing difficulty.

I bought the Legacy Edition on a heavy discount a couple of weeks ago which actually turned out to be cheaper than buying Infinite Warfare by itself on Steam. Anyway I pretty much bought it purely for Modern Warfare Remastered but since I got this with it as well I decided to give it a crack.
To begin with I am going to state that MP and Zombie Mode are both completely dead and therefore Infinite Warfare gets an automatic "Not Recommended" since two thirds of the package is unplayable. Therefore this will only be a review of the campaign. I will break this down into several sections: story and characters, visuals and performance and gameplay and replay value.
The story is just... stupid... I can't put any other way, it is just dumb and not a fun way. The characters are not memorable, there are multiple sections in the game where you lose comrades in arms and it's clear that you are supposed to feel sad because of it. You don't feel sad because the game doesn't earn it, all the characters are one dimensional and tedious, spouting nonesense and cliches. The worst of the bunch is the primary antagonist, he says the dumbest♥♥♥♥♥♥I have heard from any vilain, anywhere and he says it unironically. He is so deadly serious when he says his idiotic lines that I actually laughed quite a few times which I don't believe is a reaction the writes were gunning for.
It's not a bad looking game and it peforms reasonably well on my mid/high end rig (GTX1080 + E6700). While I didn't have any framerate dips I couldn't help but compare the visuals to Titanfall 2 which is another futuristic shooter that came out in the same release period as IW. Without a shadow of a doubt, TF2 is a vastly better looking game.
The gameplay in the campaign is not terrible but not great either, foot on the ground combat is pretty average for a CoD game. A lot of the guns didn't feel that great and sounded pretty poor. This is especially jarring after playing through Modern Warfare Remastered a week ago. MWR absolutely murders IW in terms of the feel of weapons, the sound design and the quality of setpieces. That brings me to another point, there is not a single set piece in IW  that is memorable, this game doesn't have its "Death from Above" or "All Ghillied Up". All of the ground missions feel thoroughly generic and the mechanics that are meant to set it apart such as wall running feel shoehorned in and not organic like they do in Titanfall 2. One thing that I thought that IW did well were the Jackal Missions. IW brings air to air combat with  3 degrees of freedom to CoD franchise and it was the good part. Obviously the Jackal missions aren't as involved or enjoyable as a proper flight/space sim but I thought it was best part of IW.
To close I would like to say that this game isn't worth the asking price and probably not even half of it. For anyone who is seriously considering getting this, know that you are buying a Single Player game because the MP and COOP are dead with critically low concurrent playercount.

TL;DR Yes, I would recommend this game even at its full price. It offers you a deep and well made campaing in the New World that differs from what the first game made. It also offers you a massive Mortal Empires Free-LC if you own the previous game aswell. Some might say it's not worth the price since you need the first game to play the Mortal Empire Free-LC, but I'd just argue that it only means that you got three games with the price of two.
It improved radically from the first game in the series. It has 'only' four playable races in the start of the game, but each race has two different factions to play and the factions differ from each other quite a lot (unlike the "Different starting lord" situation in TW:W1). And since they're going to offer free patches to the main game and the huge Mortal Empire campaing, you're definately gaining enough gaming material for the money. If you're against the DLC policies that companies are using nowadays I think that shouldn't really affect since the game in its current states is already giving you hunderds of hours if you just like Total War games.
Other things that might affect your purchase decision:
The game is rather demanding on your computer and specially in Mortal Empires the turn timers are quite long, but there are options in the game to help you on both occasions. It's even more about the fantasy stuff than the first one was, so if you're more into historical Total War games and don't care about the fantasy element, you might want to skip this one (if you already skipped the first one, since this one went even further).
All and all.. it's not a perfect game and it's not the perfect business model behind the game, but all that aside I still really saw it as a price worthy game, even as someone who can't afford non-sale priced games all that much.

Its more like an abstract art experience than a video game, but the concept of telling a story purely through environment and scenarios, without any real form of dialog, is one I found very interesting. I enjoyed my play-through a lot, and despite it being rather short (I finished it in about 25 minutes, but I explored every environment thoroughly as I played) I didn't feel like I was short-changed.
The story is the whole point of this game, and while not entirely groundbreaking in itself, it is delivered in a way not regularly seen in video games lately; It leaves working out whats going on up to you. If you want to, you can ignore any of the details and sprint for the next area, or you can slow down, look around, and take in all the subtleties.
It may not be a game for most, but I think its a healthy attempt at changing the rules conventional video games treat as gospel, and it should be praised for its effort.

Thirty Flights of Loving? more like Thirty Seconds of Gameplay amirite ha ha ha yeah but no. This game is weird and I love it.
There are seriously few games that can hit the note this one does, with its blend of nonsense non-linearity, unabashed smash-cuts and richly coloured surroundings. Lights and sounds blend and overlap in strange ways. strange, plastic people surge around you. those tiny noises that repeat in your mind are brought to life in an continual flow of conciousness. Overwhelmingly, it gives off the feeling of being in a dream or a half forgotten memory; The places you are have a palpable character & feeling to them, be it the oppresive paranoid rush of an airport or the comfortable warmth in a lantern-lit city roof, but the details of where you are or how you got there are often lost. If I had to compare it to anything, I'd say it's a lot like Yume Nikki, or Cat Soup, or a few songs off of Sawako's Madoromi, in how small and personal it can be, plus the drowsy, near-soporiphic (but in a good way) tone it has. I don't think I've ever played a game that so perfectly captures the feeling of waking up at 5pm in the summer, or even tries to.
This game probably isn't for everyone. It's really damn short, and you can easily blaze through it in 5 minutes or less. However, the length of it is something that doesn't exactly bother me. Actual dreams often get cut off and mixed around and forgotten at both ends, and the game leaves me with a feeling that this is neither the beginning nor the end of what happened here, so it adds to that dreamlike quality for me. Just make sure you know that you're in for a short ride if you buy it. For me, it's like revisitng somewhere in your mind. A recurring dream where you can just drift away and be lost in the whirling colour for a little while. I recommend trying it at 3am, when you're a little sleepy. It can draw you in, that way.

I wanted to make this review short and sweet, but it's hard to stop writing, even when excluding facts that could potentially contaminate an exceptionally well thought-out gaming experience. There's just so much to say. Bad Rats is, simply put, the best single-player puzzle game ever released for the PC. It does so many things right in so many ways that it might be possible to write a thesis on the topic of Bad Rats compared to other single player puzzle shooters. What Invent4 Entertainment has created is simply a masterpiece -- a work of art in the genre. Not only does it engage the mind with mysterious happenings, vagaries, and mostly intelligent dialogue, but also captures the senses with a superb visual style made possible by brilliant technology. And once the initial shock of it all wears off and it becomes possible to peel back the polished layers of sight and sound, there are some excellent puzzles here. Bad Rats doesn't do anything particularly new; it doesn't really innovate in many ways. But what it does is set a new height for all other designers of puzzle games to reach. It still isn't exactly perfect, but it's about as close as I've seen in my tenure playing video games.

Good! But Slow.
I'm not opposed to a 'grind' in a MMO.  I like when games make you work for it, and you have something  to strive for.  This game does that well when it comes to ships, and levels.
What I mean by slow, is the combat itself.  Sure you can destroy a small ship with a large ship with ease, but when it takes 20 minutes for a group of players to kill one large ship, it's just silly, and feels like a big waste of time.  The biggest pain point is that when you destroy a side of a ship, it WILL sink.  There is nothing they, or you can do about it.  You can slow the death by going into survival mode, but death is inevitable.  So my question is. WHY NOT JUST SINK ALREADY!
You cannot accelerate the sinking any faster.  If the armor is down on the ship, and you keep hitting the ship, it doesn't matter at all.  Just pound away for 3 minutes and the inevitable happens, or just turn sail and ride away and wait for it to sink.  JUST SINK, EXPLODE, DIE!
The combat is good.  High skill based shooting, and strategy.  I've been playing solo, so it's not been nearly as fun as it would be with friends, like most games.  I do see a lack of end game in the current state of the game.  You pretty much progress in ships and xp for it's own sake.  The only end game I see is either just disrupting other countries with groups of players killing them, or taking ports, which is difficult, but relatively boring.
Players of POTBS or BBO will see a lot of resemblence in this game, although this game seems more shallow, with less to do.  The boarding function is clicking what you want to do, not actually doing it.  No 'adventure' type thing.  No land based gameplay at all. (granted that was pretty lame in POTBS but it did add depth. Land combat which was boarding combat, farming, gathering ect.)
Community is solid enough.  Lots of questions get answered pretty quickly, and you will have LOTS of questions your first week.  I'd definitely reccommend it if you are playing with friends, and hopefully the devs will come out with some more engaging things in the future, rather than running boring/slow missions, and fighting fleets for the sake of fighting fleets.  PvP is good, and fun, but also rather meaningless unless you go out and hunt players which will not be worth any kind of reward for the most part.

The future is grim.  The future is cockney...
This seems to be one of those games you either love or hate.  I’m definitely in the love camp for this simple yet astonishingly over the top bloodbath.  This was my first contact with the games workshop stuff, and it’s a pretty cool IP.  Playing as Captain Titus, some sort of monastic space warrior lord, complete with chunky baby-blue armour and a few chums, you must save a factory planet from about a bazillion cockney-accented space orcs.  At its core, game design is not very nuanced or progressive; you shoot, grenade, and chainsaw your way through masses and masses of enemies, with little bits of jet-packing here and there.  Despite that, Space Marine is just so much damned fun I could barely put it down, even on my second play through.
For one, this is pure, unadulterated power fantasy with amps turned up to 11. Combat unfolds something like an early Slayer album, as waves upon wave of baddies (who all sound like Hackney cab drivers, for some reason) charge you in cathartic and blissfully chaotic battles which are exhilarating from start to finish. Your green-skinned adversaries often try overwhelm you with sheer numbers, which gives the game a crowd control element not common in these types of shooters; in small numbers, you can paint the walls red with them, but when 30 of the boys run in for a scrum, you’re in for a real slug.  By the end, you will have spilled oceans of blood, as it flies frequently and with reckless abandon.  Add in some great weapons (chain-sword and vengeance launcher, anyone?) and exquisite sound design which adds weight to your weapons and agony to the cries of your foes, and you’ve got one hell of a game.
Second, this game gives you something different in that there’s no cover system and no health packs.  Instead, health is regained by using your melee weapon to gloriously eviscerate any enemies; perhaps you’re also some sort of space vampire?  Anyway, it means you must do some gritty hand to hand fighting, and more crowd control as enemies will try to scrum you when you go to replenish your health, making battles even more desperate and ultimately fun.
Graphically, this is nothing too special, but it runs well on even modest pcs, and I had good framerates all the way.  I enjoyed the story, although I had to hit Wikipedia a few times to understand what was going on in the wider universe as well as some of the terminology.  I also though the music was very fitting, especially as ominous horn blasts herald charges of green fury.  I haven’t tried the multiplayer yet, so I can’t comment on that.
My only real beef is that that Captain Titus and his two buddies are such boring, unemotional and uncharismatic characters. From what i've read online, there are other much more interesting space marine armies, like space vikings, space ninjas and space goths.  Wouldn't you rather play as a space viking?
Even though I’m not a games workshop boy, I had a cathartic blast playing through Space Marine, twice.  It’s not subtle, nuanced, or revolutionary. What it is, is just damn good fun.  I dunno what happened to the devs after THQ went bust, but I’d love to see a sequel or successor to this one day.

Best of its kind since Baldurs Gate II. Speaking of Baldurs Gate is on sale, and it's been 10 years since I got my head around it!

This whole game feels really poorly designed. From map functionality, to the leveling curve, to the quest design, to the encounter design, to vendors and items, every single one of these areas has glaring issues which make enjoying the game difficult if not impossible for me. I was excited by the prospect of a Baldur's Gate like adventure, but instead I'm stuck in Cyseal (the beginning town), scrounging for xp and scared (and bored of being scared) to leave the town proper. So let me go through that list I set out.
The map, and controls in general, are extremely clunky and barebones. You can't click on the map to move the camera, and in fact there's no indicator on the map of where the camera is at all! I spend a great deal of time trying to figure out where I am, where I need to go, and how to get there every time I need to go somewhere that's off screen. The mouse is extremely inaccurate as well. I've had several fights that I've been forced to restart due to characters moving when I issued an attack order. Characters move sluggishly as well. This game screams for a fast forward button.
Party control is a nightmare to top it all off. It should really behave like Baldur's Gate 2, but instead everyone is either together or apart. There is no way of selecting party members individually. It's like playing as a katamari. This is not helped by the poor pathfinding.
The leveling curve is absurd, and this ties into the quest and encounter design. Experience is so hard to come by that it makes the enemies, which are overwhelming in both power and numbers, impossible to beat without casualties (more on that later). So as a result I've been trapped inside the town walls for the entirety of the 6 or so hours I've played. I have all the quests, but nowhere to go with them due to being underleveled and under-directed. It's guesswork and stagnation at its most frustrating.
Lastly the vendors and items are just... unhelpful. There's barely any melee gear in the town (kneecapping fighters and knights from the get go), and it's impossible to get enough resurrection scrolls to keep up with the losses incurred by stepping outside the gates. I've found some places I could dig up, but that would take getting a shovel which is no where to be found.
Overall this has been an incredibly disappointing and frustrating 6 hours. I will keep bashing my head against it because I'm over the 2 hour refund limit, and I don't want my $20 to go to waste. The only enjoyment I've gotten so far out of this game so far is some RP elements and the catharsis of writing this review. As a long time fan of RPGs in all their wonderful flavors I am so, so disappointed. Not a bad game I think, just very, very poorly designed and executed.

Sometimes, you might play a game that you know is bad, but for some reason, you still find it kind of fun. Sometimes, a game's poor design and glitches can be fun and even endearing if you're the right kind of person. One thing that's never fun or endearing, however, are game-breaking glitches that make the game unplayable in some way...
+ Somewhat unique concept of hitting someone/something by throwing a rock at them with your weapon like you would hit a ball with a bat. If that bores you, however, there's also a mode that just lets you fight against people using the somewhat-functional battle system of "move the mouse towards people and move it in a circle to spin".
+ There's an in-game "shop" where you can buy upgrades for your character with gold you get from winning whatever mode you pick.
+- As said before, if you enjoy semi-glitchy/broken games, you'll probably get a good 30 minutes to an hour from this. If you don't, then...
- Unfortunately, even if you do like glitchy games, there's one glitch that's not very fun at all: Sometimes when you get too close to something that's moving (I think that's how this glitch happens?),
Or it did for me at least. Not sure anyone else has played this long enough to get that glitch.
- The game by itself gets pretty boring after a short time. This isn't helped by the fact that, if you want to get upgrades, you will have to grind pretty hard, as levels pay very little gold (minus Duel mode for some reason).
- No volume sliders of any kind, so be ready to alt-tab and open Volume Mixer (and then do it again if the game crashes).
- The menus look and feel terrible.
-+ The graphics feel like they're from a low-quality Flash game from the early-mid 2000s. Some people like that aesthetic, and this might even be what the dev was going for (since there's a "Retro Mode" button that compresses the graphics from 1-4 intensity), so if you're into those kinds of graphics, you'll probably like these.
-+ The music is also...something. I don't like it myself. It's basically war drums and similar instruments, possibly to make it feel more like an arena, but the music ultimately comes off as rejected Adult Swim bumper music. If you really, really, really like "surreal sounding" music though, you might like it?
While the game is free and can be fun for a short time, the game breaking bug and overall poor layout is what ruins it for me. Even if the bug was fixed, I'm not sure I'd recommend the game to anyone outside of people who want something to have dumb fun with for less than an hour. If you are that kind of person, go ahead and roll the dice. You'll probably be done before the game crashes anyway.

[Before I go over this (hopefully) quick review, I have put more hours in this game then what is shown on my steam account. I bought it for Xbox 360 before I purchased it off steam. The hours shown on my steam account are almost all from Online play.]
STORY: This game is a must have for any Warhammer 40k fan. The Campaign is a blast, and surprisingly has a cool story that keeps you playing for the plot alone. Killing hordes of Orks with volleys of bolter fire is really satisfying, and the fighting Chaos daemons and Traitor marines feels very iconic. The story could have been longer, but for the price that you pay now it is a fair deal. It is sad that THQ went under, as this could have been a great series. Check out "Space Marine 2 plot" to see what we were missing out on. I don't want to spoil anything because it does tie in with this story, but it sounds bad♥♥♥♥♥and if you beat the campaign you need to read about it. Hopefully it can be salvaged somehow, but it sounds unlikely.
Graphics and Atmosphere: This game is several years old not, but it still looks great in my opinion, especially for its time. The atmosphere definitely feels 40k. The Forgeworld you fight on during the campaign really does in fact feel like a forgeworld. As a fan of the novels from the Black Library, I can say it is just how I imagined it. I caught myself looking out in the distance and roaming around just to take in all the cool environment details. The facilities of Adeptus Mechanicus are captured in all their glory. As a Space Marine, you really do feel like a tank. The designers did a great job of making you feel like a heavy, yet powerful superhuman. Warhammer 40,000 fans are going to love it, as will any Sci-fi fan. Sadly, there is no co-op (Exterminatus mode makes up for this). Still a total blast though!
Sound: The Gothic tone of Warhammer 40k is supplemented well through the soundtrack, but it is nothing breathtaking. However, that is excusable of course considering this was not a triple A title. Don't expect Halo level music, but it does the job. Weapons for the most part sound decent. The bolter guns fire off with a chunky and pleasing bang that you'd expect from such a powerful and iconic weapon, and tearing through enemies with them couldn't feel better. Plasma weapons have a cool sound to them and feel equally satisfying. The chainsword whirrs as we'd expect, so no complaints there. Power weapons have a searing swoosh to them when swung, but admittedly I do wish they had more depth to their sound. Over all sound quality is what you'd expect.
****(Online)****
Armor selection: Armor selection is awesome, there is plenty of armor peices unlock and they all look generally bad♥♥♥♥♥ Of course there are many chapters and chaos warbands to pick from, as well as the option to customize one's own chapter with infinite color combinations, as almost every part of armor is broken down into several parts for multi colored pieces. If you play Warhammer 40k tabletop and play a chapter you made up, I can almost 100% promise that you can replicate it perfectly here in the game. This aspect of online play is extremely rewarding and fun. The game also offers DLC chapter armor sets, which for a few more dollars may be worth it if you are a hardcore 40k fan or are fan of one of those chapters in question.
General Online Play: This is where things become more complicated. Obviously this game has been out for a while, but generally I haven't had trouble finding games for most game types using the original maps. However, most of the DLC content is completely dead, so I wouldn't purchase it separately if you didn't buy the complete edition of the game.
Versus Online Play: Game types are standard, you won't find anything new here. The maps are fun but few in number (like I said DLC maps are dead). They're a blast at first but quickly get old. The class system features 3 different classes. The well balanced tactile marines, the heavy support Havocs, and the fast attack Assault Marines/Raptors. For the most part the play between the 3 is balanced. Perks are fair and generally useful. However, many of the weapons online are simply not. Lascannons and meltaguns are ridiculously overpowered and blow you away in one shot much of the time, with no chance to retaliate. Obviously this means people use them frequently. It gets very frustrating. Team balancing is also♥♥♥♥♥♥ Maxed out players are constantly teamed up to smear casual and newer players, leading the rage quits and total stomps. The servers are also very crappy and are frequently lagging and searching for new hosts. The game is playable, however.
Exterminatus Online Play: This mode is essentially a wave game type in which you fight hordes of Orks, or as a  Chaos marine in the DLC, Imperial Guard as well (the Exterminatus DLC's aren't *as* dead..). You can pick from the 3 classes and use any perks/custom classes/weapons just like versus. You team up with 3 others and do your best to keep alive until the final wave of 20. A lot of fun, this makes the online worth it, and I can only imagine how fun it'd be if you had 3 other real life friends to play it with all at once as one group. Totally makes up for the lack of co-op campaign.
Over all, this game is a must buy for a Warhammer 40k fan. I'd definitely wait to buy it when it's on sale though, unless you absolutely are itching to play it now and can't possibly wait, just don't buy the DLC if you're going to pay full price. Most of it's dead content as said earlier. The huge 40k fan wants me to give this a 10/10, but with the unbalanced online play, bad servers, and dead content, I can not do so. However, completely dismissing it's Warhammer 40,000 setting, this is a solid game. I'd give it a solid 8.5/10. During the steam summer sale you've got to grab this.

-+-Single player only Review-+-
[Before we start this review, let me say, I'm not one of the best gamers, in fact, I'm pretty bad at games, but I enjoy them alot, I love being part of the story and blowing things up]
First half of the game, I really love.  There were some flaws, but killing endless waves of stupid green orks was a blast.  Ammo conservation was a minor issue, but I was having a really good time playing this game.
As the story and progress went on, these flaws I encountered earlier, really began to be a problem.  Enemies don't drop ammo, there is no real cover system, and the controls were a bit clunky.  I love shooters to death, but Warhammer 40K: Ultramarine wants to be a special hybrid between a melee combat game as well as a shooter.  With clunky controls, it fails to pull off a seamless transition between melee combat to ranged.
Another flaw, is your squadmates.  As you play alongside with your team, you get used to your allies being around you, and learn how to use them to your advantage, but during various points of the campaign, your buddies will leave you, and you have to face waves of enemies by yourself, which by then, being accustomed to having comrades to aid you in combat, the game becomes unbalanced and have to find new strategies to take down your enemies.
Now, its time for me to address the issue with executions.  One of the few ways to regain points in your healthbar is by performing executions on your foes. This can only be done using melee attacks, and sometimes the animation of an execution may take 3 full seconds and can't be interrupted.  That being said, if you need health desperately you may have no other option.  While attempting an execution, it leaves your character exposed and he won't be able to defend himself as he's stuck in the middle of animation.  I've actually died several times during one of those events because there's no way out of it.
The most unfair thing about this title are the boss battles.  In most games, its just player vs the boss.  Sometimes in the middle of the fight in those games, the boss would retreat and bring in his henchmen while he takes a break.  Not in this game.   While the boss is pummeling away at the player while firing all cylinders, all of his companions will be aiding him.  While there are not many of these fights, they are enough to want me to turn the game off.   Some enemies will be throwing grenades, others sniping, while the rest come fighting face to face.  There is no safeway out of boss battles, you basically have to roll around, dodge, and shoot hoping for the best outcome.
As I progressed through the game, I learned to hate it.  It had alot of fun moments, being one Ultramarine vs 10,000 Orks was a pretty badass concept and helped my drive to beat the game, but I kept wondering what  unfair disadvantage will the game deliver next?  I once exited a corridor and the game came to a cutscene that introduced a new enemy.  In the cinematic my foe began firing at me.  As the game resumed, my character was standing out of cover while taking damage.  The final boss battle did me in. I finally gave in to its cheap tactics.  I could not finish the game.  I am angry that I fought this far, but could not finish the fight, it was just too difficult and unfair, I spent 98% of my ammo in my inventory before my enemies slain me, they would not go down and there was nowhere to replenish the ammunition.
This game couldn't find its identity.  It borrows elements from Gears of War and Devil May Cry, but it didn't know what it wanted to be.  With all the complaining, the game does have some good moments. I really enjoyed the first part of this title and a few other moments in between the final chapters. Killing thousands of orks was satisfying. Very action packed, Michael Bay would be proud.  The storyline is kind of simple, but expands the imagination.

Don't let the cute look and the humor of this game fool you - This game is hardcore.  I'm not a fan of the cutesy, and this game just sucked me in right from the start. (I can't stand Torchlight 2, for instance, but love Grim Dawn..different games than this game completely, but maybe you get where I'm coming from in trying to explain my tastes?) The perfect combination of old school, party based gameplay, and new school tech. It's beautiful to look at, and a pleasure to play. The difficulty will kick you square in the♥♥♥♥♥ That's part of the beauty, in my opinion - Experimenting and working towards that perfect build over and over, discovering what works and what does not work. The beginning can be a tad slow, but when you get past the first oh...ten levels or so of character progression, things get really interesting as far as gameplay goes. This is a must-play if you're a fan of the genre. One of the best of its type since Baldur's Gate 2. As I'm writing this, the Steam Summer Sale has this game for $20. That's one of the best bargains you're going to get for your money if you like this type of game. When I purchased this game, I paid $40 and don't regret it for a second. Just don't expect Diablo 3 or for this game to hold your hand very much at all. Trust me, this game will wreck you...in a good way. When you discover the synergy of your builds and things start really coming together, it's a great feeling.

While the game isn't very long, is moderately expensensive, there are no bosses it makes up for that with good level design, beautiful art and animations + cutscenes, a story that is light-hearted while still not being afraid of incorporating say death in it, good soundtrack and enjoyable gameplay.
In other words i recommend this game.

Bad reviews do not come when your game is bad, but when you fail to deliver on your promises.

We are more forgiving these days of pixel art/bad graphics in service of a truly unique story - the problem is 30 Flights of Loving doesn't have one. There are no twists and turns, an average episode of Leverage would be a better use of your 30 minutes. Even at $3, I didn't feel like I got my money's worth.

It's not a game. Now, normally this wouldn't bother me at all. The Beginner's Guide is one of my favorite "games", and it's more of an expirience. Now, there are several things that made me return this.
1. The Length. I beat it in 15 minutes, then again in 10. This is crazily short, and it dosen't have alot of replay value. This then goes to my next point.
2. The Price. For every $5 a game costs, it should have at least 2 hours of gameplay. For example, a game that's $10 should  at least have 4 hours of gameplay. This game is $5 and has about 15 minutes of gameplay. That's terrible. This game should be a dollar, if anything.
3. The Actual Gameplay. There is none, except you just walking around. Now don't get me wrong, I'm a huge fan of walking simulators, like as I said before, The Beginner's Guide is one of my favorite games. In that game you just walk around, but there's commentary and narration that drives you through. It has a story that drives you in. In this game the story is really bad. If the stories bad, then the gameplay should be the thing to drive you through, but all you do is walk.
4. The Story. Like I said before, the story isn't good. Now, I read that it's filled with metaphors. The Beginner's Guide is also filled with metaphors. But in The Beginner's Guide, the story is good enough to make me want to know them. That makes replaying the game fun and interesting. But here, I honestly don't care. The story is bad to begin with, and that makes me just not care enough to bother to replay it. Also, the story has these seemingly random bits that are out of order, and are just dumb. The one that sticks out the most is the ending, in which
It's just stupid. I bet this is some metaphor, but as I mentioned above, I don't care enough to bother to look into it.
Overall, I'd give it a 4/10. The settings are pretty good, and the soundtract is fantastic, but the 4 points I mention above really ruins the experience. This is the type of game where you buy it, play it, the return it. You're better off watching it on youtube.

You like L4D2, but you can't shell out 20 bucks, or you're waiting for the sale? Get this.
You play as a bunch of dudes that need to plant a bomb, and once you do, you get the hell outta there. It plays similarly to Left 4 Dead, it's simple but fun. I am comparing this to Left 4 Dead 2 because in both games you are heading from point A to point B. The major differences from these two games are:
Smaller weapon selection than L4D2
This game has less variety with zombies
You can aim down sights in this game!
Five dudes v. four
The gun play is nowhere near as good as it is in titles like KF2, but it's good enough to be satisfying.
The graphics are uh... who cares? You're playing a game on the source engine. You shouldn't really care about graphics.
Sounds are fine, you'll hear a few re-used from other sources games, though not a big deal. The guns sounds are different, however.
My major gripe with this game is the terrible weapon sound quality, it sounds like it came from a bootleg MW2. However, you can fix this by getting a weapon sound pack on the workshop. Also, there's not many weapons to choose from, but it's not a big deal though because the games are short in nature, any more guns would probably be too much.
Get this game if you can't afford L4D2, you're waiting for a sale, or you just want to kill a few zeds in a short amount of time. It's simple, fun, and satisfying enough to have you coming back for more.

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

Don't let the cute look and the humor of this game fool you - This game is hardcore.  I'm not a fan of the cutesy, and this game just sucked me in right from the start. (I can't stand Torchlight 2, for instance, but love Grim Dawn..different games than this game completely, but maybe you get where I'm coming from in trying to explain my tastes?) The perfect combination of old school, party based gameplay, and new school tech. It's beautiful to look at, and a pleasure to play. The difficulty will kick you square in the♥♥♥♥♥ That's part of the beauty, in my opinion - Experimenting and working towards that perfect build over and over, discovering what works and what does not work. The beginning can be a tad slow, but when you get past the first oh...ten levels or so of character progression, things get really interesting as far as gameplay goes. This is a must-play if you're a fan of the genre. One of the best of its type since Baldur's Gate 2. As I'm writing this, the Steam Summer Sale has this game for $20. That's one of the best bargains you're going to get for your money if you like this type of game. When I purchased this game, I paid $40 and don't regret it for a second. Just don't expect Diablo 3 or for this game to hold your hand very much at all. Trust me, this game will wreck you...in a good way. When you discover the synergy of your builds and things start really coming together, it's a great feeling.

You should take in mind many factors before decide what engine would choose before start. AppGameKit is a must have but let's explain why.
I'm coming from develop games since a boy, probably as you did. I had luck finding a lot of friends where I was coding AI's for L2jServer and that experience with C++ introduced me to code games from another point of view.
So I was looking to do my own game engine based in a robust 3D library and I followed many developments since years but rarely found something solid.
COMMON ISSUES IN OTHER ENGINES
A few common problems that found in Other Engines that I worked:
- Usually you lost the control of the assets, and can't easily move any dependency without a headhache.
- Not working examples because they are moving so fast and the documentation is not updated as desired. I used to learn more fast from working examples instead pay for them.
- Lost the contact with the dev team from months without any sense. Well, some of the "best" engines users still waiting to have fixed the Network LLAPI so imagine the HLAPI.
- Well, without examples and support, we normally pay more than we could produce. It's a vital point for any Indie developer to take in mind. Many of the "best" engines licenses makes more angry bidrs than customers satisfied who can learn along the time as community.
- If you are coming from open source like me, the community get a negative point if don't share their ideas.
- These "modular" "nodes" cool IDEs, that need continuous support and never get you ride in the real programming world.
I like to make my own code, without restrictions, and it's not difficult if you give a try.
WHAT I FOUND IN APPGAMEKIT:
- A Robust Game Engine which has the best documentation ever from basic to high level advanced programmers.
- 3D working easy and better that expected, a high performance rendering anything.
- The examples introduces you quickly from Tier 1 to Tier 2 if you love C++ as me.
- A great resource of ideas and concepts to apply your own games.
- I can export and test directly in my Android and Iphone devices.
[...] And it solves for me all the points I mentioned:
- I can manage my assets as I need without any IDE restriction. I'm not buying a slow IDE; I'm buying a Robust, Tested and Knowed 2D/3D Engine coming from DBPro.
- The support is really valuable. Is cool to know they are working around and supporting the coders to improve their experience.
- PayOneTime License -under the terms of each author- instead abusive taxes or revenues.
- The community is the best. Very supportive, experienced and communicative.
So bought all the packages, and waiting the next DLCs
Keep up the good work!

Have you ever wanted to be a bad♥♥♥♥♥space marine laying waste to all the xeno and heretic scum that finds itself in-front of your bolter? Well then you have to get this game.
If you love the world of Warhammer 40K then this is the game for you, infact even if you don’t you will still enjoy blasting away enemies with huge guns whilst running around in a battle suit that effectively makes you a living tank.
The gameplay is great, the attacks and motion feel heavy and full of momentum, and considering what you are wearing this is no surprise. The many weapons, and there are a fair amount of them, all made me feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ Each shot blasting holes through enemies and leaving a trail of blood and body parts in my wake. And speaking of close combat, you get a chainsword, enough said.
The story is one that you would probably need to have some brand familiarity with before you could get the most out of it. As I said I love the lore of 40k and this was a treasure trove for me. Even if you are new to the franchise this game has a solid and engrossing story that you will want to finish. Also the voice acting is pretty sweet, always what I imagined an Ultramarine to sound like.
The scenery and environments were great, they added a lot to the game and as you traverse the war torn world you get a great sense of the monumental loss that has just taken place. A real feeling of anger against the swarm of green skins that now overrun the place just adds to the pleasure of gunning them down.
The multiplayer was a great deal of fun too, a little steep on the learning curve but with match’s still frequent to this day you will get the hang of it no time.
The asking price may be a little high if you aren’t interested in the setting but buying this on a sale is a must for everyone. On the other hand if you love 40k then it’s worth every penny.
Have fun ^_^

From what I've seen compared to my time on the PS4:
- Hackers.
No, I'm not a salty sweat-nerd who gets angry whenever someone kills me. I've recorded aimbotters, nonreloaders. I've played almost seven hours of gameplay, and I've run into 9 hackers in this game. + The game works very well without antivirus on.

Total War Warhammer 2 is the latest game in the epic grand strategy franchise. Set in the fantasy version of the Warhammer universe, the player can choose to play as one of four races – High Elves, Dark Elves, Lizardmen and Skaven (giant rats) – as they battle over control of a magical vortex.
The vortex is basically a barrier, preventing the forces of Chaos from invading the world. Some factions are trying to save the world, while others want to cause the End Times. As is usual for Total War, gameplay is divided into two major sections. The turn based campaign map is where you focus on the big picture, empire wide tasks. Train armies, move them around the map, capture and defend settlements, research technologies, construct buildings to improve your economy and public happiness, forge trade agreements and military alliances with other factions. Then fight large scale battles involving thousands of soldiers in real time. And by soldiers, I’m not just talking about your standard swordsmen, spearmen, archers and cavalry. The fantasy setting provides a wide variety of unusual creatures including giant eagles, phoenixes, dragons, hydras, rat ogres, hell pit abominations and many more.
This is the fourth Total War game I’ve played, after Shogun 2, Rome 2 and the original Warhammer. After spending almost 50 hours playing through the High Elf campaign, I can confidently say that TWW2 is easily the best version, building on what was good about the previous games, and improving in several ways.
The most obvious improvement is how the vortex affects the campaign. I was never really comfortable with the victory conditions in any of those previous Total War games. They usually required you to control a certain number of settlements, and sometimes eliminate a specific faction. I often felt like I ended up going to war with factions that I didn’t really consider to be my enemy, just to expand far enough to satisfy the victory conditions.
In order to gain control of the vortex and win the campaign, the four main races need to collect resources to perform five rituals. Each controlled settlement provides a small amount of resources, but some settlements in specific locations provide a larger amount. This means you don’t necessarily need to have the biggest empire to win. Each ritual takes place in three of your settlements simultaneously, and you’ll have to defend them for ten turns until the ritual completes. Starting a ritual will allow some Chaos armies to pass through the vortex, with the intention of destroying ritual sites. And the four races can always see each other’s ritual progress, so this naturally triggers conflict between them, especially in the later stages.
In my High Elves campaign, things were looking good at the halfway stage, as I was first to complete the third ritual. I was intending to stay defensive for the rest of the campaign, but after a while I noticed the Dark Elves had pulled in front after a period of aggressive expansion. This forced me to start an invasion of their lands to slow them down. The Lizardmen had the same idea as me, so the Dark Elves got pushed back quite far. At one point I thought that the Skaven were going to sneak a win while everyone else was fighting each other. Then one of my allies destroyed a Skaven ritual site, giving me a clear run to victory. It really felt like every faction was involved in an epic world war.
The world map is quite varied, from the frozen wastes of the north, to the Elves’ mountainous island, to the tropical jungles and deserts in the south. There are many minor races scattered around, including vampires, dwarves, bretonians, greenskins and wood elves. Any race can now claim any settlement (the previous game had some annoying restrictions), but will suffer penalties to growth, economy and army replenishment if the climate isn’t desirable. You’re also encouraged to explore the seas, as you can often find shipwrecks containing treasure which could include extra gold, weapons/armour to equip on your generals and temporary buffs for your soldiers in combat.
The AI was good in the previous game, but another improvement in TWW2 is that the AI will attack the player more often on the battlefield instead of always just sitting back and waiting for you to come at them.
Each faction can also spend gold to perform rites (different to rituals) which give temporary factionwide buffs. For example, the High Elves have a rite which makes armies immune to attrition (soldiers dying while travelling through bad weather conditions), which is perfect when attacking enemy settlements in harsh/corrupted environments.
Each of the main races has a unique mechanic which makes their playing style different to the others. The High Elves are the only one that I can talk about as I haven’t played as the other races yet – they get bonuses to diplomacy through a political intrigue system. Periodically you’ll encounter multiple choice scenarios, and your decisions will result in gaining or losing influence, as well as other temporary factionwide effects. Influence can then be spent to improve your relationship with another faction, or to damage the relationship between two of your enemies.
In the early part of my campaign, I was frequently being attacked by two minor factions, the Skaeling and the Pirates of Sartosa. Using influence, I was able to make peace with Sartosa, convince them to declare war on the Skaeling, and then I made an alliance with Sartosa and pushed the Skaeling back, completely wiping them out. My only complaints with this mechanic is that there aren’t many different scenarios, so I encountered frequent repeats, and they often referred to the leaders of other Elven factions that had long since been eliminated.
Total War Warhammer 2 is an absolute masterpiece, and I’ve loved every minute of it. Its going to get my vote for best game of 2017. If you’re a fan of Total War, or strategy games in general, Warhammer 2 is an essential purchase. Considering the length of the campaign, and the variety of playable factions, you won’t regret a full price purchase.

I can't recommend the game in its current state. Warhammer II was advertised as having a new campaign that focused on the vortex and a stitched together map that combines the new races and continent with the old.
What we recieved was the vortex campaign that while entertaining the first time through is far to similair on subsiquent playthroughs and has some majorly annoying features such as chaos and other faction intervention forces spawning randomly somewhere in your territory and then running amok. This is to say nothing about the auto resolve issues with certain factions and the abysmal naval "combat"
Most of the above should be fine though, Mortal empires was to be the meat of the game. Total War style conquest across a huge campaign map with all the factions vying for domination. Instead what we recieved was a half baked pushed out the door campaign that manages to suck much of the fun out of Mortal Empires. It is clear at this point that Mortal Empires was no where near ready for release with the main game, and is honestly not ready for release in its current state. Missing factions, Bugs carried over from the Vortex Campagin, Chaos spawning in the middle of your territories, army compositions that make no logical sense to anyone, rediculous buffs given to the AI in higher difficulties.
Overall Warhammer II was not in a state to release when it did, and almost 3 months later is still not fully ready. This game should have released early 2018 content complete. I don't like purchasing a game to find out later that major content that was promised is going to be drip fed to me months later and bugs that have been present since launch will still be around. Sometime next year Warhammer II will be a great game, but it is not that game now and it has soured my on buying any CA game until months after its release at a steep discount.

- I'll start by saying Ori and the Blind Forest is far and away my GotY 2015. Several of its components were flawless, from sound design and soundtrack to visuals and platforming/combat. The only major drawbacks were the sometimes permanent forks in the road coupled with forced autosaves, and an inability to backtrack to some areas for completion. Completed saves can not be re-entered and cleaned up which I found a nuisance, but some would argue incentivizes players to replay the otherwise fairly short (10 hour) game.
- If I had to assign a quick number, I'd give it a solid 9/10 for remarkable, memorable, and genuinely moving combinations of sound and visual design, drawn back only slightly by a few poor choices in level design and gameplay elements.
- Finally, I found the Ginso Tree to be disproportionately more difficult than any other segment of the game, finale included. It was a particularly negative experience in an otherwise unblemished and near-flawless gem.
tl;dr 9/10, a purchase you'll never regret or forget

My very first Steam review.
Audio & Visual: It's great, but you already know this, right? Most if not all reviews praise this game as one of the most beautiful 2d game game ever, and trust me, they're right. The same can be said for the full orchestra music which is either haunting, touching, soft or intense, sometimes at the same time. The sound effect is also suitable, and Ori's squeal is totally adorable.
Gameplay, Control, & Difficulty: The game offers a rather standard 2d action adventure gameplay. Ori can jump, double jump, shoot lasers, use area attack, swim, stomp, scale wall, glide and use enemy's projectile/enemy themselves to propel himself. These abilities can be upgraded to be more effective and efficient. The control is also tight and precise.
The game, however, is  quite challenging, but fair. Expect to die a lot, but you will mostly learn from those death.
The save system worth a mention. You can practically save everywhere, except near enemies or on unstable ground, at any given time. On the other hand, you need energy to save your game. In the beginning, when your energy supply is rather limited, this necessitates careful thinking as you might stuck between a rock and a hard place. But when your energy supply has grown, this system is a blessing because that means you can save your game at your leisure.
Story: Ori's tale is a touching one. I am not going to spoil anything, but it carries the themes of familial love and loss, sacrifice, rage, and adult fear. I am a parent and I can relate to why those characters, even the seemingly evil one, do what they did. I cried a bit too. The story is just that good.
So, do I recommend this game? Yes, go buy it, wait for the sale if you have to, but buy it and play it. This game deserves your money and attention, and perhaps love.

Halfway through my playthrough (completed the original edition and came back with the same friend for the enhanced version). We're playing on tactician to get a real challange and we have died a lot, but still making good progress - just killed braccus. We're playing much the same classes as before but taking advantage of the tweaks that have been made such as dual wielding and genades. At first I wasn't a fan; the voice acting I loved was gone, and no longer was my beloved rogue a killing machine. Yet as we played more, that perfection I felt before shone through. Rogues are still powerful it just requires more commitment into particular abilities and the grenades have shown their worth in many moment - still can't bring myself to take the grenade talent though :p.
Overall, we again are having a blast with the game. It has the borderlands feel with the loot mechanics, tactical turn based combat, fantastic music, consistent voice acting, even more content and soem story tweaks as compared with the first game and hasn't lost any of its charm. Easily a 9/10.
P.s. If you're playing this after finishing the original edition. I recommend going on tactician, it changes even more of the game to make it feel like an even newer experience. It adds new enemies, different status effects and makes the game a lot more "think before you act", rather than being able to plough through any fight relatively easily.

Well, its always hard to objectively and honestly review Early Acces games. This is due to the fact that theyre not a finished product.
Naval Action is one of those games that has the potential to be a true gem in the making:
- The map is huge, and i really mean huge which gives that awesome feeling of truly sailing in the caribbean.
- Lots of player factions, not just the classic 3-4, no 8 is the way to go.
- combat is awesome, it is slow-paced but feels genuine in how the ships move and behave.
Sure, alot of things are still unfinished and placeholder, for instance the interface and the menus when in a harbor are just raw and unpolished, clunky and lacking. But im pretty sure those are items that are on the development agenda and bound to get the necessary attention in due time.
For now i feel that the developers are focusing on expanding the overall game, implementing a trading system (which i havent dabbled in and do not yet understand) and a crafting system (this looks pretty easy and straightforward and works well). Offering the playerbase more to do than just float around, do missions and attack other players.
This is a good choice, imo. Polishing can come later, give us a game first.
And the game is there, free liberty to roam around with your teammates and hunt down lone traders or sailors that had the bad idea of going out on their own or without enough support.
I have joined the United Provinces (Netherlands) on the EU1 server (which is the most populated one) and from what ive come to understand is that there are clans of 200+ members that already wage large-scale wars against other faction. Matter of fact, as im writing now, the French are making a move on the United Provinces along the eastern Venezuelan coast to go and capture some of the towns. Its all-out war!
Its a true PvP-game which i think can only be compared a little to EvE in how large it is and how large battles can be. Im not 100% sure but i think a large battle can include up to 50 ships.
This might increase later, it might not.
I think its an awesome game but it really is a WiP, one that even in its current state i highly enjoy and recommend!

Passion for Age of Sail or Open Mind, if you are pickey and not particularly interested, dont even try.

With 600+ hours in AppGameKit, I will say... without a doubt... this is one of the better engines for small to medium sizes indie games. The engine is constantly being developed and expanded, the devs are totally hands on and active in the forums, and it's just incredibily easy to learn and use.

While it's 3D capabilities don't have all the bells and whistles of Unreal or Leadwerks, if you are making smaller games, or mobile or HTML games... it's more than just competant. Supporting two languages BASIC (which is a intepreted scripting language like Lua, but easier), and direct C++ linking; this engine has everything a budding, or even experienced, developer could want for projects that don't require a hefty 3D engine. But, make no mistake, the 3D engine it does have is no performance slouch, and runs incredibly well.

This is, by far, one of my favorite engines ever; and because it is, primarily, code based there's no limitations or boxing in of what kind of game you can build.

AppGameKit is more than worth its price, as are its DLCs; and given the constant updates and supports, the price is worth it.

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a third-person shooter set in the universe of Warhammer 40,000 that follows one captain of the Ultramarines, Titus, on his mission on the Forge World Graia, which is under heavy attack by a Ork horde seeking to posses the powerful weapons built in the planet's factories. Later in the game, Titus and his two accompanying Ultramarines, Sidonus and Leandros, must also face the threat of a Chaos Warband lead by a dangerous Chaos sorcerer named Nemeroth.
The main beef of Space Marine's gameplay is using the weapons you are given tocut through the hordes of enemies preventing you from advancing and then proceed in the levels. You are given both long ranged weapons (like pistols or sniper rifles) and close quarters tools (starting from a chainsaw and arriving at a huge electrified mallet): you must learn to switch between the two constantly, given you'll face various kinds of enemies (some of them dangerous on the long distances while others extremely weak if chopped down in close combat). Each weapon has different versions that are unlocked advancing in the game, each with its pros and cons. On top of his health pool, Titus can take advantage of a recharging shield that can protect him against some of the enemy fire and a super mode of some sort: the mode is charged by dishing out damage and, whenever unleashed, allows you to recover health over time and aim at enemies in slow-motion. Finishing enemies when they are weak also allows you to boost your health.
The main campaign is extremely faithful to the Warhammer 40,000 universe, both in design of the environments and characters and the references made to the general lore of the series. It lasts for aboutsix or eight hours or so and, aside from fighting your way through Graia, you can find hidden servo-skulls bearing audio recordings that further expand the game's story. There are three different difficulties (easy, normal and hard), but I'd say that even the normal mode manages to be challenging enough.
Warhammer 40,00: Space Marine also spots a rather interesting multiplayer mode. You can either play as a Space Marine or a Chaos Marine, and the game offers a customization menu that allows you to deeply personalize your marine (armor pieces, colours, insigna, ...). The multiplayer mode offers several game modes, the same you could expect into a big retail multiplayer shooter: capture the flag, capture the control point, ... The mode also features co-op missions. The player actually makes progress in multiplayer thanks to a level system, unlocking new armor pieces and/or weapons and perks as he/she gains more experience. As I'm writing this review and four years after the game's release, Space Marine's multiplayer is still really populated.
Warhammer 40,000 Space Marine, along with the Dawn of War series, is a great example about how a complex series like Warhammer 40,000 can be boiled down in a rather charming game capable of offering a great time both to the fans of the series and newcommers just wanting to enjoy some good third-person shooting action

Tom Clancy’s The Division is a SINGLE-PLAYER game that has CO-OP features with up to 4 people. This is a fact that needs to be made WAY more clear as there's a huge amount of misinformers running around calling this an MMO when It is not, as evident by the rare occassions you do see other players in safehouses simply disappear out of existence once they walk out of an exit. To play with others in the "open world" enviroment, you will need to form a party to do so.. And if someone leaves or gets kicked, the game will forcefully boot you out of the current session and load you back into your own normal private one.
I'm even tempted to question the "Multiplayer" aspect of this game as well as It only comes in the form of "The Dark Zone" which is the most poorly designed game "feature" I have ever experienced or witnessed in my entire life, making me and much of the community avoid it entirely. The CONCEPT is great. You go into a FUBAR zone to get some sweet loot from enemy NPC's that are all basically elite/boss ranked. Since all the loot you will get is contaminated, you get very limited storage that has to be "extracted" by a helicopter forcing you to go to a place to start a "defend the area" mission.
The real turd-trophy that comes up from this garbage however, is that you're going to be forced to engage in PvP against other players in the Dark Zone and these engagements have zero rules to them. Meaning as a solo player, you are gonna meet full teams of 4-8 people using mic communication (playing smurf character if its a non 30 bracket) running around and nonchalantly slaughtering & ganking anyone they come across (more than often from behind while you are fighting NPC's), even using mic-spam as a disorientation tactic as the game officially promotes and rewards the most cowardly baby behavior on the planet.
------------------------------------------
All of the above wouldn't be such a big deal for say, someone prefering a single-player experience, a non-pvp one or a non hardcore competitive scene.. But the problem with this argument is that THIS GAME COSTS 60-90 BUCKS. Cutting out the Dark Zone leaves you with randomly scattered side quests that all only have a variation of about 3 different missions of "go fix the antenna", "kill those guys", "save the civillians" and "dungeons" that are semi-scripted narrow building complexes or a sewer/subway system that you run through, clearing baddies before getting to the boss. It's all extremely repetitive with progression also being 100% RNG which will leave you majorly fùcked up in terms of possible damage output & survivability against enemies that grow exponentionally stronger every level, turning them into massive bullet sponges.
-------
TL;DR: This game does not have the content, replayability, polish or overall sustenance to justify It's price-tag with huge chunks of failed design experiments making up for most of what the average customer will run across.
