This game is truly amazing and I am greatly saddened by the fact that it's user reviews are brought down to only "very positive", just because people are too indolent to try and solve simple problems. Disregard every negative review as they are ALL complaints about easy-to-fix problems that I will explain in greater detail at the end of this review.
Fallout 3 has managed to set standards in both the FPS and RPG genres, and is possibly my favourite game of all time. Very few games come anywhere close to F3 in lore, atmosphere, combat, story, and overall gameplay, and none are on par in all of those elements combined.
Lore - the fallout franchise as a whole has some of the most developed and interesting lore that I've experienced from a video game. Though, managing to incorperate it without requiring the player to have played previous games is something that F3 has done incredibly well.
Atmosphere - Being set in a post-apocalyptic US, 200 years after nuclear war with China, F3 has done a fantastic job at making a nearly desolate nuclear wasteland something worth exploring. That combined with with themes from a 50's, anti-communist, nuclear, technologically advanced America makes F3 something truly unique and incredibly enjoyable to dwell in and explore.
Combat - F3's combat was truly revolutionary for its time. The mechanic found in V.A.T.S was something never seen before and many mechanics in current games get their inspiration from it. Nothing compares to an intense gunfight whilst you have mid-20th century swing and blues playing from your Pip-Boy.
Story - Many have complained that F3's story is too linear, and admittedly the main storyline is fairly linear, but the main quests aren't the only story. There is just as much emphasis on side quests as there is on the main one, and side quests often have a lot of decisions to be made. It's in the rest of the quests that you decide how you want to play and what kind of person you want to be.
Gameplay - After leaving the vault, you are constantly progressing. Fighting harder enemies, getting better weapons and armour, and increasing your various skills. But it never gets repetitive. While you still have quests to complete, and there are many, gameplay will never become blasé.
The complaints I have with this game are few, and all can be fixed with F3's amazing modding community. So I will include links to the mods that fix all of these problems.
No ADS - The ability to aim down your sight is one that seems to be in nearly every FPS, so it is somewhat surprising that F3 doesn't have it. Instead, you get a slight zoom by pressing what would be the ADS key. Luckily there are modders that have fixed this.
Micro stutter - This slight stutter is one that has plagued both the Fallout and Elder Scrolls games for a long time. A fix can be found here
Sprinting - It can be annoying when you need to traverse a great distance but you're stuck with that slow vanilla running. It seems odd that you wouldn't be able to sprint, but of course, we have the modding community to fix this.
Now for the problems that keep all the negative reviewers from enjoying the game.
If you press play on the first window and it closes without launching the game, more likely than not, you do not have Games for Windows Live installed. This is required to run F3.

Onto the negatives (few as they are), there are some sections that left me puzzles for a while I got stuck on one area, wondering how to proceed for about 20 minutes, I got it eventually and really enjoyed it. That being said some areas require trial and error, can I survive this? Whats down this hole that I cant see the bottom of etc. There were some difficulty spikes (you'll know them when you see them) but that being said they were welcome. I don't want the game to hand me the victory like so many new release games, the victories you make by beating these spikes feel amazing. I truely felt a sense of accomplishment after going through these challenges and surviving.
There's so much more I want to write and yet I can't because it would ruin the beautiful experience that Ori and The Blind Forest can give you. If you have a 20 spare, think about putting it into Ori, best money I've spent this year so far.

From installation to a 'compiled' test app running on my Android device in less than 10 minutes. One of the most straight-forward app creation packages around, and with a BASIC dialect rather than click-and-drag creation, allows a lot more flexibility out-of-the-box than many of its peers.
Supports two different 'tiers' of programming - tier 1 with its BASIC dialect allows you to write code which is strapped to a pre-compiled player and packaged as a stand-alone app; and with no splash screens or water-marking which you're stuck with in some products. This will be sufficient for almost all your hobbyist (and even some professional) programming. This also means no need to install Android Studio, or find the right magical combination of SDK/NDK/tools/Java that will actually let you compile.
Tier 2 gives lets you use it's libraries in native C++ and (with the addition of the aforementioned SDKs and tools) will let you compile to native code for that extra speed necessary for professional level or highly intensive software.
If you're familiar with BASIC and willing to learn the nuances of yet another dialect, give this a go before throwing much larger figures at click-and-drag studios which allow far less flexibility than AGK does.

AGK is a nice, easy-to-use game development platform. I have mainly used it for 2D games, such as
,
, and
, but it also has some quite capable 3D functionality as well.
It has its own Basic language (tier 1) or one can also develop in C++ with it (tier 2). I've been using its Basic language which is quick to learn, especially if you have prior experience with other Basic languages. Exporting to APK for Android is pretty easy to do. Being able to broadcast the game from the Windows IDE to Android for quick testing is a very handy feature as well.
It's probably important to note that AGK is not a game engine itself. One still has to create their own game. It just provides tools that simplify the rendering and other back-end processes so one can focus more on designing the game itself.
There is an active and helpful community around AGK both on Steam and at
.

Generally I would say AGK is a nice way to get started with game development. It does have a lot lacking but for its price and the rough edges it has a lot of good elements as well.  I have done two games for mobile platforms using it. These have been 2D games so I do not know about the 3D part. My points:
+cross-platform development. exporting to android and ios both with very little specific code needed. very nice.
+physics engine. has nice abstraction with very simple ways to control the 2D physics
+player apps. very simple way to broadcast your game for testing on your android/ios devices. couldn't be simpler.
+reasonably good response to questions and bugs reported
+community has some very helpful people if you go on the forums. the few that are active.
-one man show. TGC seems to be a small team and AGK is basically developed by one man. Even if Paul is great, as one man he cannot work on everything very fast.
-buggy. I have discovered several bugs that made me wonder if people actually used it for real. because them those bugs would have been found, reported and fixed a thousand times already.
-no level editor. for a game kit you really need one. compared to what gamemaker 2 looks like, the editor alone wants me to jump to it. huge amounts of time can be wasted on setting up levels. and playing with tiled etc is just klunky.
-generally the AGK IDE for the custom language works but very limited. the missing level editor is a big issue. so is the fact that you cannot see your media. and there is not git support or any other vcs. and as mentioned, the community hacks are just terrible. in general i run pycharm in separate window with the project also configured just to use git integration and to have easier search over the project.
-the custom basic language is somewhat nice in making game programming simple but at the same time limited. no advanced data structures, no function scopes (all are global), limited support for variable scoping (you can make custom types to hide some of it but that is it). you wouldn't lose the simplicity if you just added some lightweight support for at least some scoping as otherwise bigger projects become real bummers. of course refactoring etc is a real pain but that is already too far considering state of everything else...
overall a fine product that takes care of a lot of the details, frameworks, cross platform issues, physics, etc. for you. but also not very polished. good for building 2D games where you customize everything yourself. for its price a good deal. just beware the limitations.

Team up with a group of 6-4 and survive continuous waves of zombies, each amount of zombies increasing by 10.

Here's what Bomb Placement is like;

Guns: The game runs on the Source Engine, the same that Half-Life 2 and Garry's Mod runs on, It gives you a variety of Shotguns, Sniper Rifles, Pistols, SMGs, And Assault Rifles.

Just finished this. It's nice. Very reminiscent of the old point & click games, though not as long and with more logical solutions (these sorts of games were usually "guess the answer the developer was thinking of). The main feature is using different characters who have their own (single) special ability. It's not exactly lost vikings, but somewhat similar.
Despite the clean puzzle designs (e.g.: it usually makes clear which paths go nowhere) and the good pacing (the characters are nicely introduced and puzzles get progressively harder), it's actually the story that is the most engaging. It has good and charming humour, and a bit of mystery that keeps you playing and guessing what's next.
The main gripe I have with the game is that I definately no longer fit within the target audience for this. This is the sort of game I'd recommend parents buying for their children: it's non-violent, fun, keeps them engaged and tangentially (if that's a word) learns them about teamwork. Hardcore gamers should definately stay away, though. :)

This game is truly amazing and I am greatly saddened by the fact that it's user reviews are brought down to only "very positive", just because people are too indolent to try and solve simple problems. Disregard every negative review as they are ALL complaints about easy-to-fix problems that I will explain in greater detail at the end of this review.
Fallout 3 has managed to set standards in both the FPS and RPG genres, and is possibly my favourite game of all time. Very few games come anywhere close to F3 in lore, atmosphere, combat, story, and overall gameplay, and none are on par in all of those elements combined.
Lore - the fallout franchise as a whole has some of the most developed and interesting lore that I've experienced from a video game. Though, managing to incorperate it without requiring the player to have played previous games is something that F3 has done incredibly well.
Atmosphere - Being set in a post-apocalyptic US, 200 years after nuclear war with China, F3 has done a fantastic job at making a nearly desolate nuclear wasteland something worth exploring. That combined with with themes from a 50's, anti-communist, nuclear, technologically advanced America makes F3 something truly unique and incredibly enjoyable to dwell in and explore.
Combat - F3's combat was truly revolutionary for its time. The mechanic found in V.A.T.S was something never seen before and many mechanics in current games get their inspiration from it. Nothing compares to an intense gunfight whilst you have mid-20th century swing and blues playing from your Pip-Boy.
Story - Many have complained that F3's story is too linear, and admittedly the main storyline is fairly linear, but the main quests aren't the only story. There is just as much emphasis on side quests as there is on the main one, and side quests often have a lot of decisions to be made. It's in the rest of the quests that you decide how you want to play and what kind of person you want to be.
Gameplay - After leaving the vault, you are constantly progressing. Fighting harder enemies, getting better weapons and armour, and increasing your various skills. But it never gets repetitive. While you still have quests to complete, and there are many, gameplay will never become blasé.
The complaints I have with this game are few, and all can be fixed with F3's amazing modding community. So I will include links to the mods that fix all of these problems.
No ADS - The ability to aim down your sight is one that seems to be in nearly every FPS, so it is somewhat surprising that F3 doesn't have it. Instead, you get a slight zoom by pressing what would be the ADS key. Luckily there are modders that have fixed this.
Micro stutter - This slight stutter is one that has plagued both the Fallout and Elder Scrolls games for a long time. A fix can be found here
Sprinting - It can be annoying when you need to traverse a great distance but you're stuck with that slow vanilla running. It seems odd that you wouldn't be able to sprint, but of course, we have the modding community to fix this.
Now for the problems that keep all the negative reviewers from enjoying the game.
If you press play on the first window and it closes without launching the game, more likely than not, you do not have Games for Windows Live installed. This is required to run F3.

Another problem that people have is that the game will occasionally freeze. As you have seen on the store page for Fallout 3, it is not optimized for Windows 7 and 8. I've been using the Fallout Script Extender(FOSE) for a while and I've experienced no freezes.

Total War Warhammer 2 is the latest game in the epic grand strategy franchise. Set in the fantasy version of the Warhammer universe, the player can choose to play as one of four races – High Elves, Dark Elves, Lizardmen and Skaven (giant rats) – as they battle over control of a magical vortex.
The vortex is basically a barrier, preventing the forces of Chaos from invading the world. Some factions are trying to save the world, while others want to cause the End Times. As is usual for Total War, gameplay is divided into two major sections. The turn based campaign map is where you focus on the big picture, empire wide tasks. Train armies, move them around the map, capture and defend settlements, research technologies, construct buildings to improve your economy and public happiness, forge trade agreements and military alliances with other factions. Then fight large scale battles involving thousands of soldiers in real time. And by soldiers, I’m not just talking about your standard swordsmen, spearmen, archers and cavalry. The fantasy setting provides a wide variety of unusual creatures including giant eagles, phoenixes, dragons, hydras, rat ogres, hell pit abominations and many more.
This is the fourth Total War game I’ve played, after Shogun 2, Rome 2 and the original Warhammer. After spending almost 50 hours playing through the High Elf campaign, I can confidently say that TWW2 is easily the best version, building on what was good about the previous games, and improving in several ways.
The most obvious improvement is how the vortex affects the campaign. I was never really comfortable with the victory conditions in any of those previous Total War games. They usually required you to control a certain number of settlements, and sometimes eliminate a specific faction. I often felt like I ended up going to war with factions that I didn’t really consider to be my enemy, just to expand far enough to satisfy the victory conditions.
In order to gain control of the vortex and win the campaign, the four main races need to collect resources to perform five rituals. Each controlled settlement provides a small amount of resources, but some settlements in specific locations provide a larger amount. This means you don’t necessarily need to have the biggest empire to win. Each ritual takes place in three of your settlements simultaneously, and you’ll have to defend them for ten turns until the ritual completes. Starting a ritual will allow some Chaos armies to pass through the vortex, with the intention of destroying ritual sites. And the four races can always see each other’s ritual progress, so this naturally triggers conflict between them, especially in the later stages.
In my High Elves campaign, things were looking good at the halfway stage, as I was first to complete the third ritual. I was intending to stay defensive for the rest of the campaign, but after a while I noticed the Dark Elves had pulled in front after a period of aggressive expansion. This forced me to start an invasion of their lands to slow them down. The Lizardmen had the same idea as me, so the Dark Elves got pushed back quite far. At one point I thought that the Skaven were going to sneak a win while everyone else was fighting each other. Then one of my allies destroyed a Skaven ritual site, giving me a clear run to victory. It really felt like every faction was involved in an epic world war.
The world map is quite varied, from the frozen wastes of the north, to the Elves’ mountainous island, to the tropical jungles and deserts in the south. There are many minor races scattered around, including vampires, dwarves, bretonians, greenskins and wood elves. Any race can now claim any settlement (the previous game had some annoying restrictions), but will suffer penalties to growth, economy and army replenishment if the climate isn’t desirable. You’re also encouraged to explore the seas, as you can often find shipwrecks containing treasure which could include extra gold, weapons/armour to equip on your generals and temporary buffs for your soldiers in combat.
The AI was good in the previous game, but another improvement in TWW2 is that the AI will attack the player more often on the battlefield instead of always just sitting back and waiting for you to come at them.
Each faction can also spend gold to perform rites (different to rituals) which give temporary factionwide buffs. For example, the High Elves have a rite which makes armies immune to attrition (soldiers dying while travelling through bad weather conditions), which is perfect when attacking enemy settlements in harsh/corrupted environments.
Each of the main races has a unique mechanic which makes their playing style different to the others. The High Elves are the only one that I can talk about as I haven’t played as the other races yet – they get bonuses to diplomacy through a political intrigue system. Periodically you’ll encounter multiple choice scenarios, and your decisions will result in gaining or losing influence, as well as other temporary factionwide effects. Influence can then be spent to improve your relationship with another faction, or to damage the relationship between two of your enemies.
In the early part of my campaign, I was frequently being attacked by two minor factions, the Skaeling and the Pirates of Sartosa. Using influence, I was able to make peace with Sartosa, convince them to declare war on the Skaeling, and then I made an alliance with Sartosa and pushed the Skaeling back, completely wiping them out. My only complaints with this mechanic is that there aren’t many different scenarios, so I encountered frequent repeats, and they often referred to the leaders of other Elven factions that had long since been eliminated.
Total War Warhammer 2 is an absolute masterpiece, and I’ve loved every minute of it. Its going to get my vote for best game of 2017. If you’re a fan of Total War, or strategy games in general, Warhammer 2 is an essential purchase. Considering the length of the campaign, and the variety of playable factions, you won’t regret a full price purchase.

I can't recommend the game in its current state. Warhammer II was advertised as having a new campaign that focused on the vortex and a stitched together map that combines the new races and continent with the old.
What we recieved was the vortex campaign that while entertaining the first time through is far to similair on subsiquent playthroughs and has some majorly annoying features such as chaos and other faction intervention forces spawning randomly somewhere in your territory and then running amok. This is to say nothing about the auto resolve issues with certain factions and the abysmal naval "combat"
Most of the above should be fine though, Mortal empires was to be the meat of the game. Total War style conquest across a huge campaign map with all the factions vying for domination. Instead what we recieved was a half baked pushed out the door campaign that manages to suck much of the fun out of Mortal Empires. It is clear at this point that Mortal Empires was no where near ready for release with the main game, and is honestly not ready for release in its current state. Missing factions, Bugs carried over from the Vortex Campagin, Chaos spawning in the middle of your territories, army compositions that make no logical sense to anyone, rediculous buffs given to the AI in higher difficulties.
Overall Warhammer II was not in a state to release when it did, and almost 3 months later is still not fully ready. This game should have released early 2018 content complete. I don't like purchasing a game to find out later that major content that was promised is going to be drip fed to me months later and bugs that have been present since launch will still be around. Sometime next year Warhammer II will be a great game, but it is not that game now and it has soured my on buying any CA game until months after its release at a steep discount.

Thirty Fights of Loving is an abstract, explorative adventure game in which you take on the role of a member of a group of criminals living in a prohibition and police state. You simply wander through a series of environments, occasionally interacting with things, and finding yourself whisked away to another time point. It's not linear and it's not long - which is probably my main issue with it. It's not long enough for those hooks to matter - 5-10 minutes after asking those questions it's over. But that brings me to the part I liked about it - I liked that it left you to interpret/fill in the story, which admittedly won't be everyone's cup of tea.
As for actual recommendations - some people will love it and think it's a brilliant little piece of art, others will hate it and find it pretentious. I, personally, didn't mind it.. but I'm not sure I'd be happy if I paid for it outright (got it in a bundle). Which is why I'm not recommending it. :/ If you're not sure whether or not it's for you, I'd recommend waiting until it's on sale or in a bundle, otherwise you *may* feel cheated.

I've owned this game for a few weeks already, and I still haven't come to terms with its abject, unadulterated beauty. I could talk about the controls or the level design, which are normally the most important points for me for any platformer... If I did that, I would be comparing it favorably to the best platformers I've ever played. But in spite of the game's excellence in those areas, it is its visual and musical supremacy that sticks in my mind.
Friends of mine, even friends who don't normally like platformers, beg me to stream this game for them, equating it to "audiovisual crack". Occasionally—even after my third full playthrough—I find myself stopping, overwhelmed for a few moments by what I'm seeing. It has set a new visual standard for me, one which every other game I've played to date falls well short of achieving.
As for the music... In-game, it is sublime and nearly seamless. It isn't that it sets the mood of the game, nor vice versa; the soundtrack and the rest of the game simply... complete each other. Perfectly. To the note. And, listening to bits of the soundtrack outside the focusing influence of the game itself, I find myself moved in ways I have
been moved by music before.
I am normally loquacious and pride myself on my vocabulary, but words completely fail me when I try to describe how this game looks and sounds and feels. Very few games have had this kind of impact on me. This is the sort of release that comes once per decade, or less.
BUY IT.

The first thing you need to know when you buy AGK is that you are getting two products in one.  AGK comes in two flavours or tiers.  Tier One is a derivative of BASIC and Tier Two is a set of libraries for C++.  Both tiers employ a 'write once, deploy everywhere' framework. That means that you don't need to change the code in order to deploy for Android or Apple (or others).
Tier One has all the simplicity of any other variety of BASIC.  It's incredibly easy to start coding with it but that simplicity doesn't come at any cost.  The language is a powerful one and any game written in AGK Tier One will be indistinguishable from any other game on the market.
Tier Two is for the more advanced coder or someone that is already familiar with C++ but still makes creating games a very simple process.
If I had to choose a negative, it would be that AGK has a small development team, so any new feature and enhancements take a long time to arrive.  However, a recent announcement by TheGameCreators says that the development team has just been increased.  But even so, AGK is currently a very stable and very powerful language, so any enhancements are just that - enhancements .
Whether you choose to code in Tier One's BASIC environment or utilise that additional power and flexibility of Tier Two's C++ libraries, you will find AGK is a very powerful and very affordable way to quickly and easily get your games produced and into the various app stores.
When you also consider the online tutorials, documentation, commented code snippets and the very friendly online community, you can't go wrong with AGK.

I've been using AGK for several years now. In my experience, it is the single best all-in-one tool for indie coders wanting to make games for mobile and desktop platforms.
It gives a good blend between being able to code the game yourself, without doing all the work for you.
You can fully customise every aspect of your game, but don't have to deal with low level APIs, device fragmentation, complicated frameworks and unnecessary code.
AGK sits perfectly in the middle of the spectrum between coding native (eg. Android Studio) and tools that basically let you import graphics and they do everything else (eg. GM:Studio, Construct 2).
For what it does, AGK is the single best option available. It is not for everybody, but if you're looking to code games yourself with minimal effort, then it is for you.
App Game Kit is also an excellent option for beginners learning how to code.

With my knowledge of xBasic (CA-Clipper) and Basic programming (from Sinclair Basic up to VB6) I felt immediatly at home with AGK. I tried other engines, but only in AGK I was able to develop quickly a little educative game, a simple puzzle with sounds. It was easy to get it running on my tablet and my low cost chinese mobile phone. When I had a doubt, I always found the solution in the online help, or I remembered something that I saw in the examples. The examples are easy to understand; now I'm studying AGK Official Tutorial Guide to learn AGK more deeply.
I know that many people do not like Basic, some will ask for Lua or Python or C# support and object-oriented programming, but for me it would only increase the time to learn new things that I really do not have a real need. Call me a "Basic Die Hard head", but it's the way that I see the things, at least for now. You do not have to be afraid of spaghetti code, it is simple to keep the thing clean.
What I do not like in AGK is the still very basic support to 3D. I know that perhaps this is not something simple to do, but I would really love a simple to use enviroment (Game Guru-like) with AGK basic programming.
So, this is my recommendation: if you have lots of experience with Basic/xBase programming, try AGK2. It can be a good surprise to you. If you are new to computer programming, it can be very fun to learn AGK Basic.

At the time of this review i had put 100 hours into his game in 1 week after launch on steam. Its's a damn good game and certainly has the potential to be a very good MMO.  Let me start with the positives of this game, Keep in mind this is still in alpha.
1. PvP is great. Battles can go on for 1 hour 30min, however, they dont feel like that at all. machanics are all there and keeps you intrested in the battle all the way to the end. Oh, fleet size pvp can get as big as 25 vs 25.

4. A good selection of nations to pick from.
5. Arr, matey, thar be ye booty!  (Be a Pirate)
6. Crafting. Its still in its infancy but there is enough there atm to keep you preoccupied, although it still needs alot of work done to it.
7. Board and raid other ships. destroy enemy sails with 'chain shot' then whittle down the enemy crew with 'Grape' board the ship than take the loot and ship as a prize.
Now some stuff that is in the Gray zone, this stuff is a good idea but still needs alot of work in my eyes:
1. The economy. As it stands at the point of writing this review in a alpha build, the economy is broken. There are some people that have got a monopoly on some of the goods and its very hard to get hold of some of the 'goods' to build ships. so the prices of ship building are very high and you will most likely loose any sort of profit. That said i have heard that its ok on other servers but some of the ship crafting needs to be tweeked to balance things.
2. 'Durabilty'. On ships you get something called durabilty. These are effectually your lives. rate 7-5 ships have 5 dura (lifes) then rate 4-1 ships you get one less life per rate.  For me personally i would like to only see 1 life per ship but alot of people will disagree with me.
3. Small ships are pretty useless and are used as a 'stepping stone' to get the next Rate ship. I would like to find a way so small ships are used later on in game.
4. The map/ Open sea, Its well big. it fits in well with the game and how its done. you have to work out what direction to sail from your compuss and it can & will take hours to get to where you want to go. Its how it should be, however, its a bit boring for the eye. I do believe that they are planning to add things like storms and damage to your ships, etc... this will make it alot more dynamic
Now to the bad things in this current Alpha build:
1. UI is crap! its only a few blue boxes with text.
2. Its very hard to just pick up the game and start playing it if your new, There is nothing to help you apart from the ingame chat.
3. Missions are extremely repetitive yet they are one of the best ways to get exp and money.
4. Feel the grind! The first few days i thought that the exp gain was to fast, however, that changed once i got rank 1st Lt. It takes bloody ages to grind exp and it really is quite painful.
5. Current lack of content. There really isnt much in the game atm, howevewr, it is only alpha and i do know some very exciting things are going to be added and alot of rebalancing is going to happen.
6. Trading is still very poor. This will get better over time but as it stands there really is not much point as it takes along time to get to port to port.
This is what i have made of the game so far from me playing it. For an Alpha stage game it really is solid and well done. If you can keep in mind that its Alpha then alot of the bugs/ balancing issues/ lack of content can be forgiven. there are somethings that i personally need to be changed but everyone is differant.
I would suggest you watch a few streams of gameplay and ask lots of questions before buying it, i did, this will give you a better idea if you would like the game or not.

Cooperation and leadership are extremely important to fight for control of the sea, but as of right now there aren't any game mechanics that help clan leaders gently guide their squeeky sheeple contingent to victory.

If you're looking for a game about 17th-18th century sailing and warfare in the caribbean, I'd say this is the game you'd want. It has some similarities to Pirates of the Burning Sea, but it is more complex, has way better graphics, and is way more realistic, at least in my opinion.
Still, the game is in Early Access, so there's alot left to be done, as the UI for one, and I suspect there will be some sort of avatar part of the game as well.
A few things bother me though, first of all there's no real difference between nationals and pirates, wich goes pretty much straight against what this game otherwise have in terms of realism, the second major thing is that it is very hard core, and is endorsed to be so by the vocal part of the community that are active on the forums.
Overall I can say that the developers seem to listen very closely to what those active on the forums say, and not only ask for but also act on alot of the feedback they get. This however seem to further propel the hard core setup of the game, and I fear this can lead to a high degree of drop-outs among those trying this game out.
This doesn't seem to be viewed as a problem for most of the players, since there seem to be an opinion that it will create a good and healthy playerbase if "weak" players are weeded out.
A good and healthy playerbase need enough players though, and I can see that might be a problem.
Still, this game is very well made, the ship combat is good, and the graphics are beautiful, even damn beautiful. Being an online multiplayer game though, it requires a crowd, and that is lacking at the moment. Lots of what I've read has been about why players drop out, and as I mentioned earlier, my firm belief is that it has to do with the hard core approach. At least for me and my mates, spending 2 hours going back and forth across the ocean just for a missed battle was taking its toll, as did the endless grind.
This became a core component though, the need for time, or the need for endurance, or both basically. Alot of players considered it important to "weed out" weaker elements of the playerbase, basically to have a strong community, and for that reason the extreme need for time, endurance or both was something good. Weeding out players in an online multiplayer game is sort of counter-productive though, and anything not attracting new players will eventually be part of the game's demise.
As of now, it's anyones guess where this will end up, but people have left for all kind of reasons: lack of time, being ganked by numerous others, not being allowed to gank anymore, no possibility to move across the ocean quickly, the introduction of teleportation, and so forth and so on. Obviously alot of choices are made according to the will of at least some forum authors, but what it ends up with in my opinion is sort of re-inventing the wheel again when it comes to online multiplayer games.
This might sort out, or it might not. If you consider picking this up, you have to consider the risk it might not turn into a release.

Puzzle Bots is a point & click adventure game designed by Erin Robinson (famous for her indie game Spooks and Little Girl in Underland), however this game has much more in common with one of her other games that goes by the name of Nanobots.
You start as Hero, the pick-up bot and are soon joined by Ultrabot (the toughest bot) and soon find yourself exploring the world around you from the eyes of a new-born robot. You'll later be joined by a whole host of other robots who each have their own special abilities, which will come in handy as you explore further into the world.
The graphics are cute and the illustrations are provided by some famous illustrators including contributions from Harvey James of Kotaku fame.
Some of the music tracks are really good, but where the game really excels is in its voice-overs; something you should by now really ought to expect from Wadjet Eye games.
To finish then, the game is about loving cooperation, and is yet another gem in Wadjet Eye's growing IP archive.

Fallout 3 is one of my all-time favourite games, and was one of the first games i got when i started getting serious about gaming back in 2008. The feeling of being in a destroyed neo-50's american world has a great affect on gameplay; to be surrounded by a futuristic twist on what was probably the peak of American culture while listening to tracks of American Swing and Jazz Blues while beating a Deathclaw to death after it surprise-attacked you and made you soil your pants is an experience that will only be found in the Fallout games.
The story of Fallout 3 is very reminiscent of the plots behind Fallout 1 and 2, and whilst i would say that i'd rather see a completely different story to the original games, there is far more story and content to make up for the main storyline which in my opinion wasn't anything new.
This game has allowed me to understand and enjoy an old genre of music that is found constantly played through the Galaxy News Radio station. I can't begin to tell you how many times i've listen to Bob Crosby and Cole Porter.
What this game does best and what i find Bethesda Game Studios to do best at in all their games is atmosphere and the feeling of being in the world that they are trying to portray. They did an extremely good job of capturing that post-Apocalyptic feel that aligns well with the classic games, but there are subtle differences because of the location and the different developers.
Combat is very fun, but not as responsive as some of the best shooters out there, but i'll give Bethesda credit as they are known for fantasy games where there is no such thing as fast fire-rate guns, since this is there first time at making an open world shooter RPG they did a good job at least. VATS is definitely the best part about combat, and the gore is super funny. The reaction i'd make to a super mutant's head exploding after a 32. caliber round through the skull is again one of the perks of playing this game.
There is a split of opinion between the new fans and the classic fans. My first Fallout experience was Fallout 3 but eventually i bought the older games and aced both of them, and i think all of them are great. I love this franchise and always will. I definitely recommend this game if you're new to the franchise, and then move onto New Vegas and then the classics.
Overall, i rate this game a 9.5/10. There is so much to do in this game, from taking in the lore, to the happy-go music, the rich culture and the endless gory fun, you will not go wrong by spending your money on this game.

I did not know whether to vote no and praise, or to vote yes and criticize. Unless you are into games as a medium and the exploration of new artistic approaches, do not buy (if you got it free, as in a bundle, no risk there). New ideas are always welcome, so I say nice try and hope to see more stuff in this spirit in the future. But this one did not resonate with me, although at some very specific points they managed to create an interesting atmosphere. Without a doubt, the best this game does is respecting the player as a clever person.

Mechanically there isn't much to 30 Flights of Loving or Gravity Bone, just WASD movement and an action button. But like The Stanley Parable or Thomas Was Alone, this is the kind of thing you pick up not for the gameplay but for a game where the developer is trying something weird and different and beautiful. It might not work 100%, but it will certainly stand out from almost everything else you have in your game library.
30 Flights of Loving starts off as a spy story and to say anything else will spoil the story. The rest of the game may be short, but also strange, bittersweet and I thoroughly enjoyed it.

The fact that I played it to the end was testament to what is a very weird narrative experiment.
There is limited interaction and no directions (besides things you can touch, walking and looking) and yet it told a somewhat coherent story.
I'm not sure if I'm bewildered or impressed, a bit of both. Not sure I would be happy if I paid full price for it but as part of the Humble Bundle I’m glad I played it.

BIT.TRIP RUNNER, or as I like to call it "$*&% I MISSED ONE !@&#$ JUMP AT THE VERY END" is a sometimes fun but more often frustrating rhythm game. All of the elements of a great game are there, but they don't quite fall together into a cohesive package in the way that you would hope they do.
Let's talk about the gameplay first. This is simultaneously the best and worst part of this game. BIT.TRIP RUNNER is a combination of rhythm game and side-scrolling platformer, where you have to jump, kick, and slide in time with music playing in the background. The player's character, we'll call him "Bit", is programmed to automatically run to the right the whole time the game is playing. No input is required to keep moving, and you'll be glad of this because all of your attention is going to need to be focused on doing other things just to stay alive. Jumping over, sliding under, and kicking through obstacles and enemies in time with the music can be pretty fun, and the feeling of satisfication you get once you finally complete a frustrating level is great. Unfortunately, these feelings of accomplishment are few and far between due to the unforgiving nature of the game. While it may be nice to play a game that doesn't hold your hand or offer you to "Press X to Win" like so many other games these days do, it is simply too far towards the other end of the difficulty spectrum for it's own good. It doesn't matter whether you are 2 minutes from the end of a level or 2 seconds, if your timing is off by just a hair, the game punishes you by sending you back to the very beginning of the level with an unrelenting lack of mercy. This leads to many extremely frustrating moments where you have performed every nuanced movement and action seamlessly and perfectly, only to be slightly off near the end of a level, forcing you to start over. BIT.TRIP RUNNER is at it's core a game about memorization and timing, and while this is not inherently a bad thing, a little more leeway, perhaps in the form of a checkpoint or a power-up that let's you rewind time to fix your mistakes, would balance out the difficulty of this game just enough to make it not so mind-numbingly frustrating.
Now, let's talk about the music and visuals of this game. Visually, the game is extremely simple. While this is not in itself a bad thing-any look at some of the top indie games will show you a simple visual style can be both beautiful and interesting-BIT.TRIP RUNNER is really neither of those things. Levels are visually indistinguishable from one another, with the exact same obstacles, enemies, and background elements appearing over and over throughout every single one of the levels I played. Admittedly, I have not completed the game beyond the first 10 or 11 levels, and so perhaps the visual style changes after a certain point, but if this is the case then the game is still suffering from a lack of variety as I shouldn't have to beat 12+ levels just to see a change in aesthetics. There are a few visually interesting and pretty-looking elements to the design, but overall the look of the game is dull, with backgrounds and obstacles appearing in mostly purple or muted gray tones. This leads to the game being incredibly repetitive from a visual standpoint, a problem which unfortunately plagues the music of the game as well. The music itself is very nice at first listen. As a fan of chiptunes myself, I quite enjoyed it for the first few minutes of gameplay. Sadly though, the lack of variety eventually ruins any potential this game might have had in the music department. Every single level I played starts with the same exact basic rhythm as the last one. This rhythm grows and evolves as you play through the level and pick up power-ups that change it's complexity. The melody of the songs themselves comes from the player's own actions in the level. Jumping over an obstacle will produce a note, as will sliding under one, kicking through one, or picking up one of dozens of gold pieces in each level. This could potentially lead to some very fun and interesting musical moments, but unfortunately-partially due to the perpetually unchanging basic rhythm and partially due to the lack of complexity or variety in the notes and sounds created by completing actions-this is not the case. There are a few moments of excitement here and there in the music of this game, but they are completely overshadowed and nullified by it's repetition. One missed moved sends you back to the beginning of the level, where you will once again face the same basic rhythm, level after level, attempt after attempt.
Overall, I really want to like this game. I'm honestly surprised that I have come back to it as much as I did. Still, I am on the fence about whether or not I can truly recommend it, and the cruel and repetitive nature of the game is what is pushing me towards not doing so. Although officialy I will not reccomend it, I will say that if you enjoy being challenged and don't mind looking at the same graphics, hearing the same sounds, and playing through the same levels over and over again, then perhaps you will enjoy it.
Final Score: 5/10

Total War Warhammer 2 is the latest game in the epic grand strategy franchise. Set in the fantasy version of the Warhammer universe, the player can choose to play as one of four races – High Elves, Dark Elves, Lizardmen and Skaven (giant rats) – as they battle over control of a magical vortex.
The vortex is basically a barrier, preventing the forces of Chaos from invading the world. Some factions are trying to save the world, while others want to cause the End Times. As is usual for Total War, gameplay is divided into two major sections. The turn based campaign map is where you focus on the big picture, empire wide tasks. Train armies, move them around the map, capture and defend settlements, research technologies, construct buildings to improve your economy and public happiness, forge trade agreements and military alliances with other factions. Then fight large scale battles involving thousands of soldiers in real time. And by soldiers, I’m not just talking about your standard swordsmen, spearmen, archers and cavalry. The fantasy setting provides a wide variety of unusual creatures including giant eagles, phoenixes, dragons, hydras, rat ogres, hell pit abominations and many more.
This is the fourth Total War game I’ve played, after Shogun 2, Rome 2 and the original Warhammer. After spending almost 50 hours playing through the High Elf campaign, I can confidently say that TWW2 is easily the best version, building on what was good about the previous games, and improving in several ways.
The most obvious improvement is how the vortex affects the campaign. I was never really comfortable with the victory conditions in any of those previous Total War games. They usually required you to control a certain number of settlements, and sometimes eliminate a specific faction. I often felt like I ended up going to war with factions that I didn’t really consider to be my enemy, just to expand far enough to satisfy the victory conditions.
In order to gain control of the vortex and win the campaign, the four main races need to collect resources to perform five rituals. Each controlled settlement provides a small amount of resources, but some settlements in specific locations provide a larger amount. This means you don’t necessarily need to have the biggest empire to win. Each ritual takes place in three of your settlements simultaneously, and you’ll have to defend them for ten turns until the ritual completes. Starting a ritual will allow some Chaos armies to pass through the vortex, with the intention of destroying ritual sites. And the four races can always see each other’s ritual progress, so this naturally triggers conflict between them, especially in the later stages.
In my High Elves campaign, things were looking good at the halfway stage, as I was first to complete the third ritual. I was intending to stay defensive for the rest of the campaign, but after a while I noticed the Dark Elves had pulled in front after a period of aggressive expansion. This forced me to start an invasion of their lands to slow them down. The Lizardmen had the same idea as me, so the Dark Elves got pushed back quite far. At one point I thought that the Skaven were going to sneak a win while everyone else was fighting each other. Then one of my allies destroyed a Skaven ritual site, giving me a clear run to victory. It really felt like every faction was involved in an epic world war.
The world map is quite varied, from the frozen wastes of the north, to the Elves’ mountainous island, to the tropical jungles and deserts in the south. There are many minor races scattered around, including vampires, dwarves, bretonians, greenskins and wood elves. Any race can now claim any settlement (the previous game had some annoying restrictions), but will suffer penalties to growth, economy and army replenishment if the climate isn’t desirable. You’re also encouraged to explore the seas, as you can often find shipwrecks containing treasure which could include extra gold, weapons/armour to equip on your generals and temporary buffs for your soldiers in combat.
The AI was good in the previous game, but another improvement in TWW2 is that the AI will attack the player more often on the battlefield instead of always just sitting back and waiting for you to come at them.
Each faction can also spend gold to perform rites (different to rituals) which give temporary factionwide buffs. For example, the High Elves have a rite which makes armies immune to attrition (soldiers dying while travelling through bad weather conditions), which is perfect when attacking enemy settlements in harsh/corrupted environments.
Each of the main races has a unique mechanic which makes their playing style different to the others. The High Elves are the only one that I can talk about as I haven’t played as the other races yet – they get bonuses to diplomacy through a political intrigue system. Periodically you’ll encounter multiple choice scenarios, and your decisions will result in gaining or losing influence, as well as other temporary factionwide effects. Influence can then be spent to improve your relationship with another faction, or to damage the relationship between two of your enemies.
In the early part of my campaign, I was frequently being attacked by two minor factions, the Skaeling and the Pirates of Sartosa. Using influence, I was able to make peace with Sartosa, convince them to declare war on the Skaeling, and then I made an alliance with Sartosa and pushed the Skaeling back, completely wiping them out. My only complaints with this mechanic is that there aren’t many different scenarios, so I encountered frequent repeats, and they often referred to the leaders of other Elven factions that had long since been eliminated.
Total War Warhammer 2 is an absolute masterpiece, and I’ve loved every minute of it. Its going to get my vote for best game of 2017. If you’re a fan of Total War, or strategy games in general, Warhammer 2 is an essential purchase. Considering the length of the campaign, and the variety of playable factions, you won’t regret a full price purchase.

I wish I could recommend this game. The idea is really cool especially for something that seems like it may be limited since it's a rail platformer. But there are problems... a lot of problems.
Graphics: Look, I'm not going to complain about the graphics being 8bit. That's the style the game wanted to take itself (for the most part), and I'm ok with that. I actually like the basic look of the character and some of the 8bit objects in the world are pretty cool looking too. But then you have to realize that this is a game where the character never stops running. The background, the foreground, the obstacles you have to dodge... it just gets vomit inducing. It just looks so blurry that it hurts to look at this game for very long, and I'm somebody that doesn't get motion sickness very easy. If you get powerups, then the screen pretty much flashes every time you grab a gold piece. In a game where you have to have your eyes taped open to make sure you don't blink and miss a jump, having distractions like that is unforgivable.
Gameplay: It's simple, and actually provides entertainment to an extent. At first, it's fun to get pass the slightly challenging obstacles. It feels nice to pass something that seems really difficult on your first try. The problem is this game is seriously one of the most repetitive games I've ever played in my life. I guess you could say a rail platformer that uses only a few buttons will inevitably be pretty repetitive, but they could've done much more with this game. If you play the game and come across a slightly challeging obstacle, you can be damn sure that you'll be doing that same exact obstacle twenty more times through the rest of the game (that's assuming you complete the rest of the game in a perfect run, which you won't)
Replayability Value: As stated above, this game is repetitive. At first, it's repetitive because it's really easy, and not much can be done to change the repitition. Later on, it's repetitive because the level design lacks creativity and just rehashes the same things from the last few levels. After that, starting at about world 3-9, it's repetitive because you get killed by something that's actually a new challenge. Then you hit world 3-10 and it's repetitive because that new challenge is being milked for all its worth and is thrown into the next level 4 times and you get killed after completing it because you misjumped and hit the edge of a staircase. So, the replayability value is bad. Keep in mind, this is a game that forces you to start at the beggining of a level after one screw up. Yeah...
Soundtrack: At first, I liked the soundtrack. It was interesting and kept me playing the game despite its lackluster gameplay. But just like the level design, they got lazy. The soundtrack sounds the same throughout the entire game. There may be slight changes, but it still sounds so bland after playing for a while. You get a headache from the ugly background, the repetitive music, and the fact that you have to keep playing the beggining of every level 200 hundred times because you can't get through these levels like a robot.
Difficulty: Don't even get me started. Personally, this game bored the hell out of me until much later. I'll admit, 1-11 was hard because it was a couple of minutes long, and making a perfect run over a few minutes isn't easy, but I still got through it after several tries. Then the game got boring again. It got boring because the obstacles that I was coming across were the same obstacles I came across ten times in the last map. All of the sudden, I got to 3-9 and out of nowhere the game decided to throw, by far, the hardest obstacles the game has to offer. There was no warning, no slowly scaling diffculty leading up to this point, it just went haywire out of nowhere. But, luckily, it was at the very beggining of the round, so I had a good chance to practice and practice. Finally, I perfected it! Eventually I got pass the level, and even though it was difficult, I stayed positive and continued into the next level. I get through half of the level filled with obstacles I've seen before just to be greeted by this same ♥♥♥♥ing obstacle from 3-9. Then eventually I get to 3-11, and the same ♥♥♥♥ing obstacle once again. I played throughout this entire game and feel like I've only really played 4 different levels.
And, don't get me wrong, I don't hate this game because I died a lot. I love Super Meat Boy and that game infuriates me to no end. The difference between this and SMB is that SMB had good level design. They implemented some obstacles you've seen before but they did it in new, clever ways. This game does no such thing. You just do what you did before.
I wanted to like this game, but it has only provided me dissapointment and infuriation. Opinions are subjective, so take what you will from this review, but if I could do it all over again I wouldn't even get this game for free, it's just a waste of time that I've only put so many hours into because I'm obsessed with completing it.

I can't recommend the game in its current state. Warhammer II was advertised as having a new campaign that focused on the vortex and a stitched together map that combines the new races and continent with the old.
What we recieved was the vortex campaign that while entertaining the first time through is far to similair on subsiquent playthroughs and has some majorly annoying features such as chaos and other faction intervention forces spawning randomly somewhere in your territory and then running amok. This is to say nothing about the auto resolve issues with certain factions and the abysmal naval "combat"
Most of the above should be fine though, Mortal empires was to be the meat of the game. Total War style conquest across a huge campaign map with all the factions vying for domination. Instead what we recieved was a half baked pushed out the door campaign that manages to suck much of the fun out of Mortal Empires. It is clear at this point that Mortal Empires was no where near ready for release with the main game, and is honestly not ready for release in its current state. Missing factions, Bugs carried over from the Vortex Campagin, Chaos spawning in the middle of your territories, army compositions that make no logical sense to anyone, rediculous buffs given to the AI in higher difficulties.
Overall Warhammer II was not in a state to release when it did, and almost 3 months later is still not fully ready. This game should have released early 2018 content complete. I don't like purchasing a game to find out later that major content that was promised is going to be drip fed to me months later and bugs that have been present since launch will still be around. Sometime next year Warhammer II will be a great game, but it is not that game now and it has soured my on buying any CA game until months after its release at a steep discount.

Honestly, from its perfectly interwoven narrative into the gameplay to the incredibly fleshed-out characters and lore, I can say with nearly absolute certainty that Bad Rats: the Rats' Revenge is a tour de force of game design, lore building, and artistic expression through an interactive medium the likes of which have very rarely been seen in the course of human history, much less through video games.
The powerful metaphors within the game strike an ominously sincere chord with many a player, as he or she experiences the crumbling wall background signifying the decrepit infrastructure of major american roads and cities, as these mice, represented as blue-collar americans by their jobs all include physical labour such as construction, demolition or service in the military , butcher the cats, represented as the higher class of white-collar workers by the cat's usually superior intellect. This work of art is a piece that knows the times that we live in, when the societal schism between classes is at an all-time high and is festering beyong any of our control until the mice and the cats are forced to become the catalysts of chaos within our once-great nation.
Another layer is added onto this by the inclusion of one simple rat. This rat is portrayed as a suicide bomber jihadist who uses the blast created from his perceived religious martyrdom to also destroy the bourgeois cats. This is an incredibly clever satire, as the creator of this masterwork believes that, by the lower class destroying those in power, they are not unlike and would most certainly be supported by those whom they abhor most, the middle-eastern terrorist jihadists. This is but another hard-hitting commentary on the state of the rift between societal class.
I could rave onwards and onwards and about the numerous harsh realities that Bad Rats: the Rats' Revenge uncovers and shows starkly so that the awestruck public can observe the horrific visage of modern day American culture, but for the sake of brevity, I will close my review here.
This game, which is more of a perfect synthesis between an interactive medium, a work of art, and a societal statement, never wavers in its funambulism between gameplay, in itself a system worth lauding, and its bitter view of our divides as a people and as a nation.

The good:

The bad:
Grind, grind, grind (done to enable their pay2win plans)
What do I mean by grind?  I've got 80 hours into the game, and I'm still sailing the starter ship.  Sure, I could be sailing the first square rigger (I just bought a snow), but why should I?  I'm almost broke, the starter ship is free, and I need to save for the next tier ship.  The system is broken.  XP is too slow (by about 4x) and gold is far too scarce.  People will say you can do it faster (and yes you can), but add in the reroll (because I picked France, and no one speaks English in chat), the failed try at trading (which is grindy), the aborted crafting try (which is grindy), and a days worth of exploring, and you are right at about 80 hours.
80 hours (probably closer to 70 due to idling).
Still in the starter ship.
Now, you will get many saying this isn't going to be pay to win.  Call it what you want, pay to play, play to win, pay to skip the grind - it's all semantics.  The people in denial are just trying to set up an MMO with an elite class of players (the ones willing to put tons and tons of time into repetitive missions), while the rest of us sit back and wish we were part of that elite class.
Repetitive missions you say?  There's only ONE mission.  Sail out for 5 mins, kill the pirate (or pirates), sail back.  20  to 25 minutes total (if you know exactly what you are doing).  A resonable pace is 2 missions per hour.  At first, longer, and you will fail frequently.  You'll get about 90xp per mission (on your way to 1000xp for teir 2 - tier 3 another 1000, teir 4 another 3750).  You will need to get to tier 3 for your first significant ship upgrade, but you had better not been spending any gold.  You'll need every cent to buy and equip that next ship  (and after that, you won't want to sail it, because you wont want to lose it).  I like the difficulty - no complaints there.  Only problem - the grind. Rinse, repeat until you are numb.  Grind even more. Oh you can go after that unarmed trader instead for 40xp- what great excitement!  You could also play PvP for xp, which is much more interesting, but your xp rate/hour goes way down - and worst of all you will sink more often.  With anything but the free ship, sinking is expensive - so no more PvP for you!  Great design, huh?
No thanks.  Save your money.  They make excuses  (it's an alpha!), well $40 sets a pretty high bar, unfinished or not.
I should add, they will tell you that the Premium ships will only be cosmetic, but they are being dishonest. The Premium ships cannot be lost (but can be captured) (see source link below).The non-paying customers (I mean  the ones who refuse to pay more than the initial $40) get 5 sinkings per ship, then they are right back into the grind of paying for a new (expensive in terms of time) ship. That's the reason it's pay2win (or whatever you want to call it - semantics). The starter ship is free, so have fun with that, otherwise get your wallet out if you don't have hours and hours to play.
A few more things...  Although the combat model is great, the AI cheats.  It has uncanny accuracy.  Devs say they won't tone it down because players eventually get good.  Well, this just punishes the new players.  And people don't actually get good at naval tactics.  They get good at learning to deal with a computer AI.  The technique of turning your bow or stern into an enemy to soak damage is almost laughable, and so unrealistic.  Oh, and the cannons are FAR too accurate.  Players are actually aiming for specific parts of the ships (trying to hit the masts, for example, or sneak a shot into the hull below the waterline).  For Pete's sake, these were smooth bore cannons on a very unstable platform!  Imagine you are on a real rocking ship, trying to time your shot with the rocking - you certainly aren't going to be aiming at the mast.  But in this game, no problem.  Shoot that mast clean off the ship if your aim is good enough (there's effectively a gyro stabilizer better than an M1 tank's in this game).  So if you are looking for realism, you won't find it here.
For anyone considering this game, look at all those thumbs down.  This is an accurate review.  Those thumbs down show you the fan boys you'll be playing with - trying to dishonestly bury these facts.
Dishonesty seems to be a theme with Naval Action.  Shame, shame, shame.

I've been using AGK since it was first released in 2011, and despite its share of quirks (and what game development kit doesn't have those?), I have to say I'm very happy with the product.
However before you buy, it's important to understand what you are getting. AGK is not an Unreal/Unity style all encompassing game engine. It is a tool primarily aimed at those comfortable working with code, and is, by and large, a code-only solution. As a programmer, I find this makes it a delight to work with, as it is far lighter weight and more flexable than many of the alternatives on the market. That said, if you require a purely graphical solution like Unreal's Blueprints, you won't find that here.
Overall, I would say AGK has a very strong feature set. However it is worth remembering that it is strongly biased towards 2D cross platform game development, and so in general its 3D command set is somewhat less mature. The AGK BASIC language is, as of AGK V2, a very capable little language, but will feel limited if you're familiar with other programming languages, due to its lack of OO or functional programming features among other things. That said, I consider it to be an ideal beginners language. Further, any limitations of AGK BASIC are mitigated by the fact that AGK also supports working in C++, which is of course capable of pretty much anything you want.
The community around AGK isn't as vibrant as it once was, but support is still there in various places, including the TGC forums, which is still a great place to get your questions answered and share your projects with others. Support from TGC themselves hasn't always been perfect, but the fact that we're still here five years after release getting new updates, features, and platforms, says it all really. TGC supported their previous language, DarkBASIC Pro, for over a decade, and so have proven themselves committed to the long haul. The documentation of AGK is also, IMO, very good, and in fact might be a good place to look if you're still on the fence about whether to go for AGK.
All in all, I would highly recommend AGK to both beginners looking to get into games programming, and also experienced programmers looking for a solid cross platform games API which they can build their own engine on without bringing in all the cruft associated with many larger engines. However if you are primarily an artist, or looking for a mostly visual game making solution, I would suggest investigating other options such as GameMaker/UE4/Unity.

A little background:
I'm a professional developer schooled in C# and Java. I am however not schooled to create games, but I know how the mechanics work. 3D game development is more of a hobby/side-project. Please read my review as such, if you're completely new to programming, my feeling about this product can greatly differ from your perspective. Most of my pros and cons are subjective. But true in my opinion. Also: I use this product only for 3D development, I have no interest in the 2D side.
Pro's of this engine:
+ Very easy to get started, the documentation on the website and examples bundled with this software are solid and easy                 to understand.
+There is a lot build in: Getting an animated 3D object and show it on screen, couply of lines and you're done.
+Write once, deploy everywhere. This is a VERY big plus, you have to change NO code to deploy it to another platform. Your code compiles to bytecode and the AGK players handles everything. Clever way to approach a game engine.
+The code editor, which is a fork of Gedit, is the perfect tool for this engine. It just works as expected: Intellisense, code completion, snippet support, ...
+ A very good community forum (I mean on the website, I don't know about the Steam forum, never use it), very friendly folks, always ready to help you out.
+ Platforms supported: Windows, Linux, macOS, iOS, Android, Raspberry Pi, HTML5, what more could a person ask for?
+ Good FPS, fast and solid engine.
Things to consider about this engine: (not the cons)
* This is a Basic dialect, you hate it, you love it. I personally don't mind, I like the simplicity.
* This product will NOT create CryTek like results. You can create beatiful games, but not 'Stunning', 'Breath taking', 'Cutting-edge' graphics. This could be a con for you. Not for me, I knew what I was buying, and it was not my intention to  get a cutting-edge engine.
* If you're just checking out some engines, paying full price is rather steep in my opinion. But there are a lot of sales. A price of 45 EUR would be just right I think. If you're planning to make a living out of this, full price is not too much for this products
*In the beginning, I had no idea where this product was heading, what the developers really wanted. But that changed this year, they asked us (the users) with a survey what we want. This was a real con for me, the lack of communication, but I got my hopes up, I think this is turning into a pro.
*I would like faster updates of the framework. Smaller but more incremental, every 2-3 weeks would be perfect. And if an update takes longer, clear communication why that is happening.
Cons (for me)
-Not OOP. The language is fully procedural and not object oriented. For me this is a con. I think OOP would enhance this product a lot. BUT: I understand it fully that they would not implement it. I would like it, but a lot of people (also beginers) might feel it's making things WAY harder. So for the future of AGK it might be a bad idea to go to OOP way. My suggestion: make it hybrid, leave all commands procedural, but give developers the chance to create classes/inheritance/.. But leave the original framework procedural. Then only the people who are interested in OOP can actually use it.
-Focus on 2 tiers, Basic and C++. In my opinion, most people that look into this engine, want Basic. There are a lot of good C++ game devevelopment libraries out there. AGK doesn't have any USPs over other libraries.
-No roadmap (but I have hopes this might change, see considerations)
Overall, I'm VERY happy with this product. I love it. I love it's simplicity, the way it works, the results it provides, the easyness. My main worries are more of a communication kind.
Would recommend this software to anybody that has interest in game development!

Every gamer at some point of their lives get that itch: I want to make my own game. There are a bunch of different tools, engines and programming languages to get started with. Using these languages and tools, however, require years of training and education since they aren't easy for beginners.
But AppGameKit is easy for beginners since it takes care of graphics handling under the hood for you. If you want to get started fast with game programming rather that using harder-to-grasp engines like Unity or Unreal, this is the right tool for you. A cool thing about AGK is that it comes in two so called Tiers: Tier 1 is the more beginner-friendly option and is based on BASIC language. If you're already familiar with programming, and C++ especially, Tier 2 is for you.
With AGK you can make both 2D and 3D games, and if you want to have realistic physics in your games, AGK comes with integrated Box2D and Bullet physics libraries. No need to download any sources or binaries for them, they're already there, waiting for your commands.
You might also think that you want to develop your game for both iOS and Android. No need to worry, AGK code works on both devices. And I personally fell in love with AGK even more when it got support for LINUX! So no matter what platform you choose to develop for and on, AGK can handle it.
Every beginner developer needs also support and guidance. AGK has a very active community ready to help you and give you feedback.
If you still want more information, go visit
. There are basically the same information and even more that I just described and some example apps people have already made with AGK. You should also visit

This game took me by surprise.

I'm glad that I did though, as it is positively delightful.
The game follows 5 miniature robots who, after each having been invented by a different inventor at a research company, begin to explore and question their surroundings. Meanwhile (sometimes literally) in the background a larger story is taking place where the inventors question the motives and past of their employer, have crushes and dreams and in general feel very human.
The game has full voice acting for the human characters and cute robot sounds for the robots, it's clearly not AAA-budget voice acting but it's actually really good and I was consistently entertained and swept along by it.
The puzzles, which are linear and progressively more complex, are nice little one-screen environmental puzzles where the various abilities of your 5 little heroes is put to the test. The solutions are all pretty easy to figure out (maybe with the exception of one of the final puzzles, which required some more timing than I was used to until then), but that didn't detract from the enjoyment I was getting from it at all.
. That would be the one-word review of this game. It wraps up nicely, doesn't outstay its welcome and oozes personality (which is impressive considering you're controlling a (literal) handful of robots).
A perfect example on how to make a neat game without having access to a huge budget, and something I'd recommend to everybody.

Thirty Flights of Loving feels like a pitch for a bigger game. Before things could get interesting, it's over.
I'd like to point out right away that the game did not like my computer. The game crashed multiple times after trying to change settings, and I managed to somehow die during the first jump cut...and then crash. Setting the game's executable to Windows 98 compatibility mode and setting the resolution options as launch parameters seemed to fix it.
I do quite like the art style, and the music and sound effects are excellent. It's just a shame that there's not too much of any of it.
That's not to say what's there is bad. I like the general presentation of the story, for the most part. Due to the jump cuts, it can be unclear on the exact order of events that occur. You're missing parts of the story, and what's there is out of order, but piecing it together isn't ridiculously complicated. That said, I can understand why it might confuse some.
As I said before, though, it feels like a pitch to raise money for a longer version of the game. I want more details on the story. What went wrong with the job they were on, and what was the job they were doing, anyway? You have to give a reason for people to care. A summary of a story never has the impact that the full story does.
My feelings about Gravity Bone, the prequel to this (and which is included in this package), can be summed up in pretty much the same way, with one additional complaint: the gameplay. While Thirty Flights of Loving is mostly a walking simulator with very limited activity, Gravity Bone has a few items that you pick up and carry in your inventory. While having  interactivity is fine in a walking simulator, Gravity Bone makes the mistake of making what limited interactivity is in the game repetitive and unenjoyable, and honestly could have been done better with either reduced/smarter use of it, or near complete removal of it.
If Blendo Games decides to come back to this universe, I'd really like a more fleshed out experience next time. I don't mind the linearity or the absurd-yet-serious tone, but there's just not enough here to justify your time or your money.

I did not enjoy this game. It's just a bunch of confusing rooms and poorly-animated character interactions. The environments and graphics were ugly, even if the art style is meant to be simplistic. The gameplay seems to be split into 2 stories: Thirty Flights of Loving and Gravity Bone. TFOL is just exploring various environments; there is almost no interaction by the player other than walking. Gravity Bone has more interactivity, with items to use and quests to complete, but it is still extremely linear and vague in terms of what is happening.
I do give this game credit for attempting to tell a story without voice or dialogue, but it was executed terribly. Maybe I just suck at infering things, but I could not follow what sort of story this game was trying to tell.

This is at its best an ~*artistic*~ walking simulator.
This is at its worst a diminutive walking simulator.
This was an effort by its designer (apparently) to engage in storytelling without typical narrative techniques, ie. Voiceovers, random data files, etc. Commendable, but borrowing from cinema isn't anything new. Games have borrowed from cinema repeatedly.
What this game doesn't really spend much, if any, time doing is having the actual structure of the gameplay inform us of story. At one point, in his commentary, the designer explains that he used a characters acceptance of our taking an orange for ourselves to show that this was a space we belonged in. But in a game with such sparse interaction, we as players can't tell the difference between a character's acceptance of our actions, and lazy coding that failed to include consequences for our actions.
