Steam says I have played this but I haven't, so instead I'll give you a recipe for a rainbow cake:
Vegetable shortening
3 cups all-purpose flour
4 teaspoons baking powder
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 sticks (1 cup) unsalted butter, room temperature
2 1/3 cups sugar
5 large egg whites, room temperature
2 teaspoons pure vanilla extract
1 1/2 cups milk, room temperature
Buttercream Frosting
Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Brush six 9-inch-round cake pans (or as many 9-inch cake pans as you have, reusing them as necessary) with shortening. Line bottom of each cake pan with parchment paper, then brush again and set aside.
In a large bowl, whisk together flour, baking powder and salt, then set that set aside too. In the bowl of an electric mixer fitted with a paddle attachment, cream together butter and sugar. Slowly add egg whites and mix until well combined. Add vanilla and mix until fully incorporated. Add flour mixture and milk in two alternating additions, beginning with the flour and ending with the milk. Mix until well combined.
Divide batter evenly between six medium bowls. Add enough of each color of food coloring to each bowl, whisking, until desired shade is reached. Transfer each color to an individual cake pan. Transfer to oven and bake until a cake tester inserted into the center of each cake comes out clean, about 15 minutes (working in batches if necessary).
Remove cakes from oven and transfer to a wire rack. Let them cool for 10 minutes. Invert cakes onto a wire rack, then re-invert and let cool completely.
Using a serrated knife, trim tops of cakes to make level. Place four strips of parchment paper around perimeter of a serving plate or lazy Susan. Place the purple layer on the cake plate. Spread 1 cup of buttercream filling over the first layer so it extends just beyond edges. Repeat process with blue, green, yellow, and orange layers.
Place the remaining red layer on top, bottom-side up. Gently sweep away any loose crumbs, then cover the top and sides with a thin layer of frosting (also use any of the excess frosting visible between the layers). Refrigerate until set, about 30 minutes.
Optional: after refrigerating, cover cake again with remaining frosting.

I'm a huge fan of the Warhammer series.  I read the books, paint miniatures(don't enjoy the tabletop game that much though), and I'm a huge fan of the lore.  This game really keeps to the core tenants of Warhammer 40k.  What does that mean?
That Viceral Violence that only Warhammer 40k can deliver.
Close quarters combat....everywhere.
The lore: You FEEL like a space Marine.  You are a powerful being crafted for war and thats how the game makes you feel.  You're 3 meters tall, fast, strong, and incredibly hard to kill.
I would recommend this game as a good way to get into the universe of Warhammer 40k.  It's a fun, fast pased game with great core mechanics.  This game didn't have the funding of the halo series or Mass effect, but what it does have is a single player experience that is quite unique.  The multiplayer is nothing to scoff at either.  Each multiplayer class has it's own unique abilities that, when played right, can be incredibly potent in online matches.  And personally, I think that the multiplayer survival mode is one of the funnest around and it can only be beaten by a solid team effort.
On the downside, this game has contradictory moments.  The only way to gain health is by performing take downs which are spectacular displays of close quarters violence.  But, these can only be triggered in close quarters.  The problem arises when you are faced with several series of long range oponents you physically can't get at.
The environment can also be a bit...bland/repetative at times.  But again, I think that this has to do with funding of the game because Relic has made several wonderful environments in the past for the Warhammer series.
I love this game and I sincerely hope that they take the lessons learned from this game into making another.

I have well over 100 hours combined in this game between the Classic and Enhanced editions, and it is a very, very good game. It's only real weakness is a bit of a slow start. After a very brief intro section, you get to the main town, and there you stay for awhile, running around, talking to people, picking up quests, and trying to figure out where to go. There is a ton of combat in this game, but that is good thing, because D:OS has probably the best combat of any RPG ever made.  Once your characters get a few levels, and you begin unlocking not only new skills, but also figuring out new ways to use your skills together, you will be hooked.  My main character was a rogue, who started very squishy, but became an absolute beast later. The combination of the Glass Cannon perk (which increases action points significantly), maxed out Stealth (so you can hide in plain sight during combat), and Backstab (damage bonuses when attacking from stealth/flank) made him absolutely lethal.
If you like RPGs and tactical combat, you will enjoy this game.  Just make sure you stick with it past the first town.

I've followed TheGameCreators for many years (since 2003). I’ve used Dark Basic Pro and now work with their AppGameKit software.
What I most like about AppGameKit is the way you can easily make games and export them to several different platforms.  You easily have access to several options to control and optimize every part of your game engine, you don't just create your game with AppGameKit, you create your engine to suit your game the most.
Whatever I have on my mind, a 2D/3D Game or an app, I know I can go in depth with AppGameKit to make the game/app I want.
And with AppGameKit you can broadcast (stream) your game directly onto your different devices to try your game in live, it's an awesome feature.
The BASIC language is very powerful and intuitive.

App Game Kit is a very easy way to get into programming without having to learn a complex interface or engine. Things just work they way you want them to and you are not forced to do them in a specific way. This makes it very easy to get started on your projects. And what you do instantly works on multiple platforms with little to no extra work. If you want to do everything in code and not inside an editor then App Game Kit is the solution for you.

As a software developer, I need software which is both easy to use yet powerful enough for me to accomplish my development goals. AGK2 really is a simple to use language, but is powerful enough for me to create stunning in game visuals and deploy them to multiple platforms with ease.

This is the product I've been waiting for a long time.
I used to code in Blitz3D, which unfortunately is totally outdated by now, running on DX7.
I bought MonkeyX Pro, but I didn't really like the language.
Then I stumbled on AGK2.
I used to code with DarkBasic in the old days, so the syntax of AGK2 was just perfect for me.
AGK2 can export on mulitple platforms, just like MonkeyX Pro, but it's WAY easier.
AGK brings tons of useful command sets like 2D physics, 3D physics, tweening,  adverts, particles, and even supports GameCenter, Facebook and InApp-Purchases. Shaders, too? You betcha!
The learning curve is really awesome. Even a total beginner can do some impressive stuff in a couple of hours.
The forum is also great, people are very helpful.
A big plus is the free AGK 2 player, which enables you to broadcast your code right onto your Android device, without having to export to .apk. You simply hit the Broadcast button and you can play your game on your smartphone.
If you're an Indie developer and want to create games fast and easy, this is for you!!!

Although flawed, Puzzle Bots is a very enjoyable game that every adventure game afficionado should try.
It's easy to be deterred by the game's shortcomings.  It's a short game, and if you know what you're doing, you can finish it in just a few hours.  The graphics and animation, while charming, are underwhelming.  The story is almost entirely back-loaded, leaving you wondering what Dr. Hugo is thinking for almost the whole game, and introducing important characters and plot elements only at the very end, causing all but the most alert players to need to play through it again in order to understand the whole story.
However, another playthrough is not something you're going to mind.  The gameplay is easy to get into, and should be instantly familiar to anyone who enjoys the classic Lucasarts and Sierra adventure games.  The characters are memorable and likable, and their dialogue is hilarious.  The puzzles are, for the most part, both logical and whimsical.  Each level has a different feel to it, and you're likely to want to save at the beginning of one or two just to have the satisfaction of playing through them all over again.
Is Puzzle Bots perfect?  No, but it is fun, and worth your money and time.

I started off with AGK around 4 years ago because I was intimidated by other engines like Unreal and Unity. It was a foolish mistake and a setback in my career. AGK is filled with issues.
If you're interested in game development as a hobby and really like writing a lot of extra code to achieve simple functionality that is built in to other languages then AGK is for you. If you want to build a career or business then you may want to seek out a more professional and matured product like Unity or Unreal Engine (I'd even recommend GameMaker over AGK).
The community is small and filled with inexeperienced users. The experienced users are so few that there aren't enough to answer questions. There is no support for AGK, no tutorials, and the documentation is bare minimum. Every time we've gone to update our AGK apps there has been new issues in the engine. Facebook features don't work. Their Android App Package exporter isn't fully functional. They are extremely slow to update 3rd party SDKs like Chartboost and AdMob. This means you have a high chance of not being able to update your app when a security risk or even attractive new feature is released by a 3rd party.
Don't be a chump like me and struggle with this product. Go for a professional tool.

If you're in to the lore of Warhammer then go nuts with this game, it's probably fun for you... for me? Not so much.
The gameplay is more repetitive than a 2 button beat 'em up from the 80's or 90's... the problem is, 80's and 90's beat 'em up's actually had variety to them because there were hidden fighting techniques in them... this game doesn't have anything like that. Everything is basically spelled out for you by pressing start and checking the move list... it looks something like this:
X
XY
XXY
XXXY
XXXX
Those are your combos... enjoy.
The sad thing is, it's across all the weapons you find. All combos include pressing the X button 1 to 4 times followed by the Y button. If you want to get "advanced" then you finish off the combo with the B button for a non-stylish execution, if you want to leech your life back, which is 100% necessary on HARD mode... it slows the pacing of the game down a lot, thus artificially extending it to a degree.
So you'll basically be pressing some variation of X, Y, B for a solid 25 hours straight. Not my thing.
There are collectables so use a guide because repeating entire sections of this game for 1 missed item will drive you insane... I found the game boring enough just walking down the linear hallways smashing buttons.
When you die on Hard mode, be prepared to repeat about 10 minutes worth of content just to get back to where you were... no skipping dialog, no skipping in game cutscenes you've already seen before, nope, just sit back and watch time go by as you wait to get slaughtered again.
Also be prepared to collect anything you already collected if you die because the game has 1 save file, there is no system save file that keeps track of collectables separately which is just a drag.
Either way, not recommened to hardcore gamers looking for a solid game to play... Casual gamers and those of you in to the Warhammer lore will probably enjoy it.
Again, for a Warhammer fan this is probably an 8 / 10 kind of game.
For regular gamers looking for interaction and engagement, 3 / 10.

All in all well worth the 7-8 hours it'll take to coast through.
The multiplayer is much like the single player; pretty basic but done well and the love for the subject material really starts to shine through when you see the level of customizastion available for your character, right down to the actual paint varieties from citadel. The combat essentially plays like Gears of War without and cover system, if you start taking hits you roll or sprint away (If thats the type of Space Marine you are), wait for your shields and eventually vitality to regen then back into the action. On the whole its simple fun and unlike most competative shooters rarely causes rages because if you get owned by someone you can copy their loadout for 1 spawn and return the favour.
In summary I've bought this game twice and loved it both times so if you are thinking of buying it, just do because its great.

Why someone might do it, I have no idea. Thirty Flights of Loving is a videogame immitation of French New Wave cinema. Along with Gravity Bone (which is included) the experience takes about half an hour—far less time than an artsy movie. Emotionally, it carries a similar impact perhaps because you are an actor in the piece. While there is no danger of making a wrong choice, there is a sense of peril. Even though it is impossible to explore the characters, there's an impression of romance and friendship. A simple plot is complicated by a trick of chronological confusion, but I still feel it has added meaning somehow.
On the whole, this is a game you play in order to think, talk and write about later. It probably deserves a replay after you've had time to contemplate. (I haven't done that yet.) In addition, I'm looking forward to the commentary option. If you are into that sort of thing, there are far worse things to spend your money on.

Your parents gave you a notebook. Everything you write down, becomes real; It might be dark magic, it might be the devils work, you never get to know what it actually is. But one thing is clear: The notebook is definitely not from our world.
One day a beggar asks for something to eat. Fooled into eating a rotten apple, the man reveals himself as a mighty wizard and curses your sister. She is slowly turning to stone and with her life fading away, her death is certain. You have one chance to help her: Gather starites by helping people with the power of the notebook. It's not stated in the game, but it's obvious that the starites are a metaphor for the very souls of those people. It's the price they pay for using a notebook, that does not belong in the human world. Having tricked enough mortals into using the help of the notebook, thus having collected enough souls, the curse is lifted and your sister is free. Seconds after, the wizard shows up again. Was everything in vain? Will he curse your sister again? What are his true intentions? It soon becomes clear, that he is not who you think he is. It's your father. Cursing his own daugher to teach you a lesson... Why? A tear is shed, the old man laughs. The game ends.

If there's one thing I learned from this game, it's that you can pretty much do anything if you can create anything. The puzzles were easy cheese, and your only limitation was your imagination and how you utilized your knowledge of the outside world. Chop down a tree with an axe. Or a chainsaw. Or just simply destroy it with your horrifying user-created chainsaw-laser-axe monstrocity. Or just petrify it with your dad's cane.
It's an inspiration for you to actually know the words of things instead of just knowing things and what they do, that's for sure. That's the only limitation I found myself having. It's a fun game otherwise. You can send vampires to solve all your problems. Can't go wrong with that.
My largest issue with this game is that it seemed short. If they had added a level editor, it would have made this game more extensive. (those pickaxes and jackhammers would be useful again) Plus, it gives users an opportunity to put their user-created items in action, as they can show it off to others in a more interesting way than just "Oh hey, an object in the workshop that pretty much can fight dragons just like anything else."
While level editor made things aren't exactly charming like what Scribblenauts Unlimited provided for backgrounds, they could potentially add a lot more to gameplay. In Scribblenauts and Super Scribblenauts, you had both "Deluge" and standard missions (though admittedly half of those goals were solved using black holes) but at least you had plenty to do for goals.
Also, the AI is a little dumb (such as a cop unintentionally shooting another cop when they meant to shoot the dragon) but I guess when you're so busy drawing up every single possible item that you can draw, that's not surprising. They should consider keeping you from attacking allies with projectiles in Scribblenauts Unmasked. I mean, those comics are focused around combat, so it should be considered.
Aside from my complaints, it's a game worth playing.

Played this on local co-op all the way through, it was brilliant. It's got some of my favourite aspects of an RPG:
- Total customisation: custom classes, freedom to use any skill, build any build, can equip anything you want as long as you have the stats. Completely original.
- Strategic turn-based battle: it almost plays like D&D -- you plan out what you want to do, you communicate with your co-op partner, plus a bit of randomness like a die roll as you confirm and see what happens. Sometimes hilarious.
- Quest decisions: multiple ways to finish quests, your characters gain traits and bonuses depending on your roleplaying actions throughout the game.
- Fun stealth aspect. Not essential but it was fun sneaking around, pickpocketing, lockpicking.
- Great writing, voice acting and art. It's got a sense of humour and quirky writing. The in-game graphics IMO much better than that ugly anime-ish cover/splash page. Literally every NPC line is voice-acted, and done well. The amount of voice acting is on the level of Oblivion or Skyrim.
The main storyline is a very slow burn. Even at about 20 hours in, you're still kind of not sure what's going on, but it's simply so fun exploring, collecting loot, selling loot, levelling, that you don't even care.
This game really surprised me by how fun it was and how much depth there is. I highly recommend it to anyone who loves a good RPG, especially fans of old-school D&D-style RPGs.

The Cold War was a long period of tension between the democracies of the Western World and the communist countries of Eastern Europe. The west was led by the United States and Eastern Europe was led by the Soviet Union. These two countries became known as superpowers. Although the two superpowers never officially declared war on each other, they fought indirectly in proxy wars, the arms race, and the space race. Time Period (1945 - 1991) The Cold War began not too long after World War II ended in 1945. Although, the Soviet Union was an important member of the Allied Powers, there was great distrust between the Soviet Union and the rest of the Allies. The Allies were concerned with the brutal leadership of Joseph Stalin as well as the spread of communism. The Cold War came to an end with the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. Proxy Wars The Cold War was often fought between the superpowers of the United States and the Soviet Union in something called a proxy war. These were wars fought between other countries, but with each side getting support from a different superpower. Examples of proxy wars include the Korean War, the Vietnam War, the Yom Kippur War, and the Soviet Afghanistan War. Arms Race and Space Race The United States and the Soviet Union also tried to fight the Cold War by demonstrating their power and technology. One example of this was the Arms Race where each side tried to have the best weapons and the most nuclear bombs. The idea was that a large stockpile of weapons would deter the other side from ever attacking. Another example was the Space Race, where each side tried to show that it had the better scientists and technology by accomplishing certain space missions first.

But there is tons of help out there, here on steam, and on the TGC forums.
I highly recommend AGK!

App Game Kit is a game creating app which lets you create a variety of different types of games with ease. The app includes a compiler which complies the games into windows, android, iOS and other such platforms. The program comes with an IDE which is based off of Codeblocks IDE. I really liked the IDE, it has some awesome features such as parameter suggestions, auto completion of commands etc.
Unlike other ‘easy’ game makers out there which feature GUI’s and drag and drop and other WSYWYG stuff, this game creation app relies on your coding entirely. You have to know programming if you want to create a game with this app. The engine uses a custom modified version of BASIC programming language. The syntax is very similar to C. This BASIC version of App Game Kit is called tier 1 programming.
You can also program in C++ with Game App Kit as a library. This gives you great power as you can use the power of C++ with the App Game Kit features. This is called tier 2 programming. With tier 2 programming you can use the object orientation of C++ with App Game Kit.
I am a complete beginner programmer with some basic knowledge of C++ and some basic knowledge and experience in Python programming. This app is the easiest game development I have used so far. The documentation in the app is very good that anything you want to know, you can just look it up and it will be present with examples. Though if they implemented the help guide in the program itself that would’ve been much better. At this point the help documentation is HTML based and opens in your browser. It’s kind of annoying having to switch between your browser and IDE to just read the help or guides. You are also provided with example apps such as different fonts properties app which displays all the things you can do with a text object. You are given the source code, so you can open it up in AGK and mess around with it, if you don’t know what a certain command does, simple moving the cursor over the command and pressing F1 key would open up the help page file to that exact command. The guide also includes some basic examples of the most common things.
You can also find plenty of help on the Game Creators’ community forums website. The community is very helpful and when I wanted some help with something I was doing, the people even went as far as to correct my 100+ lines of code. The community is pretty active and the mods themselves are pretty knowledgeable and make sure that the beginner sections’ questions are answered. You can of course also ask questions in the AGK Steam community forums as well.
The DLC’s of this include some Royalty asset packs which include both 2D and 3D assets. A few eBooks which come in PDF file format. Including beginners tier 1 tutorials and advanced tier 2 guides. There’s also a free DLC called Educational Materials pack.
There’s a lot of different Physics properties available, lots of 3D features, particle generators. Etc. available which can be attached to any object. You can create all sorts of neat effects using all these properties. The best part about AGK is you basically have to write a code and you can deploy your game to many platforms. Windows, Linux, iOS, Android and even Blackberry platforms, even HTML 5 is an option. This is a really nice feature if you are planning on distributing your games to multiple platforms.
There are of course some limitations as well of this software, for example no 64-bit data types are present such as a long long, doubles etc. Basically very few types of games require 64-bit date types anyways, such as high numbers counting/incremental games. This limitation can be overcome by using more than 1 variable. Another problem I found was the resolution are not dynamic (or maybe I haven’t figured it out yet). I made a project which was made in my desktop native resolution of 900p. When I played that game on a different PC with lower resolution, the sprites did not fit well. There is a percentage based virtual resolution feature which should fix this problem but it’s a bit harder to understand but it does fix this problem. Another problem I noticed is the Fonts of text objects. You can’t use normal fonts. The fonts have to be in an image file along with an image mapping text file which tells the program which letter is at which place on the image. This is not a major problem per say but I can be a bit inconvenient if you want to import your own text. You have to get a community made program which turns fonts into these image files which can be used in AGK. I had problems with this though I could find some pre-made fonts on the game creators forums.
Overall I am very impressed with this software and so far this has been the easiest for me to write code with. I would as far as put this alongside Python in the ease of use department. I highly recommend this software if you want to start coding for games and learn programming at the same time. This app did clear up a lot of the confusions I had with general programming e.g. I had a sort of “memory leak” problem when I starting coding which I found out was caused by putting a “Create Sprite” command inside a do loop, which continuously kept adding new sprites on top of another sprite until the FPS started to choke. This really taught me not to create object inside the main loop.

I really wish we had a yellow "neutral" option for reviewing a game, because this game really has a lot of great things going for it. Unfortunately, it also has quite a few bad things going for it that limited my enjoyment. Overall I'm marking this negative because even though the game was enjoyable, I find that it isn't worth $10.
Before I get into the negative aspects I'll say what I liked about it. The graphic and graphic style is very nice. The sounds are pleasant and satisfying. The UI is a little finicky, but overall quite nice. Gameplay is also quite calming, and I found this game fun to play while watching something on my second monitor. Micromanagement is obviously a part of the game but not so much that its overbearing.
So here's the bad parts. First, how the game works (in brief). In this game, you develop a game. You then get a rating from 4 reviewing companies on a 1-10 scale. How high your game is on the scale directly affects sales.
This is all fine and well, but there is some obvious tom foolery in how the rating system works. You can read more about the finer details on other reviews here, but in short, if you do well early on, you'll do worse later. That's right: you can develop an amazing game with a damn near perfect design/tech ratio, release time, console match, playerbase match, ALL the matches, and get an average rating of 6.75 because you released a blockbuster game a while ago.
Effectively the game punishes you for doing well. Pretty lame, right?
There's also some more drawbacks. Things like the fact that there's no competition. Nil. You feel like you're the only person developing anything because you ARE. You're always the developer of those smash hit games like "Dance/Casual" for the "Wuu" (AKA Dance Dance Revolution). There's no such thing as a topic being overdone by anyone except you. This is a HUGE drawback for a game that is essentially a business tycoon. Hell, you can set up booths at video game conventions to build hype for your game, and the game tells you that you were the 75th most popular booth at the convention.
Who the hell are those other 75 companies ahead of you? You have no idea because they don't exist!
I wanted to play as the gamer's-dream, consumer-friendly company that eventually rises above its competitors because of how committed it is to its playerbase. But you can't do that because there's nothing to rise against except game reviewers that critique you based on a game you released 8 years ago.
Another problem I have is the lack of choices. You'd think that, being a game development company, you'd be able to be creative in how you run your company. But really, you don't do much. You make games of a certain genre and topic (which you'd think is room for creativity, but it really isn't because you're essentially just forced to methodically go through and exhaust every genre/topic combo you have). You give the game a name. That's about it. Sometimes you have choices, like some fans want you to release an old engine you made. You can choose to release it, sell it, or not release it at all. The problem is, there's virtually no drawback to NOT releasing it. You lose a bit of money by releasing it but the amount is so small that its virtually insignificant. The only reason you would choose not to release it is if you want to roleplay the "evil moneygrubbing company". Which while fun, is still roleplaying, rather than just playing the game.
So overall I found the game okay. It's worth about $5.00 in my opinion. I think the developers of this game did an alright job, especially for a first release, and what is clearly a passion project. But they left out some key components of what makes a good business/management tycoon and that's what put this review in the negative section.

A very cute puzzle game. It can only be played in single-player mode, but it's fun to solve the different puzzles together with a friend and to try to come up with the craziest objects :D Or the best ways to kill off your on-screen characters :p
Unfortunately, there were some bugs in the game. Starites I couldn't get, even if I used the objects being described in walkthroughs. I had to reset the levels concerned, and suddenly the same objects worked. No idea where the problem was.
And of course the game has to be scripted in a certain way. Sometimes more than one solution works, sometimes only _their_ solution works which can be quite annoying if you don't know what they want from you. Especially because of translation errors!!! More on this now.
The German translation is quite bad, many synonyms are not available. For example: The German word for "ship" (Schiff) is not part of the dictionary in this game, instead you have to be more specific and try a "Segelschiff" (sail boat), just to find out that this doesn't exist either, but a "Segelschoner" is proposed in the list ... (a very rare word -_-). This goes on and on ...
Another very annoying thing is grammar!! The adjectives in the dictionary are not written without declination but sometimes with female declination, sometimes with male declination ... and the adjective won't be recognized if you don't chose the one in the dictionary (!!!!).
Right now I'm playing the game in French. There seem to have been some matching errors between people and their translated names (a person being described as a "raging socialist sponge" ?!), but other than that, most things in French seem to work fine. There seem to be more synonyms in the dictionary. And it doesn't matter if you type the feminin or masculine version of an adjective, both work fine!
One very annoying matching/translation error in French that makes it impossible to solve the puzzle: You meet two children in front of a tree house. It says in the description that you should put more life into the pond. "Il faut peupler le lac." Ehm.. ok, what pond, what lake? There is no water, we are on a tree?! I checked in an English walkthrough and they were talking about help needed to repare their tree house... so the solution to this puzzle is a "DAD", a father... well, no idea what the translator was smoking, but maybe I'll stumble across another puzzle where they ask me to repair the tree house and this time i'll need fish -_-"
Being a translator myself, errors like these annoy me quite a bit - no matter whether they are in German or in French. It just means that these games have never been played once in the respective languages to do a quality check. There was no proof-reading of the actual product, in this case the game.
Errors like these can severely reduce the fun of playing the game. Furthermore, this often leads to the phenomenon that games flop in some countries, even if they are a huge success in their country of origin or in countries where the original language of the game is being widely spoken. And afterwards the developers think that those countries just didn't get the humour, are lacking in some kind of way...
@Developers & Publishers: DON'T PAY DUMPING PRICES FOR TRANSLATIONS!! DO QUALITY CHECKS WITH REAL PEOPLE! TAKE THE TIME TO DO ONE OR MORE CORRECTION CIRCLES.
Sure that will cost a bit, but guys, if you can sell 100.000 copies more throughout the world because your games are of a higher quality in all languages ... it's worth it! What's the point in doing a bad translation? Just don't translate it at all! You won't risk your reputation!!!

Several instances of wanting to throw the controller straight across the room, and frustrating bits of levels where I couldn`t figure out what to do, made me rather red-faced at times, but, this being solely my own fault, I must commend the designers for making the perfect platformer. Quite possibly the most beautiful game I have ever played, "Ori and the Blind Forest" already has me craving more platformers like this--and I'm not even two hours into the game yet. The visuals, the music, the simple controls... I have spent so many years of late playing MMO's and FPS style games that I had forgotten just how much I LOVE platform games. I grew up on Nintendo, starting with the NES, so the 2-D sidescrolling platform games always call out to the 80's kid in me.
Artistically, I am just blown away. I remember an article that was in Game Informer magazine, issue 207 (back in 2010), that poised the question:  "Are games art?" In response to Roger Ebert's proclamation that "video games can never be art", the staff writers at Game Informer made reference to the following games:
Ico
Shadow of the Colossus
Mass Effect 2
Heavy Rain
Little Big Planet
Bioshock
If that same question were asked in this day and age, "Ori and the Blind Forest" would be listed as the #1 representation of video games being a form of art (followed by the Borderlands series, the more recent Tomb Raider games, Alan Wake, Enslaved: Odyssey To the West, the Bioshock series, The Elder Scrolls: Skyrim, and so many more).
An amazing blend of graphics, music, gameplay, and story, I highly recommend this game--even at the full price point of $20. I hope to be seeing more games like this in the near future!

It's clever, challenging, easy to play and it looks and sounds really amazing! That pretty much describes the game. In short... Now for the longer review...
This has pretty much came the closest so far to the idea of game i once want to create if the future is nice enough to me. Modern games keep looking towards the reality, we have almost real looking 3-D models of stuff, yeah, hell, guess what? Overhelmed by people who are trying to push their models as close to reality as possible, we are forgeting another type of beauty - the art itself. It is true, that modern technology allows us to create great things when it comes to 3D modeling and scripting, things have probably never been easier before. But it also applies to classic digital 2D art, and Ori shows us perfectly what we can achieve simply by hand drawn graphics and effects.
Now i won't say it hasn't been here before, it has, it's just that Ori has probably pushed the limit, which brings us to a certain problem. The game runs on Unity engine, which, I thought would be a good thing, but I was wrong. There is a lot of technical problems, and I mean a lot. Some of you might be happy and won't notice a thing during your whole gaming time, some of you won't even be able to launch the game, another will experience lags, falling through solid platforms, fps drops and the list goes on. I surely hope most of these problems will be adressed in the upcoming patch, but I'm not that naive to believe all problems will ever be fixed.
Now for the good side and the reason why you should go into it and buy it and play it anyway or die trying.
First thing - the visuals. You have probably never experienced something alike, closest match is Rayman Origins and Rayman Legends. But Ori looks far better and still remains loyal to hand drawn style, minimalizing number of 3D models.
The soundtrack - Gareth Coker will be definitelly remembered by this one. It's true there are something like only three main motives, but they are epic and the way orchestra pulled it off? Let me tell you - you don't hear this in games these days.
Perfect controls - the game plays very intuitively and actions fade into each other pretty neatly. Once you get to feel it, you will hardly die in the game because of lousy controls. It will be only on your head. It's true though, that as Unity game there is no support for x360ce gamepad emu, which is sad. But on the contrary - the game plays well on keyboard and mouse, so, I don't really mind with this one.
Emotions - I'm now gonna sound like emo kid (my avatar won't help a bit there), but I experienced waves of emotions playing this. Whether it was the beginning scene or perfect match between chosen track and visuals during escape sections, I really felt like I care. Again - doesn't happen in games much these days.
There are more pros, but I'll cut it there. In summary - even if you won't be able to launch the game because of technical issues, it's well worth the effort trying. What you could miss by not trying is definitelly worth the risk. So shut that Battlefield or WoW or whatever the hell are you wasting your time with, and buy the game, play the game, enjoy the game. Get a taste of what gaming really is about. Provectus out.

This is probably the best metroidvania or 2D style game I've ever played.  I liked Super Meat Boy, Shadow Complex, Limbo and Fez but this beats them all IMHO.  The game is gorgeous, it runs amazingly well even on older hardware, and the mechanics are extremely tight and satisfying.  Navigating through previous areas after you've obtained more abilities feels great and makes you realize just how well Ori moves.  It can be frustrating at times, but then you get better at figuring out what you need to do and you get past it, which is also a very satisfying feeling.  The music is great and fits the scenes perfectly, and the story is surprisingly dark and sad.  It's just an outstanding presentation all around.
A couple of tips to help prevent some frustration: Energy is plentiful in the game so don't be afraid to drop a save point before a tricky area, and when you get the ability to fling yourself off of projectiles and enemies don't forget you can hold the button to slow everything down and give yourself a couple of seconds to aim.
Highly recommended.  Watch for this on many game of the year lists for 2015.

I was skeptical about this game reading all the reviews of greatly written it is and how emotional the story was. After playing it, I have to say, it lives up to all the hype. Who knew that game made with an RPG Maker program could be told so well? Now, this "game" is more of a interactive story, not really any gameplay at all(a few puzzles, but they are incredibly simple). The game is more meant to just tell a story. It's sad, embracing and well constructed.
Pros:
+ Well written story
+ Emotional plot twists
+ Good soundtrack
+ I like the GFX, personally, I used to play around with RPG Maker a lot when I was younger so it's awesome to see a game made from it be so good
+ Though the game can be preceived as short, you will agree that the amount of time it takes to complete was the perfect amount to get the complete story told
+ Correctly priced at $5
Cons:
- The actual gameplay is unnecessary, there's not even much any way
- Puzzles are WAY too simple
- Using a controller sucks, moving is annoying and there are parts where you have to use the keyboard or mouse
I would pick it up if you are into heavy story. DO NOT pick this up expecting a game chalked full of combat, elaborate puzzles, or whatever. It's fully a story based game.

2) Keep the sound on. Always.
3) Play the game within 24 hours. It takes around 4 hours to play it all. Try doing it in one go if you can.
4) Keep a hanky nearby.

The Cold War was a long period of tension between the democracies of the Western World and the communist countries of Eastern Europe. The west was led by the United States and Eastern Europe was led by the Soviet Union. These two countries became known as superpowers. Although the two superpowers never officially declared war on each other, they fought indirectly in proxy wars, the arms race, and the space race. Time Period (1945 - 1991) The Cold War began not too long after World War II ended in 1945. Although, the Soviet Union was an important member of the Allied Powers, there was great distrust between the Soviet Union and the rest of the Allies. The Allies were concerned with the brutal leadership of Joseph Stalin as well as the spread of communism. The Cold War came to an end with the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. Proxy Wars The Cold War was often fought between the superpowers of the United States and the Soviet Union in something called a proxy war. These were wars fought between other countries, but with each side getting support from a different superpower. Examples of proxy wars include the Korean War, the Vietnam War, the Yom Kippur War, and the Soviet Afghanistan War. Arms Race and Space Race The United States and the Soviet Union also tried to fight the Cold War by demonstrating their power and technology. One example of this was the Arms Race where each side tried to have the best weapons and the most nuclear bombs. The idea was that a large stockpile of weapons would deter the other side from ever attacking. Another example was the Space Race, where each side tried to show that it had the better scientists and technology by accomplishing certain space missions first.

In short, I recommend this game highly for a casual fun, story driven experience. It is great for those rainy days, causal relation sundays or just when you want to game after a long day of work or school but not be wrapped up for too long at a stretch. One of the other nice features of the game is your ability to save at any time during play (after cut scenes). This makes being able to pick it up and put it down again extra nice for those who may have to run on a minute's notice. None of the cutscenes are overlong, so that also adds to the fun as they add to the story rather than make you roll your hand or drum your fingers in a thoroughly "Hurry up!" manner.
Again, excellent fun game, with almost zero learning curve. Every bot you get has to pass three level-tests, to make sure you understand their abilities. Then as quickly as that they are in with your regular crew. It has taken me no longer than two minutes to get all of my bots on their tests. You couldn't ask for a easier learning curve or easier to remember what layout for what bot does what. No need to try and decode secret abilities.
If you have not had the opportunity to pick up this game, do so. True, replayability is not top of the motivations for getting this game-but it is enough fun that you will want to keep coming back to it every so often after you have beaten it, in the same way the "Monkey Island"series has become a gamer cult classic, it would not surprise me to find Puzzle Bots as another of the point and click adventure gamer cult classics in times to come.

So I finally get a  chance to see what this amazing campaign endgame is, involving the vortex. Here is the first thing that happened:
I am told that a remote faraway race have begun the first ritual. It happens to be the elves who are right next to the vortex already, with literally no chance of me logistically getting there in time due to non stop Orc, Chaos, Skaven and roaming Elven raiders, along with the 15 ish local unclaimed cities you would be foolish not to treasure hunt or control (if this was realistic at least)
But aha! You can magically click a button called intervention, and send a force to interfere with the enemy ritual. It's sort of pricey, providing a weak medium and strong force, (I went medium which costs 5000) but i figure what the hell.
It then, on the next turn, spawns a fairly legit looking 20 stack right next to the giant city they are doing the ritual in (just... how... would that even be possible). Which was defended by a serious army too. This UNCONTROLLABLE (why?!) stack proceeds to just run away, then also march stance to run further away from the ritual it is supposed to interrupt. On the same turn an enemy hero casually walks up to them, does a 'hero action' and my intervention army is just deleted. Like Seriously? How does that even work. Am I missing something here or should this game just stick to battle simulations. The campaign map feels more hashed together and clumsy than Civ 5.
As for the combat, on the whole I am enjoying it but there are moments with the Skaven constantly routing and the Lizardmen always going beserk where you realise you can't actually play the game for large chunks of time. I understand why these functions exist, but they kinda need to be toned down a bit just for the sake of smoothing out the gameplay. Theres nothing more fun than watching 3/4 of your army rout and run stupidly far from the fight, only to know that as you send them in again when they rally, there is a high chance it will just happen again in constant loop. Also having some of your most important units go completely out of your control seems fun at first, but gets old after a few fights.
Campaign 2/5
Battles 4/5
There is very little out there in terms of new decent RTS so if you want some serious battles, pick this game up, but don't expect anything stellar from the world map.

1) This is my review of Warhammer total war 2 and is my personal experience with the game and opinion of it:
2)The graphics, freaking amazing, though I have found on occasion a few glitches where the buildings begin to hover several feet in the air and the ground just cuts out for no reason.  However the majority of the time the graphics are beautiful with some breath taking vistas.  Will go into more detail in regards to repetative use of buildings and lack of more substantial variety in regards to city design and layout when regarding the battle map.  Most units are graphically astonishing though some need a few more armor pieces found myself not believing a unit was heavy infantry due to the majority of cloth i saw on it and lack of substantial armor stat.  The units are also moderately well animated however some units behave with fighting styles non-indicative of their class making the game less appealing; this is both a combat drawback and an animation failure in my view.  In additon projectiles look like white streakes rather than actual projectiles, when fully zoomed out i should see a dark cloud or a fire cloud when arrows are fired in mass not a giant flame ball or a giant arking of white light, and when fully zoomed in i should see the actual arrows themselves either onfire or not, also poison arrows should not trail green nor be illuminated in green, that is over the top fantasy only a kid would find realistic; this of course hurts the realism of combat and therefore combat overall.  Some units are graphically designed more like ragtag poverty level cannon fodder and not professional units that intend to fight a real army and survive to further victories, which makes combat seem highly suicidal.  The campaign map is beautiful and reacts to battle map results well.  Though cultural conversion of cities doesnt seem to happen on the campaign map its self which harms the overal sense of achievement as a result of conquests further more this could have been an asset to the game giving players the ability to reshape the entire world in the image of their home nation.  To me both graphically and in concept the developers seem to have taking the easy road when it comes to representing and creating proper interactives of the nationalism of patriots and the hatreds associated with being conquered not to mention a conversion system for which those who are conquered would be inducted into society of their new country either mercifully or brutally.  This is a huge hit to a game that could have been a huge asset since national management and dogma was deprioritized.  Though technically this bit isnt purely graphic based criticism rather more of a concept criticism and content criticism the graphical representation of nation management systems is both barely present in game and also in need of reference so i chose to regard this issue here.  I must also regard the fact that naval combat is litterally a minigame.  I read an article that tried to explain the rationality behind naval combat being purely a statistic driven campaign map graphic reaction; it would not change the fact that this has truely hurt the game overall as naval combat is a huge part of international warfare.  I hope they choose to resolve this in the future for it takes away from the game massively.
3) The number of races and factions is both massive and rare; most games dont have as many as this one.  On the down side i have yet to see a professional army in this game, every force is tactical and easily countered if scouted beforehand; my personal preference has always been in favor of the macedonian and roman style professional armies rather than an over complicated highly specialized force that makes the 20 unit limit feel like a massive handicap.  it does in many situations force more adaptive strategies in order to win.  As with most things fantasy keeping with lore does seem to be a large requirement in the gamer community so the ability to aquire a fully armored highly trained professional force it seems i would have to mod them in myself with my own assets since most reskin mods in this game always end up being overly lore friendly or purely cosmetic.  This is in itself a draw back for me that cheap shots the fun for the most part.  Im not a fan of paying for a game only to have to work for free to obtain the things that apparently dont make sense in any world other than our own.  Other than that the unit variety is complex and beautiful with options for further expansions in unit types and looks via mods.  However until the game changes to allow for more professional armies im not going to change my opinion on the feeling of controling pretty barbarians in mass idiotic and sometimes overly complicated strategies that always end with emense loss on all sides not mentioning the severe powerscale between late game and early game units that makes early game units meaningless by comparison.  The spear/shield units need better armor and ability to withstand a charge, the shield types should matter for they do in rl as to how they are used and to what they can achieve,  unit formations should be possible via button with realistic consequences to their use, the towers in this game should be scaled down or the field expanded to allow more realistic siege bombardment, pike units should be able to stance to "brace" rather than just stand there and get sheba slapped by massive units and or horse hooves, and should move in lock step rather than attack as if they were wielding great axes.  The archers should be able to switch between arrow types such as whisling, jagged, poison tipped, standard and heavy, and fire arrows should not be seen as an ability via convenient button or native to a unit, it should be typed "pitch tipped" or "oil tipped" then set onfire with fires near the unit and or set onfire by mages since this is fantasy game, both requiring setup time as it would in rl.  Swordsmen with shields should always be heavily armored and able to use their shields to block attacks, they should be one of the hardest units to kill without a good cavalry charge or massive volley; not the easiest.  The unit scales are also a bit megre 60-120 units per platoon is a bit small for this era of combat, and the units for whom are most armored and recieving the brunt of all the enemy damage should always be no less than 200.  The cavalry in this game is capable of being utterly wiped out by swordsmen and archers which makes zero sense to me given the fact that archers should have issue being able to hit moving cavalry and swordsmen would have to be ligh swords with highly agile combat style to dismount a rider and cleave his horse working in teams not fully armored acting like crazy people rushing into horses with total contempt for life only to come out 20% scathed.  Most units without spears should actually become "unsteady" when witnessing a full cavalry charge coming at them not stand there without moral loss this is another huge problem.  The monster units are a bit overpowered since they seem to rely on a health bar more than that of a strategic play or a tactical weakness which dulls combat to almost utter stupidity.  For all the pomp of what looks like skilled units the way combat is designed is more suggestive of ill trained barbarians and situational advantages.  In addition the units that should be strong are horrifically weak; and the units that should be weak or have weaknesses are either exactly that or godly.  In additon to all of this the total lack of gear customization and obtimization such as quality, refinement, manufacturing method, material, type, year of weaponry, technological progression and technological modifications; is a huge blow to this game.

I've been a fan of the phone version of this game for a while, so I was surprised to discover it has a Steam release. Looking at its reviews, I'm REALLY surprised that nobody seems to like the game. So, I gave it a try here...
I can't tell the difference. It's basically the phone version.
Pros:
- Very simple, turn-based RPG mechanics. (started as a phone game)
- Easy to play, hard to master (Events are a great place to challenge yourself in the game)
- Interesting, pokemon-like, rock-paper-scissors mechanic for "strong" and "weak" attacks.
- Interesting artistic style for characters to choose from. (My favorite is the bomb-throwing gremlin)
- Really non-aggressive F2P mechanics. You can get by on patience and "gold coins" alone. It's basically the good kind of free to play.
Cons:
- Capped at 30 FPS (worse in full-screen, I have no idea why)
- Janky animations at times (I'm guessing it's made in something not Unity or something.)
- Seemingly no way to use the phone account on Steam? (I don't know? I can't find a way?)
If you like a simple free game to play on the side after work or on the bus, this is fine on the phone. Not sure how well that translates through Steam, but I could see myself playing this at home if I figure out how to transfer the account from the phone version. I recommend it as a simple 10-15 minute timewaster.
I'll give updates as I get time to play it more, but I haven't seen any of the issues people are complaining about other than the above mentioned.

Want an RPG with a AAA production values yet indie sensibilities and no board-room execs making horrific changes in order to make the game more marketable?  Yes, I do, and thankfully the legend of D: OS is only just begining
Finally after playing this for what seems like years (co oped most with a buddy - hard to find time as we both work full time)  I managed to power through to the end of Divinity OS.
Hands down, this is one of the best CRPGs ever, probably the best since Dragon Age decided to become a console-friendly Mass Effect mash up.
D:OS encapsulates all the things that made the old classics like Balders Gate and Neverwinter Nights . well. classics, but also brings the genre forward and notabely improves on its forebearers/. However, this game has some huge issue (for me anyway) that don't rear their ugly head until the end of the game.
The story, writing and voice acting is top notch, often leavin me in stiches laughing at some of the bizarre dialogue and jokes.
Graphics are nothing to write home about, but pleasant and colorful enough.  Spell effects and such are pretty rocking.
The game gives you a huge amount of freedom, in that it hands you the basic tools and then lets you rip it up as you see fit.  This comes down to progressing through the story, where you can work things out in a number of ways and don't always have to default to biffing people in the face to get where you want (looking at you fallout 4).  You can use steath, deception, magic, dialogue and you wits to get where you want, solve puzzles, acquire hidden loot and so forth.
This also transfers to the stellar combat, which again gives you the tools and leaves the rest to you.  Teleporting, elementals spells, summoning, and some devestating skills give you so much freedom and make battles not only tactical but fun experimentations.  That archer in the backlines giving you trouble?  Why not have your rogue spawn a walking bomb, then have your wizard teleport said bomb right on his head?  endless possibilites and usually battles are both tense and enjoyable.  Your enemies have all the same tools, so get ready for some epic wars of attrition.
Character development is also this way.  You may start with a set class, but if you can get the stats, there's nothing to stop you diversifying your party -  tanky warrior becoming adept at which craft?  Cleric/healer becoming a master lock picker?  like i said, if you've got the stats, you can do it.
The game also has so many great features, like allowing you to create two main characters, or allowing online co op, and generally being a bit sandboxy in that you can use your skills in any way you want.  There's also no hand holding, which i loved.  while it's sometimes a bit difficult to figure out where to go, i really felt like I was figuring out a quest on my own, and ever time we figured out what to do, it was most satisfying
However, near mid to end game, a few flaws became apparant.  First, leveling up and learning new skills is a laboriously slow process.  However, the top skills are amazing, and they actualy change  the way your characters play.  For example, the sheer destructive power of my wizard late game let me to adopt a sneaking gameplay, sneaking up on enemies and smashing them with my ultimae spells before they knew what was happening. Similarly, my rogue/archer went from being an annoyance to my foes at best to an absolute death machine.  These skills allow many new options and possibilities and actually made an already great game a legendary experience, but sadly there wasn't much left of the game to experiment with them by the time i got them.  Plus, the early game under-powered state that all RPGS put you through is unnecessarily long, and really grated on me.  I hope DOS 2 corrects this and lets you upgrade and learn new skills quicker.
Finaly, the game punishes you for your choices when it comes to leveling up and assigning new attribute points.  It's never very clear what you should be putting your points into, and you can't go back and change easily.  Your NPC party members CANNOT respec at all, so your stuck with your decions.  Wanna try a differnt build, or respect to learn a differnt ability or spell?  Tough luck, sweetheart.
And your two main characters can respec, but you loose all your skills and would have to buy all the skills books for them again, making it hugely expensive and wasteful unless you want to completely rehaul them.  This really got me late game, as my  party was not kitted out-well to fight the final boss, even though we steam-rolled through the sub-bosses and enemies leading up to the big cheese.  All i needed was a few teaks and small adjustments, lose a spell here, gain a spell here. My only option was to revert to an old save, losing hours and hours of play, in order to level up again and configure my party in the very specific way the finale fight demands.  This was really annoying, and clashed so much with the freeform and experimental attitude the rest of the game has.  Unless you want to follow a walkthough, be prepared for this to happen, otherwise you want to make a new save before EVERY level up.  poor show D: OS.  This might not have been a huge problem if the final boss wasn't so specific to beat, but it is...
In conculsion, I'd give this 85% and say its the best CRPG since Dragon Age: Origins.  It could have been the best CRPG of all time imho were it not for the colossal grind that leveling up is and the problems resepcing your characters.  Still, at almost 100 hours this was a blast and much better than anthying i think Bioware or Bethesda will come out with at this point. Unless Bethesda decided to get a bit beardy again and take more ques from morrowind, but given the amount of bank these guys are pulling in I doubt it...
I am a believer in D: OS and Larian studios, and i look forward to playing more great CRPGS from them

Personally I do enjoy this game and while this game certainly does have its ups and downs, I am not here to praise or criticize this game. I am here to offer a phenomenal 4 Cheese Ravioli recipe!
Here are the ingredients you will need!
Ravioli Dough: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 pinch salt, 1 teaspoon olive oil, 2 eggs, 1 1/2 tablespoons water.
Ravioli Filling: 1 (8 ounce) container ricotta cheese, 1 (4 ounce) package cream cheese, softened, 1/2 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, 1/2 cup provolone cheese, shredded, 1 egg, 1 1/2 teaspoons dried parsley.
Pesto-Alfredo Cream Sauce: 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 cloves garlic, crushed, 3 tablespoons prepared basil pesto sauce, 2 cups heavy cream, 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese, 1 (24 ounce) jar marinara sauce.
1. Mound the flour and salt together on a work surface and form a well. Beat the teaspoon of olive oil, 2 eggs, and water in a bowl. Pour half the egg mixture into the well. Begin mixing the egg with the flour with one hand; use your other hand to keep the flour mound steady. Add the remaining egg mixture and knead to form a dough.
2. Knead the dough until smooth, 8 to 10 minutes; add more flour if the dough is too sticky. Form the dough into a ball and wrap tightly with plastic. Refrigerate for 1 hour.
3. While the dough is resting, prepare the ravioli filling. Combine the ricotta cheese, cream cheese, mozzarella cheese, provolone cheese, egg, and parsley and mix well. Set the filling aside.
4. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and pesto sauce and cook for one minute. Pour in the heavy cream, raise the heat to high, and bring the sauce to a boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the Parmesan cheese and stir until the cheese melts. Remove the pan from the heat and keep warm.
5. Meanwhile, in a separate saucepan, warm the marinara sauce over medium-low heat.
6. Preheat an oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). Beat the egg with the tablespoon of water to make the egg wash.
7. Roll out the pasta dough into thin sheets no thicker than a nickel. To assemble the ravioli, brush the egg wash over a sheet of pasta. Drop the filling mixture on the dough by teaspoonfuls about one inch apart. Cover the filling with the top sheet of pasta, pressing out the air from around each portion of filling. Press firmly around the filling to seal. Cut into individual ravioli with a knife or pizza cutter. Seal the edges.
8. Fill a large pot with lightly salted water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Stir in the ravioli, and return to a boil. Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the ravioli float to the top and the filling is hot, 4 to 8 minutes. Drain well.
9. Grease a baking sheet. Place the cooked ravioli on the sheet pan and bake in the preheated oven until brown, about 4 minutes.
10. To serve the ravioli, divide them among four warmed serving bowls. Drizzle the marinara sauce over the ravioli and then top with the cream sauce.

Doctor Eva Rosalene and doctor Neil Watts work for a futuristic agency that help people to virtually-satisfy their desires. Precisely, they are able to enter one's memories, modify some elements giving new directions to the life events, and so re-create an artificial memory about the fullfilment of some life regret.
In To the moon, they take the case of a old man about to die, whose desire is to go to the moon, despite he "doesn't know why".
With these premises, they have to enter the old man's memories and retrace his entire life backwards. In every stage of the old man's life, they look for objects or events that give them the opportunity to access to more ancient happenings, until they reach his infancy and discover the roots of his personality, life choices and destiny.
The game has its maior weaknesses in some holes in the plot (...beta blockers? why??), and in a (in my case) italian translation which has been clearly carried out by diverse authors; sometimes it is ok and well written, sometimes it is full of mistakes and ridiculous (for example, the wedding scene: ...why not simply look for the wedding priest's discourse on the internet, instead of poorly translating it??)
Beside that, the narrative is based on brilliant ideas and is able to reach some notable dramatic climaxes and plot twists. It is also adequately immersive, to the point that I found the RPG maker rendition (horrible for me) annoying for just the first ten minutes. Although not always at the top while trying to explain the various misteries of the old man's life (probably too many, not all of them necessary to the story), To the moon generally succeed in elaborating on delicate themes such as life and death, destiny, psychopathology, trauma, pain and happiness. And of course, love.
In my opinion, this is the maior strenght of the game: it probably contains one of the greatest love stories in gaming.
I have to say that I was fully engaged by the game and I played it in a row (4 to 5 hours of duration); I would give it a 8/10 as a vote. Besides of its limits, it is worth of playing.

There is a lot to like here, but I don't recommend it.  I liked the concept and the fairly sophisticated and emotional story.  I also liked the humor and references that people in their 20s or 30s would find nostalgic.  What I did not like, was the disconnect between a story for people who understand such things, and game elements that were ridiculously childish.  It's not even really a game.  It's basically just a point-and-click interactive story, which is fine, except in my opinion the "puzzle" elements weren't at all puzzling, and the "hunt for memories" was basically just the game leading you around until you click a button to go to the next phase.  There is zero cognitive challenge.  This could have been so much better in terms of the satisfaction I would have felt for completing increasingly challenging game elements to get to the next segment of a story that I found very engaging.
The piano compositions and sound effects are fantastic.  Without the music, To The Moon loses much of its emotional gravitas, and I doubt so many people would enjoy it.  Played with muted speakers, it would be hard to justify its $10 price tag.  Fortunately I picked it up on sale, and I think I got my money's worth, but I wouldn't buy again and don't recommend it as a game.  It would make a decent novel or screenplay though.  Books and films don't crash a couple of times every hour.  Might only be a Mac 10.10.1 issue, but none of my other games do this.  Also, I completed the game and didn't get the achievement for doing so.  Don't tell me why or how to fix it.  I don't care.  Now that I've finished it, there's no reason to go back to it, unless I want to fall asleep to the soundtrack.

AGK 2 is probably the engine that is
.  I say this because AGK can do most every popular output except Windows Apps, AGK 2 allows commercial production from the moment of purchase, 2D and 3D apps are possible, and the price of AGK on sale and some dlc on sale is probably about $50 USD.  Putting a few well planned apps or games into Android and iOS store will probably yield more than that price.
You probably need to read the manual.  You'll want to make your own assets, unless you're okay with the dlc asset packs available.  On the other hand, The manual on the website and the dlc guide through steam is wonderfully readable.  I haven't spent time reading a programming manual that readable since the 1980s.  These instructions are so readable, I think an entire small team could learn to program that never programmed before.
The programming languages available are a modified BASIC, known as Tier 1, and C++ which is known as Tier 2.  That is, Tier 2 AGK speaks the same language as Godot, CryEngine, and Unreal.  Unless the documentation says Tier 2, you should assume the documentation is Tier 1.
If there's any negative, it would be these three outputs are missing: windows phone 8.1 output, windows 10 universal app output, and flash swf output.

If this game was even half as broken as most claim it is, I would not have poured nearly 200 hours of my time into it. I've got my money's worth many times over.
If you want a tactical shooter, at least in the traditional Tom Clancy sense, look elsewhere. Despite being dressed up like a shooter, it's really a mixed bag of tricks, sporting MMO-esque mechanics while incorporating RPG style progression and cover-based shooting. It's easier to show/watch a video on what it's like or play it yourself than it is for someone else to explain it.
It IS a Ubisoft game. If you hate uPlay, this game uses it. Don't buy it if you don't like uPlay.
The game is fun, despite what the babies on the forums will say. Balance isn't perfect, but when you look back at other multiplayer games you've played, can you honestly say those you've loved were 100% balanced, either? Humans will exploit whatever loophole they find to gain an edge on their opponent. It's hard for any developer to account for misuse or alternative usage of game mechanics when you've got a pool of thousands of players tossing stones at each other.
Despite a rough launch and the onslaught of sh!t press that's been tossed their way for the past year, the developers didn't abandon the game or their fans like I've seen many other developers do when they just can't handle the negativity, anymore. Instead, they reworked what people didn't like, created more content for players to enjoy, and ignored the haters who could never be catered to in a million years. That's dedication. That's straight up honest work. That's something commonly overlooked when people come across information about this title, and it's something that deserves both recognition, and respect.
Granted, the developers aren't perfect, but they understand this, and they put their content through a rigorous playtesting period on the test server before releasing it to the main branch. You can't please everybody. There's always that one guy who's the diehard hater, or even the diehard shill, in some cases.
Me? I'm just a guy who found this game fun, and worth every penny. There's been bumps and bruises throughout the ride that was the Division's first year, but all in all, it's not a bad game. Trash like "Shower with your dad sim" or all the other garbage, rushed joke games out there get positive reviews, yet people feel inclined to treat AAA devs like sh!t because they expect more. I get it: they advertised the game and targeted marketing to lure in the CoD and BF kiddies, and this was misleading, considering the two genres are not the same. But just because someone expects the world, gets let down because their expectations were too high, then ♥♥♥♥♥es and moans about it to everyone and their dog, doesn't mean you should listen to them.
The gunplay is greatly satisfying. Sound effects feel authentic, and recoil not too rediculous. PvP is fun, though it greatly favors group-fighting rather than solo-play. The same can be said for most of the end-game PvE content as well. If you don't feel like working with other people, you won't have very much fun with this game. Sure, most of the content is accessible by yourself, but the game is online-locked. Almost everything you do is based in the embedded multiplayer. If you don't like multiplayer games, steer-clear.
The game's not for everybody. All of the best games, at least in my honest opinion, entice love/hate relationships (i.e. Dark Souls), and this game does just that. It's hard, punishing, and requires high-level teamwork in order to get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ done in the highest level of play. You will either love this game, or hate it.
My advice? Do your research, and try it out first-hand by playing the 6-hour trial period on uPlay. If you don't like it, don't buy it. I cannot stress this enough. The game was developed with a very niche market in mind, but it was made to look like something it is not at its core.
Whatever you do, look sh!t up before you spend your money. This applies to ALL games. I'm getting tired of seeing review scores drop on so many games these days because lazy @sses don't feel like typing a few words into Google.
The Division is fun, but it's not for everybody. Rather, it's very much an MMO-shooter like Destiny in many aspects. There's hours of content available to you, and many ways to play. The game is multiplayer-only, so if that's not your thing, do not purchase this title. It's not nearly as bad as most say it is, so if you're looking for a Destiny alternative on PC, don't hesistate in checking this out. Just be sure to use up your 6 hours of FREE trial time on uPlay before coming to a decision.

So I finally get a  chance to see what this amazing campaign endgame is, involving the vortex. Here is the first thing that happened:
I am told that a remote faraway race have begun the first ritual. It happens to be the elves who are right next to the vortex already, with literally no chance of me logistically getting there in time due to non stop Orc, Chaos, Skaven and roaming Elven raiders, along with the 15 ish local unclaimed cities you would be foolish not to treasure hunt or control (if this was realistic at least)
But aha! You can magically click a button called intervention, and send a force to interfere with the enemy ritual. It's sort of pricey, providing a weak medium and strong force, (I went medium which costs 5000) but i figure what the hell.
It then, on the next turn, spawns a fairly legit looking 20 stack right next to the giant city they are doing the ritual in (just... how... would that even be possible). Which was defended by a serious army too. This UNCONTROLLABLE (why?!) stack proceeds to just run away, then also march stance to run further away from the ritual it is supposed to interrupt. On the same turn an enemy hero casually walks up to them, does a 'hero action' and my intervention army is just deleted. Like Seriously? How does that even work. Am I missing something here or should this game just stick to battle simulations. The campaign map feels more hashed together and clumsy than Civ 5.
As for the combat, on the whole I am enjoying it but there are moments with the Skaven constantly routing and the Lizardmen always going beserk where you realise you can't actually play the game for large chunks of time. I understand why these functions exist, but they kinda need to be toned down a bit just for the sake of smoothing out the gameplay. Theres nothing more fun than watching 3/4 of your army rout and run stupidly far from the fight, only to know that as you send them in again when they rally, there is a high chance it will just happen again in constant loop. Also having some of your most important units go completely out of your control seems fun at first, but gets old after a few fights.
Campaign 2/5
Battles 4/5
There is very little out there in terms of new decent RTS so if you want some serious battles, pick this game up, but don't expect anything stellar from the world map.

I am a super completionist. I check every barrel, chest, and take every potato. I have completed this game once, so if you are like me, 150 hours is what you're looking at. That said, I certainly recommend picking this up (on sale). The combat is super fun and well balanced. I do wish I'd picked that harder mode from the start, but still fun.
Now then, for the bad.
-This game has some major issues. This is probably the worst inventory management I've ever seen. Things get mega cluttered within the first hour. I kid you not, upwards of 30 of those hours are just moving stuff around and trying to sell it.
-A classic case of RPG item/loot backlog. You will never use 95% of what you find. There is food, potions, items, and crafting; and all of it is totally unnecessary. If you actually used it, you would be severely OP.
-You will flip on mute in towns because of all the repeated dialogue. Arrow in the knee was light compared to these merchants.
-Targeting in combat is cumbersome and often leads to mistaken movement.
-There are several puzzle rooms, which are normally fine, but often contain absurd, impossible to see switches. You will use Google to find these.
-While it is nice that the game doesn't hold your hand, there were many times that you really don't know what to do next. The questlog is useless.
-Frame rate drops when multiple enemies are on screen together (but that might just be my CPU)
-Just cumbersome to do pretty much anything
-Could the NPCs talk any slower? I've read the whole paragraph before they finish the first line.
Now I know that that's a huge negative list, but I want to reiterate that this is an overall positive experience. The game is a lot of fun and worth playing if you are an RPG fan, I wouldn't have sunk a week into it otherwise. I just wish it was most polished.

Divinity managed to be the first more in-depth RPG for me that held its grasp all the way to the end, thanks to its easy to understand mechanics, co-op play and especially the humor. I did not expect the amount of cheeky dialogue and events that took place and - while at times slightly hit-and-miss in nature - it really made the game.
Be warned though, the actual main story and lore of the game my friend and i found a bit lackluster. That can be an issue if you´re heavily invested in those areas of a game. There are also slight issues with pacing and silly switch puzzles.
Very few actual technical problems during a 100+ hour co-op campaign. Only one more annoying bug that was usually corrected with a reconnect by my friend, and also seemed to disappear by the other half of the campaign. The user interface is fairly self explanatory, though a few useful options were slightly hidden.
One area that really could use some improvement is item management, as the game is stacked with different components and materials for crafting. Crafting itself is an interesting mechanic but loses some of its appeal towards late game.
Overall Divinity (despite all its critical acclaim) managed to be a bit of a pleasant surprise for myself and my friend. It may not be the game for all hardcore RPG fans, but definitely worth at least a try.
