With Ori and the Blind Forest, Moon Studios have created a truly unique game -
At first, I'd like to review the storyline:
The game conveys its plot mainly without using words. Even then, the cutscenes are highly emotional and made me cry just during the prologue. While the plot idea isn't the most original, the way it was designed made it different - it's a mystical story of hope, of love and strength, and this becomes obvious in every scene and is, in a way, truly moving. I grew fond of all of the characters without ever hearing them speak.
Now, for the graphics, a small look at the game trailer should be enough to convince everyone that the graphics in this game are incredibly beautiful - just as much as the dark blue landscapes, where everything is surrounded by glowing mist, are mysterious but calming, the sharp yellow in other areads and the burning lava in Mount Horu all stunned me with their beauty. Every screen and "level" looks different and beautiful in its own way, and I never got tired of examining every ever-so-small detail in the backgrounds. In my opinion, it's worth playing the game just to look at everything.
The music also added to the fantastic atmosphere; and as the pieces are often just variations of one "Main Theme", it's fun recognizing melodies and humming along. Especially during the rather intense levels, the music really adds to the tension, and during the calmer parts, it's often rather fun. I highly recommend listening to the whole soundtrack - it's very inspirational and calming, and it's easy to focus on working while listening to it in the background.
Last, the gameplay deserves to be reviewed as well. Unlike many other games (*cough* Assassin's Creed..."NO EZIO, STOP CLINGING TO THAT WALL TWO FEET ABOVE THE GROUND, FIGHT THE ♥♥♥♥ING GUARDS!"), every key you press makes Ori jump, climb or attack with amazing precision - if you die, which happens a lot (some parts took me, like, 50 times to get just right. I've wanted to die at least thirty times of these from being so frustrated), it's not because Ori is being a little♥♥♥♥♥♥and doing things he isn't supposed to do, it's because you, the player, are incapable of pressing the right buttons at the right time. Furthermore, I felt like the choice of keys to press in order to move around were well thought-out, after a short tutorial, new skills were easy to use and pressing the keys came naturally.
By including small things like life cells and others as well as the skill system, exploring all of the levels also got more interesting as I was determined to find everything so little Ori would be well-prepared for the final battle.
In conclusion, although I am usually not a huge fan of Jump n Run adventures, I found Ori and the Blind Forest to be one of the most captivating and stunning games I have ever played with not only a great visual and emotional basis but actually fun gameplay that I never got bored of. In my opinion, this game is definitely a must play for anyone who likes Indie/Artsy games. 10/10!!!

A very solid platformer that takes inspiration from Super Metroid and Zelda, and is the product of hours of love and effort by Moon Studios.
The first thing you'll notice is that this game is beautiful to look at. The visuals are some of my favourite I've seen in a videogame in a long time, even if the game is only 2D. Each area in the game is diverse and aesthetically pleasing to look at. There is a good variety too, ranging from icey ruins to a fiery volcano. I took several screenshots while playing as the game just looks phenomenal.
Complementing the aethetics is the soundtrack, which is also amazing and deserving of its "Great Soundtrack" tag. It's probably worth buying separately, and each soundtrack fits the zone it's associated with very nicely and really conveys the feelings and emotion the soundtrack sets out to do.
While I don't play platformers for the story, this one was interesting enough to hold my attention. It's simple, but it gives meaning to what you are doing in the game.
The gameplay is solid. You unlock new abilities at a very good pace, and there are a ton of meaningful collectibles that increase your experience, health, and mana, which you will appreciate as all these resources are very useful. With experience, you can unlock new talents in different talent trees that focus on combat, utility, and efficiency. The
element about a platformer are its controls, and here the controls are tight and responsive. I never felt like Ori moved where I didn't want him to, and the new movement skills you earn as the game progresses were very well done and will allow you to reach areas you couldn't before. As this is a platforming game, you'll likely have the best experience playing this game with an Xbox controller.
The length of this game for a platformer and its $20 price is very fair. It took me 12 hours for my first playthrough, but I did go for 100% secrets and collectibles
For achievement hunters looking to 100% this game, the achievements are fair and fun to do. The hardest achievement would be the Immortal achievement, which requires you to complete the game without dieing once.  Even with practice, this game has a lot of unforgiving moments where even a slightly mistimed button press = instant death. You will likely use the game's save-copying feature at regular intervals for this one.
In summary, this game is a must-play if you have any interest in platformers. I would have it be a contender for one of the top games of 2015.
: 22 hours played as of review | 50/50 Achievements

Doctor Eva Rosalene and doctor Neil Watts work for a futuristic agency that help people to virtually-satisfy their desires. Precisely, they are able to enter one's memories, modify some elements giving new directions to the life events, and so re-create an artificial memory about the fullfilment of some life regret.
In To the moon, they take the case of a old man about to die, whose desire is to go to the moon, despite he "doesn't know why".
With these premises, they have to enter the old man's memories and retrace his entire life backwards. In every stage of the old man's life, they look for objects or events that give them the opportunity to access to more ancient happenings, until they reach his infancy and discover the roots of his personality, life choices and destiny.
The game has its maior weaknesses in some holes in the plot (...beta blockers? why??), and in a (in my case) italian translation which has been clearly carried out by diverse authors; sometimes it is ok and well written, sometimes it is full of mistakes and ridiculous (for example, the wedding scene: ...why not simply look for the wedding priest's discourse on the internet, instead of poorly translating it??)
Beside that, the narrative is based on brilliant ideas and is able to reach some notable dramatic climaxes and plot twists. It is also adequately immersive, to the point that I found the RPG maker rendition (horrible for me) annoying for just the first ten minutes. Although not always at the top while trying to explain the various misteries of the old man's life (probably too many, not all of them necessary to the story), To the moon generally succeed in elaborating on delicate themes such as life and death, destiny, psychopathology, trauma, pain and happiness. And of course, love.
In my opinion, this is the maior strenght of the game: it probably contains one of the greatest love stories in gaming.
I have to say that I was fully engaged by the game and I played it in a row (4 to 5 hours of duration); I would give it a 8/10 as a vote. Besides of its limits, it is worth of playing.

There is a lot to like here, but I don't recommend it.  I liked the concept and the fairly sophisticated and emotional story.  I also liked the humor and references that people in their 20s or 30s would find nostalgic.  What I did not like, was the disconnect between a story for people who understand such things, and game elements that were ridiculously childish.  It's not even really a game.  It's basically just a point-and-click interactive story, which is fine, except in my opinion the "puzzle" elements weren't at all puzzling, and the "hunt for memories" was basically just the game leading you around until you click a button to go to the next phase.  There is zero cognitive challenge.  This could have been so much better in terms of the satisfaction I would have felt for completing increasingly challenging game elements to get to the next segment of a story that I found very engaging.
The piano compositions and sound effects are fantastic.  Without the music, To The Moon loses much of its emotional gravitas, and I doubt so many people would enjoy it.  Played with muted speakers, it would be hard to justify its $10 price tag.  Fortunately I picked it up on sale, and I think I got my money's worth, but I wouldn't buy again and don't recommend it as a game.  It would make a decent novel or screenplay though.  Books and films don't crash a couple of times every hour.  Might only be a Mac 10.10.1 issue, but none of my other games do this.  Also, I completed the game and didn't get the achievement for doing so.  Don't tell me why or how to fix it.  I don't care.  Now that I've finished it, there's no reason to go back to it, unless I want to fall asleep to the soundtrack.

Well, after  almost 3 months, and moren than 100 hours practice. I thingk it is now the time to re-write my review about this App Game Kit. I will still recommend this game engine, but, I think I have something new to say.
Firstly, let's focus on the good things on App Game Kit.
App Game Kit has a very simple and easy UI, which is really friendly to user.( but in another way, it is not. I'll talk it later ) Not like the other game engine ( UR 4, MAYA LT, CRY OR GAME MAKER ), the menu and commands are simply easy to understand and control, more over, you don't need to built a specify operating environment command to accommodate different platforms, App Game Kit will build the environment automaticly. Unfortunately, I'm not sure if it is also support Windows 10 moblie, due to I don't have a windows phone, but any way, you can find it is very easy and comfortable to run your code on IOS and android.
The second thing is, AGK Basic, a kind of Basic language which is very easy to learn, and fast to use. C++ will also run fantasticly on your machine with Game kit.
Now, let's talk about something not so good.
Because of App Game Kit has a very simple UI, and it doesn't have an appropriate tool to build your game screen, so, you need to code everything by yourself by using some codes to find the appropriate X, Y, Z coordinate and code them with the IDE into your game. I think maybe the placement editor should be a kind of tool to build the map, however, I realy have no idea about how to use it to build my game, and thanks for the code which I've found it in the help file, it has no help at all with my map.
Another negative point is the font system. It only supports extended ASCII characters ( bitmap fonts ). You'll find you can't write some languages like Chinese, Japanese and Korean in your game. I think everyone knows that the Chinese mobile market now is the biggest market in the world. Hope to see any good change in the furture.
Anyway, App Game Kit is a very good game engine, if you are a  begginer or a independent producer. This is my review. Sorry for my bad english.

I'm completely in love with the new AppGameKit!
To be clear: I'm a game designer, not a programmer and I'm way better at art and world building than computer science or maths! Fortunately AGK allows me to prototype ideas rapidly without learning object oriented programming or complicated interfaces. It's just really easy to pick up and has some pretty impressive capabilities -- and the fact that it deploys to a wide range of hardware is an added joy.
I did have some experience with the previous version on Windows but that was before V2 and all the 3D functionality, so I approached the new version with excitement. I'm glad to say, 50 hours into my project, the excitement has only grown and I'm having a blast!
AGK runs smoothly on Ubuntu Linux (a heavily modded 14.04) and I haven't encountered any showstoppers so far. The interpretation of BASIC is sensible and the help files and examples are easy enough to decipher. It's remarkably quick and simple to get fun things happening on-screen.
Among other tests, I generated a *massive* 3D scene with a ridiculously long viewing distance, populated it with over 10,000 giant cubes and then put in a gamepad-controlled vehicle to fly around them. It ran smoothly, even with so many polys visible in the scene, so there's clearly a lot of scope for building decent games. Personally, it's my dream game engine because I can almost forget about it and just concentrate on figuring out the game logic.
Now if you'll excuse me, I have a prototype to get on with!
(Review based on the Linux version.)

Well, after messing around with this IDE, I finally have come to an unbiased (hopefully) opinion of the software.  I haven't tested it out completely, but I do feel I have a bit to say about it.
I'm a huge fan of BASIC.  I prefer text-based languages to GameMaker and Unity, and when you combine text-based languages and BASIC, you have a match made in heaven (even though most of these kinds of languages operate on BASIC from my experience).
I find most of the commands easy to grasp, and the logic behind the program is standard.  If there's one word I could use to describe this IDE, it'd be "standard".  The program follows the basic rules of code (it loops where it is meant to loop and it does what it is told in a linear fashion) and it reminds me of Visual Basic, minus the object orientation I dislike.
With that said, at one point the code I was working on was nuked horribly and I had to start the project from scratch because I couldn't find what caused the problem.  Be sure to back up your code often.
I recommend this software to anybody who likes to code.  It's great for people who already know BASIC, and fine enough for newcomers.  I don't know if it could be used for making large projects, but I'm sure there are ways to set up the icons and whatnot to make a more professional product.  It's definitely something worth giving a try.

If you're looking to dive into simple app development, AGK provides a good jumpboard for beginners and intermediate programmers out there. It really simplifies the process by providing you with control scheme templates and making application exporting easy to implement, and delivers on the "code and deploy" idea quite well. It remains to be seen how powerful the kit is (it has support for C++ and XCode libraries but remains ambiguous on how compatible it is with the kit), but it's a great tool for those who'd like to implement app ideas immediately.

Divinity managed to be the first more in-depth RPG for me that held its grasp all the way to the end, thanks to its easy to understand mechanics, co-op play and especially the humor. I did not expect the amount of cheeky dialogue and events that took place and - while at times slightly hit-and-miss in nature - it really made the game.
Be warned though, the actual main story and lore of the game my friend and i found a bit lackluster. That can be an issue if you´re heavily invested in those areas of a game. There are also slight issues with pacing and silly switch puzzles.
Very few actual technical problems during a 100+ hour co-op campaign. Only one more annoying bug that was usually corrected with a reconnect by my friend, and also seemed to disappear by the other half of the campaign. The user interface is fairly self explanatory, though a few useful options were slightly hidden.
One area that really could use some improvement is item management, as the game is stacked with different components and materials for crafting. Crafting itself is an interesting mechanic but loses some of its appeal towards late game.
Overall Divinity (despite all its critical acclaim) managed to be a bit of a pleasant surprise for myself and my friend. It may not be the game for all hardcore RPG fans, but definitely worth at least a try.

Fallout 3 is a need-to-play in the Fallout series. The game offers hours of fun wasteland exploration. It's very atmospheric as you play the role of the "lone wanderer" in search of your dad. The story line is great and there are many ways to get through it where each choice determines how the games ending would be. It's a dramatic change from the first two Fallout games, and its more of an RPG than an FPS.  No matter what you're looking for this game has it.  You can become a ruthless raider, or a local hero.
PROS
+ Vast open world
+ Hours upon hours of main storyline, DLC, or exploration
+ Karma system effects how the AI treat/percieve you, and overall game ending
+ Amazing DLC, that adds plenty of more content (sidequests, weapons, armor, perks, and enemies)
+ The new engine is a huge turning point in the series
+ Many enemies to rip a new one
+ Many unique side-quests, that'll have you
+ Customizable stats, that make your character even more unique, and add to the RPG experience
CONS
- Pain in the a** to download if you have windows 7 or later (You'll have to look up how to do it, but it's totally worth it)
- Bethesda hates PC gamers, even though we love them so much

1) This is my review of Warhammer total war 2 and is my personal experience with the game and opinion of it:
2)The graphics, freaking amazing, though I have found on occasion a few glitches where the buildings begin to hover several feet in the air and the ground just cuts out for no reason.  However the majority of the time the graphics are beautiful with some breath taking vistas.  Will go into more detail in regards to repetative use of buildings and lack of more substantial variety in regards to city design and layout when regarding the battle map.  Most units are graphically astonishing though some need a few more armor pieces found myself not believing a unit was heavy infantry due to the majority of cloth i saw on it and lack of substantial armor stat.  The units are also moderately well animated however some units behave with fighting styles non-indicative of their class making the game less appealing; this is both a combat drawback and an animation failure in my view.  In additon projectiles look like white streakes rather than actual projectiles, when fully zoomed out i should see a dark cloud or a fire cloud when arrows are fired in mass not a giant flame ball or a giant arking of white light, and when fully zoomed in i should see the actual arrows themselves either onfire or not, also poison arrows should not trail green nor be illuminated in green, that is over the top fantasy only a kid would find realistic; this of course hurts the realism of combat and therefore combat overall.  Some units are graphically designed more like ragtag poverty level cannon fodder and not professional units that intend to fight a real army and survive to further victories, which makes combat seem highly suicidal.  The campaign map is beautiful and reacts to battle map results well.  Though cultural conversion of cities doesnt seem to happen on the campaign map its self which harms the overal sense of achievement as a result of conquests further more this could have been an asset to the game giving players the ability to reshape the entire world in the image of their home nation.  To me both graphically and in concept the developers seem to have taking the easy road when it comes to representing and creating proper interactives of the nationalism of patriots and the hatreds associated with being conquered not to mention a conversion system for which those who are conquered would be inducted into society of their new country either mercifully or brutally.  This is a huge hit to a game that could have been a huge asset since national management and dogma was deprioritized.  Though technically this bit isnt purely graphic based criticism rather more of a concept criticism and content criticism the graphical representation of nation management systems is both barely present in game and also in need of reference so i chose to regard this issue here.  I must also regard the fact that naval combat is litterally a minigame.  I read an article that tried to explain the rationality behind naval combat being purely a statistic driven campaign map graphic reaction; it would not change the fact that this has truely hurt the game overall as naval combat is a huge part of international warfare.  I hope they choose to resolve this in the future for it takes away from the game massively.
3) The number of races and factions is both massive and rare; most games dont have as many as this one.  On the down side i have yet to see a professional army in this game, every force is tactical and easily countered if scouted beforehand; my personal preference has always been in favor of the macedonian and roman style professional armies rather than an over complicated highly specialized force that makes the 20 unit limit feel like a massive handicap.  it does in many situations force more adaptive strategies in order to win.  As with most things fantasy keeping with lore does seem to be a large requirement in the gamer community so the ability to aquire a fully armored highly trained professional force it seems i would have to mod them in myself with my own assets since most reskin mods in this game always end up being overly lore friendly or purely cosmetic.  This is in itself a draw back for me that cheap shots the fun for the most part.  Im not a fan of paying for a game only to have to work for free to obtain the things that apparently dont make sense in any world other than our own.  Other than that the unit variety is complex and beautiful with options for further expansions in unit types and looks via mods.  However until the game changes to allow for more professional armies im not going to change my opinion on the feeling of controling pretty barbarians in mass idiotic and sometimes overly complicated strategies that always end with emense loss on all sides not mentioning the severe powerscale between late game and early game units that makes early game units meaningless by comparison.  The spear/shield units need better armor and ability to withstand a charge, the shield types should matter for they do in rl as to how they are used and to what they can achieve,  unit formations should be possible via button with realistic consequences to their use, the towers in this game should be scaled down or the field expanded to allow more realistic siege bombardment, pike units should be able to stance to "brace" rather than just stand there and get sheba slapped by massive units and or horse hooves, and should move in lock step rather than attack as if they were wielding great axes.  The archers should be able to switch between arrow types such as whisling, jagged, poison tipped, standard and heavy, and fire arrows should not be seen as an ability via convenient button or native to a unit, it should be typed "pitch tipped" or "oil tipped" then set onfire with fires near the unit and or set onfire by mages since this is fantasy game, both requiring setup time as it would in rl.  Swordsmen with shields should always be heavily armored and able to use their shields to block attacks, they should be one of the hardest units to kill without a good cavalry charge or massive volley; not the easiest.  The unit scales are also a bit megre 60-120 units per platoon is a bit small for this era of combat, and the units for whom are most armored and recieving the brunt of all the enemy damage should always be no less than 200.  The cavalry in this game is capable of being utterly wiped out by swordsmen and archers which makes zero sense to me given the fact that archers should have issue being able to hit moving cavalry and swordsmen would have to be ligh swords with highly agile combat style to dismount a rider and cleave his horse working in teams not fully armored acting like crazy people rushing into horses with total contempt for life only to come out 20% scathed.  Most units without spears should actually become "unsteady" when witnessing a full cavalry charge coming at them not stand there without moral loss this is another huge problem.  The monster units are a bit overpowered since they seem to rely on a health bar more than that of a strategic play or a tactical weakness which dulls combat to almost utter stupidity.  For all the pomp of what looks like skilled units the way combat is designed is more suggestive of ill trained barbarians and situational advantages.  In addition the units that should be strong are horrifically weak; and the units that should be weak or have weaknesses are either exactly that or godly.  In additon to all of this the total lack of gear customization and obtimization such as quality, refinement, manufacturing method, material, type, year of weaponry, technological progression and technological modifications; is a huge blow to this game.

I've changed my review. I thought about deleting it and posting a whole new review, but then I decided to keep it so TGC's intentions to make AGK functional on Linux would be documented in the comments. If you would like to see the old review, so you'll have some context if you read the comments,
.
Okay, I've got better things to do with my time now that AGK on Linux has notably improved, and 2 lengthy reviews is 2 too many, so let's get down to brass tacks.
Players - These are programs that let you test your games on different platforms without needing to compile, reboot, or transfer code/executables to/on said platform. You simply copy over the player once, run it, then click the broadcast button in the IDE on the machine you're writing the code on, and you can test any game any time you want. For example, I gave my wife a copy of the Windows player, while I write code on my Linux machine. Then when I want to see how well any game works in Windows, I ask her to run the player, I click broadcast and boom, the game is running on her machine. I can then click "stop broadcasting", switch to a completely different game project, click broadcast again, and boom, now that game is running on her machine. It's a fantastic tool, but it too has it's limitations, the biggest being players only work on your LAN. You can't give a player to your online friends and expect them to help you troubleshoot.
Write code once for all platforms - In case it wasn't obvious by the previous point, all code you write really does only have to be written once for all platforms. Well, within reason anyways. Occasionally you'll bump into a quirk or two, it's unavoidable. But if you don't know how many gold star stickers AGK deserves for having an API who's code really does only need to be written once(give or take), then you clearly don't know how much of a razorblade in the colon writing a port is. Java has been waving the 'cross-platform support' flag for eons and I can't even count the number of times I've seen a Java game have huge platform specific bugs and issues. So it's at least better than that.
Physics engine already built in - If you've ever looked into 2D game development before, then you've probably already downloaded (and maybe even compiled) a few SDKs, read their 'getting started' sections, and began putting PNG files into the project directory before you realized the SDK comes without any physics engine installed. Then you spent a few more hours googling "how to install physics engine", before giving up on the whole thing and going back to photoshopping funny faces on to old cartoon characters(cause at least that's doing
productive). Well, you don't have to worry about that with AGK. Box2D is already installed, configured, and ready for you to make the next Angry Birds clone. All you need to know is the list of built-in functions, which happens to be arranged neat and tidy on their website. A+ for that.
Tier 1 BASIC language - There are 2 programming tiers in AGK; BASIC and C++. I've used C++ quite often in the past, but unfortunately these days I can only do most of my programming when I'm half asleep and languages like BASIC are more forgiving with their syntax. BASIC is also very beginner friendly which makes it ideal for the audience AGK is aiming for. I think LUA would be a better choice since it's a much more powerful and versatile language, but BASIC is fine too albeit having an archaic feel. The larger point here is, if you've ever used a simple language like LUA then it should only take you a few minutes to learn BASIC. If not: spend the 3 minutes it takes to learn LUA, then come back and learn BASIC.
No level editor - I know this has already been officially addressed and I applaud TGC's ambitions for hoping to eventually add a level editor, but that doesn't change the fact you don't get one when you buy AGK. My view on this remains unchanged from what I said in the previous review. Not that I'm unsympathetic. Making an intuitive, flexible and powerful level editor that's also easily usable by beginners, is no simple task. If it were, more would exist and Tiled would be out of business. Still, for $80 software proudly boasting what kind of 2D games you can make with it, one would assume a 2D level editor would be included. The community has tried desperately to fill this void themselves by making their own level editors, and loaders/compatibility layers for other tools (such as Tiled) but, spoiler warning, they all suck. I'm sorry, but they really do. Without some kind of level editor, you will have to manually program each level by assigning a huge list of sprites to their respective X and Y coordinates. The solution I went with was to take the most stable community made level editor I could find, and rewrite huge chunks of it to suit my needs. I hope to one day finish it.
Customer support - I'm sure it seems hypocritical to put this on the list after everything that happened in the comments below, but remember: I wrote the old review because I spent 4 long months trying to get help with serious, project killing bugs and never got a single response. And it's not like the AGK forums here on Steam are that active, I opened a new topic 3 days ago and it's still on page 1 with 0 responses right now. Naturally, I gave up trying and decided I needed to warn others of AGK's Linux/SteamOS issues, and that's when I wrote that review. I'm going to state the obvious now. The only reason I got any response at all was because I wrote a review that was hurting AGK's image on Steam. Maybe it's too presumptuous to say the bugs I and other AGK users were dealing with wouldn't be fixed now if I didn't write that review, so I'll just say they wouldn't have been addressed. It should never get to the point that users have to write negative reviews before the bugs they're reporting will be fixed or even acknowledged. Especially since all it would take is a daily glance at the AGK Steam forums. I'm hopeful customer support will improve but only time will tell.
I'm giving it a thumbs up, not because I think you should buy it, but because AGK does what it sets out to do. It is a very simplified game development kit that's compatible with Linux, SteamOS, Windows, Android, iphones, Macs, just to name a few, and it is accommodating for use by people who want to make the jump from gamer/scripter/game modder/CLI programmer, to actual game developer. But is it worth buying? Well, that depends. If you're determined, I believe you can do a lot with AGK. If you're not, you'll at least gain more of an understanding of how much work goes into making a game. Personally, I think $80 is a bit steep for what it offers so you might consider waiting until it goes on sale. In the meantime, start researching sine and cosine functions.

"Please note that this guide does not cover the new animated 3D, 3D physics and other commands released in V2.0.15. These subjects will be covered in an advanced guide due for release in 2016."

The dev tool is fantastic. It's easy it pick up, a joy to use and is powerful enough to pull off any idea you have.  Yes you need to learn to code, but the tier 1 language is very easy to pick up. Yes you need to code pretty much everything, but for me this means you have total control over all elements of your game meaning you can optimise everything.
Once you've picked up the language; games can be produced, packaged and on sale on multiple outlets very quickly.  I personally have used this software for several years and I've released  six games across Windows, Linux and Android.  Don't let the number of Steam hours fool you, I use thi tool for about 10 hour a week, offline as I commute on the train to work.  I've also won various laptops, all-in-ones and tablets since 2013 and that was only possible because of the fast results possible using AGK.  Also the community linked to this software is simply amazing, there's always someone willing to help you out whenever you think you've hit a dead end and give you feedback on your projects.
The tier 1 IDE is simple, but has the features you need to develop your game.  Windows & Andoid apps can be built directly from the IDE. Linux versions can be quickly packaged by using the pre-compiled players, or build directly from the IDE when running on Linux.  The Apple versions need to be compiled using a Mac.
What I personally love about AGK is how well it performs on low end machines.  Since you have to create code to cover everything, you can cut out all the stuff your game doesn't need to improve frame rate.  This makes running 3D games with good frame rates, even on integrated graphics cards, possible.
The feature set of the product is good and is continuously being expanded by the developers. If you feel the feature set is lacking, and you have the skills, you can always use the tier 2 libraries that enable you to use the AGK commands within C++.
Simlpy said: I couldn't recommend this tool enough.

I had my doubts at first. As steam reviews half the time are riddled with sarcasm or other sorts of Banter that really do not cater to a solid review.
That being said this game is well worth the price for what it deleivers.
Pros:
+Soundtrack: I could write a paper on this games soundtrack, however playing it and experiencing it would be worth your time.
+Short Story: The story is sort of a 'Inception' Style theme to it. Most of the game could be deduced as you played through and pay attention, but there are some parts that you might not expect that make it even more interesting.
+Art Style: For a game like this i prefer the low 8-bit style. It fits the game well and actually feels as though its easier to immerse yourself into the game.
+Characters/Commentary: The banter between the two main characters is very ammusing at some points. Each character seems to come alive in their own way without going to over the top.
Cons:
-Player interaction: Now dont get me wrong i love puzzles, however to jump from one section to the next requires the finding of small 'memory fragments' to activate another thing called a 'memento'. All flow seamlessly into the story, however i found myself a little dredding the puzzle part because i wanted more of the story, rather than a point and click puzzle finder.
-Notes: When you are in the game you find objects in the world that are added to your notes folder. These however have very little to no information. While it doesnt detract anything negative from the game, i wish they were given a bit more description into the story.
Overall id give this game a solid 8/10. The Puzzle repetitiveness is its only downfall in my opinion, but the games story and OST quickly make up for that. I dont think id play it more than twice. But for $10 i cannot complain on the product. It deleivered and if you have about 3 hours of downtime one day i suggest picking this game up and having a go. You wont be dissapointed

I wanted to like this game, I really did, but in the end, it's just too poorly balanced.
Pros:
+ Nice graphics
+ The voice acting is amazing
+ Quests can be quite interesting
Cons:
- The camera will randomly stop following your character
- You have to un-link a party member to heal out of combat
- The camera will move on it's own when not expected, causing misclicks
- Far too often, enemies are difficult to select, resulting in your character walking next to them, rather than attacking
- Encounters are far too unbalanced to the point where many at-level battles are impossible due to gimmicky mechanics (ex:  Enemies auto-freeze you on contact, meaning you only get a single hit in before they kill your helpless party)
Overall, I wish I could like this game, but in the end, it just relies far too much on gimmics and status ailments.  While the quests are entertaining, the combat is far too frustrating for me to recommend this game to anyone other than the die-hard masochists.

I loved Baldur's Gate and so many people are comparing it to that game, but I have to strongly disagree. This game just pisses me off. The combat difficult was spastic, with some fights being incredibly easy due and some incredibly difficult based entirely on the luck of the dice role, rather than your skill or tactical abilities.
The combat takes ages because you have to watch every character do every action in excruciating slow motion. The pathing will get "stuck" and sometimes you'll be sitting there watching an enemy character take up to a minute to decide that he can't move anywhere, and then watch the same character do it again. Every turn.  The controller controls are awful, hope you like dying on lava. Your minion's pathing is just as bad, and they will randomly walk onto lava as well.
You *need* to level up your perception to finish some of the final puzzles, so I hope you picked a character that has high perception or you'll have no idea that there are switches 2 feet from your face.
Sometimes you have to end your turn by holding down a the b-button. Sometimes it auto ended your turn and you just skipped your next character's turn.  The pyramid/teleporation scheme of getting past random locked door is awful, because sometimes it works and sometimes the "path is blocked" and you can't tell whether it will or not until you try.
You'll see an enemy use a dispel on your summons with astounding success, so you track down and grab that spell only to discover that it only works on some of the enemy's summons with no reasonable explanation as to why.
The dialogue interface is terrible. For everything else, the b button gets you out of it, except dialogue. For that you must select the "appropriate" option, which is usually the last one. Except when talking to your companions. In that case, the last one is to dismiss them from the party. Ugh!
I could go on, but this is plenty. The game is far from perfect and not the bastion of the perfection that so many other reviewers hold it up to be.

Ori and the Blind Forest's visual presentation is striking. From the very moment the game starts its hard not to appreciate just how beautiful the game is. But don't let that beauty and artistry fool you. Beneath the vivid color pallete and wonderful animation lies a incredibly challenging 2-D platformer.
Ori is proof that you don't need a complex story to have a good story. Its story is simple but evocative. Within the first ten minutes of the game you will find your heartstrings being pulled. It also needs to be said that Ori's soundtrack and audio are superb. From the opening score the music helps to draw you into the world.
Its quite clear to me that the game drew inspiration from classic NES platformers like Metroid and Kid Icarus. But Ori finds clever new ways to use similar ideas to make it feel like a wholy unique experience. For example in Metroid you often download a map for the area using a map station; or come to areas you can't access yet. This idea is present in Ori as well but you can only do so after you obtain map fragments. This encourages exploration. And like Metroid you will find areas that are only accessible after you acquire a new ability. In one sequence there are these glowing tubes that propel you off screen only to show up on the opposite side of the screen. This is a mechanic that appeared in Kid Icarus. There are also tubes on the top and bottom of the screen. These 'tubes' have force and can send you to your death if you aren't careful.
Ori has a surprising level of character progression. You can pick up spheres to gain ability points, or increase your health/magic. These act like Energy tanks or missile expansions in Metroid. The game has save points but you are able to use a bit of your 'magic' (blue energy) to create a save point of your own. This also serves to assign ability points to upgrade your abilities. These abilites can range from increased damage, or automatic pickup of health/magic etc.
Ori is a truly gorgeous game that while perhaps inspired by classic NES platformers; it manages to stand on its own. Like its predecessor's the game isn't afraid to challenge you. And when you complete a difficult section its all the more satisfying. This game is worth every penny; and should not be missed. If you enjoyed games like Super Metroid your going to love Ori.

The IDE (integrated development environment) of AGK is good (not great) for newbies and comfortable enough for programming veterans.  However, it's primarily for programming using a custom version of the Basic programming language, a language I rather not use at all due to its syntax and lack of object-orientation.  The AGK libraries can thankfully also be used in C++, but the IDE seems geared toward the Basic language.  I'm not ever going to get into AGK development simply because I'm already spoiled by Haxe and Unity and don't feel like AGK offers a good alternative to those for any reason for me.  However, if you've never programmed anything before, AGK could be your introductory level tool to make something worthwhile.
Pros:
1. AGK's IDE is pretty simple and easy to understand.  It could use some quality of life features, like right-click project-opening capability on the tree view.
2. AGK compiles its Basic language scripts to Windows, Mac, Linux, and Android, and the company behind this tool does not charge extra for compiling to other platforms, unlike Unity.
Cons:
1. AGK's Basic language is not object-oriented and will require some pretty messy code.  Even a simple example, like a ball floating around a house, can be a little taxing on your patience.  If you want to try something similar to AGK's 3D capability, I suggest you check this out:
2. The IDE lacks many very common features I'm used to when it comes to game development.  For example, there's no 2D/3D viewport for making game scenes.  There's no real separation of code between objects. This makes it much harder to get started with 3D development in AGK.  You'll have to load the 3D models manually with the programming language.  I suggest utilizing an external tile-based editor like Ogmo or maybe design scenes in Blender and somehow separate the objects from your Blender scene to make them programmable.  That said, it may be easier to just use Blender's game engine.
3. Documentation is lax.  It's hard to find C++ examples for the AGK libraries, and there's little to go on for help getting started.  I found this "go native" article kind of hidden on the official site:
Overall, I can't recommend this IDE and library for its full price.  If it was cheaper, maybe I'd recommend it, but honestly, I'm spoiled by too many free alternatives to recommend spending the money.  Some of the free, open source alternatives are easier for me to make something in.  There are many ways this IDE could save you a lot of headache, though, if you want to develop for multiple platforms.  The libraries are very easy to develop with in C++ if you're already familiar with a good C++ IDE.  You'll basically be using AGK's libraries inside a different IDE, though, which begs the question, "What does AGK give us that's worth $80?"

I've been a long time user of Game Maker Studio and was getting up to speed on Unity when the Humble Bundle came out earlier this month. I loved Game Maker Studio because it was so easy to prototype games and, well, it was free! I've now switched solely over to App Game Kit 2 for my game prototyping and app development. Not only is prototyping even faster (you don't need art up front - you can create basic sprites on the fly and assign art to them later), but you can also export out to Windows, Mac, iOS, and Android without any costly add-ons.
For example, I wrote a simple balloon app with full physics support for my 2-year-old daughter in less than 15 minutes (plus an hour's worth of art creation and making my own sound effects). I saved my project, exported an APK for my Android phone, and my daughter was happily inflating and popping balloons. I just had an idea last night about a simple jumping game with rising and falling platforms - and within 10 minutes I created a simple proof-of-concept. What more could you ask for?
The learning curve was very simple and it comes with a lot of examples to get you up to speed quickly. The community is also very helpful when you get stuck. I think I spent maybe an hour looking through the basic examples on the website, and I was off and running.
Game Maker Studio will always have a special place in my heart, but I wish I would've started with App Game Kit a long time ago. A huge thumbs up for The Game Creators!

As a long time veteran of the Total War series and a new fan of the Warhammer universe, I really enjoy these thematic fantasy battles  that range from devastating magic to giant dragons incinerating soldiers. Warhammer II improves on the first game with UI upgrades such as being able to choose which notifications pop up during the end turn. No more will you have the reminders telling you a character has skill points if you choose to turn it off. Unit cards now have an icon for large/small size so you can effectively send your troops against the right target. There are many others, not going to list them all, but it improves the overall experience.
Diplomacy is unfortunately relatively unchanged. Other than the interesting High Elf influence mechanic where you can make factions like or hate each other, a lot of the missing options have not been added back. You still can't gift regions to other factions which with the new climate system would have made a lot of sense. Conquered a uninhabitable territory? Gift it to an ally who can reside there. In future games I would definitely like to see these options added back.
Magic has been vastly improved. Damage spells actually do damage, killing hundreds if you get a good blob of troops together. Some additional lores have been added and for the most part, magic is relatively balanced but very useful.
The AI which has always been a weak point for the series is slightly improved. They will try and dodge artillery and use tactics, although their predictability can be exploited. It could definitely be better, but very few games these days have effective AI as it's simply very hard to develop.
The new factions are also interesting, each one having a distinct playstyle. Dark Elves are aggressive and once enough units have died, they gain a massive global buff to their stats, turning the tides of battle. High Elves units have a persistent buff to attack and defense until their HP drops below 50%, allowing them to outclass or at least hold against more expensive units until they lose their buffs. Lizardmen have effective main infantry and amazing dinosaurs. Skaven have huge numbers and highly effective artillery and magic, relying on sheer force to get the job done.
Overall an improved game with the usual flaws in AI and diplomacy. However, the fantasy universe combined with the tried and true combat makes this a great game and a must own for fans of the series.

Total Warhammer II was one of my most anticipated games of the year and thankfully it lived up to my hype. at the time of making this review I have 200 hours in the game.
Gameplay- in the base game you get to play as 4 major factions in vortex campaign where you compete against the Ai to take control of the vortex. Each faction has completely different campaign and battle strategies to win the campaign. For example, The High elves will use a campaign ability called influence where they can manipulate factions into fighting each other or forming alliances. Or the Dark elves using wars to enslave people to help grow their economy. Another attribute that makes this game great is its mods which can change game mechanics that you may not like or simply wish to improve.
Optimization-I Have 3 different Pc’s. My gtx 1070 with 6600k can run the game at its highest graphical settings at 40fps loading the whole campaign map (performance is much better at the beginning of the game) and its runs the actual battles at 40-60fps on average when there are 2000 troops on the field.
Mortal Empires- If you own Both Warhammer 2 and Warhammer 1 you get a new campaign map for free which combines both maps into one. You can play as any faction from game 1 and 2 (that you own from original). One issue that I have with the map is that the game 2 maps is squished very closely to the game 1 map which is not correct to the lore and it makes exploration over the ocean not seem as grand as it would be in the lore. On the plus side this change allows better performance for your computer and it makes interaction amongst factions more common. Overall, I think it’s a great free addition to game that allows more exciting campaigns.
In conclusion. I would defiantly recommend the game, even at full price to any strategy player whether you play casually to see awesome battles unfold, for hardcore players who want a competitive multiplayer or a Warhammer fan who wants to reenact battles from the lore

Like many others, I bought this game because so many of my friends insisted it was a masterpiece. At first, I thought I'd made a mistake: while it had an interesting beginning, it seemed to go downhill from there. Up until the end of Act 1, the gameplay was repetitive and, of course, the story didn't make sense at the time.
Act 2 and beyond changed all that. Suddenly, the story made
! The story and the meaning behind it pieced themselves together in such a beautiful manner and in a way that I had never expected. Initially, I thought that going through a story backward was gimmicky and would make the story incredibly convoluted, but it
. Going through the story in the way it's presented gives everything new shades of meaning. It essentially functions as foreshadowing in reverse and it's incredibly effective. You see the pieces of a man and a woman's life come together. It's so interesting because you know where they end up before you know all those tender or tense moments that led up to them coming together.
By the time the story had ended and the game was over, my heart was officially touched. The characters I had thought a little boring at first grew as characters by the end. Every single character had personality, even the minor characters that the main story isn't about. To me, the ending was satisfying. It brought up ethical issues over what the doctors in the game were doing and those issues are brought to light even further in the holiday special. To some, it's probably a happy ending, but to others it's bound to be a concerning ending. It all depends on how you feel about the events as they unfold.
I have zero regrets about purchasing this game. It's been over a week since I've played it, and even just thinking about the game fills me with happiness and reminds me of all the great moments the game had. The story, the music, the humor and charm behind the game -- all of it creates such a positive experience that I honestly don't feel words are enough for it.
Sure, this game isn't for everyone, but even if it's not your cup of tea, you'll probably get something out of the experience. And, even if it turns you didn't like it in the end, it's obvious how much love Kan Gao and his staff put into this game. It's definitely a game worth getting.

It's the Boku No Pico of videogames.
How? That's rather difficult to explain. As a platformer it's frustrating, unfair, the controls are loose, the music is repetitive, level design is grating...but despite its numerous faults if you let it the game will suck you in for hours on end. No matter how it might enrage the player, it is *very* difficult to stop playing. To say a game is that compelling sure sounds like a great compliment, but I assure you it's not. Anger sets in after the first few minutes and builds--not declines--with each successive level. It's a Simon Says at a million miles an hour, forcing the player to perform a series of monotonous tasks to a degree of precision in the milliseconds, and there's not a moment's respite for failure. Expect to see the beginning of each level many times. While the challenge and satisfaction of success could make the game very rewarding for the few willing to take the time to master its nuance, it's plagued by control issues. Suffice to say, the input feels unacceptably loose and many times the player can expect to have quite a defeats snatched from the jaws of victory by a missed keypress or delay of only a few frames. This I cannot overstate: the game expects the player to perform to a level that it itself cannot reach. So why persist? It's succubus! The level isn't *that* hard. You can't be *that* bad at such a simple game. You were *so* close that last attempt. Surely you'll get it *this* time. It's just enough to keep playing, but not enough to feel any satisfaction for a victory.
Maybe I'm nitpicking, but I can't bring myself to recommend a game that demands so much from the player, but isn't precise enough to handle the players it's trying to court. With a little refinement and some tighter controls, I could see this as a great Super Hexagon or Audiosurf-alike, but that's simply not the case.

There's a lot of upsides and downsides to this game, by this current post.
DOWNSIDES:
-This game is graphically demanding, meaning if you wanted to have the best and smoothest experience and a constant 60 FPS, you better have a top-range computer powered by the ghosts of dead Microsoft certified system engineers. Otherwise, once you start using the Flashy and awesome looking skills, you're gonna start lagging. You do, however, get the option to reduce the terrible lag by looking around in the Preferences and turning things off or down to Low.
-Research the classes before you're sure what you want to use throughout the game, you may find certain Main/Sub classes that are too problematic for you.
-Everyone says (And whines) that C9 doesn't lag, but there always will be lag and in this game, its called Connection Lag.
-Customer Support and Service is the WORST, in fact, it makes EA Games look like an active, and helping saint. No one responds to anything, and it even goes far as Webzen banning your account if you complain to them or about them in their own forums website.
-This game is a GRINDER, meaning you go out and spend an entire day farming and looking for that one item that you'll need for something.
-RNGesus.
-There's a Trade Office, meaning you can buy and sell stuff to and from other players out there (Take a look at the prices  of what item sells for what before doing so, otherwise you're not going to get much profit, sell too little, you're ripping yourself off, sell too much, no ones ever going to buy it)
-Typical prices in Trade Office are usually in the millions, meaning you better save up and grind as hard and as fast as you can.
-You're going to be a constant customer to the Blacksmith, because there is a repair system and dying halves your equipment's durability.
-Beware turning on Intrusion, at some point, there WILL be a P2W lvl 67 (current Level Cap) with full Perfect grade equipment coming after your head and will humiliate you if you do.
-Beware using Intrusion, if you die while doing so, you don't revive in the dungeon while your target can revive as many times as they want (so long as they have spare Resurrection Scrolls), and if you strike unlucky with a veteran thats busy grinding away and you're not as good as PVP'ing as they are, your♥♥♥♥♥is automatically handed to you on a silver platter. (Some will openly humiliate you)
-There is a plot.
-There are bound items, meaning you can't store them in a warehouse, they can't be traded and they will take/waste space.
-Gold dropped by normal monsters are rarely worth picking up, completing quests of any kind will ALWAYS give more EXP and money than what you kill.
-Typical skimpy female armor exists here, meaning you get a LOT of fanservices, top and bottom.
-That trailer you saw? Those are called Ultimate Fury skills, and they're the most laggy skills you'll find out there, and they come with a pretty hefty price.
-The enchancing equipment part quickly becomes an all-or-nothing.
-And lastly, this game is dying and becoming a heavily implied Pay-2-Win. Almost every person you'll find in-game is a veteran IRL money-spender, and if you decide to join the P2W crew, Webzen will squeeze every penny out of you.
UPSIDES:
-This game is fun, extremly fun, sometimes addicting and in a few morbid cases, very satisfying. Its the MMORPG version of Dynasty Warriors, minus the politics with NPCs. You're the Big Good who's the only one competent person out there (minus the few temporary NPC allies) that goes out, tosses and paints entire mountains with enemy blood like its another Tuesday to you, and the only "Impossible Bosses and Monsters" are ones scripted to be impossible. Theres even bosses that can be tossed about and thrown everywhere before they can do much to you. You can party with 3 other players to make the massacre even more enjoyable.
-There is a plot, and its decent enough to keep you interested in the "long struggle to save Glenheim".
-There's a lot of classes you can choose, just by the (current) 5 Main classes, each having their own sub classes. And if you want to make different characters, you have plenty of slots to use. (They all share the same Warehouse, however)
-There are even Artisan Occupations which are available for you to choose at the very start of the game. (Research before you choose, though. If you pick an Occupation that won't do much for you, you're not even gonna bother using it and you can't change once you decide. Also, wait a few levels before you decide to spend time crafting, as they can be expensive.)
-RNGesus.
-There's a Trade Office, meaning you can buy and sell stuff to and from other players out there.
-If you don't want to bother using the Trade Office, you can sell or trade them by typing out in the chat and Shift-Rightclick the item you want to sell/trade, theres even a Trade channel.
-Friendly players and guilds do exist in the game, so ask around if you have any questions, they're likely to answer you. But don't be suprised when the guild you joined starts getting silent more often.
-Auspices and Legends boost your character's stats, while Titles give you a sense of impressive accomplishment, the Titles and Legends are found and given by Acheivement Grinding. Auspices are usually gotten through events and buying them.
-If you join a guild and they are at a high enough level, you can buff yourself up with Guild buffs and Guild skills (The buffs are made through Artisan Occupations such as Metalsmithing, Woodworking and Tailoring.
-You can upgrade your gear with the Blacksmith and the Artisan Metalsmithing, making you all the more godly in the dungeons.
-You can craft your own weapons, armor and accessories. Rare grades takes more time but is more worth it than the Magic grades, and the same holds true for Perfect grades over Rare grades.
-Sold something you didn't mean to, including Bound items? You can repurchase them! For double the amount they sold! (So long as you didn't quit the game, or switched characters and you realized quickly what you did)
-A LOT of scenery to go and explore.
-Theres a mentor/student system! As long as the student is below lvl 25 and the mentor is above lvl 40, the student gets DOUBLE the EXP while the mentor gets double guild points and mentor medals, which can be traded for (most of the time) useful goodies.

Alright so, leme start by saying that the 5 min steam claims i have played this game is wrong, i have spent afew hours (1 session) and for some reason it didnt count that.
now for the actual review:
This is a hack'n'slash korean mmo rpg thing or as they call it "Action mmorpg" which works fine for the most part, the skills are flashy animation is rather decent and the hits connect properly and lag dosent ♥♥♥♥ you up so this part of the game works pretty much as u would exepect.
The game is rather minimalist tho it dosent look like alot of effort went into the game, the game is devided into towns and everything other then that is just a Hub-based dungeon thing - you go to a portal, you select an area u want on the map and ur teleported there for a fight and when ur done u can either restart it or teleport back into town which is kinda boring tbh.
Dungeons can work on different diffuculty levels and the only difference between them is that mobs hit harder and have more health, the terrain stays the same, visualy the monsters are the same and thier ammount is the same so nothing too much exciting.
Ingame you have 5 classes, each class have 4 sub-classes which could be counted as "20 playable classes! woohoo" but in reality its not as exciting as that sadly since the sub classes share the same "Core" skills with some unique additions.
Also, the game seems to be populated by turks and anything other then WTS/WTB is basicly turkish chit-chat.
Ingame store has mostly cosmetics BUT WAIT! thouse cosmetics have passive dmg/deff buffs so u can draw your own conclusions from that fact, tho it seems u can purchase this items from other players with ingame currency so if thats your sort of thing, go for it.
Graphicly wise the game isnt impressive, its not bad either, its somewhere is that borring mediocre range when it dosent thrill you but dosent discust you either therefor uninteresting to talk about. Oh, and the game is littered with invisible walls which no1 even bothered to hide which seems abit lazy, but meh.
So, overall, after palying for about 3 hours or so checking different classes and running into invis walls my game just crashed behind a loading screen at 99% creating and infinite singularity of spinning graphics and it was at this point that i looks up at my ceiling and realized how bored i have been. Still tho, some people might find this gam fun, there is nothing mechanicly wrong with it as i said be4, u press the buttons and the mosters die and thats all you can ask for really, so, if ur a fan of the genere and enjoy games like Tera but looking for something less good you can give this game a bash and see where it goes!

This is easily one of the best games I have ever played.  Let's go over pro's and cons
1. Co-op. As a man that searches for games to play with his wife I love this idea. Couch co-op or online it is great. It's seemless going from sharing the same screen  splitscreen gameplay between you and another co-op player. I love playing an RPG with my life and she loved it to. It also makes it easy to share dialogue options with two players and to quest together. We had so much fun together.
2. Visually beautiful. This game has a wonderfully colorful pallette.
3. Amount of gameplay time. The amount of content makes this game easily worth $100 and yet it goes for something like $40. A great value.
4. Storyline- Wow. Just wow. A multi- layered story with many stories interweaving in one another. Fantastic. I loved the stories.
5. Voice Acting and Music- Beautiful music and great voice overs.
6. Combat- fun turn based combat that uses the elements well.
7. Beautiful and varied enviroments.
8. Great controller support
Cons
1. The monster designs wtih a few exceptions (Bracchus Rex, Trife, the undeead mini bosses), were uninspired trope fantasy stock.
2. Puzzles- Some of them I just hated. I had to actually find a stupid switch I missed and I spent a long time looking for it! ugh!
3. Broken quest system- It's easy to miss a switch, accidently drop or lose an item, etc. Be careful not to sell or drop an item, key, or book unless you know for sure you don't need it or you can be screwed.
4. The Mapping system makes orienting and finding your position difficult for the direction challenged such as myself.  There is no waypoint systems and the way the map moves makes finding east, west, north, south tricky. It could have been done better. They should have maintained it orienting north.
All that said. This game is so much fun, and playing hours upon hours with my wife was a great experience we both loved. I waited for the steam sale, but when they release a sequel we don't plan on waiting this time!

I've never written a steam review before, but at some point every gamer is bound to encounter a game that pushes them over the edge; that utterly captivates them to such an extent that they need to express why.
Ori and the Blind Forest is that game. Immersive, emotional, and jaw-droppingly gorgeous, it will sweep you up from the moment you begin watching the prologue until the last credit rolls.
The gameplay itself is meticulously designed; highly recommended to play with a controller, the controls feel very intuitive and reactive.  Rewarding in its challenge yet forgiving in its design, Ori will leave you feeling accomplished, without invoking too much frustration from repeated deaths.  Part of this is due to the save system: players may save the game almost anywhere they like by expending a collectible resource, and respawn is instantaneous allowing for a seamless experience.
To say the atmosphere of Ori is immersive would be an understatement.  The hand-painted visuals that loom in the game's background are nothing short of sublime.  It's easy to catch yourself sitting idle while staring fixedly into the screen, marvelling at the incredible detail put into every scene.  The themed colours of each area will have you lingering to absorb the environment before moving on to the next.
While I would usually include a game's score in the same paragraph as the atmosphere, Ori and the Blind Forest pushes the emotional limits of video game music to the extent that it deserves an honorable mention.  Fully orchestrated and composed by a man I had previously never heard of - Gareth Coker - the game's soundtrack warranted an immediate purchase on iTunes.  The fantastic harmonies and emotional crescendos that lead you through the forest of Nibel will haunt you long after you turn off your computer.  Gripping at times and tear-jerking at others, not enough can be said about how incredible Ori's score is.
Finally, this review wouldn't be complete without discussing the touching plot that drives the game forward.  Revolving around themes of love and sacrifice, fear and bravery, the story behind Ori and the Blind Forest is jarring in its simplistic appeal to our most coveted emotions.  The ending is satisfying, something that I don't say very often about modern video games, and the game is paced very well, logging you between 6 and 12 hours to play through depending on how thorough you want to be.  Replay value is high, and I will likely being going through a second round in about a month's time.
Ori and the Blind Forest offers an incredible gaming experience, one which is too infrequently exposed to the public, and at an incredible price for what it is.  Stop reading reviews and buy it, because nothing anyone says will ever do the game justice, and it is simply something you must experience for yourself.

Ori and the Blind Forest is among the best audio-visual experiences you can find in video games. The quality of the music and graphics is not a gimmick that wears off after a couple hours of gameplay, but an asset that continuously enhances the game and astonishes the player with unrelenting beauty. This aside, Ori is a by-the-numbers MetroidVania game with some lame level design but above average game-feel and movement mechanics.
-
: Every blade of grass and every leaf of every tree has a beautifully animated mesh distortion effect that make them appear to gently bend with the wind. Ori puts art assets in the foreground and several layers deep into the background providing every vista with a sense of depth. With all of these foreground and background elements animating, the world feels very alive. There was clearly nothing lost in translation between concept art and the final look of the game. Any screenshot looks like it might have been specifically handpainted. One minor knock on the visual side is the overuse of glow. Sometimes the oversaturated glow of enemies, health drops, experience drops and projectiles become indiscernable from one another.
-
: The soundtrack's central theme is gorgeous and catchy. The more suspenseful tracks add a lot to the mood of Ori's "chase" sequences. The echoing gibberish voice of the characters is also well done.
-
: Navigating Ori through the world of Nibel is a joy. The simple run and jump mechanics are implemented perfectly and the accompanying audio-visual feedback give it excellent game-feel. The powerups that Ori collects on her quest supplement this well with standouts including the Kuro's Feather (allows you to glide and catch gusts of wind) and the super jump ability that is unlocked near the end of the game.
-
: There must be 7 or 8 types of walls in Ori. There are ones you must explode through, ones you must hurl yourself at with a super jump, ones you must launch a specific enemy at, and the list keeps going on. One challenge of designing MetroidVanias is to make these progression barriers less contrived. Presenting the player with a ledge that they can't reach at the time, but later giving them a double jump to reach it is smart design. When the player gets the double jump they will immediately think "hey I can use this to get up to that high ledge!". Having a bunch of different destructible walls is poor design. The player will not know which abilities can break which walls intuitively and will not make the same connection they did when they got that double jump ability. Having the "blue" ability break the "blue" wall makes progression through the game feel artificial and contrived. Ori does this quite a bit.
-
: There are some fantastically designed abilities. The Kuro's Feather gets you through progression barriers in an elegant way but also factors into your moment-to-moment movement. There are some other abilities that feel redundant and are ONLY used to pass barriers and do not change the way you would otherwise play the game. One offender is the wall-climb ability which differs only slightly from the wall-jump ability. When you get the wall-climb ability, the game presents you with some almost cringingly contrived puzzles to prove to you that "this is different from wall-jumping, we swear!" Another offender is the ground-pound ability which lets you break through floors and not much else.
-
: Ori offers some small amount of RPG progression in the form of its three-branched talent tree. While providing some motivation to collect experience orbs, this mechanic fails because choosing to specialize in one of the branches does not change the way you play the game in any meaningful way. Specializing in combat is fine but, since you have to do just as much combat either way, it makes that decision feel meaningless. There is no replayability provided by this feature.
Minor design issues aside, I enjoyed almost every moment of Ori and the Blind Forest and would recommend it to anyone who admires visual beauty.

AGK2 is not a drag-and-drop game maker, it's a programming language like Blitz, DarkBasic or Amos. I always loved dabbling with those programs and I love this one too. It's an easy transition to AGK2 if you're familiar with any style of BASIC coding, and there's plenty of room to get more technical if you want to - but you don't have to. It works extremely well, and really does produce results that work perfectly on any android or iOS device. Being a language, you can do what you want with it - I've made and published a side-scrolling shooter, a quiz game, a 3D crossy-road-a-like (3D is workable but pretty basic at this point, although an upgrade to the 3D is coming) and currently I'm working on a physics-based game. The physics handling in AGK2 is excellent and by far the easiest to use I've ever seen. If you're prepared to put in the time and the polish, there are very few games on the Android Play that couldn't have been made with AGK2. Another thing I like is that end results have no watermarking. There are no forced splash screens or tell-tale signs. Most people would only know you'd used AGK2 if you told them so.
If you're a hobbyist or beginning programmer who not only enjoys making games but would like the opportunity to actually offer the finished result on a global scale, I highly recommend this superb software.
[EDIT]
Updating the review because AGK itself is updating all the time. The 3D is now vastly improved since I posted this review, and now even handles 3D physics. You can even output your games to HTML5, upload it and anyone can play it in their browser. There have also been countless bug-fixes and improvements. I paid £30 for AGK in a steam sale, and now have one app on the play store that makes me ten times that every month, a very welcome additional income to a student. It would never have been possible for me to achieve this without this excellent software.
Nah. Not much bang for buck here...

I wish that Steam would implement a star rating style system, so that we have more choices than just "recommend" or "don't recommend".  I do recommend the App Game Kit; it really does make writing games (especially for mobile) fast and easy.  Also, the possibility to write once and target multiple platforms is really nice.
That said, I do have some complaints, but they don't stop me from recommending.  Ultimately, I'd like to give the software... maybe a 7/10?  If you are already familiar with programming there will be a number of things that feel awkward about programming with AGK's Tier 1 custom language.  This is especially true if you are used to object oriented programming.  It's not a show stopper, and you should be able to work out how to do what you want to do, but it can cause some headaches when you want to do things that have become second-nature that simply can't be done that way here.  There are no objects, no pointers, very few datatypes, and essentially no scope management aside from functions.  Global variables, something generally frowned upon in best-practices for most languages, are almost unavoidable here.  One can use the Tier 2 system, which allows for coding in an external compiler and just use the AGK libraries, but then you lose the cross-platform targeting, which is one of the beauties of this system.
The documentation is often sparse and occasionally inacurrate, and the user-submitted code samples they include should be taken with a grain of salt - they are often useful to get the idea of what the API functions do, but they often get the details wrong, especially when you get into the 3D functions.  The program IDE itself is pretty sparse, and the autocomplete/hint system very quickly gets confused about uer defined type structures and functions.  The debugger is only somewhat useful - if you're used to any enterprise level IDE you will be very dissapointed in the features there.
Oh, I almost forgot to mention something that came as a bit of a surprise to me.  Maybe I didn't read closely enough, but I did not initially realize that to deploy to iOS, you need to be running on a Mac.  Period.  As far as I can tell, there is no way to deploy an iOS app from Windows or Linux.  The menu item is there, but it tells you it needs Apple's XCode to be installed.  So that kind of diminishes the whole "target multiple platforms" perk.  It still counts, but with an asterisk.
If the devs ever read this, the one language feature I would wish for (out of the many that I think would be nice) would be function pointers.  If you could implement function pointers, then we could come close to some simple OOP, which would be nice.
***
Edit:
Oh, man, I just started trying to use arrays, and holy hell.  I said the one feature I would ask for is function pointers?  Well, strike that.  Fix the goddamn arrays first.  After banging my head against the desk for about an hour, I finally noticed something in the docs that I had overlooked:
Seriously, what? myArray as integer[2] would have 3 elements? An array with 0 elements returns a length of -1, and an array with 1 element returns a length of 0? What?  The developers of this software obviously must know how to code, otherwise how could they create the software in the first place?  But knowing how to code, how could they possibly think that made any sense at all? I can think of no language I have ever used that works like that, ever.  I understand that some things are done in this system to make it more useable to non-coders, but that is super unintuative.
For the sake of all that is holy, please fix that insanity.
***
Still, if you're looking for a way to quickly create games, especially mobile games for both Android and iOS, this is a good way to do it.  It could use some improvement and polishing, but it does get the job done.
I would recommend this program for mobile and cross-platform 2D development.
