My honest review after having just finished "To the Moon": This is an OK story told through the wrong medium, simple as that.
The gist of the story is, a dying man wants a final "wish" granted, which is basically a personally tailored dream he receives just before death. In this case, the man wants to go to the Moon. The dream is somehow constructed by wading through his life's memories and finding the place and time where the wish first occured. However, a problem soon becomes apparent as no one, including the dying man, really knows why he wants to go to the Moon. I won't spoil the story, only say that the man has some childhood traumas that must be "sorted".
The story is certainly emotional, just not THAT deep in my opinion; I couldn't really connect that much to the characters involved, Especially since the 2 protagonists were incredibly childish and constantly made infantile jokes during the game, destroying any mood that could have been.
That however, is not the problem of this game - it is the game itself. The game mechanics are completely superficial: you must hunt around the man's memories for objects of particular importance to the memories. Most of these objects are important for no rhyme and reason whatsoever: a sofa, a football, an umbrella; it can be anything. When you have them all, you must solve a flip puzzle to continue. The game hardly require any cognitive facilities on the players part.
If the story had been told as a film, or perhaps a book, I think I could have related better to it. As it stands though, I did not find it worth my time.
Nonetheless, there is one brilliant part about the game: The music is incredible, in particular the piano piece "For River". It is beautiful, and the composer has been so nice as to make the piano sheet available. That alone was worth the price I paid for the game.

While I would recommend this program for mobile and cross-platform 2D development, I feel that development has been wayyyy too slow for 3D as well as for other important features. Also, don't pay attention to the hours I've spent on the Steam version. I've used the standalone AGK 1 and AGK 2 for hundreds of hours (version 1 and 2 are pretty much identical, even at this point in my opinion).
A little story for context: I originally had bought AGK 1 almost 2 years ago when it was priced at $60. For the price, it was a solid program with an incredibly easy learning curve (this is a HUGE strength). It's huge weakness though was exporting iOS and Android apps (the process was just ridiculous-they had like a 70-step guide or something that was missing steps and stuff). Then, AGK 1 had trouble getting funding because it seemed that it was underpriced for what it offered. Then, the AGK 2 came along (as part of a massive Kickstarter campaign) to replace AGK 1, promising a bunch of new features and such. I understood that they made a business mistake, and I wanted to help them out, so I pledged (you also got the beta version). AGK 2 luckily fixed the export with a new IDE and such.
Anyway, I spent months on a 3D mobile game (probably my most impressive and time-consuming project to date) since 3D animation was promised to come out a few years ago, but still has yet to arrive. In fact, I stopped working on the project a year ago, waiting for the promised 3D animation, and it's still a long way from coming. What's worse is that there were other stretch goals for 3D that haven't even been touched yet. The worse part about all of this is that the deadlines for when these features would arrive were months, if not years off, which made it difficult to plan. This isn't even just for the 3D parts, certain 2D features have also taken absurd amounts of time to be released.
Unfortunately, since those almost two years, not too much else has changed. I don't want to give a negative review (I wish you could use neutral) for AGK 2, because I feel that it's worth the money for 2D games. However, this product continues to frustrate me on how little it delivered from what was promised. I really don't understand how long it can take to incorporate 3D animation or even some other 3D commands; it really shouldn't be that difficult. It appears that the product is understaffed (I think there is like one programmer working on it for like 5 devices), and the countless delays and limited updates (both in scale and in time) have really made this product suffer. It really is a shame because this product could have been so much better.
Anyway, sorry for the rant. It is a decent product if all you wish to use it for is 2D stuff, but its 3D has been lacking for years. I know it doesn't advertise this on the store page, but it is part of the product as well as other promised 3D features. If you are expecting features in the future, it's too hit-or-miss.
In short, the 2 after AGK is so misleading, it really should just be called AGK 1, and even then, an incomplete version.

As an old AMOS coder from the good old days of the Amiga, I picked up AGK2 pretty quickly and had things wizzing around the screen in no time.  I've been looking for something like this for a long time and this reminds me of the ease and flexibility of AMOS.  It's not as comprehensive or as polished as AMOS, and I'm afraid not by a long way but it is early days and the potential is positively tangible.  The biggest difficulty for me is the lack of a comprehensive, technical manual for the BASIC language.  There is online documentation, but it is frustratingly sparse with more of an 'overview' of commands rather than an in depth explanation with examples.  For example, I have been trying to find information about variable scope, returning values (as an array?) from functions and examples of file handling (how are values separated in the file) but, to my frustration, there's no information.  I'm sure I can engage with the great community, but I don't want to have to wait for an answer (that a manual would give you straight away)!
Overall, I'm very keen to support this software and will have to soldier on.  It has certainly rekindled my passion for game coding!

No, this is programming. If you are afraid of programming, this program might not be for you, nor the game industry for that matter. However, if you aren't afraid to get your hands dirty with some basic programming, this is the program for you!
Using a pretty easy language, this program eliminatesthe problem of creating your own game engine. It basically gives you the freedom of creating a video game without spending an eternity of creating your own engine. This program is also made so that you program your game once, and then it will be playable cross-platform for pretty much all popular devices. And with an awesome broadcasting tool and an AGK app on your phone, you can stream the game from your computer to your phone/tablet, and test it there.
Ok, it's 12:24 AM now, and I have a big presentation tomorrow, so I won't write much more.
But I'll leave you with this.
If you are interested in making video games, and are not afraid of some lines of code, this is the program for you.

Overall, I think this is a good product.  Not great--not yet at least--but good.  I see what this company did with DarkBasic and I hope that they intend to stuff as much of that as they can into APK2, and the indications are that they intend to do just that.  I tried GameMaker last year, and I found that the games I was interested in making didn't fit very neatly into the GM model (although I'm sure it's a good tool for some games).  The nice thing about AGK is that it is more flexible--so much that I can't think of a 2D game that can't be done with it.
My sense is that this is the initial release of a product that will see many updates, especially in the 3D world.  The features for 3D appear to be fairly basic, although I haven't tried them yet.  That said, let's get to the pros and cons:
Pros:
+ Handles all of the graphics-related stuff I don't feel like dealing with, and plenty of nice features
+ "Easy enough" that I've got a (very rudimentary) game prototype within a week
+ Very flexible--basically it's a library of game functions with an IDE wrapped around it
+ Nice IDE, fairly intuitive and hasn't caused me any headaches
+ BASIC compiler points out most silly mistakes, like using a variable before setting it
+ Pretty reasonable physics model  (take it as a compliment, as Physics was one of my majors)
+ Handles collisions pretty well
Cons:
- Documentation is...pretty basic.  It exists and gives you a decent idea of what the functions do, but it's just not up to a great level yet.  I suspect that they and the community will rectify this with time.
- There are a few non-obvious behaviors (bugs?) and call sequences.  It increases the learning curve because you spend time dealing with things that "ought" to work.
- There seem to be certain ranges of values that the physics model "likes" to deal with.  Don't expect to place planets and astronauts in the same program with their real masses.  Fortunately, you shouldn't ever need to do that.
- I wouldn't use this to make a 3D game, yet.  I believe I read that 3D animations are not supported yet.
Overall, I'd say:  it's good, and getting better.
About the reviewer:
I have 11 years of experience as a professional computer scientist.  I have more than the layman's knowledge of physics.  What I do not have (yet) is game development experience.

This IDE is great to learn coding, although there should be some more guides for noobs like me.

It does require a desire to learn programming, but the BASIC style language you can use makes it a great tool to learn how to program and the community is really helpful both here in Steam and on the TGC forums. once you are comfortable with you prgramming skills you can easily move on to C++.

This is easily one of the best games I have ever played.  Let's go over pro's and cons
1. Co-op. As a man that searches for games to play with his wife I love this idea. Couch co-op or online it is great. It's seemless going from sharing the same screen  splitscreen gameplay between you and another co-op player. I love playing an RPG with my life and she loved it to. It also makes it easy to share dialogue options with two players and to quest together. We had so much fun together.
2. Visually beautiful. This game has a wonderfully colorful pallette.
3. Amount of gameplay time. The amount of content makes this game easily worth $100 and yet it goes for something like $40. A great value.
4. Storyline- Wow. Just wow. A multi- layered story with many stories interweaving in one another. Fantastic. I loved the stories.
5. Voice Acting and Music- Beautiful music and great voice overs.
6. Combat- fun turn based combat that uses the elements well.
7. Beautiful and varied enviroments.
8. Great controller support
Cons
1. The monster designs wtih a few exceptions (Bracchus Rex, Trife, the undeead mini bosses), were uninspired trope fantasy stock.
2. Puzzles- Some of them I just hated. I had to actually find a stupid switch I missed and I spent a long time looking for it! ugh!
3. Broken quest system- It's easy to miss a switch, accidently drop or lose an item, etc. Be careful not to sell or drop an item, key, or book unless you know for sure you don't need it or you can be screwed.
4. The Mapping system makes orienting and finding your position difficult for the direction challenged such as myself.  There is no waypoint systems and the way the map moves makes finding east, west, north, south tricky. It could have been done better. They should have maintained it orienting north.
All that said. This game is so much fun, and playing hours upon hours with my wife was a great experience we both loved. I waited for the steam sale, but when they release a sequel we don't plan on waiting this time!

I for one would continue but I feel like all the people I met along the way soon give up and go back to the Dark Zone. Speaking of which DLC 2, Survival or whatever. Someone still remembering the age-old title
I loved that title for it's atmosphere and approach to realistic sailing and shooting mechanics.
In many aspects, Naval Action seems to be a worthy successor.
Ship handling is difficult and demanding, but incredibly rewarding when you finally get the hang on it (I certainly have no arrived at that point. Still missing broadsides at point blank.) It feels very immersive, too.
Now add a pinch of Pirates! to the lot and mix it with classical MMO features:
Naval action circles around PvE and PvP (there is a PvE only server, too) sea battles in an open world sandbox (yes, that time of the year again).
Choose a faction to side with and gain ranks and riches by doing missions, privateering, trading and, well: naval action. Grind your rank from petty midshipman all the way up to rear admiral while sailing the infamous caribbean waters.
The AI is decent but not stunningly smart. It benefits from cheating and bonuses, too. Still lots of room for improvement here.
As to be expected you can find balancing issues, bugs and glitches but so far I did not discover a game-braking one. Remember: Early Access.
If you were disappointed by gamey ship handling in Empire: Total War but loved it's graphics and atmosphere, Naval Action will interest you.
you're willing to look beyond the Early Access issue and the heavy Elite:Dangerous style rank grind, which still feels dull and pretty unrewarding.
If you ever wanted to be Jack Aubrey, Mr. Hornblower, Arr! Blackbeard or Surcouf, this is your chance. Don't forget to have a looped volley of shanties running on your music player, though.
Sailing ships roll and pitch in the seas in all their detailed, glorious splendour. Mighty Ship-of-the-Lines exchanging rolling broadsides under a waning moon, their dim stern lanterns lit while the whole sea is enlightened by muzzle flahes just to be swallowed by dense gun powder clouds again.
Listening to the creaking sound of ships rolling in heavy waves and the impressive thunder of firing 32 pounders is impressive.
Ah, the ocean! It's colour sheme and rolling wave's look even more realistic and impressive than in World of Warships, and that ocean already looks stunning.
Spotting a lone sail or traces of a slowly growing landmass on the fog-shaded horizon amidst the sheer endless, foaming sea really succeeded in immersing me right into the game.
I've exclusively playing PvE until now- so I can't give a verdict about the PvP servers or the state of PvP in general.
As of update 9.7 there have been many additions to PvE content like gargantuan AI fleets, AI can sail all ship types, a stronger, very challenging AI opponent (as of update 9.73 made easier for lower skill levels), land-in battles (meaning the battle terrain will reflect the open world terrain).
The only thing that needs to be added for atmosphere are decent music (and by the way, those STUPID COMMENTS ON THE LOADING SCREENS NEED TO GO! They are not even close to be funny.) and more modelled sailors. Right now you've only got one sailor manning a gun each, the helm is unmanned and no one cares to deal with sails. Which looks kinda silly! Albeit the sailors models themselves are well done and the textures detailed.

‘Bad Rats: The Rat’s Revenge’ is a 2009 title released by “Invent 4 Entertainmento”. It features a ball, a cat, and 9 different rats: Batter Rat, who is a rat with a baseball cap and bat designed to, well, bat the ball. Tractor Rat, who is a rat inside a tractor wearing a hard hat who pushes the ball slowly. Bomber Rat, who has a long beard, a turban, and a suicide vest, who blows up upon touching the ball and sends it directly upward. Archer Rat, who is dressed like Robin Hood and has a bow and toothpick arrow, who shoots the ball directly forward with mediocre aim. Fat Rat, who’s never seen without a piece of cheese and has a main goal of being the weight in a lever system. Rocket Rat, who’s tied to a rocket with a soldier helmet, and, when his adjustable timer runs out, will shoot directly upward until redirected and he explodes. Runner Rat, who is a normal rat in a hamster wheel who can launch the ball directly forward. Vacuum Rat, who has a vacuum pack on his back and a vacuum in his hand and can pull the ball directly upward. Lastly, there’s Cannon Rat, who has a similar timer to Rocket rat but goes directly forward instead of upward. The game also sometimes features a dog character.
The idea of the game is to place these rats (along with some planks and barrels) in various areas to complete each level by killing the cat. Many ways to do this include slicing it with a knife, burning it, microwaving it, shooting it, crushing it, and more. The previously mentioned dog character will sometimes eat it.
Bad Rats costs 99 cents on steam and is known as “one of the worst games ever made” by many game reviewers. It is, in fact, commonly gifted to friends as a joke due to its cheapness and badness. The prankster will often convince his victim that it’s the best game ever made, and try to get them to play it while they can talk, so the prankster can listen to their victim’s utter dismay when they find the game’s true nature.
Some things that contribute to this game’s awfulness include Its concept. The idea is that these rats would like to get revenge on the cat by killing it, although we never see what the cat actually does. Also, the idea that a dog will eat a cat is absurd. Other than this, the animation is godawful, making a 2009 game look worse than CGI from 2003. The look is not complimented by the fact that most of the animations are 112% broken. Not only this, some levels are completely unbeatable, and the time limit of 10 minutes for 44 levels does not help. Another thing that doesn’t help is that doing the same thing 20 times has the ability to lead to 20 different results, so often times players will reset think the correct answer was wrong. Speaking of the correct answer, not only will the game’s suggested solution not work half the time, but sometimes the game will display the completed puzzle without the player asking for it. Most infuriatingly, the game will sometimes switch from 2d with 3d modeling to 3d to with 3d modeling, making it so the ball will just roll off the screen without prompting. The game doesn’t even go past 1240p. All these factors are what earn the game it’s awful status.
10/10

In the beginning computer programming was restricted to an elite of scientists and mathematicians then, created in 1964, there was BASIC (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code), popularized in the late 1970s and became almost ubiquitous with home computers of the 1980s.  Designed from the start to be easy to learn, it is a high level computer language, meaning it reads, almost like the English language.
e.g. Print("Hello World")  - will print Hello World on your screen.
Basic Continued to evolve during the 1990s with the likes of AMOS and into 2000 with languages like Dark Basic.  In the 2010s, with the explosion of mobile devices, BASIC has again evolved to meet demand and AGK was born.
AGK2 can be used 2 ways -
1) As a BASIC scripting language. This is a fully featured, standalone solution for people who want to program.
2) As libraries for C++.  This extends the power and simplicity of AGK to people who prefer to use C++.
The basic language has a plethora of powerful features supporting 2D and 3D game and APP development. These include a 2D physics engine, Shader support for  both 2D and 3D, access to Sensors like GPS and Gyro meters, Joy pad support, HTTP, Multiplayer, Video, Particles, and much more.
AGK2 compiles finished, ready to install packages for Android, IOS, Blackberry, Windows and Apple Mac.  It is then up to you how to use those packages either for personal programs to release the potential in your device or to make money at any or all of the various app stores (e.g. Google play, Amazon, Apple, OUYA).
The unrivalled level of personal support offered by The Game Creators and their very active community is amazing.  AGK2 is still undergoing development and has frequent updates and the developers listen to the community new feature requests.  The best just gets better.
Overall -  10/10  want to program that device in your pocket, or the one you are reading this on ?  Then
and unleash the power of your devices and perhaps even make some money.

I've been coding for many years one way or another from my early Amiga days, and AGK is one of the best cross platform development languages going. The basic language is easy to pick and up run with, while the C integration allows more advanced users almost unlimited freedom to develop and distribute across multiple platforms with a single build. Basic idea's can be prototyped in an afternoon by an experienced coder, while the base engine is more than fast enough to handle complex and advanced games with a bit more time spent on it, even across mobile platforms. It's not up their with Unreal or Unity, but it's far easier to use and has a great user community. Recommended to anyone looking for an intorduction to game development, easy and accessable cross platform development or serious applications development.

I am an hobbyst developer. In one year I have published 8 apps on Google Play, using the built-in powerful BASIC. Each app features from 500 to 8000 lines of code. The apps span from educational software to arcade, puzzle and action games. The compiler is really fast (few seconds to compile the biggest project). The number of commands is the largest I have ever seen, including 2D/3D graphics, Box2D physics, sensors, input including touch, keys, gestures, controllers, and so on. IDE is based on Geany, and is really powerful, with command completion features. Testing is easier than having a coffee in the morning: you broadcast by WiFi the app to your preferred device (Android, iOS, PC, BlackBerry, Mac etc) and instantly you have your app live and running. Last but not least, the local export to APK on PC or IPA on MAC is really useful. For sure, if you love to create apps, especially games and educational rapidly, easily, with tons of features, a growing community of developers and supporters that will help you...well AGK is to be seriously considered...and it is the cheapest tool too. And if you are an advanced C++ programmer, AGK comes with equivalent C++ API that will allow you to exploit the best of AGK in addition to  be able to use native OS or 3rd party libraries.

For cheap, easy, multi-platform game making from a company with the BEST and most helpful community I've ever come across on the internet you will not be disappointed.

Hello! This is my first review, so sorry for how bad it is.
Just before we start, I bought this game for £6.99 on
, wouldn't do it for an indie game but Activision are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, so I why not and bought it. I highly recommend you do the same.
I am a fan of the COD series, and unlike most, I quite like the jump-around-your-head type stuff. People never gave this game a chance in the first place, hence all the negative reviews. I am just going to get the only really bad thing (in my opinion) out of the way, and that is the supply drop system. I don't care if you say you can grind the game, if you buy supply drops, you are at a considerable advantage. You can earn them, but the rates for earning keys and salvage are stupid. Luckily, if you do spend a lot of money on supply drops, if you don't get the thing you want, you can just buy it using salvage gained from the supply drops. Also, there are weapon variants that are not available through supply drops, so get grinding!
Now the good bits. I know there are bots in the online service floating around, but the Matchmaking service is genuinely brilliant. Considering that there are only 1500 people in the game, 10 seconds as the longest time to get into a match is amazing. The feeling when you get a kill is amazing and very satisfying. The campaign is one of the best campaigns in a COD game, ever. I genuinely like the campaign as much as the one from Modern Warfare, and no other COD game has ever come that close in my opinion. The air combat is brilliant and frenetic, especially on high difficulty. The zero-gravity combat is really good as well. There are a few scenes where characters die, and I genuinely felt sad when it happened.
Moving on to Zombies. It is good. The feeling of killing a fairly difficult boss is very satisfying, and there is no BO3-like usable items that give you an insane edge. I've never felt like I needed a Fate & Fortune card. I have not played them, but I have been told that the other zombies maps aren't great (DLC4 Excluded, it hasn't come out yet). Look further into it if buying Season Pass/Map Packs for Zombies.
Overall, I genuinely feel like this is a great game. Shame about the Supply Drops though.

I was expecting multiplayer games to be comprised of both players' characters. Instead, one player joins and controls one or more of the host's characters from the host's game save. It works, if you play regularly with the same person and only play together. But it's not conducive to standard ad-hoc multiplayer gaming.
I play only with my girlfriend, and we only play the game together. If you're looking for something like that, this game can be a lot of fun. However, turn-based combat with character development and emphasis on tactics can cause frustration if you're playing with an inexperienced gamer.
Aside from the problems, the game is quite fun. If you're playing alone, or dedicated with one other person, I recommend it. If you're looking for something like Diablo 2/3, PoE, Torchlight 2 multiplayer, this is not it.

I wasn't sure I was going to like this game, but I took a chance on it because it was quite cheap during a sale, and I am so glad I did. No other game I have ever played has moved me like this one, and that prompted me to write a review, which I rarely do. Because the only reason to play the game is for the story, it wouldn't be right to talk about it here in great detail; however, be assured that the story is well worth the cost of admission, even at the base price of $10.
The game itself involves you and your partner fufilling a dying man's wish to go "to the moon," and this is accomplished by using a machine that allows the duo to examine the man's memories, beginning with the most recent and progressing through earlier memories from there after finding things within the memory that hold significance to other memories, which creates a link between them. The gameplay is top-down and relatively simple, but that's okay because gameplay obviously isn't the star of the show in this case—story is.
The soundtrack itself is also incredible and covers a wide range of emotions, and it is used to great effect within the game; it really sets the mood in each scene.
is where the developer sells the soundtrack, and you can also listen to it there for free if you don't want to buy it. I would give some of the tracks a listen even if you don't intend to buy the game (although you should, definitely). Half of the profits of the soundtrack sales (and I believe the game sales as well, but I'm not sure) go to charities for autism, so it supports a good cause if you choose to purchase anything.
The game is lacking in terms of options. Most notably, the resolution cannot be changed, which I found annoying upon first starting the game, but I quickly got over it as I settled into the story. I think I read at one point that this was a limitation of the engine and not as much a failure to add the option. The graphics are simple, but effective, and there's a surprising amount of feeling conveyed through the small expressions on the characters' faces and their actions. It controls about as well as you'd expect it to for a game of this sort. I never encountered any bugs on my playthrough.
The engaging story and excellent music are the strengths of this game, and honestly, that's all it needs to succeed at what it's trying to do. I would give this a 9/10. It's truly just an exceptional game; I want to call it a near-masterpiece, but that could possibly be taking it too far. It has a nice style, but I do have some slight gripes with the inability to edit resolution. The dialouge and story isn't overly philosophical and pretentious, and I'm quite okay with that; I think the story benefits from its use of colloquial language—it kind of makes it feel more real, and not like it's someone trying to preach anything or shove a message in your face. It's a great game, just buy it already!

I have played Ori with keyboard and mouse on PC five times in total: just for fun (1), to discover all secrets (2), without skill points (3), under three hours (4) and deathless (5) - it's the best 2D platformer in a very long time. The following is an overview of what points I like and don't like about Ori and the Blind Forest:
[++] = very good, [+] = good, [°] = neutral, [-] = bad:
[++] soundtrack. Atmospheric, emotional sounds of instrumental orchestra are a real pleasure to listen to. I even died intentionally before the end of the Ginso Tree just to listen to the music a bit more, and the interpretation of the Sorrow Pass nearly made me cry, that's how good the soundtrack is. Probably one of the best soundtracks ever in a videogame.
[+] graphics. Very detailed, colorful, varying landscapes reveal the game's great aesthetics, and the character models are beautiful as well. The performance is really smooth, too; I had no problems running the game on maximum settings on an ATI Radeon HD 5870 1GB on HD resolution (1680x1050 @ 60fps).
[+] level design. Great level design rewards you for being an explorer to discover all the life cells, energy cells, skill points, experience points, map fragments and map stones scattered all across the giant map. These secrets will most likely require backtracking, but I never had a problem with that since I always discovered new locations and secrets on the way. Everything about the map is coherent and makes sense. You might for instance wonder why some enemies respawn occasionally, until you find out that there is an ability which you can use to take advantage of enemies and their projectiles to reach areas you might never thought you could reach. It feels really fulfilling to discover these areas and achieve 100% completion.
[+] skill system. This game comes with some RPG elements, you can use your skill points to unlock skills for Ori on three different skill trees. To unlock the better abilities on a particular skill tree, you at least need to have unlocked all the previous abilities, so your choice really matters and affects your gameplay experience. Do you want to fire multiple shots at once, to collect experience points more easily or to resave in locations where you have already saved? Do you prefer the ability to hit four targets at once or a triple jump and better defense? (I would recommend the rightmost tree with the triple jump and better defense, these abilities are the best in my opinion, but again - it's all up to you.) In addition to the skill tree, you earn 8 abilities through so-called ancestral trees, which will not only help you tremendously throughout your adventure, but also make the combat more diversified, because you won't have to rely solely on your standard attack to kill enemies - you can stomp on them, reflect their projectiles, bash them into dangerous obstacles which will kill them instantly and so on. My favourite ability has to be the bash ability, because it can be used in a very versatile way and rewards your skill more than any other ability.
[+] story. To be honest, I didn't pay that much attention to it on my first playthrough, because I was too busy listening to that awesome soundtrack, but later I realized how emotional and stirring, but also how coherent and logical it was within the game's context. You can skip the five "movie cutscenes" (but not everything, see below). I won't spoil anything for you, so I'll just move on to the next point.
[+] price. You get more content from Ori for 20€ than you get from some so-called AAA-titles for 60€ and more. The only problem is the lack of multiplayer (but on the other hand, what should a multiplayer in a 2D-platformer look like?), you only have some meaningless leaderbords with people who completed the game the fastest.
[°] difficulty. Don't be fooled by the cute graphics into thinking that this is the easiest game ever, it's actually really difficult in comparison to all the other 2D-platformers currently on the market. There will be some tricky passages that you will almost certainly die on your first attempt, and the enemies can be a real pain in the beginning of the game when you don't have the bash skill. I would love to tell you how often I died on my first playthrough, but I can't (see below). Regardless, I think I died about a hundred times. The last area seems to have enraged some bigger reviewers out there, and sure it is challenging, but it's also fair since it really tests how well you can handle the abilities given to you. People who claim otherwise either want an easy final level or have no skill. Do you like challenging games? If not, this might not be the game for you. In my case, I liked the challenge in this game, so I classified this point as neutral.
[-] no post-credits play. You can't explore the world after you beat the game, you can't even select your save file to see how often you died in total. You should also make sure to collect everything you can before Mount Horu, because you won't be able to return. However, the creature next to Ori tells you just that before entering Mount Horu, so that's not such a big issue for me.
[-] save game system. To save, you have to use one (with upgrades: half of a) skill point. When you need four skill points to open a gate and you have just mastered a difficult passage, you better not save, because otherwise you'll not be able to open that gate, you will have to backtrack just to refill that one missing skill point, which almost frustrated me on some occasions. On top of that, you can't save when you're near an enemy or on fragile grounds, but that makes sense in my opinion, because when you reload your save file, you want to be safe in that spot and not be killed by some enemy before you can even react. Besides that, I recommend to save a lot on the first playthrough, since there can always be some instant death trap a few centimeters away from you or a different unfortunate hazard like spikes which you can't get out of, so you'll die as a result (prime example has to be the enormous spider's web, which falls on the spikes below. I jumped down and was dead because of spikes I couldn't see in the first place, which was really frustrating). And remember, when you die, you'll have to do everything again from your last save: if you collected some secret cells or went to numerous locations you wanted to explore and then died because of an inconveniently placed hazard, good luck recalling all the places you've been to.
[-] instant death. Without a doubt, there are too many instant death traps for my taste. I often thought that I have so much life left that it's not necessary for me to save, and a few moments later I was dead because of some laser beam or spikes one could not get out of, so that I got hit over and over again until I died. By the way, some spikes really are instant death traps, while others are not - that's inconsistent and confusing at times.
[-] unskippable scripted sequences. You can skip five "movie cutscenes", but you'll have to watch the smaller cutscenes with text overlay, whether you want it or not. Yes, the story is really good, but on my fourth and fifth playthrough I already know the story, so I don't think it's necessary to forcibly show me them again.
[-] rebinding keys. Though you can play with a controller on PC or play with keyboard and mouse (or keyboard exclusively, which I've never tried out), I have not found the option to rebind keys, which is just laughable, sorry. I prefer the arrow keys over wasd-controls, but I couldn't change the controls, so I had to get accustomed to the predefined control set. Luckily, I could get used to the controls easily, but considering the game's difficulty, I can understand that people who can't get used to them might get frustrated, especially when the assignment of keys becomes the reason for not being able to complete a passage (instead of the lack of skill).
[-] minor glitches/bugs

The developers know what they're doing and listen to the players in their forums.
In game, you start by choosing your player name and nation, then you are brought to the Capital of your faction in the port screen (User Interface is a bit clunky right now, but they are obviously planning to improve it) where you can see your ship, buy equipment, trade, craft items, upgrade your ship and accept missions or simply jump in a random battle room and fight.
But if you press Sail you get to the open world, which is really huge, ranging from the northern coast of South America to Florida with the Caribbean Islands in between, of course, and the gulf of mexico, with lots of settlements and places to explore, fight or trade.

Sailing and fighting might seem hard at the beginning. but you will quickly get used to the various keys and maneuvers.

So, get the game, find some friends or invite yours and build up a fleet to join the great community already present in Naval Action.

I loved the sailing in AC4; it's the main reason I picked this game up because it took that aspect that I loved and built upon it. You spawn in your little dinghy at a port full of a bunch of other people in their little dinghies and one guy with a giant♥♥♥♥♥frigate showing off. This game doesn't have much curb appeal. You step in and it's clearly unpolished (as expected). The UI is bad and confusing, boarding ships is this minigame that people have described as "rock paper scissors" but really if you just always go offense you can't seem to lose, there are no tutorials or help in-game, and many items/descriptions are ambiguous like "Marines" give me "cannon_reload_time = 10%." What does that mean? Is my reload time going up or down? Or is it 10% of the original value? I also didn't figure out different wood types affect ship speed/health until about 15 hours in. That would be important. Also I didn't know that your rank affected how many crew you can have, not which ship you can buy. Would've been nice before buying a 200 crew ship so early on. I have encountered a few bugs, namely capturing ships and then not receiving them in the loot screen.
Still, despite all these flaws, it is a damn fun game. Now that I've figured out how most of the mechanics work, there is a lot of depth to the overworld content as well as combat. The roar of cannons in the big 20+ ship battles is music to my ears, not to mention the game looking really good for an EA title. Also, the lag seems to be non-existant. I play on the EU PvP server since it's the most populated and don't notice any lag at 150ms nor have I seen anyone rubber-banding and such. Finally, the devs appear to be very responsive. They're active on Twitter answering questions and posting about updates as well as being very reactive to player feedback before the Steam launch went live.
All in all I give it a 8/10. The core mechanics are good fun and there's definitely enough content to keep you occupied. The devs have a solid base that's rough around the edges; once you get past the initial "wtf is this" from the UI and confusion, the game is really fun. Am I sure this game will move in the right direction? No. But from what I've seen the devs have a good head on their shoulders. Still, it's an EA title so take that with a grain of salt.

You need to learn where your cannons are placed on your ship, how your sails are setup, and what that means with regards to elevation and firing angles (ie. are the waves too high, or are the sails too full and canting the ship too much).
This is an early access game, but it has been fleshed out quite well since the open world was first introduced to early backers. The devs listen and interact with the community as well, so use the official forums to give suggestions and use the bug report feature to help make the game even better.
Despite it still being Early access, I love this game.

‘Bad Rats: The Rat’s Revenge’ is a 2009 title released by “Invent 4 Entertainmento”. It features a ball, a cat, and 9 different rats: Batter Rat, who is a rat with a baseball cap and bat designed to, well, bat the ball. Tractor Rat, who is a rat inside a tractor wearing a hard hat who pushes the ball slowly. Bomber Rat, who has a long beard, a turban, and a suicide vest, who blows up upon touching the ball and sends it directly upward. Archer Rat, who is dressed like Robin Hood and has a bow and toothpick arrow, who shoots the ball directly forward with mediocre aim. Fat Rat, who’s never seen without a piece of cheese and has a main goal of being the weight in a lever system. Rocket Rat, who’s tied to a rocket with a soldier helmet, and, when his adjustable timer runs out, will shoot directly upward until redirected and he explodes. Runner Rat, who is a normal rat in a hamster wheel who can launch the ball directly forward. Vacuum Rat, who has a vacuum pack on his back and a vacuum in his hand and can pull the ball directly upward. Lastly, there’s Cannon Rat, who has a similar timer to Rocket rat but goes directly forward instead of upward. The game also sometimes features a dog character.
The idea of the game is to place these rats (along with some planks and barrels) in various areas to complete each level by killing the cat. Many ways to do this include slicing it with a knife, burning it, microwaving it, shooting it, crushing it, and more. The previously mentioned dog character will sometimes eat it.
Bad Rats costs 99 cents on steam and is known as “one of the worst games ever made” by many game reviewers. It is, in fact, commonly gifted to friends as a joke due to its cheapness and badness. The prankster will often convince his victim that it’s the best game ever made, and try to get them to play it while they can talk, so the prankster can listen to their victim’s utter dismay when they find the game’s true nature.
Some things that contribute to this game’s awfulness include Its concept. The idea is that these rats would like to get revenge on the cat by killing it, although we never see what the cat actually does. Also, the idea that a dog will eat a cat is absurd. Other than this, the animation is godawful, making a 2009 game look worse than CGI from 2003. The look is not complimented by the fact that most of the animations are 112% broken. Not only this, some levels are completely unbeatable, and the time limit of 10 minutes for 44 levels does not help. Another thing that doesn’t help is that doing the same thing 20 times has the ability to lead to 20 different results, so often times players will reset think the correct answer was wrong. Speaking of the correct answer, not only will the game’s suggested solution not work half the time, but sometimes the game will display the completed puzzle without the player asking for it. Most infuriatingly, the game will sometimes switch from 2d with 3d modeling to 3d to with 3d modeling, making it so the ball will just roll off the screen without prompting. The game doesn’t even go past 1240p. All these factors are what earn the game it’s awful status.

I have played this game for about 4 months now and I have to say I am enjoying it very much. What I like the most about it is that you can make a "party" and play with your friends. This option gave many many in-game hours of fun to my husband and me and obviously finishing quests is a lot easier if you're not going alone. There's plenty of different classes to choose from and after level 20 you get even more options because every class splits into some sort of sub-class (normally there is 4 or 5 of them). The game allows you to have 12 characters at the same time so you can switch between them any time you want if you get bored. I like the variety of skills that characters have, each one unique and (for me at least) interesting to watch :-)
If I had to say something negative about it, it would be very small inventory space but somehow between your personal inventory, warehouse and guild warehouse (if you are a member of one), you manage. Sometimes it takes a couple of tries to actually log into game but I'm more than willing to overlook that considering it doesn't take long to log back in and you get hours and hours of fun once you're in.
Even though I played for months I have very little hours on record purely because I was too lazy to look into it and see why is steam not recording. A couple of days ago I looked around a little bit and found out that if you run steam as an administrator on initial launch it will record hours and show you as "in-game" . Steam did not record hours because the game has it's own launcher and apparently this is also the case with other games that have their own launcher.
Game is free to play although there are in-game items you can buy through "cash shop" with Wcoins (you top up on your webzen account) but in my experience it is not essential for winning to buy anything, therefore I would have to say it is not pay to win, but that's just my opinion. If you are willing to spend some cash, you can get adorable pets that follow you around and have their own abilities or boost your own. You buy "mysterious egg" so you can't actually choose your pet, drops are completely random.
I like everything about this game, from characters and their attractive attire to crafting and many other perks and options. I would recommend this game to anyone.

I got this mostly for my kid.. but that is not saying it can't be used professionally. It most certainly can, and is. It is powerful, and can create pretty much anything you can imagine. It is fast, and because it offers byte code (via the build in BASIC language) its iteration time is stunningly short. A little background for context: I have been coding for 30 years in a wide variety of languages and using AGK, and more recently AGK2, for a couple of years now.
So let's clear something up straight away, despite the name AGK isn't just for creating mobile style apps, it can create anything you want on a multitude of platforms.  Your imagination is the only real limit.
If you're a beginner or just prefer it then you can code in good old BASIC, or like me you might prefer to use C++ and the added flexibility that brings.  Whichever you choose the comprehensive list of commands and features within AGK2 are identical (all explained well in the supporting help files).
In today's constantly changing market no language can afford to stand still and the developers at The Game Creators have realised that too.  They are always listening, with feature requests, updates and bug fixes dealt with promptly and the AGK user community are always consulted on any major decisions.  It's a language whose future we can all help shape.
The one area I was initially skeptical of was the claim that you could "code once and deploy easily to multiple mobile & desktop platforms".  Surely some platform specific changes would be required?  Well no, once you have your development environment setup it really does do what it claims.  PC, Mac, iOS, Android, OUYA etc. it works.  Want to develop for the iPhone but don't want to deal with Object-C?  No problem, with user-friendly AGK2 you'll never see a line of Obj-C code.
AGK2 is already a great language to work with, The Game Creators plans for the future are exciting (advanced 3D, extra platform support etc.) and the current price really is unbelievable.
If you're a developer, whether an absolute beginner or experienced, I recommend you look at AGK2.

I've really enjoyed using App Game kit and have created a number of published products using it.  It may seem a little daunting at first but once you read through the examples and experiment with a few lines of code it all makes sense.  You can learn the areas that you want to focus on to start with and it’s a quick way of realising your ideas on a number of platforms.  I have struggled with other languages and have found the learning curve incredibly high and I guess AGK brought me back to my childhood in many ways to when I was 9 coding on a Sinclair spectrum.  I say this because you can get visual results quickly and easily which is very rewarding.  AGK is also a great way for kids to start programming and it’ll encourage them to learn new techniques and explore their ideas further.  Why shouldn’t you make the games you always dreamed of playing?   So, if you want to make games at an affordable cost and publish them easily on a number of app stores / platforms then I recommend AGK.

I have not played COD since MW3 and after 2 hours of playing IW in story mode I can say that im very happy with it.
The graphics are amazing, the sounds are realistic, the voice acting and lip sync is on point. The gameplay is the usual COD gameplay and since it's in space, the weapons are high tech and there's thrusters on your suit so you can hover, wall ride and double jump, these mechanics gave the game a higher and more dynamic feel.
I don't get why people hate this COD so much, I understand that for someone who bought COD every year it might have felt like more of the same but is it a bad, broken and unplayable game that deserves such low reviews? There are far worse games that do not deserve positive ratings such as those JRPG's that look all the same, made in RPGMaker just for a quick cash in from the Otakus that drool over drawn females or the games that exist just so people can farm cards and make money out of the Steam market.
I look at COD IW as a Sci-Fi Casual Action Shooter and it does an amazing job at that. You play as a Lt. in the military from Earth which is at war with the army from Mars (now colonized). It's rebel leader wants to conquer the rest of the solar system because Mars had been neglected and only served to gather materials to bring back to Earth (this reminds me a lot of when the African colonies start to revolt against the empires that owned them).
I'm having tons of fun playing IW. I did not buy it for it's online gameplay so I can't say anything about that but if you're looking for a casual shooter that has a good sci-fi feel and a good story then this is your go-to.
Just dont buy it on steam for it's full price since you can get it for $15 or lower in other resellers.

This game does exactly what it means to; and that is, fulfills the desire of everyone with an interest in the age of sail to captain their own ship and venture the high seas of the Caribbean and Atlantic coast. Despite being early access, it's relatively content complete insofar as the open world is available. People have called the game "EVE:Online at sea", take of that what you will.
Combat is instanced and content complete. If you've ever played the naval battles in Empire: Total War it's pretty similar to that. Although there's an auto Skipper, it pays to learn how to manage your sails as the wind is fully simulated. This game probably has the most realistically simulated water I've seen in a game too, as waves can rock a ship and knock your cannons' line of fire. You can switch your cannonballs out for chain shot to demast your enemy's sails and follow that up with grapeshot to knock out their crew enough for a successful boarding. You can even ram them if you're feeling particularly cavalier, I once got lucky and capsized someone's ship but I doubt that happens as much with the bigger hulls.
I look foward to seeing what else the developers have in store for this game, so far they've promised a better economy and enhanced inter-factional diplomacy. For now I'd have to say it's one of the few impulse buys I actually didn't end up regretting.

Amazing game, large PvP battles are epic!!
Countries fight for domination, captains for fame - it is simply just THE game.
EDIT:
You begin the game with as a low rank captain with a low amount of crew in a ship called "Cutter", which is a 12 gun ship (40 crew).
When I started playing, it was a looooong way to the top rank, grinding alot of XP towards getting more crew and thereby a larger ship. Max crew under ones command is 1050, which is needed to fully crew the largest ships in the game.
The 1st rate battles are EPIC but already as a captain with 200 crew, you will be able to sail frigate class ships with 40 guns, like the famous Suprise. The 200 crew rank is a milestone as a player in this game, because it really kicks off here! This is where you have to learn to manually control sails and PvP will be much more fun. 5 guys in frigates can do some serious damage and take out the largest ship if done right.
Its possible to craft your own ships, but this takes some time. When you buy the game and create an avatar, you are given "labor hours" (LH) - 42 LH pr. real time hour. These hours can be used to craft materials and in the end combine these and craft a ship. To create materials, resources are ofcourse needed.
Ress are produced and consumed in all ports around the map, which means you must sail in trader ships and buy where its cheap(being produced) and earn money by selling in ports that consume a certain resource, if you are meaning to earn cashe - ofcourse pirates or enemies of ones nation are lurking on the seas, around the cays and isles - so dont sail with high value without an escort. Many players like myself are hunting for lone traders, this may take hours but the loot can be worth it.
The game is really exciting that way. In this game, you are an asset to your nation, every gun is needed in the large coordination of fleets and clans within a nation. Every nation has been on the verge of destruction, which require all hands on deck and collaboration!
- Part of the community is really toxic, put these guys in the ignore list ASAP.
- Often its hard for new players to survive - find a good clan in your nation, but be careful. Toxic players tend to team up as well, be sure to join the good guys ^^
- It takes time to master a ship in battle, gaining the wind, keeping the upper hand and wrecking your opponent. All ships have different stats, speed, turning, speed compared to degrees in the wind etc etc. Thats why it can take some time to learn the small things but the depth is also amazing.
The game is still under development and within the next few days a new patch will be implemented. This will reset the map and RoE will be changed completely - I look forward to this.

A diamond in the rough, not as polished as it may seem. Greatly optimised, more than the first Warhammer. With the arrival of Mortal Empires, it is quite rich in pronouncedly distinct races and factions, yet still expensive (counting the base game, all DLC packs, and the expansion-like sequel). Moddability adds a whole new dimension to the game; mods are the only reason why the game series is worth buying. Yet...
... its cons and issues, still:
- no tax gauging
- no region gifting
- no puppet states, no liberation (only the Chaos hordes have it, and it's half-baked, can't seem to be able to create more than one tribe? iirc)
- the trade system across different races is wacky and wobbly
- no naval battles (yeah, Warhammer is all about land battles, why not talk it over with the IP owner and change it just for this game?)
- barely any distinct factions of the same race to choose from, and most of them are eaten up and locked behind the DLC, for instance, can't play as Skaven in the Old World, my rats had to swim to get there
- balanced and imbalanced at the same time; the issue of archers across races (OP Wood Elves versus Sea Archers on sea versus Normal Archers versus Bad Archers of greenskins for example)
- reinforcement range antics continue on and they still suck; settlements can't be besieged now immediately after disembarking (even when the army had full movements points, supposedly). Other issues such as having enough movement points to besiege (the movement arrow is all yellow) but not be able to do it because of lacking that 1% or less than 1% of M-points (which translates to one turn wasted, strategically), or that broken movement gauge which says 50% does not equal 50% most likely because it is an inaccurate floating value (because you can't strike a fortified camp after using up 50% of your movements points, at least here)
- aye, you barely receive 4 races, 8 factions in Warhammer II, and probably still more than in the base, DLC-cut Warhammer I game (when you exclude all the races and factions from DLC packs, excluding free Bretonnia as well)
Having to wait for the Norsca to arrive in Mortal Empires is not an issue, having to wait for one single new lord to play a new, "different" faction is a problem. It would be better if we got a big set of Lords and their factions of the same ilk as those in the base or expanded game instead of one or two just to play another faction of the same race. Rationing the game content like this is terrible.
Recommending the game? Yes. Recommending to wait for some more free packs (such as Bretonnia) to justify the buy? Yes. Recommending to play it with mods? Yes. Recommending to buy the whole series (all DLC)? Hell no, unless you really want to, or unless CA adds more content (more factions of the same type to select from) or fixes the goddamn overpriced, downsized DLC.

Bad Rats is a revolutionary first person shooter that sets a new standard for this era of gaming. This is game published by Electronic Arts and is developed by Dice on the new Frostbite 4 engine to provide a superior graphic fidelity compared to other marvellous titles including Crisis 3. The story of the game takes place in the year 2035 when North Korea officially ends the cease fire for the Korean War and launches a series of surprise attacks on the United States of America and South Korea. North Korea launches an overwhelming amount of long range ballistic missiles towards major metropolitan areas in the United States which devastates the population and cripples the infrastructure of the government to be able to function properly to contain control of the United States. North Korea launches a full scale aerial campaign on Seoul with a relentless wave of troops pouring across the DMZ of North Korea and South Korea. China and the rebuilt Soviet Union organized by Vladimir Putin has been supplying North Korea with highly advanced military technology and expertise has secretly been supporting North Korea for a war since 2006! You play as a squad in the Navy Seals for the United States called “Bad Rats” Your objective is to assassinate all cats in the region of Asia to cut off all food supplies from the North Koreans and collapse the regime of Kim Jong Un. Using the destructible environments from the Frostbite 4 engine you must use the environment for a tactical advantage to exterminate all cats from Asia. Fan favourite maps return including Seige of Shainghai where you must collapse a skyscraper to kill all cats in the building. Facial scanning technology from LA Noire returns to add an extra layer of realism with realistic facial animation movements to add more emotion to the already immersive world. This is a highly addicting shooter that takes place in locations across the world from nuclear wasteland America to the glorious lands of North Korea. You have a massive arsenal of over 500 weapons to use with thousands of gadgets and gun camouflages. Bad Rats is integrated with the Steam Workshop which has created thousands of community maps and gun skins to be submitted into the game for future free DLCs called “Operations”. Each operation adds an extra layer of immersion into the game with a huge variety of community maps and skins to be added to expand the already masterpiece of a game. Bad rats is a very skill based shooter and requires extensive training to truly shine in multiplier. Bad Rats is the only first person shooter on the market to add a innovative competitive mode with ranks to determine your skill level. In multiplayer there are 2 teams. Counter Cats and Cats. The counter cats must plant a bomb on one of the two locations on the map to kill the population of cats in the area. The cats must prevent the counter cats or the “bad rats” from planting the bomb by either killing all the Counter Cats or defusing the bomb to save the population of cats in the premise.Bad Rats is a highly addicting shooter that any seasonal gamer should try out but I assume you already have! Bad Rats global sales have exceeded 1 billion on the first day outselling the Call of Duty franchise. It is very rare to see game a game this flawless since the release of Half Life 2. If you like first person shooter games you already own bad rats, if you don't you are missing out on one of the most brilliant game of this century.
Final verdict
Pros
Immersive environments
Balanced multiplayer
Overwhelming amount of content
Gorgeous Graphics
Revolutionizes the FPS genre
Fantastic and inspiring story
Great voice acting
Like Half Life 3 but better
Cons
Too much graphics
10/10

Don't judge a book by its cover.
Imagine opening a tabloid newspaper for a quick read about the Kardashians and finding inside scientific journals.
From the outside this excellent RPG looks like Diablo had a threesome with Disney and Torchlight.
Inside this is a complex, funny and innovative game. There is no RPG like it.
Fire + Poison = Explosions.
100% fire resistance + immunity to burning = walking on lava.
105% fire resistance = healed by fire.
You can talk to the animals!
At the beginning of the game my mage was using Air magic in combat and shocking themselves into missing a few turns in combat. Lol - I am so lame. Don't stand in a puddle of water retard.
I used a rain spell to douse a burning ship and got involved in a love human/ orc thing going on.
I investigated a murder that took me to the end of time and came across and elderly deranged elf looking for justice for his murdered family. (Very creepy voice - lovely acting).
It's all not fun and games. There is a dark side too where you come across great evil and undead. Of blood and sacrifice and the end of the world.
Combat is turn based and quite a joy. The combination of elements and battlefield layout allow almost infinite possibilities in battle.
Use telekinesis to bash enemies on the head with water barrels. Use your bow or sword. Conjure zombies and fire elementals. Throw grenades. Quaff a healing potion. The world is quite open and you will often come across battles you can't win. Either innovate or come back later.
Do it your way and have bags of fun. Recruit some companions or play through with your original two. Play through a rock, paper, scissors mini game to convince NPCs to accept your views. "These are not the droids you are looking for."
Inventory and Crafting. Literally millions of things to pick up which can be crafted into millions of combinations. You uncover recipes as you read books but you can experiment too. Slipping on ice too often? Bang some nine inch nails to the bottom of your boots.
The developers have also brought a Legend of Grimrock 2 type puzzle element to the game. It's strange. Requires brain function. What? In this game. Really? I can separate my party? In fact one puzzle requires you to kill a party member and teleport to their dead body 'on the other side'. Scary. Amazing.
I really struggled to get into the final location in the game until I retrained my brain and used these teleport pyramids given to you early on. When I solved the puzzles it was like I passed my school exams again. I did me proud.
Negatives needed right?
Crafting - overwhelming at first. Confidence gained in second play through.
Mission items - they are not tagged. You can't sell them. You can't find them in your inventory. Where is that stupid, STUPID reveal scroll? Have I broke the game?
Missions - you really can go round and round and round trying to progress. There is only a little hand holding.
Summary
I really, REALLY love this game. It's beautiful. Innovative. It looks like Disney but inside there is iron and steel. It will chew you up and spit you out. It will test your RPG credentials unlike Wasteland 2 or Pillars of the Eternity did.
If you are looking for a proper RPG, with C&C and complexity - take it on.

The game is amazing. Story is interesting so far, the tactical combat is even better than back in BG2, there's lots of humor in the game and the co-op feature is really well designed, allowing me to share the experience with my GF as one of our favorite co-op experiences of all time.
When I still can't recommend this amazing game, it's because the co-op has some of the most critical bugs I've ever seen, even 6+ months after the release of the enhanced edition:
The "minor" nuisances is that hp bars and initiative order in combat is consistently wrong on the client. We've gotten used to both looking on the host's monitor to see what the real health values are, and when each character acts in combat, but I imagine this will be quite the deal-breaker if you're not sitting next to your partner.
The true critical issue for us has been that the co-op saves break, making it impossible to continue. We're not talking the occasional game crashes (which are reasonably rare) but that we reach a state where the client will consistently freeze up upon joining the game. We were initially able to suppress the issue a bit with help from Larian support and then bypass it for a while by switching the save to the other computer - yet the bug has returned every time. We are now 35 hours into the game and unable to continue. Larian support was initially quick and helpful, but it's now been 2 weeks since we sent them crash reports and we still cannot continue the game.
We've been loving the game, and I'd change my review to recommended in a heartbeat if it wasn't broken for us to the point of not being playable at all.

This is the second review I have written for Naval Action. The first one was written shortly after the game was released on Steam when I purchased it in January 2016. The review was brief, and recommended the game. Ultimately, I don't think it was particularly helpful as it was vague, but indicated the promise of the game.
However, after 18 months and about a thousand hours of playing, I need to amend the review accordingly and most importantly change from "recommend" to "don't recommend". I will try to be clear and helpful in why I have done so.
First, I should point out that the world within Naval Action is beautfifully rendered. The graphics of the open world, ships, ocean, sky, and every other facet are incredible. The sound is rich, vivid, and during battle scenes perfectly accurate and enthralling. In a battle, smoke from powder obscures your vision and wafts with the wind creating a truly realistic picture of what naval combat was in the age of sail. Naval Action is, simply put, a gorgeous game. The developers should be incredibly proud of the visual masterpiece they have created.
The UI when a ship is in port is extremely plain and utilitarian, with no hints or tooltips on what to do, or what things are for. This is problematic to new players, though at this point there are many tutorials online on Youtube or individual's channels and there is ample help from the community in the forum and in game. The developers seem to believe that the lack of an appealing UI is costing them players but I do not think this is the case. Yes, it's dull, but the people who play the game and get sucked into it (like I originally did) will learn how to use it and make due. After all, a captain's desk isn't particularly exciting but it's where the nitty and gritty details of running a ship get done.
Where the game has failed in its promise and expectations is in several other areas.
Naval Action has, over the last 18 months or so, gone through several major patches. Each one has changed a major aspect of gameplay. Some of them, especially the early ones, were very much for the better. More detailed crew control, the necessity to replace crew after battles, and a more vibrant crafting system have all been good steps forward. More recently, however, and primarily it would seem due to either a vocal minority of "hard core" players or the developers own tastes, many changes have marginalized or severely curtailed the ability of all but full time players to be successful.
It has now likewise become impossible for a solo player, or even a small clan, to thrive. Below are some examples:
1) In earlier versions of the game, a player could purchase additional "outposts" which allowed you to have a base at various locations on the ingame map of the Caribbean. You would still have to sail to a new place on your own first, which in the open world would take several hours to sail from one edge of the map to the other, but once you set up an outpost there, you could freely "teleport" from one outpost to another (a player was limited to a maximum number of outposts, and even before reaching that point, the cost of additional outposts became progressively more expensive). You could have an outpost in a port owned by your nation, which would allow you to construct various buildings: plantations, mines, and so forth to produce raw materials for crafting which you could either use or sell elsewhere for profit. Or, you could set up an outpost in a "Free Town" which was not owned by any nation, thereby allowing entry to all, but which could not be used for producing resources. The benefit was that 1) it could not be captured by an enemy and thus deprive you of your outpost and 2) they were usually near hotspots of activity thereby creating a good area for PVP. After one patch, you were even allowed to transfer goods (at a much steeper cost than sailing yourself, but without the danger of piracy or the time it took to do so) from one free town to another.
Now, most of those features are gone. You cannot teleport to a free town, and you cannot ship goods. The developers argue this supports "realism" and while they are correct it is more important to recognize that if it takes you three hours to sail a shipment of gold from Mexico to Jamaica and you are attacked and captured before you get there then you are not likely to keep many players. If it was a 20 minute trip, that's one thing, but then of course you lose the majesty of exploring the massive world. It was better the way it was where it was possible to ship things, but with some limitations and cost increases accordingly.
Most seriously, the ability to teleport from a free town has been removed meaning if you want to fight in a specific area you have to spend 30 to 60 minutes sailing there from your nearest outpost, hope you find someone to fight, and then another 30 to 60 minutes sailing back. Realistic? Sure. But it's also a lot like having a part time job.
2) Prior to patch 10.0, players could generate a reasonable income doing the PVE missions, regardless of if they were on a PVE or PVP server. In a combat mission given by the ingame Admiralty, you sail to a designated location and enter a battle instance based upon the difficulty level you select. Inside, you fight a certain number of ships. For an individual combat order, it is usually 1 or 2 (1 would be comparable to your ship, 2 would be smaller ships but still a challenge since you are outnumbered). If you complete the mission, you receive money and "combat marks" for sinking the ship and completing the mission. If you fail to sink a ship, you get nothing - even if you inflict massive damage. Previously, you received rewards for damaging ships, which was especially good if you fought a fight against a superior force and managed to inflict damage but were ultimately sunk without sinking an enemy. This is now gone since 10.0. There were also fleet combat missions which were very fun, where you would be part of a large fleet with AI help against other AI. Now, the AI fleet on your side is gone so it is not possible to have a large fight if you don't have anyone to sail with you.
3) Despite being an early access game catering to a niche market where there is a small number of active players, the developers insist on maintaining several servers. They are supported in this by a tiny group who either complain about server lag (I have played from a mobile hotspot in the middle of the Pacific and can do so without issue) or complain because certain events or port battles (RVR activity) would happen during the night in Europe. Since Games Labs is a Ukrainian company, they have sided with those people and refused to merge severs into one global server for maximum player activity and maximum player feedback for an early access game.
4) In every instance where the player base as a whole or as individuals have questioned or suggested alternatives, the attitude from the developers (represented by Admin on the Naval Action forum) is often hostile. It's tough to be criticized, but if you are going into the public eye in this way you have to be thicker skinned and take the high road. This is something that the developers of the game seem unable to do. If they are attacked in any way, they will retaliate and ban or block players in the game or the forums.
5) Every major patch reinvents the wheel. Rather than stick with a system - combat, crafting, diplomacy, hostility generation, etc and tweak it over time, every few months the whole system is thrown out in favor of something new. Yes, it's early access, but it is getting ridiculous.
This is the only game of its type out there, and even in its flawed form is still enjoyable, but it is stressful due to nonsensical game mechanics and requires a SIGNIFICANT investment of time. If you do not have 4 hours a day to devote to the game, you will not be able to advance very far in it.

This game brought massive improvements to the first one. 85% of the complaints I had with the first one have been fixed.
Sieges. My biggest problem with Total War: Warhammer (TWW) was the terrible sieges. Sieges have seen minor improvements in Total War: Warhammer II (TWW2). The problem with TWW was that the sieges were far too basic. There was 1-3 main streets that were 50ft wide and other "minor" streets that were about 30ft wide in cities. There was only 1-3 walls. In previous Total Wars we saw 360 degrees seiges. TWW2 has put minor improvements on sieges. We now have thinner, minor streets and more of them. We also have larger maps which helps make up for the lack of 360 degrees. As far as minor settlements go they still dont have maps which is frustrating. Thankfully mods fix this, however mods shouldn't fix the game, they should improve the game.
Battles. Battles have seen major improvements. I hated how short they were in TWW a 20v20 battle would last 15 minutes at the maximum. In TWW2 They aren't longer, however they are more intense which makes up for it. River battles have been added back in! Yay! The battle AI has also seen many improvements not just off of TWW but to TW games in general. The AI now uses forests better to their advantage. They will sometimes even wait in them for one of your units to pass by and then strike. Don't get me wrong, it's not like Total War: Rome II (TWR2) where there would be a 30 minute long search of tracking down hidden units, the AI will still reveal the main [art of their army, only leaving small groups of 1-5 units in forests.
Campaign. TWW had my favorite campaign of any Total War title. TWW2 topped it. We now have the unique events from TWW combined with rituals needed to complete the Vortex. Campaign AI is better than any previous TW title. Enemy AI will now sometimes siege your cities until they surrender.
Factions. Factions are all very unique with very different playstyles required to excell with them. For example the Skaven rely heavilly on numbers and rushing the opponet, the Lizardmen have excellent infantry and monsters but lack ranged ect. Very well balanced.
Overall a 9/10.
