Thirty Flights of Loving and its predecessor, Gravity Bone, are both wonderfully quirky adventures of espionage made by Blendo Games. I recommend them as experiences but that is all they are. They hardly qualify as games so I wouldn't pay full price for them. Gravity Bone was originally available as a free download on the Blendo Games website. While it was short, it had some minor gameplay elements. It had the use of items and some minor platforming but ,overall, the game felt like a tech demo. It felt like it was only a sample of what was to come. So when Thirty Flights of Loving was released I assumed that it would be a full length game with more items, more locations, more vague Gravity Bone spy story, and more platforming, puzzle solving, etc. But Thirty Flights of Loving has even less gameplay. You more or less walk through the story with little to no interaction. While it was a fun experience, I don't believe that it is something that should be advertised and sold as a game. It should have been released for free alongside Gravity Bone on the Blendo Games website.

This game is full of charm and always manages to put a smile on my face. It's a simple platformer game on rails. You jump, slide, kick and spring your way through each stage, broken up into levels with a boss at the end to the infectious beats provided by the games' addictive soundtrack.
Gold coins are scattered throughout each level, collecting them all gives you access to a bonus round if you make it to the end of the level. Bonus rounds are retro-stylised versions of the main game where you play for extra points to improve your high score.
Death in BIT.TRIP.RUNNER is caused by hitting any obstacle, be it a knee-high ledge you were supposed to jump over or a UFO you needed to slide under. The best feature this game posseses is that, upon death you don't face loading screens or some mocking text, you are visually dragged back to the start of the level to instantly resume in the fun, this makes death (almost) painless and doesn't break the flow of your gaming.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys video-games but perhaps not to those who detest the sort of precise gameplay that BIT.TRIP.RUNNER demands in its latter levels.

Honestly? The game would've stood a bit better if it wasn't a Call of Duty game. The Story at times seemed to make little sense (i.e. 2 characters would be at odds with each other but within 1 mission (Ignoring the side missions you can do) would be best buddies, which seems unlikely to really happen). The Gameplay seemed to feel like the enemies were either too easy to shoot, or bullet sponges for your ammo.
The story did have some interesting moments (which I won't spoil in this), but there were also moments where a "critial" plot moment felt like a movie cliche in how it was telegraphed to the player.
The Jackal missions were fun at first, but they seemed to become very repetitive with each iteration of the mission, while the Stealth aspects they tried to add in seemed to be done sub-par, being very easy to miss a melee and cause the whole room to be alerted to you.
The Multiplayer was very unbalanced, with people being able to spawn trap you (if done correctly) other players and became very stale after a few matches.
Overall, the game had some good moments but felt more of the same from Advanced Warfare, but with more elements done far worse than expected.

Even writing about this game has me taking deep breaths trying to keep calm and not flame. If I had to list the purchases I regret the most on Steam, this would probably be placed very high up on the list.
The developers clearly thought they couldn't mess up RPG and RTS, then learned the hard way that real-time strategy isn't an easy genre to develop for at all. The game is unfinished to a sometimes hilarious extent, and it ends in a cliffhanger that was never ever continued because losses were up the roof and the planned trilogy was dropped.
The first few chapters can fool you, but the truth is, there was never any planning done for chapters past four. Usually, you get swarmed by a horde of enemies right as the chapter starts, a battle in which you lose your pre-deployed army and have to spend the rest of the mission endlessly microing your hero back and forth trying to get somewhere. "Thousands-strong armies"? For your enemies, maybe. Not for you.
Speaking of the hero, Elhant is one of the most uncooperative, arrogant♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥I have ever seen in a protagonist role, and I spent the entire game wishing he'd die a horrible death. Not that I saw half of what you're supposed to see of him, because the movie cutscenes wouldn't load on my PC. For a while, I went into the game folder to watch them, but then I realized the loading bug was probably for the best.
And yes, to top it all off, the game is filled with bugs. It's funny when they allow you to kill a boss by shooting them from behind a wall - I did that several times while I grabbed a snack - but it's not so funny when the AI takes a ridiculous path or the game simply crashes mid-mission.
Never mind the massive feature list shown on the Steam Store Page, most of it is broken, unfinished, or simply not as good as you'd expect. Now, I've heard multiplayer used to be rather decent, but as expected from a 2006 game, it is now dead. Do yourself a favor,
HoAE. There are far, far better strategy games on Steam.

Enhanced Edition as a title fails for what Larian did this to game. These aren't just new textures, or models. It plays like a whole new game. I think that Divinity: Original Sin - Enhanced Edition should be an example of how other RPG games should work. If you are looking for a fun co-op game to play online, or in your living room look no further. Co-op gameplay is seamless and fun. They have really built co-op into the story mechanics, as much as they have the gameplay. If you are looking for a long game, this is supposedly 100 hours of content. I don't believe that, because I've spent almost 50 hours and I am not even halfway. (No, I haven't been dying constantly.) Between the sidequests, puzzles, combat, the main story, and the crafting you will spend well over 100 hours on this game. I commend Larian studios for their incredible attention to detail, and their love for the game is shown in the work they put into it. Looking forward to Divinity 2.

"As a historian I find myself both pleased with the results and revolted we may never know the veracity of our efforts. Regardless of whatever headaches I have, may you enjoy the fruits of our labor.
We may never know who Citizen Abel truly is, but we do have stories about him." -- Brendon Chung,
I'm not going to lie: This is a difficult game. It will anger you. It is meant to do so.
But if you pretend it doesn't have a story that is desperately trying to make its way to you, you are deluding yourself. And you are falling for the trap that Chung has so meticulously designed for the average player.
I don't mean that this is a difficult game insofar that it's hard to complete. It's level design is agonizingly linear, and excruciatingly short in length. It's difficult because the most important events in the story don't happen on the screen. It's difficult like a jigsaw puzzle without a picture on the box -- difficult because you don't know what you're putting together, let alone how.
It's short because most of what it's trying to tell you, it tries to communicate by not telling you at all. Just leaving hints, out of order, tucked away in parts that don't seem important. That is not to say that Chung is lazy and expects you to make the story for him, simply that he respects the player enough to understand what's on the table and what that means is likely being dealt under it.
This isn't really much of a game in the usual sense of a game. It is a linear short-story, told in a fragmented non-linear fashion. It is so short a story, in fact, that it is really closer to a poem in that vein: its decided brevity poses more questions than it answers, and that is its main storytelling technique -- in typical crime-mystery fashion.
That is what I love about Thirty Flights of Loving, and what so many people hate: it gives you but a blink of an eye, from a view of limited scope, in a world promised to be much larger than it shows. A world that Chung has obviously given much thought, more thought than a passer-by might think he has given the game itself. And like a poem, agonizingly short, its parts are so few that they have been chosen with such care that they tell more than the pieces themselves ever could. Like in poetry, how sometimes the story resides as much in the silence between the words as the words themselves.
Thirty Flights of Loving isn't really so much a game, as it is a question. A series of questions, posed to the player, answers known by the characters, if they could only speak. And it sparks a rare kind of intense and frustrated curiosity that I have experienced but few times in my entire life.
It does so by being more than what it is: it is incredibly consciously constructed, made for consumption from the very beginning. And if you try to wolf it down and casually digest it like you would a hamburger and fries, it will tear through your gut like a box of nails. It is uncompromising, and it will make you angry.
It is difficult like that, it was made to be. That is what makes it so uniquely wonderful to me. Chung dares to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, and asks you what you're going to do about it.
That part is up to you.

Originally an early prototype for Blendo Games’s Gravity Bone, TFOL is difficult to classify within traditional gaming genres. Is it an adventure game, an action game, an art game, or an elegiac love poem? Well, it’s all of these and none. 30 Flights is an indie gamer's indie game. It occupies the same experimental vein as Proteus, The Path, and Journey. I know that may scare some of you off, but it shouldn’t. TFOL is basically a slick crime caper gone awry. Like Reservoir Dogs? You’ll probably enjoy this.
As one comes to expect from indie indies, TFOL features simple graphics, quirky humor, an innovative yet enigmatic narrative structure, and great music. Despite its age, the Quake 2 engine has never looked this good. The blocky retro-visual style is utterly charming: think Minecraft meets No One Lives Forever.
Thirty Flights of Loving focuses its sharp satirical lens on the over-the-top cinematism rife in video games and their tendency to imitate big-budget Hollywood Action movies. But it is also a powerful and moving homage to the stylish, discontinuous narration of French New Wave films. The game has often been compared to the work of Tarantino, but both the plot and razor sharp editing owes more to the formal innovations of Jean-Luc Godard's seminal film, A bout de souffle.
Much of the central game experience involves trying to piece together its intricately crafted story. Temporal and spatial leaps await the player at every turn. Brendon Chung has a knack for capturing the gritty underworld vernacular that our anti-heroes inhabit. Interspersed throughout the game are moments of transcendent beauty. In one, Anita sits peeling oranges overlooking her vast apartment courtyard. The sound is particularly used to great effect here, realistically capturing the nocturnal soundscape of a large urban metropolis. In the climactic gunfight, the action recalls the poetic rhythm of Koyaanisqatsi and Baraka. Without relying on dialogue text, voiceover narration, or UI, Brendon Chung manages to convey an entire world and story through the environment.
To what degree any of this makes sense depends on the player’s perception. What exactly went down at Cugat airfield? Who is Winston Borges (a.k.a. Mo Golden, Moco Rococo, The Big Pai-Goo)? Is Bernoulli’s Principle the key to unlocking this puzzle? These are just some of the many questions you’ll ask yourself in 30 Flights of Loving.

Fixes for FPS:
- Messing with NVIDIA Control Panel (you can actually turn off V-sync and get over 100 FPS).
-- Update 1: I think the issue is respawning when you have died. I went from 50 - 60 FPS in 1 area, I died and then I dropped to 16 FPS again when I respawned at a checkpoint. Cons;
- Game is unoptimized. I get 11 - 21 FPS in cut-scenes/quick time events.
- If you quit the game (aka back to the desktop), the game will still appear in the background processes. When you close the game from the background processes and if you reopen the game, it will ask if you want to run the game in 'Safe Mode.'
- You can't tab out, not even in fullscreen borderless.
Tips:
- You can easily miss 4 achievements during the campaign called 'Captain’s Log, Reality TV, You Know Nothing & Peace to the Fallen.' Try and watch a guide about them before so that you know in the future where to look.
- Pick up every weapon. They're like 'collectibles.'
- Upon starting the game, be sure to preloading/precache the shadows. If you don't you will receive server timeout messages when entering a match in multiplayer and who knows what it will do in Single Player if you don't have it (probably 5 FPS and longer load times).

First of all, I only played the campaign.  I don't do multiplayer shooters anymore, I just don't have the spare cycles to suffer cheaters, delinquents, and map memorizers anymore.
Summary
The campaign was OK.  The game is plagued by too many "howevers" as you will see below.  If you're like me and only want the story campaign, then it's worth a go if $20 or less.  I got it on sale for $29, which I felt was slightly high for what I played.  My hours are off because I accidentally left it running all night one night.
What I liked:
I liked the fact that I could choose side missions from a mission map what I wanted to do, however, you are able to do almost all the side missions before doing the first campaign mission after becoming captain of your Space Carrier.  This almost completely caused a continuity disconnect with the story campaign.
I liked the most wanted board and chose missions to hunt down these NPCs, however, the last 5 or 6 you never get to see the cards completed for reasons I can't get into for spolier reasons.
I liked that the gear was 3D printed and you had to scan weapons you found to add them to your ship's database..however, it was obnoxious that the weapons you haven't scanned yet show up in the database and some of them you don't even encounter until you reach the point where you won't enter the armory again.
I liked that there was customization of the weapon attachment and scopes, however, the limitations should be based on position of the attachment on the weapon, not the number of attachment slots in the UI.
I liked that there was transition from FPS to Space Fighter and back again in the same mission, however, it was all scripted so there was always the "guard rail" feeling, though I think this is an issue present in the entire franchise.  You never really get to roam your entire ship though there is no reason in this engine that you couldn't aside from the developer's willingness to do so.  I know its not Star Citizen, but some freedom would be nice.
Ethan was just great, no however here.
What I just couldn't stand:
The target locking pursuit thingy...nothing like it running you into enemy capital ships or asteroids all the time.
Missiles...fairly pointless as the gun upgrades you get are pretty much all you need.
The story gets a little too ham fisted with the "burden of command".
The captain's computer is pretty much worthless.
*sigh*

Not a huge fan of the COD series mp, I think the run and gun in a shoebox concept is absolute garbage and it's a shame so many mp games have moved in that direction, but I have taken the time to beat the sp capaigns of each series entry as sales pop up on steam. And while I don't think any of the recent entries have been particularly noteworthy; this game included, I am inclinded to leave a favorable review in light of the excessively negative press. And for the most part, the game is actually decently done. Still a dated engine, but the level design isn't bad. There is definitely a sense of scale. Dialogue is well written for the most part. And the conversation flows and doesn't seem forced. Besides one awkward moment where people were laughing at one of Ethan's joke that wasn't particularly funny. Would I go out of my way to recommend Infinite Warfare to my friends? No, absolutely not. In some sense, the outrage is justified. The franchise is done to death. It needs fresh life. This game is certainly not worth full price. I can appreciate the scale of new games and the manpower required, but games are absolutely not worth $80. I still believe profit margins should be reduced. And it's absolutely outrageous that Activision thinks they can charge $50 for COD4 remastered and force you to buy Infinite Warfare to purchase it. Thankfully that was later rectified. But I hear they're charging more for DLC that was included free in the original title. Hopefully that was also addressed. I don't care if it's a remaster, you can't charge full price for a decade old game. Halo gave you 4 games for the price of 1 COD game. The remaster is worth $30 at most and I'm leaning more towards $20.
My review will be mainly focused on the single player campaign of Infinite Warfare. As a fan of Ace Combat and HAWX, the arcade style space combat was a welcome addition. It certainly filled the void where Starwars Battlefront failed *cough* And with the exception of a few scripted events and level sequences, it was not a rail shooter. It was definitely satisfying to see the transition from ground to orbit to docking or forced entry on hostile ships, followed by descending into the bay and moving about the ship. Definitely gave a sense of scale. Especially with the ftl/slipspace travel. Watching the jump from the bridge. The hanger did seem a bit bare though. Given the amount of armor you later see. And knowing there's more than 2 gunships. But all the detail, did add to the immursion. Story delivery-wise, the campaign seemed to jump around too much, with the side missions giving too much freedom to play them in any order. One second you get this sense or urgency of an impending invasion, the next you can choose to protect a salvage run rather than defend your home planet.... That feels unnatural and runs the immersion. On earth, I defintiely got a 2142 vibe every time I saw a Titan.. err Destoryer in low orbit. Gameplay mechanics like avoiding the burning sun, or popping a door slowly or kicking it in were thoughtful. Turning robots on humans seems a bit repetitive. New material please. The boosters..... those need to go. I still keep my boots firmly planted on the ground despite the boosters. It will always feel forced and ridiculous performing wall runs. And boosts should be saved solely for landing high jumps with minimal impact. That's minor, and I can appreciate the vaulting system in place.
On the other hand, some things did seriously irritate me... the entire concept of the SDF hating freedom and hating the people of earth seems a bit ridiculous. The quotes when you die especially.. It's not believeable. Most wars, however ridiculous, e.g. religion, are fought by people who fight and believe in something... people tend to be rational, even if misguided. The idea that a group would hate freedom is implausible.. The SDF are fighting for independence, they want FREEDOM. Quotes saying they hate freedom are a bit ridiculous. The delivery was off. And I really don't see someone so young being an admiral and leading such a large movement. Especially someone with such lack of emotional discipline. And on that subject, WHY THE F*** IS A LIEUTENANT NOW A COMMANDER. I understand 95% of the fleet was wiped out, but before then the lieutenant and admiral were in contact. An admitral wouldn't even acknowldege a lieutenant in the military. A kid straight out of academy or university would be granted the rank of lieutenant.. And why was a private first class leading the marines after the Sgt. died?! Am I missing something.. a PFC is the lowest rank of all. Anyone flying in the airforce/navy would likely be a major or a colonel. The choice of navy did seem more fitting than air force, given the concept of battleships. Back to the enemy forces, the entire SDF seemed void of personality. And there was a total lack of effort on the voice department. Unless I'm fighting the 501st again. The same voice over and over.. really destracted from the experience. AND FOR THE LOVE OF GOD WHAT THE F*** IS WRONG WITH THE CUTSCENES. Cutscenes were horrifically laggy... I have a 1080ti, 6700k, 16GB DDR4, 1TB SSD, etc. THis should not be happening in a released product, nevermind one that's been out on the market for over a year. You can't expect me to turn down cache or shadows with $6000 of the best hardware on the market. Back to characters, The UNSA characters are more memorable than the SDF, but I'll still forget them, just not Ethan <3 and as usual everyone dies and you feel horrible at the end. gg COD. At least the developers suceeded at delivering a powerful ending. It's an interesting story, but at this point I feel the entire franchise is stale, living off of bad multi-player. The campaigns are far too short. There isn't enough content for the price being asked. Don't buy this game unless you want a quick thrill and have cash to burn. Otherwise, go buy playerunknown's battleground, killing floor 2, payday 2. There's plenty of other franchies with more to offer. This is not a game where you're going to get $1/hr out of. More like $10/hr.

First thing that you need to know is that the movement goes by momentum - similar to Genesis Sonic. (slow start, goes faster over time)
It makes controls a bit harder to grasp, and some stages require tight maneuvers.
Overall once you get past the controls barrier, you'll find a rather challening platformer.
Stages aren't long, so the game can be played in short bursts.
Overall difficulty - 7/10

If you like cute platformer games then you're in the right place. Squirreltopia has, by far, surpassed my expectations. It not only has fun background music but adorable character designs as well. The mini games are pretty fun too once you unlock them. It challenges the player much more than you'd expect, but don't take your frustrations out on the squirrels. Overall, great game to pass some free time with.

I can definitely see why people like the game. There were a lot of things I liked about the game: Graphics, level design, attention to detail (like, for example, that your character sprite changes every time you die).
However, it ran really slowly on my computer, and even at it's best, the controls were far too sluggish for me. For me, personally, responsiveness of controls are the most important thing for a precision platformer. It's what maintains that fine line between getting frustrated with myself and wanting to do better, or getting frustrated with the game and wanting to quit.
Most computers might run it fast enough to be enjoyable, but even though mine is far above the recommended specs, it's not nearly fast enough.

Squirreltopia is a 2D platformer that has you controlling a squirrel and his other squirrel companions to defeat another squirrel! Sounds cute and friendly right? Wrong. This game is brutal and unforgiving even on easy mode. Easy mode gives you checks points while hard mode takes those away and adds a timer. The levels themselves stay the same and there are very few checkpoints so this game won't be a walk in the park either way. You start off on the overhead map which is like a tiny level in itself and access the actual levels via doorways. Though strangely enough a large chunk of them are locked off until near the end when you collect a certain colored key that opens them.
Controls are very simple, you move and you jump. That's it, no sprinting, ducking or double jumping. It's not as bland as you may think, they introduce balloons, bombs and other contraptions to keep things interesting. One thing they do not have is a pause button for some odd reason. Their are collectible game cartridges and acorns hidden throughout some levels, the latter is to unlock minigames, the former I have no clue what they do. Minigames are neat and usually involve you collecting or avoiding objects in a small area but it is unlikely you'd want to go back to them after trying them at least once.
Music is pretty catchy but the same song plays throughout both the over-world menu and the levels which can make it get repetitive fast. Songs only change when you head to a new “world”. The levels are all themed from forest, snow, desert, etc. Once you finish enough levels you are allowed to fight the world's boss and they are not really fun to fight. They have no real movement patterns to recognize and move around at random which can be really annoying when a boss has to drill down and spends nearly a minute floating back and forth while you sit and wait. Those are the only real enemies of the game and the other levels obstacles consist of hazards like spikes, endless pits and lasers. Each time you die you spawn as a different looking squirrel which is a cool little feature.
Overall it's a fun little game if you are looking for a challenge. It's sure to have you dying countless times in your attempts to clear a level. It's recommended that you are experienced with platformers before attempting to tackle this game. Over 1000 squirrels were killed to make this review and I only managed to collect one acorn. There are a decent amount of levels but it will take you quite a bit of time to finish due to difficulty and a couple of simplistic minigames to keep you entertained for awhile. If you are looking for a game offering an immense challenge or you simply hate squirrels and want to see them electrocuted Squrrieltopia is certainly worth your time.
Honestly, its a great game. If squirrels met mario, it would be squirell topia. It is lots of fun if you like platformers, and it really brings back the old days of playing mario.

Note: I deleted my old review because with so many updates since last Octobers release, it was simply too out of date to warrant an edit. So here is a new one, reviewing the game as of V1.10, released today!
Chaos Reborn is a hex based, turn based, card based strategy game where you are a wizard and you have to kill the other wizards. This is done by casting spells which can either summon creatures to attack other creatures and wizards, cast magic attack spells to kill almost anything, or create growth spells that hinders mobility. You'll soon learn that different creatures have different strengths and weaknesses, far too many to list here but you'll learn them.
You have a choice of what kind of game you want to play - if you love managing risk and playing with lots of RNG, there is Chaos Mode. This is the mode that was not only the only way to play the original, but was the only mode when the game was in development, so it has a strong following from many of the core players. It's also my favourite. Basically, every spell has a % chance of being cast, and there are many factors that can affect what that % is going to be. Stronger spells have a lower chance of being cast than the weaker ones. Killing creatures also has % chance, based again on many factors but the main one being attack + defence of the creatures in combat.
In v1.8, a new mode was introduced called Law Mode. Law Mode is a more standard affair, a lot of the RNG is stripped away for players who are not comfortable with playing with a lot of RNG. So, instead of % chance of being cast, spells have a mana cost to being cast. The more powerful ones are more expensive than the less powerful ones. Combat is also very different - everything now has Health Points, and the amount of damage dealt is influenced by attack + defence of the creatures in combat.
In amongst Law and Chaos Mode, you have two ways of playing (so much choice!) - Classic or Equipped. Classic gives all wizards the same bodygear and staff with equal stats for a truly level playing field. Equipped mode however gives you the chance to be creative, allows for customisation and creates far more exciting games - you get staffs and bodygears that have special features and particular alignments to certain spells, and so allows you to customise your wizard based on your play style.
But wait, there's more! There is an Offline Mode where you can play offline games and a single player campaign. There are also some tutorials. Use these to familiarise yourself with the game first before jumping into Multiplayer.
Multiplayer offers up to 4 different ways of playing - PvP Matchmaker (Friendlies and Ranked), PvP Private Games with your mates, Online Realms (with ally and invading options, where you can help your friends or fight them), and the all new Duels mode - jump into a 1v1 match to win Forge crystals so you can build your own staffs and bodygear.
But wait, there is EVEN MORE. There are social ranks - so at the end of each month, if you've met certain criteria, you level up to a new rank. Apprentice is your base rank - which goes up to Lord, where you can offer yourself up as a Lord defender for a King and his realm - which goes up to King, where you can make your own Realm, and then up to Demi God and God, which I understand that in the future, you can create guilds and tournaments, but no details on this as of yet, which has disappointed some, certainly those who participated in the Kickstarter, but hasn't bothered most (at least, that is the impression I get).
So is the game any good? In a word, yes absolutely. It looks gorgeous, it sounds good - it's easy to play but difficult to master. Lots of stats to learn, lots of spells to choose from, great community, and above all a lot of fun. I highly recommend Chaos Mode as that is the most exciting, but if you don't like its outcome dependancy on RNG, there is Law mode that may be more to your taste.
However, the game does suffer from minor balance issues here and there. Also, the tutorials don't do a fantastic job in selling the game as well as it could. Plus, personally, I think the offline campaign is boring as hell. However, Julian and the Snapshot team do their best to address the most serious issues with regular updates, which now and again come with new features. And yes, there are still issues.
But overall, yes I sing the praises much of this game, but 900+ hours and still enjoying it everytime I login, I have much to praise. Great game, highly recommended.

I've spent almost 80 hours playing just the classic Chaos PvP multiplayer alone (ie. flat/standardised with no wizard gear) which should speak volumes about how fundamentally solid the core of this game is. Snapshot recently introduced a more deterministic 'Law' mode in contrast to the chance and risk management of the Chaos mode. Personally I don't find it nearly as interesting but it could be just your bag if you're not big on RNG and carefully manipulating odds in your favour.
The thing that I love most about Chaos Reborn is how simple and lean it is, but without sacrificing depth and excitement. The breadth of spells to cast and creatures/structures to summon makes each game unique, and if you're playing the Chaos mode then chance can make things even more unpredictable. Yes, plans can crash and burn, but new ones can unexpectedly rise out of their ashes. The illusion system is perhaps the defining aspect of the game and opens it up to all kinds of risk and reward, bluffing and second guessing your opponents.
Anyway, I'll leave it at that. Chaos Reborn is a perfectly formed strategy gem, up there with Frozen Synapse for me, which is high praise indeed. If you're at all interested in this kind of game then you owe it to yourself to at least give the demo a whirl, perhaps even try it out with some friends.

Weapons are pretty standard, you have an assault rifle (A.K.A bolter) sniper rifle, etc. The only real interesting ranged weapon I have come across is a remote detonation grenade launcher. I would also like to add that the game is extremely well optimized, lowest fps I got was 40 on med-high settings and I am fairly below the recommended system requirements. Something like that is hard to find anymore.

Fragmented isn't a bad game. I repeat it's not a bad game. Some might be wondering, yes I bought The Repop 3 years ago as a 3rd backer, but overall I was not that impressed with the game. It seemed incredibly unpolished. I played this game a while back and still didnt like it but it was slightly more polished than repop. Fast forward a few months or a year and I play the repopulation again and it's still unpolished, but I tried Fragmented out and it's incredibly polished now. The character movements are pretty fluid now, there is no frame dropping, lag or anything. This game is actually really good now.
Character Customization
Is pretty terrible. The hairstyles for women aren't good at all. All of the characters look 'white'. There are no black facial features never mind any other ethnicity. The character models look good however. They actually have somewhat of superhero bodies.
Story
There is no story.
Gameplay
This is where Fragmented shines but also fades out. The gameplay itself is decent. It could be more fluid like Andromeda fluid but its not too bad. I never got to use anything more than a few melee weapons but there is no auto lock on mechanics you actually have to aim which is nice. There is crafting which is great. The only problem with this is that the materials required to craft some items is ridiculous. Fragmented seems to have an identity issue, it doesnt know if it wants to be a survival game or rpg game. So it leaves in high material costs for items, but because there is no system to set up harvesters or trade items or set up work orders, it leaves you spending your entire time foraging and looking for materials.
The environment is gorgeous and looks 10x better than repopulation does. Everything is much more fluid for some reason. There is also environmental effects such as rain.
There is a survival system which forces you to perform certain actions such as craft clothes because you dont want to freeze. If you geth ot you take off some clothes. Drinking water keeps you hydrated or you can swim as well, and etc.
Crafting - I crafted a few structures to get a general feel for the game, I think the construction aspect to the game is nice. I have no problems with it. Some of the recipes need to be toned down because this isnt an rpg, and on some harcore pvp servers, it would take you 10 hours to craft some items and thats if you can survive. When you die on these servers you lose everything.
So In summary
Pros
-Nicely polished compared to years ago
-Character movement is fluid
-Enviroment is amazing
-There are survival aspects to the game
-The crafting system is decent
Cons
-Character customization is horrible
-Has identity crisis, crafting items costs too much
-Combat could be polished to meet 2017 standards
Overall for $9.99? Id recommend you try it out. It's a pretty fun game that has unlimited amounts of possibilites.

Features
Authentic Age of sail naval combat game that blends realism and gameplay for an enjoyable and unique experience. Era of game: mid 1700s to the 1820s. It is not a sim. It is not an arcade. It is not fully realistic nor fully historical, but a blend of all these.
Authentic and Addicting Combat System
Naval Action features one of the most beautiful and authentic Age of Sail combat systems to date. Every cannonball, every wave, and many parts of the ships are all tracked to see where the ball hits. Accuracy is not based upon rng or a magical skill number but actual gunnery, which is your own ability to judge the following three things: the distance between you and the target, the characteristics of your smoothbore cannons, and the pitching and rolling of your ship through the waves. I don’t know if this is well known or not, but I have hit the wheel of enemy ships and seen their ship go into “rudder shock,” which means they cannot turn.
Open World (OW)
Explore a massive world that would take weeks to fully explore. It is time compressed because otherwise it would take days of real time sailing just to go between ports, let alone the weeks needed to cross the Caribbean. How it is right now, it takes 4-12+ hours of real time sailing to cross the map. Travel can be long. Local knowledge of the area, the channels, shallows, and hiding spots are all vital. However, at the moment, the islands can seem a little boring beyond the majestic views. There is dynamic weather and you can get lost, especially in storms and heavy fog. Venturing out of sight of land for the first time can be a little intimidating.
Map
There is a very rough ingame map that shows the ports. The devs plan to beautify the map once UI is decided upon. There is no “You are Here” marker. You will have to keep track of that yourself. Navigation is a skill you will want to learn if you want to venture outside the Arena. It is extremely daunting at first but easy to pick up. Soon you will be pretty good at it. The map lacks navigation tools.
Battle Instances
Because every shot, every wave, and detailed parts of the ships are all tracked by the server, battles have to be instanced. Instances can have up to 50 ships, whether they are small cutters or ships of the line. When a battle starts, the participants are pulled into an instance of that spot on the Open World.
Realistic Sailing Model
Sailing in the battle instances is fairly realistic and authentic. To tack properly (turn through the wind), you have to learn manual sailing. Easy to pick up, fairly easy to master. It becomes second nature, like learning manual shift in vehicle.
UI
Battle Instance UI is pretty good in my opinion. I am a minimalist when it comes to UI. I don’t want all the extra crap blocking my view of the beautiful ships and environment. The Open World and Port UI are horrible (tech demo).
Economy and Crafting
Economy and Crafting is becoming more complex all the time and requires quite a bit of time and money to get involved.
Boarding Combat
There are no avatars. You cannot walk about your ship. When you board the enemy, a tactical mini game appears. Some people compare it to Rock Paper Scissors. Some like it, some hate it, I think it is fine. If this is a deal breaker, watch YouTube first before you buy.
PVE
There is Player Vs Environment (AI). The AI can be difficult at first, even very difficult. But they soon become easy and boring once you get to know them. There is a pve only server if you don't want to play against players.
PVP
This is where the heart of the game is. Expect Ganks. Expect great 1v1 fights. Expect on-the-edge-of-your-seat group fights, where teamwork and skill is needed to clutch victory from defeat. This is the addicting part of the game.
Port Battles:
Port battles take place at regional capital ports where hostility has been driven up. The port battle has up to 50 players and contains the land and forts surrounding the port (so tight harbors are hard to manage 50 ships in) providing different options for tactics for each port. A successful port assault will change the current owner to your nation. Do not open player outposts in national ports except the capital city. All other national ports can be captured and you will lose access to anything in the port until it is recaptured. Port captures are way too frequent (negative).
Arena
There is an arena option available.Technically you never have to access the open world if you don't want to. Battle seems daunting at first, but in the Arena you can practice in a low stress environment with the free basic ships. Combat is easy to get the hang, very difficult to master.
Progression
You start with a small cutter.You can progress to a ship of the line.The progression can be long. Just pvp and have fun; no need to grind. You will get into the larger ships in due time and you will want to learn the game first. This game is all about the process.Forget the end game. If you get to the end game without learning the game you will cry when your extremely expensive ship ends up on the bottom of the ocean or in someone else’s dock. If you grind, it isnt any worse than WoWS.
Price
The price is expensive for an early access game. But in my opinion, it is very worth it. At almost 3000 hours, I have paid about 1 cent an hour to play Naval Action. When considering what I spend on other entertainment, it is actually pretty cheap if you stick with it. I know many AAA games that I have spent a fortune on and only play it for a couple of weeks.
Stability
Even though the game is Early Access, I've only had 1-2 crashes in 2 years. It is very stable on my machine. There are annoying bugs from time to time and very rarely something is wrong with the server. People do report fps problems. People say the game is poorly optimized, but with a 980 ti, I get 70-100fps on Open World and typically 100+ fps in battle. I play on 1920x1080 and ultra.

Learning curve means you are always learning new things. After almost 3000 hours, I am still learning new things.

I have to say I bought this on sight mostly for the incredible James Benson animation but then also got one of the most incredible Metroid style games I've ever come across. This is quite possibly one of the most beautiful looking games I've seen in some time. It's that I don't like a good apocolypse game of grey hues but man do I like to see a game that has some color.
The gameplay itself is a 2D platforming game that is very much inspired by the Metroid games. Many areas with cool things in them that can only be gotten once you have a certain ability. There is also abilities that you unlock with points that are gained by collecting spirit from enemies you kill but that are also found in hidden areas. Most of the abilities give you bonuses to your already existing skills such as damage boosts, increased blast radius, revealing where hidden secrets are, etc. You could play the entire game without them and still be fine, in fact there is an achievement for doing just such a thing.
The game is a very good challenge. I would call it "funstrating". When you get in the zone and can go through an area unscathed you just feel so good and the platforming is so fun you just never want it to end. Then you get cocky and try to go fast and then die on the same spikes 7 times in a row. While there are stationary save points in the game they are certainly nothing to rely on. What you do have is the ability to make a save point anywhere you want other than by enemies or on an unstable platform. That makes it sound really easy but what was cool was that they made you use energy to make the save points. This same energy can be used for more powerful attacks and obviously if you are making too many save points you're going to have to go a fair distance until you get more energy back. Many times I would forget to put a save point down only to die foolishly and have to start WAAAAAAY back at last checkpoint. i'd rage quit but it really was my own fault. I never felt that game gave me a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t death. If I died I usually wasn't being careful enough and fell straight into spikes.
The game is somewhat short but man is it worth it. Buy it. Play it. Think about replaying it.

From time to time a game appears that gives a lesson to every developer and company about how to make games properly. Well, Ori is one of those games.
Even though perfection will never exist in videogames IMO, I find it really hard to search for cons into this game. Just notice that I was very hyped about Hotline Miami 2 for almost a year and I honestly admit that this hype banished once I purchased Ori.
Ori and the Blind Forest brings something new, something fresh, something NEEDED. I can't imagine the amount of work required to build a game like this but trust me people, devs can be hugely proud of it.
Visuals are the closest to perfection I've ever seen in a videogame. Just see it for yourselves and get stunned about what a 2D platformer can give you. Seriously, you don't need to go to an art museum anymore. This game is well enough. From beginning to end it'll be impossible for you not to stare at every single detail, every singe hand-made background.
The tag "Great Soundtrack" is not one of the most voted without a reason. Such a great visuals strongly need a great soundtrack too, and that's what you'll find. Tracks add so much feeling and emotion into this game that together with the visuals it becomes one of the greatest combinations of the WHOLE industry.
Controls are tight and super fair. Mind this words: the game is challenging and every single death will be of your fault. This is the regular metroidvania where you get more movement skills as soon as you progress into the story. I found quite some similarities to the experience I got with Guacamelee (in terms of gameplay).
The story... OMG. Just when I thought I saw everything a 2D platformer could give (mostly soft and simple plots), this game appears. 20 minutes were enough for me to start clapping in front of the screen. This game has one of the strongest prologues I've ever played. AND IT'S IN 2D. SO MANY LIMITATIONS, YET SUCH AN INCREDIBLE EXECUTION.
The length is also good enough. Not too long, but not too short either. Map is extremely well planned, together with collectibles and secrets. Getting everything can perfectly give you 8-10h, which is more than the average platformer can offer.
Finally, achievements are very well written too. This sounds stupid but it's sad to see some nice games where the achievements are completely senseless or wrongly directed. This game has every kind of achievement I like: storyline achievements, collectible achievements, movement achievements, and hardcore achievements.
I think that the only con I can find to this game is that sometimes there are so many glowing things together that you can't really distinguish the friendly ones against the enemy bullets. But this mainly applies to one particular enemy and I'm partially colorblind so I can't say it's a con at all.
Overall, just stop buying mediocre bundles nor triple A games. Do yourself a favor and pay 20€ for this game. We're in front of one of the best games of the year, and we're still on March. But seriously, this game is something I've never seen before (and I've played more games than I can count) and probably no one will dislike this game (aside from fake haters and people pretending to be funny).
: 9.75/10 this is one of the best 2D platformers you'll play in a very long time.

So I've played about 7 hours so far and have had a blast. I have 2 ARK accounts with well over 4k hours between them and left ARK some time ago when they introduced Power Armor and Lasers and all that bunk. I was looking for something not so crazy and unbalanced as ARK and discovered this game on sale for $7.50 and thought, what the heck, let's try it out. The idea of being a pirate and having a ship with cannons seemed to appeal to me. My 7 hours of initial play were on an official Standard server called Timberfrost or something like that. Ping was around 53. My computer is about 5 years old with a GTX 670 Ti Video card and on high graphics I am getting a consistant 43 FPS. The graphics are nice, not too shabby at all, reminds me of ARK so they are probably using the same engine.
You wake up with a broken ship's rudder as your weapon/tool. Do the basic collect this and that, while you are guided by a tutorial questline that teaches you the basics and advanced elements of the game. Learn to hunt, go into caves for metal, yada yada. I was in a cave and came across some poor smuck and killed him for all his booty. I'm a pirate after all! 600 copper and 100 tin he donated to me, after which he logged out and probably rage quit. Sorry bud! I'm not really much of a PKer but what the heck. I built a little wooden base and logged out after 5 hours to take a short break. Upon logging back in about 30 minutes later, I heard a knock-knock, knocking of my door. Seems someone was trying to bash their way in. I patiently awaited on the other side of the door and after a couple more swings, he was in. Or rather he tried to get in because at that moment I leapt upon him and whacked, smacked, and cracked him with my bronze axe. Down he went... and he was only able to hit me once. Boy he had lots of loot on him, including a steel axe, some seige bolts, and a flintlock pistol with 10 bullets, along with some pirate armor. Oh Boy! I repaired the damage he did to the house, fortified it, and then moved away, knowing he would come back eventually when I was offline. Now he can waste his time bashing down the 20 doors and extra walls I placed just to find nothing.
So I'm having fun... and this is what playing a game is about. Heck I would pay full price for this at $15 but at $7.50 it's a steal. I haven't noticed any bugs in my short time. Sure it's a slowly evolving game but all the elements are there for you to enjoy. The server population might not be the greatest but so far I'm content with not running over a bunch of other players all the time. Anyway, if you buy the game, come to Timberfrost and look up Jadeheart. Don't mind helping new people out.

Open Sorcery was a very nice little experience. I was heavily invested within minutes. Cute, clever writing with an interesting

Open Sorcery is an exquisite text experience--the way choices have been implemented in dialogue makes it flow smoothly and naturally, and the rich, deep world gives every action context that changes how you perceive it in retrospect.
Your actions and growth as a sapient firewall feel very, very organic; the game just oozes verisimilitude. And the non-player characters all reacting like a living system to your choices. This game can vary between a hopeful exploration of what it means to be a person ... to a tragedy that ends with those you love dead or scattered, and you broken down into an unfeeling copy of yourself.
This game does incredible things with its text format, and between entrancing prose and dialogue that shines, has my highest recommendation.

An open-world combat and trading experience, Naval Action is a pretty damn good sailing game. It is heavily in alpha, however: UI elements are plainly unfinished, there are very few tooltips to help anyone get started, and even statistics are poorly formatted and explained.
With all that being said, what exactly are you getting?
You're getting an open world experience whereby you sail around, encounter enemy players (read: not a member of your nation) and then challenge them to battle. You and them begin an instanced ship-on-ship battle whereby you can either stand and fight or run by avoiding fire for a minute or so.
Ship customization isn't here yet, though equipment and crafting is. It is possible, but difficult, to craft an entire ship from scratch by buying the components for it. Obtaining these resources other than buying them, however, is apparently not possible.
The game prides itself more towards realism than arcade simulation: physics make targeting enemies on the open sea difficult, as both your ship and the enemy ship bob and crest with waves. There is a map, but it does not tell you where you are. You have to navigate the world the old-fashioned way: using your compass.
It does support PvP and PvE servers, and in PvE you can only fight NPC ships. In PvP you can be challenged by just about anyone, and trading becomes far more challenging. Hiring fleet vessels to protect you in a PvP scenario is a must.
Overall, it's highly unpolished but well worth $55 CAD. If you like this concept, but are intimidated by its skill ceiling, take a look at the Steam game Windward instead.

I have spent 20 hours on this in one week, while also working 40 hours, to give you an idea of how much of my free time has been spent on the game.  Is this game for everyone?  No, however, if you want a game that is a mix of poker with tactical acumen, this game is for you.  Combat is by dice rolls, but just like Blood Bowl, the good player stacks the dice in his favor and will win more often than he loses.  Yes, there are times where you will fail something with a 90%+ chance to succeed and it will cost you the game, but most of the time, you could have spent resources to increase your success rate.
There is also a low RNG impact mode as well.  While it is fun, it is very deterministic.  I prefer the original mode because while random, you have more decisions to make.  Whereas, once someone gets a lead in Law mode, it is a matter of just grinding the game out to a win.

Firstly I like this game a lot at least half of the time and a bit most of the rest of the time. The nature of games that use RNG will always at times lead to frustration, especially amongst people who are statistically illiterate.
Firstly if you can't help crapping your pants when a bunch of 20% rolls go against you then this is probably not the game for you.
Secondly if you only want to play single player this is also probably not the absolute best option. They have made a brave effort to make the SP interesting and fun but quite frankly it will never grip you like the mplayer. I can't quite decide why but it feels like the more you play against the CPU the more you start to find it a little predictible, or maybe playing against an AI in arena is just not as fun as teabagging your mates.
The game really comes to life when you play against another human, you'll find yourself gripped by every dice roll, pleading with the gods of chance to smile kindly upon you. You'll curse every failed spell and delight as your opponents best laid plans are crushed by fickle lady luck. I really can't explain to you how gripping a game that is in many ways quite simple can grip you, you'll really just have to try it out for yourself.
There are a few other minor quibbles I would love to see addressed. It would be nice if they implemented a dynamic camera that really took you into the action when spells were cast. It would be nice if the wizard (your avatar) stood out more impressively. They've made some good effort with gear and stuff but he never really stands out on the battle field, he needs more impressive animations (idle and spell casting). Finally the battlefields themselves are bit sparten and graphically plain.
It has to be said that most of my problems are minor and cosmetic and shouldn't be a reason for anyone who knows they enjoy turn based games. If you have even a passing interest in the genre then this is really a game you should pick up.

Though I had never played the original game on which this was based, I purchased it during Early Access, as it seemed a very unique blend of turn-based strategy incorporating a card-based system.   Now that I am actually putting a little time into it post-release, I am extremely pleased with the outcome.  I highly recommend it for fans of turn-based strategy looking for something a little different.

Ignore my shown play time, I always play on the non-Steam version. I've found that online games, and Steam don't tend to mix that well often enough, so use the non-Steam version whenever possible, and strongly suggest that others do the same, especially for C9.
C9 is a PvE centered (not massively) multiplayer online brawler/hack n' slash, with RPG mechanics like character, and skill leveling, equipment, crafting, guilds, and loot to gather. You can largely play it just fine solo, but it can be more fun when playing with up to three of your friends. The controls are solid, and the action is fast, so if this is the kind of game you're into, it can be a lot of fun.
This is one of those games with a town hub, and instanced dungeons like others of this genre (Dungeon Fighter Online, Dragon Nest, Vindictus, etc..). Major game zones are split up into continents, and as of the time of this review at least most of the sixth continent has been released. The level cap increases as more zones are added, then the difficulty of mobs, and number of mechanics at work you need to make use of increases the further along you go.
One warning is that it's a peer to peer game published to a global area (bad combination), so if you play with others, it's best to stick with people that at least live in the same continent as you. If you join up with anyone, and they're on the other side of the planet or such, the latency/lag could be pretty bad.

amount of PvP as a PvP game, no matter of how little importance PvP may be to the game. In C9, and other games of this genre, PvP is just optional side content affecting really nothing outside of PvP, whereas PvE is an unavoidable necessity, which all aspects of the game, including the PvP, is based on. I would say no. Although, the thing about pay to win (P2W) is that it is when a game provides a significant pay advantage, and as such is a completely subjective description. Yes, but unless you for instance spend all day playing, or hammer through dungeons you're over powered for as fast as you can, you likely won't run out of stamina.
The common misconception about stamina systems is that they're there due to social causes, like certain laws in Korea. That is not the case, as for one, they're completely incapable of enforcing what people claim they do. Instead, it's a game mechanic. Games using something like a stamina system restrict the amount of content you can consume per day, per character rather than how rewarding that content is like games using grind exclusively do. The result is the two methods make games better suited to different people. If you want to focus on one character, and play for long hours a day, play a grind game. If you want something more casual, or one that even encourages playing alts, play a game using something like a stamina system.

I simply have no words for this game. I bought it simply because of the ratings it received a few days after it was released. The screenshots looked spectacular as well, so I was expecting something pretty amazing.
After completing the game, I can say without a doubt: this is the most refined, most polished, the deepest and certainly the most beautiful platformer I have ever played. And I don't think there's any game quite like it.
The game immediately lets you know what you're in for: a charming story set in a surreal fantasy world that looks absolutely incredible. And while the story is not at all complex or long, it's exactly what it needed to be to satisfy me. A lovely tale of love, friendship and loss that will make you weep occasionally. At first it may seem a bit black and white (good characters are good, bad characters are bad), however in the second half of the game, you realize that this is not the case and the story earns even more respect.
The visuals are simply stunning. They fit the mood of the game perfectly and manage to draw you into the world even further than the story did. Combine this with the incredible music and you have a game that never loses your attention. You could honestly just look at the screen and listen to the music and it would still be a worthwhile experience. Not only that, the world feels incredibly varied. You'll visit many different places and all of them will have a different mood, music and visuals. And they all feel incredible.
And what about the gameplay? It's fantastic. There's a ton of different mechanics for you to use (double and triple jumping, shooting, bashing, climbing walls, swimming, gliding, slamming on the floor, power jumping off the walls and many more), and sometimes obstacles can approached in more than one way, making the game feel more varied. There's even three skill trees for you to put your skill points in, so you can decide what you want to do. And there's no real obligation for you to invest in one specific skill tree, you'll be fine with picking the first thing the game offers you. The controls are ever so slightly stiff, but honestly it doesn't matter too much as you'll get used to them quickly.
Another thing worth mentioning about this game is its difficulty. I personally believe that this game is just slightly too difficult to be enjoyed to its full potential. Most of the time you won't have any problems, as the game has a great saving mechanic, but there are a few sections where saving is prevented and you have to beat the entire section without dying (specifically the escape sections). These can be frustrating at times, but the feeling when you finally beat them is worth it. Like I said, it's just SLIGHTLY too difficult, you'll still probably enjoy this game far more than many other games.
The game has very few other issues. For some reason if I Alt-Tab the game, I get a weird graphical glitch happenning, but it's no big deal. Sometimes, the voiced sections repeat the exact same thing that was said an hour ago, but with different subtitles, and I guess the Bash ability is kind of wonky and hard to aim sometimes. But these errors are so minor  they don't actually affect the game in any significant way.
At 20€, this game is an absolute steal. The moment the game was over I was in tears (stay until the end of the credits and you'll se why) and I knew that the price was worth it. If you want a platformer that is incredibly polished, looks amazing and makes you cry, look no further: this is the game you've always wanted to play.

The controls were clunky - with no crosshair, it was hard to select small items such as light switches. Controller support was poor and incomplete - I could not remap the controller buttons and there seemed to be no way to examine items with the controller - I had to use the mouse every time.
I didn't play this game for long, maybe it gets better, but I'm not going to spend the time to find out.

Full disclosure - I only played this game for an hour, and about a quarter of that was messing with the controls. Partly, this was down to control issues and basic mechanics; there is a major bug where if you try to bind certain keys to an action, the game will either not respond at all or will respond intermittently with no rhyme or reason. In some areas, jump is disabled, and even where it works, it often doesn't because the space you want to jump to is occupied by another of the invisible walls that infest the game world. The inventory system is also very difficult to get used to, jarring to look at (whatever you interact with floats next to a badly rendered hand with a beam of light connecting the hand to the object - am I holding these things with the force?), and inconsistent to interact with. Some items don't seem to do anything at all, and others do...something...but it's unclear what, if any, effect they have on the game. One time, I was in a dark place and kept selecting the flashlight over and over, but nothing happened. Turns out, you can't access items while swimming. Once I got out of the water, the light floated next to my hand...and still didn't light things up.
The game also seems to have totally missed the memo that it's supposed to be a dream - the majority of the "dream world" seems quite real (at least the part I bothered to explore) and the character keeps reacting to it as if it is a real place, wondering aloud why a computer lab is in the middle of a desert, scoffing that the user left their password and login details right out in the open (why does a dream computer need a password, btw?), etc. Admittedly, a computer lab in a desert could be a dream-like juxtaposition, but not when there's a generator to power the machine and a post-it note for login details; that's just somebody putting a real computer in a very odd place for reasons that probably made sense to them.
All these things were bad, but the real killer was that the whole thing is deadly dull - I wandered around the main character's house for several minutes before deciding there was nothing worth interacting with. Then I piloted the character to bed, which transitioned me to an equally dull and sterile 'dream world' full of cubes and objects that looked interactive but weren't, and then through a door to the desert. In the desert, there was a computer, and on the computer, there was a long file full of exposition that suggested some sort of upcoming action sequence with smoke creatures (but it also made them sound about as dangerous as a speeding ticket), but I couldn't get any of the commands listed on the computer to work, and after an interminable time wandering the desert in search of the labyrinth of scary smoke beings, I decided enough was enough.
This game is full of bad design choices and bugs, and the story is about as engaging as an instruction manual for a stereo you don't own anymore, or maybe one of those ghastly work-orientation videos that tries to make learning fun. I can't actually think of anything nice to say about it, which is sad, because I definitely get the impression that somebody put a lot of work into this game. Sometimes passion and effort are enough to overcome lack of experience and even lack of talent, but not this time :(

"Dream is an exploration game that takes place within the subconscious mind of Howard Phillips, a young man whose waking hours are tedious and dull, but whose dreams are lucid and powerful." --Steam description
That's what the game promises, and it's why I was an early backer.  (I just now got a computer that can handle the game properly, so that's why I'm reviewing it now.)  In reality, Howard's dreams are not very powerful or atmospheric.  They're quite dull and lifeless.
The game does create some realistic environments, but they fail to create any kind of mood.  Are Howard's dreams scary?  No.  Are they depressing?  No.  Are they suspenseful?  No.  Are they at least creative and interesting to explore?  No.  Does anything bizarre and dreamlike happen in any of his dreams?  No.  Every dream he has is just meh.  They are expansive, but there's so little to do it all feels like an enormous waste of space.
You don't do much in them aside from one or two thoughtless, contrived puzzles that have nothing to do with the environment or story.  The only things that tie the dreams to the story are the snippets of interpretation pages which spell out what everything is supposed to mean, but they are not enough.
The game has one cutscene (audio only), and it makes you listen to this longwinded conversation after each act, and then once again to complete the game!  It progresses more each time, which means you must listen to parts you've already heard up to 4 times, and it is tedious, not to mention trite.  The entire conversation goes like this:
"My mum and dad want me to get a job, but I dunno what I want to do."
"If you work hard enough, Howard, you can achieve your dreams, and everything will be all right.  Just look at me!  I worked hard and I succeeded, so if you do the same, you'll succeed, too!."
"Bloody hell, you're right!  Thanks!  This emotionless conversation has changed my outlook on life!"
Puh-leeze.
This conversation is all we learn about Howard.  For all that work you do traversing Howard's dream worlds, you learn little about him, and the big revelation at the end is lukewarm: Howard doesn't have a job, he wants to be a writer, and in the end he decides to get a job and start writing on his free time.  Is that it?  Is that the whole story?  It's not nearly enough, and the dreams he has are not interesting and do not mirror his life situation or convey any emotions regarding it.  (Except for the first nightmare.  That one came the closest to furthering a story and connecting me with Howard's situation, and it's the only dream Howard has that creates any kind of mood and takes the player for a ride.)
In terms of creating realistic models and utilizing its game engine, Dream shines.  In terms of creating atmosphere and telling a story, the creators didn't take the idea far enough.

All of the reviews I saw about Gabe Newell Simulator said that it was awful.
But I thought "No worries, at least it will be a bit of a laugh".
Boy, was I wrong!
I should have paid heed to the wise advice of the reviewers who told me to keep away from it.
But did I listen to the voice of experience? No, I did not - and I suffered for it.
There are two modes of play: "Story Mode" and "Steam Mode".
The "Steam Mode" gives you a number of click options, as if you are running the Valve company.
Release Half Life 3 and your money count starts to go up.
Then you can upgrade your games, to make more money.
For what purpose? To see some big money numbers? Very pointless.
Then there is the "Story Mode", which is the main game.
You can select a level, from 1-2 and 4-7 (the game is missing level 3 - no idea why).
First off, make sure that you set the screen size to your computer's settings.
I know that probably sounds obvious, but with every other game I've played the game itself would automatically choose the best screen size for you; but not so with this one.
I spent some time playing this game on the wrong screen size.
This not only meant that I could not read all of the relevant text, but I couldn't play level 1 either.
For level 1, when I had the incorrect screen size setting, a text-based announcement (the first screen) was as far as I could go; there was no option whatsoever to do anything.
Once the screen size had been fixed, you could see a "Skip" button to click on to continue.
(But, as it turned out, I probably shouldn't have bothered.)
Finally, with the game screen widened, I could play level 1.
Level 1 starts with a dark theatre, which then goes to a screen which inicated that Half Life 3 to be released.
Unfortunately, this scene can't be skipped, so if you are going to play level 1 again (which can only be done by closing and restarting the programme), you have to sit through it all again (which is annoying).
In level 1, you start off as Gabe Newell, in his office at Valve.
There is a pistol on the table - pick it up by using the E key.
You can engage in some text-based dialogue with a guy in your office.
You pick up a rifle from the next office.
If the rifle doesn't pick up straight away, keep hitting E on the keyboard (and move around a bit beside the gun whilst doing so, to make sure you are in the right position).
Then you get to shoot an overgrown moth, and then some other aliens.
I spent some time clicking away at the aliens, but my guns wouldn't shoot.
It turns out that you have to right-click to aim to shoot - as, in this game, you can't shoot off the hip at all.
(I would have known that if I did the training with the correct screen size).
There was one alien standing in a room who I shot at through the open doorway (emptying an entire magazine) but who wouldn't die - it turns out you have to be in the same room as him to kill him (go figure).
I tried the other levels as well, but . . . yawn.
The game isn't thrilling at all.
There is an attempt at humour when you engage in some text-based dialogue with the guy in your office, but it's not particularly amusing.
I was thinking that the one saving grace of this game would be some brilliant humour (hey, even some half-decent humour would have sufficed), but it just wasn't funny.
Quite frankly, Gabe Newell Simulator is a rubbish game.
The game play is poor.
The sound effects and ambience are not much chop.
The graphics are usable, but that's about it.

I owned and played this game often when I was younger and was stuck at my grandmother\'s house for days. When I purchased this game, it was from pure nostalgia. I remembered when I would play this game for hours on end, and I recalled how much enjoyment I got from it...
...After I bought this game, I remembered that the only reason I played this game was because the choices at my grandmothers place was 1) play this game 2) go to Church or 3) watch re-runs of the Andy Griffith show, and there is only so much of Deputy Don i can take before I\'m willing to do almost anything...and I\'m not a Christian, so I chose Prison Tycoon.
Don\'t waste your money. The only reason this game should be bought is as a prank gift to a good buddy when you have a few extra bucks to spend.
The graphics are sub-par (even when it was first released), UI is almost worthless, no tutorial (let me say that im not a huge advocate for tutorials...i don\'t usually need EVERY small detail explaned over the course of a half hour. ________________________________________________________________________________
You could say that this game is "Spellbinding" an amazing world that really gets you wrapped up in it, now you may notice i only have 0.7 hours play time, this is because most of my play time is actually on the demo version of the game, and i eventually purchased the game, totally worth it.
the world is so beautful, really good art style, the singleplayer is awesome and fun, really engrossing to be honest, the complex strategem, difficult boss fights (im looking at you lords in the end castles), and most of all, player invading, yep thats right, a player can drop in and help the boss or lord your playing against! really fun to do it yourself as well, i think ive screwed up like 3 boss fights for people this way.
okay so to the game itself:
there are 3 different schools of spells, Law, neutral and chaos
Law consists of typical RPG monsters to summon such as pegasus (which you can ride), elf archers, dwarves and my personal favorite summon in the game, paladins (paladins are beast, dont worry, you will understand soon), they focus on buffing your minions and yourself (you can even give yourself a sword or bow to allow your wizard to attack, or a shield to protect you) neutral is all about big creates and some crowd control, you will be summoning things like spiders, wolves, ogres and packs of rats (the card for them summons three rats), chaos summons undead, goblins, hydra's and manticores and has some crowd control, like sticky goop which can root an opponents minion or wizard in place, and it spreads so watch out for your minions so they dont get stuck too (it creates copies of itself and places them on tiles near the previous one, turn by turn, then expires and disappears after a good amount of turns), and terrorfying trees! evil trees with arms that you can place in sets of up to 5 at a time, all must have at least one empty tile between them, they can attack enemy minions that get near them but can't move (they are trees afterall) which is really cool. you have gear, like talismans, staves and robes which give you additional spells or little abilities to activate for a mana cost. a really good trick is that as an law player (which i am) you can spawn these blue trees, with one empty tile between them, now not only do these give your wizard and minions protection (you can hide inside them) BUT with the right talisman, you can spawn the trees, then activate this talisman and two of the trees will turn into elf archers for you to fight with (and they can move, since they are elves now) then the next round, two more trees will turn into elf archers, then the next round the last one will turn, now you have five archers to kill your foes with.
WARNING: killing foes and your minions being killed relies on an RNG (random number genrator) the game will give you the percentage chance of how likely you are to kill that minion or wizard, there is no health bar for any of them, just armor that lowers that percentage chance, for example an ogre usually has like a 3%-5% chance to be killed by one of your less powerful minions and so on.
thats just the basic jist of the game, i advise giving the demo a go to see if you like it (even if this game doesn't sound good to you, you never know till you try) and i thurrully recommend playing/buying it.

Chaos Reborn is a turn-based fantasy tactical game with a strategy element, where wizards do battle by casting spells and summoning creatures to fight for them.
I will not describe it as it's been done by many reviewers before, but I will talk about a somewhat misunderstood aspect of the game: randomness.
Every action in the game has a chance of success. The more powerful a spell you cast, the lower the chance.
A creature has a chance of hitting a target, and the result is all or nothing: either the target dies, or it remains unscathed.
All this means the game relies heavily on an RNG (random number generator), causing some people to feel the game is too random, therefore frustrating.
The game is indeed based on randomness, but that's its most interesting feature.
What it's really about is risk management and bluffing, and the most important game mechanic for this is illusion.
When summoning a creature (the majority of available spells) you have the option of risking failure or casting an illusion.
Illusions hava a 100% chance of success, and the creature will behave exactly as its real counterpart, but it can be instantly dispelled.
Every wizard has a Disbelieve spell always available. If it's cast on an illusion, it will disappear and the wizard will still be able to cast a spell in his turn. Basically this equates to killing a creature (or any number of creatures) at unlimited range for free. But if the target creature is real, the Disbelieve spell will fail and the wizard will have wasted his precious spell for the turn.
This leads to an interesting game of reading and second-guessing your opponent, where the perceived strength of the enemy force never matches reality, and every creature summoned has a psychological impact that exceeds its actual value.
Some players have noted how Chaos Reborn brings together features of chess and poker, and rightly so.
This is a sophisticated and deep game that requires planning for multiple outcomes to effectively hedge your bets.
Don't try to play it as an ordinary tactical game where all you do is overpower your opponent, this gem is on another level entirely.
EDIT: This review was written just before the dev caved in to the whiners and introduced an alternate set of game mechanics called Law Mode.
To enjoy the game as it was meant to be, I recommend you play Chaos Mode.
